c64.name: Commodore 64 (breadbin, ASSY 250407)
c64.description: A home computer sold from 1982. This tree traces every physical component back through the industrial processes of the early 1980s to the ore, crude oil and quartz sand it began as. Roughly 320 discrete parts from about twenty distinct manufacturing industries. The chips were designed in Pennsylvania and fabricated there; the board was populated and the machine was boxed in Hong Kong, with some runs contract-manufactured in Japan.

c64.bottoms-out.name: Where every branch terminates
c64.bottoms-out.description: Everything above ends in one of three trunks: refined metals, petrochemicals, and the plants and utilities that supply both. Most component subtrees carry their own shorter copy of the relevant chain - a capacitor really does carry its own aluminium, and an ABS case really does carry its own acrylonitrile - so these are the canonical, deepest versions of the same chains, kept together so that one can be read end to end.
c64.bottoms-out.note: An index of where the supply chains bottom out, not a plant: nothing is made, mined or operated here. It is the only route from the root to the metal, chemical and industrial branches, and the unlinked catalogue is parked here, so any canonical subtree that no branch links stays reachable rather than being dropped. Not established: that every branch terminates in one of three trunks - several subtrees bottom out at process equipment or at plant utilities rather than at a refined metal or a petrochemical, so the three-trunk claim is a simplification of the tree's own shape and is not a documented supply-chain fact.

unlinked.catalogue.name: Published but unlinked materials
unlinked.catalogue.description: These 10 nodes were written as canonical, reusable subtrees — a fragment's "made from" chains in full detail — but no other branch ended up referencing them, so nothing linked them into the tree. They are collected here rather than deleted. Where a component subtree inlines its own shorter version of the same material chain, this is the long one.
unlinked.catalogue.note: Generated by scripts/build.mjs. Nothing in the tree points here; the connection exists only in prose, in each node's own branch.

si.polysilicon.gangue.name: Feldspar and mica gangue, hand-picked away
si.polysilicon.gangue.description: The pegmatite that hosts the quartz veins contains albite and K-feldspar with muscovite and biotite. Alumina in feldspar is the enemy - it survives all the way to the aluminium metallisation - so the lump is sorted by hand and by hydrofluoric-acid washing before it is even shipped.
si.polysilicon.gangue.note: Biotite in particular carries a lot of iron and is a classic contaminant marker in a quartz shipment.

si.polysilicon.coke.crude.name: Sour crude residue, vacuum distilled
si.polysilicon.coke.crude.description: Heavy Venezuelan or Middle East crude sent to a vacuum tower at 350-400 C and 30-50 mmHg; the bottoms are a dense black pitch of asphaltenes and metal porphyrins, and are the feed for the coke. Vanadium and nickel concentrate in this residue, so coke made from it carries trace vanadium that the silicon plant has to tolerate.
si.polysilicon.coke.crude.note: Not established: that any particular silicon supplier fed its furnaces with vacuum-residue coke rather than coal-tar pitch, anthracite or low-ash coal, nor the vacuum-tower pressure, the coking-heater temperature or the vanadium figure. Traces of vanadium and nickel in metallurgical silicon, and hence in its carbon reductant, are real, but the level a silicon plant had to tolerate is not a published number.

si.polysilicon.coke.calciner.name: Delayed coking and calcination of petroleum coke
si.polysilicon.coke.calciner.description: Vacuum residue from crude oil distillation is heated in a battery of delayed-coking heaters to 500 C and held in a large coking drum for 12-24 hours; the green coke is then calcined in a rotary kiln at 1200-1350 C to drive off volatiles and leave needle coke at 0.5-2% sulphur. Silicon furnaces blend petroleum coke with anthracite coal.
si.polysilicon.coke.calciner.note: Not established: the coking-heater temperature, the drum residence time, the calcining-kiln temperature or the sulphur content for any specific producer. Delayed coking and rotary-kiln calcination are standard, but each supplier blends several carbon sources to hit a target ash and sulphur figure that is not published.

si.polysilicon.coke.anthracite.name: Anthracite coal as a coke substitute
si.polysilicon.coke.anthracite.description: The other traditional reductant for the submerged arc furnace, mined from the hard coal fields of Pennsylvania, Wales and Shanxi. Lower carbon, higher ash and higher iron than petroleum coke, so it was used as a blend component.

si.polysilicon.brine.name: Chlor-alkali brine electrolysis
si.polysilicon.brine.description: Salt dissolved in water and electrolyzed in a membrane or mercury cell at 3-4 V to make chlorine and hydrogen. The hydrogen is what reduces the trichlorosilane, and the chlorine is one half of the hydrochloric acid that chlorinates the metallurgical silicon in the first place.
si.polysilicon.brine.note: The hydrochloric-acid route is documented: metallurgical-grade silicon is hydrochlorinated to trichlorosilane with hydrogen as a co-product. But the trichlorosilane is then reduced by its own decomposition on hot silicon filaments, not by hydrogen from a chlor-alkali cell, so the claim that cell hydrogen does the reduction is not supported. The cell voltage is also unestablished.

metal.salt-brine.name: Rock salt and solar salt brine
metal.salt-brine.description: Two very different-looking things that are the same feedstock. Rock salt is a bed of halite pushed up by evaporation of a restricted sea and then mined; solar salt is the same chemistry done in the sun, in shallow evaporation ponds that turn a square mile of bay into a crystalliser. The chlor-alkali cell does not care which it gets: what matters is a saturated brine with the calcium and magnesium removed, because both precipitate as scale in the diaphragm cell and would otherwise carry oxygen into the chlorine.
metal.salt-brine.note: Not established: the saturated-brine figure of about 310 g/L NaCl, the 1.0-1.1 t of NaCl per tonne of chlorine, and the calcium/magnesium scale argument, which no general reference states. What the references do support is that the cell runs on concentrated NaCl brine and that rock salt forms as evaporite beds from restricted seas.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: rock salt (halite) mined at Wieliczka, Michigan and along the saltbelt; solar salt evaporated in the San Francisco Bay and the Great Salt Lake

facts.label: Purity to the chlor-alkali cell
facts.value: brine made up to saturated, about 310 g/L NaCl before it enters the cell

facts.label: Per tonne of chlorine
facts.value: roughly 1.0-1.1 t of NaCl, plus about 1 t of electrical energy

metal.salt-solar-pan.name: Evaporate brine in a solar salt pond
metal.salt-solar-pan.description: A series of shallow ponds, from 2 m down to 30 cm, through which seawater is stepped down in salinity, precipitating gypsum first and then halite. A hectare of pond evaporates tens of thousands of tonnes of salt a year. The leaf is a solar pond on a coastal lagoon.
metal.salt-solar-pan.note: Yields are strongly climate-dependent; medium confidence on the per-hectare figure.

facts.label: Depth steps
facts.value: 2-5 m intake, 0.3 m evaporator, 0.2 m crystalliser

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: order 100-200 kg per m2 of pond per year

metal.salt-rock.name: Halite bed: Wieliczka, Michigan, the saltbelt
metal.salt-rock.description: Salt deposited in an evaporating sea and buried later; mined by room-and-pillar, with the salt crushed and screened for the brine saturator. The Wieliczka mine in Poland is the oldest deep salt mine still working, and Polish rock salt was the classic feed for the eastern European chlor-alkali industry.
metal.salt-rock.note: Not established: the NaCl 95-99% assay. The references give room-and-pillar mining at the Sifto mine under Lake Huron and describe mined salt as halite extracted from evaporite formations; neither states an assay, and the Wieliczka and Michigan saltbelt claims are not in either.

facts.label: Typical assay
facts.value: NaCl 95-99%, with calcium and magnesium salts as the impurity

facts.label: Method
facts.value: room-and-pillar underground mining

metal.salt-evaporite.name: Halite evaporite: the rock
metal.salt-evaporite.description: The leaf of the sodium branch: a bedded evaporite sequence of halite with interbedded gypsum and clay, laid down when a restricted sea evaporated. Nothing chemical about it - just a dried-up ocean.

facts.label: Lithology
facts.value: massive to bedded halite with gypsum, anhydrite and clay partings

si.cz.seed.name: Seed crystal for CZ pulling
si.cz.seed.description: A short (100)-oriented sliver cut from a previous ingot, used to set the orientation and the defect-free growth of the new boule. Its diameter has to match the finished boule, so a seed is cut and ground for each crystal-pulling station.

si.cz.crucible-sand.name: Quartz sand melted into crucible glass
si.cz.crucible-sand.description: High-purity quartz sand, acid-leached to remove aluminium and iron, is melted in a flame or arc furnace around a rotating graphite mandrel at about 2000 C into a clear, annealed vitreous silica blank. The graphite is then burnt off in air at 800-1000 C.
si.cz.crucible-sand.note: Not established: how a particular puller supplier made its crucible blank - the acid leach for aluminium and iron, the flame or arc melting around a rotating graphite mandrel, the roughly 2000 C melt and the 800-1000 C burn-off. Standard CZ practice is a high-purity quartz crucible, but the blank-manufacturing route is a supplier trade secret and is not described in any source available here.

si.cz.atmosphere.name: Helium over the CZ melt
si.cz.atmosphere.description: High-purity helium, bled over the melt to carry off the intense blackbody heat and to sweep volatile boron compounds away. Argon, or a helium-argon mix, was the cheaper alternative and produced more oxygen precipitation in the finished boule.
si.cz.atmosphere.note: Not established: that helium was the blanket gas over the melt, or that an argon atmosphere produced more oxygen precipitation. The documented practice for Czochralski silicon is an inert atmosphere such as argon, and the oxide concentration in CZ silicon is attributed to the quartz crucible dissolving into the melt rather than to the choice of cover gas.

chem.silane.name: Silane and organosilane chemistry
chem.silane.description: Monosilane, SiH4, is a gas made by redistributing trichlorosilane, and it is the precursor for the polysilicon films deposited inside the fab that made the 6510 and the 4164s. Organosilanes are the opposite: a methyl- or ethylchlorosilane that has been reacted with methanol or ethanol instead, so the molecule ends up carrying an alkoxy group and an organic group and is a liquid rather than a gas. They are the surface chemistry that bonds glass fibre to epoxy resin, and every FR-4 board in the world contains them. Both families come out of the same silicon-chlorine-hydrogen chemistry; that shared feedstock is the only relationship between them, and conflating the two is the usual first mistake.
chem.silane.note: A statement about the supply chain rather than a substance: it covers monosilane gas and organosilane liquid chemistry together, and the two real materials hang beneath it.

facts.label: Shared feedstock
facts.value: trichlorosilane, from metallurgical silicon and HCl

facts.label: The split
facts.value: redistributing HSiCl3 gives SiH4, a pyrophoric gas; alkylchlorosilane plus alcohol gives RSi(OR')3, a liquid coupling agent

chem.silane.coupling-agent.name: Organosilane coupling agents
chem.silane.coupling-agent.description: Bifunctional organosilanes: a hydrolysable alkoxy or chloro group that bonds to the silanol groups on a glass surface, and an organic group - vinyl, amino, epoxy or methacrylate - that reacts with the resin. Aminopropyltriethoxysilane and vinyltrimethoxysilane are the workhorses; methacryloxypropyltrimethoxysilane and 3-glycidoxypropyltrimethoxysilane were the ones chosen where the resin was an epoxy. They are made from the same silicon-chlorine chemistry as monosilane by substituting an alcohol for the hydrogen: methyltrichlorosilane plus methanol gives the trimethoxysilane and releases HCl. Applied to woven glass cloth at a few tenths of a per cent by weight, they are the reason epoxy bonds to glass rather than merely wetting it - and therefore the reason a C64 mainboard does not delaminate in a solder pot.
chem.silane.coupling-agent.note: A coupling agent is a substance with a composition, and the operation that applies it to cloth is a separate step in the glass-fibre branch (chem.glass-fiber.cloth-sizing). Methanol is the route to the methoxy silanes, and the silicon-chlorine front end is the same one that makes trichlorosilane.

facts.label: Typical loading
facts.value: 0.3-1.0 wt% of the glass

facts.label: Preparation
facts.value: alkylchlorosilane plus methanol or ethanol, releasing HCl; the alcohol replaces the chlorine, not the hydrogen

facts.label: Form
facts.value: colourless to pale liquid, hydrolysed and condensed to a siloxane oligomer in the applied solution

facts.label: Competing chemistry
facts.value: titanate and zirconate coupling agents do the same job for glass-filled thermoplastics, without the silicon

chem.silane.monosilane.name: Monosilane (SiH4)
chem.silane.monosilane.description: The polysilicon precursor: a colourless, pyrophoric gas that decomposes on a hot surface to lay down a conformal silicon film. A fab in 1982-84 that used it ran a small silane plant, because the gas is both too dangerous and too cheap to ship far. It goes into the machine's own logic: the polysilicon gate of the 6510, and the second of the three polysilicon levels in each 4164 DRAM, were deposited from silane by low-pressure CVD. It did not make the 9N polysilicon charge for the crystal pullers - that was still the Siemens trichlorosilane process until the late 1980s.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 4N-5N (99.99-99.9999%) electronic grade

facts.label: Boiling point
facts.value: -111.8 C, so it is handled as a liquefied gas

facts.label: Storage
facts.value: refrigerated bulk liquid in stainless or carbon-steel tanks at -60 C or below; cylinder supply at low pressure

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: pyrophoric in air, acutely toxic, flammable from about 1% in air

chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd.name: Deposit polysilicon by low-pressure CVD
chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd.description: Silane decomposes on hot silicon in a diffusion tube at 600-850 C, laying down a conformal film of polycrystalline silicon. This is the step that changed how the C64's own chips were made. A self-aligned gate needs a gate material that survives ion implantation into the source and drain on either side of it, and that can be laid down and then oxidised around; aluminium can do neither, because it is destroyed by the implant and it diffuses into the oxide at the temperatures every later step needs. So once implantation replaced diffusion for source and drain doping, polysilicon won, and with it a gate that is chemically bonded to its own dielectric rather than merely resting on it.
chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd.note: Dichlorosilane was the cheaper alternative and was used for the same films; silane won where the film had to be phosphorus- or boron-doped in the same step.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: 100-500 nm of poly-Si, doped n+ or p+ from a gas in the same tube

facts.label: Reactor wall
facts.value: cold-wall quartz or silicon carbide tube; SiH4 decomposes appreciably above about 400 C, so a hot-wall tube would coat itself

facts.label: On the C64's own parts
facts.value: the 6510's gate, and the second of the three polysilicon levels in each 4164

chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route.name: Disproportionate the trichlorosilane
chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route.description: The industrial route to monosilane: trichlorosilane redistributes into silane and tetrachlorosilane, catalysed, with the whole reaction run in a hydrogen atmosphere: 4 HSiCl3 -> SiH4 + 3 SiCl4. It suits a fab because the trichlorosilane it consumes is the same material the polysilicon plant already makes by the ton, delivered in bulk ISO containers or road tankers, and the tetrachlorosilane that comes back out is reclaimed by hydrogenation at the same plant. The silane leaves the reactor diluted to roughly a tenth or a quarter in hydrogen, which is what the crackers and the adsorption columns downstream were designed for and is far easier to handle than neat silane.
chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route.note: This is a disproportionation of trichlorosilane, not a reduction by hydrogen - the hydrogen is the carrier and diluent gas, and the equation balances without it. Direct synthesis from metallurgical silicon and hydrogen also exists but was not the commercial route in this period.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 4 HSiCl3 -> SiH4 + 3 SiCl4 (disproportionation, run in H2)

facts.label: Crude output
facts.value: 10-25% SiH4 in H2, purified before use

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: SiCl4, hydrogenated back to trichlorosilane at the polysilicon plant

chem.glass-fiber.name: E-glass fibre
chem.glass-fiber.description: Continuous glass filaments about 5 microns across, drawn in thousands from a tank furnace and woven into cloth. The C64 needs it twice on the board side of the machine: as the reinforcing cloth in the FR-4 mainboard laminate, and as the laminate core of the keyboard matrix board. E-glass is a lime-alumino-borosilicate, and the 15-19% of its weight that is not silica exists for one reason - it brings the working temperature down far enough that a 5 micron filament can be drawn from an affordable non-lead melt. That is why it is made in millions of tonnes a year and why it is the cheapest structural reinforcement known. Everything it is made of is weighed once, in a batch: silica sand, limestone, soda ash, a borate and a clay.
chem.glass-fiber.note: Chopped strand for glass-filled phenolic connector bodies and glass-filled nylon is the same melt run through a hammer mill instead of a winder, so it shares this batch but not this filament.

facts.label: E-glass composition
facts.value: typical analysis ~54 wt% SiO2, ~15% Al2O3, ~16% CaO, 0-10 wt% B2O3, 1-2 wt% Na2O+K2O, Fe2O3 under 0.5%

facts.label: Filament diameter
facts.value: about 5 um continuous roving; 9-24 um for chopped and mat grades

facts.label: Tensile strength / modulus
facts.value: 2-3.5 GPa / 70-76 GPa on the sized filament

facts.label: Softening point
facts.value: about 820 C, against a 1400-1500 C melt

chem.glass-fiber.cloth-sizing.name: Size the woven cloth with silane
chem.glass-fiber.cloth-sizing.description: For laminate grade the woven cloth is desized and then treated with an organosilane coupling agent - sprayed or dipped, dried and cured at 100-150 C - before it is impregnated with epoxy. The molecule has one end that hydrolyses and bonds to the silanol groups on the glass surface and an organic end that reacts with the resin, so the glass is covalently joined to the epoxy instead of merely being wetted by it. That chemical bond across the cloth is what keeps a mainboard from delaminating along its own reinforcement when the assembly goes through a solder pot, and the 0.3-1.0 wt% of silane that buys it is invisible in the finished part.
chem.glass-fiber.cloth-sizing.note: The 20-50% interlaminar shear figure is a commonly quoted range for aminosilane versus no treatment rather than a measurement of a C64 panel, and the coupling agent used for a brominated-epoxy FR-4 was typically a methacrylate or glycidoxy silane rather than an amino one. The chemistry is the same in all three cases.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 0.3-1.0 wt% of the glass

facts.label: Application
facts.value: spray or dip, then dry and cure at 100-150 C

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: an aminosilane-sized epoxy laminate shows roughly 20-50% higher apparent interlaminar shear strength than the same laminate on unsized cloth

chem.glass-fiber.packaging.name: Spin, rove and weave the cloth
chem.glass-fiber.packaging.description: The attenuated strand is wound onto a rotating package at high traverse speed, then a few hundred filaments are gathered into a roving and woven on an air-jet loom into plain-weave cloth. The loom is the reason a laminate is isotropic: a plain weave with a square fill puts equal glass in both directions, so the board does not creep along one axis when it is heated. That is why PCB cloth is woven rather than chopped or randomly matted. The kraft liner in the finished laminate panel is paper, not glass - a softwood pulp sheet - and belongs to the resin and liner branch, not here.
chem.glass-fiber.packaging.note: The 100-300 g/m2 range and style 7628 are the better-supported figures; the yarn tex and ends-per-cm figures are not checked against a 1983 laminate datasheet.

facts.label: Cloth weight for FR-4
facts.value: about 100-300 g/m2; roughly 200 g/m2 (style 7628, 7.9 oz/yd2) was the common one for 1.6 mm two-layer board

facts.label: Weave
facts.value: plain, or crow/twill where higher stiffness was wanted

facts.label: Yarn
facts.value: about 9-22 tex per 100 filaments, 8-18 filaments per cm of cloth

chem.glass-fiber.attenuation.name: Attenuate and size the strand
chem.glass-fiber.attenuation.description: A blast of air at constant pressure across the wicket pulls the emerging cone out to about 5 microns before it has travelled half a metre, and the filament is wound onto a rotating package at 10-25 m/s. As it passes the sizing apron it picks up a thin film - starch or oil for the textile trade, and a light dose of silane for laminate grade. Continuous filament is not chopped: chopped strand is a separate product made by running the same strand through a hammer mill, which is what the glass-filled phenolic and glass-filled nylon parts elsewhere in this tree are made from.

facts.label: Filament diameter after attenuation
facts.value: about 5 um

facts.label: Strand length per package
facts.value: tens of kilometres

facts.label: Sizing on the strand
facts.value: starch or oil; a light silane for laminate grade

chem.glass-fiber.bushing.name: Forehearth and bushing plate
chem.glass-fiber.bushing.description: The glass leaves the furnace through a refractory forehearth and arrives at a bushing plate: a small alloy block, a couple of hundred millimetres across, drilled with 200 to several thousand holes of 10-40 microns. Gold-platinum-rhodium is the usual alloy because nothing else survives 1400 C in contact with a boron-bearing melt; the cheapest bushings are rhodium-plated nickel. Pressure pushes the melt through each hole, surface tension rounds the emerging cone, and gravity and attenuation do the rest.

facts.label: Bushing material
facts.value: Au-Pt-Rh alloy, or rhodium-plated nickel in the cheaper grades

chem.glass-fiber.melt.name: Melt, refine and condition the batch
chem.glass-fiber.melt.description: The batch is charged into a regenerative tank furnace held at 1400-1500 C - hot enough to keep the viscosity low enough to draw a filament through a 10 micron hole, and then held in that narrow window for tens of hours. What comes out is not merely molten: it is refined until every bubble larger than a few microns has risen out or been broken by a rotating stirrer, and then conditioned - held just above the liquidus so that beta-eucryptite crystallises out on the refractory. That conditioning is the slowest step in the plant and the one that makes continuous fibre possible: without it the drawn fibre devitrifies into a crystalline, brittle mass the moment it cools.
chem.glass-fiber.melt.note: Fuel was natural gas or fuel oil, and the two regenerators either side of the tank put 40-60% of the heat back into the incoming air, which is why a glass furnace is a net consumer of a few GJ per tonne of glass rather than a large one.

facts.label: Refining bubble target
facts.value: no bubble above 1-50 um, depending on the grade

chem.glass-fiber.borax.name: Borax (sodium borate)
chem.glass-fiber.borax.description: The boron source, and the reason E-glass is a borosilicate at all. Borax decahydrate, Na2B4O7.10H2O, goes into the batch either as the decahydrate or as boric acid made from it; either way the boron ends up in the glass network as B2O3. A few per cent of B2O3 lowers the liquidus and widens the working range enough to draw fine filament at a temperature the bushing alloy can survive, and it improves chemical durability - which is what stops the finished fibre dissolving in the warm caustic etch bath the board house puts it through.
chem.glass-fiber.borax.note: Borax appears under other names elsewhere in the supply chain: tincalconite or boric acid for the electrolytic capacitor electrolyte, and a separate borax for the television funnel glass.

facts.label: B2O3 in E-glass
facts.value: 0-10 wt% depending on the melt; the boron is what makes this a borosilicate

facts.label: Borax as batched
facts.value: Na2B4O7.10H2O (decahydrate, 47 wt% water) or calcined anhydrous, or as H3BO3

facts.label: Where the boron came from
facts.value: colemanite and ulexite ore, Turkey and California dominant by the 1980s

chem.glass-fiber.borax.ore.name: Colemanite and borate ore
chem.glass-fiber.borax.ore.description: The borates are mined from evaporite deposits and altered limestone-tuff beds, in Turkey (Bigadiç, Emet) and California's Boron and Kramer districts. Ore is 25-35% B2O3 and is shipped as run-of-mine lump, so this is as close as the boron in a C64 mainboard gets to the ground.

facts.label: Principal districts
facts.value: Bigadiç and Emet (Turkey); Boron and Kramer (California)

chem.glass-fiber.borax.acid.name: Boric acid from colemanite
chem.glass-fiber.borax.acid.description: Colemanite ore is crushed and boiled with sulfuric acid, which drives the calcium out as gypsum and leaves boric acid in solution: Ca2B6O11.5H2O + 2 H2SO4 + 2 H2O -> 2 CaSO4 + 6 H3BO3. The liquor is filtered hot and crystallised by cooling, and the crystals are dried at low temperature because boric acid dehydrates to B2O3 above about 100 C. Glass makers bought either this acid or the crude ash from dry lakes such as Searles Lake; the acid was the easier way to get a clean batch.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: colemanite + H2SO4 -> boric acid + gypsum, by boiling aqueous digestion

facts.label: Drying limit
facts.value: below about 100 C, or the acid dehydrates to B2O3

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: roughly 0.7-0.9 t of boric acid per tonne of 30% B2O3 ore

chem.glass-fiber.batch.name: Mix the batch
chem.glass-fiber.batch.description: The raw materials are weighed and dry-blended to about +/-1% on each constituent before a single tonne is melted. The tolerance matters more than it looks: the melt fixes the viscosity curve, and the viscosity curve decides whether 5 micron filament can be drawn from the bushing at all. A modern batch is tens of tonnes, and it is the last point at which the composition can be corrected.
chem.glass-fiber.batch.note: The five raw materials are children here rather than made-of edges: a glass batch is a mixture, so its constituents are siblings that melt into each other, and a reader following the chain needs to land on the sand and the limestone, not on a link list.

facts.label: Batch size
facts.value: 1-40 tonnes

facts.label: Mixing time
facts.value: 2-8 minutes in a ribbon blender

facts.label: Target tolerance
facts.value: +/-1 wt% on the major constituents

facility.power.kaolin.name: Kaolin (china clay)
facility.power.kaolin.description: A white kaolinite clay from a kaolin pit, washed and beneficiated for the ceramic and paper trades. Ends at the clay pit.

metal.soda-ash.name: Soda ash (Na2CO3)
metal.soda-ash.description: Sodium carbonate, the second half of the sodium story. It goes into glass (a huge 1980s user, though the glass agent owns that branch), into detergents, and into the Bayer plant as the carbonate that lime converts back into caustic. The Solvay process, still the dominant route in 1982, makes it from salt, limestone and coke in a solution-and-precipitation tower - no molten salt, no electrolysis.

facts.label: Solvay tower
facts.value: ~10 m diameter, 20-30 m tall, cooled to about -10 C at the top

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl, then 2 NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O

facts.label: Net
facts.value: 2 NaCl + CaCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CaCl2

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: order 1 t of CaCl2 brine per t of soda ash

metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery.name: Causticise the spent brine to recover the salt
metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery.description: The Solvay process does not consume the salt: the ammonium chloride in the spent brine is causticised with lime back to ammonia and sodium chloride, and the brine is re-saturated. The plant therefore closes its salt loop, and its only real consumption is limestone and energy and the ammonia. That closure is the whole reason Solvay was so cheap for a century and why it was so hard to displace until the chlor-alkali-soda ash route had caught up.
metal.soda-ash.salt-recovery.note: Medium confidence on the salt consumption figure; the chemistry is standard.

facts.label: Causticisation
facts.value: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NH3 + CaCl2 + 2H2O

facts.label: Re-saturation
facts.value: brine is re-saturated with mined salt and returned

metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln.name: The lime kilns that feed the Solvay tower
metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln.description: The Solvay process needs carbon dioxide and it gets it by burning limestone in a shaft kiln beside the tower, in the same way a sugar mill burns bagasse. The kiln gas, after the dust is knocked out and the gas is cooled and scrubbed, is about 40-45% carbon dioxide on a dry basis - lower than the 98% a dedicated CO2 plant would produce, but it came free with the lime the process also needed. The Solvay works was therefore a self-contained chemical plant that took limestone and salt and made soda ash, calcium chloride and CO2 in one site.
metal.soda-ash.lime-kiln.note: The Solvay reference gives the limestone calcination as 950-1100 C, not 1000-1100 C, and says nothing about a shaft-kill gas of 40-45% carbon dioxide. Not established: the dry CO2 concentration of the kiln gas.

facts.label: Kiln
facts.value: shaft kiln, 1000-1100 C, beside the tower

facts.label: CO2 concentration
facts.value: 40-45% dry after dust removal

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: the lime itself, sold to steel and to agriculture

metal.limestone.name: Limestone (CaCO3) quarry
metal.limestone.description: High-calcium limestone for the Solvay towers, the blast furnaces, the Bayer plant, the lead sinter and the lime kilns. Quarried by bench mining with a face shovel or a chain dragline, crushed, and graded; a blast furnace wants roughly a third of a tonne of limestone per tonne of hot metal. The same rock is the flux in the copper flash furnace, the causticisation reagent in alumina refining, and the neutraliser at the board fab.
metal.limestone.note: Documented: limestone is mostly calcite and aragonite, and in the blast furnace it binds with silica and other impurities to remove them from the iron. Not established: the CaCO3 92-98% / SiO2 0.5-2% assay, the 0.2-0.35 t per tonne of hot metal consumption rate, and the bench and crushing detail.

facts.label: Use rate
facts.value: order 0.2-0.35 t per tonne of hot metal in the blast furnace

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: surface quarry, 5-15 m benches, crushed to 10-50 mm

metal.limestone.quarry.name: Limestone quarry and crushing plant
metal.limestone.quarry.description: A 5-15 m bench taken out of a 10-40 m face with a face shovel or a chain dragline, drilled and blasted where the rock is competent, then a primary jaw or gyratory crusher to 50-150 mm and a crushing and screening plant that produces three fractions: 0.5-5 cm for the sinter plant, 5-40 mm for the blast furnace and the kilns, and a fines fraction that goes back. A limestone quarry is one of the least complicated mines there is, which is why lime is cheap everywhere and why the Bayer process's caustic and lime costs are the alumina industry's real cost base.
metal.limestone.quarry.note: Not established: the 5-15 m bench height, the 10-40 m face, the 50-150 mm primary product, the three product fractions and the 0.2-5 Mt/year output. No reference fetched describes limestone quarrying practice at this level of detail.

facts.label: Product sizes
facts.value: 0.5-5 cm sinter feed, 5-40 mm furnace and kiln feed, plus fines

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 0.2-5 Mt/year for a chemical-grade supplier

metal.limestone.bed.name: Carbonate platform limestone
metal.limestone.bed.description: The leaf: a fossiliferous carbonate rock, mostly calcite, laid down on a shallow warm sea floor and now quarried a few metres at a time out of a 10-40 m face.
metal.limestone.bed.note: Not established: this node's specific claim that the rock is a carbonate-platform deposit quarried a few metres at a time out of a 10-40 m face. The limestone reference documents the rock's composition and its fossiliferous reef and shelf settings but gives no quarry geometry.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: fossiliferous limestone, commonly a carbonate platform deposit

metal.soda-ash.ammonia-source.name: Make ammonia from coke in the gasworks
metal.soda-ash.ammonia-source.description: In 1982 most ammonia in the soda industry still came from the gasworks: coke plus steam and iron passed over a hot carbonaceous catalyst, then cracked to nitrogen and hydrogen. Natural gas-based steam reforming had largely displaced this in North America and Western Europe, but coke-based ammonia remained standard in India, China and much of Eastern Europe - which is where much of the world's soda ash, and hence much of its glass, was made.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: iron promoted with K2O, or activated coke

metal.soda-ash.ammonia.name: Carbonation tower and the rotary calciner
metal.soda-ash.ammonia.description: A 20-30 m steel tower with a conical bottom, fed at the top with ammoniated brine and in the side with CO2 from the lime kilns. Sodium bicarbonate precipitates as a fine white slurry in the upper third and settles into the cone; the temperature is held near 40 C because below that the ammonium chloride in the liquor crystallises out and fouls the tower. Bicarbonate is then calcined at 200-250 C in a rotary kiln to soda ash.
metal.soda-ash.ammonia.note: Tower internals varied; the conical settler is universal.

facts.label: Tower temperature
facts.value: near 40 C at the precipitation zone

facts.label: NH3 loss
facts.value: order 0.1-0.3 t ammonia per t of soda ash, mostly vented

metal.silica-sand.name: Industrial silica sand (quartz dune sand)
metal.silica-sand.description: Siliceous sand from a dune or a beach, washed, screened and often magnetically separated to take out the heavy mineral concentrates that would be a nuisance. This is a distinct node from the silicon-grade quartzite: the purity required here is far lower, and this sand is a commodity that the foundry, the glass and the copper industries all pull on. The quartzite that goes into the silicon furnace is a different, much rarer rock.

facts.label: Processing
facts.value: wash, screen, dry, magnetite separation; <150 um for foundry and smelter use

facts.label: Vitrified silica
facts.value: used in foundry moulds and in fused silica, at 99.9%+

places: map of the Mississippi valley dune sands

metal.silica-sand.dune.name: Aeolian dune sand and beach placer
metal.silica-sand.dune.description: The leaf: quartz grains rounded by wind or wave, in an unconsolidated surface deposit a few metres to tens of metres thick sitting on older sediment. Dunes along the Mississippi valley, the Great Lakes shorelines and the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States were the standard sources, mined with bucket-wheel or dragline dredges - a sand mine is the commonest kind of open pit in the world.

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: surface dune and beach sand, over bedrock or older sediment

industry.name: Foundries, factories, utilities and logistics
industry.description: The plant and the plumbing behind the Commodore 64: who made the chips, who assembled the box, what burned to light the lights, where the water came from, where the waste went, and how many hands and hours it took. A C64 is an artefact of eleven industries, not one. The eleven branches below are the shared utilities and the two hard-industry branches - manufacturing geography and freight - that every other subsystem points at.
industry.note: Category answers what industry made a thing. energy is reserved for the generating plants, the grid and the plant's own steam and compressed-air distribution, and only for plant and process nodes - so the boilers, turbines, transformers, switchgear, insulators and fuel commodities inside those plants are filed under industry (heavy equipment, mining) or power (electrical hardware) instead. industry also carries the extractive ends: coal and ore bodies, sand, limestone, sulphur, biomass. fluids is water and water chemistry, bulk process gases, solvents and process chemistry. Several nodes here are notes: commentary about the supply chain rather than things in it.

facility.test-equipment.name: Factory and engineering test equipment
facility.test-equipment.description: Every C64 that left the Hong Kong line had been through a functional test, and the boards had been tested electrically before population and after soldering. In-circuit testers and flying probes were the technology of the era; the automated ATE industry of the 1990s did not exist yet. The capital equipment here was made by the test-and-measurement industry, which is why it is categorised `industry` rather than `assembly` - assembly is reserved for the operations themselves.

facility.test-equipment.bare-board.name: Bare-board test and flying probe
facility.test-equipment.bare-board.description: Bare PCB test came first: a bed-of-nails grid fixture to prove every net was etched and plated correctly, catching a shorts-heavy board before it was populated and therefore before the parts were on it. The flying probe - a robot or CNC head with a moving needle that touched nets individually without a fixture - existed by the early 1980s as an engineering diagnostic, and only later became the standard production tester once it got fast enough.
facility.test-equipment.bare-board.note: Today the flying probe has largely displaced the bed-of-nails in production, which removes the per-revision fixture cost - a genuine change in the economics of board design between 1983 and now.

facility.test-equipment.needle-probe.name: Spring probe and tungsten needle
facility.test-equipment.needle-probe.description: The bed-of-nails is a field of sprung tungsten-rhenium or beryllium-copper pins on a 2.54 mm grid, each pressing a few grams onto a pad to make contact. The 1980s fixtures were drilled and wired by hand or on a numerical-control machine from the Gerber artwork - which is why a board layout change meant a new fixture.
facility.test-equipment.needle-probe.note: Tungsten-rhenium was the common needle alloy in this era; beryllium copper became the standard later, and both carry real occupational-exposure caveats for the operators who handled them.

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 2.54 mm (0.1 inch)

facts.label: Contact force
facts.value: typically 100-300 g per pin

facility.test-equipment.burn-in.name: Burn-in oven and sockets
facility.test-equipment.burn-in.description: A forced-air oven at 70-100 C with burn-in sockets, holding hundreds of boards for 24-72 hours so that early-life component failures - bad solder joints, marginal ICs, leaky capacitors - showed up on the line instead of in the customer's house. Commodore's 1982-83 quality record suggests it was not always run long enough.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: typically 70-100 C

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 24-72 hours

facility.test-equipment.test-rom.name: Test ROM in the final-test fixture
facility.test-equipment.test-rom.description: A dedicated test ROM - the '501' diagnostic ROM is the one most C64 owners meet - loaded into the machine's own ROM socket during factory final test so the machine could self-test its own RAM, character ROM, CIA timers and VIC registers. It is the same object a user later used to prove the machine worked.
facility.test-equipment.test-rom.note: Not established: that Commodore's factory final test loaded the 501 diagnostic ROM into the machine's own ROM socket, or that the 501 ROM was the diagnostic most C64 owners met. The existence of a 501 test ROM is not in doubt; its use in final-test fixtures is.

facts.label: Test ROM
facts.value: the 501 diagnostic

facility.test-equipment.functional.name: Functional tester
facility.test-equipment.functional.description: A powered-up test station running a test program from ROM that exercised the VIC-II registers, checked the RAM, drove the keyboard matrix and read back the RAM. On a Commodore line this was a dedicated fixture with a monitor and a keyboard, and the operator's job was to load, run, read the result, box or quarantine.

facility.test-equipment.ict.name: In-circuit tester (ICT)
facility.test-equipment.ict.description: A bed-of-nails fixture pressing 1000 or so spring-loaded probes onto the bare board's pads, measuring resistance, capacitance, diode voltage and, at an increasing share, functional signatures at each node - all in a few seconds. By 1983 the analogue resistance-only tester was giving way to the analogue-plus-functional 'in-circuit functional tester' that could catch an unpopulated IC or a wrong-orientation part without a board-level functional test.
facility.test-equipment.ict.note: The bed-of-nails fixture itself is bespoke per board revision - which is one of the reasons a new motherboard revision was expensive to introduce and why the 250407 revision mattered.

logistics.people.name: The labour content of a C64
logistics.people.description: Two labour populations with almost nothing in common: a tiny, very senior, very expensive American engineering team in Pennsylvania and Japan, and a large, low-paid, mostly female production workforce in Hong Kong and Japan. The design labour is amortised over millions of units and is invisible in the $35-50 bill of materials; the assembly labour is a few dollars per unit and is the reason Commodore could hit a $135 production cost. The Hong Kong branch of Commodore Electronics Ltd employed approximately 2,500 people when mass production of the production-redesigned C-64A began there in March 1983 - the single best-documented headcount in the whole Commodore manufacturing story.
logistics.people.note: Almost every node in this branch is a note: what is documented here is people and wages, which is commentary about how the machine was made rather than a thing in the supply chain. The wage figures come from the Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department's 1983 quarterly report and from ILO Bureau of Labour Statistics hourly compensation indices for SIC 36 electronic and other electrical equipment.

facts.label: Hong Kong branch headcount
facts.value: ~2,500 persons at the start of C-64A mass production, March 1983

logistics.people.qa-defects.name: The labour cost of the quality problems
logistics.people.qa-defects.description: Commodore's labour did not just build machines, it found and reworked other people's mistakes. The 'sparkle' defect was traced after three weeks to a ROM - not the VIC-II - with a pre-charging circuit that was sensitive to a bus contention spike; three million such ROMs were already in service. A logic error put 64 clock cycles on a scanline instead of 65 and took about five months into production to fix. Assembly-line workers over-adjusted the colour potentiometer until it saturated the colour and wiped out the luma. Electric screwdrivers cut traces on the disk-drive connector, and because those traces went to a connector nobody tested, they passed final inspection. Charles Winterble: 'It takes a very tough person to say I'm not shipping these because they're not as good as they could be - especially when people are clamoring to buy them.'

facts.label: ROMs affected
facts.value: 3 million already in service when the sparkle cause was found

facts.label: Bus timing fix
facts.value: about five months into production

facts.label: Cost of the C64A redesign
facts.value: a substantial redesign was required to fix the Santa Clara build

logistics.people.production-engineering.name: The production engineers who fixed it
logistics.people.production-engineering.description: The unsung labour in Commodore's story: David Ziembicki (production engineer, then Commodore West Chester), Bruce Crocket and Charles Winterble, who had to debug the project and bring it into production, and Robert H. Lane, who became president of Commodore Business Machines Inc in November 1982 and was fired by Tramiel after the June 1983 CES. Kentron's 150 Japanese engineers and technicians - brought in specifically because Commodore Japan's production engineering had worked on the VIC-20 - are the documented reason the C64 was eventually manufacturable at all.

logistics.people.development-cost.name: Nobody knows what the C64 cost to develop
logistics.people.development-cost.description: Winterble's answer to the question was direct: 'I had no formal budget accountability, other than Jack watching me. Jack said that budgets were a license to steal.' The reason the answer was 'nothing much' is that the fab was not running at full capacity and the design chips were absorbed into existing overhead with no supplier margin at all. Ziembicki: 'We were using people who were there anyway.' Software, per Charpentier, 'wasn't tangible - you couldn't hold it, feel it, or touch it - so it wasn't worth spending money for.'

logistics.people.c64-system-team.name: The C64 system design team
logistics.people.c64-system-team.description: After Tramiel decided in late November 1981 that the VIC-II and SID would go into a 64 KB home computer rather than a game console, the machine itself was designed in about five weeks. The architecture was laid out on paper in two days; five working prototypes were finished just before the new year. The team was Bob Yannes, Bob Russell, Shiraz Shivji and David Ziembicki, with Yash Terakura of Commodore Japan involved on the Japanese variant. They worked over Thanksgiving and Christmas. Charlie Winterble had set the deadline; Tramiel had decided the machine had to be at the January 1982 CES.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: laid out on paper in two days

facts.label: Prototypes
facts.value: five working units in under five weeks

facts.label: Show
facts.value: January 1982 Consumer Electronics Show, Las Vegas

logistics.people.design-team.name: The C64 chip design team
logistics.people.design-team.description: A team of about seven people, working in parallel on two chips, in nine months. Al Charpentier designed the VIC-II with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Bob Yannes designed the SID with two draftsmen and one CAD operator. Charles Winterble, then director of worldwide engineering, authorised and managed the project. The whole effort began in January 1981, spent about two weeks studying the Mattel Intellivision, the TI 99/4A and the Atari 800, and finished with first-pass silicon in November 1981 that worked except for one bad sprite. The chips were designed in a modular, deliberately uncompact style - Yannes built one oscillator module and repeated it rather than multiplexing - because design time was the scarce resource, not die area. Neither designer had a modern CAD workstation; logic was simulated by hand.
logistics.people.design-team.note: Six months is often quoted for this design and the sources do not support it: Charpentier and Yannes both worked the full nine months from January 1981 to November 1981, a figure documented in IEEE Spectrum's 1985 case history and in the C64 design histories. The system-level C64 (architecture on paper in two days, five working prototypes in under five weeks) was a different and much shorter effort by Yannes, Bob Russell, Shiraz Shivji and David Ziembicki in December 1981.

facts.label: Team size
facts.value: about 7 (2 designers, 4 draftsmen, 1-2 CAD operators, plus a manager)

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: January 1981 to November 1981 (9 months)

facts.label: VIC-II process
facts.value: 5 micrometre features

facts.label: SID process
facts.value: 7 micrometre, scaled to 6 in places

logistics.people.wave-solder-worker.name: The worker at the wave-solder line
logistics.people.wave-solder-worker.description: The single most recognisable job in a 1980s electronics factory. She stood or sat at one end of a 2-3 m wave-solder machine, fed pre-inserted boards into the conveyor, watched for bridging and dry joints, pulled the rejects, and often did the visual inspection and the component-insertion handwork at the same station. Almost always female, usually in her twenties or thirties, on a piece rate or a small hourly premium for yield, and living within an hour's bus ride of the plant in a New Territories squatter village or a public housing block. Hong Kong's 1983 wage survey listed 'soldering worker' as a distinct occupational category for exactly this reason.
logistics.people.wave-solder-worker.note: The 1980s photographs of the Commodore Hong Kong line show a robotised through-hole populating machine followed by a long line with bench test desks, consistent with this description, but they date from December 1992, not 1983.

logistics.people.hk-wages.name: Hong Kong electronics wages, 1983
logistics.people.hk-wages.description: The Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department's Quarterly Report of Wages, Salaries and Employee Benefits Statistics carried explicit occupational breakdowns for the electronics industry in 1983 - assembler, soldering worker, tester/aligner, quality control operator, packer, machine operator - with average daily wages and normal hours, and it separately flagged that piece rates were common in manufacturing and that the survey therefore reported them on a time basis. Operative daily wages across manufacturing generally sat around HK$60-100 in 1983, so an assembler earned roughly HK$9-14 per hour at a 7-8.5 hour day. Hong Kong had no statutory minimum wage at all in 1983.
logistics.people.hk-wages.note: The scanned 1983 Census and Statistics Department tables are OCR-garbled; the HK$60-100 daily figure is read off the reported range across manufacturing occupations and should be treated as a range, not a single number.

facts.label: Typical operative daily wage
facts.value: about HK$60-100 in 1983

facts.label: Implied hourly
facts.value: about HK$9-14

facts.label: Minimum wage law
facts.value: none before 2011

logistics.people.direct-labour.name: Direct assembly labour per machine
logistics.people.direct-labour.description: Roughly 0.5-1.5 person-hours per machine across population, insertion (automated), wave-solder, assembly, test and packing, plus a share of the test and rework. At 1983 Hong Kong and Japanese electronics wage levels of roughly HK$9-14 or JPY 500-700 per hour, that is about US$1-3 per machine of direct labour - between 3% and 8% of the $35-50 production cost. Direct labour is genuinely tiny compared with the IC content, which is exactly the point Commodore's vertical integration strategy rested on.
logistics.people.direct-labour.note: Not established: a documented Commodore standard time for C64 assembly. The person-hour estimate is derived from the process steps (insertion is automated; a wave-solder pass plus test plus pack is on the order of 30-60 minutes of attended time) and should be treated as an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a measured value.

facts.label: Share of BOM
facts.value: roughly 3-8%

logistics.people.bom.name: The bill of materials (1983 estimate)
logistics.people.bom.description: Brian Dougherty of Berkeley Softworks gave the most-cited contemporaneous breakdown, used as a production cost of $35-50 by 1985: three ROMs at $1 each; eight 64K DRAMs at $1.85 each; SID and VIC-II at $4 each; RF modulator $3; 6510 at $1-2; TTL, buffers, regulators and capacitors together $5; keyboard under $10; PC board $1-2; plastic case $1-2; power supply and connectors $5-10; packaging and manual $1-2. Note what this says: the eight DRAM chips alone were $14.80, more than the case, the board and the modulator combined.
logistics.people.bom.note: These are Dougherty's estimates, not Commodore's accounts - Commodore never confirmed them. The $135 initial production cost is a Commodore figure.

facts.label: Total estimate
facts.value: $35-50 by 1985; $135 at introduction in 1982

logistics.shipping.name: Moving 100,000 C64s
logistics.shipping.description: The C64 was assembled in East Asia and sold in North America and Europe. In 1983 that was containerised cargo on liner services, not break-bulk: a 40-foot box holds 250-350 C64s depending on how they were packed, and the whole industry's economics were shaped by the 1966-1980s transition from weight/measurement cargo to box rates.

logistics.shipping.customs-valuation.name: Customs valuation and the paper trail
logistics.shipping.customs-valuation.description: US customs value was the transaction value - the price actually paid or payable - which is why Commodore's transfer-pricing between Commodore Electronics Ltd (Bahamas), Commodore Japan Ltd and the Hong Kong branch became the subject of a US Tax Court case that ran from 1991 and shifted $116 million of income between entities. The same transfer prices determined the duty. The documentation for a 1983 shipment would have included a commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading and, in a bonded warehouse or an export-processing-zone deal, a certificate of origin.

facts.label: Section 482 adjustment
facts.value: $65.6 M for 1985 and $50.5 M for 1986 added to CBM income

logistics.shipping.commercial-documents.name: Commercial invoice, packing list and certificate of origin
logistics.shipping.commercial-documents.description: The three documents that travelled with the container besides the bill of lading. The invoice stated the price actually paid or payable, which is the number customs used; the packing list was the count and weight the carrier checked against the manifest; the certificate of origin was what made the 807.00 assembly-relief deduction claimable. In a bonded warehouse or an export-processing-zone deal all three had to be issued and retained for years - which is why the tax case could reconstruct Commodore's internal transfer prices two decades later.

logistics.shipping.import-duty.name: US import duty on a computer in 1983
logistics.shipping.import-duty.description: The C64 entered the United States under the Tariff Schedules of the United States (the TSUS - the HTS did not exist until 1989), classified as an accounting, computing and other data processing machine incorporating a calculating mechanism, item 676.15, dutiable at 5.5% ad valorem. Separately, item 807.00 gave a duty allowance for the US components shipped out for assembly abroad - which for Commodore meant a deduction for the value of the MOS chips and the case shipped to Hong Kong, so only the value added in Hong Kong paid duty.
logistics.shipping.import-duty.note: The 5.5% figure for TSUS 676.15 is verified from a 1987 Court of International Trade decision. Not verified: the exact 1983 rate for item 676.15; it is flagged as medium confidence for that reason. Note also that in 1983 the HTS did not exist (it was introduced in 1989) and the Customs Tariff Index, not a searchable database, was the practical reference.

facts.label: TSUS item
facts.value: 676.15, data processing machines

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: 5.5% ad valorem (rate confirmed for 1987; 1983 rate not directly verified)

facts.label: Assembly relief
facts.value: TSUS 807.00: duty on full value less US component value

logistics.shipping.demurrage.name: Demurrage, detention and the inventory cost
logistics.shipping.demurrage.description: Two separate costs. Demurrage is the charge for leaving a container on the terminal beyond the free time; in 1983 free time was commonly four to five days and the daily charge escalated. Detention is the charge for keeping the container beyond the time allowed at the other end. On top of both sat the real cost: eight to twelve weeks of sea transit each way meant Commodore had to hold inventory in transit and in the destination warehouse, which is exactly the cost structure that rewarded the 'just-in-time' port-to-port discipline and punished Commodore's famous spotty availability in 1983.
logistics.shipping.demurrage.note: Modern practice: much longer contractually-guaranteed free time (7-10 days), published terminal tariffs and time-and-demurrage clauses that convert demurrage into a rental. The published per-day figures quoted today ($65-$315/day at LA/LB) are anachronistic for 1983.

logistics.shipping.air-freight.name: Air freight for the high-value parts
logistics.shipping.air-freight.description: Customs values tell the story: a box of 300 C64s entered at, say, $150-200 declared value each would carry $45,000-60,000 of electronics inside a container whose ocean freight was a few hundred dollars. The ICs were the opposite case: a 6510 and a VIC-II at internal transfer value were a tiny fraction of the customs value of the finished case, so nobody flew the chips - the chips came by sea inside the container, and the container moved once. Air freight was for prototypes, for a replacement part in an emergency, and for the tape and the spares.
logistics.shipping.air-freight.note: Air freight in 1983 was priced by weight with a minimum weight, so the economics made it essentially unusable for consumer electronics inbound freight; it was used for sample and prototype shipments and for urgent replacement parts.

logistics.shipping.bill-of-lading.name: The bill of lading
logistics.shipping.bill-of-lading.description: The negotiable document that made containerised trade possible: a carrier-issued contract of carriage naming the shipper, the consignee, the port of loading and discharge, the freight terms, and the description of the goods. Without it the goods did not move; with it, the bank paid on presentation. The 1983 electronic BOL did not exist - the paper document was the mechanism.

logistics.shipping.routes.name: Route times: transpacific and Europe-Asia
logistics.shipping.routes.description: Kaohsiung or Hong Kong to Long Beach is about 4,500-5,000 nautical miles via the Luzon Strait and the great circle; at 16-18 knots that is roughly 12-14 days port to port, plus 3-7 days in the terminal on each end. Hong Kong to Rotterdam via the Suez Canal is about 11,000 nautical miles, 22-26 days, with 5-7 days of canal transit and waiting. These were the numbers that set Commodore's inventory position: eight weeks of sea transit each way on the Pacific route, eleven to twelve weeks each way on the Europe route.
logistics.shipping.routes.note: These are order-of-magnitude figures derived from distances and 1980s liner speeds; No published 1983 schedule for a specific Commodore carrier service was found.

facts.label: Transpacific
facts.value: ~12-14 days port to port

facts.label: Europe-Asia via Suez
facts.value: ~22-26 days port to port

logistics.shipping.ports.name: The ports
logistics.shipping.ports.description: Kaohsiung was Taiwan's largest container port and was ranked the world's fifth-largest container port in 1982; its first container terminal was built 1969-70 and Container Terminal No. 4 in the Zhongxing Commercial Harbor Area was built from 1983. Keelung, on the northern approach to Taipei, opened the first Taiwanese container ship movements in January 1972 and worked on a filled jetty because of the terrain. Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour terminals, Rotterdam, and Long Beach or Oakland on the US West Coast, plus New York and Newark on the East Coast, completed the set.

facts.label: Kaohsiung first container terminal
facts.value: built 1969-70; storage capacity 2,500 TEU

facts.label: Kaohsiung ranking 1982
facts.value: world's 5th largest container port

logistics.shipping.c64-count.name: The volume Commodore was moving
logistics.shipping.c64-count.description: By March 1983 the C64 was shipping at about 25,000 units a month and had passed the Apple II in monthly unit sales; roughly half a million had sold in the first six months. At 300 units a 40-foot box, that is about 83 TEU a month - about four to five ships' worth of containers a month, which sounds trivial until you remember it was compounding 20-30% a month.

facts.label: Ship rate March 1983
facts.value: about 25,000 units/month

facts.label: First six months
facts.value: about 500,000 sold

logistics.shipping.containerisation.name: Containerisation (40-foot box)
logistics.shipping.containerisation.description: ISO 40-foot general purpose container: 12.192 m x 2.438 m x 2.591 m internal, holding up to about 32-36 tonnes. One TEU is a 20-foot box; a 40-foot box is two. Box rates had replaced weight rates on the main east-west lanes by the end of the 1970s, so a low-density, high-value cargo like a C64 paid per box rather than per tonne.
logistics.shipping.containerisation.note: The C64 weighed roughly 4 kg boxed; a 40-ft box at 32 t payload would in principle hold hundreds, but in practice the limit was volume and the fact that C64s were not stackable with the packaging of the day, so 250-350 is a working estimate, not a documented figure.

facts.label: Payload
facts.value: roughly 32-36 t

facts.label: C64s per box
facts.value: 250-350 (estimate, at 4-5 kg each)

facility.foundries.name: The Commodore supply-chain geography
facility.foundries.description: Where a C64 physically came from, and the only place in this tree where the map is Commodore-specific rather than industrial. Commodore owned one fab, in Pennsylvania. The boards were printed in Hong Kong. The boxes were assembled in Hong Kong, Japan, West Germany, the United States and - from 1984 - Britain. The corporate records that survived the bankruptcy are unusually detailed and are the best source for this branch.
facility.foundries.note: Evidence discipline for this branch: the headcounts, dates and production-start figures below come from the US Tax Court record of Commodore Holding B.V. v. Commissioner, which reproduces the parties' own stipulations of fact. They are Commodore-specific facts about Commodore's own plants and are not industry figures - nothing here should be read as an average for electronics manufacturing. Where a figure is general rather than Commodore-specific (the ILO wage index, the generic fab capital costs) it says so.

facility.foundries.subcontract-network.name: The sub-contractor geography: Japan, Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines
facility.foundries.subcontract-network.description: Commodore's own factories were few; its supply base was enormous. Japan supplied the disks and a great deal of the precision mechanics and passives. Taiwan and Korea supplied the display-grade passives, the transformers, the coils, the keyboards and the power supplies, through the export processing zones. The Philippines and Malaysia supplied the switching power supplies and the magnetics by the late 1980s. Hong Kong was the assembly and test node, sitting between them, with the boards printed locally and the chips arriving from Pennsylvania.
facility.foundries.subcontract-network.note: The wage index here is general, not Commodore-specific: ILO Bureau of Labour Statistics hourly compensation costs for production workers in US SIC 36 electronic and other electrical equipment. It is the cleanest single measure of why the work was in Hong Kong and Taiwan - roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the American cost per hour - but it says nothing about Commodore specifically.

facts.label: Hourly compensation index (US=100), electronic equipment
facts.value: 1975: Hong Kong 15-16, Korea 16, Taiwan 18-19; 1984: Hong Kong 19, Korea 23, Taiwan 22

facility.foundries.other-sites.name: The rest of the manufacturing map, 1983
facility.foundries.other-sites.description: By 1983 Commodore described itself as an international company with manufacturing in Japan, Hong Kong, West Germany, the UK, Pennsylvania and California in the United States, and Scarborough in Metropolitan Toronto. C64 units carried the MADE IN HONG KONG, West Germany or England marks, and were assembled in at least 11 factories worldwide over the model's life. Commodore did not, at this stage, have a Commodore Taiwan plant - the Taiwanese supply chain in this story is the sub-contractor base, not a Commodore factory.
facility.foundries.other-sites.note: The $680 M / 44.7% figure is Commodore's own reported fiscal-1983 sales, not an industry figure, and it is here only because the 1983 annual review is the source for the list of manufacturing countries beside it. Commodore Taiwan as a subsidiary is a later-1980s development; No 1983 evidence of a Commodore-owned Taiwan factory has been found. A Philippine assembly operation definitely existed by the 1990s (the Philippine government seized Amiga and CD32 stock after Commodore's 1994 bankruptcy over a debt to a factory there), but that is outside the 1982-84 window.

facts.label: Fiscal 1983 sales
facts.value: $680 million, up 44.7% on 1982's $304.5 million

facility.foundries.corby.name: Commodore Business Machines (UK), Corby
facility.foundries.corby.description: The British end. Commodore UK's head office was in Slough and it built calculators at a factory on Teesside; in 1983 it announced a new GBP 20 million home computer factory at Corby, Northamptonshire, as the European manufacturing and distribution centre for the C64 and VIC-20, expecting 300 jobs by the end of 1984 and 700,000 units a year by then. The Corby plant was in place by September 1984 with 850 jobs on a ten-acre site, ran flat out sixteen hours a day, and was closed as a manufacturing base in January 1986.
facility.foundries.corby.note: Corby post-dates the C64's 1983 peak, so it belongs here as the European logistics and finishing node rather than as a 1983 production source.

facts.label: Capital
facts.value: GBP 20 million announced 1983; a little over GBP 2 million of UK grant

facts.label: Jobs
facts.value: 300 planned for 1984; 850 by opening; 170 retained at closure

facts.label: Closure
facts.value: January 1986

facility.foundries.braunschweig.name: Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH, Braunschweig, West Germany
facility.foundries.braunschweig.description: The European production base. Commodore launched production for the European market in Braunschweig in 1980 and it once employed up to 2,000 people. Commodore GmbH also designed products. The PET had been imported from Braunschweig, and Commodore UK in the 1970s bought calculators at a factory on Teesside. After the 1983 Corby decision, the more expensive business systems stayed in Braunschweig.

facts.label: Peak employment
facts.value: up to 2,000

facility.foundries.japan-vendors.name: Japanese assembly vendors for the VIC-20
facility.foundries.japan-vendors.description: The VIC-20 - the machine whose case, board size and BASIC the C64 inherited - was first built in Japan by Shinwa Electric Company, then by Japanese Cash Register (JCR), both assembling and manufacturing to Commodore Japan Limited's specifications and under its direction. Japanese Cash Register also owned a factory on Ina road; CJL's engineering headquarters was at Isaka.
facility.foundries.japan-vendors.note: The C64-Wiki list of Commodore entities includes 'Commodore Japan Limited in Japan (Isaka)'; the Tax Court record confirms Shinwa Electric and Japanese Cash Register as the VIC-20 assemblers but does not give their locations.

facility.foundries.kentron.name: Kentron Co., Ltd., Ina, Japan
facility.foundries.kentron.description: The small Japanese production-engineering company that Commodore Japan acquired in October 1982 and that actually fixed the C64. Kentron had about 150 employees at its height and expertise in production engineering, quality control, work standards, purchasing and materials control. Commodore Japan substantially redesigned the machine into the 'C-64A' with Kentron's help; Kentron produced prototypes in late 1982 and began mass production in January 1983 - two months before the Hong Kong branch started, which is why Kentron, not Hong Kong, is where the machine was made buildable. Kentron was a CJL subsidiary from October 1982 to June 1986, when it was sold to an unrelated party.
facility.foundries.kentron.note: The acquisition dates and the January 1983 production start are stipulated facts from the US Tax Court record, not published Commodore accounts.

facts.label: Headcount
facts.value: ~150 employees at height of operations

facts.label: Owned
facts.value: October 1982 - June 1986

facts.label: Mass production
facts.value: January 1983

facility.foundries.hong-kong.name: The Hong Kong operation (CE(HK)L and the CEL Hong Kong branch)
facility.foundries.hong-kong.description: Where the C64 really got built. Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd had been making watches and calculators since 1979, and manufactured VIC-20 units from April 1982; later the Hong Kong branch of Commodore Electronics Ltd took over. Mass production of the production-redesigned 'C-64A' began at the Hong Kong branch in March 1983, and that branch employed approximately 2,500 people. Commodore's Hong Kong operation bought or produced watches, calculators and computers, and by 1983 it was the assembly centre for the whole company's output. Commodore had Hong Kong subsidiaries listed as Commodore Business Machines Ltd (Hong Kong) and Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd.
facility.foundries.hong-kong.note: The 2,500 headcount and the March 1983 mass-production start are the parties' stipulated facts in the US Tax Court record, not Commodore's published accounts and not industry averages. The exact street address of the Commodore Hong Kong plant is not established in the sources consulted; it is not confirmed as Kwai Chung, Tsuen Wan or Kwun Tong. Photographs of the plant taken in December 1992 by Robert Baker, a Commodore production engineer sent from West Chester PA for the Amiga 600 pilot run, show a robotised through-hole insertion machine, a long assembly/test line and bench test desks.

facts.label: Headcount
facts.value: ~2,500 persons at the Hong Kong branch of CEL

facts.label: Mass production start
facts.value: March 1983

facts.label: VIC-20 production in HK
facts.value: from April 1982

facility.foundries.psu-maker.name: Power supply / transformer sub-contractor
facility.foundries.psu-maker.description: The linear power supply inside the C64 - the big orange or black transformer, the rectifier and the linear regulators - came from outside suppliers, cost an estimated $5-10 including connectors, and one of Ziembicki's complaints was that a supplier that had passed engineering approval then quietly changed the design without telling anybody.

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $5-10 for supply and connectors

facility.foundries.hk-injection.name: Hong Kong / Taiwan injection moulding sub-contractor
facility.foundries.hk-injection.description: The ABS case, the keyboard keycaps and the cassette-port door were moulded by a sub-contractor, not by Commodore. Hong Kong and Taiwan each had hundreds of small toolrooms and presses in 1983, and Commodore used both. The case cost an estimated $1-2 in 1983 prices.
facility.foundries.hk-injection.note: The identity of the moulder is not documented in the sources consulted.

facts.label: Case cost
facts.value: $1-2 per set (1983 estimate)

facility.foundries.hk-pcb.name: Hong Kong PCB fabricator
facility.foundries.hk-pcb.description: All sixteen versions of the C64 motherboard were manufactured in Hong Kong. Hong Kong in the early 1980s was a genuine centre of bare-board fabrication - dozens of small plants doing gold-impregnated or tin-lead plated FR-4 double-sided boards on a 0.3-0.4 mm grid with the pads drilled and plated by a subcontractor. Commodore did not own one; it bought them.
facility.foundries.hk-pcb.note: The bare-board manufacturer is not named in any source consulted; 'manufactured in Hong Kong' is the documented claim.

facility.foundries.santa-clara.name: CBM Santa Clara, California
facility.foundries.santa-clara.description: Commodore's US assembly line, where production of the C64 began in late summer 1982. It had automated component-insertion equipment. It went badly: excessive video and audio noise, excessive heat, and semiconductors incompatible with the design, so yield was low, cost high and returns came back. Only a limited number of units came out of Santa Clara before responsibility was shifted to Commodore Japan in the autumn of 1982.

facts.label: Start of production
facts.value: late summer 1982

facility.foundries.board-layout-dispute.name: The automated-insertion board layout fight
facility.foundries.board-layout-dispute.description: Commodore's US plant used automatic component insertion; the Japanese plant did not, and the two wanted different component spacing. Charpentier's group won: the C64 board was laid out for automated insertion, and production was moved to a Hong Kong plant that had the automated tools. This single decision is why every C64 motherboard was made in Hong Kong.

facility.foundries.mos.name: MOS Technology / Commodore Semiconductor Group fab, Norristown PA
facility.foundries.mos.description: The fab that made the 6510, the 6567/6569 VIC-II, the 6581 SID, the 6526 CIA and the ROMs. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 by John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe and Don McLaughlin as a second source for Texas Instruments' calculator chips, was majority-owned by Allen-Bradley from 1970, and built its own plant on 14 acres of the Valley Forge Corporate Center, 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Pennsylvania. It was a 1-micron NMOS fab running 4-inch wafers, and it is the only place the C64's silicon came from - none of the five custom chips could ever be second-sourced. Commodore bought MOS outright for a 9.4% stake in CBM in November 1976 and merged it in 1981. The fab was closed in 1992 after Commodore's bankruptcy.
facility.foundries.mos.note: Sources variously call the location Norristown, Valley Forge or Lower Providence; the EPA documents put the plant at 950 Rittenhouse Road in Lower Providence Township, Norristown PA, in the former Valley Forge Corporate Center.

facts.label: Building
facts.value: constructed 1970-71 for MOS Technology

facts.label: Site
facts.value: 14 acres; purchased from Allen-Bradley in 1978

facts.label: Process
facts.value: 1 micron NMOS; 4-inch wafers

places: 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Montgomery County, Pennsylvania

facility.foundries.mos.csg-successor.name: After Commodore: GMT Microelectronics
facility.foundries.mos.csg-successor.description: The fab was bought out of bankruptcy in December 1994 for about $4.3 million plus $1 million of liabilities (including the EPA licence), reopened in 1995, ran a 1-micron process for third parties, and was shut down by the EPA in 2000-01. 183 employees and $21 million of revenue in 1999. It is a rare, well-documented instance of a 1970s fab surviving the death of its owner.

facility.foundries.mos.captive-prototypi.name: The captive fab as a prototyping advantage
facility.foundries.mos.captive-prototypi.description: The reason Commodore could design a chip in nine months: the fab was not full, the mask shop and the processing line were on site, and a designer could pull a test chip in a few weeks - or, in an emergency, four days. Ziembicki's line is the whole story of Commodore's speed: 'We were using people who were there anyway... You waste a little bit of silicon, but silicon's pretty cheap. It's only sand.'

facts.label: Turnaround
facts.value: a few weeks; 4 days in an emergency

facility.foundries.corporate-structure.name: The corporate chain that owned all of it
facility.foundries.corporate-structure.description: From the US Tax Court record: Commodore Holding B.V. (Netherlands) at the top; Commodore International Ltd (Bahamas); Commodore Electronics Ltd (CEL, Bahamas) as the principal operating corporation; Commodore Business Machines Inc (CBM, West Chester PA) as the US sales subsidiary and the site of the semiconductor division; Commodore Japan Ltd (CJL); Commodore Electronics (Hong Kong) Ltd (CE(HK)L) and, after April 1982, the Hong Kong branch of CEL; Commodore Buromaschinen GmbH (West Germany); and CBM International Sales Inc, the DISC. MOS Technology became a division of CBM on 1 January 1981 - which is why all the chips were still stamped with the MOS logo until 1989.

facts.label: MOS acquisition
facts.value: CBM agreed to buy MOS in November 1976 for a 9.4% equity stake in CBM; merged into CBM 1 January 1981

facility.foundries.vertical-integration.name: Vertical integration as a strategy
facility.foundries.vertical-integration.description: Tramiel's thesis, and the reason the whole tree looks the way it does: if you own the chip, you do not pay a merchant supplier's margin, you control the schedule, and nobody can raise your price. The concrete results: a $135 initial production cost against a $595 retail price, and a production cost driven down to $35-50 by 1985.

facts.label: Initial production cost
facts.value: $135 (target was $130)

facility.cleanroom.name: The semiconductor fab building
facility.cleanroom.description: Where the C64's five custom chips were made. A 1-micron NMOS fab: a raised access floor over a service plenum, a ceiling of HEPA filters feeding laminar-flow hoods and open cleanroom, Class 100 in the process bays and Class 1000 in the support areas, and a yellow-lit room for photolithography. Air changed 100-1000 times an hour and consumed most of the plant's electricity.
facility.cleanroom.note: The 1980s standard was US Federal Standard 209E (1963), which is why everyone said 'Class 100' rather than ISO Class 5. ISO 14644 only arrived in 1995.

facts.label: Class definition
facts.value: Class 100 = <=100 particles >=0.5 um per cubic foot of air

facts.label: MOS process
facts.value: 1 micrometre NMOS, 4-inch wafers

facts.label: Fab capital cost
facts.value: roughly $4 M in 1970 (a small fab) rising through $100-300 M for a full 1980s 100-300 mm fab

facility.cleanroom.workforce.name: Fab workforce, 1980s
facility.cleanroom.workforce.description: A large 1983 fab ran 5,000-10,000 employees, of whom the majority working on the wafer lines were women - the largest single female industrial workforce in many of the regions where the plants went, because the tool operators and the wafer handling were culturally coded as women's work even though they were skilled and tightly controlled.
facility.cleanroom.workforce.note: Commodore's own Norristown fab was far smaller than a 5,000-10,000 employee plant, so this figure describes the industry-wide pattern and not Commodore. Not verified: a firm headcount for any single named 1983 plant.

facts.label: Typical large fab
facts.value: 5,000-10,000 employees

facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools.name: Wafer carriers and handling hardware
