facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools.description: In 1983 a wafer still travelled in a quartz boat inside a plastic carrier, or hand-carried in a PTFE-wafer cassette from process to process. The SMIF FOUP - the sealed nitrogen-purged single-wafer container that made the whole modern fab possible - arrived with SEMI E10 in the early 1990s. Before that, every transfer was an opportunity for a particle, and a large fraction of the total defect budget.
facility.cleanroom.bobbin-and-tools.note: Modern practice is the 300 mm FOUP in a minienvironment with automatic material handling; the 1980s practice was a person carrying a cassette.

facility.cleanroom.quartz-boat.name: Fused-quartz wafer boat
facility.cleanroom.quartz-boat.description: A slotted quartz holder that carries 25-50 wafers through the diffusion furnace. Fused quartz is used because it survives 1000 C, expands predictably, and is chemically inert to the dopants. Made from high-purity synthetic quartz rod, ground and flame-polished.

facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies.name: Garment and consumable supply
facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies.description: Garments were not laundryable in the era - a hooded coverall was worn once and destroyed. The plant bought enormous quantities of spun-bonded polypropylene garments, hoods, overshoes, gloves, wipes and tacky mats, and washed nothing. One 1980s 5,000-person fab burned something like a million garments a year.
facility.cleanroom.gowning-supplies.note: The garment figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate; No published 1983 consumption figure was found. Modern fabs launder and reuse garments and use more reusable materials, which was one of the first sustainability targets in the industry.

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order of 1 million garments per year at a large fab

facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp.name: Spun-bonded polypropylene
facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp.description: Polypropylene melt-spun into continuous filaments and laid down in a random web, then bonded by heat or needle punching. Cheapest possible cleanroom garment material, and the raw material for the 'tacky mat' that caught shoe-borne particles at every airlock.
facility.cleanroom.spunbond-pp.note: Not established: that spun-bonded polypropylene was the standard 1980s cleanroom garment material or the standard tacky-mat material. Spun-bonded fabric has no separate encyclopaedia article, and no standard or industry document was located for this material in the cleanroom trade in that decade.

facility.cleanroom.prefilter.name: Pre-filter bank
facility.cleanroom.prefilter.description: Bag or panel filters (2-5 micrometre) ahead of the HEPA units, on the make-up air ducts and on the return air. The 1980s standard pre-filter was a 5-ply disposable bag of coarse glass fibre in a steel frame, or a V-bank of 1-inch washable aluminium-header panels. It existed because a HEPA that gets loaded with dust is an expensive mistake.

facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media.name: Coarse glass-fibre filter media
facility.cleanroom.prefilter-media.description: Glass melted and blown into coarse fibres and felted into a mat. The same glassfibre technology as the HEPA medium but 100-1000x coarser and far cheaper. Ends at the glass batch.

facility.cleanroom.cost.name: What the building cost (1983 dollars)
facility.cleanroom.cost.description: For scale: a small 4-inch fab cost about $4 million in 1970 (about $31 million in 2024 money); a full production fab in 1983 ran from roughly $100 million to several hundred million dollars - National Semiconductor announced a $100 million, 290,000 sq ft plant in August 1983, and UMC spent about $200 million on a 1.2 micron fab in the same year. That is why owning a fab was only ever available to very large firms.
facility.cleanroom.cost.note: The $100-300 M figure quoted for a 1980s production fab is right for a 1980s production fab; the $4 M figure is right for an early small 4-inch fab like MOS's, and the two should not be compared without saying which decade and which class of plant is meant.

facts.label: UMC, 1983
facts.value: ~$200 M for a 1.2 micron fab

facility.cleanroom.airlock.name: Gowning and airlock
facility.cleanroom.airlock.description: A two-stage airlock - a 'dirty airlock' for incoming components and personnel in street clothes, and a 'clean airlock' with a cross-over bench for gowning. The costume of the era was a hooded coverall plus boots; in the amber room a yellow-coated garment as well.

facility.cleanroom.hvac.name: Temperature and humidity control
facility.cleanroom.hvac.description: 20-22 C and 40-60% relative humidity, tighter than any other building of the era, and the single most expensive thing in the building to get right. The 1980s control was a system of pneumatic controllers and a mechanical chart recorder; a modern fab uses thousands of sensors and a BMS.

facility.cleanroom.makeup-air.name: Make-up air and air change rate
facility.cleanroom.makeup-air.description: The fab's single largest utility load. Because the Class 100 rooms were almost entirely recirculating, the make-up air was only the leakage plus the exhaust: the acid and solvent fume hoods, the furnace exhaust, the ion-implant exhaust. Even so, a 1980s fab typically ran 100-1000 air changes per hour in the clean bays and 20-60 in the support areas, and the air-handling plant cost tens of millions of dollars and dominated the energy bill.
facility.cleanroom.makeup-air.note: Modern practice is roughly the same air-change figure but with far better heat recovery, a 6-second air exchange in Class 1 areas, and much higher total electrical intensity per square foot because the process tools now dominate.

facts.label: Clean bay ACH
facts.value: 100-1000 per hour (vs 5-10 in an office)

facility.cleanroom.passivation.name: Passivation and packaging areas
facility.cleanroom.passivation.description: Passivation (the final silicon nitride or phosphosilicate glass over the completed aluminium) and then the back-end: wafer probe, dice, die attach, wire bond, and the moulding of the ceramic or plastic package. The back end in 1983 was Class 10000 to Class 1000, not Class 100 - the contaminating work (bonding, moulding compound) happened there.
facility.cleanroom.passivation.note: Not established: that the 1983 back end ran at Class 10000 to Class 1000 rather than Class 100. No standard or manufacturer document was located stating the cleanroom class of a 1980s semiconductor assembly and test area.

facility.cleanroom.litho-area.name: Photolithography area
facility.cleanroom.litho-area.description: Mask aligners, coat/develop tracks, bake ovens and the mask storage cabinets. In a 1980s 1-micron NMOS fab the lithography bay was Class 100 with the amber lighting, the operators wore yellow-room coats and face shields, and the photoresist was spun from a solvent (Shipley AZ1350, based on a novolak resin sensitised with a diazonium salt) with xylene or cellosolve acetate.

facility.cleanroom.amber-room.name: Amber (yellow) room for photolithography
facility.cleanroom.amber-room.description: The lithography bay was lit only through yellow filters - either yellow-lens fluorescent fixtures or, later, a laminated film - so that no light below about 500 nm reached the photoresist. The 1980s specification was that irradiance from 350 to 500 nm should stay below roughly 0.5 W/m2 at the work surface, with the rest of the spectrum unrestricted. Resists of the period were sensitive to the mercury g-line (436 nm), h-line (405 nm) and i-line (365 nm).
facility.cleanroom.amber-room.note: The classic 1980s yellow room was a room with yellow fluorescent tubes. That alone was often not enough - later measurement work has shown legacy 'yellow' tube lighting can still expose resist within an hour - so good fabs added a second, external filter film. Modern practice is to run the room in white light and rely on the area's low-actinic-UV requirement plus dosimetry.

facts.label: Actinic lines
facts.value: g 436 nm, h 405 nm, i 365 nm (mercury lamp)

facility.cleanroom.classes.name: Class 100 and Class 1000 zoning
facility.cleanroom.classes.description: Federal Standard 209E Class 100 in the lithography, etch and metallisation bays; Class 1000 in the diffusion, cleaning and packaging areas; Class 10,000 in the corridors, the airlock and the material store. The class was maintained by air pressure differentials - the Class 100 room slightly positive to the Class 1000 room, which was positive to the corridor - which is why the doors of a 1980s fab always felt like they were being blown open.
facility.cleanroom.classes.note: Modern practice: ISO 14644-1/2, ISO Class 5 (equivalent to the old Class 100) and Class 7 (Class 1000), with ISO Class 8 corridors and much tighter pressure control.

facts.label: Pressure differential
facts.value: 0.01-0.05 in. water (2.5-12 Pa) between classes

facility.cleanroom.ffu.name: Fan filter unit and laminar flow
facility.cleanroom.ffu.description: A 2.4 x 1.2 m fan-filter unit or a fan coil with an integral HEPA, blowing filtered air down through perforated ceiling tiles at 0.3-0.5 m/s to give unidirectional ('laminar') flow. Open cleanroom used ceiling FFUs over the whole floor; the 1980s move was to a 'minienvironment' - a small FFU box over each process tool inside a Class 1000 room - which was the direct ancestor of today's SMIF pods.

facts.label: Face velocity
facts.value: 0.3-0.5 m/s (about 30-90 fpm)

facts.label: Filter bank
facts.value: typically 5-10% of floor area in FFU ceiling

facility.cleanroom.hepa.name: HEPA (absolute) filter
facility.cleanroom.hepa.description: Deep pleated borosilicate glass-fibre media in a galvanised steel casing, rated 99.97% efficient at 0.3 micrometres - the most penetrating particle size, hence 'most penetrating diameter'. A 2.4 m x 1.2 m filter was the ceiling module of every 1980s fab, ceiling and laminar-flow bench alike.
facility.cleanroom.hepa.note: HEPA rated at 0.3 um is the number quoted then; it is a worst-case penetration figure, not the true 0.5 um count the class designation used.

facts.label: Efficiency
facts.value: 99.97% at 0.3 um (HEPA), i.e. 0.03% penetration

facts.label: Media
facts.value: borosilicate glass microfibre on aluminium separator

facility.cleanroom.hepa-glass-fibre.name: Borosilicate glass microfibre
facility.cleanroom.hepa-glass-fibre.description: Glass melted at 1400 C and blown into fibres a few micrometres across, then laid into a paper and fired at 800-900 C to set a bonding agent, and chopped into slivers. Every 1980s fab consumed tens of thousands of these filters a year and changed them on a schedule rather than on condition.

facility.cleanroom.silica.name: High-purity silica
facility.cleanroom.silica.description: The same raw material as the fused-quartz diffusion tube, the photomask substrate and the ceramic package: high-purity SiO2. In 1983 most came from Brazil or from the US inland deposit, and by the mid-80s the industry moved to synthetic vapour-deposited silicon tetrafluoride because natural high-purity quartz was getting scarce.

facility.cleanroom.access-floor.name: Access floor panel
facility.cleanroom.access-floor.description: A 600 mm square steel or aluminium-frame panel with a steel or cast-iron skin, on adjustable pedestals with seismic and electrical bonding. The panel had to be load-rated for a 1000 kg diffusion furnace cart and still be light enough for two people to lift.

facility.cleanroom.raised-floor.name: Raised floor and plenum
facility.cleanroom.raised-floor.description: A 600 mm or 900 mm void under a load-rated pedestal floor, with all the process exhaust, the cold water, the nitrogen, the vacuum and the electrical cabling running underneath. The whole architectural idea of the fab is that the floor is a duct. This is also why the 1980s fabs needed full basements and 4.5-6 m ceilings.

facility.hazardous-waste.name: Hazardous and industrial waste, 1980s practice
facility.hazardous-waste.description: The part of the story usually left out. A 1980s electronics plant generated, per fab, tens of thousands of gallons of spent acid, spent solvent, cyanide-bearing rinse, and metal-bearing sludge a year, plus a smaller amount of contaminated equipment and packaging. What happened to it was loosely governed - in the US by RCRA, which had only been in force for three years in 1983 - and often not well.

facility.hazardous-waste.commodore-site.name: Commodore's own solvent site: the CSG Superfund case
facility.hazardous-waste.commodore-site.description: The clearest documented example in this whole story. A 250-gallon underground concrete tank at the MOS Technology site at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Norristown, Pennsylvania - installed with the building in 1970 - leaked in 1974. It stored the trichloroethene and other solvents used to clean silicon wafers. MOS replaced it with an unlined steel tank, which leaked too. In 1978 the Audubon Water Company, which supplied the public water system, detected trichloroethene in its wells. PADER concluded by 1979 that the contamination could not be excavated. A ground-water recovery well and a spray/treatment system began in November 1981; an air stripper began in February 1984. The site went on the Superfund National Priorities List on 4 October 1989 and the fab was closed in 1992.
facility.hazardous-waste.commodore-site.note: The site history is documented in unusually fine detail because it was litigated for 15 years: the tanks, the replacement, the recovery well VFCC-4, the stripper, and the 1981 practice of spraying pumped groundwater onto surrounding fields to volatilise the VOCs. All of that is in the public record.

facts.label: Tank
facts.value: 250-gallon (946 litre) underground concrete tank

facts.label: Leak
facts.value: 1974; TCE found in public wells in 1978

facts.label: NPL listing
facts.value: 4 October 1989

facility.hazardous-waste.trichloroethene.name: Trichloroethene (TCE)
facility.hazardous-waste.trichloroethene.description: A chlorinated solvent, 1,1,2-trichloroethene, once the standard vapour-degreasing and wafer-cleaning solvent in the semiconductor industry. A suspected carcinogen; a common groundwater contaminant; the specific reason the Norristown site is on the National Priorities List.

facility.hazardous-waste.tce-feedstock.name: Ethylene from the steam cracker
facility.hazardous-waste.tce-feedstock.description: The chlorination of ethylene, or the oxychlorination of 1,2-dichloroethane, which is itself from the chlorination of ethylene. The ethylene came from naphtha steam cracking - the same petrochemical chain as everything else on this tree. Ends at the crude oil still.

facility.hazardous-waste.ocean-outfall.name: Ocean outfall
facility.hazardous-waste.ocean-outfall.description: In the coastal Far East - Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, the Philippines - dilute effluent was and is discharged through a permitted outfall diffuser into the sea, often at a designated ocean disposal zone beyond the territorial limit. The dilution argument is real; so is the fact that the 1980s outfalls had almost no metals monitoring.
facility.hazardous-waste.ocean-outfall.note: The offshore dumping of raw sludge - not diluted effluent - was also common in the Far East until the early 1990s and was progressively banned.

facility.hazardous-waste.manifest.name: The RCRA manifest
facility.hazardous-waste.manifest.description: A multi-part paper form - the shipping paper, the generator certification and the transporter and facility certifications - carried with the load from generator to treatment, storage or disposal facility, with signed copies returned to the generator. This is the paper trail that later made it possible to reconstruct where Commodore's waste went.

facts.label: Copies
facts.value: at least 4 (generator, transporter, TSDF, and the returned copy)

facility.hazardous-waste.incineration.name: Incineration of solvent vapours
facility.hazardous-waste.incineration.description: Vapour incineration (afterburner / thermal oxidiser) for the xylene, toluene and trichloroethane vapour from the resist track and the degreaser, plus a wet scrubber or a carbon absorber on the cool side. By the time the air came out it passed an oxidiser at 800-1000 C with a residence time of about one second. The afterburner burned gas or fuel oil, which is what put a burner on the roof next to the acid scrubber.
facility.hazardous-waste.incineration.note: Solvent recovery by activated-carbon adsorption and distillation was increasingly preferred for cost reasons even in 1983 - recovery plant cost money to buy but paid back in solvent.

facts.label: Residence time
facts.value: ~1 s at temperature

facility.hazardous-waste.neutralisation.name: Acid neutralisation with lime
facility.hazardous-waste.neutralisation.description: The cheapest and by far the most common treatment: slaked lime or limestone slurry is dosed into a reaction tank, the acid is neutralised, the metal hydroxides precipitate out, and the tank is then settled and the supernatant discharged. It converts an acid into a sludge - which is still a hazardous waste, just a solid one.
facility.hazardous-waste.neutralisation.note: No document located that describes lime or limestone neutralisation of semiconductor waste streams as the commonest treatment. The general chemistry is not in question; the claim about frequency of practice in the 1980s electronics industry is unsourced.

facility.hazardous-waste.landfill.name: Hazardous waste landfill
facility.hazardous-waste.landfill.description: In 1983 a hazardous landfill was typically a clay-lined cell with a leachate collection system and groundwater monitoring wells, licensed under RCRA or operating under interim status. Because the Land Disposal Restrictions did not yet exist, most of it received untreated sludge and incinerator ash.

facility.hazardous-waste.settling-pond.name: Settling pond / lagoon
facility.hazardous-waste.settling-pond.description: An unlined or clay-lined earthen basin into which treated effluent was discharged and solids allowed to settle, with the supernatant decanted to a stream or a municipal sewer. Thousands of these existed in 1983; the liner requirements came later. The pond was often the plant's cheapest and worst idea.
facility.hazardous-waste.settling-pond.note: Not established: that thousands of unlined settling ponds existed in 1983, and the claim that liner requirements came later is not tied to a dated regulation here.

facility.hazardous-waste.metal-hydroxide.name: Heavy-metal hydroxide sludge
facility.hazardous-waste.metal-hydroxide.description: A wet, low-solids sludge of iron, aluminium, chromium, copper, nickel, zinc and cadmium hydroxides, filtered on a plate-and-frame or belt press to 15-25% solids and trucked to a hazardous landfill in a lined, covered cell. In 1983 this was the default destination and the reason so many US sites are now Superfund sites.
facility.hazardous-waste.metal-hydroxide.note: Not established: the 15-25% solids figure after plate-and-frame or belt press dewatering, and the characterisation of lined covered cells as the default 1983 destination. The sludge composition claim is not sourced either.

facts.label: Solids
facts.value: 15-25% after dewatering

facility.hazardous-waste.generation.name: Spent acid, solvent and plating waste streams
facility.hazardous-waste.generation.description: The three physical waste streams that carried almost all of a 1980s electronics plant's hazardous load: the spent acids and alkalis from etching and cleaning, the spent organic solvents and resist stripper from photolithography and degreasing, and the cyanide- and metal-bearing rinses from gold and tin plating. Each was a bulk liquid, collected in a tank, and each needed its own treatment route. Small generators - which in 1983 was most of Commodore's Hong Kong subcontractor base - had almost no obligations at all beyond a monthly manifest.
facility.hazardous-waste.generation.note: Not established: that small generators such as Commodore's Hong Kong subcontractor base had almost no obligations beyond a monthly manifest in 1983. RCRA's small-quantity-generator rules are in the Subtitle C regime, and the number of copies on a manifest is set by regulation, not established here.

facility.hazardous-waste.plating-rinse.name: Cyanide- and metal-bearing plating rinse
facility.hazardous-waste.plating-rinse.description: Rinse water carrying gold, tin, copper, nickel and chromium out of the plating line. The cyanide-bearing stream needed alkaline chlorination before discharge; the acid-bearing stream went to the neutralisation tank. Both ended up in the same hydroxide sludge.

facility.hazardous-waste.spent-solvent.name: Spent organic solvent and resist stripper
facility.hazardous-waste.spent-solvent.description: Acetone, xylene, toluene, isopropanol and cellosolve acetate from the degreasers, plus the spent developer (tetramethylammonium hydroxide from positive photoresist) and stripper from the coat-develop track. Recovered by activated-carbon adsorption and distillation where that was economical, and otherwise vapour-incinerated.
facility.hazardous-waste.spent-solvent.note: Not established: that tetramethylammonium hydroxide developer and cellosolve acetate stripper were the specific 1980s resist-track waste streams, and that activated-carbon recovery was preferred for cost reasons even in 1983. No document was located for the photolithography waste chemistry of that decade.

facility.hazardous-waste.spent-acid.name: Spent acid and alkali
facility.hazardous-waste.spent-acid.description: Sulfuric and hydrochloric acid exhausted by the etchers and the wet benches, plus the caustic and the alkaline develop and strip baths. Neutralised with lime into a metal hydroxide sludge; the arsenic-containing liquor from the diffusion furnaces went the same way.
facility.hazardous-waste.spent-acid.note: Not established: that the diffusion furnaces' arsenic-containing liquor was neutralised into the same hydroxide sludge stream. No document was located on 1980s semiconductor arsenic waste handling.

facility.hazardous-waste.rcra.name: RCRA: the cradle-to-grave regime
facility.hazardous-waste.rcra.description: The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act became law on 21 October 1976. Its Subtitle C hazardous waste regulations were promulgated 26 February and 19 May 1980 and took effect 19 November 1980 - so in 1983 the whole American electronics industry was three years into the most consequential change in waste handling since the Clean Air Act. Generators must determine whether a waste is hazardous, accumulate it in a closed, labelled, inspected area for no more than 90 days, describe it on a manifest, and ship it only to a permitted treatment, storage or disposal facility.
facility.hazardous-waste.rcra.note: A regulatory regime, not a thing in the supply chain, hence a note. The 1984 Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments tightened this substantially, including the ban on land disposal of untreated hazardous waste; in 1983 that ban did not yet exist and land disposal of untreated sludge was routine and lawful.

facts.label: Law
facts.value: RCRA, enacted 21 October 1976

facts.label: Regulations effective
facts.value: 19 November 1980

facts.label: Accumulation limit
facts.value: 90 days (later tightened)

facility.compressed-air.name: Instrument air and plant air
facility.compressed-air.description: Every factory ran on compressed air. Instrument air was dried, oil-free air fed to the air-line and to the logic valves; plant air was for the pneumatic tools, the automated insertion machines and the ejectors. The classic 1980s split was a dedicated compressor for instrument air and one or more dirty machines for everything else.

facts.label: Header pressure
facts.value: 6-7 bar at the ring main

facility.compressed-air.fab-exhaust.name: Process exhaust (fab wet-bench and furnace)
facility.compressed-air.fab-exhaust.description: A separate, larger system from the instrument air: a scrubbed chemical exhaust ducting the acid, base, solvent and furnace exhaust out of the building, usually to an alkaline scrubber on the roof. The neutral brine it discharges and the metal-bearing sludge it produces are the liquid and solid waste streams of the plant.

facility.compressed-air.scrubber-packing.name: Alkaline scrubber packing
facility.compressed-air.scrubber-packing.description: A packed column of plastic Raschig or saddle rings on a support grid, fed with caustic soda or sodium carbonate, stripping acid mist and the base-mist equivalent out of the exhaust. Discharge is a neutral brine sent to the effluent system.

facility.compressed-air.pvc-packing.name: PVC / PP packing media
facility.compressed-air.pvc-packing.description: Moulded plastic ring or saddle packing, chemically inert to acid and alkali where ceramic or metal would be attacked. The same vinyl chloride monomer chain that makes the conduit and the cable in the plant.

facility.compressed-air.nitrogen-purge.name: Nitrogen purge of the air system
facility.compressed-air.nitrogen-purge.description: Before opening a vessel, a line, or a tank that had held flammable or reactive material, it was purged with nitrogen and tested with an oxygen analyser. The purge itself was fed from the nitrogen header or, in a small plant, from a bottled cylinder.
facility.compressed-air.nitrogen-purge.note: Not established: that purging with nitrogen and testing with an oxygen analyser was the 1983 practice before opening a vessel, and that small plants purged from a bottled cylinder. No standard or process-engineering source was located for purge practice of that decade.

facility.compressed-air.ring-main.name: Ring main and distribution
facility.compressed-air.ring-main.description: Black steel pipe - galvanised or, better, painted steel - in a ring around the plant with drop-legs to each machine. A ring rather than a spine so that a single closed valve could isolate a section for maintenance. Drops went through a service unit with a tap, a pressure regulator, a filter and a flowmeter at each bench.
facility.compressed-air.ring-main.note: Not established: the 6-7 bar working pressure, the choice of black steel pipe, the ring-versus-spine layout and the service unit (tap, regulator, filter, flowmeter) at each bench. The compressed air article covers moisture in the distribution system, not the piping design.

facts.label: Working pressure
facts.value: 6-7 bar

facility.compressed-air.receiver.name: Air receiver (accumulator)
facility.compressed-air.receiver.description: A vertical ASME code air vessel, 1-10 m3, acting as a buffer so the compressor could unload on a pressure switch. It also stored enough air to ride through a power cut for a few minutes - which in a fab meant keeping the wet-bench exhaust and the compressors together.
facility.compressed-air.receiver.note: Not established: the 2-10 m3 capacity at 8 bar and the claim that the receiver rode through a power cut for a few minutes. The ASME code vessel is sourced; the sizing is not.

facts.label: Typical
facts.value: 2-10 m3 at 8 bar

facility.compressed-air.dryer.name: Air dryer
facility.compressed-air.dryer.description: Two chemistries in 1983. Refrigerant (absorption or adsorption, e.g. a zeolite unit chilled to 1-3 C) gave a pressure dew point of about 2-10 C, good enough for most pneumatic machinery and marginal for instrument air. Desiccant (two alternating towers of silica gel or molecular sieve with a heatless regeneration on the off-line tower) got the dew point down to -40 to -70 C, which was what a pneumatic logic valve or a moisture-sensitive process needed.
facility.compressed-air.dryer.note: Modern practice is a zero-pressure-change desiccant dryer with a heated purge and dew-point controlled switching; in 1983 the purge air was thrown away, which is why instrument-air plants were noisy and hot. Not established: the 2-10 C refrigerant and -40 to -70 C desiccant dew points, and the claim that the purge air was thrown away in 1983. The compressed air article shows a Joule-Thomson refrigerated dryer on a compressor set; it gives no dew points and says nothing about desiccant units of that period.

facility.compressed-air.separator.name: Water (and oil) separator
facility.compressed-air.separator.description: An automatic drain pot or cyclone knock-out that removes the condensed water and, in an oil-injected screw machine, the injected oil. This vessel was the source of most of the 'the air is wet' complaints in the shop.

facility.compressed-air.aftercooler.name: Aftercooler
facility.compressed-air.aftercooler.description: A water-cooled or finned-air heat exchanger that takes the discharge air from ~100 C down to ~40 C. Without it the machine would not hold pressure in a hot climate and the separator would not work.

facility.compressed-air.compressor.name: Air compressor
facility.compressed-air.compressor.description: Reciprocating or, from the 1960s onward, oil-injected rotary screw machines. A large electronics plant ran several 100-300 kW screw units; a small sub-contractor ran one 30 kW reciprocating machine under a concrete acoustic enclosure.
facility.compressed-air.compressor.note: Not established: the 150-400 kW per machine and 7-8 bar discharge figures, and the claim that oil-injected screw machines were standard from the 1960s onward. The air compressor article documents the reciprocating, vane and screw types only.

facts.label: Plant machines
facts.value: 150-400 kW free air delivery each

facts.label: Discharge
facts.value: 7-8 bar

facility.compressed-air.motor.name: Drive motor
facility.compressed-air.motor.description: A TEFC or, in a corrosive coastal plant, an explosion-proof motor. 400 V three-phase induction motor with a direct-on-line or star-delta starter; speed control only by pole changing.
facility.compressed-air.motor.note: Not established: that speed control on a 1983 compressor was by pole changing only, and that explosion-proof motors were used in coastal plants. The induction motor article documents three-phase squirrel-cage drives and TEFC enclosure cooling only.

facility.compressed-air.intake-silencer.name: Intake silencer and inlet filter
facility.compressed-air.intake-silencer.description: An intake filter-silencer combination that kept the machine from eating the dust and the unfiltered outside air. In a coastal site (Kaohsiung, Hong Kong, Long Beach) the sea salt went straight onto the rotors if this was neglected.
facility.compressed-air.intake-silencer.note: Not established: the sea-salt corrosion mechanism at coastal sites and the intake filter-silencer combination as a distinct item. No document located.

facility.gases.name: Industrial gas supply
facility.gases.description: The bulk gases a 1980s electronics plant bought by the tanker load: nitrogen, oxygen, argon and hydrogen, plus helium and carbon dioxide. Supplied either by an on-site air separation unit, an on-site PSA/membrane/electrolyser, or delivered as liquid from a merchant producer in a road tanker. Everything in this branch except helium and CO2 starts from the same place: atmospheric air.
facility.gases.note: Attach these gases with  rom, never children: a nitrogen generator or a tube trailer is an ingredient of a process step, not a component of it. Nitrogen, argon and oxygen are also published as ids other fragments reference directly, so they must keep their names and ids stable. Not established: the 1980s merchant purity specification quoted in the facts (N2 99.99%+, O2 99.5%, Ar 99.99%, H2 99.99%). The air separation article supports ASU output purities of 97.5-99.5% oxygen and co-production of argon, not a merchant-grade table.

facility.helium.supply-constraint.name: The 1980s helium shortage
facility.helium.supply-constraint.description: US Bureau of Mines and then BLM administered the supply; the Cliffside field ran out in the mid-1970s and production was rationed, so helium became genuinely rationed and expensive for laboratories and for leak testing. This is a real constraint on the 1980s helium supply chain, not a later phenomenon.

facility.argon.uses.name: Where argon went in a 1980s plant
facility.argon.uses.description: TIG welding of the sheet metal and the transformer laminations, the inert blanket over the 1800 C silicon melt in the crystal puller, and - increasingly - argon sputter deposition of the aluminium interconnect in a fab. Almost all of it went into joining metal, not into making silicon.
facility.argon.uses.note: Not established: the claim that argon sputter deposition of aluminium interconnect was growing in fabs by 1983, and that almost all argon went into joining metal. Argon is documented as a by-product of air separation; its 1983 distribution of uses is not.

facility.gases.hydrogen.uses.name: Where hydrogen went in a 1980s electronics plant
facility.gases.hydrogen.uses.description: Hydrocarbon and silicone greasing, hydrogen annealing of the copper and the metallisation, the reducing atmosphere in the diffusion furnace and the epitaxial reactor, and - for the tie-in with this story - the hydrogen atmosphere in the case of a lamp or a nickel/plated through-hole fill was not yet standard practice.

facility.gases.carbon-dioxide.name: Carbon dioxide (dry ice)
facility.gases.carbon-dioxide.description: Used in the plant for refrigerant cargo, for the dry-ice shipping of perishables, and - in the electronics plant - for nothing much; the two dry-ice applications in a 1980s C64 supply chain were chilling the shipped goods and cleaning moulds of frost. A large part of the 1980s merchant supply came not from an oil refinery but from hydrogen- and ammonia-based fertiliser plants, where the shift-reactor CO2 was captured and dried; it ends at natural gas and air.

facility.gases.hydrogen.name: Hydrogen
facility.gases.hydrogen.description: Three routes in 1983: (a) bulk hydrogen from a merchant plant by tube trailer or by liquefaction; (b) on-site steam methane reforming of natural gas, the standard for anything above about 100 Nm3/h; and (c) electrolysis of demineralised water for the last, and highest, purity.
facility.gases.hydrogen.note: Not established: the 100 Nm3/h threshold above which steam methane reforming was the standard, and the 95% reformer / 99.99% electrolytic purity pair. Steam methane reforming as the cheapest source of industrial hydrogen is documented; the sizes and purities are not.

facts.label: Purities
facts.value: 95% (reformer), 99.99% (electrolytic, with deoxo polish)

facility.gases.hydrogen.electrolysis.name: Electrolysis of demineralised water
facility.gases.hydrogen.electrolysis.description: In a diaphragm or, from the 1970s, an alkaline cell, a nickel-plated or activated-titanium cathode makes hydrogen while a nickel anode makes oxygen. Fed with conductivity-grade water at 20-25 C. Output purity is 99.99% once the cell gas is passed over a palladium diffuser or an oxygen getter - the 'deoxo' step that killed the last 0.1% of oxygen.
facility.gases.hydrogen.electrolysis.note: Not established: the 50-55 kWh per kg energy figure, the nickel anode and activated-titanium cathode construction, the palladium diffuser deoxo step, and the 99.99% output purity. The electrolysis article confirms water electrolysis gives hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode and describes the palladium-diffusion problem; it does not state the specific cell chemistry or energy figure of that era.

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: about 50-55 kWh per kg of hydrogen

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99% after deoxo

facility.gases.hydrogen.reforming.name: Steam methane reforming
facility.gases.hydrogen.reforming.description: Natural gas is desulphurised to under 0.5 ppm sulphur, mixed with steam at 3:1 and passed over a nickel-molybdenum or chromite catalyst at 800-850 C and 15-25 bar. This gives hydrogen plus CO, and the CO is shifted over an iron-chrome catalyst to CO2 and more hydrogen. Then CO2 is removed by amine scrubbing or molecular sieve.

facility.helium.name: Helium
facility.helium.description: In 1983 helium was a genuinely scarce, genuinely odd commodity. Most of the world's supply came from a handful of natural-gas fractionation plants in Texas, Wyoming, Kansas and New Mexico, which extracted the 0.0005-0.005% helium in the gas as a crude 50-75% mixture. The rest came from four dedicated underground helium fields - the hug gas of Amarillo, Texas, and the Dixon and Harley fields in Kansas. Cryogenic separation of helium from LNG did not become industrial until the late 1990s.
facility.helium.note: Helium was rationed and price-controlled in the US until the 1996 helium policy change; a factory that needed it in 1983 wrote to a supplier, waited, and paid whatever was quoted. Not established: the helium content of natural gas quoted here (0.05-0.5 vol%, and 0.0005-0.005% in the description) and the 50-75% crude purity. Reference sources give helium in natural gas as up to several per cent by volume in the richest fields, which does not support these figures either way. Also not established: that cryogenic separation of helium from LNG did not become industrial until the late 1990s. Cryogenic separation from natural gas was in commercial use from the 1920s, and no source was located that dates LNG-based recovery as claimed.

facts.label: Content in natural gas
facts.value: 0.05-0.5 vol% typically

facts.label: Crude purity
facts.value: 50-75% He before purification

facility.helium.hug-gas.name: Hug gas from an underground helium reservoir
facility.helium.hug-gas.description: The Permian Basin of west Texas and the southwest Kansas gas fields hold helium that never migrated out of the crust, trapped under impermeable salt and anhydrite since geological time. These are drilled specifically for helium, at tiny volumes - Amarillo field production was only tens of millions of cubic feet a year even in its peak.
facility.helium.hug-gas.note: Partly established: the Cliffside field near Amarillo, Texas and the Bushton, Kansas connection are documented. Not established: the field list (Cliffside, Amarillo and Bush in Texas; Hugoton in Kansas), the Dixon, Kansas place entry, the Precambrian radiogenic accumulation as the age of the specific source, and the claim that Amarillo production was only tens of millions of cubic feet a year at peak.

facts.label: Fields
facts.value: Cliffside, Amarillo and Bush, Texas; Hugoton, Kansas

facts.label: Age of the source
facts.value: helium accumulated since Precambrian radiogenic decay

facility.helium.cryo-separation.name: Cryogenic helium separation from natural gas
facility.helium.cryo-separation.description: The gas is chilled to -190 C through a train of plate-fin heat exchangers; helium, having the second-lowest boiling point, stays in the vapour phase and is drawn off from the top of the cold box as a crude 50-75% helium stream. Then purified by cryogenic adsorption, catalytic dehydrogenation of the residual hydrogen and activated-carbon adsorption of the nitrogen - the last step adsorbs the nitrogen on a char bed at 77 K to give 99.995% (5N) or 99.9999% (6N) helium. The same activated-carbon adsorption principle as the water-treatment carbon, run at liquid-nitrogen temperature.
facility.helium.cryo-separation.note: Not established: the -190 C cold box temperature, the 77 K char-bed temperature, the catalytic dehydrogenation and cryogenic adsorption steps, and the 6N (99.9999%) grade. The helium article confirms that the crude gas is purified by successive cooling and that activated charcoal is the final step giving 99.995% Grade-A helium.

facts.label: Purified purity
facts.value: 99.995% (5N) to 99.9999% (6N) after the char bed

facility.helium.liquid-helium.name: Liquid helium dewar (4.2 K)
facility.helium.liquid-helium.description: A double-walled stainless vessel with a superinsulating vacuum jacket, holding 4.2 K liquid helium for a cryostat or a superconducting magnet. Expensive, evaporating at about 0.5-1% a day, and topped up by truck in a dewar that looked like a scaled-down rocket stage.
facility.helium.liquid-helium.note: Not established: the 4.2 K figure, the 0.5-1% per day evaporation rate and the truck top-up practice. The helium article confirms that most helium is liquefied by a cryogenic process and that the safety issues resemble liquid nitrogen; the numbers are not in it.

facility.argon.name: Argon
facility.argon.description: Argon is not made; it is separated out. It is the third component of air and comes off the top of the ASU's nitrogen column, either as an argon-nitrogen mixture from a simple unit or as 99.99% pure from a dedicated argon column. Most 1980s plants bought it by the tanker as a by-product of someone else's oxygen plant.
facility.argon.note: Not established: that most 1980s plants bought argon by the tanker as a by-product of someone else's oxygen plant, and the 99.99% typical purity. The 0.93% abundance in air is the standard figure.

facts.label: In air
facts.value: 0.93% by volume

facility.argon.argon-column.name: Argon recovery column
facility.argon.argon-column.description: A second, smaller column that separates the nitrogen-argon mixture from the top of the nitrogen column into pure argon bottoms and nitrogen tops. Installed when the oxygen plant needed the argon value or the customer paid for it - usually in a semiconductor or welding-wire plant, not in a steelworks.
facility.argon.argon-column.note: Partly established: a separate argon column downstream of the nitrogen column, and the high reflux ratio it needs, are documented. Not established: the description of pure argon bottoms and nitrogen tops, and the claim that it was installed in semiconductor or welding-wire plants rather than steelworks.

facility.gases.oxygen.name: Oxygen supply
facility.gases.oxygen.description: Supplied as liquid oxygen from a merchant AS U or from the site unit. Used for the oxy-acetylene flame of the mechanical and maintenance shops, the gas-shielded welding of the metal frames, and increasingly for the oxygen plasma strip in a fab.
facility.gases.oxygen.note: Not established: the 99.6% industrial grade figure and the oxygen plasma strip use in fabs. Air separation units producing 97.5-99.5% oxygen are documented; merchant liquid oxygen grades are not.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.5% O2 merchant, 99.6% industrial

facility.gases.acetylene-cylinder.name: Acetylene cylinder
facility.gases.acetylene-cylinder.description: Dissolved acetylene at 15 bar in a porous monolithic mass (calcium carbide + acetone), in a steel shell. Calcium carbide came from the electric arc furnace carbide plant, i.e. ultimately from coal coke and quicklime.
facility.gases.acetylene-cylinder.note: Not established: the 15 bar filling pressure and the porous monolithic calcium-carbide-and-acetone mass. The acetylene article confirms acetylene solubility in acetone and that calcium carbide production needs an electric arc furnace; the cylinder charging pressure is not stated in the text read.

facility.gases.oxygen-acetylene.name: Oxy-acetylene flame for tool and frame welding
facility.gases.oxygen-acetylene.description: Oxygen plus a locally generated acetylene from calcium carbide (in the Far East, imported cylinder acetylene was common). This is the flame that welded every sheet-metal chassis, rack and jig in the factory.
facility.gases.oxygen-acetylene.note: Not established: that locally generated carbide acetylene was the practice in the Far East with imported cylinders common, and that this flame welded every sheet-metal chassis in the factory. Acetylene's use for welding and cutting is documented; the site practice is not.

facility.nitrogen.name: Nitrogen supply
facility.nitrogen.description: The single largest bulk gas. Used for inerting storage tanks and vessels, blanketing, purging, and as the carrier gas in diffusion furnaces and plasma etchers. Small plants bought a few tonnes a month of liquid N2; a furnace-loaded fab wanted tens of tonnes a day and built its own ASU.
facility.nitrogen.note: Not established: the three purity grades quoted (99.9% roughing, 99.99% blanketing, 99.999% furnace) and the tonnage split between small plants and a furnace-loaded fab.

facts.label: Purity grades
facts.value: 99.9% (roughing/purging), 99.99% (blanketing), 99.999% (5N, furnace and process)

facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer.name: Tube trailer (bulk gas road delivery)
facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer.description: A tractor-trailer carrying 30-40 high-pressure cylinders or a single multi-compartment tube bundle of 6,000-15,000 litres, delivering liquid nitrogen, oxygen or argon from a merchant plant. In 1983 this was how a factory without an on-site ASU got its gases; the driver's unload was a vent line that fogged the yard and alarmed the neighbours.
facility.nitrogen.tube-trailer.note: Oxygen road tankers in that era were often marked with a diamond placard and were the single most dangerous vehicle in the industrial park. Not established: the 30-40 cylinder or 6,000-15,000 litre capacity, the 2,000-9,000 m3 gaseous equivalent figure, and that this was the 1983 delivery method for a factory without an on-site ASU. No document located on bulk cryogenic road delivery of that decade.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: roughly 2,000-9,000 m3 of gaseous equivalent

facility.nitrogen.liquid-storage.name: Bulk cryogenic liquid storage
facility.nitrogen.liquid-storage.description: A double-walled vacuum-insulated stainless tank on a skirt, with a vacuum-insulated transfer line (a double pipe with perlite or multilayer reflective insulation between) from the ASU or the delivery tanker. The tank is a pressure vessel rated to about 700-1000 kPa on the inner shell.
facility.nitrogen.liquid-storage.note: Not established: the 700-1000 kPa inner-shell rating, the perlite or multilayer insulation detail, and the 5-60 m3 tanker and 50-500 m3 on-site tank sizes. No cryogenic tank standard was located.

facts.label: Tank sizes
facts.value: 5-60 m3 merchant tankers; 50-500 m3 on-site bulk tanks

facility.nitrogen.membrane.name: Membrane nitrogen generator
facility.nitrogen.membrane.description: Hollow-fibre asymmetric polyimide or cellulose acetate membranes in a pressure vessel, 20-40 bar feed, with N2 diffusing through the wall faster than O2. Cheap, silent, no regeneration heat, and limited to about 90-95% nitrogen - which is fine for blanketing and not fine for a furnace. By 1983 membrane units were new and uncommon; they took the small-plant market from PSA in the 1990s.
facility.nitrogen.membrane.note: Not established: the 90-95% purity ceiling, the 20-40 bar feed pressure, and that membrane units were new and uncommon by 1983 and took the small-plant market from PSA only in the 1990s. Membrane separation is documented as an alternative to cryogenic air separation; the numbers and the dated market history are not.

facility.nitrogen.membrane-polyimide.name: Hollow-fibre polyimide membrane
facility.nitrogen.membrane-polyimide.description: A thin-walled asymmetric fibre, about 0.1-0.2 micrometre wall, with a selectively permeable outer skin. Making a defect-free fibre over a 1 m length was, and is, the hard part.

facility.nitrogen.psa.name: PSA / molecular-sieve nitrogen generator
facility.nitrogen.psa.description: Pressure swing adsorption: compressed air is adsorbed on beds of zeolite molecular sieve at 7-10 bar, then dropped to near atmospheric and purged with a slice of product to release the nitrogen. Gave 90-99% nitrogen cheaply at small scale; the 1980s workhorse for factories of under a few hundred kW load.
facility.nitrogen.psa.note: A PSA unit will not deliver oxygen, at any pressure; 4-6 MPa is a liquid-oxygen or high-pressure-pipeline convention and belongs to the cryogenic branch, not to this one. Not established: the 90-99% nitrogen output and the 7-10 bar operating pressure. The pressure swing adsorption article documents the mechanism and the adsorbents (zeolite, activated carbon, silica gel, alumina, synthetic resins) but states no product purity or pressure.

facility.nitrogen.zeolite.name: Zeolite molecular sieve (synthetic)
facility.nitrogen.zeolite.description: Crystalline hydrated aluminosilicate with a uniform 3-5 angstrom pore, made by hydrothermal crystallisation of bentonite, kaolin or synthetic gels. Uniform aperture size is what makes PSA possible - a zeolite with 3A pores excludes N2 and adsorbs only O2 and H2O; the 4A and 5A grades are used elsewhere in gas drying.
facility.nitrogen.zeolite.note: The same chemistry gives the 4A sieve that fills the R-2400 filter's perforated shell in the C64's power supply, if the cartridge was the zeolite type rather than the coil type. Not established: the 3-5 angstrom pore size and the claim that a 3A pore excludes N2 while adsorbing O2 and water. The zeolite article confirms that the major molecular sieves 3A, 4A and 5A are all LTA type and defines molecular sieving by size exclusion; the pore figures and the selective-adsorption detail are not in it.

facility.nitrogen.cryogenic-asu.name: Cryogenic air separation unit (ASU)
facility.nitrogen.cryogenic-asu.description: Air is filtered, compressed in a large multi-stage compressor to about 6-7 bar, cooled against the cold product streams until it liquefies, then fractionally distilled in a low-temperature column to make oxygen and a nitrogen-argon mixture. A unit also making argon has a separate argon column fed from the top of the nitrogen column. Typical small unit: 1,000-5,000 Nm3/h of oxygen.
facility.nitrogen.cryogenic-asu.note: Oxygen delivery pressure is the one number that gets conflated: 4000-6000 kPa is the high-pressure liquid-oxygen case, pumped at 50-100 bar before the warm end of the vaporiser, while a plant that piped oxygen directly would normally run at 400-600 kPa. Not established: the 1,000-5,000 Nm3/h small-unit size and the oxygen delivery pressures as figures. The air separation article describes the cycle and the high- and low-pressure columns; it gives no delivery pressure and no unit size.

facts.label: Oxygen delivery pressure
facts.value: typically 0.5-0.6 MPa at the battery limit, piped up to 3-4 MPa

facility.nitrogen.expander.name: Expansion turbine (expander)
facility.nitrogen.expander.description: A turbine in the cold box that recovers the enthalpy drop of the expanding nitrogen and uses it to generate power, offsetting part of the ASU's compression energy. Standard from the 1960s onward.
facility.nitrogen.expander.note: Not established: that expansion turbines were standard from the 1960s onward and drove the air compressor. The air separation article says modern ASUs use expansion turbines for cooling with the output helping to drive the air compressor; it does not date the practice.

facility.nitrogen.asu-tower.name: Fractionating columns
facility.nitrogen.asu-tower.description: Insulated stainless-steel columns 5-10 m tall with trays or packing, holding the low-temperature distillation that separates oxygen (bottoms, warmer) from nitrogen and argon (top, colder). A common 1980s arrangement was a single low-temperature column producing oxygen plus a nitrogen-argon mixture, with a side argon column.
facility.nitrogen.asu-tower.note: Not established: the 5-10 m insulated stainless column height and the claim about the common 1980s single-column arrangement. The air separation article documents the high-pressure and low-pressure distillation columns and the 1.2-1.3 bar LP column, not column dimensions.

facility.nitrogen.asu-heat-exchanger.name: Cold box (plate-fin heat exchanger)
facility.nitrogen.asu-heat-exchanger.description: A stack of aluminium brazed plate-fin exchangers, some 10-20 m tall, in which the compressed air is progressively cooled to -196 C by the outgoing oxygen and nitrogen. The heart of every ASU.
facility.nitrogen.asu-heat-exchanger.note: Not established: the 10-20 m height of the cold box. The air separation article confirms the plate fin brazed aluminium heat exchangers inside a cold box and the 1-2 K approach between the combined condenser and reboiler; the height is not stated.

facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.name: Atmospheric air
facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.description: 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon, plus water and CO2. The single source of every bulk industrial gas. Delivered to an ASU intake through a windowless, acoustically baffled multi-bay intake so it arrived at a steady temperature, humidity and free of the dust that would plug a cryogenic plant.
facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.note: CO2 figure uncertain: the quoted 0.03% is the pre-1990 concentration. The standard reference composition of dry air gives carbon dioxide as 0.04%. The nitrogen, oxygen and argon figures are the standard 78.08 / 20.95 / 0.93%.

facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.intake.name: Air intake stack
facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air.intake.description: A tall concrete or brick stack with louvres facing away from the prevailing wind, feeding a plenum and the air compressor. Intakes were sited so that no two of them - for air, for cooling water, for the coal yard - were close enough to contaminate each other.

facility.water.name: Water for a factory
facility.water.description: Every 1980s electronics and metals plant drank more water than it realised, and it arrived from one of two places. Two distinct demands sit on top of it: ordinary industrial water for cooling, rinsing, process and human use, and, in the fab, water pure enough to grow an oxide on silicon without introducing a defect. Point consumers at facility.water.industrial or facility.water.ultrapure rather than at this node, and attach them with `from` - a water treatment plant is an ingredient of the process, never a component of the product.
facility.water.note: Not established: the water volumes. Hundreds of m3 per day for cooling and tens of m3 per day of ultrapure water are not tied to any document for a plant of this size in 1983.

facts.label: Industrial process water
facts.value: hundreds of m3 per day for cooling; tens of m3 per day of ultrapure

facility.water.industrial.name: Ordinary industrial water
facility.water.industrial.description: The 99% of the plant's water use: cooling, washing, rinsing, boiler feed, human use. Deliberately not ultrapure, deliberately recycled. This branch is what a factory that needs cooling towers, a degreasing line or boiler make-up should point at; it draws the same raw intake as the ultrapure plant. Everything the plant throws away comes back through two routes: acid, solvent and dump rinses are collected, neutralised, filtered and returned to the pretreatment inlet - water conservation in a 1983 fab was a cost decision, not an environmental one, and a mature plant typically recovered 50-70% of its demand - while the liquid that could not be reclaimed was neutralised, settled and, where the acidity and fluoride demanded it, lime-neutralised with fluoride precipitation, then discharged to a municipal sewer under a permit or to an outfall.
facility.water.industrial.note: Not established: that a mature 1980s plant typically recovered 50-70% of its water demand, and the description of the fluoride-precipitation discharge route. Water reuse of that order is plausible industrial practice but no document states it.

facts.label: Reclaim recovery
facts.value: 50-70% of plant demand in a mature 1980s plant

facility.water.chiller.name: Reciprocating chiller
facility.water.chiller.description: A compressor, condenser and evaporator in a packaged unit, cooling water or air cooled. The alternative to evaporative cooling wherever the wet-bulb was too high. 1980s chillers were almost all ammonia or R-12/CFC-11, and therefore both a refrigerant-ozone problem and a safety problem.
facility.water.chiller.note: Not established: that 1980s chillers were almost all ammonia or R-12/CFC-11. Modern chillers are documented as vapour-compression units on a separate condenser water loop; the refrigerant mix of the 1980s is not sourced here.

facility.water.evaporative-cooling.name: Evaporative (swamp) cooler
facility.water.evaporative-cooling.description: A finned coil with water sprayed over it and an induced-draft fan. Far cheaper than a chiller and it worked well in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore, where the wet-bulb temperature was already low; useless in a humid July in Pennsylvania.

facility.water.cooling-tower.name: Induced-draught cooling tower
facility.water.cooling-tower.description: A 20-60 m concrete or steel shell packed with fill, with fan blades in the base drawing air up through the falling film of circulating water. Water evaporates, concentrates the dissolved solids, and is purged to the drain or the recovery plant.
facility.water.cooling-tower.note: Not established: the evaporation loss of about 1% of circulating flow per 10 C of wet-bulb depression, the 4-8 cycles of concentration figure, and the 20-60 m shell height. The cooling tower cited describes evaporative cooling and drift eliminators but gives none of these figures.

facts.label: Evaporation loss
facts.value: ~1% of circulating flow per 10 C of wet-bulb depression

facts.label: Cycles of concentration
facts.value: 4-8 typical

facility.water.chem-treatment.name: Cooling-water chemical treatment
facility.water.chem-treatment.description: Chromate-based corrosion inhibitors (the dominant, and environmentally toxic, 1980s chemistry), or the newer phosphate/phosphonate/zinc formulations, plus biocide (chlorine or an organomercurial/isothiazolinone blend) and an antiscalant acid. This is where a large share of the plant's chemical consumption went.
facility.water.chem-treatment.note: Chromate inhibitors were being phased out across the industrial West in the 1980s - the same decade Commodore's own site was a Superfund listing because of chlorinated solvent handling.

facility.water.chromate.name: Sodium chromate inhibitor
facility.water.chromate.description: A dichromate/chromate film former that passivates the steel of the cooling system. Enormously effective, and the reason thousands of 1980s cooling towers are a chromate source in the groundwater.
facility.water.chromate.note: Not established: that chromate was a film-forming corrosion inhibitor in cooling systems, and the claim about thousands of chromate-bearing cooling towers in the 1980s. The encyclopaedia article on sodium chromate is a bare formula page and states none of this.

facility.water.chromite.name: Chromite ore (FeCr2O4)
facility.water.chromite.description: The only economic source of chromium. Mined by underground stoping in the Bushveld Complex of South Africa and elsewhere, then smelted to ferrochrome.

facility.water.chromite-mine.name: Chromite mine
facility.water.chromite-mine.description: A stratiform chromite seam (UG2 in the Bushveld) worked by stoping or by open pit. Ends at the chromitite layer in the ground.

facility.water.tower-filling.name: Tower fill and eliminator
facility.water.tower-filling.description: Cellulose (Kraft), PVC or polystyrene film fill media in a lattice or dendritic pack, plus a drift eliminator of PVC chevron sheets at the top. Cellulose fill was being replaced by flame-retardant PVC in the mid-1980s for fire reasons.

facility.water.ultrapure.name: Ultrapure water
facility.water.ultrapure.description: The water that rinses a silicon wafer between every process step, and the water in which the thermal oxide grows. Target in 1983 was 10-15 MOhm-cm (roughly 1 ppb total ionic impurities) held at 20-25 C, distributed in 304 stainless or PVDF-lined piping. The yellow-lit photolithography bay and the wet chemical benches were the biggest consumers; the C64 itself was an assembly operation, not a fab, but every IC on its board came from a plant running exactly this chain. A modern practice note: the same chain now ends with UV and ultrafiltration, not with a mixed bed.

facts.label: 1983 practice
facts.value: 10-18 MOhm-cm; modern fabs specify 18 MOhm-cm at 25 C as a minimum

facts.label: Specification
facts.value: TOC <5 ppb in modern practice; 1980s practice often 50-100 ppb

facility.water.di-loop.name: Ultrapure distribution loop
facility.water.di-loop.description: Slotted 316L stainless or PVDF-lined pipework in a continuous recirculating loop, running hot at 60-80 C to suppress bacteria, with take-off points at each wet bench. A loop that is not constantly moving will grow biofilm within a day - the single hardest problem in 1980s ultrapure water. Modern fabs add a terminal ultrafiltration barrier here (1-100 nm hollow-fibre membranes at 1-4 bar, stripping colloids, bacteria and endotoxin); in the 1980s the state of the art was a 0.2 micrometre-rated PTFE or nylon cartridge on the last loop, or nothing at all, and the loop ran hot instead. The liquid leaving the plant is the 10-15 MOhm-cm water the wet benches are plumbed to.
facility.water.di-loop.note: Modern fabs run the loop cold and sterilise it; running hot was the 1980s answer to bio-growth. Not established: the 60-80 C hot-loop practice, the 10-15 Mohm-cm offtake figure, and the terminal ultrafiltration comparison for 1980s plants. No document was located on 1980s ultrapure water distribution loop temperature.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: electropolished 316L stainless, or PVDF-lined

facts.label: Loop temperature
facts.value: 60-80 C (1980s practice); 20-25 C (modern practice, with UV/UF)

facility.water.pp.name: Polypropylene piping
facility.water.pp.description: Polypropylene was the cheapest acid- and chemical-resistant pipe for wet-bench waste lines and reclaim, and (as spun-bonded fabric) the material of the 1980s 'class 100' air filter pre-filter.
facility.water.pp.note: Not established: that polypropylene was the cheapest acid-resistant pipe for 1980s wet-bench waste lines, or that spun-bonded polypropylene was the standard air-filter pre-filter material of the decade.

facility.water.pvdf.name: PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride)
facility.water.pvdf.description: A fluoropolymer from vinylidene fluoride, chemically inert to ultrapure water and to most process acids, used as a liner or as solid pipe in ultrapure service. Melting point about 170 C, and it will not support microbial growth.
facility.water.pvdf.note: Not established: the 170 C melting point and the claim that PVDF will not support microbial growth. The PVDF article supports its origin by polymerising vinylidene difluoride and its non-reactive character; the numbers are not in it.

facility.water.uv.name: UV sterilisation
facility.water.uv.description: A 254 nm germicidal lamp in a stainless vessel, dosing typically 30-40 mJ/cm2, to kill bacteria and oxidise the last of the organics. Added in the late 1980s onward, mostly for the reclaim loop, because a 1970s fab did not sterilise its ultrapure water at all.
facility.water.uv.note: 1948-1983 practice: no UV, no ultrafiltration in most plants; bacteria were managed by keeping the loop hot (60-80 C for hot DI water) or by chlorination upstream.

facility.water.uv-lamp.name: Low-pressure mercury lamp
facility.water.uv-lamp.description: A quartz envelope with a low-pressure mercury vapour discharge emitting 254 nm, immersed in a quartz sleeve in the water. Same lamp chemistry as the germicidal fittings in hospitals.
facility.water.uv-lamp.note: Not established: the 254 nm emission figure and the low-pressure mercury quartz-envelope construction. The germicidal UV article covers lamp dose and EPA dosage guidance but gives the emission wavelength only in an unsourced table template.

facility.water.ro.name: Reverse osmosis
facility.water.ro.description: Cellulose acetate or thin-film composite spiral-wound elements in 6-inch pressure vessels rejecting 90-99% of dissolved ions, 95-98% of organics and, importantly for the 1980s plant, most of the silica and hardness. The first RO units were installed at plants like this from the mid-1970s; by 1983 they were displacing two beds of ion exchange ahead of the polishers.
facility.water.ro.note: Modern practice is two-pass RO with antiscalant dosing and a final UV and ultrafiltration; the 1980s plant had a single pass and no antiscalant. Not established: the 10-15 bar brackish and 55-70 bar seawater operating pressures and the 95-99.5% salt rejection figures. The reverse osmosis article gives 2-17 bar for fresh and brackish water and 40-82 bar for seawater, and states no rejection percentage.

facts.label: Operating pressure
facts.value: 10-15 bar (brackish) to 55-70 bar (sea water)

facility.water.ro-membrane.name: Cellulose acetate / TFC membrane
facility.water.ro-membrane.description: A 0.2-1.5 micrometre-thick selective layer on a polysulphone support, wound into a spiral and potted with epoxy. This is the same membrane family as the 1541 floppy's read/write head gap in spirit - a nanoscale selective barrier - but the RO element was 1 m long.

facility.water.mixed-bed.name: Mixed-bed deioniser
facility.water.mixed-bed.description: A single resin bed with the cation and anion beads thoroughly mixed, polishing the effluent of the two-bed demineraliser down to a few tens of parts per billion of the sodium-chloride equivalent. It was the top of the 1980s purity curve and was standard offtake to the wet benches; the resin was regenerated with caustic and acid at the same time rather than in sequence, which is what gave the single-pass polish its quality.
facility.water.mixed-bed.note: Not established: the few tens of parts per billion NaCl equivalent outturn and the 10-18 Mohm-cm resistivity figure. The ion-exchange resin article documents resin types and regeneration but not the mixed-bed polish performance of a semiconductor water plant.

facts.label: Resistivity
facts.value: 10-18 MOhm-cm

facility.water.ion-exchange.name: Demineralisation by ion exchange
facility.water.ion-exchange.description: Strong-acid cation then strong-base anion exchange, then a mixed-bed polish. Removed >95% of the ionic load of the filtered water and got to 10-15 MOhm-cm. It could not remove silica, organics or colloids, and the resin was a huge organic load in itself.

facility.water.pretreatment.name: Water pretreatment plant
facility.water.pretreatment.description: Coagulation, clarification, multimedia filtration and activated carbon, all in one reinforced-concrete block that dominated the plant footprint. The purpose is to strip the water of the things that would poison an ion-exchange resin or foul an RO membrane: suspended solids, colour, hardness, chlorine, organics and silica. It feeds both the ultrapure plant and the ordinary industrial side.

facility.water.activated-carbon.name: Activated carbon adsorption
facility.water.activated-carbon.description: A tall bed of coconut-shell, coal or lignite carbon catalytically activated in a furnace, removing humic colour, trihalomethane precursor, pesticide and industrial organics. In the ultrapure plant it was the last chance to remove organics before the ion-exchange resin and the RO membrane.

facility.water.multimedia-filtration.name: Multimedia (sand) filtration
facility.water.multimedia-filtration.description: Pressure filters in lead/catalysed iron tanks, 3.5-4.5 m diameter, containing 600-700 mm of graded media - typically 100 mm anthracite on 50 mm sand on 25 mm garnet. Backwashed with air scour plus water at 20-40 m/h.
facility.water.multimedia-filtration.note: Not established: the 3.5-4.5 m vessel diameter, the 100/50/25 mm anthracite-sand-garnet bed and the 20-40 m/h backwash rate. No standard or waterworks manual was located stating multimedia filter bed specifications.

facts.label: Media
facts.value: anthracite / sand / garnet

facility.water.anthracite.name: Anthracite filter coal
facility.water.anthracite.description: Hard, coarse anthracite crushed to 1-2 mm as the coarse top layer. Same material as the boiler fuel, just graded differently.
facility.water.anthracite.note: Not established: the 1-2 mm grading as a filter medium. Anthracite is documented as a hard, high-carbon coal used for power generation and metallurgy; its use as crushed filter coal is not stated in the cited article.

facility.water.filter-sand.name: Silica filter sand
facility.water.filter-sand.description: Washed, graded, nearly pure SiO2 sand with effective size 0.5-0.7 mm. A large, unglamorous, and genuinely scarce mineral input to any waterworks.
facility.water.filter-sand.note: Not established: that filter sand has an effective size of 0.5-0.7 mm and that it is a scarce mineral input. The encyclopaedia has no article on filter or silica sand for water treatment (the Silica sand article redirects to sand casting), and no waterworks standard was located.

facility.water.sand-quarry.name: Sand and gravel extraction pit
facility.water.sand-quarry.description: A pit worked by river dredging or by bank excavation beside a watercourse, screening the outwash into a concrete-aggregate fraction and a finer silica fraction. Filter sand is scarce: it has to be nearly pure SiO2 with an effective size of 0.5-0.7 mm, and most river gravel is too dirty to wash up to standard. Ends at the sand deposit.
facility.water.sand-quarry.note: Not established: that filter sand is scarce because most river gravel is too dirty to wash up to standard. No document located.

facility.water.coagulation.name: Coagulation and clarification
facility.water.coagulation.description: Alum or ferric chloride plus lime and a coagulant aid is flash-mixed, then the floc is grown in a flocculation bay and settled out over 2-4 hours in a clarifier. Residual turbidity had to be under about 1-2 NTU for the sand filters to be worth having.
facility.water.coagulation.note: Not established: the 20-80 mg/L alum dose, the 2-4 hour settling period and the under-2 NTU target. The coagulation article supports the mechanism and the role of alum but states none of these figures.

facts.label: Dose
facts.value: 20-80 mg/L alum

facts.label: Target
facts.value: <2 NTU after clarification

facility.water.alum.name: Alum (hydrated aluminium sulfate)
facility.water.alum.description: The workhorse coagulant. Made from bauxite (or domestic low-grade bauxite/clay) digested in sulphuric acid and crystallised. Ended at the bauxite mine by way of the same chain that makes the aluminium in the grid conductor.

facility.water.raw-intake.name: Raw water intake
facility.water.raw-intake.description: Either a surface intake from a river or reservoir, or a deep well into a confined aquifer. Surface water for cooling, well water for the ultrapure plant - because groundwater is already filtered by geology and low in organics.

facility.water.surface-intake.name: River / reservoir intake and pump house
facility.water.surface-intake.description: A screened intake structure with travelling-bar screens, coarse screens and a low-lift pump house on the bank. In practice many 1980s plants - including Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors in the export-processing zones - bought municipal or industrial-zone water from the local authority and paid a tariff, rather than taking their own.
facility.water.surface-intake.note: Not established: that Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors in the export-processing zones bought municipal or industrial-zone water rather than taking their own. No waterworks or government document located on Taiwanese industrial water supply in that period.

facility.water.river-intake.name: The river or reservoir
facility.water.river-intake.description: Turbid, hard, seasonally variable. The Schuylkill at Norristown, the Sham Chun at Hong Kong, the Tamsui at Taipei, the Keelung river, and the many dams that supplied Hong Kong from the 1960s (Plover Cove, 1973).
facility.water.river-intake.note: Not established: the named intakes and their characterisations. In particular the Sham Chun, Tamsui and Keelung river claims and Plover Cove's 1973 date are not tied to a water authority document here.

facility.water.well.name: Deep well and well pump
facility.water.well.description: A 150-300 mm steel or PVC casing to 100-300 m with a deep-turbine or submersible pump. In the Lehigh Valley the sand-and-gravel aquifer gave soft, iron-bearing water that had to be degreased; in Taiwan the wells hit 100-300 m of Pleistocene gravel.
facility.water.well.note: Not established: the 150-300 mm casing to 100-300 m depths, and the specific claims about Lehigh Valley iron-bearing water and 100-300 m of Pleistocene gravel under Taiwan. No hydrogeological document located for these places.

facility.water.well-screen.name: Well screen and gravel pack
facility.water.well-screen.description: Wire-wound or slotted screen with a graded silica-sand or garnet gravel pack, wrapped in geotextile. Stops the well pumping sand and the aquifer silting up the pump.

facility.water.aquifer-gravel.name: Aquifer sand and gravel
facility.water.aquifer-gravel.description: Glacial outwash and alluvial gravel forming the confined aquifer; the raw material of the well itself and the source of the hardness and iron.
facility.water.aquifer-gravel.note: Not established: that the Lehigh Valley, Chianan Plain and Hong Kong aquifers are confined sand-and-gravel of Pleistocene age. Aquifers as a concept are sourced; the per-place geology is not.

facility.water.aquifer.name: Confined sand-and-gravel aquifer
facility.water.aquifer.description: The buried glacial outwash and alluvial gravel bed, laid down in the Pleistocene and now saturated under pressure by an impermeable cap. It is the rock the well is drilled into, the source of the hardness and dissolved iron that the treatment plant has to remove, and the reason groundwater was preferred over river water for an ultrapure plant. Ends at the ground.
facility.water.aquifer.note: Not established: the Pleistocene age and glacial origin of the buried outwash the node describes, and the claim that groundwater was preferred over river water for an ultrapure plant. The aquifer article supports the confined-aquifer concept only.

facility.steam.name: Industrial steam plant
facility.steam.description: Process steam for soldering, cleaning, degreasing, autoclaving and heating the building. Most industrial steam plants of 1983 were coal- or oil-fired package/field-assembled water-tube boilers, often with their own turbo-alternator so that the site exported some of its own electricity.
facility.steam.note: Not established: that most industrial steam plants of 1983 were field-assembled water-tube boilers with their own turbo-alternator, and the 6-10 bar process and 25-45 bar turbo-alternator pressure figures.

facts.label: Typical pressures
facts.value: 6-10 bar saturated for process; 25-45 bar / 250-400 C for turbo-alternator schemes

facility.steam.feedwater-treatment.name: Boiler feedwater treatment
facility.steam.feedwater-treatment.description: Two chemistries: lime-soda softening for the low-pressure plant, and ion-exchange demineralisation for anything above about 20 bar. By 1983 the whole industry standard was sodium-cycle cation plus strong-base anion demineralisation with a mixed-bed polish.

facility.steam.demineralisation.name: Ion-exchange demineralisation
facility.steam.demineralisation.description: A cation exchanger in the sodium form swaps Ca/Mg for Na; a strongly basic anion exchanger then swaps the bicarbonate/sulphate/chloride anions for OH; CO2 is degassed between the two beds by a packed or bubble column, because skipping the degasser overloaded the anion resin with carbonic acid and shortened its life; the effluent is then polished in a mixed bed to the sodium-chloride equivalent of a few tens of ppb. Resin is regenerated with 10-20% caustic and 6-12% hydrochloric or sulphuric acid, and each regeneration blew a large slug of acidic or alkaline brine once or twice a day that had to go somewhere - in 1983 usually a lined lagoon, a settling pond and then a discharge permit.
facility.steam.demineralisation.note: Modern practice adds a second pass of RO/mixed bed and typically achieves 18 Mohm-cm; the 1980s benchmark for a good mixed bed was 10-15 Mohm-cm.

facts.label: Demineralised water
facts.value: typically 0.1-1.0 us/cm (10-100 Mohm-cm) after a mixed bed

facts.label: Regeneration frequency
facts.value: once or twice a day per bed

facility.steam.ion-resin.name: Ion-exchange resin (polystyrene-DVB)
facility.steam.ion-resin.description: A gel-type cation resin (sulfonic acid groups) or an anion resin (quaternary ammonium groups) on a cross-linked polystyrene-divinylbenzene bead. Beads of 0.3-1.0 mm, sieved into size fractions so the fine resin could be kept out of the top of the bed.

facility.steam.divinylbenzene.name: Divinylbenzene crosslinker
facility.steam.divinylbenzene.description: A small fraction of a C10H10 comonomer added to the styrene so the bead does not dissolve in the caustic used for regeneration. This crosslinking is what makes the resin insoluble and gives it its capacity.

facility.steam.styrene.name: Styrene monomer
facility.steam.styrene.description: Produced by dehydrogenating ethylbenzene or by cracking benzene, both from the aromatic fraction of an oil refinery. A C8H8 molecule - the same feedstock family as the styrene in the ABS case of the C64.

facility.steam.lime-soda.name: Lime-soda softening
facility.steam.lime-soda.description: Slaked lime Ca(OH)2 and soda ash Na2CO3 are dosed into a hot reaction basin, converting the scale-forming calcium and magnesium hardness into calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide sludge, which settles in a clarifier. This is the classic 1900-1960 process, still running at small industrial plants in 1983. Produces a lot of sludge.

facility.steam.hardness-sludge.name: Calcium carbonate / magnesium hydroxide sludge
facility.steam.hardness-sludge.description: The lumpy waste from lime-soda softening, pumped to a thickener and then to a drying bed or trucked to landfill wet. This is the sludge that fills the lagoons around old steel and chemical works.

facility.steam.lime.name: Burn and hydrate lime
facility.steam.lime.description: Quicklime CaO is burnt from limestone in a vertical or flash calciner at about 1000 C, losing its carbon dioxide as CO2 and leaving a caustic porous solid; it is then hydrated, an exothermic reaction that turns it into slaked lime Ca(OH)2 for the lime-soda process. Ends at the limestone quarry face.

facts.label: Calcination temperature
facts.value: about 1000 C

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: roughly 0.56 t CaO per tonne of pure CaCO3

facility.steam.condensate-return.name: Condensate return
facility.steam.condensate-return.description: Steam traps in every steam-consuming process returned hot condensate to the hotwell. Recovering it saved both fuel and water-treatment chemical, and the copper condensate pipework of a 1980s plant was a continuous, weeping mess of unions and gaskets.

facts.label: Typical recovery
facts.value: 50-70% of steam as condensate

facility.steam.trap.name: Steam trap
facility.steam.trap.description: A thermostatic (bimetallic or liquid-expansion) or mechanical bucket trap with a strainer upstream. Failed-open traps cost fuel; failed-closed traps flooded the plant. Every steam system of the era leaked at a few percent of its steam load, largely from these.

facility.steam.header.name: Steam header and distribution
facility.steam.header.description: A large-diameter steel pipe - 300-800 mm - with flanged or socket-welded branches to each user, insulation lagged in magnesium-block or calcium-silicate, and a trap at every low point. Steam was distributed at constant pressure from a header rather than generated at each machine.
