facility.steam.header.note: Not established: the 300-800 mm header diameter, the magnesium-block and calcium-silicate lagging practice, and the socket-welded branch detail. No piping or steam-distribution standard was located.

facility.steam.insulation.name: Steam pipe insulation
facility.steam.insulation.description: Moulded magnesium-block sections, calcium silicate or, on hot surfaces, an asbestos-based rope and canvas wrap. Asbestos lagging was utterly routine on a 1980s steam line and is the reason so many power and chemical plants have mesothelioma claims decades later.

facility.steam.asbestos.name: Asbestos (chrysotile) mineral
facility.steam.asbestos.description: Fibrous magnesium silicate mined from open pits and shafts in Quebec, South Africa, Italy and the Soviet Union, and spun, carded and woven into rope, cloth and board. This is the single most under-acknowledged raw material in any 1980s industrial plant.

facility.steam.asbestos-mine.name: Asbestos mine and mill
facility.steam.asbestos-mine.description: A serpentinite or chrysotile orebody worked by open pit or underground, then crushed, graded and carded. Ends at the serpentinite rock in the ground.

facility.steam.turbo-alternator.name: Industrial turbo-alternator
facility.steam.turbo-alternator.description: Where a plant burned coal continuously it made sense to take steam past 300 C and put it through a small turbine to make some of its own electricity. A 2-6 MW pass turbine driving a 480 V alternator, exporting a few hundred kW and buying back the rest at peak rates, was a standard arrangement in Taiwan, Korea and Britain.
facility.steam.turbo-alternator.note: These units were called 'pass turbines' or 'back-pressure turbines' and were the main cogeneration technology before the 1980s gas-engine programme; natural-gas-fired turbine-generator sets took over from about 1980.

facility.steam.turbine-governor.name: Speed governor and overspeed trip
facility.steam.turbine-governor.description: A flyball or hydraulic governor on the turbine shaft plus a mechanical overspeed trip and, in larger sets, a turbine protective device that tripped the generator breaker. The overspeed trip was the last line of defence against a runaway.

facility.steam.boiler.name: Water-tube boiler
facility.steam.boiler.description: Two-drum or three-drum evaporators with a superheater. Industrial boilers of 4-20 t/h fired coal at about 6-9 bar saturated, directly into the plant's heating and process network. Economisers and feedwater heaters recovered heat; a fraction of the boiler water was blown down to keep total dissolved solids and alkalinity inside limits, which is why the make-up had to be soft or demineralised or the cycles of concentration collapsed. That blowdown went to a flash tank for heat recovery and then to the cooling-water basin. Two spring-loaded safety valves per drum, a feedwater level regulator and a refractory-lined sight-glass port were the bits an operator actually watched.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: 2-20 t/h industrial; 50-300 t/h for power-house duty

facts.label: Working pressure
facts.value: 6-9 bar saturated

facility.steam.safety-valves.name: Safety valves and drum level control
facility.steam.safety-valves.description: Two spring-loaded safety valves per drum, a feedwater level regulator on the drum, and the refractory-lined sight-glass port that operators actually looked at. A steam plant is a place where the concrete is usually older than the manager.

facility.steam.fuel.name: Industrial boiler fuel
facility.steam.fuel.description: Anthracite, bituminous coal, fuel oil or - very commonly in Hong Kong, Japan and Taiwan - coal briquettes pressed from imported anthracite fines in a ring-die or pillow press.

facility.steam.briquette.name: Coal briquette (hongsha / pressed coal)
facility.steam.briquette.description: Binderless or starch-bound anthracite fines pressed at 200 bar into egg-shaped briquettes about 100 g each, fired on a grate. Hong Kong's thermal power and much of its industrial boiler load ran on exactly this fuel.
facility.steam.briquette.note: Not established: the 200 bar pressing pressure, the 100 g egg-shaped briquette and the claim that Hong Kong's industrial boiler load ran on this fuel. The encyclopaedia has no article on coal briquettes, and no Hong Kong fuel document was located.

facility.steam.anthracite.name: Anthracite fines
facility.steam.anthracite.description: Hard, high-carbon coal, largely imported to the Far East from South Wales, Vietnam and China. Ends at the anthracite seam.

facility.steam.boiler-house.name: The boiler house
facility.steam.boiler-house.description: A tall, heavily built single-storey steel-framed building with a travelling crane, the boilers in a row, coal bunkers or an oil day tank alongside, and the chimney outside. Even in 1983 it was the tallest building on most industrial sites.
facility.steam.boiler-house.note: Not established: the description of the era's boiler house as a tall single-storey steel-framed building with a travelling crane, and that it was the tallest building on most industrial sites. Architectural description, not a sourced claim.

facility.steam.fuel-handling.name: Fuel handling and bunker
facility.steam.fuel-handling.description: A conveyor, a hopper and a boiler feed screw, or an oil tank and a pump skid. Manual barrow-and-shovel coal handling was still normal at plants below about 10 t/h.

facility.power.name: Industrial electricity supply (1983)
facility.power.description: The electricity that ran every press, oven, wave-solder machine, conveyor and test rig. In 1983 the world's grids were coal, oil, gas and hydro - not the gas-turbine-dominated grids of today - and industrial customers bought it on a two-part tariff with a demand charge. This node is the utility's own end: the generating stations, the transmission network and the price. The customer's end, from the service drop to the machine tool, is the separate node facility.electricity.
facility.power.note: The Taiwan mix figures are the grid that actually powered Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractor base, which is why they are quoted here rather than a world average. Natural gas barely existed as a grid fuel in 1983: the first LNG cargo (Algeria) reached Kaohsiung in 1983 and Hong Kong's town gas came from manufactured coal gas, not natural gas.

facts.label: US industrial price
facts.value: 7.0 US cents/kWh (all sectors 6.4 c/kWh) in 1983

facts.label: Taiwan 1980 supply mix
facts.value: oil 58.8%, coal 17.1%, hydro 13.9%, nuclear 10.2%, gas 1.2%

facts.label: Taiwan 1990 supply mix
facts.value: coal 38.4%, oil 25.6%, hydro 24.5%, nuclear 7.7%

facility.power.tariff.name: The industrial electricity tariff (1983)
facility.power.tariff.description: Industrial customers never paid a simple price per kWh. The tariff was two-part: an energy charge per kWh plus a demand charge per kW of measured maximum demand over a 15 or 30 minute interval. The demand charge rewarded flat load and punished a factory that ran its ovens and its wave-solder line together. Tariff classes ('medium general service', 'large power and light') were negotiated against contract demand and often a five-year commitment.
facility.power.tariff.note: Modern practice is the same two-part structure, but with hourly and time-of-use pricing and, in some markets, deregulated retail suppliers; the 1980s tariff was a regulated cost-of-service tariff set by a public utility commission.

facts.label: US industrial average
facts.value: 7.0 c/kWh in 1983 (total average 6.4 c/kWh)

facts.label: Tariff structure
facts.value: energy charge (c/kWh) + demand charge ($/kW)

facility.electricity.name: Electricity at the factory wall
facility.electricity.description: The chain from the utility's service drop to the machine tool. This is the branch other subsystems should reference whenever they need 'mains power': the substation, the transformer, the low-voltage switchboard, the motor control centre, and finally the cord and plug.
facility.electricity.note: Not established: the factory service voltages quoted in the facts (11-13.8 kV in, 480 V three-phase or 220 V single-phase out in the US, 380-415 V in Hong Kong and Europe). No utility or standards document was located for these values.

facts.label: Factory service voltage
facts.value: 11-13.8 kV into the plant, 480 V three-phase or 220 V single-phase out of the transformer in the US; 380-415 V in HK/Europe

facility.electricity.distribution-busbar.name: Busbar trunking and cable
facility.electricity.distribution-busbar.description: Copper or aluminium busbar in an epoxy-impregnated sandwich ('busway') for high-current runs, and PVC/PVDF-insulated copper or aluminium cable in conduit or tray for the rest. Flexible conduit was still common above machine tools.

facility.electricity.substation.name: Customer substation
facility.electricity.substation.description: Where a large factory bought at transmission or sub-transmission voltage: a fenced yard with the utility's metering, an incoming circuit breaker, a main transformer, a secondary switchgear line-up and the plant's own protection relays.

facility.electricity.switchgear.name: Low-voltage switchboard
facility.electricity.switchgear.description: Air-circuit-breaker switchboards at 480/415 V, with bolted busbar, fuses/MCCBs per outgoing way and a transformer tap-selector. Most factory power for small machines was tapped off the board at 120/230 V through a plug.
facility.electricity.switchgear.note: Not established: that factory switchboards were air-circuit-breaker type at 480/415 V with a transformer tap selector, and that small machine power was tapped at 120/230 V through a plug. The switchgear article read does not state board construction or factory voltage practice.

facility.electricity.earthing.name: Earthing grid and lightning protection
facility.electricity.earthing.description: Copper rod or bare conductor bonded under the floor and up the steelwork, plus air terminals and down conductors to earth rods. The grid is not decoration: it is the reference for every protective device on the switchboard, and in a fab with a raised floor the earth grid and the electrostatic-dissipative floor were often the same conductor, bonded to the pedestals.

facility.electricity.power-factor.name: Power factor correction capacitors
facility.electricity.power-factor.description: Motor loads are inductive, so a big factory runs at 0.7-0.85 power factor and gets penalised by the utility. Banks of switched capacitor kVAr corrected it. A capacitor is the cheapest industrial electronics ever made - a polypropylene film between two aluminium foils.

facility.electricity.mcc.name: Motor control centre
facility.electricity.mcc.description: A vertical lineup of combination starters and contactors with a fused disconnect per motor, feeding the compressors, injection-moulding presses, conveyors and extract fans. The 1980s unit had no variable-frequency drives at all - speed control was a pole-changing or slip-ring motor.
facility.electricity.mcc.note: Adjustable-frequency drives only became normal in the late 1980s-90s, and the first-generation IGBT VFDs cost more than the motor.

facts.label: Typical
facts.value: 415 V, 30-250 A per cubicle

facility.electricity.contactors.name: AC contactors and overload relays
facility.electricity.contactors.description: Silver-alloy contacts on a moulded phenolic base with a shading ring to stop contact chatter, plus a bimetal or electronic overload. The bimetal overload relay, unchanged since the 1920s, was the industrial motor's main protection.

facility.electricity.transformer.name: Distribution transformer
facility.electricity.transformer.description: A laminated silicon-steel core with copper or aluminium windings on pressboard and paper insulation, immersed in mineral oil or Askarel. Oil-immersed units dominated until the 1980s-90s fire codes and the economics of dry-type began to change the picture in Europe and Japan.

facts.label: Typical rating
facts.value: 500-2500 kVA, 480/277 V or 400/230 V secondary

facility.electricity.porcelain-bushing.name: Porcelain bushings and standoff insulators
facility.electricity.porcelain-bushing.description: Glazed porcelain sheds, cemented with epoxy onto the winding ends, to bring the winding out to a terminal. These are the tall ribbed 'sheds' you see on any pole-top transformer.
facility.electricity.porcelain-bushing.note: Not established: the epoxy cementing of porcelain bushings onto transformer winding ends. Porcelain and glass insulators are documented for overhead lines; transformer bushing construction is not covered by the sources read.

facility.electricity.feldspar.name: Feldspar
facility.electricity.feldspar.description: A potassium-sodium aluminosilicate used as a flux in porcelain and in the electrolytic alumina bath. Ends at the pegmatite quarry.

facility.electricity.insulating-oil.name: Transformer insulating oil
facility.electricity.insulating-oil.description: Mineral oil (naphthenic or paraffinic), a by-product of vacuum distillation of crude. Also Askarel (PCB-filled chlorinated dielectric) in older units - a PCB source that explains part of the PCB contamination of the Hudson/Superfund sites.
facility.electricity.insulating-oil.note: Askarel transformers were phased out in the US after the EPA began classifying PCBs as hazardous in 1979; by 1983 new units were mineral-oil or dry-type.

facility.electricity.askarel.name: Askarel (PCB-filled transformer dielectric)
facility.electricity.askarel.description: A chlorinated biphenyl dielectric used from the 1930s until the 1980s ban. Ends at the chlorinated benzene/aromatics stream.

facility.electricity.chlorobenzene.name: Chlorinated aromatic feedstock
facility.electricity.chlorobenzene.description: Chlorobenzene and biphenyl feedstock for the askarel blend, itself from the chlorination of benzene over a chloride catalyst. Ends at the aromatic hydrocarbon still.
facility.electricity.chlorobenzene.note: Not verified for a specific 1980s askarel producer.

facility.electricity.electrical-steel.name: Grain-oriented silicon steel (GOES)
facility.electricity.electrical-steel.description: 3.2% silicon steel rolled so its crystallographic grain lies parallel to the flux direction, giving a core loss an order of magnitude lower than hot-rolled steel. Made in a special continuous-annealing line. This is the same material used in the C64's switch-mode transformer and in every mains transformer in the world.
facility.electricity.electrical-steel.note: Deliberately stiff magnetically so it laminates easily and does not ring when punched - 'GOES' is stamped on the laminations.

facility.electricity.grain-oriented-mill.name: Grain-oriented steel rolling mill
facility.electricity.grain-oriented-mill.description: Hot band rolled to 2 mm, cold rolled to 0.3 mm, decarburised in a hydrogen atmosphere and given a final magnetic anneal. Ends at the ore and the coke oven.

facility.electricity.service.name: Utility service and metering
facility.electricity.service.description: A pad-mount or pole-mounted transformer on the utility side of the fence, with revenue metering and a fused cut-out. The customer owned everything downstream of the meter.

facility.power.coal-plant.name: Coal-fired steam power plant
facility.power.coal-plant.description: The workhorse baseload of the 1980s. Coal from a mine or a rail/barge unloading dock is crushed, pulverised to talcum fineness, blown into a furnace with preheated air, burned under a boiler, and the resulting steam drives a turbine-generator. Net efficiency typically 33-38% thermal to electricity on a unit built in the 1960s-70s.

facility.power.grid.name: Transmission and distribution network
facility.power.grid.description: High-voltage transmission from the plant's switchyard to the city, then medium-voltage distribution to the industrial park, then the service drop to the customer. This is the piece almost nobody thinks about: roughly 8% of generated electricity is lost in transmission and distribution before it reaches the meter.
facility.power.grid.note: Losses have fallen by only a few percentage points since 1983 because the physics of I2R dominates; a modern grid still loses 5-8%.

facts.label: T&D losses
facts.value: ~8% of generation (1970s-80s developed grids)

facts.label: Transmission voltage
facts.value: 230-765 kV AC, some 500 kV DC by 1983

facility.power.grid.distribution.name: Medium-voltage distribution feeder
facility.power.grid.distribution.description: Overhead or underground 11-13.8 kV feeders with reclosers, sectionalisers and fuses. Underground feeders were standard in the new Hong Kong industrial estates and in Japanese and Korean industrial parks; overhead was normal in the US outside cities.

facts.label: Typical voltage
facts.value: 11 kV (Hong Kong), 20-22 kV (Taiwan), 13.8 kV (US)

facility.power.grid.substation.name: Utility substation
facility.power.grid.substation.description: Transformer bays, circuit breakers, buswork and the control house that steps transmission voltage down to the 11-34.5 kV distribution level. Utility substations outnumbered the plants; a 1980s industrial park typically had one primary substation feeding a ring of unit substation transformers.

facility.power.grid.line.name: Overhead transmission line
facility.power.grid.line.description: Steel lattice towers or wooden H-poles carrying three phases on aluminium conductor, with shield wires and porcelain or glass suspension insulators. The thermal rating of the conductor, not the voltage, is the limit.

facility.power.insulator-porcelain.name: Porcelain suspension insulator
facility.power.insulator-porcelain.description: Glazed (glassy) or unglazed (ceramic) insulator strings, 10-20 discs to hold a 230-500 kV line up in the air. Replaced later by composite polymer strings, which is why the classic transmission silhouette disappeared after 1990.

facility.power.acsr-conductor.name: Aluminium conductor steel-reinforced (ACSR)
facility.power.acsr-conductor.description: Aluminium strands around a steel core for tensile strength, twisted and stranded on the line. Ends at an aluminium smelter fed by alumina.

facility.power.nuclear-plant.name: Nuclear power plant
facility.power.nuclear-plant.description: Not a 'coal/oil/gas/hydro' machine, but it was 10.2% of Taiwan's electricity in 1980 - the first reactor at Chinshan came on line in 1978, followed by Chinshan 2 (1979), Chinshan 3, Feitsui and Lungmen. Any 1983 power bill in northern Taiwan could legitimately be traced to a uranium fuel rod.

facts.label: Taiwan nuclear share 1980
facts.value: 10.2% of grid supply

facility.power.uranium.name: Uranium fuel
facility.power.uranium.description: Uranium concentrate converted to UF6 and enriched from natural 0.71% U-235 to 2.5-3.5%, then fabricated into ceramic UO2 pellets 8 mm across, sintered, ground to length, clad in zircaloy and made into a fuel assembly. In 1983 the US HEU was being phased down and the world's enrichment market was switching to centrifuge cascades.

facility.power.uranium-ore.name: Uranium ore (U3O8)
facility.power.uranium-ore.description: Graded and leached in the 1970s-80s, largely from the Colorado Plateau (Uravan) and New Mexico, plus Namibia and Canada. Ends at the orebody.

facility.power.uranium-vanadium-ore.name: Vanadiferous uraninite ore
facility.power.uranium-vanadium-ore.description: The US Colorado Plateau ore was processed mainly for vanadium with uranium as a by-product, in mills that roasted the ore with salt and soda ash and leached it with chlorine.

facility.power.gas-plant.name: Gas-fired power plant
facility.power.gas-plant.description: Two different things share this name. For the 1983 industrial economy the honest answer is that almost none of the grid came from natural gas - gas turbines ran mainly for peak load, standby and cogeneration. Taiwan's first LNG cargo arrived in 1983 and natural gas did not become a grid fuel until the 1990s.
facility.power.gas-plant.note: In the US the big gas-fired build-out came after 1990, with the EPA NOx rules; in 1983 a gas turbine plant was an unusual and expensive thing to run on a peak-load schedule.

facts.label: Taiwan gas share 1980
facts.value: 1.2% rising from ~0

facility.power.gas-plant.turbine.name: Gas turbine
facility.power.gas-plant.turbine.description: A compressor, a combustor at 1400-1600 C and a turbine in a single shaft or two. Open-cycle efficiency only 25-35% in 1983 - the poor number that made gas peakers expensive until combined cycle became standard in the 1990s.

facility.power.oil-plant.name: Oil-fired steam power plant
facility.power.oil-plant.description: The 1980s default in much of Asia and the Middle East, and the reason Taiwan's grid was 58.8% oil in 1980. Residual fuel oil and fuel oil burned in a boiler instead of coal - cheaper to handle, dirtier, and dead on arrival once the 1979 oil shock and OPEC reset prices.
facility.power.oil-plant.note: Not established here: that Taiwan's grid was 58.8% oil in 1980. That figure is quoted with sources on the parent node facility.power; it has not been checked against a primary statistical series for this node. The description of oil-fired generation as the 1980s default in much of Asia is not sourced either.

facility.power.oil-plant.stack.name: Tall chimney
facility.power.oil-plant.stack.description: A 150-250 m concrete or steel chimney to get the plume above the inversion layer and disperse sulphur dioxide over a large area. Not a pollution control device - a dilution device.

facility.power.oil-plant.boiler.name: Oil-fired boiler
facility.power.oil-plant.boiler.description: Same water-tube boiler as the coal plant, but with oil burners instead of a pulveriser and an induced-draft fan sized for the lower flue-gas volume. Two to four boilers typically share one stack.

facility.oil.name: Crude petroleum and fuel oil
facility.oil.description: The liquid fuel of the whole industrial world in 1983. Kuwait and Saudi Arabian Light for the Far East, plus North Sea Brent and US domestic crude for Europe and the US East Coast.

facts.label: Residual fuel oil price
facts.value: ~$25-30/bbl in 1983, down from ~$37 in 1980

facility.oil.refinery.name: Refinery
facility.oil.refinery.description: Atmospheric and vacuum distillation plus hydrotreating to make fuel oil and, in a complex refinery, the naphtha feed for the hydrogen and ethylene crackers. Ali Qaido in Kuwait (1945) or Amuay in Venezuela (1962) typified the scale.

facility.oil.lpg.name: LPG (propane/butane)
facility.oil.lpg.description: The liquid the Hong Kong and Japanese industrial estates burned for process heat and factory heating, and the feedstock for the 1980s alkylation route to isobutylene. Ends at the well or the refinery.

facility.oil.well.name: Oil and gas well
facility.oil.well.description: A rotary or cable-tool hole completed into sandstone or carbonate. In 1983 the Far East's oil was largely onshore (Gawair in Kuwait, Ghawar-equivalent fields) with growing offshore production.

facility.oil.reservoir.name: Sandstone or carbonate oil reservoir
facility.oil.reservoir.description: Porous sedimentary rock (typically Tertiary sandstone or Jurassic carbonate) saturated with oil under pressure. This is where the story actually ends for oil.
facility.oil.reservoir.note: Not established: that the reservoirs supplying the Far East trade of 1983 were typically Tertiary sandstone or Jurassic carbonate. No petroleum-geology document was located for these fields.

facility.power.hydro-plant.name: Hydroelectric power plant
facility.power.hydro-plant.description: Genuinely important for the 1980s Far East: Taiwan took 13.9% of its supply from hydro in 1980 and 24.5% by 1990 (Sun Moon Lake, Tachia, Feitsui, Wujie), and Taiwan's run-of-river stations are exactly the kind of small plant Commodore's Taiwanese subcontractors drew from. Elsewhere hydro was the cheap baseload of Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Canada.

facts.label: Taiwan hydro 1980
facts.value: 13.9% of grid supply

facility.power.hydro-plant.tailrace.name: Tailrace and reservoir
facility.power.hydro-plant.tailrace.description: Where the water goes back to the river - and, downstream of the dam, the river itself is the raw water intake for the industrial park that the dam's power attracted.

facility.power.river.name: The river itself
facility.power.river.description: A glacial or monsoonal river carrying suspended sediment, hardness and organic colour. This is the actual origin of most of the ultrapure water in this tree.
facility.power.river.note: Not established: the named rivers and reservoirs and their characterisations, including Sun Moon Lake, the Sham Chun, the Han River basin, and the claim that this is the actual origin of most of the ultrapure water on the tree. No water authority document located.

facility.power.hydro-plant.turbine.name: Francis turbine
facility.power.hydro-plant.turbine.description: The standard medium-head machine: water enters the spiral casing, turns a runner on a vertical or horizontal shaft at 100-750 rpm, and exits into the draft tube.

facts.label: Head
facts.value: 60-250 m typical

facility.power.hydro-plant.penstock.name: Concrete penstock and headrace tunnel
facility.power.hydro-plant.penstock.description: A 3-6 m diameter steel or concrete conduit carrying water from the intake at head to the turbine, usually several hundred metres and dropping 50-300 m of head.

facility.power.cement-portland.name: Portland cement
facility.power.cement-portland.description: Limestone plus clay, fired in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, ground with gypsum. The universal structural binder of the 1980s industrial plant: dams, cooling towers, substation foundations, effluent tanks, the fab's raised floor.

facility.power.cement-kiln.name: Rotary cement kiln
facility.power.cement-kiln.description: A 60-150 m inclined steel tube rotating 1-2 rpm, burning coal or oil at 1450 C to drive off CO2 and drive the reaction forward. Ends at the limestone and clay pits.

facility.power.rockfill.name: Rockfill dam and riprap
facility.power.rockfill.description: Dams of the era were built of quarried rock tipped into the river and compacted, faced with concrete or asphaltic membrane. Ends at the quarry face.

facility.power.aggregate-quarry.name: Aggregate and riprap quarry
facility.power.aggregate-quarry.description: Granite/gneiss quarried, crushed and screened for dam rock, concrete aggregate and filter material. Ends at the rock in the hillside.
facility.power.aggregate-quarry.note: Not established: that granite or gneiss was quarried for dam rock, concrete aggregate and filter material in this supply chain. No quarry or aggregate statistics document was located.

facility.power.coal-plant.turbine.name: Steam turbine
facility.power.coal-plant.turbine.description: A multistage expansion turbine: high-pressure, intermediate-pressure and low-pressure sections, the last with the long bladed rotor of a wet-steam half-pressure machine. Exhaust goes to the condenser at about 0.05 bar. Steam rate for a 1980s unit was roughly 9-11 MJ/kWh.

facts.label: Steam rate
facts.value: 9-11 MJ per kWh

facts.label: Rotor speed
facts.value: 3000 rpm (50 Hz) or 3600 rpm (60 Hz)

facility.power.coal-plant.switchyard.name: Switchyard and circuit breakers
facility.power.coal-plant.switchyard.description: Outdoor busbars, disconnectors, dead-tank and live-tank oil circuit breakers and surge arresters, on a steel lattice gantry. The step-up point where the plant connects to the transmission network.

facility.power.coal-plant.stepup-transfo.name: Generator step-up transformer (GSU)
facility.power.coal-plant.stepup-transfo.description: A single-phase or three-phase bank of 240-500 kV oil-filled transformers that takes 21 kV from the alternator to the transmission line. This is the piece of iron that makes the whole grid possible, and it is why every power station has a lumpy, oil-filled, bunded yard next door.

facility.power.coal-plant.generator.name: Generator (turbo-alternator)
facility.power.coal-plant.generator.description: The turbine shaft turns a 2- or 4-pole alternator at 3000/3600 rpm. A 500 MVA water-cooled unit is about 12 m long and 6 m wide. Output was 13.8 kV or 21 kV - far too low to transmit, hence the step-up transformer next door.

facts.label: Terminal voltage
facts.value: 13.8 or 21 kV

facility.power.coal-plant.condenser.name: Surface condenser
facility.power.coal-plant.condenser.description: Thousands of stainless-steel tubes with condensing exhaust steam outside and cooling water inside. The condensate is the plant's own feedwater; cleanliness here directly sets boiler-tube life.

facility.power.coal-plant.turbine-steel.name: Nickel-alloy rotor and casing steel
facility.power.coal-plant.turbine-steel.description: For a 540 C steam turbine the high-pressure rotor needed 0.5-0.8% Cr-Mo-V steel and the last stages austenitic stainless; the whole thing was forged, normalised, stress-relieved and then creep-rupture proof-tested.

facility.power.coke.name: Metallurgical coke
facility.power.coke.description: Bituminous coal coked in batteries of 30-45 ovens to make the fuel and the reductant for the blast furnace. Ends at the coking plant.

facility.power.coking-coal-seam.name: High-Bituminous coking coal seam
facility.power.coking-coal-seam.description: A very specific subset of bituminous coal - the seam that swells and fuses in the coke oven, distinct from the steam coal the power station burns. The Pennsylvania/Kentucky/West Virginia 'High Bituminous' field.

facility.power.iron-ore.name: Iron ore (hematite/magnetite)
facility.power.iron-ore.description: The blast-furnace feed, and the reason a power station's turbine steel has a supply chain at all. US supply was Mesabi Range hematite and taconite in the Lake Superior district, shipped by rail to the blast furnaces of the Great Lakes steel belt; Europe and Japan imported Brazilian pellets and ore. Ends at the orebody.

facility.power.iron-ore-pit.name: Iron ore open pit (Mesabi)
facility.power.iron-ore-pit.description: Taconite and hematite are dug by 15-tonne payload shovels and hauled in 90-tonne trucks from a strip 60 m deep. Ends at the orebody.

facility.power.coal-plant.boiler.name: Water-tube boiler and evaporator
facility.power.coal-plant.boiler.description: Drum-type water-tube boiler, typically 300-900 MW, drum at ~15 MPa and 340-370 C. Feedwater circulates through downcomers and up risers around a flame path several hundred passes long; saturated steam leaves the drum to be superheated. Superheaters raise that saturated steam to 540-565 C by hanging banks of tube bundles in the radiant and convective pass, and reheaters do the same again to the steam coming back out of the high-pressure turbine - higher steam temperature is the single biggest lever on plant thermal efficiency. An economiser, a bank of finned tubes in the flue-gas path, preheats feedwater from about 120 C to the saturation temperature using the last 8-10% of the flue-gas heat. Ash from the boiler hoppers was quenched, then either dewatered and trucked to a landfill or put wet into a hopper and pumped as slurry; fly ash was collected in electrostatic precipitators or baghouses and trucked dry or ponded.

facts.label: Steam temp
facts.value: 540-565 C at the turbine inlet

facts.label: Superheat
facts.value: saturation (~340 C) to 540-565 C

facts.label: Ash yield
facts.value: 8-15% of coal mass

facility.power.coal-plant.furnace.name: Boiler furnace and combustion
facility.power.coal-plant.furnace.description: A refractory- and water-wall-lined firebox. Coal and preheated air enter at the burners, burn at 1300-1600 C, and give up radiation to the water walls lining the furnace walls.

facility.power.coal-plant.scrubber.name: Wet flue-gas desulphuriser (scrubber)
facility.power.coal-plant.scrubber.description: Required in the US from about 1978 onward once new-source performance standards took effect. Slaked lime or limestone slurry absorbs SO2 to calcium sulphite, which is then forced-oxidised to gypsum; the stack gas is reheated so the plume still rises.

facts.label: SO2 removal
facts.value: 85-95% typical

facility.power.limestone.name: Limestone (calcium carbonate) slurry
facility.power.limestone.description: Crushed and slaked to calcium hydroxide for wet scrubbing, or used directly in dry/semi-dry scrubbers. Ends at the quarry.

facility.power.air-preheater.name: Ljungstrom / regenerative air preheater
facility.power.air-preheater.description: The flue gas gives up its heat to the incoming combustion air through a slow-rotating bank of corrugated steel plates - exhaust gas at ~300 C, air at ~300 C. This alone recovered several percent of the coal's energy.

facility.power.coal-plant.pulveriser.name: Coal pulveriser (mill)
facility.power.coal-plant.pulveriser.description: A ball or roller mill grinds run-of-mine coal to a powder with at least 70% through 200 mesh (75 micrometres) so that it will burn in suspension. This was the technology that made the 1950s-80s boiler possible at all.

facts.label: Fineness
facts.value: >=70% through 75 micrometre (200 mesh)

facts.label: Mill power
facts.value: 40-70 kW per mill, 2-4 mills per boiler

facility.power.coal-plant.fan.name: Hot-air fan and primary air
facility.power.coal-plant.fan.description: A fan supplies the 60-80% of combustion air that dries and suspends the powder in the furnace and the remainder that sweeps it out between the boiler tube banks.

facility.power.coal-plant.receiving.name: Coal receiving and stockyard
facility.power.coal-plant.receiving.description: Unload from rail unit trains or self-unloading barges into a yard. In the 1980s the East Coast plants were fed by unit trains; Japan's and Korea's coal came by Panamax and post-Panamax bulker.

facility.coal.name: Steam coal (run-of-mine to sized)
facility.coal.description: The fuel. Bituminous coal, 20-35 GJ/t, 0.5-3% sulphur, bought on the international steam coal market or delivered by rail from the field. Its ash and sulphur content set the flue-gas desulphuriser and the bottom-ash grinder bill.

facility.coal.prep-plant.name: Coal preparation plant
facility.coal.prep-plant.description: Crushed, screened, washed and dried at the mine mouth. 1980s plants were dense-medium washers plus hydrocyclones; the resulting 2-inch x 0 coal with 8-12% moisture is what a boiler of that era was designed to burn. Thermal drying was the last step - a screen-deck or flash dryer brought the fuel down to about 8-12% moisture, because wetter coal burns slower, raises stack temperature and can quench a boiler screen tube.
facility.coal.prep-plant.note: Not established: that 1980s plants were dense-medium washers plus hydrocyclones, and the 8-12% product moisture figure and 2-inch x 0 top size. The encyclopaedia has no article on coal preparation (the title does not exist), and no coal preparation manual was located.

facts.label: Product moisture
facts.value: 8-12% after drying

facility.coal.washing.name: Dense-medium coal washing
facility.coal.washing.description: Raw coal is floated on a magnetite/water slurry of specific gravity ~1.35; the light coal floats, the ash-rich shale sinks. This is where the mountaintop-removal debate's 'coal refuse' piles come from.

facility.coal.magnetite.name: Magnetite sand for dense-medium fluid
facility.coal.magnetite.description: Fe3O4, a natural iron oxide sand used as the density medium because it is dense, cheap, recoverable magnetically and chemically inert.

facility.coal.magnetite-ore.name: Magnetite ore body
facility.coal.magnetite-ore.description: Magnetite is rare as a bulk ore and common as a concentrates: the dense-medium coal washer only needs a few grams of Fe3O4 per litre of circulating slurry, so the ore was mined in small tonnages - often lake-shore or gabbro deposits - and concentrated by flotation and magnetic separation. Ends at the ore body in the ground.

facility.coal.mine.name: Coal mine
facility.coal.mine.description: In 1983 the relevant supply was room-and-pillar underground mining in the Appalachian basin (Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky) for the US East Coast grid, and open-pit truck-and-shovel or bucket-wheel in the Powder River Basin, Silesia, the Ruhr, the Bowen Basin and the Witbank coalfield.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: typically 150-600 m underground in the Appalachians

facility.coal.opencut.name: Open-cut coal mine
facility.coal.opencut.description: Overburden stripped by dragline or shovel, coal ripped by bulldozer, loaded into 100-tonne rear-dump trucks. Dominant in the Powder River Basin, the Ruhr, Limburg, New South Wales and Limpopo.

facility.coal.overburden-strip.name: Overburden strip of shale and clay
facility.coal.overburden-strip.description: Burden stripped in benches to reach the coal seam - often 10-60 m of rock and dirt per metre of coal in the Powder River Basin. The overburden itself becomes a backfill and a landfill-pond liner.

facility.coal.room-pillar.name: Room-and-pillar mining
facility.coal.room-pillar.description: Still the dominant method for Appalachian metallurgical and steam coal: rooms driven to the pillar, pillars left behind to hold the roof. Cheap but leaves 30-50% of the seam underground.

facility.coal.room-pillar-seam.name: Seam between shale and sandstone beds
facility.coal.room-pillar-seam.description: The same Carboniferous coal-bearing sequence as the longwall face, mined from a shaft or slope rather than a portal. Ends at the rock in the ground.

facility.coal.longwall.name: Longwall face
facility.coal.longwall.description: A mechanised shearer cuts a 2-3 m slice across the panel; the roof is allowed to cave into the goaf and the coal flows to a shearer loader. High recovery, high output, and a lot of subsidence.

facility.coal.seam.name: Bituminous coal seam in sedimentary rock
facility.coal.seam.description: The raw input, full stop. In the northern Appalachian basin the commercial coal is in the middle and upper Pennsylvanian (Conemaugh, Monongahela, Kittanning, Freeport) formations - Carboniferous, roughly 300 million years old, laid down in swamp forests and buried under Pennsylvanian sediment.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: ~300 Ma (Pennsylvanian) in the Appalachians

facts.label: Typical seam
facts.value: 1-6 m thick

chem.name: Petrochemicals and process chemistry
chem.description: Everything on the C64 that began as crude oil or natural gas: the polymers of the case and the keyboard, the solvents of the assembly plant, the wet chemicals and photoresists of the silicon fab, the laminate resin and flux of the board, and the fuels that moved all of it. Traces roughly a tonne of hydrocarbons per kilogram of plastic back to a barrel of light sour crude. The two feedstocks are named as ingredients, not children, because a petrochemical complex does not contain the oilfield it buys from.
chem.note: The two shared commodities, light sour crude oil and field gas, are supplied to this branch rather than produced by it: no chemical plant contains an oil reservoir or a gas field.

chem.petroleum.name: Petroleum: light sour crude oil
chem.petroleum.description: The dig-it-out endpoint of the whole petrochemical chain. Crude is a mixture of thousands of hydrocarbons from methane to asphaltenes, plus sulphur compounds, nitrogen compounds, resins, asphaltenes and trace metals. The grades that feed the 1980s steam crackers are light, low-sulphur: Arab Light at 35-36 degrees API and Brent Blend at 38-39 were the benchmarks of the era.
chem.petroleum.note: Saudi Light at 38-39 API is the classic light sour grade; Arab Light (35-36 API) is the heavier sour crude that historically dominated Saudi exports. Assay figures vary by stream and year. A barrel of crude is a bulk hydrocarbon stream, not a power-generation one, so it is a fluid rather than energy. This is the commodity the whole petrochemical trunk consumes, and other branches reference it as an ingredient.
inputs: organic matter buried in marine shale

facts.label: Arab Light (Saudi), 1983 assay
facts.value: 35.0-36.0 deg API, 0.9-1.5 wt% S, ~2.2 wt% S (typical)

facts.label: Saudi Light
facts.value: 38.0-38.5 deg API

facts.label: Mass of C64 case in crude
facts.value: about 1-3 litres of crude oil per machine (plastic + energy)

chem.solder-chemicals.name: Solder, flux and rosin
chem.solder-chemicals.description: A wave-soldered through-hole board of 1983 is assembled with a 60/40 tin-lead solder and a rosin flux core. The two facts that make this branch worth tracing are that the flux is pine rosin - a forestry product, the clearest non-fossil material in a C64 - and that the solder is 40% lead by weight, which is the reason solder is now the single most restricted substance in electronics. By the late 1980s the halide-free no-clean flux had arrived and was beginning to replace the RMA flux that the C64 was assembled with. A solder joint is not tin-lead metal. The technology change that arrived in the middle and late 1980s was a flux with no halide at all, built on organic acids and esters rather than amine hydrochlorides and leaving an ionic residue mild enough that the board did not have to be washed.
chem.solder-chemicals.note: No-clean fluxes arrived commercially in the mid-1980s; the halide-free specification is measured against a standard ion chromatography test, and the figure quoted for it is halide not detected - under 0.001% by that test.

facts.label: Halide content
facts.value: not detected (<0.001% by the standard test)

chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.name: The thermal profile is the process
chem.solder-chemicals.reflow-profile.description: The reason the soldering chemistry is mostly temperature management: a through-hole joint sees 250-260 C for one to three seconds in the wave, which is enough to make the intermetallic and not enough to damage the flux or the laminate; a surface-mount joint sees a 220-245 C peak for 30-120 seconds in a reflow oven or a hot plate. Over-temperature grows the intermetallic and dulls the joint; under-temperature makes a cold solder joint that fails in service. Every one of these numbers is a chemical property, because the eutectic is a chemical fact.

chem.solder-chemicals.cleaning.name: Board cleaning after soldering
chem.solder-chemicals.cleaning.description: The flux residue had to come off, and the 1980s answer was either an organic solvent (1,1,1-trichloroethane, or isopropanol after 1983, or a mixture) or an aqueous detergent wash. The solvent was the same molecule as the degreaser, and its replacement by isopropanol is one of the cleanest single substitutions in the file: the board plant's solvent went from a chlorinated hydrocarbon to a propylene oxidation product in about two years, for regulatory and cost reasons rather than performance ones.

chem.isopropanol.name: Isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol)
chem.isopropanol.description: C3H8O, boiling 82.6 C, and by the mid-1980s the solvent that had taken over most of the cleaning work the chlorinated solvents used to do. It is flammable, it is cheap, it evaporates cleanly, it dissolves flux residue and oil, and it does not dissolve the ABS or the polycarbonate the way a chlorinated solvent can - which is exactly why it became the electronics cleaner. Almost all of it was made from propylene, so the electronics plant's replacement solvent is the same cracker as the case plastic. The older route hydrogenates acetone over copper or nickel-zinc at 100-150 C and 5-20 bar with 95-98% selectivity and was still fully in use in 1983; both routes end at the same molecule and differ only in whether the plant owns a propylene oxide unit.
chem.isopropanol.note: Not established: the 82.6 C boiling point, the 2-12% flammable range, the acetone-hydrogenation conditions of 100-150 C and 5-20 bar at 95-98% selectivity, and the 99.5-99.9% electronics purity. The two industrial routes - hydration of propene and hydrogenation of acetone - are standard.

facts.label: Flammable range
facts.value: 2-12% in air

facts.label: 1980s purity for electronics
facts.value: 99.5-99.9%, low water, low residue

chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.name: 60/40 tin-lead solder
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.description: A tin-lead solder melting in the high 180s C, which is why a wave-solder bath sat at 250-260 C and a hand iron at 300-350 C: 70-80 C of superheat above the melting point, which keeps the bath molten at the top and fluxes the joint as it passes through. In 1983 about 60-70% of the world's solder was 60/40 tin-lead for electronics; the alloy is cheap, it has a low melting point, and its oxide comes off in a flux. The 40% lead was the subject of the entire lead-free soldering programme of the 1980s and 1990s, and the lead itself came out of a flotation concentrator, not out of a refinery.
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.note: Lead comes from the lead/zinc mining and flotation chain, not from this subsystem. The 183 C eutectic is 63/37 Sn-Pb, not 60/40; 60/40 is not a eutectic alloy and melts at 188 C. Not established: the 250-260 C wave-bath temperature, the 300-350 C iron temperature, and the 60-70% share of world solder in 1983.

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: 188 C for 60/40. The 183 C eutectic belongs to 63/37 Sn-Pb, which is a different alloy and melts at a true point rather than over a range.

facts.label: Lead content
facts.value: 40 wt% (and later restricted)

chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.name: Where the tin came from
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.description: The tin in a 60/40 solder was smelted from cassiterite, the tin ore, and cassiterite is one of the rarer tin deposits in the world: Bolivia's placer and vein cassiterite, the Cornish tin belt, the Nigerian and the Indonesian deposits, and the alluvial cassiterite of Malaysia and Thailand. In 1983 the world mined something like 25,000-30,000 tonnes of tin a year - a small metal market by volume and a strategically awkward one, because the electronics industry's solder demand is a large fraction of it.

chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.name: Cassiterite (SnO2)
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.description: Tin oxide, 78.8% tin by mass, the principal tin ore. Recovered from placer deposits by panning and gravity concentration and from hard-rock veins by flotation, then smelted or reduced to tin. The C64-scale observation is the interesting one: a single soldered joint holds a few milligrams of tin, and there are a hundred and fifty million of them, so the tin industry exists in part because of solder joints.
chem.solder-chemicals.solder-alloy.tin-s.note: Not established: the 78.8% tin by mass figure, the panning and flotation recovery route, and the Llallagu, Cornwall and Kinta Valley attributions as 1983 supply sources.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.name: Rosin flux (RMA)
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.description: The flux core of the solder wire, or the liquid flux of the wave-solder machine: 25-40% rosin in a flux base with an activator. The rosin's job is to dissolve the surface oxide of the copper and the solder - the abietic acid is a mild acid and a mild chelant - and its virtue is that it is a good flux and then leaves an ionic residue that is not corrosive. RMA fluxes were specified with a halide content under 0.05% because halides are what makes a flux corrosive and what makes a circuit hiss. The C64's board was very likely assembled with a halide-bearing flux and cleaned afterwards.

facts.label: Activation
facts.value: organic acids, fatty acid salts, or amine halides

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-f.name: The flux base and its solvent
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.rosin-f.description: A liquid flux is rosin, activator and solvent, and the solvent is what makes it a liquid. Through the 1980s the solder wire's core was a rope of activated rosin flux in an alcohol or glycol ether solvent (isopropyl alcohol, or a glycol ether), and the core was drawn into a wire of solder by a wire-drawing machine. The active rosin in the core had to be clean enough to be drawn: any acid-value drift or gum would tear the wire. A solder wire is a core-drawing operation: a rope of activated flux is drawn together with a tube of alloy through successive dies until the wire is 0.3-0.8 mm across and the flux core 0.1-0.3 mm.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.name: Flux activator
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.description: Rosin alone is a weak flux. The activator is what makes the flux work, and it is also what makes the residue corrosive, so the whole specification of a flux is a trade: enough acid to remove the oxide, not enough ion to eat the board. The 1980s activators were carboxylic acids (stearic acid, abietic acid itself, succinic acid and its anhydride), fatty acid salts such as the zinc and amine stearates, and - in the older RMA grades - amine hydrochlorides, which is where the halide came from.

chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.name: Amine halide activator (the halide source)
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.description: A triethanolamine or an alkylamine neutralised with a mineral acid, giving a halide ion in the flux. It is the reason a halide flux is corrosive if the residue is left on, and it is the reason the halide-free no-clean flux of the mid-1980s removed them rather than replacing them: the halide was never functional, it was just the most convenient way to get an acid and an amine together. The MIL-F-14161 halide-free standard of the late 1970s is what the industry measured against. The whole trick of a halide flux is the neutralisation: enough amine to dissolve the resin, enough mineral acid to supply the fluxing acidity and the halide ion, and not so much of either that the residue eats the board.
chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux.activat.note: The halide-free flux specification (MIL-F-14161) is the standard US military specification that the 1980s flux industry measured against; its date is the origin of the practice rather than of the specification's current form.

chem.rosin.name: Pine rosin (colophony)
chem.rosin.description: The sticky amber solid left when turpentine is distilled out of pine resin. Most rosin is made from pine stumps - the resinous wood left behind when a tree is cut for pulp - by destructive distillation: the stump is chipped, heated in a still to about 150-200 C, turpentine and pine oil come over, and the residue is the rosin, which is then graded by colour and by softening point. About 700,000-800,000 tonnes of rosin were made in the early 1980s, mostly in China, the United States and Brazil. The black liquor from a kraft pulp mill carries resin acids and fatty acids - tall oil - which is distilled into fatty acids, tall-oil fatty acids and a pitch and can be processed further into rosin equivalents.
chem.rosin.note: Rosin production figures for the early 1980s are order-of-magnitude; the chemistry and the softening point ranges are standard. Rosin (colophony) is a resin and is treated as a plastics material. Tall oil, which comes from a kraft mill, stays packaging.

facts.label: Rosin acids
facts.value: abietic acid ~60-70% of pine rosin

facts.label: Ring and ball softening point
facts.value: 70-90 C (batter to stick grades)

metal.rosin.activator.name: The halide activator in the flux core
metal.rosin.activator.description: Plain rosin is a weak flux. The electronics industry improved it by adding a small amount of acid activator - in 1982 almost always zinc chloride, or in the more aggressive grades a zinc chloride-ammonium chloride mixture - so the flux can remove oxides that rosin alone would leave. The trade is real: more activator means a better joint and a corrosive residue that, if it is not washed off, eats the copper. This is why the flux grade is a specification on the wire, and why the electronics-grade rosin wire of 1982 was normally a mildly activated (MA) or activated (A) flux rather than pure RMA.
metal.rosin.activator.note: Flux grade nomenclature and the activator levels are standard; medium confidence on which grade Commodore specified in 1982.

facts.label: Activator
facts.value: zinc chloride at 0.1-2%, or zinc-ammonium chloride

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: RA (rosin-ammonia), RMA (rosin mildly activated), MA, A

facts.label: The trade
facts.value: more activator means better oxide removal and worse corrosion of copper if residues remain

metal.pine-resin.name: Pine resin from a plantation or a pulp mill
metal.pine-resin.description: The leaf: resin bled from the trunks of Pinus species in managed plantations in the American Southeast, Brazil, India, Malaysia, Portugal and China. In the 1980s most rosin came not from tapping but from distilling pine stumps and pulping residues left over from the paper industry - a pulp-mill residue. So the flux in a C64 solder joint is, quite literally, a by-product of making pulp, which makes it a convergence point with the paper and pulp side of the organics chain.
metal.pine-resin.note: By the 1980s the pulp-mill (wood rosin) route supplied the majority of industrial rosin; medium confidence on the exact 1982 split between gum and wood rosin.

facts.label: Rosin yield
facts.value: roughly 1-3% of softwood pulp-mill residue

places: Kraft pulp mill, southeastern United States

metal.turpentine.name: Turpentine from the same stump
metal.turpentine.description: When pine stumps are distilled for rosin, the first thing off is turpentine - alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene - and it is the solvent the flux paste is made with. So the same 5 kg of pine stump that ends up as the flux in a C64's solder joint first gives up its turpentine, and the two are the two halves of one stump-distillation plant. The turpentine went into the paint and printing-ink industry, which means the soldering branch of this tree converges with the coatings branch through a barrel of distilled turpentine.
metal.turpentine.note: Medium confidence on the order-of-processing; the distillation sequence is standard.

facts.label: Product
facts.value: alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and camphene, by steam distillation of the stumps

facts.label: First fraction
facts.value: turpentine, then rosin as the residue

chem.rosin.distillation.name: Stump distillation and grading
chem.rosin.distillation.description: Rosin is made by distilling the resin out of pine stumps. The stump is chipped into 5-10 cm pieces, charged to a still, and heated; turpentine comes over first and is condensed and separated by distillation into alpha-pinene, beta-pinene and dipentene, and then pine oil and a heavy residue come over, and what is left in the pot is the crude rosin. The rosin is then graded - by colour (X, WW, WW, W) and by softening point (batter 75 C, fir 80 C, Norway 85 C, I 90 C, P 110 C, S 120 C) - and the Y grade, at about 165 C softening point and clear, is the one the flux core needs because it has almost no crystallisation and it does not go brittle. Grading is colour against a reference chip, softening point by the ring-and-ball method and acid value by titration, and the flux maker's specification is colour and softening point with the abietic acid content following from them.

facts.label: Ring and ball softening point
facts.value: 70-120 C by grade

facts.label: Acid value
facts.value: 150-170 mg KOH/g

chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.name: Chipping and the still
chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.description: A whole-tree distillery burns about 1.5-2.5 tonnes of dry pine stumps per tonne of rosin plus its turpentine, and yields about 5-8% rosin, 3-4% turpentine and 1-2% pine oil by mass of dry wood. The stumps come from pine killed by beetle attack, from pine cut for pulp, and from the thinning of a plantation - so the rosin business is downstream of a forestry, and specifically of a beetle, in a way that is often overlooked when the flux is described as a petrochemical.
chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.note: Yields vary a lot with the species, the age of the stump and the method; the ranges are the commonly quoted ones.

facts.label: Rosin yield from dry pine wood
Wood per tonne of rosin
facts.value: ~1.5-2.5 t dry stumps

chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.r.name: Retort and the batch cycle
chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.r.description: The classic stump still is a cast-iron or steel retort holding one to two tonnes of chipped wood, charged, closed, and fired with the turpentine vapour going to a condenser and the rosin staying in the pot. A cycle takes 12-20 hours and the still is charged by hand - which is why the business has barely changed since the 1850s in its mechanics while every other part of the 1980s chemical industry has been rebuilt twice. The 1980s changes were in the condenser and in the chip size, not in the process.
chem.rosin.distillation.stump-chipping.r.note: Stump distillation cycle times and charge sizes vary by still design; the figures are representative of the small-batch practice that survived into the 1980s.

facts.label: Batch time
facts.value: 12-20 hours

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: 1-2 tonnes of chipped wood

chem.pcb-chemicals.name: The chemistry of making the board
chem.pcb-chemicals.description: A 1983 bare board goes through about eleven wet operations, and each one is a chemical plant: laminate impregnation and pressing, copper foil treatment, dry-film lamination, alkaline or ferric etching, drilling, electroless copper, electroplating, solder mask, silkscreen, and a final clean. The C64's board is a single-layer FR-4 board with through-hole parts, which is the simplest case - one copper layer, no plating on the holes - and that removes the electroless copper and the gold entirely. Solder mask and silkscreen are two inks rather than one operation: the mask is an epoxy or acrylate screen-printed or curtain-coated through a 100-150 micron stencil and cured at 150 C, the green being a phthalocyanine green in a novolac epoxy vehicle, and the legend is a separate white epoxy ink cured the same way through a 150-200 micron stainless mesh.
chem.pcb-chemicals.note: The solder mask and the silkscreen legend are two inks and one cure rather than two separate operations.

facts.label: Solder mask thickness
facts.value: ~100-150 microns

facts.label: Silkscreen
facts.value: ~150-200 microns wet, cured at 150 C

chem.pcb-chemicals.chlorine-free.name: Chlorine-free chemistry, and why it took twenty years
chem.pcb-chemicals.chlorine-free.description: Nothing in the 1983 process list was unusual except that it was chlorinated: ferric chloride, trichloroethane, a chlorinated epoxy and a brominated one. By 1995-2000 the industry had moved to alkaline etching, alkaline dry-film development, and epoxy laminates with a non-halogenated flame retardant system - and the drivers were the Montreal-adjacent ozone debate, the effluent limits on copper and hexavalent chromium, and the RoHS-style restrictions that arrived later. This node is the marker for where 1983 practice differs from today, not a description of a 1983 process. The industry answer by 1995-2000 was alkaline etching, alkaline dry-film development and epoxy laminates with a non-halogenated flame retardant, driven by the ozone debate, effluent limits on copper and hexavalent chromium, and the restrictions that came later.
chem.pcb-chemicals.chlorine-free.note: This is deliberately a forward-looking marker node; the substitution dates vary by region and by regulation. It marks where 1983 practice differs from today and is not itself a 1983 process.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.name: Plating baths
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.description: A 1983 double-sided board is copper plated in an acid copper sulphate bath (with levelers and brighteners), then tin plated or gold plated. The chemistry is a small industry of its own: a copper electroplate with organic additives at 2-6 A/dm2 and 25-30 C; a tin or tin-lead bath; and, for the connectors, a nickel and gold stack. Immersion gold is not electroplated gold - it is a displacement reaction, a few hundred nanometres of gold out of a complexing bath, over a nickel layer that the board chemistry has to deposit first.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.name: Immersion gold over electroless nickel
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.description: Electroless nickel-phosphorus (hypophosphite reducer) gives a hard, corrosion-resistant, solderable surface, and immersion gold in a cyanide-complexed bath gives the contact surface its low contact resistance. The gold bath contains a complexing agent (EDTA, a phosphate or a cyanide) whose job is to hold the gold in solution so the surface reaction is slow and self-limiting at a few hundred nanometres. For a C64's single-layer board none of this is used - the pads are bare copper with a surface treatment.
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.note: Immersion gold chemistry and thickness are process-specific; the general mechanism (a displacement reaction with a complexing agent) is what is reliable here.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.name: Electroless nickel-phosphorus and its reducer
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.description: The nickel under a gold surface is deposited by a chemical reduction: hypophosphite gives up a hydrogen atom to the nickel ion on the surface and the nickel comes down as metal, with phosphorus co-deposited at 3-9 wt% to make the layer hard and amorphous. The bath is nickel chloride or sulphate at 5-10 g/L, hypophosphite at 10-30 g/L, and 85-95 C for 30-90 minutes, and its uniformity is the reason it is the standard under immersion gold - it coats a via wall as evenly as it coats a pad.

chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.name: Sodium hypophosphite and white phosphorus
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.description: The reducing agent is made from yellow phosphorus, caustic soda and sodium carbonate. So the nickel under the gold on a connector - the part that made a C64's edge connector and its I/O socket reliable in a humid climate - was plated out of phosphate rock, coke, silica and an electric furnace, and the C64-scale quantity of phosphorus in it is vanishingly small and the C64-scale quantity of phosphate rock behind it is not. Yellow phosphorus is reacted with sodium hydroxide under pressure and the sodium hypophosphite comes off with hydrogen, which is why the plant has a hydrogen vent and a flare; the reaction is violent and it is a scale-up of a bench reaction from the 1840s.
chem.pcb-chemicals.plating.immersion-gol.note: Hypophosphite is made by reacting yellow phosphorus with caustic soda under pressure; the chemistry is standard.

chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.name: Copper etching
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.description: Ferric chloride at 35-42 degrees Baume, or cupric chloride, dissolves the exposed copper in 30-60 minutes. Ferric chloride was the 1980s default: cheap, fast, and it etches copper at a rate that keeps the undercut manageable. Its problems were regeneration (the spent etchant is worthless unless it is oxidised back, which needs chlorine or a peroxide and an electrolytic cell) and the ferric ion's attack on the epoxy of the laminate if the etch went long. By the early 1980s the alkaline sodium persulphate etch was spreading because it regenerated in place with peroxide and sodium hydroxide and because it would etch a finer line.

chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.name: Ferric chloride etchant
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.description: FeCl3 at 35-42 degrees Baume (about 3-5 molar), which is an oxidising acid: the ferric ion takes an electron from the copper and the cupric ion falls back to ferrous. Regeneration is done either with chlorine (the industrial way, in a cell) or with hydrogen peroxide and acid. The byproduct is copper chloride, which in the 1980s was becoming a problem in its own right because of the copper discharge limits.
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.note: Copper etching by ferric chloride, with the copper(II) chloride rinsed away, is standard. Not established: the 35-42 degrees Baume working concentration, the about 3-5 molar figure, and the chlorine-cell and hydrogen-peroxide regeneration routes.

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: 35-42 degrees Baume

chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.name: Regenerating the ferric chloride etchant
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.description: Spent ferric chloride is ferrous chloride and copper chloride, and it has to be oxidised back to ferric before it can etch again. The industrial way was a chlorination cell: chlorine into the ferrous solution at 60-80 C, converting ferrous back to ferric and precipitating the copper as cuprous chloride. The cell was a piece of the chlor-alkali plant's technology, and the chlorine in it was often the same chlorine that the plant bought for its own electroplating line. Chlorine regenerates the feric ion and the copper comes out as a precipitate, which in 1983 meant a chloride concentration that climbed and had to be bled off and a copper sludge with its own disposal limits.
chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chlori.note: The alkaline etch was spreading through the 1980s; the exact adoption date in a given plant is not documented here.

chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.name: Dry-film photoresist
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.description: A 25-40 micron dry film laminated hot onto the copper - a polyester or polyethylene terephthalate base carrying an acrylate photopolymer and an acrylated monomer that crosslinks on exposure. The exposure crosslinks the acrylate, so the exposed areas become insoluble and the unexposed areas are developed away, and the resulting image is negative - the opposite polarity to the wafer resists of the same decade, and the reason the two industries use opposite conventions for the same word. This is the clearest dated marker in the board chemistry.
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.note: The commercial introduction of aqueous-developable dry films dates from the early 1980s; by the middle of the decade they were the standard in North America. Not established: the 25-40 micron film thickness, the polyester (PET) or polyethylene base, the acrylate photopolymer and acrylated monomer chemistry, and the negative image convention as a description of 1980s dry film. The claim that aqueous-developable films arrived in the early 1980s and were standard in North America by the middle of the decade is the softest statement in this node.

facts.label: Film thickness
facts.value: 25-40 microns (2-4 mil)

facts.label: Base
facts.value: polyester (PET) or polyethylene

chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.name: Laminating the dry film
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.description: The dry film comes off a protective polyester or polyethylene release liner, is laid on the cleaned and dried copper, and is squeezed onto it by a hot laminator at 110-150 C and 3-5 bar with a silicone rubber roller. The rollers are silicone because the film must not stick to them and the liner must, and the whole operation is a controlled vacuum or a controlled pressure depending on the machine: without the pressure, the air trapped between the film and the copper becomes a bubble and the bubble becomes an etch defect.

chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.name: Release liner and its disposal
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.description: A 25 micron polyester or polyethylene film with a slightly adhesive surface, peeled off and wound onto a take-up reel. In 1980s board plants the liners went into the waste stream by the kilogram - a 500 mm square panel of dry film consumes about a tenth of a square metre of liner - and a solvent-free laminator could run a plant's whole reel without a solvent drum in the room, which is another reason the industry went dry.
chem.pcb-chemicals.dry-film-resist.lamin.note: The liner consumption per panel is an order-of-magnitude figure; the solvent-free trend is the reliable part of this node.

chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil.name: Electrolytic copper foil
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil.description: A 35-70 micron copper foil, electrodeposited on a rotating drum from a copper sulphate-acid bath and then treated on the bonding surface. The treatment is the interesting part chemically: the foil's teeth are made mechanically or electrochemically, and the surface is then covered with a nodular copper layer bonded to an organo-chrome or a zinc-oleate layer, and in the 1980s increasingly with a benzotriazole layer. Benzotriazole replaced the chromate because hexavalent chromium was being regulated out of the process.

chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil..name: Benzotriazole coupling agent
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil..description: BTA, a seven-membered ring with three adjacent nitrogens, adsorbs onto copper and stops it reacting with anything else - it is the corrosion inhibitor and the adhesion promoter in one. It is a beautiful small molecule for this tree because the same triazole ring chemistry appears in the corrosion inhibitors of every other metal in the book, and because the copper underneath is a metal chain node and the BTA is a petrochemical.
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.copper-foil..note: BTA's use as the standard copper coupling agent dates from the 1970s and displaced chromate-based treatment; the exact formulations are proprietary.

chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.name: Epoxy-glass laminate (FR-4)
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.description: Woven glass cloth impregnated with a brominated epoxy resin at 50-60% resin content, then pressed at 170-180 C and 0.3-1.5 MPa in a multi-daylight press. The cloth comes from the mineral chain (chem.glass-fiber); the resin is chem.epoxy; the hardener in a high-temperature board is the DDS of the epoxy branch. In 1983 FR-4 was the default board material and a typical single-layer C64 board was 1.6 mm of it.
chem.pcb-chemicals.laminate.note: Not established: the 170-180 C and 0.3-1.5 MPa press cycle, the 50-60 wt% resin content, the brominated epoxy content and the 1.6 mm nominal thickness for a 1982 FR-4 board.

facts.label: Board thickness
facts.value: 1.6 mm (nominal)

chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy.name: Brominated epoxy for FR-4
chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy.description: Tetrabromobisphenol A based epoxy, brominated to about 20-40% bromine, blended into the resin at 10-30% so the laminate meets UL 94 V-0. The bromine works by releasing hydrogen bromide in the flame and smothering it, and it works so well that the industry continued using it through the 1980s even as the first brominated flame retardant ban had already arrived. It is the epoxy in the C64's board.
chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy.note: FR-4 formulations vary; not all consumer FR-4 of the 1980s was brominated, and the C64's board grade is not documented.

facts.label: Bromine content of FR-4 resin
facts.value: about 10-20% Br

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: UL 94 V-0 at 1.6 mm

chem.epoxy.branched-epoxy.name: Branched and novolac epoxies
chem.epoxy.branched-epoxy.description: Reacting DGEBA with a dihydroxy or trihydroxy compound - trimethylolpropane, bisphenol A again, or an epoxy cresol novolac - builds a molecule with more than two epoxide groups and higher functionality, which raises the glass transition temperature and lets a laminate hold a solder temperature. The epoxy novolac also carried the bromine: brominating the ring gives the flame-retardant epoxy that FR-4 used.

chem.fab-chemicals.name: The wet chemicals of a 1980s silicon fab
chem.fab-chemicals.description: A 1983 wafer fab consumed tens of thousands of gallons a day of ultrapure water and a few thousand gallons of five electronic-grade acids, and its entire chemistry was aimed at one thing: keeping a few hundred metallic atoms per square centimetre off the wafer. This branch traces those chemicals - sulphuric acid, hydrogen peroxide, the buffered HF etch, the plasma etch gases, the dopant gases and the photoresist - back to the sulphur, the chlorine, the fluorine, the ammonia and the natural gas they were made from. The wet bench of the period used 10-20 litre recirculating baths of buffered HF and piranha, and the chemicals came in returnable fluoropolymer containers or, for the largest users, by bulk tanker.
chem.fab-chemicals.note: This node deliberately flags where practice diverged from today's; the specific substitution programmes and their dates vary by process step.

chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.name: Electronic-grade ammonium hydroxide
chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.description: Aqueous ammonia at 20-29 wt% in ultrapure water, made by sparging anhydrous ammonia into the water under a scrubbed laminar-flow hood, then filtered to sub-micron and to low sodium. It is the alkaline clean and the alkaline developer companion, and it is the one wet chemical that arrives as a gas: a fab's supply was a battery of electro-polished or fluoropolymer bottles on a nitrogen-purged cabinet, refilled from a bulk ammonia tank outside the cleanroom. The ammonia arrives as a liquid tanker from a Haber-Bosch plant about a day's drive away, is vaporised through a water or steam-heated vaporiser and is sparged into ultrapure water; the purity demanded was surprisingly modest next to the acids, because ammonia's job is to leave no alkali residue, and 99.9% anhydrous was generally adequate.
chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.note: The ammonia itself is a natural-gas product: chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammonia.ammonia. Commercial ammonia solution is graded on the Baume scale, with about 30 wt% ammonia as the typical high-concentration product. Not established: the 20-29 wt% electronic-grade figure, the sub-micron filtration and low-sodium specification, and the 99.9% anhydrous ammonia a fab received.

chem.fab-chemicals.spec-purity.name: The purity ladder
chem.fab-chemicals.spec-purity.description: The 1980s specification ladder, from technical grade to the electronic grade that a wafer demanded: a technical acid at about 5N with metals at tens and hundreds of parts per million; an electronic acid at about 8N; and the 9N-10N grade with a total metal content under 10 parts per billion. The reason the ladder existed was the relationship between a metal atom's concentration and the device: a wafer with 10 parts per billion of iron in a cubic centimetre of silicon has more iron atoms in the active volume than it has dopant atoms.
chem.fab-chemicals.spec-purity.note: The purity ladder is a way of describing the chain, and its numbers are the substance of the node. Not established: the 5N, 8N and 9N-10N ladder and the sub-10 ppb total metal specification as 1980s figures. The comparison the node makes - that at 10 parts per billion the metal atoms in the active volume outnumber the dopant atoms - follows from the atomic density of silicon and is the part that holds.

facts.label: Technical grade acid
facts.value: ~5N, metals at 10-100 ppm

facts.label: Electronic grade acid
facts.value: 8-9N, metals under 100 ppb

facts.label: Highest grade (1980s)
facts.value: 9N-10N, total metals under 10 ppb

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.name: Bulk process gases
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.description: The three gases a fab inhaled by the thousand: nitrogen for inerting, purging and sparging; argon for the sputtering cathodes and for the anneal; and helium for the leak detector, the cryopump and some of the photolithography optics cooling.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.argon.name: Argon
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.argon.description: A by-product of the air separation unit at 1-3% of the air, purified to 99.999%. It fills the sputtering cathodes - the argon ions are accelerated across the gap and knock atoms out of the aluminium or titanium target - and it is the inert atmosphere of the annealing and ashing steps. The sputtering itself is the metals chain, but the gas that drives it is an air separation product.
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.argon.note: Argon is a byproduct of cryogenic air separation. Not established: the 1-3% of air figure, the 99.999% purity, and the description of argon filling sputtering cathodes and inerting the annealing and ashing steps in a 1980s fab.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.helium.name: Helium
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.helium.description: Almost all helium is recovered as a by-product of the cryogenic separation of natural gas liquids - 0.05-0.7% of a helium-rich gas stream, separated to 99.999%. It is the cleanest gas in the plant and it is used in the helium leak detector that is how a fab proves a chamber is sealed, and in the cryopumps of the etch machines. It is the one process gas in a fab whose feedstock is unambiguously natural gas.
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.helium.note: Helium separation from a natural gas plant belongs to the gas processing branch: chem.natural-gas.processing.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.name: Nitrogen
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.description: 99.999% and, for the very best, 99.9999%. Produced by cryogenic air separation for the large users and by pressure swing adsorption for the small ones. Its uses were the furnace tube atmospheres, the photoresist spin-coat bowl, the drying cabinets, the solvent flush and the packaging seal. A large C64 production line would have used a few hundred cubic metres of nitrogen a week.

chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.name: Cryogenic air separation
chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases.nitroge.description: Air is filtered, compressed to 30-100 bar, cooled and expanded through a cold box to fractionate it into oxygen, nitrogen and argon at -180 C. A unit producing 5,000-30,000 tonnes a day of nitrogen was a large industrial plant in its own right, and it shared its cold box technology with the natural gas processing business in this file.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.name: Dopant sources
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.description: The chemicals that put boron, phosphorus and arsenic into the silicon. The chemistry here is a closed loop back to the ammonia, the chlorine and the fluorspar of the rest of this tree, and the whole business is about the fact that a dopant source is gaseous, toxic and must be delivered to a few cubic centimetres of reactor at a controlled partial pressure. Diffusion in 1983 used a gas or a solid source - phosphorus from phosphine or a doped oxide, boron from diborane or boron nitride, arsenic from arsine - in a furnace at 800-1,100 C.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.note: The C64 chips were 2 micron NMOS designs of the late 1970s fabricated in the early 1980s; both diffusion and implantation were in use for that generation.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.name: Diborane (B2H6) and boron trifluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.description: The p-type sources. Diborane is made from boron trifluoride and sodium hydride or from boron trichloride and a hydride, and it arrives at 0.5-5% in hydrogen; boron trifluoride was delivered neat from a cylinder. In 1983 p-type implantation was moving from boron to BF2+ (a molecular ion made in the ion source) because the heavier ion gave a shallower, more controllable junction - a change in the ion source chemistry, not in the wafer chemistry.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.bora.name: Boron trifluoride from fluorspar
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane.bora.description: BF3 is made by treating fluorspar with sulphuric acid or with fluosilicic acid, so the p-type dopant of a 1983 NMOS process is, three steps back, the same rock as the HF that etched the oxide. This is the tightest single chain in this whole tree from a mineral to a transistor.
