chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.arsine.name: Arsine (AsH3)
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.arsine.description: The other n-type source, used for heavier and shallower implants and for the arsenic source oxide. It is made by reducing arsenic trichoxide with zinc and hydrochloric acid or with hydrogen, and the arsenic comes from arsenic metal or from gallium arsenide production. Arsine is the most acutely toxic gas routinely used in a semiconductor fab; the 1980s limit of a few parts per billion in the exhaust was enforced with an ionising-type monitor, not a badge.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.arsine.note: Arsine is made by reducing arsenic(III) oxide with zinc in acid, and is flammable, pyrophoric and highly toxic. Not established: its use for heavier and shallower implants and for the arsenic source oxide, the dilution in hydrogen, and the parts-per-billion exhaust limit enforced with an ionising monitor.

facts.label: Dopant
facts.value: n-type (donor)

facts.label: Delivery
facts.value: diluted in H2

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.name: Phosphine (PH3)
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.description: The n-type dopant source. In 1983 it was supplied two ways: as an ion-implantation source, and as a dopant gas diluted to 5-15% in hydrogen or nitrogen for the dopant gas deposition reactor. Phosphine is pyrophoric in the pure state and is one of the most acutely toxic gases in a fab, which is why it arrived diluted and in a gas cabinet.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.note: Not established: the 5-15% dilution in hydrogen or nitrogen for the dopant gas reactor, the ion-implantation use, and the gas-cabinet practice in 1983.

facts.label: Delivery
facts.value: 5-15% in H2 or N2

facts.label: Dopant
facts.value: n-type (donor)

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Where the phosphorus comes from
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: The phosphine of a 1983 fab has a longer ancestry than most people assume. Elemental phosphorus is made in a submerged arc furnace from phosphate rock, coke and silica at 1,400-1,500 C, condensed as white phosphorus under water, and then either burned to phosphorus pentoxide (for fertiliser and for the pure phosphoric acid of this file) or reduced to phosphorous acid, which is then converted to phosphine. So an n-doped transistor junction in a C64's VIC-II traces back through a gas cylinder, an electric furnace, and a phosphate rock mine. Yellow phosphorus plus phosphorus pentasulphide is treated with caustic soda and water to give phosphorous acid and sodium hypophosphite, and acid plus hypophosphite is the standard industrial route to phosphine; the electronic gas is then diluted to 5-15% in hydrogen or nitrogen and cylinder-packaged, because pure phosphine is pyrophoric and because the cylinder is what the gas cabinet expects.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.note: Phosphine preparation routes include the hypophosphorous acid route and the phosphorus pentasulphide/caustic route; the latter is the common industrial one.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Phosphoric acid (the wet-process acid)
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: The wet process beats the phosphorus furnace, and it beats it because the furnace is only economical at a very large scale: ground phosphate rock is digested in 30-40% sulfuric acid, the calcium sulphate is filtered off as gypsum, and the phosphoric acid is concentrated to 54% P2O5. The C64-scale relevance of this acid is indirect - it is the fertiliser that came out of the phosphate rock, and it is also the semiconductor-grade acid a fab used for its own processes, purified further to 9N. Rock at 1-2 mm is digested in 30-40% sulphuric acid at 70-80 C and filtered, giving about 54% P2O5; the chemistry is a century old and limited by the solubility of calcium sulphate, so the gypsum cake is the waste stream and its disposal - often offshore or in a lined lagoon - is the industry's continuing environmental problem.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.note: This acid chain is a fertiliser and commodity chain that is nominally outside this subsystem; it is included because the semiconductor-grade version is one of the fab's wet chemicals.

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 54% P2O5 typical

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: Phosphate rock
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: A sedimentary rock of calcium phosphate - apatite - mined from the Florida phosphate belt and the Moroccan and Chinese deposits. It is one of the four rock types this whole tree ends in, alongside crude oil, natural gas and sand. The C64-scale fact is absurd but true: the quantity of phosphate rock mined for fertiliser every year is measured in tens of millions of tonnes, and the quantity used to make the phosphorus in a C64's transistors is a few grams, most of it going into fertiliser for somebody's field.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.note: The phosphate rock mining and fertiliser chain is nominally outside this subsystem; this node exists because the n-type dopant chain terminates there. Category metals, for the same reason: phosphate rock is a mineral, not wafer chemistry. Phosphate rock is mined mainly in Florida and North Africa. Not established: the tens of millions of tonnes a year mined for fertiliser, and the Florida and Moroccan attributions as the supply actually behind semiconductor-grade phosphorus.

chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.name: The submerged arc phosphorus furnace
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.description: A 30-100 MW furnace in which phosphate rock, coke and silica are heated to 1,400-1,500 C by three graphite electrodes dipped into the charge, and the phosphorus vapour - P4 - is taken off, condensed under water and stored under water because it ignites in air. A 1980s US plant made 100,000-150,000 tonnes of yellow phosphorus a year, and the greater part of that went to phosphoric acid for fertiliser rather than to any electronics use.
chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.phosphine.pho.note: Phosphate rock with sand and coke is heated to 1,200-1,500 C to give P4. Not established: the 30-100 MW furnace rating, the three graphite electrodes, the condensation and storage under water, and the 100,000-150,000 tonne per year US figure for a 1980s plant.

facts.label: Product
facts.value: P4 vapour, condensed under water

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.name: Plasma etch gases
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.description: The gases that a barrel or planar plasma etcher used to etch silicon dioxide, polysilicon, aluminium and organic films. They are the fluorine and chlorine family, and they are the most expensive part of the etch cost after the electricity.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.barrel-etc.name: The barrel plasma etcher
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.barrel-etc.description: A quartz or alumina tube with electrodes at the top and bottom, gas fed in at the top, RF at 13.56 MHz, and wafers standing vertically in slots around the tube wall. It was the workhorse of the 1980s for silicon dioxide and aluminium etching and for resist ashing, and it was cheap, simple and gently non-uniform - which was acceptable when the field of view was small and the line was a couple of microns. The planar (magnetron) etcher, where the plasma is generated above the wafer by a magnetically confined source, gave the flatness that a later generation of chips needed.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.barrel-etc.note: Plasma etching uses RF excitation at 13.56 MHz, and a fluorine-bearing gas etches silicon dioxide selectively in conjunction with photolithography. Not established: the quartz or alumina barrel with top and bottom electrodes, the vertical wafer slots, the 0.1-10 torr range, and the barrel's description as the workhorse of the 1980s.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.nf3.name: Nitrogen trifluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.nf3.description: An emerging chamber-cleaning gas in the 1980s, and later a feedstock for the NF3-based etch chemistry. It is a very strong oxidiser, it is a gas at room temperature, and the reason it took so long to industrialise in the United States was a supply constraint rather than a performance one - the production chemistry needed fluorine.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.nf3.note: NF3 chamber cleaning was in commercial use in the late 1980s; this node's presence is a marker rather than a core technology of the 1983 C64 chips.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cl2.name: Chlorine and boron trifluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cl2.description: A chlorine-based plasma - Cl2, or BCl3 with Cl2 - is used for aluminium, because fluorine does not etch aluminium cleanly. BCl3 also supplied boron, so the etch gas doubled as the p-type dopant source, which is one of the reasons the boron trifluoride and boron trichloride business ended up as one business.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cl2.note: BCl3 is made by chlorinating boron oxide or elemental boron; the chemistry is standard but the 1980s supply details are not well documented.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.name: Tetrafluoromethane
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.description: CF4, the workhorse oxide etch gas and the fluorine chemistry's workhorse generally. It is made from fluorine (from fluorspar) and carbon, or from a chlorofluorocarbon feedstock. In a plasma etcher it dissociates to fluorine radicals that etch silicon dioxide - it does not etch silicon, which is what made the selectivity possible - and it is the gas that made the barrel reactor the standard 1980s oxide etch.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.note: CF4 boils at -128 C. Not established: the dissociation to fluorine radicals as the reason selectivity against silicon works, manufacture from fluorine and carbon or from a chlorofluorocarbon feedstock, and CF4 as the standard 1980s oxide etch gas.

facts.label: Boiling point
facts.value: -128 C (a gas at room temperature)

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.name: Fluorine from fluorspar
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.description: Every fluorine atom in a fab's chemistry started as calcium fluoride. Fluorspar is treated with concentrated sulphuric acid at 200-250 C in a kiln or a retort to make anhydrous hydrogen fluoride, and the HF is either sold as the aqueous etch acid or chlorinated with chlorine to make the CFCs and the fluorocarbons. It is the same sulphuric acid, the same chlorine and the same rock as the oxide etch, the freons in the packaging and the halogenated degreasers.

chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.name: Anhydrous hydrogen fluoride
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.description: Fluoride plus concentrated sulphuric acid at about 265 C gives anhydrous HF, which is distilled off and shipped in a fluorine-lined tanker or a nickel tank. It is a strong acid, a violent poison, and it will dissolve most metals; the 1980s storage practice was a tank with a fluorine polymer lining and an emergency water curtain, and the fundamental tension in the whole HF business is that the only thing that will hold it is the same fluorine chemistry that makes the etch gases.
chem.fab-chemicals.etch-gases.cf4.fluori.note: Anhydrous hydrogen fluoride is made by treating fluorite, CaF2, with concentrated sulfuric acid. The 200-250 C figure in this node is not established: industrial practice is quoted at about 265 C. Also not established: the fluorine-polymer-lined tank, the water-curtain protection, and the emergency arrangements.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CaF2 + H2SO4 at about 265 C

facts.label: Product
facts.value: anhydrous HF, distilled

chem.photoresist.name: Photoresist chemistry
chem.photoresist.description: The organic photoresists of 1983 were almost all positive-working diazonaphthoquinone resins on a novolac: the light-sensitive group is a diazonaphthoquinone sulphonate ester on a phenolic novolac made from phenol and formaldehyde. Exposing the resist converts the ester to a carboxylic acid, which makes the exposed resin soluble in the alkaline developer, so the image is positive. It is a strictly positive image because of the mechanism, not because of anything clever - the exposure destroys the very group that was holding the resin together. Development ran 0.2-0.3 N TMAH at 20-25 C by spray or immersion for 30-60 seconds, controlled to a fraction of a degree and a fraction of a per cent because the image is only about half a micrometre deep and the process window is correspondingly narrow; spray development, introduced in the early 1980s, removed the meniscus and particle problems of immersion and became the standard within a few years.

facts.label: Developer
facts.value: 0.2-0.3 N TMAH at 20-25 C

facts.label: Resist thickness
facts.value: 0.5-2.0 microns (1.5-2.0 typical for 2 micron processes)

chem.photoresist.plasma-resist.name: Polysilane and plasma-polymerised resists
chem.photoresist.plasma-resist.description: The silicon-containing resists, in which a Si-Si backbone absorbs the deep ultraviolet and generates a silyl radical that crosslinks the exposed area. In 1983 they were in development for the 1 micron and sub-micron layers, and they are the reason the industry needed a deep-ultraviolet lithography tool at all. Their problem was exactly the same as everything else in this branch: a new chemistry with a contamination story attached.
chem.photoresist.plasma-resist.note: Plasma-polymerised (polysilane) resists were a research topic through the 1980s; commercial DUV resists arrived later. The silicon-containing resists were a research topic through the 1980s, which is a statement about the state of the art rather than a step in the process. Confidence stays low.

chem.photoresist.negative.name: Negative resists and image reversal
chem.photoresist.negative.description: A small share of 1980s production was negative-working - the exposed areas crosslink and stay - and image-reversal resists, where a photoacid generator makes a carboxylic acid in the exposed areas and an amine in the top layer diffuses into them and makes the exposed areas soluble, so a positive image is made with a negative resist chemistry. The reversal chemistry existed in 1983 because of the contrast it gave with the deep-ultraviolet exposure tools of the late 1980s.
chem.photoresist.negative.note: Negative and image-reversal resists are a family of chemistries described here rather than an operation in the 1980s line.

chem.photoresist.hard-bake.name: Dehydration bake and hard bake
chem.photoresist.hard-bake.description: A dehydration bake at 150-200 C to drive the water out of the spin-coated film before exposure, and a post-exposure hard bake at 120-180 C to crosslink or densify the remaining image. The hard bake is what makes the resist resistant to the plasma etch and to the buffered HF, and it is also what makes it harder to strip - which is why the industry moved to plasma stripping and to ozonised water by the late 1980s, and why the old solvent strippers (phenol and sulphuric acid) disappeared from the process. Stripping progressed through a phenolic-plus-sulphuric-acid liquid strip to an ozone/water clean and an oxygen plasma ash, driven by the ion contamination of the liquid strippers and by the fact that a hard-baked resist had become impossible to remove in a controlled way; plasma ashing runs at about 1 mbar and 250-400 C.
chem.photoresist.hard-bake.note: Resist stripping belongs to this step; the stripping numbers are in its description.

chem.photoresist.diazonaphthoquinone.name: Diazonaphthoquinone sulphonate
chem.photoresist.diazonaphthoquinone.description: The photosensitive ester: 1,2-naphthoquinone-2-diazide-5-sulphonic acid esterified onto the phenolic hydroxyls of the novolac. The 1,4-isomer was the one the 1980s photoresist industry settled on because it gives the higher photospeed and less outgrowth. The whole resist is about 20-30% diazo compound by weight; the rest is novolac and a small amount of sensitiser.
chem.photoresist.diazonaphthoquinone.note: Diazonaphthoquinone sulfonate esters are mixed with novolac resin and act as a dissolution inhibitor; a conventional resist is resin, sensitiser and solvent, and novolac is a phenol-formaldehyde condensation polymer. Not established: the 1,4-isomer preference, the 20-30 wt% diazo content, the g-line, h-line and i-line exposure figures, and the outgrowth comparison.

facts.label: Diazo content
facts.value: ~20-30 wt% of the resist

facts.label: Typical exposure
facts.value: g-line 436 nm, h-line 405 nm, i-line 365 nm

chem.photoresist.novolac.name: Novolac resin from phenol and formaldehyde
chem.photoresist.novolac.description: Phenol condensed with formaldehyde under acid to a thermoplastic, low-molecular-weight resin with no epoxide or methylol functionality left. The resin is not the photosensitive part; it is the part that gives the film its mechanical integrity and its dissolution behaviour in the developer. Its phenolic hydroxyl groups are why the novolac dissolves so readily in TMAH - and why an alkaline developable resist could not have worked with the old novolac-epoxy resists of the early 1960s.
chem.photoresist.novolac.note: The phenol chain is chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol and the formaldehyde chain is chem.pom.formaldehyde. The node is the resin, not the making of it.

chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.name: Tetramethylammonium hydroxide
chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.description: TMAH, sold at 25 wt% in ultrapure water, used to develop the positive photoresists and - from the late 1970s - to wet-etch the aluminium interconnect of a dynamic random access memory. It arrived as a photoresist developer in the single most consequential materials change of the early 1980s: a chemist at IBM demonstrated in 1979 that an alkaline developer could work on a diazonaphthoquinone resist without image reversal, and that single result is the ancestor of essentially all modern photolithography. TMAH is made by the electrolysis of trimethylamine hydrochloride or by ion exchange from trimethylamine and a methyl chloride-derived quaternary salt, and the commercial 25% solution in ultrapure water had to be filtered sub-micron and low in sodium, because any sodium on a wafer is a threshold-shift defect.
chem.fab-chemicals.tmah.note: TMAH manufacture is either the electrolytic route from trimethylamine hydrochloride or an ion-exchange route; both are industrial.

chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.name: Electronic-grade nitric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.description: 70% HNO3 at about 10N. Nitric acid was the oxidising component of the older cleaning recipes and a component of some of the early aluminium etchants. It was the least-used of the four big wet chemicals by the early 1980s because it had been largely replaced by hydrogen peroxide.

chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.ostwald.name: Ostwald process
chem.fab-chemicals.nitric-acid.ostwald.description: Ammonia oxidised over a platinum-rhodium gauze at 800-900 C to nitric oxide, then to NO2 in excess air, then absorbed in water. Nitric acid is therefore an ammonia product, which means it is a natural-gas product: the Haber-Bosch ammonia of the 1980s was the source of the nitric acid and of the ammonium hydroxide, both of which a fab bought.

facts.label: Ammonia oxidation
facts.value: 800-900 C, Pt-Rh gauze

metal.cyanide-precursor.name: Ammonia (NH3)
metal.cyanide-precursor.description: The nitrogen source for the cyanide that dissolves the gold. Ammonia is made in enormous tonnage for fertiliser and the cyanide plant buys a small part of it: natural gas and steam are reformed to hydrogen and nitrogen, the mixture is shifted, and about 15-20 MPa of hydrogen with nitrogen passes over a promoted iron catalyst at 400-500 C to give ammonia. The ammonia is then oxidised with air over a platinum or manganese dioxide catalyst to hydrogen cyanide and hydrolysed to sodium cyanide. The same ammonia is what the Sherritt-Gordon nickel leach and the potash-ammonia Solvay works buy.
metal.cyanide-precursor.note: Medium confidence on the numbers; the Haber-Bosch conditions are standard.

facts.label: Haber-Bosch
facts.value: 400-500 C, 200-300 bar, iron catalyst, order 20-40 GJ per tonne of NH3

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: fertiliser ammonia ran to tens of millions of tonnes a year in 1982; a cyanide plant used tens of tonnes

metal.habers-catalyst.name: Iron catalyst for ammonia synthesis
metal.habers-catalyst.description: The hydrogen in the cyanide comes from ammonia, and the ammonia's Haber-Bosch reaction runs over a promoted iron catalyst made from magnetite or from mill scale. So the cyanide that leaches the gold, and the chlorine that makes the hydrochloric acid, and the aluminium in the case all hang off an iron-ore-derived catalyst in a gas works. This is the last of the deliberate cross-branch loops in this file, and it is a real one: the Haber-Bosch catalyst is a 1980s version of the same magnetite that this tree mines for steel.
metal.habers-catalyst.note: The Haber-Bosch catalyst is manufactured from natural magnetite or from mill scale; medium confidence on which predominated in 1982.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: magnetite reduced to alpha-iron, promoted with K2O and Al2O3

facts.label: Link
facts.value: the same magnetite mined for iron ore in this tree

metal.magnetite.name: Magnetite (Fe3O4) and the taconite route
metal.magnetite.description: The other main ore. Magnetite is magnetic, so it can be separated from a low-grade run of rock by magnetic separation, and that changes the economics of the whole business. The Mesabi taconite of Minnesota at 25-32% Fe is ground to 30-45 um and concentrated to 65-70% Fe pellets on a concentrator with a 3 m diameter separator. Krivoy Rog and the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly in the Soviet Union are magnetite districts at 55-65%, worked down to 100 m depths with sublevel stoping. The magnetite is also roasted in a fluidised bed to hematite before magnetic separation, or sintered and reduced.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 25-32% Fe for taconite; 55-65% for the Krivoy Rog magnetite

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: grinding to 30-45 um and magnetic separation; roasting of the concentrate

facts.label: Product
facts.value: taconite pellets at 65-70% Fe

metal.magnetite.roasting.name: Fluidised-bed roasting of magnetite concentrate
metal.magnetite.roasting.description: The Krivoy Rog and Finnish magnetite concentrates were roasted before magnetic separation and before the blast furnace, because a magnetite concentrate that has been oxidised to hematite sinter is far easier to reduce - hematite is the reducible oxide, magnetite is not. A fluidised bed of concentrate with a magnetite-gangue composition can be held at 700-800 C indefinitely without sintering, and it is the only economical way to oxidise a hundred thousand tonnes of fine concentrate. The plant is a tall rectangular refractory-lined box with a bed of nozzles on the floor and water-cooled walls, and its throughput is enormous.
metal.magnetite.roasting.note: Medium confidence; the fluidised-bed roast is standard Soviet and Finnish practice but the parameters are plant-specific.

facts.label: Feed size
facts.value: under 0.1 mm concentrate

facts.label: Product
facts.value: hematite sinter, with the sulphur and the alkalis driven off

metal.magnetite.speciality.name: Oxide pellets and the direct reduction route
metal.magnetite.speciality.description: A different branch of the same ore: magnetite concentrate is the only ore that can be reduced to sponge iron directly, without coke, by a hydrogen-nitrogen mixture at 1100-1200 C in a shaft furnace. That is the MIDOR and HYL processes, which by 1982 were the strategic reserve of the steel industry in the oil shock years - a few per cent of world steel but a hedge, and the reason a Soviet or Brazilian or Venezuelan integrated steelworks would spend a decade building an ore-based direct-reduction plant. It is also the only ore that can be shipped as a pellet and reduced at a distant site without smelting.
metal.magnetite.speciality.note: Direct reduction was a genuine 1980s strategic technology; medium confidence on the 1982 share.

facts.label: Gas
facts.value: natural gas reformed to H2/N2 at 55-65% H2

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: magnetite or hematite pellets, 8-16 mm

facts.label: 1982 share
facts.value: a small percentage of world steel, but a strategic one after 1973

metal.magnetite.underground.name: Deep underground magnetite mining
metal.magnetite.underground.description: The Soviet iron ore industry - Krivoy Rog, the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly, and the Khibiny - mined massive magnetite bodies at 300-1000 m with sublevel stoping, sublevel caving and room-and-pillar, on a scale with no real comparison anywhere else. The magnetite ore was magnetic enough that the mine was lit by the ore's own remanence in the early shafts. It is included to mark that the iron chain has two completely different mining geometries: a 300 m wide surface pit in Western Australia, and a 100 m thick tabular body a kilometre down in Ukraine.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sublevel stoping with delayed fill, sublevel caving, or panel caving

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: 300-1,000 m, with shafts to 1,500 m

metal.magnetite.separators.name: Magnetic separation and the taconite concentrator
metal.magnetite.separators.description: The separator is a rotating drum 1-2.5 m in diameter with a 4-10 pole magnet of 400-1,200 gauss at the drum surface, or a high-gradient can of ferrite pole pieces that achieves 10,000-20,000 gauss on the tips. Slurry flows past and the magnetic grains are held to the drum and carried around until they fall off the other side. With the magnetoferrite in the drum the recovery of a 30-45 um magnetite grain is above 95%. A taconite concentrator at 20-40 Mt a year is one of the largest single streams of water and solids in the world, and the tailings are a billion-tonne deposit in their own right.
metal.magnetite.separators.note: Separator field strengths and grind targets are standard class values; medium confidence.

facts.label: Drum separator
facts.value: 1-2.5 m diameter, 400-1200 gauss at the surface; high-gradient types to 20,000 gauss

facts.label: Grind
facts.value: 30-45 um before separation

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 65-70% Fe, 2-4% silica

metal.magnetite.ferrite-magnets.name: Ferrite magnets in the separator
metal.magnetite.ferrite-magnets.description: A short and important cross-link: the permanent magnet inside a magnetic separator is a ferrite - barium ferrite or strontium ferrite, sintered like the power ferrites but with a different composition and without the permeability requirement. So the ore concentrator that feeds the blast furnace contains ferrite magnets, and the ferrite branch of this file is the same powder metallurgy.
metal.magnetite.ferrite-magnets.note: Nd-Fe-B magnets were commercialised around 1982-84, so an 1982 separator would be ferrite or alnico, not Nd-Fe-B. Medium-high confidence.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: SrFe12O19 or BaFe12O19, sintered; remanence ~0.3-0.4 T

facts.label: In 1982
facts.value: ferrite magnets had largely displaced alnico in small motors and magnetic separators; the modern Nd-Fe-B magnets did not arrive until the 1980s

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrochloric-acid.name: Electronic-grade hydrochloric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrochloric-acid.description: 20-37% HCl purified to about 10N. It was the second half of the piranha mix in some recipes, the dilute etch for the native oxide, the source of the chloride chemistry in the plasma etchants, and the chemical that keeps a fab's chemical room smelling of a swimming pool. It is made by absorbing the HCl gas from a chlorine and hydrogen burner in ultrapure water.
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrochloric-acid.note: The hydrogen for the chlorine and hydrogen burner is chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.

chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.name: Electronic-grade hydrogen peroxide
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.description: 30-50% aqueous H2O2 purified to 99.999% with a total metal content in the tens of parts per billion. It was the other half of the piranha mix and the workhorse cleaner and oxidiser of the wet bench, and by the 1980s it had largely displaced the older sodium hydroxide and nitric acid cleaning recipes. Naphthalene or anthracene is converted to 9,10-anthraquinone over sulphuric acid, hydrogenated to the anthrahydroquinone at 50-60 C and 3-5 bar over palladium on carbon and re-oxidised by air at the same temperature and pressure, in a working solution 0.2-0.5 M in anthraquinone and at 90-95% yield.
chem.fab-chemicals.hydrogen-peroxide.note: Anthraquinone is now usually made from naphthalene; the anthracene route is the older one.

facts.label: Hydrogenation
facts.value: 50-60 C, 3-5 bar H2, Pd on carbon

chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.name: Electronic-grade sulphuric acid
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.description: 96-98% H2SO4 purified to 9N-10N, with a total metal content under 10-100 parts per billion depending on the grade. It was delivered in a fluoropolymer-lined tanker or in a 2,000-litre high-purity container and was used for the piranha clean, for the dehydration bake, for the sulphuric acid-hydrogen peroxide resist strip, and for the oxidation furnace as a carrier gas alternative. Its raw material is the elemental sulphur of a Claus plant, burned in a contact process. The last step to semiconductor grade is an azeotropic or vacuum distillation that takes the acid to 9N, driven by the fact that every metal with a volatility near the acid's has to be pumped out of it; that distillation, and the quartz or Teflon equipment it needed, is why electronic-grade acid cost 20-100 times a technical grade. The piranha clean mixes three parts concentrated sulphuric acid to one of 30% hydrogen peroxide at 80-120 C and strips all organic matter off a wafer, a quartz boat or a process chamber.
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.note: Purification routes for high-purity sulphuric acid have varied (distillation, ion exchange, isopropanol extraction); the general point is that a dedicated purification step exists and that it is expensive.

chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.contact.name: Contact process and sulphur burning
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.contact.description: Sulphur is burned to SO2 in a 900-1,200 C furnace, converted over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst at 420-450 C to SO3, and absorbed in 98% acid to make oleum, which is then diluted. The feedstock in 1983 was overwhelmingly recovered elemental sulphur, because the Claus plant had made it cheap; earlier the pyrites (iron pyrite, FeS2) route was used, and a number of Japanese plants still burned pyrites into their own acid.
chem.fab-chemicals.sulfuric-acid.contact.note: The sulphur feedstock for sulphuric acid is chem.sulfur, and it arrives from the Claus plant. Industrial SO2 oxidation is carried out at about 420-620 C over vanadium(V) oxide catalysts, typically around 450 C, at near-atmospheric pressure. Not established: the 900-1,200 C sulphur burning furnace, the 98% acid oleum step, and the Japanese plants still burning pyrites into their own acid.

chem.sulfur.name: Elemental sulphur (brimstone)
chem.sulfur.description: Bright yellow solid sulphur, one of the four commodities - alongside crude, natural gas and coal - that a 1980s chemical plant could buy. It is used in vulcanisation, in the manufacture of sulphuric acid (which is then used to make titanium dioxide, fertiliser and phosphates), in 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid herbicides, and in the elemental sulphur vulcanisation of rubber. World sulphur production in 1983 was of the order of 8-10 million tonnes a year, essentially all of it recovered from H2S by Claus.

facts.label: World sulphur production 1983
facts.value: ~8-10 Mt/year

chem.solvents.name: Solvents and degreasers in a 1980s plant
chem.solvents.description: Between half and three quarters of the organic solvent used in a 1980s electronics plant went into degreasing, mostly in a hot vapour degreaser. The solvent was almost always a chlorinated hydrocarbon - 1,1,1-trichloroethane or trichloroethylene in Europe and Asia, perchloroethylene in the United States - and the entire decade's regulatory story is the story of removing them. By 1990 in the United States, vapour degreasing with perchloroethylene and trichloroethylene was over, and what replaced it was isopropyl alcohol, N-methylpyrrolidone, or a hydrocarbon.

chem.solvents.regulation.name: Regulation: why the solvent list changed
chem.solvents.regulation.description: Three forces rewrote a 1980s solvent shelf. The US Clean Air Act's 1970 and 1977 amendments and the resulting state implementation plans constrained volatile organic compound emissions, and because a chlorinated degreaser is an emission source, they hit the degreaser directly. The 1983-1989 federal halogenated solvent action set dates for the chlorinated degreasers. And the Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, removed the CFCs and the halon-cleaning gases.
chem.solvents.regulation.note: A regulation or a treaty is a statement about the supply chain, not an operation in it. The whole regulation branch is commentary about why the solvent list changed; its children keep the detail.

chem.solvents.regulation.occupational.name: Occupational exposure limits
chem.solvents.regulation.occupational.description: The other half of the story. In 1980s practice every one of these solvents had a 1980s-era recommended limit, every one of them was under active review by the ACGIH, and the direction of travel through the decade was downward. Perchloroethylene's limit fell from 400 to 100 ppm, trichloroethylene from 200 to 50 ppm, and methylene chloride from 500 to 250 ppm. The engineering response was local exhaust ventilation with a hooded enclosure and a solvent recovery unit, not a respirator. Every one of these solvents carried a recommended limit in the 1980s and every limit was under active review: perchloroethylene fell from 400 to 100 ppm, trichloroethylene from 200 to 50 ppm and methylene chloride from 500 to 250 ppm.
chem.solvents.regulation.occupational.note: The specific 1980s limit values changed year to year and differ between the ACGIH TLV and the OSHA PEL; the values here are indicative of the direction and magnitude of change. Exposure limits and their revision are commentary about the chain, not a step in it.

chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.name: Montreal Protocol
chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.description: Signed in 1987, in force from 1989, and the most effective environmental treaty ever agreed. It phased out CFCs and halons, and it is the reason expanded polystyrene packaging lost its CFC blowing agent and the electronics plant lost its CFC cleaning gas. A C64 in 1983 was packed in a CFC-blown foam box; a C64 in 1993 was not. The most visible effect of the Protocol on a household object was in its packaging: until about 1987 the end caps and fitted inserts in consumer electronics cartons were expanded polystyrene blown with CFC-11, and pentane blowing took over, which made the foam softer and slightly heavier and pushed the structural part of the problem into the carton.
chem.solvents.regulation.montreal.note: The C64's corrugated shipping carton was a paperboard box; the polystyrene foam end caps in consumer electronics packaging of that era commonly used CFC or HCFC blowing agent. A regulation or a treaty is a statement about the supply chain, not an operation in it. Signed 16 September 1987, in force 1 January 1989, with the developed-country CFC phase-out complete by 1996. Not established: CFC-11 as the blowing agent in consumer-electronics polystyrene end caps and fitted inserts until about 1987, and pentane as the replacement that made the foam softer and heavier.

facts.label: Signed
facts.value: September 1987 (Montreal)

facts.label: In force
facts.value: 1 January 1989

chem.solvents.regulation.epa.name: US EPA VOC and solvent rules
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.description: The 1970 Clean Air Act amendments listed chlorinated solvents as hazardous air pollutants, and the states' implementation plans in the early 1980s put specific limits on degreaser emissions. New Jersey's solvent programme in the early 1980s was the strictest of them and effectively banned chlorinated degreasers in much of the state. The federal halogenated solvent action followed, banning trichloroethylene vapour degreasing by 1990.
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.note: US solvent regulation is jurisdiction-specific and layered; the dates above are the commonly cited anchors rather than a single statute. A regulation or a treaty is a statement about the supply chain, not an operation in it.

chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.name: The 1980s substitution: isopropanol, NMP, hydrocarbons
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.description: What actually replaced the chlorinated degreasers, and why it took about ten years rather than two. The candidates were isopropyl alcohol, N-methylpyrrolidone, and increasingly hydrocarbon solvents and aqueous detergents. Each was available, each worked, and none of them was free: isopropanol is flammable, NMP has reproductive toxicity concerns, and hydrocarbons have a low flash point too. The substitution was driven by regulation and by the fact that a chlorinated degreaser needed a permit and an oxygen emission permit and a reporting line to the regulator, and by nothing else at all. The substitution was easy because it was a move along an existing supply chain: isopropyl alcohol sat next to the acetone plant in a complex that already had propylene, and the chlorinated solvent it replaced was the only one on the list that needed a mercury-catalysed acetylene route or a chlorine plant to make.
chem.solvents.regulation.epa.substitutes.note: This node summarises a substitution whose timetable varied by country and by sector; it is a direction-of-travel statement rather than a dated claim. The substitution of isopropanol, NMP and hydrocarbons for the chlorinated solvents is a statement about what industry did.

chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.name: Xylene, toluene and hexane
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.description: The hydrocarbon solvents. Xylene is the classic silkscreen and coatings solvent and it is what the screen printing ink of a PCB is thinned with. Toluene was the coatings and adhesive solvent. Hexane (extracted from the light ends by solvent extraction with furfural or NMP) was the degreaser for precision metalwork and the extraction solvent for the edible oils. All three are refinery fractions, and they are also the most flammable solvents on the shelf. Furfural (161 C) and NMP (202 C) were the classical solvents for separating aromatics from paraffins in a refinery, both displaced from most of their other duties during the 1970s and 1980s by better solvents and by pressure-swing and adsorption processes.
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.note: The same two solvents appear in chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby and in the solvent replacement business.

chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.white.name: White spirit and mineral spirits
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.white.description: A petroleum distillate boiling 150-200 C - roughly C8-C12 - sold as the standard paint and stencil solvent. It was the cheapest coating solvent there was and it was used in the silkscreen shop, in the stencil shop and in the assembly shop's fixture cleaning. Its defect was the same defect as xylene's: flash point around 30-40 C, which means it belongs in a room with no open flame and a bonded-earth tank.
chem.solvents.aromatic-hydrocarbon.white.note: White spirit definitions vary by standard; the 150-200 C range and the flash point are representative.

facts.label: Flash point
facts.value: about 30-40 C (typical)

chem.solvents.other-oxygenated.name: Ketones, esters and glycol ethers
chem.solvents.other-oxygenated.description: The rest of the 1980s solvent shelf: methyl ethyl ketone and methyl isobutyl ketone (the latter made by condensing acetone to diacetone alcohol and then hydrogenating), ethyl acetate and isobutyl acetate, propylene glycol ethers, and dimethylformamide. Each had a niche - the ketones for coatings, the esters for cleaning, the glycol ethers for the controlled evaporation of a coating, DMF for the film and fibre industries.

chem.solvents.acetone.name: Acetone
chem.solvents.acetone.description: Propanone, boiling 56 C. It was the general cleaning solvent for glass, for the epoxy residues of a coil winding operation, and for some stencil and screen operations, and it is the solvent in the acetylene absorption step of the acetylene process and in the electrophotography of copying. It came out of the cumene process and the acetone cyanohydrin process, both of which are propylene plants.
chem.solvents.acetone.note: About 83% of acetone is made by the cumene process and about a third of world supply is used as a solvent. Not established: the 56 C boiling point, the 2.5-13% flammable range, and the use for the epoxy residues of a coil winding.

facts.label: Flammable range
facts.value: 2.5-13% in air

chem.ethanol.name: Ethanol
chem.ethanol.description: C2H6O, boiling 78.4 C. In 1980s electronics it was a solvent and a cleaning fluid for a few specialist applications, and it was the fuel additive competing with MTBE for the octane that lead had given up. Chemically it can be made either by hydrating ethylene over phosphoric acid at 300 C and 60-70 bar, or by fermenting sugar. Both routes existed in 1983; the fermentation route made most of the world's ethanol in that decade because it was cheaper. The synthetic route hydrates ethylene with steam over phosphoric acid on silica at 280-330 C and 60-70 bar for 4-6% ethanol per pass with the off-gas recycled; the limit is thermodynamic, since the reaction is an equilibrium, and the industry spent decades on catalysts and on pervaporation and extractive distillation to get around it. Sugar from cane, beet or starch is fermented by yeast at 30-35 C for two to three days and rectified to 95% or dehydrated to absolute.

facts.label: Hydration conditions
facts.value: 280-330 C, 60-70 bar, H3PO4 on silica

chem.isopropanol.kpo.name: KPO process (from propylene)
chem.isopropanol.kpo.description: Propylene plus acetone gives propylene oxide; propylene oxide isomerises to acetone over a base catalyst; acetone plus hydrogen is hydrogenated to isopropanol. The isomerisation-hydrogenation loop is the unit that makes the process economical, and the 1970s introduction of the low-temperature isomerisation catalysts was what made the KPO route beat the older acetone-hydrogenation route on the balance sheet. About 0.6 t of acetone per tonne of isopropanol is circulated and has to be bought in or made on site, so an isopropanol plant without an acetone source was not viable; that is why the isopropanol business grew up attached to cumene plants, and why the electronics cleaner's supply chain in 1983 ran back through cumene, phenol and the cracker.
chem.isopropanol.kpo.note: The KPO acetone circulation ratio is commonly quoted around 0.6 t/t; exact values depend on the loop design.

chem.solvents.cfc.name: CFCs and HCFCs (halons and freons)
chem.solvents.cfc.description: Trichlorofluoromethane (CFC-11, boiling 23.8 C) and trichloro-1,2,2-trifluoroethane (CFC-113, boiling 48 C) were the 1980s cleaners, refrigerants and foam blowing agents, and CFC-11 was the blowing agent in expanded polystyrene packaging until the late 1980s. In 1983 there was no regulation on them at all; by 1987 the Montreal Protocol had been signed and by 1989 the phase-out of the developed countries had begun.
chem.solvents.cfc.note: CFCs are useful solvents and their boiling points make them suitable as refrigerants. Not established: the specific boiling points of 23.8 C for CFC-11 and 48 C for CFC-113, and CFC-11 as the expanded-polystyrene blowing agent until the late 1980s.

chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.name: CFC synthesis from chloroform
chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.description: CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) is chloroform plus hydrogen fluoride in an antimony halide catalyst at 50-100 C; CFC-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane) is carbon tetrachloride plus hydrogen fluoride. Both therefore start from the chlorination of methane - the same methane the plastics industry buys - and both end in the ozone layer. The chain from a gas field to a chlorofluorocarbon is four steps long and it took twenty years of argument before anything was done about it.

chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.methane-.name: Methane chlorination
chem.solvents.cfc.cfc-synthesis.methane-.description: Chlorine plus methane at 250-400 C gives chloromethane, and further chlorination gives chloroform and carbon tetrachloride. The chlorination is a free-radical chain reaction in a fluidised bed, and the product is a mixture that has to be distilled. The chloroform route to CFC-11 is therefore a natural gas route: methane, chlorine, fluorine - and fluorine is from fluorspar, the same rock as the HF that etched a silicon wafer. Methylene chloride, chloroform, carbon tetrachloride, the trichloroethane degreaser, vinyl chloride monomer and epichlorohydrin all start from the same brine electrolysis, and one electrochemical cell in a chemical park supplies the chlorine atom that appears in a dozen different industrial molecules.

chem.solvents.methylene-chloride.name: Dichloromethane (methylene chloride)
chem.solvents.methylene-chloride.description: CH2Cl2, boiling at 40 C, made by chlorinating methane to chloromethane and then to dichloromethane, or by the chlorination of formaldehyde. It was the fastest-evaporating chlorinated solvent and was used for paint stripping, for the epoxy and flux residues that a slow solvent would not remove, and in place of perchloroethylene in some cleaning operations. Its 1980s regulatory moment came at the end of the decade, when the US EPA designated it a hazardous air pollutant and set a phase-out of its use in degreasing and in the aerosol propellant market.

chem.solvents.perchloroethylene.name: Tetrachloroethylene (perchloroethylene)
chem.solvents.perchloroethylene.description: Cl2C=CCl2, boiling at 119 C, made by chlorinating ethylene to 1,2-dichloroethane and then to tetrachloroethane followed by chlorination and dehydrochlorination, or by the oxychlorination route. It was the American electronics degreaser of choice because it dissolves grease and flux residue and does not evaporate as fast as 1,1,1-trichloroethane. It is the clearest case in this file of a solvent killed by regulation rather than by performance: the US EPA's 1984 halogenated solvent rule set a phase-out schedule for vapour degreasing - all sources by 1989, with the smaller degreasers going first - and perchloroethylene was also being restricted as an air pollutant.
chem.solvents.perchloroethylene.note: The exact sub-schedules of the US halogenated solvent rule (1984) had tiered deadlines by source size; the 1989 completion date is the one usually quoted.

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: non-flammable in air

facts.label: US EPA phase-out of vapour degreasing
facts.value: small sources from 1985-1986, all sources by 1989

chem.solvents.trichloroethylene.name: Trichloroethylene (1,1,2-TCE)
chem.solvents.trichloroethylene.description: Boiling at 87 C, made from acetylene by chlorination to tetrachloroethane followed by dehydrochlorination. It has excellent solvency for grease and for the epoxy and phenolic residues of an electronics line, and it is also a solvent for the vapour degreaser that handles the cleaned parts. It is a suspected carcinogen, and the United States removed it from vapour degreasing in 1990 under the federal halogenated solvent rule; by then the replacement across the industry was largely done. The original industrial route to this degreaser: acetylene chlorinated to tetrachloroethane and then dehydrochlorinated, still the route in much of the world in 1980. It is the acetylene-HCl chemistry of vinyl chloride with a different degree of chlorination.
chem.solvents.trichloroethylene.note: The US prohibition dates: the halogenated solvent rulemaking began in 1983 and the prohibition on TCE vapour degreasing took effect in 1990. Trichloroethylene remained widely used outside the US into the 1990s.

facts.label: Flammable range
facts.value: ~8-11% in air (with an oxygen-enriched flammability)

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: 1,1,1-Trichloroethane from acetylene
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: The synthesis that links a degreaser to a natural gas field. Acetylene plus HCl over a mercuric chloride catalyst gives vinylidene chloride, CH2=CCl2, and chlorinating that with chlorine gives 1,1,1-trichloroethane. Both steps are the same chemistry, and the same catalyst, as the vinyl chloride process - and therefore so are the same upstream, the same natural gas and the same mercury liability. Vinylidene chloride plus chlorine at 20-50 C gives 1,1,2-trichloroethane first and then 1,1,1-trichloroethane, separated by distillation.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: Mercury catalyst and its recovery
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: HCl is adsorbed onto a mercuric chloride-charcoal catalyst and acetylene adds across it. The catalyst is what makes the chemistry work and what makes the plant a mercury emitter, and the 1980s answer was a mercury recovery system: the reactor effluent was stripped with an acid stream, the mercury concentrated to a recoverable 10-20% solution, and that solution taken back to the catalyst maker. It is the same engineering problem and the same answer as the PVC plant's, for the same reason.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.name: Activated charcoal support
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.description: A 2-4 mm charcoal pellet, impregnated with mercuric chloride and dried. Activated charcoal is made by carbonising wood or coal at 800-1,000 C and steam activating it, so it is - like the rosin in the solder flux - a forestry product. The charcoal support in the degreaser's ancestor chemistry is therefore, like almost everything else in this file, something dug up or grown and then refined.
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.vinylidene.note: Activated charcoal manufacture by steam activation of a carbonised precursor is standard; the specific precursor used for this catalyst is not known here.

chem.solvents.trichloroethane.name: 1,1,1-Trichloroethane (methyl chloroform)
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.description: CH3CCl3, boiling at 74 C, a non-flammable solvent that was the standard degreaser for precision metalwork and electronics through the 1950s to the 1980s. It was made from acetylene by hydrochlorination to vinylidene chloride and then chlorination to 1,1,1-trichloroethane - so it shares its whole upstream with vinyl chloride and with natural gas. It is toxic to the liver and kidney, mildly carcinogenic, and it was banned as a non-essential aerosol propellant in the United States in 1987 and phased out as a degreaser through the late 1980s and 1990s.
chem.solvents.trichloroethane.note: The flammability of 1,1,1-trichloroethane is a special case: it is non-flammable in air but burns in oxygen-enriched atmospheres, which is a hazard in a large open vapour degreaser. Exposure limits in the early 1980s were under active revision.

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: non-flammable in the usual range (flammable limits ~6-13% with an oxygen-rich atmosphere)

facts.label: 1980s occupational limit
facts.value: 200 ppm 8-hour TWA (ACGIH), with a 300 ppm ceiling

chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.name: The vapour degreaser
chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.description: A tank of boiling solvent with a cold condenser coil above it. Parts are lowered into the vapour, the vapour condenses on the part and washes the grease off, the condensate runs back into the boil tank, and the distilled clean solvent is pumped to the sump. It was astonishingly effective and astonishingly cheap, and it filled a plant with vapour - which is why it was also the plant's largest solvent loss and its largest occupational and air-emission exposure. A large plant had three or four machines with 20-40 litre tanks. The tank runs continuously with a boiling sump and a distilled-solvent reservoir, and in practice 5-20% of the charge had to be replaced each month through dragout, evaporation and the azeotroping of oil and water back into the tank.

facts.label: Monthly solvent make-up
facts.value: ~5-20% of tank charge

chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.condenser.name: The condenser and the tank
chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.condenser.description: The machine has two working parts: a boiling sump at the bottom that supplies the vapour, and a water-cooled coil above it that condenses the vapour and drips it back clean. The whole design depends on the vapour being kept out of the room, so the machine had a lid and a draught, and the lid was opened to put the parts in - which is exactly when the vapour left. A 20-40 litre tank boiled away 1-3 litres of solvent a day in a well-run plant, and that vapour was the emission the regulator was measuring. Three losses ran at once - evaporation out of the open tank, drag-out on the parts and carry-over into the room ventilation - and the 1980s answers were a lid that stayed shut, a water-cooling coil with more area, a basket that dripped over the tank rather than the floor and, at the largest sites, a vapour condenser returning condensate to the distilled reservoir.

facts.label: Typical unrecovered loss
facts.value: 1-3 L/day from a 20-40 L machine

facts.label: Worst-case make-up
facts.value: up to 20% of tank charge per month

chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.ultrasoni.name: Ultrasonic cleaner
chem.solvents.vapour-degreaser.ultrasoni.description: A tank of hot solvent or water with a 20-80 kHz transducer. In 1983 the electronics plant used ultrasonic cleaning before the vapour degreaser for fine work - the watch crystals, the gears, the small press-fit parts - because a vapour degreaser will not clean a crevice and an ultrasonic tank will. It is also the machine that put solvent into the ultrasonic cleaner market, where 1,1,1-trichloroethane and perchloroethylene were the usual fills.

chem.abs.name: ABS resin plant, and the C64 case
chem.abs.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene is not a copolymer but a polymer blend: a SAN matrix with a grafted polybutadiene rubber phase dispersed in it as 0.1-10 micron particles. Making it is four separate unit operations - make the rubber, graft styrene and acrylonitrile onto it, make the matrix, blend and pelletise - and then a fifth that most people forget, drying. The C64's case, its keyboard surround and the beige plastic of its keys are this material.
chem.abs.note: The two feedstock edges make this branch terminate at the barrel: ABS is made of naphtha, and naphtha is a fraction of light sour crude. It also reaches butadiene, styrene and acrylonitrile through the three children below.

c64.case.abs-resin.phthalo-blue.name: Phthalocyanine blue pigment
c64.case.abs-resin.phthalo-blue.description: Copper phthalocyanine (PB15), an intensely coloured, heat-stable, lightfast blue used for the cool grey-blue tones on some cases. Copper plus four phthalonitrile rings, assembled in a violent exotherm.

facts.label: Colour index
facts.value: Pigment Blue 15 (PB15)

facts.label: Form used
facts.value: PB15:3 (non-flocculating / gamma form)

c64.case.abs-resin.phthalic-anhydride.name: Phthalic anhydride
c64.case.abs-resin.phthalic-anhydride.description: Made by air oxidation of o-xylene over vanadia-titania catalysts at ~450 C. It is the classic route to phthalocyanine pigments and to glycidyl ester epoxy resins.
c64.case.abs-resin.phthalic-anhydride.note: Partly established, and in part in conflict: the source gives vanadium pentoxide as the catalyst, not vanadia-titania, and puts the o-xylene oxidation at about 320-400 C, not the 400-460 C and ~450 C quoted here. The reactor type is not stated by the source at all.

facts.label: Reactor
facts.value: fixed-bed or fluidised-bed, 400-460 C

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: vanadia-titania

c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene.name: o-Xylene
c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene.description: One of the three xylene isomers separated out of the mixed aromatics from the reformer by adsorption (UOP Parex-type) or by distillation. The ortho isomer is the one that gets oxidised to phthalic anhydride.
c64.case.abs-resin.o-xylene.note: The o-xylene to phthalic anhydride step is established; the separation route is not. The source describes o-xylene as produced by cracking petroleum, which affords a distribution of aromatic compounds including the xylene isomers, with m-xylene isomerized to o-xylene, and does not describe an adsorption unit separating the isomers. A Parex-type unit is understood to adsorb the para isomer and leave the ortho and meta isomers behind, so it does not by itself isolate o-xylene.

c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separati.name: C8 aromatics separation (UOP Parex)
c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separati.description: Para-xylene is selectively adsorbed from the mixed C8 aromatics onto a zeolite molecular sieve, desorbed with a purge, leaving o- and m-xylene. It is a swinging adsorption unit with hundreds of adsorbent beds and rotating valves.
c64.case.abs-resin.c8-aromatics-separati.note: Not established: the sorbent grade, the number of beds and the 96-99% para-xylene recovery figure, and that a 1982 ABS supplier used a Parex unit at all. No encyclopaedia article covers the Parex process, and the C64 own documents say nothing about the petrochemical chain feeding the resin.

facts.label: Sorbent
facts.value: X/Y zeolite molecular sieve

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: ~96-99% para-xylene recovery

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: mixed C8 aromatics from the reformer

chem.abs.other-polymers.name: Other polymers in and around a C64
chem.abs.other-polymers.description: A 1983 consumer electronic device used perhaps eight different engineering plastics and two rubbers. This branch traces each of them to its monomer, because they all come out of the same crackers, the same benzene and the same phenol. Each is a node with its own subtree; chem.pvc, chem.epoxy, chem.rubber, chem.polyester and chem.silicone are the ones other parts of this tree reference.

chem.thermosets.name: Phenolic and amino thermosets
chem.thermosets.description: The two oldest synthetic plastics, still in a 1983 machine in the places where a thermoplastic will not do: phenolic for the switch and socket housings and the old-style bakelite knobs, and urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde for the white insulating parts, the plug bodies and the coil-formers. Both are condensation networks: once cured they do not melt, and they are made from phenol or from urea, which comes from the same cumene and ammonia chain as everything else in this file.

chem.thermosets.urea-formaldehyde.name: Urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde
chem.thermosets.urea-formaldehyde.description: Urea condensed with formaldehyde gives a thermoset used for the white insulation of plugs, sockets and coil formers, and melamine gives the tougher, heat-resistant version used for the panel fittings. Both are white, both are cheap, and both are moisture-sensitive, which is the defect that kept them out of anything structural. The urea comes from ammonia and carbon dioxide - the Haber-Bosch product - so this is a nitrogen branch rather than a hydrocarbon one. 2NH3 plus CO2 at 180-220 C and 15-25 bar gives ammonium carbamate, which dehydrates to urea, and the ammonia comes from the Haber-Bosch loop fed by steam-reformed natural gas: a white appliance plug of 1983 is, four steps back, a gas field.

chem.thermosets.phenolic.name: Phenolic resin (phenol-formaldehyde)
chem.thermosets.phenolic.description: Phenol condensed with formaldehyde under acid (novolac, with hexamine as the curing agent) or under base (resol, self-curing). Bakelite, patented in 1907, was the first wholly synthetic plastic. In 1980s electronics it was in the switchgear, the relay covers and the phenolic laminate (paper or cotton cloth in phenolic resin) for the low-cost circuit boards and for the insulating barriers in a power supply.

chem.thermosets.phenolic.hexamine.name: Hexamethylenetetramine (hexamine)
chem.thermosets.phenolic.hexamine.description: Formaldehyde plus ammonia, and it does double duty: it is the curing agent for novolac phenolic and it is a slow accelerator and a decomposition source of formaldehyde in rubber compounds. It is one of the few molecules in this file that reaches into three unrelated chemistries.

chem.thermosets.phenolic.formaldehyde.name: The formaldehyde in a phenolic
chem.thermosets.phenolic.formaldehyde.description: Methanol oxidised to formaldehyde over silver at 600-700 C. The same formaldehyde as the acetal plastics, from the same methanol, from the same synthesis gas. Phenolic resin and POM sitting a few hundred metres apart in a 1980s chemical park is not a coincidence; both are formaldehyde chemistry.

chem.pom.formaldehyde.name: Formaldehyde from methanol
chem.pom.formaldehyde.description: Methanol plus a controlled amount of oxygen over silver at 600-700 C, giving 25-35% formaldehyde in air (the Formox process), then concentrated to 60-70%. The methanol comes from synthesis gas, so this is a coal-or-gas-to-methanol-to-formaldehyde chain rather than a direct petroleum one - although in a 1980s plant the methanol would typically have been made from natural gas. Methanol plus about 0.4 mol of oxygen per mole over silver gauze at 600-700 C gives 25-35% formaldehyde at above 90% selectivity, in a packed bed of thousands of tubes.

facts.label: Product formaldehyde
facts.value: 25-35% in air (Formox)

chem.pom.name: POM (acetal homopolymer and copolymer)
chem.pom.description: Polyoxymethylene, made by polymerising formaldehyde - from the oxidation of methanol - either with an acetic anhydride chain transfer (giving the homopolymer, Delrin) or with a small amount of a diacetate comonomer (giving the Celcon-type copolymer). It is the 1980s precision engineering plastic: gears, cams, hinges, tolerance rings and the moving parts in a mechanism. The homopolymer route runs formaldehyde with acetic anhydride, the growing chain's hydroxyl end reacting with the anhydride to give an acetoxy end that stops polymerisation; the copolymer route uses formaldehyde with a 2-4% fraction of a methylol-substituted diacetate so the chain stops at an inert C-O-C end.
chem.pom.note: Acetal chemistry is standard; the exact comonomer loadings vary by grade.

chem.pom.uses.name: Where POM sat in a 1983 machine
chem.pom.uses.description: Small precision parts: the gear and cam of a fan, the hinges and catches, the insulator of a switch mechanism, the arm of a relay. In a 1983 home computer it was present in tens of grams at most, but it was there because nothing else moulded to a 0.05 mm tolerance with a low friction coefficient.
chem.pom.uses.note: POM use in a C64 is likely but small and not documented in the sources used here. Where POM sat in a 1983 machine is a statement about the machine, not a substance.

chem.rubber.name: Elastomers: natural rubber, neoprene, EPDM
chem.rubber.description: Three rubbers for three different jobs in and around a 1983 machine: natural rubber for the feet and plinths and the moulded grips, neoprene for gaskets and the flexible cable jacket, and EPDM for the cable's weather-resistant insulation. The C64's case feet are elastomer pads stuck to the underside of the case, and they are the only rubber on the outside of the machine.

chem.rubber.epdm.name: EPDM
chem.rubber.epdm.description: Ethylene copolymerised with a diene (norbornene or a cyclic diene), the diene content giving the vulcanisable double bonds. It has no unsaturation in the main chain, so it is ozone-resistant and will not crack in sunlight, which is why it replaced natural rubber in weather-exposed cable insulation and in the C64's power cord as the flexible jacket material of preference.
chem.rubber.epdm.note: The ethylene comes from the cracker: chem.ethylene.

chem.rubber.neoprene.name: Neoprene (polychloroprene)
chem.rubber.neoprene.description: Chloroprene polymerised in emulsion at 40 C. It is oil-resistant, weather-resistant and flame-resistant, which makes it the rubber for gaskets, for the flexible jacket of a power cord, and for the cable's outer sheath when the cable is not PVC. It is made from acetylene and chlorine through vinylacetylene and dichloroacetylene - one more route that ends in acetylene, and therefore in natural gas. Acetylene dimerises to vinylacetylene, which chlorinates to 1,2-dichloro-2-butene; dehydrochlorination gives chloroprene, which polymerises in emulsion at 40 C.
chem.rubber.neoprene.note: Neoprene's process chemistry is standard; the intermediate toxicity warnings are well established.

chem.rubber.natural.name: Natural rubber (cis-1,4-polyisoprene)
chem.rubber.natural.description: Field latex tapped from Hevea brasiliensis, coagulated, smoked and pressed into bales. In 1983 world production was of the order of 3.0-3.5 million tonnes a year, two thirds of it in Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. It is cis-1,4-polyisoprene with a glass transition near -70 C, so it is the most resilient rubber at room temperature, and it needs vulcanisation with sulphur because the cis double bond is what makes it elastic. A quarter-spiral cut is made into the tapping panel about every other day and the latex is collected in a cup; about 30% of a mature tree's latex can be taken without killing it over a 25-30 year tapping life. Before the 1930s the whole article had to be vulcanised in the mould; by the 1930s the compound could be prevulcanised in a mixer - deliberately introducing some crosslink - so it was a flowable, uncured-on-the-surface material that could be shaped and then cured in the mould. Heated with sulphur and an accelerator, a thiuram or a sulphonamide, the cis double bonds get a short sulphur bridge between neighbouring chains: crosslinked, so the chains can no longer slide.
chem.rubber.natural.note: World natural rubber production in the early 1980s was around 3 million tonnes a year; the figure is approximate.

chem.silicone.name: Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane)
chem.silicone.description: The only engineering polymer whose backbone is not carbon. Built from chlorosilanes made by the Rochow direct process - silicon plus methyl chloride over copper at 280-350 C - then hydrolyzed and condensed. In 1983 silicones were everywhere in electronics: as RTV sealing gaskets, as conformal coatings and encapsulants, as dielectric greases for the variable capacitors, and as the flexible key domes.

chem.silicone.polymer.name: Silicone rubber and fluids
chem.silicone.polymer.description: The chlorosilane is hydrolyzed to a silanol and condensed with a silanol-terminated chain stopper, giving a silicone oil (low viscosity) or, with reinforcing silica and peroxide cure, a silicone rubber (elastomer). The 1980s mix in electronics was dominated by room-temperature-vulcanising silicone - a moisture-cured acetoxy or hydroxyl-terminated compound - because it cures in a fixture without heat, and by the fluorosilicone mould releases.

chem.silicone.polymer.key-domes.name: Conductive elastomer key domes
chem.silicone.polymer.key-domes.description: A switch contact made of a silicone or neoprene elastomer filled with carbon black - or with metal-plated hollow glass spheres - so that the rubber itself conducts. When the dome is pressed it shorts to a printed conductor beneath; the dome's force curve (about 0.5-2 N operating, 8-12 mm travel) is the feel of the keyboard. The conductive filler is a petroleum carbon black or a silvered microsphere, and the elastomer is usually a peroxide-cured silicone or a neoprene, chosen for its fatigue life in millions of actuations.
chem.silicone.polymer.key-domes.note: The C64 keyboard used elastomer-dome membrane technology; the exact elastomer and filler for a given revision are not documented here.

chem.silicone.polymer.conformal-coating.name: Conformal coating
chem.silicone.polymer.conformal-coating.description: A 20-100 micron film of room-temperature-vulcanising silicone brushed or dipped over a populated board, cured in humid air, to keep water, dust, sulfur dioxide and salt off the conductors. In 1980s practice it was used on power supplies and on automotive electronics rather than on consumer boards, and the industry debate was whether a conformal coating is better than a conformal coating removed badly - the rework risk is the problem. The C64's mainboard is generally described as uncoated.
chem.silicone.polymer.conformal-coating.note: Whether a given board was conformal-coated is a plant practice, not a material fact; most consumer boards of this era were not. Conformal coating is a practice described in commentary, not a substance or an operation.

chem.silicone.rochow.name: Rochow direct process
chem.silicone.rochow.description: Metallurgical silicon plus methyl chloride over copper at 280-350 C gives dimethyldichlorosilane. The silicon comes from the quartz and coke reduction that the whole semiconductor industry depends on, so the silicone business and the chip business share an upstream - and share the same four-nines purity problem in their own way. The methyl chloride comes from the natural gas chlorination business, so the silicone plant and the semiconductor plant are both fed by chlorine and by methane.

chem.polyester.name: Polyesters: PET, PBT and unsaturated polyester
chem.polyester.description: Three families that share the same two feedstocks - ethylene glycol or propylene glycol, and a terephthalic or maleic/fumaric acid. PET in 1983 was overwhelmingly a fibre and bottle business, PBT was the engineering thermoplastic, and unsaturated polyester was the resin of the glass-reinforced mouldings. In a 1983 electronic assembly, the polyester was the transformer bobbin insulation, the relay base, the film capacitors, and any glass-filled moulding. PBT is polymerised by transesterification and polycondensation like PET but with butanediol, giving a melting point of about 225 C against PET's 260 C and a faster crystallisation, which is why it is the engineering grade: it sets in a 5-10 mm wall in 5-10 seconds where PET needs a minute.

chem.polyester.unsaturated.name: Unsaturated polyester resin
chem.polyester.unsaturated.description: Maleic anhydride plus propylene glycol condensed to about 1,000-2,000 molecular weight and dissolved in styrene; the crosslinker is styrene itself and the cure is a peroxide (usually methyl ethyl ketone peroxide) at 20-80 C. In the 1980s it was the resin of glass-reinforced moulding compound and of the cast reinforced parts - and it is the resin family most associated with the styrene emission complaints of boat building, which is the same styrene that the ABS matrix uses.
chem.polyester.unsaturated.note: The styrene comes from chem.styrene; the propylene glycol from the propylene and ethylene oxide chains.

chem.polyester.pet.name: PET from ethylene glycol and dimethyl terephthalate
chem.polyester.pet.description: Dimethyl terephthalate plus ethylene glycol transesterified at 180-280 C over an antimony or titanium catalyst, then polycondensed at 270-290 C under 1-50 mbar. The bottleneck is the transesterification methanol coproduct, which is recovered and returned to the terephthalate plant, so the plant is a big methanol recovery column. The route through dimethyl terephthalate rather than terephthalic acid was chosen in the 1970s and 1980s because the acid route's oxidation step had the corrosion and the purity problems; by the late 1980s the acid route had caught up. Para-xylene is oxidised to terephthalic acid over cobalt-manganese acetate at 175-225 C and 15-30 bar, and it is that oxidation rather than the polymerisation which is where the capital in a PET plant sits.

chem.polyester.pet.ethylene-glycol.name: Ethylene glycol
chem.polyester.pet.ethylene-glycol.description: About 2.2 tonnes of ethylene glycol per tonne of PET resin, from the ethylene oxide hydration branch. The glycol is purified to 99.9% because the water it carries ends up as a hydrolysis chain terminator and it is the single largest cause of high-acid-value polyester.

chem.polyester.pet.terephthalic-acid.name: Para-xylene and terephthalic acid
chem.polyester.pet.terephthalic-acid.description: Para-xylene is separated from the C8 aromatics by adsorptive separation (UOP Parex, 4A zeolite) or by crystallisation, then oxidised with air over a cobalt-manganese-acetate catalyst at 175-225 C and 15-30 bar in acetic acid. The para isomer must be more than 99.5% pure because the meta and ortho isomers cannot be polymerised into a useful fibre.
chem.polyester.pet.terephthalic-acid.note: The node is the acid, and the oxidation that makes it is described in the text of the acid itself; the feedstock is the refinery aromatics complex.

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: 175-225 C, 15-30 bar, Co/Mn/Br in acetic acid

chem.polyamide.name: Nylon 6 and nylon 6,6
chem.polyamide.description: The two polyamides that a 1980s machine used for its precision parts. Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine, or nylon 6 from caprolactam which itself comes from phenol. Both are condensation polymers of a diamine and an acid or of a lactam, and both need the phenol-aromatic chain, so both are downstream of the same cracker benzene as the ABS.

chem.polyamide.nylon-6.name: Nylon 6 from caprolactam
chem.polyamide.nylon-6.description: Caprolactam is opened with water at 250-270 C in a hydrolysis-polymerisation reactor under 1-15 bar, giving a nylon 6 with a very narrow molecular weight distribution because the chemistry is a step growth from a single monomer. Nylon 6 is the form used where a low melt viscosity matters, and it was the standard for the textile filament and the carpet fibre trade.

chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.name: Caprolactam from phenol
chem.polyamide.nylon-6.caprolactam.description: Phenol hydrogenated to cyclohexanol, then dehydrogenated to cyclohexanone; cyclohexanone oximation to cyclohexanone oxime; the oxime rearranged with oleum (the Beckmann rearrangement, which expands the ring from six to seven members) to caprolactam, and the ammonium sulphate byproduct stripped and recycled. This is a five-step route from phenol and it is one of the longest petrochemical chains in the C64's ancestry. Phenol is hydrogenated over nickel or palladium at 120-180 C and 10-30 bar to cyclohexanol and dehydrogenated over copper at 250-300 C to cyclohexanone; the phenol comes from cumene and the cumene's propylene from the cracker, so nylon 6 is a third-generation descendant of the naphtha cracker. The Beckmann rearrangement needs concentrated sulphuric acid or oleum and produces 1.1-1.3 tonnes of ammonium sulphate per tonne of caprolactam, which has to be sold as fertiliser - the same sulphuric acid and the same fertiliser market the Claus sulphur plant feeds, which is why the industry was moving to oleum-free rearrangements over solid acid or a zeolite.

facts.label: Ammonium sulphate by-product
facts.value: ~1.1-1.3 t per t caprolactam

chem.polyamide.nylon-66.name: Nylon 6,6 from adipic acid and HMDA
chem.polyamide.nylon-66.description: Adipic acid plus hexamethylenediamine condense to nylon salt at 250-270 C and 10-20 bar in a batch or continuous process, then polymerise at 270-280 C under a small nitrogen pressure. Adipic acid in 1983 came mostly from the oxidation of cyclohexane or of a C4 route with nitric acid; hexamethylenediamine came from adiponitrile hydrogenation or from adipic acid plus ammonia. The 1980s feedstock route was hydrocyanation of butadiene with hydrogen cyanide over a nickel catalyst followed by hydrogenation of both nitriles, which is what made a cracker-based nylon 6,6 possible at all.
chem.polyamide.nylon-66.note: Upstream: chem.butadiene. Nylon 66 is a polycondensation of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid; equal amounts are combined in water and the salt is heated in batches or continuously. Not established: the 250-270 C and 10-20 bar salt conditions, the 270-280 C polymerisation under a small nitrogen pressure, and the butadiene hydrocyanation feedstock route attributed to the 1980s.

facts.label: Polymerisation
facts.value: 270-280 C, low nitrogen pressure

facts.label: Nylon salt
facts.value: equimolar acid + diamine, 250-270 C

chem.polycarbonate.name: Polycarbonate
chem.polycarbonate.description: Bisphenol A polycarbonate, made by the interfacial phosgene route from BPA and phosgene in dichloromethane, then melt polycondensed at 250-290 C. It is the transparent, tough, dimensionally stable engineering plastic of the 1980s, and in electronics it went into connector housings, terminal blocks, relay covers and the housings of the switchgear it replaced metal in. The C64 itself was not made of polycarbonate - the case was ABS - but the material surrounds the machine in the peripherals and in Commodore's later machines, and it shares the bisphenol A and the cumene chain with the epoxy and the polyester. Bisphenol A dissolved in aqueous caustic is reacted with phosgene in dichloromethane at 20-40 C with a tertiary amine catalyst; the chloroformate-terminated oligomer is washed and then polymerised by melt condensation at 250-290 C under 0.1-1 mbar.

facts.label: Interfacial step
facts.value: 20-40 C, dichloromethane, caustic, tertiary amine

chem.polycarbonate.properties.name: Why it was chosen
chem.polycarbonate.properties.description: Amorphous at 100-150% linear retention, glass transition near 145 C, tensile strength 60-70 MPa, and a notched Izod of 8-15 kJ/m2. It is the transparent tough polymer of the 1980s: sunglasses lenses, camera and instrument housings, the disc of a compact disc from 1982, and the dome of the keyboard on some machines. It was also the first engineering polymer to be explicitly targeted at the electronics market as a metal replacement.
chem.polycarbonate.properties.note: The why it was chosen question is the reason polycarbonate is on a C64, not a property of a substance. The glass transition temperature is about 147 C, so this node's 145 C is slightly low, and compact discs are a major polycarbonate market. Not established: the 60-70 MPa tensile strength, the 8-15 kJ/m2 notched Izod, and the 100-150% linear retention figure.

chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.name: Phosgene
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.description: Carbonyl chloride, COCl2, made by oxidising carbon monoxide with chlorine over activated carbon at 100-150 C. It is acutely toxic, and it is one of the reasons the polycarbonate industry of the 1980s was moving toward the non-phosgene route based on bisphenol A carbonate and on the methylene chloride and pyridine route. The bisphenol A it consumes is the same bisphenol A as the epoxy, and the chlorine is the same chlorine.

chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine.name: Chlorine and carbon monoxide
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine.description: Chlorine from brine electrolysis plus carbon monoxide from a reformer or from coke. This is the point at which the chlor-alkali industry - which needs hydrogen to sell its chlorine, and therefore needs natural gas - touches the plastics industry through a molecule with two chlorine atoms and one oxygen.
chem.polycarbonate.phosgene.chlorine.note: Chlorine electrolysis belongs to the chlorine subsystem; the hydrogen requirement is chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.
