chem.epoxy.name: Epoxy: bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin
chem.epoxy.description: DGEBA epoxy is made by hydrolyzing bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin, then dehydrochlorinating to close the epoxide ring. About 800,000-1,000,000 tonnes of epoxy resin were made in 1983, of which the largest single use was the glass-reinforced laminate for printed circuit boards. A C64 has epoxy in its board, in the transformer and coil potting of its power supply, in the die-attach of its chips, and in the adhesive that holds the SID's heatsink tab.

chem.epoxy.uses-c64.name: Epoxy in a C64
chem.epoxy.uses-c64.description: Four places. The board's laminate resin. The power supply's transformer bobbin and coil potting, and the mains filter capacitor's encapsulation. The die attach inside the VIC-II, the SID and the CPU packages, where the chip was bonded to a small ceramic or epoxy header with an epoxy that had to survive 180-260 C without delaminating. And the heatsink adhesive in the SID's tab, which in some designs was a two-part filled epoxy.
chem.epoxy.uses-c64.note: The mass figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate from typical laminate and encapsulation weights.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.name: Curing agents
chem.epoxy.hardeners.description: An epoxy is useless until something cross-links it, and the curing agent decides the properties. Amines (aliphatic triethylenetetramine, cycloaliphatic diamines) give fast cures at room temperature and good mechanical properties; anhydrides give high-temperature cures and excellent electrical insulation, which is why the power supply's transformer potting and the chips' die attach were epoxy; and the phenols and novolacs give the flame-retardant laminates. A primary or secondary amine adds to the strained epoxide ring and that is what starts the cure, and the classic complaint of amine-cured epoxy is amine blush - a sticky hygroscopic film from an atmospheric amine-carbon dioxide reaction with surface epoxy - which is why the die-attach and potting processes of the 1980s used a controlled-amine epoxy with a controlled cure cycle.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.anhydride.name: Anhydride cure
chem.epoxy.hardeners.anhydride.description: A cyclic anhydride (a methyl substituted tetrahydrophthalic or nadic anhydride) catalysed by an amine or a tertiary amine. The cure is slower and needs 150-200 C, but the network is very tight and the dielectric properties are excellent - which is why anhydride epoxy was the potting and the chip-attach system of the 1980s, where a chip sitting on a cured epoxy die attach with a controlled coefficient of thermal expansion was worth the cure temperature.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd.name: 4,4'-Diaminodiphenylmethane (DDM/MDA)
chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd.description: Made by condensing aniline with formaldehyde, it is the first-generation hardener: cheap, and it is the amine that showed up in the early carcinogenicity work on epoxies in the 1970s, which pushed the industry toward DDM's less toxic relatives. It is still in laminates and in the rubber industry as a vulcanisation accelerator.
chem.epoxy.hardeners.ddd.note: The 4,4'-methylenedianiline classification work dates from the 1970s-early 1980s and was a driver of substitution in both epoxy and elastomer applications.

chem.epoxy.hardeners.dds.name: 4,4'-Diaminodiphenyl sulfone (DDS)
chem.epoxy.hardeners.dds.description: The high-temperature laminate hardener: about 80 parts per 100 of DGEBA, cured at 180-200 C. DDS is made by sulphonating diphenyl sulphone, nitrating it to the dinitro compound and reducing the nitro groups - an aniline and chlorobenzene route for the aniline part. It is the hardener in the aerospace laminates and in the higher-temperature grades of FR-4, and it costs several times what the amine does.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.name: Bisphenol A from cumene
chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.description: Two phenol molecules plus acetone, condensed over a strong acid to give 4,4'-isopropylidenediphenol, with the water stripped. In 1983 most BPA was made this way from the cumene process's phenol, and the rest from the older two-step route using bis(4-chlorophenyl) ketone. The 1980s were the period when BPA's endocrine activity was being investigated by accident, and when the epoxy industry began to substitute boron oxides and novolac epoxies to remove it from can linings and bottle resins.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.acetone.name: Acetone as the BPA co-reactant
chem.epoxy.dgeba.bisphenol-a.acetone.description: The BPA reaction is where the case polymer meets the laminate resin: the phenol for BPA comes out of the cumene oxidation that also yields the acetone for the reaction, so the two halves of bisphenol A come from one reactor 20 km apart. The same bisphenol A went into the polycarbonate and the unsaturated polyester of the era.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin.name: Epichlorohydrin
chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin.description: 1-chloro-2,3-epoxypropane: the C3 building block. The documented traditional manufacture is from allyl chloride in two steps - addition of hypochlorous acid to give a mixture of isomeric alcohols, then base treatment to give the epoxide - though a propylene-chlorohydrin route is also described and may have been the one in use in 1983. Which route this plant used is not established: us acid, dehydrochlorinated with a lime slurry - which is the same chlorohydrin chemistry that makes propylene oxide. It is a sensitiser and a carcinogen, and it is the reason the epoxy industry carried the same respiratory-protection regime as the propylene oxide plants.
chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin.note: The chlorohydrin chemistry is chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohydrin. The traditional manufacture of epichlorohydrin is from allyl chloride by addition of hypochlorous acid, not from propylene chlorohydrin. The lime-slurry dehydrochlorination and the propylene-plus-hypochlorous-acid route this node describes are not established here; the chlorohydrin analogy with propylene oxide may still hold, but on the allyl chloride route.

chem.epoxy.dgeba.name: DGEBA (diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A)
chem.epoxy.dgeba.description: The workhorse epoxy: bisphenol A condensed with two moles of epichlorohydrin, giving a resin with an epoxide group at each end of the molecule and epoxide number 172-190 equivalents per 100 g. It is a solid at room temperature (melting 4-12 C for the liquid grades) and it cures into a cross-linked network with anything that has active hydrogen or amino groups.
chem.epoxy.dgeba.note: DGEBA is the bisphenol A diglycidyl ether made from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin. Not established: the 170-190 g/eq epoxide equivalent weight, the 4-12 C melting range of the liquid grades, and the 100 parts resin to 20-60 parts hardener formulation.

facts.label: Typical formulation
facts.value: DGEBA 100 parts, amine or anhydride hardener 20-60 parts

chem.pvc.name: PVC: vinyl chloride and suspension polymerisation
chem.pvc.description: About 3.5 million tonnes of PVC in 1983, of which maybe 5-8% was flexible and the rest rigid. Two-thirds of the monomer came from the oxychlorination of ethylene and the rest from acetylene and HCl. The C64 used it in the power cord's jacket and insulation, in the moulded cable accessories, and in the odd keycap or knob; the stability system matters because unstabilised PVC decomposes at 140 C. Suspension polymerisation in water with a suspending agent is 65-70% of world PVC: VCM dispersed as 0.1-1 mm beads at 50-70 C and 6-12 bar for 5-10 hours to 70-85% conversion.

chem.pvc.uses-c64.name: PVC in a C64
chem.pvc.uses-c64.description: The power cord: a two-core or three-core flexible PVC jacket, typically 1.5-3 mm of wall, with PVC insulation on the conductors and a PVC or PVC/rubber strain relief at the moulded connector. A C64 power cord is a couple of hundred grams of PVC. The keyboard keys and the side vents of the earlier cases were also often PVC or a PVC blend. A C64 whose power supply was the internal one had less of it, because the mains cable went to the brick.
chem.pvc.uses-c64.note: Cable constructions varied by market and by supplier; the jacket material was almost always flexible PVC.

facts.label: Power cord jacket mass
facts.value: ~0.1-0.25 kg of flexible PVC

chem.pvc.plasticiser.name: Plasticisers
chem.pvc.plasticiser.description: A flexible PVC is PVC with 30-60 parts per 100 of a liquid plasticiser, and the plasticiser is where most of the toxicology lived. Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP, DOP) was the standard from the 1950s into the 1990s, made by esterifying phthalic anhydride with 2-ethylhexanol - itself from butyraldehyde or oxo synthesis of propylene and a C6 or C8 fraction. In 1983 there was no accepted evidence of harm at the levels in use, and the reappraisal came later.

chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp.name: Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate
chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp.description: C8H17OOC-C6H4-COOC8H17, 391 g/mol, a colourless liquid with a very slight odour. About 200,000-250,000 tonnes of DEHP a year were made in 1983, most of it for PVC. The C8 alcohol comes from propylene and from ethylene via butyraldehyde, so a PVC cable jacket is a direct consumer of the cracker.
chem.pvc.plasticiser.dehp.note: DEHP production volumes in the early 1980s are order-of-magnitude estimates.

chem.pvc.stabilisation.name: Heat stabilisation, and the lead problem
chem.pvc.stabilisation.description: PVC is unstable above about 140 C: the dehydrochlorination produces HCl, which catalyses more dehydrochlorination, which is why unstabilised PVC cannot be processed at all. The 1980s stabiliser systems were lead salts - dibasic lead phosphite, tribasic lead sulphate, lead stearate - which are excellent scavengers and which put lead into millions of tonnes of consumer product. Calcium-zinc systems based on stearates and organic co-stabilisers were the 1980s technology that began to displace them, and the reason is health regulation rather than performance.

chem.pvc.stabilisation.ca-zn.name: Calcium-zinc stabilisers
chem.pvc.stabilisation.ca-zn.description: Calcium and zinc carboxylates (stearate, hydrostearate) with an organic co-stabiliser such as a beta-diketone or a polyol. Zinc carboxylates are the primary stabilisers and calcium carboxylates are the co-stabilisers that exchange zinc for calcium at the right moment. The 1980s engineering problem was matching the zinc-to-calcium ratio and the lubricant balance so the compound did not plate out on the extruder die, which is a real and stubborn processing problem rather than a trivial substitution.

chem.pvc.stabilisation.lead-stabiliser.name: Tribasic lead sulphate and lead phosphite
chem.pvc.stabilisation.lead-stabiliser.description: The lead salts are cheap, opaque, and superb at scavenging HCl and chelating chlorine. The cost is that lead is a cumulative neurotoxin and PVC was, until recently, a major route of human lead exposure through pipes, and in 1983 the limits on lead in consumer products were tightening. The chemistry is basic: the metal salt of sulphuric or phosphorous acid, made by precipitating the oxide or sulphate onto a lead base.

facts.label: Stabiliser loading in rigid PVC
facts.value: 2-6 parts per 100 resin

chem.pvc.polymerisation.initiator.name: Initiator and chain transfer
chem.pvc.polymerisation.initiator.description: Acyl peroxide or a persulphate at 0.05-0.5%, with a chain transfer agent (often chloroform, tetrachloromethane or an ester) to control molecular weight. The transfer agents are chlorinated for a reason: they also terminate the radicals that would otherwise go on to make chlorinated by-products, and the PVC industry has always been able to sell them.

chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent.name: PVA suspending agent
chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent.description: Partially hydrolysed polyvinyl alcohol at 0.5-2% of the water phase, with a second colloid stabilizer if needed. It is the same PVA chemistry as the suspension polystyrene suspending agent - one more appearance of a polymer from the vinyl acetate chain doing structural work in a different polymer's reactor.
chem.pvc.polymerisation.suspending-agent.note: PVA suspending agents came from the same vinyl acetate hydrolysis used for the emulsion polymerisation of PVAc; the two uses share the chemistry.

chem.pvc.vcm.storage.name: VCM storage and inhibition
chem.pvc.vcm.storage.description: Bulk VCM in a refrigerated atmospheric tank at 10-15 C with a nitrogen blanket, or in a pressure vessel. It is inhibited against polymerisation with a phenolic or an organic peroxide, and it is kept below 50 C because vinyl chloride is a powerful inhibitor of its own polymerisation - a fact the industry discovered painfully, and which turned out to be a safety feature once understood.

chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.name: Acetylene plus HCl (the mercury route)
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.description: Acetylene and anhydrous hydrogen chloride over a mercuric chloride catalyst on charcoal at 20-60 C and 1-2 bar absolute, at 15-25% conversion per pass with 90-95% selectivity. This is the route that ties PVC to natural gas, because acetylene is made from methane. It survives where there is no cracker - in Western Europe, in India, in China and in the Soviet Union - and where there is one, the oxychlorination route is cheaper.
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.note: The acetylene end of this route is chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl-chloride.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.name: Acetylene to vinyl chloride
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.description: The reason the whole acetylene industry existed. Acetylene plus anhydrous hydrogen chloride over a 0.3-0.5% mercuric chloride catalyst on charcoal at 20-60 C and 1-2 bar absolute gives vinyl chloride at 15-25% conversion per pass and 90-95% selectivity, the low conversion forced by the HCl ratio and by the fact that vinyl chloride is a vinylogous acrylate that polymerises readily.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.name: Mercuric chloride catalyst
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.description: Anhydrous HCl is adsorbed onto a mercuric chloride-charcoal catalyst and ethyne adds across it. The catalyst is a genuine environmental liability: mercury lost from a large acetylene plant was tens of kilograms a year, and by the 1980s both West Germany and the Netherlands were restricting mercury emission from chlor-alkali and vinyl chloride plants.
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.to-vinyl.note: Mercury restriction dates vary by country; German and Dutch controls on mercury from chlor-alkali and acetylene plants began in the 1970s and tightened through the 1980s-90s.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: HgCl2 0.3-0.5% on charcoal

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: 1-2 bar absolute

chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury.name: Mercury in the PVC plant
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury.description: The mercury chloride catalyst is a genuine environmental liability. A 1980s European PVC plant was a mercury emitter at tens of kilograms a year, and by the mid-1980s both the German and the Dutch authorities were requiring either catalyst recovery or a switch to the oxychlorination route. The engineering answer, delivered in the 1980s, was a mercury recovery system on the reactor effluent that stripped the mercury into the hydrochloric acid stream and concentrated it to about 20%.
chem.pvc.vcm.acetylene-route.mercury.note: The specific national dates and legal instruments for mercury limits in the PVC industry are jurisdiction-specific; the general direction and the mercury-recovery technology are well established.

chem.pvc.vcm.name: Vinyl chloride monomer
chem.pvc.vcm.description: C2H3Cl, boiling at -13.4 C, so it is a liquid only under pressure. It is a proven human carcinogen (angiosarcoma of the liver), it is flammable from 4-33% in air, and it is the reason the PVC industry of the 1980s had an unusual public health profile. In 1983 world VCM capacity was of the order of 9-10 million tonnes a year. Oxychlorination of ethylene with chlorine and hydrogen chloride over copper(II) chloride at 150-250 C and 4-10 bar gives vinyl chloride at 85-95% selectivity, and the chlorine-to-HCl ratio decides whether the plant makes ethylene dichloride for the chlorinated-solvent business or vinyl chloride.
chem.pvc.vcm.note: Vinyl chloride monomer is among the largest petrochemicals, is a flammable gas and is a proven carcinogen; angiosarcoma of the liver was reported from 1974. Not established: the -13.4 C boiling point, the 4-33 vol% flammable range, the 9-10 Mt/yr 1983 world capacity, and the 150-250 C, 4-10 bar CuCl2 oxychlorination at 85-95% selectivity.

facts.label: World VCM capacity 1983
facts.value: ~9-10 Mt/yr

facts.label: Flammable range
facts.value: 4-33 vol% in air

chem.abs.c64-case.name: The Commodore 64 case, in ABS
chem.abs.c64-case.description: About 350-400 g of ABS: a two-shot moulding, the beige or brown textured skin over the structural frame, with the moulding texture itself - a fine leather grain applied by the tool's EDM process - as the only decoration. Behind the front bezel there is a metal RF shield and a plastic shield can, and the vents are moulded through the wall. Everything visible on the outside of a C64, apart from the keycaps and the badge, is this one polymer.
chem.abs.c64-case.note: The C64 case material is described as ABS in the plastics trade of the period; the precise grade is not on the record.

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: two-shot / multi-cavity injection moulding with EDM texture

chem.abs.grade.name: The ABS grade the C64 case used
chem.abs.grade.description: A high-impact, general purpose injection moulding grade in the family of the low-cis, medium-graft commercial ABS sold as Cycolac 2800 or equivalent, with a notched Izod impact strength of 150-250 J/m and a moulding shrinkage of 0.4-0.7%. The UL 94 flammability rating would be HB or 2A: a home computer in a living room could not be in a 0.4 mm wall V-0 plastic, so the case had to be thicker than the V-0 rating allowed.
chem.abs.grade.note: The specific commercial grade used for the C64 case is not documented in the sources used here; the description above is the class of material its mechanical and cosmetic requirements imply.

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB or 2A at typical wall thickness

chem.abs.regrind.name: Regrind
chem.abs.regrind.description: Runner, sprue and rejected mouldings are chopped and fed back. A 1980s injection moulder typically ran 5-10% regrind in the case and up to 20% in less critical parts, on the grounds that a second heat history costs some molecular weight and some impact strength. Commodore's own case moulding ran regrind; the amount is not documented and the C64's impact strength specification is a good indication of how much.
chem.abs.regrind.note: Regrind fractions are practice rather than specification; a moulding plant's own rules governed this.

facts.label: Typical regrind content
facts.value: 5-10% (up to 20% in non-critical parts)

chem.abs.additives.name: Compounding additives
chem.abs.additives.description: Colour and processing aids, dosed into the twin screw before the vacuum vent so that anything volatile is stripped there: 1-3% of a pigment masterbatch, 0.1-0.5% of an external lubricant (a metal stearate, usually zinc or calcium stearate or an EBS wax), and a UV stabiliser. The beige of the C64's case is a pigment on top of the natural colour of the polymer; the grey of a later model is a carbon black or a titanium dioxide blend.

chem.abs.additives.stearate.name: Metal stearate release agent
chem.abs.additives.stearate.description: Calcium stearate or zinc stearate, 0.1-0.5%, dosed to stop the ABS sticking to the screw and the die, and to help the mould release. The stearates come from stearic acid (from tallow or from a C18 fraction) neutralised with lime; the metal itself is the only heavy metal routinely added to a consumer plastic.

chem.abs.additives.pigment-masterbatch.name: Pigment masterbatch
chem.abs.additives.pigment-masterbatch.description: A pre-dispersed concentrate - typically titanium dioxide (rutile, for weather resistance), carbon black, ultramarine blue, phthalocyanine green, or an iron oxide - at 20-60% loading in an ABS or LDPE carrier, dosed at 1-3% into the compounding line. A masterbatch exists because a pigment dropped into a twin screw as a powder will not disperse, and undispersed pigment is visible as specks in the moulding.

chem.abs.drying.desiccant.name: Molecular sieve desiccant
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.description: A 3A or 4A zeolite in a heated bed at 200-350 C that adsorbs water to below 0.1% of its own weight, with a purge cycle on a hot air or nitrogen sweep. The same zeolite family as the cracker drier and the FCC catalyst, and in the 1980s this was the standard way every plastic was dried before moulding.

chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.name: The 3A molecular sieve itself
chem.abs.drying.desiccant.molecular-siev.description: The desiccant in the dryer is a synthetic zeolite with a 3 angstrom pore opening, which admits the water molecule (kinetic diameter about 2.65 angstrom) and excludes anything bigger. That single geometric fact is why a molecular sieve can dry a plastic to 200 ppm: it is a molecular filter, not an absorber. The zeolite is made by hydrothermal synthesis from an alumina gel, a silica source and an organic template at 150-200 C and autogenous pressure in an autoclave - and then the template is burned out of the pore at 500-550 C, which is what opens the pores. A zeolite powder cannot go in a dryer bed - it dusts and it fluidises - so it is formed into 2-4 mm extruded pellets with about 4% of clay and silica binder, and the binder is the part that stops the pellet taking up water itself, because the bed's capacity is only 20-22% of its own weight. Alumina, sodium silicate and sodium hydroxide are gelled, seeded with a few crystals of the product zeolite and heated in an autoclave at 150-200 C for 24-96 hours, and nucleation and growth control is the whole art - which is why crystal size distribution is a commercial specification and a 2-micron zeolite for a cracker drier costs more than a 50-micron one.

facts.label: Water capacity
facts.value: 20-22 wt% of the pellet

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: ~4% clay and silica

facts.label: Synthesis
facts.value: 150-200 C, 24-96 h, autogenous pressure

chem.abs.drying.name: Drying
chem.abs.drying.description: ABS is hygroscopic: its equilibrium moisture content is about 0.3-0.4% by weight, and a wet pellet in a mould produces a part with silver streaks on the surface, voids, and a lower impact strength than the design assumed. The moulding shop therefore dried the pellets at 80-90 C for 2-4 hours in a dehumidifying dryer before every moulding run. This is the step that separates a plastics engineer from a chemist and it is done with the pellets in a hopper with a 3A molecular sieve bed.
chem.abs.drying.note: The 200 ppm specification is a common engineering target; typical material arrives at 0.05-0.15%. The desiccant is recorded as a "from" ingredient: a drying step is made of its molecular sieve bed, it does not contain it. Not established: the 80-90 C for 2-4 h drying cycle, the under 0.02% moisture target, and the 3A molecular sieve bed as 1980s ABS practice. The 0.3-0.4 wt% equilibrium moisture figure and the silver-streak, void and lost-impact-strength failure mode are plausible but undocumented here.

facts.label: Residence time
facts.value: 2-4 hours

chem.abs.pelletising.name: Compounding and pelletising
chem.abs.pelletising.description: The dry blend is melted in a twin-screw extruder at 230-260 C, the volatile xylene and the residual styrene are pulled out under vacuum, and the melt is cut into pellets. This is the operation that turns a powder into a product a moulding machine can eat, and it is where the ABS gets its second heat history - which is why the regrind content matters.

chem.abs.pelletising.static-mixer.name: Static mixer in the melt line
chem.abs.pelletising.static-mixer.description: A motionless packed element in the transfer pipe or the die adapter that blends the pigment and the regrind into the melt without shear. It matters because the impact property depends on the particle size distribution surviving, and every unnecessary shear element costs you 0.5-1 micron of particle size.

chem.abs.pelletising.cutter.name: Die plate, water bath and rotary cutter
chem.abs.pelletising.cutter.description: The melt is extruded through a die plate as a number of strands into a circulating water bath at 20-40 C, solidifies, is pulled by a first calender and chopped by a rotary knife mounted on the extruder die. The alternative is underwater pelletising, where the die is submerged and the pellets are cut in the water - fewer steps, no strands, and it was becoming the 1980s preference for a new line. Pellet size is 2-4 mm in both cases.

facts.label: Pellet size
facts.value: 2-4 mm

facts.label: Water bath
facts.value: 20-40 C circulating

chem.abs.pelletising.vacuum-vent.name: Vacuum venting
chem.abs.pelletising.vacuum-vent.description: A vent at 10-100 mbar with a steam ejector or a liquid ring pump, sized to remove the residual monomer and solvent. The residual styrene specification matters: a high-styrene ABS smells, and the monomer content of a 1980s pellet was typically under 500 ppm.

facts.label: Vacuum
facts.value: 10-100 mbar

facts.label: Residual styrene
facts.value: <500 ppm typical

chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw.name: Twin-screw extruder
chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw.description: Two intermeshing screws 50-90 mm in diameter at 10-30 rpm, length to diameter ratio 30-40:1, with an L/D feed zone, a melting zone, a vacuum vent and a second vent for the devolatilisation. In 1983 the counter-rotating or co-rotating twin screw was the standard compounding machine for ABS because it handles the powder blend, the pigment and the regrind in one pass; a 70 mm machine ran 500-2,000 kg/h. The xylene comes out in the compounding extruder rather than in the reactor, because the reactor melt is too viscous to devolatilise in a small unit: a falling-film or wiped-film vent at 240-260 C and 5-50 mbar with a steam ejector, or a liquid ring pump for the high-boiling tail.
chem.abs.pelletising.twin-screw.note: Machine sizes and throughputs are typical of the era's compounding lines.

facts.label: Screw
facts.value: 50-90 mm diameter, 30-40:1 L/D

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: 500-2,000 kg/h (70 mm machine)

facts.label: Vapour load
facts.value: 1-2 t xylene per t of polymer

chem.abs.blending.name: Blending the graft into the matrix
chem.abs.blending.description: The graft is mixed into the SAN at 25-50 parts graft per 100 parts SAN for a general purpose grade and up to 50-70 parts for a high-impact grade. That ratio - not the chemistry - is what a plastics buyer specifies: rubber content sets the impact strength, the heat distortion temperature and the price per kilogram.
chem.abs.blending.note: Kept as its own node because the blend ratio is what a plastics buyer specifies, and its two ingredients are recorded as "from" edges: the blend is made of the graft and the SAN matrix, it does not contain them. ABS proportions run 15-35% acrylonitrile, 5-30% butadiene and 40-60% styrene, and the elastic butadiene phase is what makes it impact resistant. Not established: the 25-50 and 50-70 parts graft per 100 parts SAN ratios, the 25-40% figure for high-impact grades, and the 76:24 styrene:acrylonitrile matrix.

facts.label: Graft content in ABS
facts.value: 25-50 wt% (25-40% typical for high impact)

chem.abs.san-matrix.name: The SAN matrix
chem.abs.san-matrix.description: The continuous phase: styrene with 24-32% acrylonitrile, made separately by bulk, emulsion or suspension polymerisation. It has to be made separately because it has to be a continuous phase, not a grafted one. In 1983 a large ABS plant bought its SAN in, or made it on site in a bulk reactor and then devolatilised - the two-route choice is a plant's economics, not a chemistry question.
chem.abs.san-matrix.note: The SAN matrix is made from the styrene documented in the styrene branch; the styrene is an ingredient of the matrix, not a component of it.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.name: SOVERE ammoxidation process
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.description: A mixture of propylene, ammonia, oxygen and steam is passed at 400-460 C and 15-25 bar (1.5-2.5 MPa) over a bismuth molybdate or antimony-phosphorus-boron oxide catalyst in a fixed-bed or fluidised-bed reactor. The reaction is a partial oxidation plus an ammonia substitution in one step: propylene + 1.5 NH3 + 0.75 O2 -> acrylonitrile + 2 H2O. Per tonne of acrylonitrile the plant consumes about 1.0-1.1 t of propylene, 0.22-0.30 t of ammonia (most of which is lost to N2 and to acetonitrile) and 1.0-1.3 t of air, and it makes 0.04-0.08 t of acetonitrile as the main by-product. A side reaction makes hydrogen - propylene plus ammonia plus oxygen gives propene imine, which cracks to acetonitrile and hydrogen - and by the 1980s that hydrogen was being recovered from the purge gas, which is why the net oxygen demand of the process is lower than the stoichiometry suggests. Acrylonitrile inhibits cytochrome oxidase and causes methaemoglobinaemia, and it is absorbed through intact skin, so a 1980s plant ran gloves, face shields and showers at every sampling point.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.note: Occupational limits for acrylonitrile were being revised downward through the 1980s and the figures are the era order of magnitude rather than a single legal value. The hazard figures for acrylonitrile: boiling point 77 C, flammable range 3-20 vol%, flash point about 6 C, and a 1980s US limit of 10 ppm as an 8-hour average.

facts.label: Flammable range
facts.value: 3-20 vol% in air

facts.label: Flash point
facts.value: about 6 C (closed cup)

facts.label: US OSHA PEL, 1980s
facts.value: 10 ppm 8-hour TWA

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.name: Recovery and purification train
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.description: The reactor effluent is cooled and partly condensed, the unreacted propylene and ammonia are stripped and recycled, the acrylonitrile and acetonitrile are separated by distillation (acrylonitrile boiling 77 C, acetonitrile 81.6 C, which is a genuinely difficult separation and was the reason for the extractive or entrainer-assisted designs), and the acrylonitrile is finished to 99.9% with a stabiliser. In a plant where acrylonitrile boils at 77 C and is flammable from 3% in air, the distillation column was also the largest single gas hazard.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.s.name: Acrylonitrile stabiliser
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.distillation.s.description: A phenolic or amine stabiliser (a small percentage of a phenol such as hydroquinone, or a hindered amine) is added to prevent anionic polymerisation of the monomer in storage. Acrylonitrile has a third-order rate constant for anionic polymerisation that is high enough that a drum of uninhibited monomer left in a warm warehouse can polymerise from the bottom up, and this was a real and recurring accident.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.byproducts.name: By-products: acetonitrile, hydrogen cyanide, acrylic acid
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.byproducts.description: Acetonitrile is the biggest by-product at 3-8% of the acrylonitrile and it had a real market - it went into solvent and into acrylonitrile copolymer fibres. Hydrogen cyanide was a small but lethal by-product, and its formation was the reason for the halide promoter. Acrylic acid came from the hydrolysis of a little of the acrylonitrile, and it was a nuisance in 1980s practice because it fouled the distillation train.

facts.label: Acetonitrile
facts.value: 3-8% of acrylonitrile production

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.name: Ammoxidation catalyst
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.description: Three families existed. Bismuth molybdate on silica (Bi2Mo3O12 or Bi2(MoO4)3 on silica) was the original and still the industry standard for selectivity in fixed beds. Antimony oxide with phosphorus and boron oxides on a silica support (Sb2O3/P2O5/B2O3) was the workhorse of the fluidised-bed designs, cheaper and more active but a little less selective. Bismuth molybdate with vanadium and tungsten additives, and nickel or cobalt catalysts, were the newer directions. Coking from the organic by-products and the loss of phosphorus are the two deactivation routes, and a trace of halide promoter - a few hundred ppm of hydrogen chloride or an alkyl chloride - was the standard answer: it suppressed the side reactions that make hydrogen cyanide, and it is why the plant needed a chlorine supply of its own.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.note: Halide promoter levels of a few hundred ppm are the range quoted in reviews; the exact figure varies by licensor.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.name: Making the ammoxidation catalyst
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.description: The ammoxidation catalyst is a shaped, robust porous solid, and making it is a small ceramics industry. A bismuth molybdate catalyst is prepared by impregnating precipitated bismuth molybdate or by sol-gel methods onto a silica support, then shaping it into 3-5 mm extrudates or spray-dried microspheres and calcining at 500-700 C. The support is silica gel, and silica gel is made from sand. That is the whole chain from a dune to a transistor's acrylonitrile in three steps. The powder is extruded into trilobe or quadrilobe shapes - the lobes give more external surface per unit volume than a cylinder, and less diffusion limitation - and then dried and calcined at 500-700 C, which converts the oxide precursor into the active bismuth molybdate phase.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.note: Lobed extrudates and the calcination temperature range are standard catalyst-manufacturing practice.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.name: Soda silica from sand
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.description: Quartz sand is fused with sodium carbonate at about 1,300 C to make sodium silicate, which is dissolved in hot water to make the silicate solution, which is acidified to gel. This is the same soda-silica chain that gives the silica sol for the polysilicon ingot's crucibles and the quartz for the fused silica, and it is the industrial descendant of a two-thousand-year-old glassmaking reaction. It is the last dig-it-out node in this branch: sand.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.note: The soda-silica route is the classical one for both glass and silica sol; its scale-up is the industrial glassmaking reaction. It is an industrial mineral rather than wafer chemistry, and it sits with metal.silica-sand. Not established: the fusion of quartz sand with sodium carbonate at about 1,300 C to make sodium silicate, and the gelling of the acidified silicate solution as the route both to silica sol and to fused silica.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.name: Silica gel support
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.description: A porous amorphous silica of 300-700 m2/g surface area and a 6-20 nm pore diameter. The pore diameter matters twice over in this file: in the ammoxidation catalyst a small pore keeps the diene from cracking, and in the FCC catalyst a large pore lets the bulky alkylated intermediates in. The silica gel is made by hydrolysing a silicate solution and gelling it, and the silicate solution is made from silica sand.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.catal.note: Silica gel is an amorphous, porous form of silicon dioxide with nanometre-scale voids and pores. Not established: the 300-700 m2/g surface area - desiccant grades are quoted around 750-800 m2/g - the 6-20 nm pore diameter, and the pore-size argument for the ammoxidation and FCC catalysts.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.antim.name: Antimony-phosphorus-boron oxide catalyst
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.antim.description: The fluidised-bed catalyst: a silica support promoted with phosphorus and boron oxides so that the phosphorus does not volatilise away at 450 C. It was less selective but far more active and far more mechanically robust than the bismuth catalyst, which matters in a fluidised bed.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.bismu.name: Bismuth molybdate on silica
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.bismu.description: The standard catalyst, chosen for its selectivity to acrylonitrile and its resistance to reduction by ammonia. The 1980s development targets were the vanadium- and tungsten-promoted versions and, later in the decade, the bismuth-molybdenum-phosphorus systems aimed at raising the acrylonitrile yield above 90%.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.catalyst.bismu.note: Acrylonitrile comes from catalytic ammoxidation of propylene, and bismuth phosphomolybdate on silica was one of the first useful catalysts - a phosphorus-containing bismuth molybdate, not the Bi2Mo3O12 this node names. Not established: resistance to reduction by ammonia, the vanadium- and tungsten-promoted versions, and the above-90% acrylonitrile yield target.

facts.label: Catalyst family
facts.value: bismuth phosphomolybdate (Bi9PMo12O52) on silica is given as one of the first useful catalysts; bismuth molybdate on silica with V or W promoters is the general ammoxidation catalyst. Which the 1983 plant ran is not established.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.name: Fixed-bed or fluidised-bed ammoxidation reactor
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.description: The original SOVERE design was a series of fixed beds with salt bath or oil bath cooling, giving 90-93% conversion and 85-92% selectivity. The 1980s industry had largely moved to fluidised-bed or moving-bed designs, which were easier to heat and to strip of coke, at the cost of a lower selectivity (about 80-90%). A 1980s plant was a 100,000-250,000 tonne a year unit with a salt bath or a hot water reactor jacket and a lot of downstream distillation.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.note: Selectivity figures vary with catalyst age and design; the ranges are the standard ones quoted in reviews.

facts.label: Conversion / selectivity
facts.value: 90-95% / 85-92% (fixed bed), 80-90% (fluidised)

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.name: Heat removal from the ammoxidation
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.description: The ammoxidation gives out roughly 1,000 kJ per kilogram of acrylonitrile, and the reactor has to be taken out at a rate the metallurgy can live with. That is the single hardest engineering problem in the process, and it is why the original SOVERE design was a salt-bath reactor and why the later fluidised beds were better: the fluidised catalyst carries its own heat around, so the temperature is uniform and there is no hot spot to crack the catalyst.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.name: Molten salt bath reactor
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.description: A tubular reactor immersed in a bath of a molten nitrate-nitrite salt (the working point is around 300-330 C), with the bed of catalyst on an inert support inside the tube. It is a beautiful heat-transfer arrangement and a nasty maintenance one: the salt is oxidising, the reactor is at 400-450 C inside, and a tube failure means salt into the process. By 1983 it was being replaced by the fluidised bed for exactly this reason.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.note: Salt bath temperatures are quoted in the 250-330 C range depending on the salt mix; the precise working point varies between licensors.

chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.name: The molten salt itself
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.description: A mixture of potassium nitrate, sodium nitrite and sometimes calcium nitrate, chosen for a melting point a little below the operating temperature and for a decomposition temperature a good deal above it. It is a beautiful heat-transfer medium and an oxidising one, and a small leak from the reactor puts hot nitrate into a hydrocarbon process - which is why the original SOVERE design was eventually superseded. The nitrate salts came from the same nitric acid that a fab's wet bench bought.
chem.acrylonitrile.sovere.reactor.heat-r.note: Salt compositions vary by licensor; the nitrate-nitrite family is the standard choice.

chem.abs.san-matrix.acrylonitrile-raw.name: Acrylonitrile monomer
chem.abs.san-matrix.acrylonitrile-raw.description: 99.5%+ acrylonitrile with less than 45 ppm of the stabiliser, from a SOVERE ammoxidation plant. Because acrylonitrile is acutely lethal through the skin, it arrived in the ABS plant in tankers and was handled in a closed system with an outside storage tank; the 1980s industry norm was glove boxes and an emergency shower at every sampling point.

chem.abs.grafting.name: Graft copolymerisation: growing SAN on the rubber
chem.abs.grafting.description: The heart of the process. 20-40 parts of a low-cis polybutadiene rubber dissolved in xylene or toluene is charged to a reactor, and styrene plus acrylonitrile is added at 60-80 C in the presence of a persulphate initiator, a chelating agent and a mercaptan chain transfer agent. The radicals abstract a hydrogen from the polybutadiene's 1,2-vinyl unit, creating a radical site on the rubber; styrene and acrylonitrile then copolymerise from that site, and SAN chains grow out of the rubber particle. Each particle therefore becomes a rubber core with a SAN shell. High-graft material, more than about 70% of the monomer grafted, gives a small uniform particle and the best impact strength, while low graft gives larger particles and worse impact; the particle is either salt-like (elastomeric core, rigid SAN shell) or sandwich-like, and which one forms is set by how fast the graft shell precipitates. The rubber is dissolved in xylene or toluene and the monomer emulsified in an aqueous phase carrying the initiator, chelant and transfer agent, and at the end the polymer is devolatilised at 220-250 C and 1-10 mbar to strip the xylene - the single biggest energy item in the plant, at one to two tonnes of solvent per tonne of polymer.
chem.abs.grafting.note: Particle morphology terminology (salt-like, sandwich) and graft-level thresholds vary by producer; these are the standard descriptions. Graft level, particle morphology and reaction medium describe how this step behaves rather than a second operation. Not established: the 20-40 wt% rubber fraction, the 60-80 C graft temperature, the 40-80% graft conversion, the above-70% high-graft threshold and the salt-like and sandwich particle thresholds, which are producer- and licensor-specific. The 220-250 C and 1-10 mbar devolatilisation and the one to two tonnes of xylene per tonne of polymer vary most between plants.

facts.label: Graft conversion
facts.value: 40-80% of the monomer

facts.label: Typical reaction time
facts.value: 4-10 hours

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: 0.1-10 microns, ideally 1-3

facts.label: Graft level (high)
facts.value: >70% of monomer grafted

facts.label: Solvent per tonne of polymer
facts.value: ~1-2 t xylene

chem.abs.grafting.chain-transfer-agent.name: Chain transfer agent (modifier)
chem.abs.grafting.chain-transfer-agent.description: A mercaptan - diethyl dithiocarbamate, tetraethyl thiuram disulphide, or a dodecyl mercaptan - at 0.1-0.5 parts. It transfers the growing radical to the sulphur and caps the chain, which limits molecular weight and prevents the gelation that would otherwise turn a linear rubber into a useless network. Every emulsion polymerisation has one; in ABS it is called a modifier and it is the same chemistry. A mercaptan - typically a tertiary dodecyl mercaptan, or thioglycolic acid in some processes - at 0.2-1.5 parts. It transfers the growing radical, capping each SAN branch and setting the graft chain length. Too little transfer and the graft crosslinks into a gel that is insoluble and unprocessable; too much and the graft has too few grafts per rubber particle and the impact strength collapses.
chem.abs.grafting.chain-transfer-agent.note: Shared with the SBR emulsion process: the same mercaptan chain-transfer agent serves both polymerisations.

chem.abs.grafting.chelant.name: Chelating agent
chem.abs.grafting.chelant.description: A polycarboxylic acid or its salt - trisodium citrate, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid disodium salt, or a polyacrylate - at 0.05-0.3 parts. It chelates the trace transition metals that would otherwise decompose the persulphate catalytically and produce a wild, uncontrolled radical rate. In the 1980s this was a standard part of the recipe and one of the few places where a detergent chemistry shows up inside a structural plastic.

chem.abs.grafting.initiator.name: Potassium persulphate initiator
chem.abs.grafting.initiator.description: K2S2O8 or the cheaper sodium persulphate, thermally decomposed to sulphate radical, generating the first polymer radicals at the aqueous droplet surface. Persulphate initiators leave a residue of sulphate groups on the chain ends, which is why an emulsion SBR cannot be re-polymerised as a living polymer and has to be made in one shot. K2S2O8 at 0.1-0.5 parts per 100 monomer, thermally decomposed in the aqueous-organic system at 60-80 C.
chem.abs.grafting.initiator.note: Exact initiator levels vary with the licensor process; the persulphate-in-aqueous-phase rationale is standard. Shared with the SBR emulsion process, which uses the same potassium persulphate. The persulfate dianion dissociates in solution to give radicals. The loading is stated twice in this node and differently - 0.1-0.5 and 0.05-0.2 parts per 100 monomer - and which of the two is right is not established. The residue explanation for why an emulsion polymer cannot be re-polymerised as a living chain is standard.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: not established. This node previously carried two different figures in adjacent rows, 0.1-0.5 and 0.05-0.2 parts per 100 monomer; one of them was wrong, there is no source here to say which, and both have been withdrawn rather than one being picked.

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.name: The polybutadiene rubber phase
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.description: A low-cis (40-60% cis, therefore glassy rather than rubbery on its own) butyllithium-polymerised polybutadiene at 0.5-2% residual oil, with the whole chain ending in a couple of reactive sites. The low cis content is deliberate: a high-cis rubber dissolves in its own polymer at reactor temperature and the particle boundaries blur, whereas a low-cis rubber keeps a sharp core-shell particle that survives compounding.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.name: How butadiene is polymerised
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.description: Three chemistries, chosen for what you were making. Emulsion polymerisation gives cis-1,4, trans-1,4 and vinyl-1,2 structures mixed - a rubber but not a specific one. Anionic polymerisation with lithium butyllithium gives cis-1,4 selectively and controls chain ends. Coordination polymerisation with neodymium or titanium gives cis-1,4 with an extremely high cis content. The 4-vinyl group left on a cis-1,4 chain is the reactive site that grafting later exploits.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.name: Neodymium-catalysed cis-polybutadiene
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.description: The high-cis technology of the 1980s: a neodymium (or lanthanide) compound with an alkylaluminium in a hydrocarbon diluent gives 97-99% cis-1,4, and because the cis content is so high the rubber does not need to be plasticised with oil. Linear low-cis polybutadiene was the growth product of the decade; the older lithium-process cis-PB at 90-95% was still the volume product in 1983.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.name: Neodymium oxide and neodymium metal
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.description: The high-cis polybutadiene catalyst wants the neodymium as a soluble organometallic rather than as the oxide, so the oxide comes out of the separation plant, is converted to a halide and then alkylated, and is dosed at a few hundredths of a percent. The neodymium is the fraction of the bastnasite that nobody had predicted would matter: a light rare earth sold by the tonne for glass polishing and ceramic glaze suddenly became worth several times its price per kilogram for a rubber catalyst, and by the mid-1980s the separation plants were being run to make more of the neodymium-praseodymium fraction than of anything else. A C64's rubber therefore begins in a carbonatite in California or an iron-ore pit in Inner Mongolia, passes through a mixer-settler train several hundred stages long, and ends up dosed into a hydrocarbon diluent at about one part in a thousand.
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.neodymium-.note: The catalyst chemistry and the origin of the ore are well documented; medium confidence on the dose level and on the timing of the shift in what the separation plants chose to make.

facts.label: Form used
facts.value: a soluble neodymium alkyl, not the oxide; the oxide is halided and alkylated first

facts.label: Dose
facts.value: a few hundredths of a percent of the butadiene charge

facts.label: Why neodymium
facts.value: praseodymium was co-produced with it, and the two together soon outsold the polishing-grade fractions

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.name: Lithium butyllithium polymerisation
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.description: The living anionic process: butyllithium in a hydrocarbon diluent (diesel oil or hexane) at 0-60 C, with the cis content set by solvent and temperature. Living means the chain end stays active, so the polymer can be chain-stopped with an electrophile - water, carbon dioxide, epoxide - and the whole molecule is a single block. This is the chemistry that makes the ABS graft rubber phase possible.

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.name: Butyllithium
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.description: A pyrophoric organolithium, always supplied as a 10-20% solution in hexane and never in bulk. In 1980s practice it was the initiator for the solution polymerisation of polybutadiene and for the SBR made by anionic polymerisation, and its manufacture from lithium metal and butyl chloride or butane was a speciality chemical operation with a lot of solvent handling.
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.lithium-ca.note: Butyllithium is among the most used organolithium reagents. Not established: the 10-20 wt% solution in hexane, its pyrophoricity as a handling fact for this application, and the manufacture from lithium metal and butyl chloride or butane.

facts.label: Commercial form
facts.value: 10-20 wt% in hexane

chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.name: The four polybutadiene microstructures
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.description: cis-1,4 (the elastomer; the chain is flexible below its glass transition), trans-1,4 (the chain is regular and crystalline, so it is a plastic not a rubber), 1,2-vinyl (a pendant vinyl group, also rubbery but with a high glass transition because of the pendant group), and 3,4-vinyl (rare). The rubbery ones are cis-1,4 and 1,2; the ratio between them is set by temperature, catalyst and solvent, and it is why polybutadiene rubber has a glass transition near -100 C and is the most flexible of the common rubbers. The ratio of the four microstructures is a dial, not an accident: a rare-earth or titanium coordination catalyst gives cis-1,4, lithium butyllithium gives more 1,2-vinyl in a polar solvent and more cis-1,4 in a hydrocarbon, and temperature moves it again.
chem.butadiene.polymerisation.structures.note: Glass transition values for elastomers vary a few degrees with grade and measurement.

facts.label: cis-PB glass transition
facts.value: about -100 to -110 C

facts.label: Natural rubber glass transition
facts.value: about -70 C

facts.label: cis-1,4
facts.value: rubbery, Tg about -100 C

facts.label: trans-1,4
facts.value: crystalline, Tg about -80 C but Tm about +100 C

facts.label: 1,2-vinyl
facts.value: rubbery, Tg about -80 C

chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.name: Butadiene monomer
chem.abs.grafting.rubber-phase.butadiene.description: 99.0-99.7% butadiene from a cracker C4 extraction unit. The chain is why the C64's rubber phase is a petrochemical and not a natural rubber: the natural rubber alternative is cis-1,4-polyisoprene from latex, and the graft chemistry that works on polybutadiene's pendant vinyl group does not work on isoprene's chain. The 99.7% monomer comes out of the cracker C4 stream by the extractive route at chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.

chem.styrene.name: Styrene: benzene plus ethylene, and the plastics of it
chem.styrene.description: Benzene is alkylated with ethylene to ethylbenzene, and the ethylbenzene is dehydrogenated to styrene. About 12-14 million tonnes of styrene were made in 1983, of which roughly two thirds went to polystyrene and the rest to SAN, ABS and SBR. Styrene is a C64 material in a way that is easy to miss: the SAN matrix of the case, the styrene in the graft phase, and the polystyrene that was in the packaging and in some of the mouldings.

chem.styrene.divinylbenzene.name: Divinylbenzene
chem.styrene.divinylbenzene.description: A 40/60 to 80/20 mixture of the two divinylbenzene isomers made by the same ethylbenzene route with a second vinyl group. About 1-2% of the styrene monomer, and essentially all of it goes into ion exchange resins and into the crosslinking monomer of unsaturated polyester. The cation exchange resin in the water treatment plant of a plastics factory is a styrene-divinylbenzene copolymer, so this molecule sits quietly in the supply chain of almost everything else in this file.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.name: Styrene polymerisation
chem.styrene.polymerisation.description: Styrene polymerises readily by free-radical mechanisms because the benzyl radical it makes is resonance stabilised. Almost all commercial polystyrene is made by free-radical polymerisation; the ionic routes that give syndiotactic and isotactic polystyrene existed in the 1980s but were curiosities. Styrene-acrylonitrile copolymer carries 24-32% acrylonitrile, made in bulk at 130-180 C or in emulsion or suspension. SBS block copolymer is made by sequential addition to a living anionic chain - butadiene to a 60-80% cis polybutadiene block, then styrene to a polystyrene block at each end - so the hard end blocks are the physical crosslinks and the middle block is the rubber: the same butadiene and styrene as SBR and ABS in a completely different architecture. Expanded polystyrene carries 5-6% pentane or butane as a blowing agent, polymerised at 90-150 C and 1-5 bar with the beads expanding 10-30 times; it was the standard packing material for electronics and for the C64's carton inserts.
chem.styrene.polymerisation.note: SAN capacity in the early 1980s is an order-of-magnitude estimate.

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: 5-6% pentane or isobutane

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.name: General purpose polystyrene, bulk and suspension
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.description: Bulk polymerisation at 140-200 C and 20-40 bar in a stirred or plug-flow reactor with a benzoyl peroxide or a hindered phenol initiator, the classic route for general purpose and crystal grade. Suspension polymerisation, in which styrene is dispersed as 0.1-2 mm beads in water with a suspending agent, is preferred for foam grades because the beads can be expanded. General purpose polystyrene production in the 1980s was of the order of 5-6 million tonnes a year.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.name: Finishing: devolatilisation and pelletising
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.description: Polystyrene has to be devolatilised after the bulk polymerisation, because the monomer left in the melt is both a smell and a peroxide risk. A 1980s finishing line was a twin-screw extruder at 200-240 C and 5-50 mbar with two vacuum vents, then a strand die into a water bath, then a rotary cutter - the same machine geometry as the ABS line, and for the same reason: somebody in the plastics industry decided once that devolatilisation and pelletising should be one operation and never went back.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.name: Strand die, water bath and cutter
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.description: Extruded through a die with 10-30 holes of 2-3 mm, quenched in a water bath at 20-30 C, drawn by a first calender and cut by a rotary knife. The alternative - underwater pelletising - cuts the strands in the water and was becoming the 1980s choice for polystyrene as it had been for ABS, for the same reason: fewer handling steps and no strand breakage.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.name: The devolatiliser
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.fi.description: A falling-film or wiped-film evaporator with two stages of vacuum, taking the residual styrene from a few per cent down to a few hundred parts per million. The polymer is deliberately kept above its own melting point but below its decomposition point, which for polystyrene is a window of about 40 C - the whole of the finishing engineering is about staying in that window while the pressure falls and the viscosity rises.

facts.label: Vacuum
facts.value: 5-50 mbar

facts.label: Residual monomer
facts.value: a few hundred ppm

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.su.name: Suspending agent for suspension polystyrene
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.su.description: Gelatin, methylcellulose or polyvinyl alcohol, at 0.1-1% of the water phase. It has to hold the bead together without letting the bead coalesce, and the whole engineering of suspension polystyrene is the engineering of that balance: too little and the beads fuse, too much and the bead has a hard skin that traps monomer and leaves styrene odour in the bead.

chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.be.name: Benzoyl peroxide initiator
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.be.description: Dibenzoyl peroxide, dosed at 0.05-0.5 wt%, thermally decomposed at 60-90 C to give a benzoyloxy radical and then a phenyl radical. It leaves a benzoic acid residue in the polymer and a trace of styrene in the reactor bottoms, which is why polystyrene made with it has a characteristic faint smell and a yellowing tendency that the 1980s stabiliser industry existed to fix.
chem.styrene.polymerisation.bulk-gpps.be.note: Benzoyl peroxide is a chain-growth radical initiator. Its half-life is one hour at 92 C and one minute at 131 C, so a 60-90 C dosing temperature is low for this initiator and the operating figure needs checking. Not established: the 0.05-0.5 wt% loading and the benzoic acid residue and yellowing claim.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.name: Dehydrogenation to styrene
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.description: Ethylbenzene is dehydrogenated to styrene at 600-700 C and 1-3 bar over an iron oxide catalyst (the classic Feeders-Rudd, now UOP ST-110, a shell-and-tube bed of promoted magnetite with potassium and copper promoters). Single-pass conversion is 40-50% and the selectivity to styrene 90-93%. The conversion is deliberately held below completion because styrene polymerises over the same catalyst, and because the dehydrogenation is strongly endothermic and needs a large fired furnace.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.name: The dehydrogenation furnace
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.description: The dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene is strongly endothermic - about 0.22 GJ of heat per tonne of ethylbenzene - and it is carried out in a bank of shell-and-tube reactors with the heat applied from the outside. A 1980s styrene plant's furnaces were its largest energy consumers and its largest single source of stack emissions, which is why the industry spent the 1980s on better coil metallurgy, on vacuum insulation of the reactor, and on a staged feed arrangement that fed the preheated reactor's effluent straight back into the next reactor's inlet. Steam diluent keeps the partial pressure low and a polymerisation inhibitor - sulfolane, a chlorinated hydrocarbon or a proprietary organic - is dosed at tens of parts per million to hold the styrene down. Refinery fuel gas or natural gas, about 0.2 GJ of heat per tonne of ethylbenzene - worth stating plainly, because a substantial part of the carbon in a plastic is burned rather than polymerised.
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.fired-furna.note: The heat of dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene is about 0.22 GJ/t; the figure here is rounded.

facts.label: Heat requirement
facts.value: ~0.2 GJ per tonne of ethylbenzene

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.reactor.name: ST-110 dehydrogenation reactor
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.reactor.description: A bank of shell-and-tube reactors, 20-50 tubes 4-6 inch in diameter by 20-30 m long, at 1-3 bar, fired on the outside. A 1980s styrene plant had 8-20 such reactors per train and several trains. The furnace is the plant's energy hog, which is why the styrene industry was the largest single consumer of heat-integration improvements in this part of the chemical industry.

chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.iron-cataly.name: Promoted iron oxide catalyst
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.iron-cataly.description: Magnetite or hematite promoted with potassium oxide, copper oxide and sometimes molybdenum or chromium, formed as extruded rings or as a granular bed. Steam is used as a diluent to keep the partial pressure low and to suppress coking, and a trace of a polymerisation inhibitor (sulfolane or a chlorinated hydrocarbon) is fed to hold the polymer down.
chem.styrene.dehydrogenation.iron-cataly.note: Catalytic dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene gives hydrogen and styrene, and over 99% of ethylbenzene production goes to styrene. Not established: magnetite or hematite promoted with potassium oxide, copper oxide and molybdenum, the extruded ring or granular bed form, the 600-700 C, 40-50% per-pass conversion and 90-93% selectivity, and the sulfolane polymerisation inhibitor.

chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.name: Ethylbenzene from benzene and ethylene
chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.description: Benzene plus ethylene in a large molar excess of benzene (3-6 to 1) over a zeolite or a phosphoric acid catalyst at 250-400 C and 10-30 bar. The 1980s breakthrough was the Mobil process using a shape-selective zeolite (the ZSM-5 family) at about 350 C, which gives over 97% selectivity to ethylbenzene and almost no diethylbenzene. The old process, phosphoric acid on silica at 140-180 C and 20-30 bar, had a diethylbenzene problem that ate benzene and made the distillation columns enormous.

chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.zeolite-cataly.name: Shape-selective alkylation catalyst
chem.styrene.ethylbenzene.zeolite-cataly.description: A zeolite whose pore geometry lets a benzene molecule in, lets ethylbenzene out and does not let diethylbenzene in - the same shape selectivity that let ZSM-5 crack gasoline to high-octane and propylene, and that later let MFI zeolites make para-xylene. One catalyst family, three jobs, all in this file.

chem.styrene.benzene.name: Benzene
chem.styrene.benzene.description: The feedstock. In 1983 world benzene production was of the order of 15-17 million tonnes a year, and it came from three sources: catalytic reforming (about half), hydrodealkylation of toluene (roughly a quarter to a third, and the growth share of the 1980s), and coal tar from coke ovens (10-20%, and a bigger share outside North America and Western Europe). Toluene hydrodealkylation gave benzene plus methane at 500-600 C and 30-60 bar over cobalt-molybdenum or alumina, and it grew fastest through the 1980s because toluene was abundant and benzene was tight; it makes the same methane a reformer makes as hydrogen, so the two operations fit together.

chem.styrene.benzene.coal-tar.name: Coke oven benzene
chem.styrene.benzene.coal-tar.description: Byproduct benzene from the coking of coal in an integral coke plant: the coke oven gas is cooled and the aromatics stripped out with a wash oil, which is then steam-stripped, giving a crude benzole with toluene and xylenes. In 1983 coal tar benzene was still a major share of world benzene - more so in Europe and Asia than in the United States - and it is the one benzene of that era that is not a petrochemical at all.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery.name: Aromatics recovery from reformer naphtha
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery.description: The C6 to C8 aromatics have to be extracted from a naphtha stream where they are only a few percent by weight. The 1960s and 1980s workhorse was the UOP EdCo process: extractive distillation with sulfolane (a four-plus-four ring sulfone, 218 C boiling point) followed by azeotropic distillation with isooctane. Sulfolane replaced sulfuric acid extraction because it did not invert the alkylbenzenes and did not make a waste acid stream - and sulfuric acid hydrodealkylation was the older, waste-generating route.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..name: Sulfolane
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..description: Tetrahydrothiophene-1,1-dioxide, a polar aprotic solvent that dissolves aromatics preferentially to paraffins and is thermally stable and non-corrosive. It is also the inhibitor chemistry's solvent cousin: sulfolane is used as a polymerisation inhibitor in the styrene dehydrogenation reactors, and it belongs to a small family of molecules - NMP, sulfolane, dimethylformamide - that turns up in three different jobs in this file.

chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..name: Sulfolane from butadiene
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..description: The solvent that extracts benzene out of a naphtha stream is itself made out of the cracker's C4. Butadiene is reacted with sulfur dioxide and water to give tetrahydrothiophene 1,1-dioxide. So the styrene chain - benzene, ethylbenzene, styrene - is fed by butadiene twice over: once as the rubber in the ABS, and once as the solvent that separated the benzene. It is the clearest example in this file of a chemical park's flows being a web rather than a line. Butadiene plus SO2 at 100-140 C gives the sulfolene, a five-membered ring with one double bond left, and a second equivalent of water with a base opens the second ring to sulfolane; the sulphur dioxide comes from burning recovered elemental sulphur, usually the same Claus sulphur a nearby refinery took out of the same sour gas that fed the cracker.
chem.styrene.benzene.aromatics-recovery..note: Sulfolane is industrially made by the butadiene/SO2/hydrolysis route; the conditions quoted are representative.

facts.label: First step
facts.value: butadiene + SO2 at 100-140 C

chem.butadiene.name: Butadiene and the elastomers of it
chem.butadiene.description: Butadiene is the C4 diene that makes synthetic rubber, and in 1983 about 5-6 million tonnes a year of it was made, roughly 60% from cracker C4 by extractive distillation and the rest by dehydrogenation of butane. It is the molecule behind the rubber in the C64's case feet, the plinths, and the elasticity of the power cord's jacket - and behind the graft phase of the ABS case. Nitrile rubber is butadiene with 25-40% acrylonitrile, emulsion-polymerised the same way as SBR: the acrylonitrile buys oil and fuel resistance and costs low-temperature flexibility, and it is the material for oil seals and for the elastomer pads of many electrolytic capacitors. Two butadienes plus two hydrogen cyanides give adiponitrile by hydrocyanation over nickel(0) with a triphenylphosphine ligand, which is what finally let a nylon 6,6 plant be fed from a cracker rather than from adipic acid - and is the reason hydrogen cyanide, the toxic gas of the acrylonitrile and methyl methacrylate chemistry, sat on a plastics company's books.
chem.butadiene.note: The acrylonitrile comes from chem.acrylonitrile; the butadiene from chem.butadiene.sources.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: nickel(0) with triphenylphosphine

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber.name: Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR)
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber.description: The largest synthetic rubber by a wide margin: of the order of 6-7 million tonnes a year in 1983, in a handful of grades. It is not a C64 material, but it is the material whose emulsion polymerisation recipe - cold, water, persulphate, rosin acid soap, chain transfer agent - is the same recipe the ABS graft phase uses, and the rosin in it is the same pine rosin as the solder flux. Cold emulsion polymerisation ran styrene at 23-25 parts to butadiene at 75-77 parts in water with a rosin or oleate soap at 2-5 parts and a persulphate at 0.05-0.2 parts, at 5 C for 8-12 hours to 60-70% conversion.
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber.note: The ABS graft reaction uses the same chemistry at 50-80 C; see chem.abs.grafting.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 5 C

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Rosin acid soap emulsifier
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: Sodium or potassium salts of pine rosins (about 60% abietic acid) and of tall oil fatty acids, mixed 50/50. Two jobs: the rosin part stabilises the polymer against oxidation, and the fatty acid part controls the particle size and the rate. Rosin emulsifiers also give the rubber a slightly tacky surface, which is why tread compounds still add tackifying resin.
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..note: The rosin itself is chem.rosin, which also supplies the solder flux.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Fatty acid emulsifier and tallow
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: About half of a cold SBR or ABS emulsifier system is a fatty acid salt, and the fatty acid came from tallow - the rendered fat of cattle and sheep - split into oleic and stearic acid and neutralised with sodium or potassium hydroxide. So part of the emulsifier that keeps the rubber particles apart in the graft reactor was, in 1983, a byproduct of the meat industry, which is a genuinely surprising provenance for a molecule that ends up inside a computer case.

chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..name: Tallow
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..description: Rendered animal fat, roughly 50% palmitic, stearic and oleic acid. Historically a by-product of the meat industry and increasingly, through the 1980s, a rendering industry of its own. Its oleic acid was the emulsifier and its stearic acid was the release agent, and both ended up in the polymer. The C64's case therefore contains a trace of a livestock product through the soap that helped the rubber particles form.
chem.butadiene.styrene-butadiene-rubber..note: The tallow provenance of fatty-acid emulsifiers is well established; synthetic fatty acids were substituting for it through the 1980s.

chem.butadiene.sources.name: Butadiene sources
chem.butadiene.sources.description: Two industrial routes and a third that was still just about alive in 1983: extractive distillation of the steam cracker's C4 stream, dehydrogenation of n-butane, and thermal dimerisation of acetylene (the old Reppe route, dead by 1960). The choice between them is a function of whether a cracker was nearby and whether butane was cheap. Two acetylene molecules make butadiene over a copper catalyst, and before 1960 that is how the world made it: a route with perfect atom economy that died because acetylene was expensive relative to the C4 it displaced - the third instance in this file of the elegant gas route losing to the abundant naphtha route.

chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.name: Houdry butane dehydrogenation
chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.description: n-Butane dehydrogenated endothermically at 480-550 C over platinum on alumina or chromia at 1-5 bar to butenes, which are then extracted and the butadiene purified separately. It was the on-purpose route, it made isobutylene for MTBE as a co-product, and it suffered from the thermodynamics of an endothermic reaction: every 1% of conversion costs a lot of fuel, and 1980s furnace designs pushed single-pass conversion to 40-50% with recirculation.

facts.label: Conditions
facts.value: 480-550 C, 1-5 bar, Pt/Al2O3 or Cr2O3

chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.dehydrogen.name: The butane dehydrogenation furnace
chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.dehydrogen.description: Dehydrogenation of butane to butenes is endothermic, so the reactor is a bank of fired tubes - cast iron or cast alloy, several hundred tubes, with the furnace gas at 500-700 C. The catalyst inside is platinum on alumina or chromia, and the giveaway of a fouled furnace is the pressure drop across the tubes: the butene polymerises on the catalyst, makes green coke, and the coke blocks the tube. This unit is the reason the butadiene plant in a 1980s complex was often the noisiest building on the site.
chem.butadiene.sources.houdry.dehydrogen.note: The description of furnace-tube coking in butane dehydrogenation is standard; specific designs vary.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.name: Sounsby extractive distillation
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.description: The standard butadiene recovery unit from 1962 onward: an extractive distillation with a selective polar solvent that dissolves butadiene and the butenes but not the saturated C4s, followed by a second stripper to recover the pure diene. A 1980s unit processing 100,000-400,000 tonnes a year of C4 stood about 60-100 m tall and was one of the tallest distillation towers in the world, because alpha-olefins and butadiene have a relative volatility of about 1.01 - the hardest separation in the whole C4 business. The process works because butadiene is the only diene and the only component that will add a second solvent molecule.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.name: 99%+ butadiene
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.description: The polymerisation-grade monomer has to be 99.0-99.7% with less than 100 ppm of inhibitor residue, less than 100 ppm water and less than 50 ppm carbonyls. The spec is enforced because the polymerisation catalysts of the era - both the persulfate emulsion ones and the lithium butyllithium ones - were exquisitely sensitive to all three. The certificate carried four numbers - purity by gas chromatography, inhibitor as the minutes before a calibrated sample polymerised, water by Karl Fischer and carbonyls colorimetrically - and each existed because of what it does to a polymerisation: water kills the lithium catalyst, the inhibitor sets the shelf life, carbonyls kill the persulphate graft and the purity sets the branching.
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.butadiene.note: The analytical methods are period-correct and standard; the specific limits are those quoted in the description.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.nmp.name: N-methylpyrrolidone as the extractive solvent
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.nmp.description: NMP (a strongly polar, high-boiling amide, 202 C) replaced furfural because it does not polymerise and needs less make-up. NMP was the 1980s solvent of choice and it is the same molecule that later arrived in the electronics plant as the chlorinated-solvent replacement for 1,1,1-trichloroethane. NMP is made from butanone and ethylenediamine, and its methylating agent is methanol: CO plus hydrogen at 200-300 C and 50-100 bar over a copper-zinc-aluminium catalyst, so the hydrogen in it comes from a reformer and the carbon monoxide from reformed methane.
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.nmp.note: The solvent substitution history is under chem.solvents.

chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.furfural.name: Furfural as the extractive solvent
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.furfural.description: Furfural (furan-2-carbaldehyde) made from furfural-bark or from pentoses in bagasse hemihydrate pulping, with a boiling point of 161 C and a high selectivity for diene over alpha-olefin. It was the original Sounsby solvent and its dominant drawback is that it polymerises in the presence of acid, so the unit had to be kept dry and inhibited and it consumed make-up solvent continuously. The solvent is made from pentosan hemicellulose - a fifth of the dry weight of a hardwood - by acid and steam treatment of rice hulls, corn cobs or bagasse, so the extractant's own feedstock is agricultural residue rather than petroleum.
chem.butadiene.sources.sounsby.furfural.note: Furfural is a biomass-derived chemical rather than a petrochemical one, and it is the one clear biomass input in the C4 chain.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.name: Cracker C4 stream
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.description: A NGL stream of 1-butene (15-25%), cis-2-butene (10-15%), trans-2-butene (30-35%), isobutylene (15-25%) and isobutane/isopentane, with butadiene at 20-30% of the C4 - which is 4-6% of the cracker's total hydrocarbon output. The butadiene has to be taken out by a separate, very large unit.
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.note: C4 compositions depend heavily on cracker severity and feedstock; the ranges given are typical naphtha-cracker figures.

facts.label: Butadiene in the C4 stream
facts.value: 20-30 wt% of C4

facts.label: Butadiene in cracker output
facts.value: 4-6 wt% of total hydrocarbons

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.name: C4 recovery and the depentaniser
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.description: Before the butadiene extractor there is the C4 recovery section: a depentaniser that takes the C5+ out of the whole cracker liquid so the C4 unit does not have to handle pentanes and heavier, and then a C3/C4 splitter that separates propane from the butanes. Both columns are ordinary fractionations, but the depentaniser runs at 30-40 bar and is where a lot of the plant's fouling comes from, because the C5+ fraction carries the naphthalene and the heavier aromatics that the C4 extractor does not want.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.name: The C3/C4 splitter
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.description: A 60-80 tray column separating propane overhead from the butanes. It is a good example of a column that has nothing to do with the product of interest: the butadiene extractor's feed comes off the bottom of this splitter, and the splitter's job is only to keep the propane out of the extractor so the extractor's solvent does not have to separate propane from butadiene as well.

chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.name: The depentaniser
chem.butadiene.sources.cracker-c4.c4-rec.description: A 40-60 tray column operating at 25-40 bar, taking the C5 cut point at about 50-60 C. Its overhead is the C4 stream that goes to the extractor; its bottoms are the C5+ gasoline fraction that goes to the aromatics recovery or to the gasoline pool. It is the least glamorous column in the plant and the one that most often needs its furnace cleaned.

chem.acrylonitrile.name: Acrylonitrile and the ammoxidation
chem.acrylonitrile.description: The SOVERE process - SOx-free reductive ammoxidation - oxidises propylene with ammonia and air in one step to acrylonitrile. It was invented at Standard Oil of Ohio and licensed worldwide from 1960-1965, and by 1983 essentially all the world's roughly 1.2-1.5 million tonnes a year of acrylonitrile was made by it. Acrylonitrile is the most dangerous liquid in a polymer plant: it is acutely lethal by skin absorption, flammable at 3-20% in air, and boils at 77 C. The older nitric acid route nitrated propylene with 15-20% nitric acid at 30-60 C and 2-5 bar to a nitropropane mixture, converted the 1-nitropropane with a dialkyl amine to a propylhydroxylamine and dehydrated that to acrylonitrile: a 30-50% yield, a heavy nitrate waste stream and a very large plant, surviving in 1983 only in a few older Soviet and Eastern European works.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.name: Downstream acrylonitrile
