chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.description: What the acrylonitrile was for in 1983: acrylic fibre (Orlon, Dralon, and in Japan the acrylics), nitrile rubber (butadiene copolymer), SAN and ABS copolymer, and the polyacrylonitrile precursor for carbon fibre. More than half the acrylonitrile made in the early 1980s went into acrylic fibre, and a growing slice of the fibre grade went into polyacrylonitrile precursor for carbon fibre, which needs a very pure comonomer (methyl acrylate at 0.5-3%) because any ionic impurity ends up as a carbon defect.
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.note: Carbon fibre for aerospace became a real commercial product in the late 1970s-early 1980s but had essentially no place in a 1982 home computer; the link here is the shared acrylonitrile supply.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.name: Methyl methacrylate (acetone cyanohydrin route)
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.description: A separate molecule with the same nitrile: acetone plus hydrogen chloride gives acetone cyanohydrin, which is esterified with methanol and then dehydrated with sulphuric acid to methyl methacrylate. The acetone cyanohydrin route was introduced from 1938 and became dominant in the 1950s-60s. The hydrogen cyanide for it came either from the acrylonitrile plant's by-product or from its own Andrussow process, and the methanol came from synthesis gas.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.name: Acetone cyanohydrin
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.methyl-met.description: A compound that made the C64 possible twice over: it is the intermediate for methyl methacrylate, and the HCN it carries is the feedstock for methyl methacrylate and for the older butadiene-adiponitrile route to nylon 6,6. It is acutely toxic and it has killed people by being absorbed through the skin, which is the reason the ACH plants had such aggressive containment.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.name: Acrylic acid
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.description: Made by hydrolysis of acrylonitrile in an 85-93% sulphuric acid solution at 90-120 C in a batch or continuous reactor in the 1980s (the later propane-oxidation route came later and took over). The acrylonitrile had to be purified first because the hydrolysis is irreversible and the by-product ammonium sulphate ends up in the polymer. Superabsorbent diapers drove the growth of this route from the late 1970s.

chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.name: Ammonium sulphate by-product
chem.acrylonitrile.downstream.acrylic-ac.description: One tonne of acrylic acid from acrylonitrile hydrolysis throws out about one tonne of ammonium sulphate, which is a low-grade fertiliser that is expensive to dry and transport. It is the classic penalty of the hydrolysis route and the reason the later oxidation route won.

chem.propylene.name: Propylene and its derivatives
chem.propylene.description: Propylene is the C3 that the cracker makes whether you wanted it or not, and for two decades the propylene splitter process existed purely to turn that unwanted C3 into more of it. By 1983 most propylene came from the cracker and from FCC, and it went into polypropylene, propylene oxide, cumene for phenol and bisphenol A, and the acrylonitrile ammoxidation.

chem.propylene.cumene.name: Cumene route to phenol and acetone
chem.propylene.cumene.description: Benzene plus propylene gives cumene; cumene plus oxygen gives cumene hydroperoxide; the hydroperoxide is cleaved with acid to give phenol and acetone. About a million tonnes a year of phenol in 1983 came out of this route, and phenol went to bisphenol A (and therefore to the C64's epoxy laminate resin), to phenol-formaldehyde plastics, and to caprolactam. Acetone came out of the other end of the same reaction, which is why acetone supply in the 1980s was really cumene capacity in disguise.

chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.name: Acid cleavage to phenol and acetone
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.description: The cumene hydroperoxide is cleaved with sulphuric acid (or with a zeolite in later plants) at 50-80 C, giving phenol and acetone with 85-95% selectivity. The 1980s safety concern was the rearrangement of the cumene hydroperoxide to the phenol and acetone, which is violently exothermic: a small holdup upstream of the cleavage reactor would flash-boil, and the famous 1979 and 1985 phenol plant incidents are what the modern design rules are written around.

chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone.name: Acetone
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone.description: The co-product of the cumene process and, from 1960s, a major product in its own right from the acetone cyanohydrin process. Acetone was the electronics plant's solvent of choice for degreasing and photoresist stripping in 1980s practice, and it is also the feedstock for methyl methacrylate and for the bisphenol A plus chloroform route to epoxy.
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.acetone.note: The solvent uses are under chem.solvents.acetone.

chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol.name: Phenol
chem.propylene.cumene.cleavage.phenol.description: The molecule that goes into bisphenol A for epoxy, into phenol-formaldehyde for the phenolic plastics of switches and sockets, and into caprolactam for nylon 6. 1983 world phenol production was of the order of 3.5-4 million tonnes a year, essentially all of it from cumene.

chem.propylene.cumene.oxidation.name: Cumene oxidation to the hydroperoxide
chem.propylene.cumene.oxidation.description: Cumene with air at 120-140 C, either with a hydroperoxide initiator or with a cobalt or manganese catalyst, gives cumene hydroperoxide at 20-40 wt%. This is a liquid-phase autoxidation, and it has the classic autoxidation hazard: the reaction is exothermic, it runs away above 150 C, and the product is a shock-sensitive organic peroxide.
chem.propylene.cumene.oxidation.note: Cumene is oxidised in air to cumene hydroperoxide. Not established: the 120-140 C liquid-phase autoxidation, the hydroperoxide initiator or cobalt/manganese catalyst option, the 20-40 wt% hydroperoxide concentration, and the runaway above 150 C.

facts.label: Conditions
facts.value: 120-140 C, air, initiator or Co/Mn catalyst

chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.name: Cumene alkylation
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.description: Benzene with excess benzene over phosphoric acid on silica at 140-180 C and 20-30 bar in an adiabatic bed, or over a solid acid. The large excess of benzene (3-5 mol per mol of propylene) is deliberate: it suppresses the diethylbenzene and triisopropylbenzene by-products and stops the reactor polymerising the propylbenzene.
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.note: Propylene and benzene are compressed together at 30 bar and 250 C over a catalytic Lewis acid, with phosphoric acid often favoured over aluminium halides. The 140-180 C, 20-30 bar, H3PO4-on-silica adiabatic-bed conditions and the 3-5 mol benzene per mol propylene ratio in this node are the licensor's industrial figures and are not established here.

facts.label: Conditions
facts.value: 30 bar at 250 C over a Lewis acid catalyst; the source notes phosphoric acid is often favoured over the aluminium halides

facts.label: Benzene to propylene
facts.value: 3-5 mol/mol

chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.name: Phosphoric acid on silica
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.description: The classic cumene alkylation catalyst is orthophosphoric acid on a silica carrier: the acid is absorbed into the silica's pore structure and the pore structure holds it there, and the catalyst's whole life is the slow loss of that acid to the reactor walls. The 1980s industry answer was a solid acid and a moving-bed or slurry reactor; the answer that arrived later was a zeolite. Three catalysts for one reaction in fifty years, and the C64's epoxy resin is downstream of all three.

chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.name: Silica carrier (the same silica as the cracker drier)
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.description: A silica gel of 200-400 m2/g surface area, and a strong family resemblance to the 3A molecular sieve's carrier and to the FCC catalyst's matrix and to the ammoxidation catalyst's support. One amorphous silica, made from sand by the soda-silica route, appears in this file as a support four different times, and it is the petrochemical branch's quietest link to a mineral.
chem.propylene.cumene.alkylation.phospho.note: Silica gel is amorphous and porous with nanometre-scale voids, and the same material does appear as a support elsewhere in this chain. Not established: the 200-400 m2/g surface area of the alkylation catalyst's carrier, and the claim that all four supports in this file are one material.

chem.propylene.flame-retardants.name: Chlorinated flame retardants from propylene
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.description: Polymers and elastomers for electronics and furniture were made to burn slowly by chlorinating a paraffinic or a phosphate ester. Chlorinated paraffins, and the phosphorus esters derived from propylene oxide and phosphorus oxychloride, went into the flame-retardant grades of ABS, polypropylene and polyurethane foam that a consumer electronics company would specify for enclosures but not for a home computer.

chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp.name: Tris(2,3-dichloropropyl) phosphate
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp.description: The organophosphate flame retardant made from propylene oxide and phosphorus oxychloride. It is an effective flame retardant for ABS, rigid polyurethane foam and polyester resins, and its precursor, tris(2,3-dibromopropyl) phosphate, is the classic story of a flame retardant that was banned in the United States in the 1970s after it caused animal tumours. That ban is the single clearest link between a 1960s consumer polymer and a 1990s regulation.
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.tdcpp.note: The US ban on tris(2,3-dibromopropyl) phosphate under the Consumer Product Safety Act dates from 1977; the chlorinated phosphate was its less-toxic replacement.

chem.propylene.flame-retardants.chlorina.name: Chlorinated paraffin
chem.propylene.flame-retardants.chlorina.description: Paraffins chlorinated to 40-70% chlorine, used as a secondary flame retardant and, in the 1970s, as a plasticiser for PVC. It is a cheap and effective flame retardant and a persistent environmental contaminant, which is why the 1980s trend in electronics housings was towards phosphorus systems and towards thin walls that did not need as much of it.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.name: Propylene oxide
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.description: Propylene epoxidised, then made into propylene glycol, polyether polyols for polyurethane foam, and propylene chlorohydrin. World production was of the order of 0.7-0.9 million tonnes in 1983. Because the epoxidation of propylene was historically done with hypochlorous acid, a chlorinated by-product stream came with it, and that is why 1,2-dichloropropane and the flame retardants derived from it were part of the same business.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.hydrogen-.name: Hydrogen peroxide epoxidation
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.hydrogen-.description: Propylene plus hydrogen peroxide over a titanium-on-silica catalyst at 40-80 C and 1-10 bar, with the propylene chlorohydrin recycled as the phase-transfer catalyst. It makes no chloride, it is nearly quantitative, and it depends on a cheap supply of hydrogen peroxide - which in 1983 was the reason the anthraquinone peroxide plant and the propylene oxide plant sat next to each other in a few integrated sites.
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.hydrogen-.note: The chlorohydrin-recycling hydrogen peroxide route was the commercially important one in the 1980s; the halide-free TSCA process came later.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: titanium on silica (TiO2/SiO2)

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.name: Chlorohydrin route
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.description: Propylene plus hypochlorous acid gives 1-chloro-2-propanol (about 90%) and 2-chloro-1-propanol (about 10%); the mixture is dehydrochlorinated with a lime or caustic slurry to propylene oxide and the chlorides are recycled as chlorine. The 10% isomer is the problem: it goes on to make propylene chlorohydrin and then the toxic 1,2-dichloropropane, so the plant had a dedicated caustic hydrolysis section for it.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.name: 1,2-dichloropropane
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.description: The unwanted isomer stream, made when propylene chlorohydrin is treated with excess caustic. It is a solvent and a flame-retardant intermediate, and it is toxic to the liver and kidney. In the 1980s the industry reduced its production by selling propylene oxide as a propylene glycol monomethyl ether ether or by shifting to the hydrogen peroxide route, both of which avoid the chloride.

chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.name: 1-chloro-2-propanol
chem.propylene.propylene-oxide.chlorohyd.description: The intermediate whose dehydrochlorination is propylene oxide. It is mildly toxic, it is the reason propylene oxide workers were exposed to a chlorinated alcohol, and it is the direct chemical relative of propylene chlorohydrin, the skin sensitiser that caused occupational dermatitis in the plastics industry before closed systems became normal.

chem.propylene.polymerisation.name: Polypropylene
chem.propylene.polymerisation.description: About 7 million tonnes of polypropylene in 1983, the fastest-growing major plastic. It needs a stereospecific catalyst to be anything but glue: isotactic polypropylene is crystalline and rigid, atactic is a sticky amorphous gum, syndiotactic is a curiosity in the 1980s. The 1980s advances were the high-yield supported catalyst and, on the way in, gas-phase and slurry-loop reactors.

chem.propylene.polymerisation.loops-and-.name: Slurry loop, gas phase and slurry reactor
chem.propylene.polymerisation.loops-and-.description: The 1980s reactor competition: the slurry loop (heptane diluent, polymer as a slurry, then solvent recovery and devolatilising), the loop slurry with 30-50% solids, and the gas-phase fluidised bed with no solvent at all. The gas-phase process was the 1980s newcomer and its whole commercial case was the elimination of the solvent recovery section.

chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospec.name: Stereospecific titanium catalyst
chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospec.description: Titanium trichloride or titanium tetrachloride on magnesium chloride with an aluminium alkyl, refined in the 1970s and 1980s to give activities high enough that no catalyst removal was needed. The MgCl2-supported catalyst with an internal donor (a phthalate or a diether) was the technical development that made modern polypropylene economics work, and the diether donors were commercialised around 1980-83.
chem.propylene.polymerisation.stereospec.note: The activity figures for late-1980s catalysts are order-of-magnitude and were rising quickly year to year.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: TiCl4 or TiCl3 on MgCl2 with AlEt3/AlEt2Cl, internal donor

facts.label: Activity (late 1980s)
facts.value: >20,000-40,000 t polymer per tonne catalyst

chem.propylene.separation.name: Propylene purification
chem.propylene.separation.description: The propylene has to be at 99.5-99.9% with less than 10-20 ppm of carbonyl compounds, because propanal and acetone stop an ionic polymerisation dead. In 1980s practice the purified propylene was made by distillation plus an alkaline wash, and by the later 1980s by hydrazine or hydrazone treatment which converts the carbonyls into something removable.

chem.propylene.sources.name: Where propylene comes from
chem.propylene.sources.description: Three sources, in order of size in 1983: the steam cracker (roughly 40-45% of world propylene supply), catalytic cracking (roughly 30-35%), and dedicated processes. A naphtha cracker makes propylene at about 15% of its hydrocarbon product, so a cracker and a propylene splitter were bolted together in the 1960s to turn the whole C3 stream into pure propylene; by the 1980s the splitter had mostly been bypassed because the C3 could just be purified. The other half of the cracker C5 problem: isoprene was isolated from the FCC C5 stream or synthesised from isobutylene and formaldehyde until synthetic isoprene replaced it in the 1980s, and natural rubber was never seriously displaced because isoprene only gives cis-1,4-polyisoprene with a stereospecific catalyst, and that is a poor substitute for the natural article.
chem.propylene.sources.note: Isoprene is not a C64 material; it is here because it shares the C5 stream and the same cracking chemistry.

chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation.name: Depolymerisation of polypropylene
chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation.description: Reheated polypropylene was fed back to a reactor to recover the propylene it was made from. This was developed as a recycling route in the early 1970s when the word recycle meant something and it survived as a niche process for decades, mostly because the chemical plant could not discharge a plastic waste stream.
chem.propylene.sources.depolymerisation.note: Reactor operation temperatures and the commercial fate of the process in the 1980s are not well documented; treat as a minor route.

chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitte.name: Propylene splitter (the older dedicated unit)
chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitte.description: A dedicated thermal cracker that re-cracked propane and the cracker's propylene-rich C3 stream at 500-600 C to make more propylene, at 15-25% selectivity, with a big furnace and a bad energy balance. It was the standard propylene route of the 1960s, it was still running in 1983 in a few places, and it was generally obsolete by the mid-1980s because the selectivity was hopeless and the cracker had become the cheaper source.
chem.propylene.sources.propylene-splitte.note: Splitter conditions and selectivity vary; the key point is the low selectivity relative to modern routes.

facts.label: Selectivity
facts.value: 15-25% propylene

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.name: Cracker C3 stream
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.description: The propylene and propane that distil out of the cracker's quench separator. Naphtha crackers make roughly 0.15 t of propylene per tonne of feed, which on a 500,000 t/yr cracker is about 75,000 t/yr of propylene - more than a small polypropylene plant needs.

facts.label: Propylene from naphtha cracker
facts.value: ~0.15 t/t feed

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: C3 recovery and the propylene column
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: How the propylene actually leaves the cracker. The C3 and C4 streams are separated in a deethaniser, then the propane and propylene go to a propylene splitter column where the propylene is taken overhead. Before that column, the stream is caustic washed to remove the carbonyls and the oxygenates; in the 1980s this was an option rather than an obligation, and the plants that skipped it were the plants whose polymerisation catalyst was drinking acetone.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: The propylene splitter column
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: A 50-70 tray column 50-70 m tall that separates the propylene overhead from the propane that has to be recycled back to the furnace. Propylene and propane have a relative volatility of about 1.1, so this is a distillation with a reflux ratio of 15-25 and a lot of energy; the 1980s development was a packed or tray hybrid with a side stripper and a low-pressure-drop design, because the column's cost is its energy consumption.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: Chlor-alkali (brine electrolysis)
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: Salt water electrolyzed in a membrane or mercury cell at 60-90 C and 3-4 V DC to give chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. It is the source of every chlorine molecule in this file - the PVC monomer, the epichlorohydrin, the chlorinated solvents, the hypochlorous acid of the propylene chlorohydrin, the phosgene of the polycarbonate, and the trichlorosilane precursor chain of the silicones - and the source of the caustic and the acid that made the phenol-formaldehyde and the ester plasticisers. It is the largest single tonnage of chemistry that a 1983 computer sits on top of, indirectly.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: Brine (salt)
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: A saturated sodium chloride solution, made from a salt mine or a solar evaporation pond, purified to remove calcium and magnesium because they foul the membrane and foul the diaphragm. Salt is the one raw material in this branch that is dug out of the ground rather than taken from a refinery, and it is the true end of the chlorine chain.
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.note: Chlor-alkali electrolysis is conducted in a mercury, diaphragm or membrane cell, so the fouling this node describes is real. Not established: the saturated brine feed, the calcium and magnesium removal specification, and the Stassfurt, Salina and Hockley attributions.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: Membrane cell
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: The cell type that replaced the mercury cell through the 1980s: a perfluorosulfonate membrane separating the anode and cathode, giving chlorine at 99.5%+ without the mercury the older cell had to manage. The conversion of the world's chlor-alkali from mercury to membrane was one of the largest and fastest industrial changeovers of the decade, and it was driven by mercury emissions - the same environmental logic that removed mercury from the PVC acetylene process.
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.note: The membrane cell commercialised from the late 1970s and displaced mercury cells through the 1980s-90s; the timetable varied by region.

chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.name: Caustic wash
chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3.c3-rec.description: A 10-20% sodium hydroxide wash column that neutralises the acidic oxygenates - propanal, acetone, propionic acid, and the phenol and cresols from the C9+ - that the cracker makes. The spent caustic is a refinery effluent problem: it is a phenolic wastewater with a high chemical oxygen demand, and in the 1980s it was often incinerated on the site.

facts.label: Caustic strength
facts.value: 10-20 wt% NaOH

chem.ethylene.name: Ethylene: steam cracking and the polymers of it
chem.ethylene.description: Steam cracking naphtha at 800-900 C over cast alloy coils is the largest single chemical reaction in the world by tonnage. World ethylene capacity in 1983 was about 27-30 million tonnes a year, and roughly half of it went into polyethylene and the rest into ethylene oxide, styrene and solvents. Every polyethylene cable sheath, every styrene monomer and every polyester fibre in a C64 starts in a coiled coil furnace.

chem.ethylene.uses-c64.name: Where the C64's ethylene ends up
chem.ethylene.uses-c64.description: Concretely: the styrene monomer for the ABS case and the SAN matrix, the ethylene oxide route to ethylene glycol for anything polyester in the power supply, the polyethylene in the power cord's insulation and in the moulded cable accessories, and the C2 in the vinyl chloride monomer for the PVC jacket and for the keyboard's keycaps in the less common grades. A C64's ethylene demand is a few tens of grams.
chem.ethylene.uses-c64.note: This figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate from typical material masses and is not a measured value.

facts.label: Ethylene per C64
facts.value: tens of grams of ethylene monomer

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.name: Polyethylene
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.description: The largest use of ethylene: about 12-14 million tonnes of polyethylene were made in 1983, split roughly between low-density (free radical, high pressure) and high-density (coordination catalysis, low pressure). The C64-scale uses are the power cord's insulation and jacket, the moulded cable accessories, and the keyboard membrane's insulation. Metallocene catalysis - one sandwich compound with a zirconium atom between two cyclopentadienyl rings, activated with methylaluminoxane - was first reported in 1980 and was not yet industrial in 1983, but it was the obvious next step because it gives a narrow molecular weight distribution and predictable comonomer placement.

facts.label: First reported
facts.value: 1980 (Kaminsky / Sinn)

facts.label: Industrial use
facts.value: mid-1990s

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.name: Polyethylene additives
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.description: Antioxidants (hindered phenols such as BHT, and phosphites), stabilisers, and pigment. The antioxidant is the reason a polyethylene cable in a C64's power supply does not go brittle: a radical from the mains or from a metal ion attacks the chain and causes scission or cross-linking, and a phenol traps it.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.bht.name: BHT (2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol)
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.bht.description: The workhorse antioxidant, dosed at 0.05-0.2 wt%. It is made by alkylating para-cresol with isobutylene over a solid acid or an aluminium chloride catalyst, and it was also in the C64's power supply as a capacitor-filling fluid (as the antioxidant of the impregnant).
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.additives.bht.note: Not established: the 0.05-0.2 wt% loading and the para-cresol alkylation with isobutylene. In particular the claim that BHT was the antioxidant of the C64 power supply's capacitor-filling fluid is unsupported - no such material appears in the 1992 service manual parts list.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.name: HDPE: coordination catalysis at low pressure
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.description: Ethylene at 20-60 bar and 150-260 C over a transition-metal catalyst gives linear polyethylene with almost no long-chain branching, so it crystallises tightly and has a density of 0.94-0.97. Because the polymer comes out of the reactor as a powder or a slurry rather than a melt, HDPE in 1983 was made in a slurry loop or a gas-phase fluidised bed and then converted by extrusion. The Phillips chromium oxide process (1952) ran chromium oxide on silica at 20-40 bar and 150-200 C in a slurry loop, and it is the reason a 1980s plastics plant had the diluent-recovery section that was its largest single energy consumer. Union Carbide's Unipoly gas-phase process polymerised ethylene as a gas in a fluidised bed at 20-30 bar and 70-100 C with the catalyst on a support: no diluent to recover and no slurry to centrifuge, and by the early 1980s the technology for every new large plant.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: CrOx on silica

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe.name: Linear low density polyethylene
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe.description: Copolymers of ethylene with a small amount of alpha-olefin - 1-butene or 1-octene - which gives a linear chain with short branches: low density with high stiffness. LLDPE was the fastest-growing polyethylene family of the 1980s (about 10-15% of PE production by 1983 and climbing), and the switch from 1-butene to 1-octene was a change in the crackers' product slate rather than in the polymer plant.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.sllpe.note: The exact LLDPE share of 1983 is an estimate; growth in this period was rapid.

facts.label: World LLDPE share of PE, 1983
facts.value: ~10-15% and rising

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Ziegler-Natta polymerisation
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: Titanium tetrachloride or titanium dichloride with an aluminium alkyl (triethylaluminium or diethylaluminium chloride) at 50-100 bar and 50-80 C in a hydrocarbon diluent. Ziegler was the 1953 discovery that started the whole low-pressure polyethylene industry; by the 1960s it had become Ziegler-Natta by supporting the titanium on magnesium chloride, which gave the multiplicity of active sites and therefore the control of molecular weight distribution that made high-density pipe grades possible.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Triethylaluminium
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: The cocatalyst. It alkylates the titanium and reduces Ti(IV) to Ti(III), and it scavenges the water and oxygen that would kill the catalyst. It is pyrophoric, and the 1980s industry response to that fact was the standard practice of diluting it to 5-10% in a hydrocarbon before it ever left the cylinder.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.note: Triethylaluminium is exceedingly pyrophoric and is the organoaluminium cocatalyst paired with titanium-based catalysts. Not established: its alkylation of titanium and reduction of Ti(IV) to Ti(III), its water and oxygen scavenging, and the 5-10% dilution in hydrocarbon as 1980s handling practice.

facts.label: Cocatalyst
facts.value: Al(C2H5)3, 5-10% in hydrocarbon for handling

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Titanium-magnesium chloride catalyst
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: TiCl4 supported on finely divided MgCl2, activated with an aluminium alkyl. The MgCl2 support is the whole trick: it generates about a hundred active titanium sites per gram of catalyst with a range of stereospecificity, and that is what turned HDPE from a family of blends into a graded set of grades.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.note: All modern supported Ziegler-Natta catalysts use TiCl4 as the active ingredient on an MgCl2 support, and the 1970s discovery that magnesium chloride greatly enhances titanium catalyst activity is what made the supported catalyst family dominant. Not established: the roughly hundred active sites per gram, the 50-80 C and 50-100 bar conditions, and the AlEt2Cl alternative cocatalyst.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: TiCl4 on MgCl2, AlEt3 or AlEt2Cl cocatalyst

facts.label: Polymerisation
facts.value: 50-80 C, 50-100 bar, hydrocarbon diluent

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.name: Titanium tetrachloride and the sponge route
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.hdpe.ziegler-.description: The titanium tetrachloride of the Ziegler-Natta catalyst is made from titanium ore - rutile or ilmenite - by chlorinating it with coke and chlorine at 900-1,000 C, then distilling the TiCl4 out at 136 C. Titanium metal comes back by reducing the tetrachloride with magnesium (the Hunter process, which is the Kroll process in reverse) and distilling the magnesium chloride off. So the most important catalyst in the low-pressure polyethylene business is made in a plant that looks exactly like the zirconium and hafnium plants of the nuclear industry, because they all make volatile tetrachlorides. Rutile or ilmenite plus coke plus chlorine at 900-1,000 C gives TiCl4 with iron and vanadium chlorides that have to be removed by distillation - making a volatile chloride the cheapest way to get a pure element out of an oxide. TiCl4 plus magnesium at 800-900 C under argon in a sealed can, then vacuum distillation of the magnesium chloride at 1,000 C, leaves a porous titanium sponge.

facts.label: Carbochlorination
facts.value: 900-1,000 C, coke plus Cl2

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.name: LDPE: free-radical high-pressure process
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.description: Ethylene is polymerised at 200-300 C and 1,000-2,000 bar in a jacketed or tubular reactor with a peroxide initiator, in the liquid phase (below about 280 C) or the gas phase (above it). The density of 0.91-0.93 comes entirely from chain branching: the very high pressure creates radicals on the growing chain, the chain folds, and the branches that stop it crystallising. In 1983 the process was mature to the point of being a cost exercise, and it still made most of the world polyethylene.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.autoclav.name: Autoclave versus tubular reactor
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.autoclav.description: The autoclave process (Union Carbide, 1930s) stirred the gas-phase reaction; the tubular process (Sons, 1950s) had plug flow with injection quills and much better temperature control. By the 1980s the tubular reactor was the standard large unit because it gave a narrower molecular weight distribution and better ethylene conversion, and because the autoclave's bulk polymer needed devolatilising.

chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.initiato.name: Peroxide initiator
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.initiato.description: Di-tert-butyl peroxide, or in the autoclave process a mixture of di-tert-butyl peroxide with di-tert-butyl percarbonate. The initiator decomposes at temperature to give the two tert-butoxy radicals that start the chain, and the choice of half-life at operating temperature sets the run length.
chem.ethylene.polyethylene.ldpe.initiato.note: Not established: di-tert-butyl peroxide with di-tert-butyl percarbonate as the 1980s autoclave initiator pair, the 200-300 C and 1,000-2,000 bar autoclave condition, and the 0.91-0.93 g/cm3 density range.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.name: Ethylene glycol and the glycols
chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.description: Monoethylene glycol, diethylene glycol and triethylene glycol, made by hydration of ethylene oxide in a 1:1 to 1:20 mole ratio of oxide to water, with the ratio chosen to steer the product distribution towards the wanted glycol. In 1980s practice monoethylene glycol was about half the output and went into polyester, antifreeze and diester coolant, and diethylene glycol went into antifreeze and into the unsaturated polyester resins of the same family as the C64's case resin. One tonne of ethylene glycol needs about 3.5 tonnes of ethylene oxide at full selectivity, world MEG capacity was around 4-5 million tonnes a year in 1983, and the big consumers were polyester fibre and film and PET. The older catalytic hydration put ethylene oxide over phosphoric acid on silica at 200-220 C and 60-70 bar with about 20% of the glycol recycled as diluent to suppress ether side products, at 85-90% selectivity to monoethylene glycol - and the whole plant economics is that selectivity, because the diethylene glycol and dioxane have to be sold at a discount. The Shell direct oxidation-hydratation, commercialised in 1965, converted ethylene, oxygen and water in one step over a supported silver-phosphorus-tungsten catalyst for a higher MEG yield and less waste water, at the price of needing very pure oxygen; both routes were still running side by side in 1983.

facts.label: Ethylene oxide per tonne of glycol
World MEG capacity 1983
facts.value: ~4-5 Mt/yr

chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.vacuum-dis.name: Glycol finishing by vacuum distillation
chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.vacuum-dis.description: Water is removed in a multi-column vacuum system because the glycols boil at 197, 245 and 285 C and water outranks them everywhere; a set of vacuum columns at 30-100 mbar separates mono-, di- and triethylene glycol and recovers the unreacted oxide. This is one of the clearest cases in the whole tree where the separation, not the chemistry, is the expensive part.
chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.vacuum-dis.note: Diethylene and triethylene glycol are the major byproducts and separating them from water is energy-intensive, which is the point this node makes. Not established: the 197, 245 and 285 C boiling points, the 30-100 mbar vacuum and the multi-column configuration.

facts.label: Boiling points
facts.value: MEG 197 C, DEG 245 C, TEG 285 C (1 atm)

facts.label: Vacuum
facts.value: 30-100 mbar

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.name: Ethylene oxide
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.description: The oxidation of ethylene over silver at 200-300 C and 20-30 bar, in which every eighth or tenth ethylene molecule is burned to carbon dioxide and water instead of being oxidised. It was about 1.5-2.5 million tonnes a year in 1983, most of it going to ethylene glycol for polyester and to surfactants, and it is one of the most hazardous large-scale chemical processes in existence.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.safety.name: Ethylene oxide safety
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.safety.description: Ethylene oxide boils at 10.7 C, so it is a liquid only just below ambient and a gas in a warm tank; its flammable range in air is 3-80% by volume and its ignition energy is about 0.06 millijoule. It is acutely toxic, it polymerises without catalyst into a runaway, and it is kept in equilibrium by a trace of tertiary butyl alcohol or hydrochlorinated hydrocarbon inhibitor. In 1980s practice the industry standard was a fixed tank or a pressure vessel with an inert blanket, nitrogen purging and a quench section that could handle a deflagration.
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.safety.note: Flammability limits for ethylene oxide are commonly quoted as roughly 3-80% by volume; the flash point is about -20 C. This is the hazard commentary about ethylene oxide, kept with the substance it is about.

facts.label: Flammable range
facts.value: 3-80 vol% in air

facts.label: Inhibitor
facts.value: tert-butyl alcohol (TBC) or hydrochlorinated hydrocarbon

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.name: Air-oxidation process (the industrial one)
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.description: Ethylene and air over silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina in a multi-tubular reactor at 200-300 C and 20-30 bar. Per-pass conversion is only 10-15% and the selectivity to ethylene oxide is 80-90%, so the unreacted ethylene is recycled with the inert diluent. The alternative process - the chlorohydrin route, ethylene plus hypochlorous acid to chloroethanol to oxide - was still running in the United States in the early 1980s but had been almost entirely displaced by air oxidation elsewhere. The superseded chlorohydrin route chlorinated ethylene in water and dehydrochlorinated with lime, and made a chlorinated calcium salt waste for every tonne of product, which is why it survived only in the United States: a process displaced not by yield but by waste.
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.note: Chlorohydrin EO production was already minor by the early 1980s and was essentially gone by the mid-1980s in Europe and Japan.

chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.name: Silver on alpha-alumina catalyst
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.description: 10-20% silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina, promoted by chlorine. Silver is the only catalyst that works: it is the only metal that both activates oxygen and lets ethylene through, and the geometry matters as much as the chemistry, because the low surface area keeps the pore diameter small enough to suppress the combustion pathway. Catalyst life is 2-5 years and the silver is recovered at the end of it.
chem.ethylene.ethylene-oxide.air-oxidati.note: Almost all industrial ethylene oxide has been made by direct oxidation of ethylene over a silver catalyst since 1940. Not established: 10-20% silver on low-surface-area alpha-alumina, the chlorine promoter, the 80-90% selectivity and 10-15% per-pass conversion, the 2-5 year catalyst life, and the silver recovery.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: 10-20% Ag on low-surface-area alpha-Al2O3

facts.label: Selectivity
facts.value: 80-90% to ethylene oxide

chem.ethylene.purification.name: Ethylene purification
chem.ethylene.purification.description: Before the ethylene can be polymerised it has to be dry and essentially free of oxygen and carbon dioxide, because both water and oxygen poison a radical or coordination polymerisation catalyst irreversibly. A cracker therefore had a molecular sieve drier taking water to under 1 ppm and a CO2/CO removal stage. 3A or 4A zeolite molecular sieve in beds switched in parallel took the water below 1 ppmv - the same family of material as the FCC catalyst and the styrene alkylation catalyst, which is the clearest single illustration that one piece of chemistry runs through the whole tree. Oxygen was held under 1 ppm and carbon dioxide under 5 ppm by an amine or a solid bed, and the CO2 was the dangerous one: it poisons the coordination catalysts and it reacts with the organoaluminium cocatalyst of a Ziegler-Natta polymerisation.
chem.ethylene.purification.note: Drying and oxygen/CO2 removal are part of this step; the four numbers that define the grade are its facts.

facts.label: Water specification
facts.value: <1 ppmv

facts.label: Molecular sieve
facts.value: 3A or 4A

facts.label: Oxygen
facts.value: <1 ppmv

facts.label: Carbon dioxide
facts.value: <5 ppmv

chem.ethylene.quench.name: Quenching and acetylene control
chem.ethylene.quench.description: The cracked gas leaves the coil at 800-900 C and has to come down to under 40 C in a second or two before anything can be separated, or the reactor metallurgy melts. The choice of quench is a real fork in the road: a gas quench to 350-400 C followed by selective hydrogenation, or a direct spray quench to under 40 C. A spray quench injects liquid hydrocarbon or quench oil straight into the cracked gas, which is cheap and puts the gas into the quench-oil circuit at once but cannot be combined with selective hydrogenation, because the acetylene has already polymerised in the cooler.

chem.ethylene.quench.decanter.name: Decanter and quench oil circuit
chem.ethylene.quench.decanter.description: The condensed liquid is settled and decanted, separating the heavy C9+ tar from the gasoline and C4 streams. The heavy fraction - about 5-10% of the cracker feed - was the benzene, toluene and xylenes rich C9+ cut in the 1980s, and it was the aromatics feed for the styrene plants and the solvent plants.

chem.ethylene.quench.gas-quench.name: Gas quench to 350-400 C
chem.ethylene.quench.gas-quench.description: The cracked gas is quenched with recycled process gas rather than directly with liquid, stopping at 350-400 C. This keeps the gas hot enough that the acetylene survives, so the acetylene can be destroyed deliberately afterwards in a selective hydrogenation reactor (palladium on alumina at 130-180 C, 10-30 bar hydrogen) rather than being allowed to polymerise into gums in the cooler. Ethylene purity of 99.9%+ with acetylene under 5 ppm is the target. Palladium on alumina at 130-180 C and 10-30 bar of hydrogen converts the acetylene to ethylene, and it is why a cracker carried a few tonnes of 0.5-2% Pd: the hydrogen partial pressure had to be held tightly, because too much of it makes ethane and costs ethylene yield.

facts.label: Acetylene in product ethylene
facts.value: <5 ppm

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.name: Steam cracking
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.description: A hydrocarbon feed mixed with steam is brought to 800-900 C in a few tenths of a second in a serpentine coil inside a radiant furnace, at 1-3 bar. The chemistry is brutal free-radical chain cracking: the large molecules fall apart into smaller ones and a large hydrogen-rich tail gas. What decides the plant is how fast the coil can be taken to temperature without coking it, and how fast it can be cooled again. Steam does two jobs: it lowers the hydrocarbon partial pressure so radicals recombine into smaller molecules rather than into carbon, and it carries the heat into the coil.

facts.label: Ethylene yield (naphtha)
facts.value: 25-35 wt% of feed

facts.label: Coke on coil
facts.value: 0.05-0.2 wt% of feed before decoking

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.expander.name: Cracked-gas expander turbine
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.expander.description: The cracked gas at 800-900 C is not simply cooled; in the 1980s it was let down through a turboexpander that recovered most of the sensible heat as work, doing the job of the quench exchanger. The expander recovered 10-20% of the cracking energy and was one of the reasons the energy crisis of the 1970s produced a generation of much more efficient crackers.

facts.label: Work recovered
facts.value: 10-20% of the cracking enthalpy

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.name: Coke and decoking
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.description: Coke builds up on the coil, which insulates it, raises the skin temperature and finally blocks the tube. 1980s practice was to shut the furnace and decoke in place by burning the coke out with steam and air (off-line decoking), taking several hours and costing several thousand dollars a cycle; a shift to shorter, more frequent on-line decokes came later with the high-performance coils. The coke itself is a fine, hard, low-metal material that has to be disposed of.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.co.name: Cracker coke
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.decoking.co.description: A granular, high-carbon, low-hydrogen solid with vanadium and nickel that came out of the feed. It is a nuisance rather than a product in the 1980s - the FCC coke market was far bigger and the cracker coke was dirty - and a large cracker made a few hundred to a few thousand tonnes a year of it.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epo.name: Ceramic (CHA) coil coating
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epo.description: Cracking alumina or silicon carbide coated onto the coil inside the furnace. The industry spent the 1970s and early 1980s trying to reduce coil metal temperature by 50-100 C; silicon carbide coatings (the CHA process, from Combustion Heat Exchanger) were the commercially successful route and let a furnace run hotter for the same metal temperature, which is worth several percent of ethylene yield.
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.epo.note: Coating technologies and their names vary by licensor; the general point - coatings lower the metal skin temperature - is solid.

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coi.name: Cracker coil metallurgy
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coi.description: The coil is cast alloy, not steel: 25Cr-35Ni (Incoloy 800, 800H, 802) or the HP-modified 35Cr-45Ni alloys of the 1980s. The radiant fire gas is oxidising and its metal skin runs 30-50 C above the process temperature, so at 850 C process the skin is 880-900 C; a carbon steel coil crept and failed. Incoloy 800 became the industry standard, and its nickel content is one reason a cracker is so expensive.
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.coi.note: Coil alloy compositions vary between licensors (Sons, Lummus, Mitsubishi, Linde) and the alloy detail is a metals-chain item; what matters here is that it is a cast high-nickel alloy bought in tonnes.

facts.label: Tube size
facts.value: 4 in (100-114 mm) OD, 4-6 mm wall, cast

chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.name: Cracker furnace and radiant section
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.description: A refractory-lined box 20-40 m long with 40-80 coiled coils hung side by side, each coil 30-80 m of 4 in (100 mm) cast tube in ten passes of 10-20 m. The fire is gas- or oil-fired at 30-50 MW per furnace, and the radiant duty is the whole point: roughly 70% of the process heat has to arrive by radiation because convection through the gas is too slow to get the coil to 850 C in half a second.
chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.furnace.note: Feed is mixed with very hot steam and briefly heated in a furnace with the reaction temperature around 850 C. Not established: the 20-40 m box with 40-80 coiled coils, the 4 in cast tube in ten passes, the 30-50 MW firing rate, and the roughly 70% radiant duty. The 800-900 C range is for modern units, not a 1982 figure.

facts.label: Gas outlet temperature
facts.value: 800-900 C (modern units 850-870 C)

facts.label: Coil count
facts.value: 40-80 coils per furnace

facts.label: Residence time in coil
facts.value: 0.1-1 second

facts.label: Firing rate
facts.value: 30-50 MW per furnace

chem.ethylene.feedstock.name: Cracker feedstock
chem.ethylene.feedstock.description: Naphtha was 70-80% of world cracker capacity in 1983, ethane and propane 20-30%. The choice is regional and historical: US Gulf crackers run on ethane piped from the Gulf's gas fields because the ethane price under a gas contract made it unbeatable; European and Japanese crackers run on naphtha because they had no ethane to hand. A naphtha cracker is the one that makes propylene and butadiene as well as ethylene, which is why the older chemical industry grew up on it.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.gas-oil.name: Gas oil feedstock (the third choice)
chem.ethylene.feedstock.gas-oil.description: The heavier option, chosen when naphtha and gas oil were both dear: a 300-700 F cut cracked harder to get ethylene, coking heavily, and yielding the most propylene of the three. Gas oil cracking existed in the Middle East and in Japan through the 1970s and mostly disappeared in the 1980s because its cost per tonne of ethylene was the worst of the three.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.ethane.name: Ethane feedstock
chem.ethylene.feedstock.ethane.description: Ethane cracks cleanly with little coke and needs almost no steam dilution, so an ethane cracker is cheaper to run and its ethylene yield (50-55%) is much higher. But it makes almost no propylene and no butadiene, so a pure ethane cracker has to buy its co-products. The 1980s US Gulf argument about ethane versus naphtha was really an argument about whether propylene and butadiene were worth more than the extra ethylene.

facts.label: Ethylene yield from ethane
facts.value: ~50-55% of feed

facts.label: Steam dilution (ethane)
facts.value: 20-40 mol% vs 200-400 mol% for naphtha

chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-prop.name: Ethane and propane (LPG)
chem.natural-gas.composition.ethane-prop.description: The C2 and C3 that make natural gas liquids, recovered as LPG at 1.5-8 bar in the field and as a debottlenecking liquid at the gas plant, then split for heating or fed to a cracker. LPG was the preferred cracker feedstock precisely because it is already light and needs no naphtha handling. A dedicated propane cracker needs far less steam dilution (20-40 mol% against 200-400 mol% for naphtha) and so makes far less process gas per tonne of ethylene, but it makes almost no co-product: the propylene and butenes streams shrink and the C4 stream effectively disappears.

chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha.name: Naphtha feedstock
chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha.description: A C5 to 200-220 F hydrocarbon cut, hydrotreated to under 0.5 wt% sulphur and under 0.5 ppmw nitrogen. Beyond its hydrocarbon content what matters is the coniocarbon and the asphaltene content: those are what coke the coil. The naphtha from an Arabian light crude is comparatively clean, which is one reason Gulf crackers could run at a lower steam dilution than a naphtha cracker fed with heavy California naphtha.
chem.ethylene.feedstock.naphtha.note: The refinery side of this handover is chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha-to-ethylene. A refinery fraction: naphtha is cut from light sour crude, so this leaf now terminates the whole cracker chain at chem.petroleum.

chem.ethylene.scale.name: The ethylene industry in 1983
chem.ethylene.scale.description: About 27-30 Mt/yr of world ethylene capacity in 1983, of which the United States held roughly 19 Mt (about two thirds) and Western Europe about 8 Mt, with the Gulf Coast of the US, the Rhine-Ruhr, Antwerp, the Suez Gulf and the Japanese and Korean coasts as the clusters. A 1980s cracker cost $150-400 million and took three to five years to build.
chem.ethylene.scale.note: Capacity and cost figures for this period are approximate; cracker capital costs roughly doubled between 1978 and 1981.

facts.label: US share
facts.value: ~19 Mt (~2/3 of world)

facts.label: Grassroots cracker cost
facts.value: $150-400 million (late 1970s-early 1980s)

chem.refining.name: Refining: turning crude into fuels and feedstocks
chem.refining.description: Atmospheric and vacuum distillation to cut crude into fractions, then conversion and upgrading processes to make the specific products industry wants. For the C64 the interesting products are not the fuels but the naphtha that gets steam-cracked to ethylene, the benzene for styrene, the LPG for crackers, and the elemental sulphur recovered from hydrogen sulphide. In 1983 world refining capacity was roughly 65-70 million barrels a day, about 30% above demand, and the industry was running at 65-75% utilisation.
chem.refining.note: Category industry for the refinery units themselves and fluids for the hydrocarbon streams, catalysts and specs they handle: refining is a plant, and energy is reserved for power generation and the grid.

chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.name: Refinery to polymer: the handover
chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.description: Three handovers matter. Naphtha plus steam into a cracker gives ethylene and propylene. C4 from the same cracker gives butadiene and isobutylene. Reformer naphtha into the aromatics complex gives benzene, which with ethylene gives styrene. This node is the place where the fuel industry stops and the polymer industry starts, and it is the join that makes a C64 physically possible. The cracker hands over a C4 stream of 1-butene, the 2-butenes and isobutylene, and extracting the butadiene out of it is a second plant; the isobutylene left behind goes to MTBE or alkylate and the butenes go to hydroformylation for plasticisers. Benzene out of the aromatics complex is alkylated with ethylene in excess benzene (to suppress diethylbenzene) to give ethylbenzene, which is then dehydrogenated.

chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha.name: Naphtha to ethylene
chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha.description: The handover. Naphtha plus steam at 800-900 C over a cast alloy coil, giving 25-35% ethylene by weight with propylene, butenes and a benzene-rich C9+ residue. Roughly 70-80% of world cracker capacity in 1983 was naphtha-based, with the rest ethane and propane; the Gulf Coast and the Far East were naphtha and the Texas Gulf was liquid-fuelled ethane.
chem.refining.polymer-feedstocks.naphtha.note: The steam-dilution numbers for a naphtha cracker are recorded on the steam cracking step at chem.ethylene.steam-cracking.

chem.refining.products.name: Refinery products and by-products
chem.refining.products.description: Fuels, lubricants, waxes, coke and sulphur. For this tree the interesting list is short: naphtha to the crackers, benzene to styrene, LPG to crackers, propylene and butylene to the older chemical plants, and sulphur to rubber and to sulphuric acid.
chem.refining.products.note: Refinery products and by-products is a heading for the three streams beneath it rather than a substance of its own. Lubricant base oils, waxes and fuel oil remain as nodes.

chem.refining.products.fuel-oil.name: Fuel oil
chem.refining.products.fuel-oil.description: The bottom of the barrel: a 1-3% sulphur residue sold to power stations and ships. After 1973, and especially after the 1980s tanker accidents, the political life of fuel oil in Europe and the US got hard, and the refinery's answer was more conversion. In 1983 fuel oil still took about 25-30% of world refinery production.
chem.refining.products.fuel-oil.note: The fuel-oil share of 1983 refinery output and the regulatory context are order-of-magnitude figures; exact shares varied widely by region.

chem.refining.products.waxes.name: Petroleum waxes and slack wax
chem.refining.products.waxes.description: Waxy distillate from solvent deasphalting, deoiled on a centrifuge train to give hard, medium and soft paraffin wax and microcrystalline wax. Slack wax goes into paper, board and packaging film; the microcrystalline waxes are the petroleum fraction that was blended into the first generation of hot-melt adhesives.

chem.refining.products.lubricants.name: Lubricant base oils
chem.refining.products.lubricants.description: Distillate fractions solvent-extracted (2,700-5,000 Ns at 100 C) and hydrofinished, or in the 1980s increasingly hydroisomerised. The C64 link is not the lubricant in the gearbox but the fact that the same hydrofinishing catalysts and the same additive chemistry (zinc dialkyldithiophosphate, made from phosphorus pentasulphide) appear in the machine's grease and in the rubber and plastic stabilisers.
chem.refining.products.lubricants.note: The C64-scale claims here are inferential; the base-oil processes described are standard but the specific link to a 1983 consumer machine's lubricants is not documented in the sources used here.

chem.refining.octane.name: Lead phase-down and the unleaded problem
chem.refining.octane.description: Tetraethyl lead was phased out of most industrialised markets between 1978 and 1985 as catalytic converters spread. The lead phase-down is the single most consequential fuel specification change of the decade and it is the reason MTBE, alkylate, isomerate and the ZSM-5 additive were all developed on that timescale. Without lead the refiner needed 3-8 octane numbers from somewhere, and in 1983 the United States solved it with MTBE, ZSM-5 and alkylate while Europe, with a smaller and cleaner car fleet, was much less short - which is why MTBE uptake was overwhelmingly American.

facts.label: Lead phase-down
facts.value: 1978-1985 across OECD markets

chem.refining.octane.tetraethyl-lead.name: Tetraethyl lead
chem.refining.octane.tetraethyl-lead.description: Pb(C2H5)4 blended at a few grams per litre, discovered in 1921 and the cheapest octane technology for fifty years. It was the cheapest route to octane and the most expensive in externalities: it destroyed the lead and phosphorus catalysts that were the whole point of the catalytic converter. Teledyne and DuPont stopped adding it to road fuel in most markets by 1985.

chem.refining.isomerisation.name: Isomerisation and octane boosting
chem.refining.isomerisation.description: The C5 and C6 straight-chain paraffins in naphtha have terrible octane numbers; isomerising them to the branched isomers does something about that with almost no yield loss. This is the cheap half of the unleaded-gasoline story; MTBE and alkylate were the expensive half. C5/C6 isomerisation over platinum on chlorided alumina, or from the 1980s a zeolite unit at 250-350 C with an aromatics-rich recycle, yields 98-99% and buys 8-12 octane numbers - trivial per barrel, material at a million barrels a day. Alkylate is isobutane plus isobutylene or propylene over anhydrous HF at 20-40 C, and HF alkylation was a large and dangerous business in 1980s practice: an HF cloud is dense, water-soluble and burns deeply, so the units had their own HF storage and a dedicated water curtain.

facts.label: Alkylation conditions
facts.value: anhydrous HF, 20-40 C, 1-3 bar

chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.name: MTBE (methyl tert-butyl ether)
chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.description: Methanol plus isobutylene over an acidic ion-exchange resin (Amberlyst, sulphonic acid polystyrene, about 100 C, 5-10 bar), giving a 100+ octane component. MTBE was the big gasoline technology story of the late 1970s and early 1980s in the United States, and its feedstock - isobutylene - came from the crackers and the FCC, which is the direct petrochemical link: the same C4 that becomes butadiene rubber becomes the octane booster in American petrol.

chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.ion-exc.name: Ion-exchange resin catalyst
chem.refining.isomerisation.mtbe.ion-exc.description: A macroporous or gel-type sulphonic-acid polystyrene resin, the same chemistry as the ion exchange resins used in water treatment. MTBE resins had to be replaced every 10,000-20,000 hours in the 1980s as they aged.

chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.name: Catalytic reforming and the aromatics complex
chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.description: Reforming naphtha over platinum at 500-540 C and 15-30 bar converts paraffins and naphthenes into aromatics, releasing about 0.2-0.3 tonnes of hydrogen per tonne of feed and upgrading the octane number. It is where the world's benzene comes from, and therefore where the styrene in the C64's ABS comes from. Platforming (UOP, 1943) is the process that made the aromatised gasoline era possible: naphtha from C5 to about 220 C over 0.3-0.4 wt% platinum and rhenium on chlorided alumina at 500-540 C and 15-30 bar with an H2/hydrocarbon ratio of 5-6. The benzene plant extracts the C6 aromatics from the reformer effluent, separates benzene, toluene and the C8 isomers and hydrogenates the xylenes back to benzene, because a tonne of xylene is worth less than a tonne of benzene. Deactivated catalyst was shipped out and the platinum, rhenium and gallium recovered by chlorination, aqua regia dissolution and solvent extraction, which also disposed of the refinery's radioactive coke from the feed's radium.

facts.label: Hydrogen to hydrocarbon
facts.value: 5-6 molar

facts.label: Benzene in reformer feed
facts.value: 2-5% of naphtha when run for octane, up to ~50% when run for aromatics

chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platin.name: Platinum-rhenium on chlorided alumina
chem.refining.catalytic-reforming.platin.description: Platinum crystallites of about 1 nm on gamma-alumina promoted with chlorine to keep the metal and the acid function in balance. Platinum is one of the most expensive catalysts in the plant, so catalyst regeneration and platinum recovery are real economics: the platinum in a 1980s reformer was worth tens of thousands of dollars, and the catalyst was shipped off site for reclamation.

chem.refining.claus.name: Claus process: recovering elemental sulphur
chem.refining.claus.description: Three-quarters of a mole of oxygen is used to burn a third of the hydrogen sulphide to sulphur dioxide, then the two react over an alumina catalyst to make sulphur and water: 2 H2S + SO2 -> 3 S + 2 H2O. The Claus unit turns the refinery's or gas plant's worst stream into a saleable commodity, and its output is the elemental sulphur that the whole 1980s chemical industry - rubber vulcanisation, fungicides, sulphuric acid - depended on. The Canadian oil sands' sulphur problem and the Arabian gas sweetening builds both exist because of this unit.

chem.refining.claus.catalyst.name: Claus catalyst (activated alumina)
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.description: High-surface-area alumina, sometimes promoted with titanium, in two or three fixed beds at 200-350 C with interstage reheating. Because the reaction is exothermic and reversible, a multi-bed converter with controlled quench keeps the equilibrium favourable; a single-bed converter cannot get above about 80% overall recovery.

chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.name: Claus alumina catalyst and its support
chem.refining.claus.catalyst.alumina-cat.description: The catalyst is not a mystery material: it is activated alumina, and the alumina is refined from bauxite. A Claus unit's catalyst life is measured in years and its loss rate is what sets the unit's sulphur recovery, so a good 1980s unit used a promoted, high-surface-area alumina with a shape (extrudate or cylindrical) chosen to hold surface area at 300-400 C.

chem.refining.claus.furnace.name: Claus furnace
chem.refining.claus.furnace.description: A refractory-lined furnace at 250-400 C where a third of the H2S is burned with oxygen or air. The burn has to be kept on the rich side: too much oxygen and the H2S is oxidised all the way to SO2, which wastes the sulphur; too little and soot forms and plugs the catalyst.

facts.label: First stage conversion
facts.value: 30-40% of the H2S to SO2

chem.refining.hydrotreating.name: Hydrotreating and desulphurisation
chem.refining.hydrotreating.description: The refinery's chemistry of taking things out: sulphur, nitrogen, oxygen and metals, plus saturation. It is the answer to sour crude, and it is the process that made Arab Light and Mexican crudes usable in 1980s refineries. It also produces the acid gas from which elemental sulphur is recovered. Naphtha hydrotreating at 300-400 C and 20-50 bar of hydrogen over cobalt-molybdenum on alumina to 0.2-0.5 wt% sulphur is the pretreatment that makes a crude usable in a cracker. Gas oil was hydrodesulphurised at 300-400 C and 30-80 bar over Co-Mo or Ni-Mo to 0.1-0.3 wt% S, with a 0.05 wt% deep-desulphurisation variant developed in the late 1970s for the 1990 fuel specifications; every barrel desulphurised is a barrel of fuel oil turned into saleable middle distillate. Jet kerosene has to be under 3 wt% sulphur and free of water, because it passes through a turbine at 800-1,000 C with water condensing in the fuel-oil nozzles, so the kero hydrotreater runs at 300-400 C and 30-50 bar and carries a naphthenic acid problem of its own.

facts.label: Deep desulphurisation
facts.value: 0.05 wt% S (late 1970s-80s development)

chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.name: Acid gas to the Claus unit
chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.description: Every hydrotreater and every amine unit makes an acid gas of mostly H2S with some CO2. In 1983 that stream was worth real money: recovering its sulphur turns a disposal liability into a product, and about 80-90% of world sulphur production was elemental sulphur recovered this way. A 20-35 wt% MEA or DEA absorber took the H2S and CO2 out of the hydrogen recycle gas and the rich amine was stripped in a 120-130 C reboiler; the amine was degraded by the oxygen and hydrocarbons in the gas, and the amine/oil/water effluent was one of the refinery's worst waste streams of the period.
chem.refining.hydrotreating.acid-gas.note: Same amine chemistry as the gas sweetening plant: chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-gas.discovery-and-drilling.sweetening.

chem.refining.vacuum-residue-processing.name: Converting the vacuum residue
chem.refining.vacuum-residue-processing.description: The 2-5% of crude that will not distil is the hardest material in the refinery. It must be converted - into coke, into gasoline, or into distillate - or it is sold as fuel oil. This is where the refinery's biggest single units and its biggest capital decisions sit. Hydrocracking cracked heavy oil and hydrogenated the fragments in one step at 350-450 C and 80-200 bar of hydrogen over cobalt-molybdenum or nickel-molybdenum on alumina, giving 70-90% diesel with almost no sulphur - the process that let a refinery make diesel rather than fuel oil.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.name: Fluid catalytic cracking
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.description: Vacuum gas oil is contacted with a zeolite catalyst at 500-530 C and 1-3 bar in a riser, cracked into gasoline, light ends and coke, and the catalyst is continuously regenerated in a fluidised-bed regenerator at 650-750 C. FCC was the largest refinery process by capacity in the early 1980s - a large unit processing 40,000-100,000 bbl/d - and the source of most of the world's leaded-free gasoline blending components and of the propylene that fed the older chemical crackers.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.c.name: Cracked gasoline and the propylene route
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.c.description: FCC gasoline is high in olefins, aromatics and isoparaffins, with an octane number well above the reformer's, and it is the blending component that let the industry drop lead. Its propylene stream - 2-4% of FCC feed - fed the old chemical industry: by 1983 propylene from FCC and from crackers together supplied roughly half the world's propylene, and the older propylene splitter process existed precisely to make more of it.

facts.label: Propylene from FCC
facts.value: 2-4% of FCC feed by mass

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: FCC zeolite catalyst
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: A synthetic zeolite (USY, made by dealuminating Y zeolite) dispersed in a silica-alumina or silica matrix, rare-earth exchanged by lanthanum and neodymium. The zeolite gives shape-selective acid sites; the matrix gives attrition resistance and heat capacity. This is the same family of materials as the zeolites that would crack naphtha for styrene a decade later. Vanadium and nickel in the feed deposit as mobile vanadates and nickel species that destroy zeolite acid sites and accelerate dehydrogenation, so passivation additives - an aluminium monohydride slurry, antimony compounds - were standard by the 1980s, with gasoline desulphurisation additives appearing at the end of the decade.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: Making the FCC zeolite
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: A synthetic zeolite is not mined; it is crystallised. The reagents are an alumina source, a silica source, an alkali and a template, and the product is a 3-5 micron crystal of a lattice so regular that it was named after the mineral zeolite. The FCC catalyst's lattice is what makes it a shape-selective acid, and the same recipe with a different template and a different silica-to-alumina ratio gives the MFI zeolite of the styrene alkylation and the 3A sieve of the cracker drier. One family of chemistry, four jobs, and about a tenth of a tonne of catalyst per year for every 10,000 bbl/d of FCC capacity. The Y zeolite is grown from an aluminosilicate gel at 100-200 C with a seed and then dealuminated - by acid leaching, by chlorination with HCl or ammonium persulphate, or thermally with steam - to raise its silica-to-alumina ratio from about 5 to about 6-10.
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.note: Dealumination silica-to-alumina ratios vary by process and product; the values are representative of the era's USY.

facts.label: Crystallisation
facts.value: 100-200 C, aqueous, seeded

facts.label: USY silica-to-alumina
facts.value: about 6-10, from about 5 for Y

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: ZSM-5 octane additive
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: A small-pore zeolite (mordenite framework, 10-membered rings) blended at 3-15% into the USY catalyst to crack the C7-C10 straight chains that were killing octane after the lead phase-down. This is the direct ancestor of the propylene and isobutylene it also made: ZSM-5 selectively shapes the products towards C3 and C4 olefins.

facts.label: Blend level
facts.value: 3-15% of the catalyst

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.name: Silica-alumina matrix
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.z.description: Amorphous silica-alumina, precipitated from sodium silicate and aluminium sulphate and caustic-gelled, then spray dried as 40-90 micron microspheres. The matrix is what gives the catalyst its attrition resistance and its heat capacity; it also carries a good part of the cracking, because the matrix surface area is large and the zeolite is expensive.

chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.r.name: Riser and regenerator
chem.refining.fluid-catalytic-cracking.r.description: The riser reactor is a vertical pipe 10-20 m long with the catalyst and feed entering at the bottom; the cyclone separators strip entrained catalyst back; the regenerator burns the coke off the catalyst with air. A 1980s unit's two-stage regeneration was the standard answer to how to get more heat into the reactor while cutting carbon monoxide from the stack.

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: 1-3 bar absolute

facts.label: Coke yield
facts.value: 4-6% of feed

chem.refining.delayed-coking.name: Delayed coking
chem.refining.delayed-coking.description: Vacuum residue is heated to 350-400 C and held in large coke drums for 12-24 hours, during which it cracks to 15-25% petroleum coke while the vapours are continuously drawn off and fractionated. Delayed coking was the dominant residue conversion process of the 1960s and remained so through the 1980s, handling maybe 40-50% of vacuum residue in a complex refinery, largely because it makes the anode-grade coke the aluminium industry needs.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.green-coke.name: Green coke
chem.refining.delayed-coking.green-coke.description: The unreformed coke straight out of the drum: 85-92 wt% carbon, 8-15% volatiles, with all the feed's sulphur and metals still in it. Green coke is the intermediate between the coker drum and the calciner, and it is also what the plastics industry noticed in the 1980s: green coke is a needle-coke precursor, and it is the reason carbon fibre of aerospace grade became possible after the large-scale-carbon-fibre work of the late 1960s.

chem.refining.delayed-coking.coke-drum.name: Coke drum
chem.refining.delayed-coking.coke-drum.description: A 6-11 m diameter vessel 20-35 m tall holding 100-400 tonnes of coke per cycle, switched in parallel with a fractionator overhead. Switching a drum is the highest-risk operation in a refinery: the drum is water-quenched and de-coked with a full-diameter drill and coke cutter while the neighbouring drum runs at temperature.

facts.label: Coke yield
facts.value: 15-25% of vacuum residue

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 12-24 hours

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.name: Atmospheric distillation
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.description: Fractional distillation of crude at atmospheric pressure in a 35-50 m fractionating tower, separating a barrel of crude into naphtha, kerosene, gas oil, and a 700 F residue. It is the first process every molecule of the polymer industry passes through, and it is where the difference between a 30 and a 40 degree API crude turns into a 200 versus 260 dollar a tonne cracker feedstock. The naphtha overhead is where refinery corrosion happens: water condenses out of the vapour, dissolves the HCl that came in with the crude brine and dissolves H2S into very aggressive sulphuric acid, and 1980s practice attacked it with an ammonia or amine neutraliser injected into the overhead condenser plus a wash-water draw.
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.note: Total acid number values are crude-specific and the threshold for accelerated attack is generally quoted as above about 2 mg KOH/g at the column temperature.

facts.label: Typical naphthenic acid index
facts.value: 1-3 mg KOH/g for Arabian heavy crude

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.name: Vacuum distillation
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.description: A second column at 25-50 mmHg absolute (740-760 mmHg vacuum) that distils the 700 F plus residue down to a vacuum gas oil and a vacuum residue of 2-5% of the crude, without cracking it. Lowering the pressure raises the boiling points' relative spacing so heavy molecules can be distilled instead of decomposed, and the vacuum is made by steam ejectors or by a barometric leg. Below about 350 C the residue cracks rather than distils, so the flash zone is run at 340-370 C and the vacuum gas oil carries some cracked material; the side reactions make coke and acids, which is why the column needs wash sections and anti-fouling coatings.

facts.label: Vacuum residue yield
facts.value: 2-5% of crude

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.name: Steam ejectors and vacuum
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.v.description: Three-stage steam ejectors holding 25-50 mmHg, using 10-25 t of steam per hour for a mid-size unit. Ejectors are simple but they cost a lot of steam; by the 1980s mechanical vacuum pumps (rotary or liquid-ring, with a surface condenser) were being installed to save that steam, and most plants still had ejectors as backup.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Fractionating tower
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: A 35-50 m column with 40-50 trays, at about 1.1-1.5 bar overhead and 2.5-3 bar at the bottom, condensing a vapour-liquid staircase in which each tray separates hydrocarbons by boiling range. A large atmospheric tower is a pressure vessel of 100-200 tonnes, and it is still the cheapest separation device ever built per tonne of product. A modern valve tray is 70-90% efficient against an ideal stage and the tower needs enough reflux (a few per cent of the feed) to wet the trays; cutting reflux to save furnace duty is the classic operating trade and it costs separation.

facts.label: Valve tray efficiency
facts.value: 70-90% Murphree

facts.label: Typical reflux
facts.value: 2-6% of feed, as liquid

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Naphtha hydrotreating before the cracker
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The cracker feedstock was almost never straight-run naphtha. It was hydrotreated to under 0.5 wt% total sulphur (often 0.05-0.3 wt%) and under 0.5 ppmw nitrogen, because sulphur poisons the reforming and cracking catalysts and nitrogen poisons the polymerisation catalysts downstream. Naphtha hydrotreating is the first place refinery chemistry meets polymer chemistry.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Sour water stripper
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The hydrogenating reactors make water and ammonia, and the separator water carries dissolved H2S and NH3. A stripper removes them, otherwise the recycled hydrogen carries ammonia into the cracker, where ammonia poisons the polymerisation catalysts and shows up as a colour defect in the polymer.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Cobalt-molybdenum / nickel-molybdenum catalyst
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: Sulphided Co-Mo or Ni-Mo on alumina in a fixed bed at 300-400 C and 20-50 bar hydrogen, with an H2/hydrocarbon ratio of 200-1,000. Lumping several reactors in series gave 0.2-0.5 wt% sulphur naphtha; a naphtha cracker in 1980s practice wanted 0.5 wt% S or less. The cobalt is not a promoter in the small sense - it is roughly 2-6% Co2O3 beside 10-30% MoO3 on the same alumina support, and the two together are what makes the catalyst active, so a refinery bought the same refined cobalt that a drill-bit maker bought, and it arrived as oxide on a support rather than as anything recognisable as a metal.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: about 2-6% Co2O3 with 10-30% MoO3 on alumina

facts.label: Product sulphur
facts.value: 0.2-0.5 wt% S (pre-cracker)

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Cut points and the product slate
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The fractions a refinery aims for, by boiling range: naphtha (C5 to about 200 F end point, roughly 30-40% of crude), kerosene/jet (200-300 F, 8-15%), gas oil (300-700 F, 20-30%), and the atmospheric residue (700 F plus, 25-40%). Naphtha is the fraction that matters to this tree: it is the steam-cracker feedstock, and its exact end point and sulphur decide whether a cracker will run at 800 or 850 C.
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.note: All the low boiling fractions of crude oil are separated by atmospheric distillation, vaporising below about 400 C at atmospheric pressure. Not established: the C5 and 200-220 F naphtha end point, the 30-40%, 8-15%, 20-30% and 25-40% yields, and the claim that naphtha end point and sulphur decide whether a cracker runs at 800 or 850 C.

facts.label: Naphtha
facts.value: C5 / 33 C to 200-220 F end point; 30-40 vol% of crude

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Overhead condenser and gas recovery
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: The naphtha overhead is condensed in a shell-and-tube condenser with a reflux drum, and the non-condensable gas (methane, ethane, hydrogen, H2S) goes off to the fuel gas header. In 1980s practice the gas was usually simply burned, although the recovery unit for ethane and propane (an absorber) was standard in complex refineries because it paid for itself. In complex refineries an absorber or a deethaniser-absorber recovered 60-90% of the ethane and propane from the fuel gas before it was burnt, and that recovered propane and butane is the LPG which feeds the crackers.

facts.label: Off-gas recovery
facts.value: 60-90% of the ethane and propane

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Reboilers and side strippers
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: A fired or steam reboiler supplies the vapour to the bottom of the tower, and side strippers remove the light ends from the kerosene and gas-oil draws so the side columns are not loaded with vapour. Kerosene is stripped with a few hundred kPa of steam; diesel often went straight to the bottom because the vacuum column handled its light ends.
