chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.name: Distillation trays
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.description: Valve, sieve, bubble-cap or proprietary proprietary-type trays at 0.4-0.6 m spacing. In 1980s practice a new refinery would install valve or sieve trays, and an old one would often be kept and given a new tray-packing section on the vacuum side.
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.f.note: Tray packing on the atmospheric side was rare in the 1980s; structured packing arrived mainly on vacuum columns and on hydrotreaters.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.name: Crude preheat train
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.description: A train of shell-and-tube exchangers that takes crude from ambient to 220-300 C by recovering heat from every hot stream in the refinery, then the fired heater takes it the rest of the way to 350-370 C. Preheating was the classic refinery heat-integration project: a crude preheat train alone recovers tens of megawatts and pays for itself in fuel. Everything in the refinery hotter than crude - coker bottoms gas, FCC slurry oil, diesel bottoms, hot water - fouls one exchanger in the hundred, and the 1980s counter-measures were a deliberately high shell-side velocity, online cleaning with a pigging system and, in a few cases, a differential-pressure monitor as a leading indicator.
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.note: Fouling monitoring practice varies; the mechanisms described are standard.

chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.name: Fired crude heater
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.description: A radiant box furnace with 150-400 coils of cast alloy or wrought-alloy tube (Cr-Mo, 5 in outside diameter, 0.3 m apart), firing gas at 30-80 MW. Tube metallurgy matters: the coil sees a 30-40 C metal temperature above the oil temperature, and the 1980s move to coiled tubing and to higher radiant efficiency cut fuel use several percent.
chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.c.note: Coil counts and duty vary widely by refinery; these are typical 1980s figures.

facts.label: Tube outside diameter
facts.value: 5 in (127 mm), 4-6 mm wall

facts.label: Firing rate
facts.value: 30-80 MW per heater

chem.refining.scale.name: The refining industry in 1983
chem.refining.scale.description: Around 750-850 refineries existed worldwide, of which more than 300 were in the United States alone (US capacity about 19 million bbl/d). The largest refining regions in 1983 were the US Gulf Coast, the US Midwest, Western Europe (Rotterdam, Antwerp, Fos-sur-Mer), the Caribbean (USVI, Curaçao), Japan and Singapore, and the Middle East (Ras Tanura, Ruwais, Kuwait). About 3-5% of the crude throughput was burned as refinery fuel gas.
chem.refining.scale.note: Refinery counts and capacities are approximate; the 1983 figures bracket a decade-long plateau in OECD capacity. The refinery count and capacity figures are commentary about the industry, not a substance.

facts.label: World refining capacity 1983
facts.value: ~65-70 million bbl/d

facts.label: US capacity 1983
facts.value: ~19 million bbl/d

facts.label: Refinery fuel gas
facts.value: 3-5% of throughput

chem.natural-gas.name: Natural gas: the gas field
chem.natural-gas.description: Methane, mostly: either the gas cap sitting on an oil reservoir or a gas-only field. In 1983 world gas production was roughly 2.9-3.0 trillion cubic metres a year, of which about 70% was still associated with oil and much of it was flared or burned at the wellhead. Gas matters to a C64 three ways: as acetylene for PVC and chlorinated solvents, as hydrogen for ammonia and hydrochloric acid, and as the fuel that moved the plastics.
chem.natural-gas.note: This is the shared commodity node, reaching the tree as a from ingredient.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Gas reservoir
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas fills a porous sandstone or a fractured carbonate just as oil does, but with a lower density and a higher compressibility, so gas in place is quoted in trillions of standard cubic feet rather than billions of barrels. The largest gas fields in the world in the early 1980s were the giant Permian Basin fields (US), Urengoy and Yamburg in West Siberia, and Groningen (Netherlands, discovered 1959).

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Gas in place
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Trillions of standard cubic metres of gas in the pore space. The C64-scale fact: all the natural gas used worldwide in 1983 was of the order of 3,000 billion cubic metres a year, so one machine's plastics and energy are far below a thousandth of a cubic metre.

chem.natural-gas.uses.fertiliser-ammonia.name: Fertiliser ammonia
chem.natural-gas.uses.fertiliser-ammonia.description: About 80% of ammonia goes to fertiliser, a demand that sets the size of the hydrogen industry and therefore, indirectly, the amount of ammonia available for the acrylonitrile ammoxidation. The link to the C64 is indirect but real: the same ammonia plants that fertilised the fields also supplied the nitrogen that went into the case polymer.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.name: Hydrogen by steam methane reforming
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.description: CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3H2 over nickel at 750-850 C and 20-30 bar, followed by the water-gas shift (iron oxide/chromia, 350-450 C) to raise the hydrogen fraction, then CO2 removal and cryogenic or PSA purification. A world-scale 1980s plant made 50-100 million m3 of hydrogen a day. Almost all of it went to ammonia; the rest to hydrotreating and to hydrochloric acid. The second largest industrial use of hydrogen is hydrochloric acid: H2 + Cl2 at 250-400 C over a synthesis catalyst, absorbed into demineralised water to 31-37%. The refinery's hydrogen - desulphurisation, hydrocracking, reforming - came from naphtha reformers and, as sour crudes grew, from dedicated gas reformers; in 1983 hydrogen was roughly 3-5% of refinery energy consumption and a genuine bottleneck.
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.note: Chlorine electrolysis itself belongs to the chlorine subsystem; the hydrogen requirement belongs here.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Hydrogen to ammonia (Haber-Bosch)
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 over promoted iron or ruthenium at 400-500 C and 150-250 bar, in a 1,000-2,500 tonne a day synthesis loop fed from a purge cascade. Ammonia is the single largest use of hydrogen, and it matters to the C64 in two places: the nitrogen for the polybutadiene and SAN polymerisations, and the acrylonitrile ammoxidation. The aqueous form the fab buys is at chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Ammonia synthesis catalyst
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: The Haber-Bosch catalyst is promoted iron: magnetite reduced to alpha-iron, promoted with potassium oxide and with alumina or calcium oxide. Ruthenium is better by an order of magnitude but was, in 1983, still a research curiosity as far as ammonia plants were concerned. The catalyst is made by melting magnetite with the promoters, granulating, and reducing it in situ with hydrogen, and a 1980s ammonia plant had a few hundred tonnes of it.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.name: Magnetite from iron ore
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.description: Fe3O4, the reduction product of hematite, and the raw material for the ammonia catalyst. It is also the mineral in the Claus catalyst's neighbourhood and in the polishing lapidary industry. A tonne of ammonia carries about 0.3-0.4 tonnes of iron in its catalyst, and the catalyst is replaced every few years, so the ammonia business has a real, if modest, appetite for iron ore.
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.to-ammoni.note: The iron ore chain itself belongs to the metals subsystem; this node marks where it enters the ammonia catalyst. The industrial ammonia synthesis catalyst is obtained from finely ground iron powder, itself obtained by reduction of high-purity magnetite. Not established: the 0.3-0.4 tonnes of iron per tonne of ammonia, the catalyst replacement interval, and that this is where the iron ore chain enters.

chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.nickel-ca.name: Nickel reforming catalyst
chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen.nickel-ca.description: Nickel on alumina, or the older nickel-chromium used in the pre-1957 Topsoe SMR-180. By the 1980s the modern multi-bed reformer ran 25-40 tubes of 10-16 inch diameter at 30-50 bar, with an inlet temperature near 550 C and an outlet at 850-870 C, burning gas in a process furnace alongside the tubes.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.name: Acetylene from natural gas
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.description: The Reppe process, commercialised from 1959-1965: a mixture of roughly 6-8% methane with 30-38% air and 55-60% hydrogen is fired through a water-cooled burner at 1,200-1,800 C and quenched to below 100 C within milliseconds. The acetylene yield per pass is only 2-3% of the feed, so the process has to recycle a large stream, and the furnace consumes several GWh of electricity per tonne of acetylene. It survived because it made a C2 unit out of a C1 feed - the only route that can make vinyl chloride, and hence PVC, without cracking a barrel of naphtha. Cracking acetylene at 1,200-1,400 C in a water-cooled steel retort and quenching in nitrogen gave a fine high-surface-area channel black for rubber reinforcement and printing inks, largely displaced in tyres during the 1960s by furnace black made from natural gas. Acetylene plus chlorine also gives tetrachloroethane and from it trichloroethylene and chloroform, while methyl chloride for the chlorosilane chain comes from the same high-temperature HCl chemistry, so field gas reaches the C64's chips as well as its case.
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.note: The semiconductor chain itself belongs to the silicon subsystem; the chloromethane source is gas-derived and belongs here.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.name: Quench and acetylene recovery
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.description: The hot gas is quenched to below 100 C within milliseconds, then acetylene is absorbed selectively from the acetylene-hydrogen-methane-hydrogen-sulphide mixture by acetone at 10-20 C and 5-15 bar (about 2.2 volumes of acetylene per volume of solvent), stripped and the solvent recirculated. Recovered acetylene is 99.5-99.8% pure once hydrogen sulphide and water are removed. The last step before the acetylene goes to the vinyl chloride plant is a drying and finishing train - a molecular sieve or a chilled water wash to get the water under 10 ppm, then a caustic or amine wash for the last of the hydrogen sulphide - because vinyl chloride hydrolyses in water and the last drying step is not optional.

facts.label: Solvent
facts.value: acetone (selective absorbent)

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.name: The absorption and recovery train
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.description: The acetylene is absorbed out of the cracked mixture in a solvent and taken off the top of the tower at high purity, which is the whole reason for doing the separation this way. Acetone's job is to hold acetylene - which at 20 C and 12 bar will dissolve to about 2.2 volumes of solvent per volume of acetylene - while letting the hydrogen, methane and carbon monoxide straight through. The dark, dangerous part of this plant is not the chemistry but the acetylene itself: above 2 bar in the presence of a metal, acetylene will detonate into its own decomposition products, and the whole extraction plant is designed around never letting that happen.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.name: Absorber and stripper
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.description: A 20-40 tray absorber at 10-20 C and 5-15 bar with the acetone circulated, and a stripper that takes the pure acetylene overhead at 3-5 bar and the solvent off the bottom for recycle. The solvent must be regenerated at intervals because it accumulates the hydrogen sulphide and the water from the feed gas, and because the acetylene polymerises in it if it is left standing - the plant has a permanent low-temperature nitrogen blanketing problem.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.name: Acetone as the selective solvent
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.quench.a.description: The choice of solvent is a compromise. Acetone has a high acetylene solubility and a low methane solubility and a manageable vapour pressure, and it is made from cumene on the same site, which is the practical reason it was chosen. It is also flammable and it is a reproductive toxin, which is a modern objection to a molecule the industry has used since 1945.

chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.partial-.name: Partial oxidation burner
chem.natural-gas.uses.acetylene.partial-.description: Methane is partially oxidised to CO and H2, which then combine to acetylene at flame temperature. The furnace runs at atmospheric to 2 bar with the flame held above the acetylene decomposition point; the burner is water-cooled because copper and steel both survive the flame while the mixture would otherwise decompose to soot. The process is violently sensitive to soot: any carbon in the gas feed poisons the burner.

facts.label: Furnace temperature
facts.value: 1,200-1,800 C depending on variant and measurement point

facts.label: Acetylene per pass
facts.value: 2-3% of feed gas

chem.natural-gas.sources.methane-hydrate.name: Gas hydrate (a hazard, not yet a resource)
chem.natural-gas.sources.methane-hydrate.description: Methane trapped as a clathrate of water, stable below about 20 C at surface pressure. Known since the 1930s and already recognised in the deep ocean and permafrost as a potentially enormous resource, but in the early 1980s it was a hazard - it plugged subsea pipelines and was one reason offshore gas lines carried inhibitors and heated risers - not a supply.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Non-associated (gas-only) field
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: A gas reservoir with no oil at the contact. The North Sea fields of the late 1970s - Frigg (1977), Heimdal, Sleipner, Troll (discovered 1979) - turned Europe from an import market into a gas market, and the Norwegian and British gas grids of the early 1980s were built around them. In the US the equivalent discovery was the tight and geopressured gas of the Anadarko and Rocky Mountain basins. Tight low-permeability sandstone and coalbed methane had to be stimulated rather than merely completed, with the oil branch's massive hydraulic fracturing and with dewatering for coal seams; in 1983 tight gas was a real but small share of US supply.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: A gas field is a place that is worked, not an operation. Gas and oil extraction is industry, and the energy category is reserved for power generation and the grid.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Discovering and drilling a gas field
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas fields are found by the same seismic and drilled with the same rig as oil fields, but the completion differs: the log response that proves a gas column is high resistivity with low neutron density, and the well must be tested for absolute gas flow rather than liquid rate. Gas viscosity is about a hundred times lower than oil but its compressibility ten times higher, so the well responds to drawdown very differently. Gas sands are often visible before they are drilled, because gas lowers the acoustic impedance of the rock so the reflector dims and sometimes inverts; the amplitude anomaly is also produced by a shale lens or a tuning effect, which is why the prospect still had to be drilled. The casing and completion hardware is identical to an oil well but the discipline is not: a gas well perforated below the point of no return has to be tested to destruction of casing and tubing, because the column is light and there is no fluid level to swallow a leak. A wellhead separator and a test separator drop the liquid out of the gas at 30-70 bar before the gas goes to a knockout drum and the gathering system; the liquid is the same crude or condensate as in the oil case.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: The seismic acquisition chain is shared with the oil branch: chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Dehydration to pipeline dew point
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas must arrive at the pipeline dew point or the higher-pressure steps downstream condense water out and the line fills with liquid. By 1980s practice that meant a glycol unit (triethylene glycol at 80-95 wt% purity, contactor at 20-50 C and 40-70 bar, reboiler 120-140 C) and increasingly a 3A or 4A molecular sieve adsorption unit for the last kilogram of water per million standard cubic metres.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Triethylene glycol
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: A heavy glycol made by reacting ethylene oxide with diethylene glycol; the standard dehydration absorbent because of its low vapour pressure at the contactor temperature. The 1980s trend was towards 95 wt% TEG purity, because glycol vapour carried upstream into a gas turbine or a carburettor was a real emission problem.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: Glycol synthesis is the ethylene oxide branch: chem.ethylene.ethylene-glycol.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Sweetening to pipeline specification
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: H2S and CO2 are removed with a 20-35 wt% alkanolamine in an absorber at 30-45 C and 20-70 bar, with the rich amine regenerated at 120-130 C and 1.5-2 bar in a reboiler. By the early 1980s the trend was to diethanolamine for economy and MDEA for lower heat duty and no carbamate degradation.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Alkanolamine
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Monoethanolamine (MEA, primary), diethanolamine (DEA, secondary), methyldiethanolamine (MDEA, tertiary). MDEA was the growth amine of the 1980s because it does not form carbamate with CO2, so its degradation and reboiler duty are lower; the penalty is a slower absorption rate and a lower equilibrium loading.

chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.name: Drilling fluid for a gas well
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.description: Gas wells were drilled with the same bentonite mud as oil wells, with two differences: a low filter loss was mandatory because filtrate invasion had to be reversed before logging, and a gas-cut mud had to be controlled because entrained gas reduced hydrostatic pressure and made the well hard to control. The standard 1980s control was a mechanical gas trap plus defoamer.
chem.natural-gas.sources.non-associated-.note: The mud is the same oilfield bentonite mud as on an oil well.

chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas.name: Associated (oil-associated) gas
chem.natural-gas.sources.associated-gas.description: Gas from the gas cap of an oil field, produced at roughly 50-150 m3 of gas per barrel of oil. Around 70% of world gas production was associated gas in 1983, and a large share was still flared: world flaring ran at the order of 100-130 billion m3 a year in the early 1980s, several million tonnes of hydrocarbons a year simply burned at the wellhead. A flare tip burns whatever the oil plant cannot handle, and in 1980s practice it was sized for peak oil rate, so routine gas-cap growth had to be reinjected into the reservoir or sold.

chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s.name: Hydrogen sulphide (sour gas)
chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s.description: A lethal, corrosive, smelly component that must be taken to a few ppmv before the gas enters a steel pipeline, because H2S embrittles steel and attacks copper alloys. Sweetening it produces a concentrated acid gas stream whose H2S is the feedstock for the Claus sulphur plant in the refining branch.
chem.natural-gas.composition.h2s.note: The amine plant and the Claus plant are under chem.natural-gas.sources and chem.refining.claus.

chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen.name: Nitrogen in natural gas
chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen.description: 1-15% N2 in many fields. It is the impurity that most affects heating value, that forces the Wobbe index (a measure of interchangeability between gas supplies) onto a pipeline tariff, and that makes a gas which is 90% N2 unsaleable as town gas.
chem.natural-gas.composition.nitrogen.note: Nitrogen content is highly field-specific; the Wobbe index framing is standard.

chem.natural-gas.composition.methane.name: Methane
chem.natural-gas.composition.methane.description: CH4, 80-98% of a dry gas, 39.8 MJ/m3 gross calorific value, -161.5 C boiling point. The single molecule most of this branch is about: because methane is hard to polymerise and hard to functionalise, the industry of the 1980s broke it into acetylene at extreme temperature or into hydrogen over a nickel catalyst, and those two products underwrote most of the polymer industry.

chem.natural-gas.uses.name: What the gas is for
chem.natural-gas.uses.description: Three jobs in 1983: burn it, crack it, or reform it. Burning dominated volume; the petrochemical jobs - acetylene, hydrogen, ammonia - were small in tonnage but disproportionate in value, and they are the reason the polymer industry existed at all. The largest single use of gas is plain combustion: boilers, industrial furnaces and gas turbines. A 40-100 MW gas turbine of the 1980s fired gas at 15-25 bar through a dual-fuel combustor, and a gas-fired polyethylene furnace ran 10-30% excess oxygen.
chem.natural-gas.uses.note: Acetylene, hydrogen, fuel and fertiliser ammonia hang directly off the gas field.

chem.natural-gas.processing.name: Gas processing and transport
chem.natural-gas.processing.description: The plants that turn a wet, sour wellstream into a pipeline gas, a liquefied gas or a natural-gas-liquids fraction. A large 1980s gas plant handled 5-30 billion standard cubic feet a day; the North Sea, Gulf and Middle Eastern plants of that decade were among the largest chemical plants ever built. Ethane, propane, butane and pentane are stripped out as natural gas liquids - ethane for crackers, propane and butane for LPG, C5+ for gasoline - and a cryogenic plant recovers 90-99% of the methane but less of the heavy end, so the design trade is expander against absorption.

chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.name: Gas pipeline
chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.description: Line pipe 0.6-1.4 m in diameter, API 5L grade X52-X70, laid by a lay barge or a trenching spread and internally coated with epoxy and polyethylene powder. Transmission lines run at 60-100 bar with compressors every 100-200 km. The 1980s were the years of the great gas transmission builds: the Central Asia-Centre system, the Norwegian and North Sea systems and the Trans-Med pipelines all date from this decade.
chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.note: A pipeline and an LNG carrier move a bulk stream, they do not make one, so transport is the category here and the gas plant that feeds them is a plant.

chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.sub.name: Subsea pipeline and riser
chem.natural-gas.processing.pipeline.sub.description: Concrete weight-coated line with a hot-water or electrical trace heater for hydrate prevention, and a wet-insulated riser with a buoyancy module for the first 100-300 m of water. Deepwater gas tiebacks of the 1980s established the standard development: subsea wellhead manifold, a dedicated line to a central platform, gas gathered ashore.

chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.name: LNG liquefaction
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.description: Chilling gas to -162 C so it becomes a liquid at atmospheric pressure, cutting volume about 600-fold for the same energy. In 1983 world LNG trade was roughly 55-70 billion m3 a year, about 2-3% of world gas production, on a network of roughly 60-70 liquefaction trains. The dominant cycles were the propane-precooled mixed refrigerant (9 stages, about 7-8% specific power) and the nitrogen expander cycle.

chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.name: LNG carrier
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.description: A 70,000-125,000 m3 membrane or independent-tank ship with a re-liquefaction plant, because LNG boils off at 0.1-0.3% a day and the load has to be reliquefied in transit. The world LNG fleet in 1983 was of the order of 90-130 ships at $40-90 million each.
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.note: LNG carrier prices and fleet size in the early 1980s are order-of-magnitude figures.

chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.name: LNG storage and regasification terminal
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.description: A vacuum-insulated cylindrical tank of 20,000-160,000 m3 with a nickel-alloy inner tank over perlite insulation, plus a jetty for a 125,000-165,000 m3 carrier. Regasification burns about 0.3 tonnes of fuel gas per tonne of LNG, which is where the C64-scale fact becomes visible: the fuel burned to regasify enough LNG to make one machine's plastics is tens of grams.
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.note: The regasification fuel figure of about 0.3 t/t LNG is the standard design value; the C64 extrapolation is order-of-magnitude.

chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.name: Mixed refrigerant cycle
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.description: Propane pre-cooling to -30 to -40 C, then an ethylene/ethane/propane mixture expanded through a series of exchangers to -120 C, then a nitrogen expander to -162 C. The hydrocarbons in the refrigerant are the same ones the petrochemical industry buys; the nitrogen expander cycle burns almost nothing but needs a lot of power and very large exchangers, which suited a plant with cheap power and no other outlet for its fuel gas.
chem.natural-gas.processing.liquefaction.note: Kept as a node because its three numbers (the -162 C liquefaction temperature, the 1:600 volume reduction and the 7-8% specific power) are the cycle, not a detail of it. The refrigerant hydrocarbons are recorded as ingredients.

facts.label: Volume reduction
facts.value: about 1:600

facts.label: Specific power
facts.value: ~7-8% of LNG energy (mixed refrigerant)

chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.name: Cryogenic separation (expander plant)
chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.description: The JT-expander process that became the industry standard for large gas plants in the 1980s: the gas is chilled by expansion through a turbine to -30 to -80 C and the resulting cold box distils methane from ethane and heavier. The plant cost is dominated by the aluminium cold boxes, which remain one of the largest single uses of aluminium in the world per tonne produced.

chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.name: Aluminium cold box
chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.description: A brazed plate-and-fin aluminium exchanger 10-30 m long, cryogenic to -80 C, containing dozens of channels. Aluminium-brazed cold boxes replaced copper wound exchangers in the 1970s and are one reason the gas plant business grew so fast in that decade.

chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.name: Cryogenic turboexpander
chem.natural-gas.processing.cryogenic-se.description: A radial or axial turbine in the cold box, handling 10,000-40,000 kW on a big plant, recovering 5-15% of the gas enthalpy and reaching -30 to -80 C. The expander train was the mechanical heart of the 1980s gas plant and its efficiency set the plant cost.

chem.natural-gas.sources.name: Where the gas comes from
chem.natural-gas.sources.description: Associated gas from the gas cap of an oil reservoir, and non-associated (gas-only) gas. The distinction matters industrially: associated gas was a by-product that had to be flared or reinjected until the late 1970s made it commercial, while gas-only fields carry the pipelines and the LNG trains.
chem.natural-gas.sources.note: Associated gas, the gas-only field, the gas reservoir and the gas hydrate hang directly off the gas field.

chem.natural-gas.composition.name: What natural gas is
chem.natural-gas.composition.description: A mixture, not a compound. A sour gas well may deliver methane with 2-10% ethane and propane, 1-8% C4, 1-20% hydrogen sulphide, 0.5-5% carbon dioxide and up to 15% nitrogen. Everything downstream - the pipelines, the dew point specification, the hydrogen plant - is set by those five impurities.
chem.natural-gas.composition.note: Methane, ethane and propane, nitrogen and hydrogen sulphide hang directly off the gas field.

chem.crude.name: Crude oil: finding it, drilling it, lifting it
chem.crude.description: The upstream end of the chain. Seismic surveys pick a structure, a rig drills a 5-7 km hole through rock, casing and cement line the hole, the well is completed and perforated into the reservoir, then often artificially stimulated. An 8 kg C64 case corresponds to only 1-3 litres of crude oil, but that crude was found under 5-10 km of overburden using a drilling rig that cost tens of millions of dollars.
chem.crude.note: Category industry throughout the exploration, drilling, completion, stimulation, separation and assay branches: upstream oil and gas is an extraction industry, and the category table reserves energy for power generation and the grid. The bulk process fluids inside it (muds, cement slurry, acid, fracturing fluid) stay fluids, and the crude itself is fluids.

chem.crude.c64-fraction.name: One Commodore 64's share of the wellhead
chem.crude.c64-fraction.description: The plastic mass of a C64 is about 350-400 g of ABS in the case plus 100-200 g in the keys, and ABS comes from roughly 2 kg of crude oil per kilogram of polymer. Add the energy to make it, the fuel to ship it and the polymer's own energy in the burning, and one machine corresponds to roughly 1-3 litres of crude oil - about one minute of production on a small Arabian field, and undetectable in the world oil balance. This node is the reminder that the whole upstream industry exists to supply a mass flow, not a concept.
chem.crude.c64-fraction.note: The 2 kg crude per kg of olefin-derived polymer figure is a widely used mass-balance rule of thumb; the 1983 world production number is approximately 57-60 Mb/d for liquids. One C64 share of the wellhead is an order-of-magnitude aside. The crude itself is chem.petroleum.

facts.label: Crude per kg of ABS
facts.value: about 2 kg crude (mass balance across cracker to polymer)

facts.label: Crude per C64
facts.value: about 1-3 litres, i.e. 0.8-2.5 kg

facts.label: World crude production 1983
facts.value: ~57-60 million bbl/d, ~9 x 10^9 tonnes/year

chem.crude.assay.name: Crude assay
chem.crude.assay.description: What the seller is paid for: a barrel of crude is specified by a handful of standardised numbers, and every downstream decision - which cracker, which desulphuriser, whether it can be shipped - is made from them. Density and API gravity set the transport economics, sulphur splits sweet from sour, the simulated boiling curve sets the cut points, the trace metals set the catalyst life, and the cold-flow properties decide whether it can be pumped.
chem.crude.assay.note: The five standard measurements are API gravity, sulphur, simulated distillation, Conradson carbon residue and pour point, and their numbers are facts of this node. Its from edge is the crude it measures.

facts.label: Saudi Light
facts.value: 38.0-38.5 deg API

facts.label: Arab Light
facts.value: 35.0-36.0 deg API

facts.label: Light sweet reference
facts.value: West Texas Light 40 deg API, 0.3% S

chem.crude.separation.name: Wellhead and terminal separation
chem.crude.separation.description: The wellstream arrives at 15-100 bar and 60-100 C as an oil/gas/water froth. It is separated in stages: test separator, stock tanks, heaters and desalters, gas-oil separator, and finally a train of electrostatic and coalescing vessels that make a storable crude. Field separation is where the crude assay is determined and where the oil is counted.

chem.crude.separation.oil-water-coalesce.name: Oil-water coalescer
chem.crude.separation.oil-water-coalesce.description: A packed or membrane device that lets separated water droplets out of the crude without carrying oil. Produced-water disposal in 1983 was to a pit or a treatment plant; the offshore discharge limit under the 1983 amendments to the US Clean Water Act required 42 ppm oil and no visible sheen, which is why coalescers and hydrocyclones appeared on offshore platforms.
chem.crude.separation.oil-water-coalesce.note: The 42 ppm / 30 ppm benchmark figures for produced-water oil content are the long-standing offshore standard; the 1983 date for that particular rule reference is a common citation but the precise effective date varies by jurisdiction.

chem.crude.separation.electrostatic.name: Electrostatic coalescer (electrogravitational)
chem.crude.separation.electrostatic.description: Charged droplets are attracted into the water phase, collapsing the emulsion in seconds instead of hours. Small pipeline electrocoalescers were introduced in the mid-1980s for crude pretreatment, cutting the demulsifier dose; they were used in 1980s practice wherever the crude conductivity allowed (hence electrogravitational not electrocoalescing for most crudes).
chem.crude.separation.electrostatic.note: High-conductivity crudes could not be electrocoalesced in the 1980s; that limitation is why electrogravitational units (large DACC-type vessels) were preferred for crude.

chem.crude.separation.heater-treater.name: Heater-treater and desalter
chem.crude.separation.heater-treater.description: A crude preheater to 150-200 C followed by a settler and then a desalter, where the crude is washed with recycled water to strip salts. Needed because sour Middle East crudes carry 1-3 wt% dissolved salts, and because naphthenic acids plus water at 200 C will corrode the hot exchanger on the way to the refinery. A crude desalter separates maybe 90-95% of the salt in one stage.

facts.label: Typical crude salt content
facts.value: 0.2-3 wt% dissolved chlorides

chem.crude.separation.three-phase.name: Three-phase separator and stock tanks
chem.crude.separation.three-phase.description: A horizontal or vertical vessel at 2-10 bar with a mechanical or electrostatic coalescing section that separates oil, gas and water, then atmospheric storage tanks that settle the remaining water and sediment. Stock tank bottoms and the settled water carry the production's salt and heavy ends, and their disposal was the field's environmental problem in the 1980s.

chem.crude.separation.three-phase.demuls.name: Demulsifier chemistry
chem.crude.separation.three-phase.demuls.description: Nonylphenol- or alcohol-based surfactants dosed at 5-50 ppm to break the oil-water emulsion; in the 1980s a growing share of demulsifiers were polyalkoxyamine and polyglycol ethers. A stable water-in-oil emulsion (chocolate mousse) could hold 20-50% water into the crude and was the single largest quality loss on a wet field.

chem.crude.separation.test-separator.name: Test separator
chem.crude.separation.test-separator.description: The first vessel, sized 1-5% of the field's liquid capacity, where the wellstream is bled at 25-70 bar to a stable pressure and temperature. Its records are the raw data for reservoir performance, gas-oil ratio and oil assay. A field with 100,000 bbl/d of oil needed a test separator of a few hundred bbl.

chem.crude.stimulation.name: Well stimulation: fracturing and acidising
chem.crude.stimulation.description: Almost no reservoir delivers its whole potential through a millimetre perforation. Stimulation makes the rock permeable by fracture or by dissolving the rock; it is one of the biggest single levers on oil and gas supply and it consumes enormous volumes of water, sand and, for acidising, corrosive acid. Heavy oil and tar sands were stimulated with steam at 250-350 C, injected, soaked and then produced on at Cold Lake and Athabasca scale; one steam cycle costs several tonnes of water and roughly 0.5-1 barrel of 60% fuel oil per tonne of steam.
chem.crude.stimulation.note: Heavy-oil thermal work existed but was marginal to light-sour supply; the numbers are order-of-magnitude.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.name: Matrix acidising and fracture acidising
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.description: Hydrochloric or hydrofluoric acid injected to dissolve or acid-fracture the rock, typically 15-28% HCl in sandstone and HF-containing mud acid in carbonate. Sandstone acidising only reached the late 1970s as a standard service; carbonate mud-acid fracturing with a 12% HCl-3% HF system had become the standard carbonate treatment by the mid-1980s. Placement mattered more than chemistry: acid was bullheaded down casing or coiled-tubed into the perforation tunnels, and because HF precipitates calcium fluoride a 1.2-1.5 m HCl preflush was always pumped first to keep calcium out of the rock.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.name: Acid-resistant tubing
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.description: Coiled tubing and the acid lines were, by the mid-1980s, routinely nickel alloy - a nickel-molybdenum alloy such as Alloy C-276 or a titanium grade - rather than carbon steel, because the inhibitor was never perfect and the steel was never quite good enough. Nickel alloys and titanium come out of a metallurgical chain rather than a petrochemical one, but it is the acid chemistry that puts them into this operation.
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.note: Alloy selection for acid service is metallurgy rather than petrochemistry; this node marks the boundary of the subsystem. Acid-resistant tubing is used by the acidising step, not contained in the inhibitor.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.name: Mud acid (HCl + HF)
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.description: Hydrochloric acid to dissolve carbonate, with 1-3 wt% HF to attack the clay in sandstone and 2-5 wt% HF in carbonate muds. The reason for mud acid was a reserve shift: by the early 1980s mudstone was around 80% of world oil reserves, and mudstone cannot be treated with pure HCl because of its clay reactivity. Acid is pumped downhole in steel or titanium coils, with corrosion inhibitors (amines, thiourea) and a surfactant.
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.note: HF and HCl chemistry is the same as chem.fab-chemicals in this file; HF from fluorspar, HCl from chlorine. HCl and HF are ingredients, not components: both are now "from" edges. The hydrogen route that makes the hydrochloric acid is chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen, which absorbed the deleted "hydrogen to hydrochloric acid" step.

chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.name: Acid corrosion inhibitor
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.description: Hydrofluoric acid at 12% and hydrochloric acid at 12%, pumped down a steel coil, will remove a hundredth of an inch of steel a day. The inhibitors - a long-chain amine, thiourea, an acetylenic alcohol - adsorb on the steel and cut the corrosion rate by several orders of magnitude without touching the rock. It is a thin grey film of chemistry doing the work, and it is the reason mud-acid jobs of the 1980s could be pumped downhole at all.
chem.crude.stimulation.acidising.mud-aci.note: An amine corrosion inhibitor is a substance sold in drums, not an operation.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Hydraulic fracturing
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: A water-based or gel fluid pumped down the casing into the pay, then into the perforations at 40-100 bbl/min and up to 6,000-10,000 psi surface pressure to part the rock; a proppant is carried in to hold the fracture open when pressure is released. Born in 1947 (experiments) and industrialised in the late 1950s (Massive Hydraulic Fracturing, 1961-1965), by the 1980s it was routine on low-permeability gas reservoirs and increasingly common on oil wells. A big 1980s job used 10,000-100,000 bbl of fluid and 500-2,000 tonnes of sand. A propped fracture's job is conductivity times length: the first fractures were vertical and planar, so 1980s design moved to multiple parallel fractures per zone, and conductive area had to be raised by resin-coated proppant or by larger grains because proppant embedment in soft rock closed fractures within months.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Fracturing pumping equipment
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: Blender trucks, sand trucks and a high-pressure pump unit (one pumping unit at 25,000 psi), laid out in a yard over the rig. A 1980s job mobilised 10-40 trucks and 100-200 people, and it was the largest single water consumer in the oilfield outside steam flooding.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Proppant sand
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: Sized, round, silica sand or resin-coated sand, typically 20/40 or 30/50 mesh (0.4-0.6 mm), graded to carry a hundred thousand tonnes a year in a region. Ottawa River and Illinois Basin sands were the standard, with regional sources in Texas and Arkansas. It was a heavy, low-value, high-bulk freight commodity.
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.note: Sand proppant is the same silica route as the glass fibre and fused silica branches.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Fracturing sand and its plant
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: The proppant is a silica sand that has been sieved, washed, resin-coated and graded, and the plant that does it is a small mineral processing operation that exists in the Permian basin because the proppant has to be nearby. The oilfield sands of the Permian have a problem that glass sands do not: a weak grain crushes under the closure stress of a hydraulic fracture, so the 1980s industry coated a fraction of the proppant with a phenolic resin to make it stronger. By the late 1980s a fraction of the sand (5-30% depending on the basin) was coated with a cured phenolic or furfural resin so it would not embed on closure, which turned a mineral commodity into a single-use consumable and created a solid waste stream of its own.
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.note: Coating fractions and the date of commercial introduction vary by basin and supplier.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Frac sand mine
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: A sand quarry that happens to contain almost pure silica in a dune, worked at 1,000-10,000 tonnes a day. The last dig-it-out node of the crude branch's stimulation chain, and a reminder that a hydraulic fracture is largely a mineral supply chain: the water, the sand and the chemicals are all mining and manufacturing, and only the pressure is petroleum engineering.
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.note: Not established: the 1,000-10,000 tonne per day working rate and the near-pure silica dune grade. That a hydraulic fracture is largely a mineral and chemical supply chain rather than petroleum engineering is the reliable part of this node.

chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.name: Fracturing fluid and gel
chem.crude.stimulation.hydraulic-fractur.description: Water plus a viscosity builder (hydroxyethyl cellulose in water, or a hydrocarbon gel), often crosslinked with borate or an organometallic zirconium/titanium chelate to hold the proppant in suspension at high temperature. Waterfracs (no crosslinker, friction-reducer only) took a large share of the market by the mid-1980s because they were cheaper and left less residue.

chem.crude.well-completion.name: Well completion
chem.crude.well-completion.description: Turning a drilled hole into a producing well: set production casing, cement to the pay, run and perforate the tubing, pack the annulus, and install a tree. This is where the reservoir is deliberately connected to the borehole for the first time. A completed well was logged with spinner and turbine flowmeters, noise logs and temperature logs, and tested with a multi-hour rate and pressure buildup.

chem.crude.well-completion.christmas-tre.name: Christmas tree (wellhead assembly)
chem.crude.well-completion.christmas-tre.description: The valve stack on top of the casing: casing spool, tubing spool, master valve, wing valves with gauges, and the flowline tee off the wing. Every stream the well ever produces has to pass through this steel gatework, which is why it is the most pressure-rated cluster of parts in the business.

facts.label: Parts count
facts.value: 80-200 components, several hundred kg of forged steel

chem.crude.well-completion.packer.name: Packer and completion hardware
chem.crude.well-completion.packer.description: An elastomer-sealed packer run and set in the casing to isolate zones and provide a seat for the tubing hanger. In 1980s completions this was single- or dual-packer tubing with sliding sleeves or selective stimulation, increasingly mechanical rather than hydraulic.

chem.crude.well-completion.packer.elasto.name: Packer elastomer (nitrile / HNBR)
chem.crude.well-completion.packer.elasto.description: A nitrile (acrylonitrile-butadiene) or HNBR element that swells or mechanically expands to grip the casing. Nitrile is the same chemistry as chem.butadiene in the polymer branch: acrylonitrile copolymerised with butadiene.
chem.crude.well-completion.packer.elasto.note: Cross-link: chem.butadiene. The nitrile rubber it is cut from is described under chem.butadiene; the copy of that node that used to sit here was folded away as a duplicate.

chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.name: Perforation
chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.description: Shaped charges fired down the casing to punch 1-3 cm holes through steel, cement and formation in one shot, linking pay zone to borehole. A 1980s completion might be 4-6 perforations per metre of pay; perforation is done in stages so only the best footage is shot.

chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.e.name: Entry hole into the pay zone
chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.e.description: The first connection to the reservoir is itself a jet-perforated hole in cement, and it is the smallest diameter in the whole production system: a few millimetres through which the entire well flow must pass.

chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.s.name: Shaped-charge perforator
chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.s.description: A copper or steel cone lined with a high explosive (RDX/HMX or HMX-wax, 5-30 g per shot in the 1980s) with a steel or ceramic liner; the detonated cone forms a copper or tungsten-alloy jet at 8-10 km/s which drills the hole. Charges were fired on a wireline in a gun barrel or in a TCP (tubing conveyed perforator).
chem.crude.well-completion.perforation.s.note: Charge weight and composition varied widely with depth and rock toughness; the jet mechanism is well established.

chem.crude.rig.name: The drilling rig
chem.crude.rig.description: Rotary drilling: the drill string is rotated from the surface, the bit mills a hole, mud circulates to carry cuttings out and to control formation pressure. Offshore this is a jack-up, a semisubmersible or a drillship; onshore it is a land rig with a derrick. 1980s rigs reached 6,000-7,500 m total depth on routine programs.

chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.name: Core drilling and coring
chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.description: Diamond core barrels cut 1-4 in core in a special drilling string, giving the reservoir rock, its porosity, its saturation and its capillary properties undamaged. A cored well is the most expensive way to get reservoir data, so it was used on 1-3 wells out of 20 and almost always on the discovery well.

chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.core-barrel.name: Diamond core barrel
chem.crude.rig.core-drilling.core-barrel.description: A steel or aluminium tube with a diamond-set reaming shell and a core lifter, run on the bottom hole assembly at low RPM (20-100) and low weight. Carbit tungsten-carbide bits dominated abrasive sandstone, PCD for softer beds, and set diamond for carbonate.

chem.crude.rig.pressure-control.name: Well control: BOP, diverter and kill
chem.crude.rig.pressure-control.description: The blowout preventer stack (annular preventer plus 3-5 ram preventers) and the choke manifold above the wellhead, rated 5,000-15,000 psi. Before the 1970s and 1980s safety emphasis, the classic profile was a vertical string, overbalanced mud and a diverter; 1980s practice added the above-the-bit diverter packoff for kick tolerance.

chem.crude.rig.rig-types.name: Rig types and their 1980s cost
chem.crude.rig.rig-types.description: Jack-up rigs (4-6 legs, 60-90 m water-depth limit) and fixed derricks onshore; semisubmersibles (700-1,000 m, self-propelled, expensive); drillships (ice-strengthened, for deep water and harsh climates). Costs in the early 1980s: onshore rig $1-3 million, jack-up $20-45 million, drillship $30-70 million, semisubmersible $60-120 million. Offshore dayrates in 1983 ran $25,000-60,000 a day.
chem.crude.rig.rig-types.note: Rig newbuild prices moved violently through 1981-83 (a deepwater rig that cost $60m in 1980 was quoted above $100m in 1983); treat these as order-of-magnitude figures.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.name: Casing and cementing
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.description: Steel casing is run to isolate the hole and to carry the pressure; cement is pumped between casing and formation (and sometimes inside the casing) to seal the annulus. Without a good cement job the whole completion leaks and stimulation injects into the wrong zone. Cementing is one of the few oilfield jobs that is nearly a repeatability disaster: 10-30% of wells take a cement squeeze.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.casing-stri.name: Casing string and cement sheath
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.casing-stri.description: Conductor, surface, intermediate and production casing, each cemented across its shoe. The C64-scale point: even a modest producing well consumes tens to hundreds of tonnes of cement and hundreds of metres of steel, dwarfing the machine it ultimately supplies.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant.name: Cement dispersants and additives
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant.description: Sulfonated naphthalene formaldehyde condensates (BNS) or sulfonated formaldehyde melamine (SFM) to keep the slurry workable at low water; and bentonite as an extender. Early 1980s practice was to optimise with laboratory thickening-time tests before the job, because a primary cement job cost $0.2-1 million.
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.dispersant.note: Exact additive ranges vary widely by job; the chemical identities are standard.

chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.api-class-g.name: API Class G oilwell cement
chem.crude.rig.casing-cement.api-class-g.description: Portland-type cement with 40-60 wt% Class G sulphate-resisting blend, gypsum for set control, silica flour as a retarder for the thickening time, and additives for fluid-loss control. Mixed on location with water and spacers at 1.7-2.0 g/cm3 and pumped at 30-90 bbl/min.

chem.crude.rig.bit.name: Drill bits
chem.crude.rig.bit.description: The cutting tool at the bottom of the string. In 1980s practice a soft-formation bit was a sealed journal bearing with a cone of natural diamond, a medium bit a sealed or unsealed mud turbine with tungsten-carbide nose buttons, and a hard rock bit a milled-steel body with tungsten-carbide inserts on the three cones.

chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.name: PDC (polycrystalline diamond compact) bit
chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.description: The emerging bit of the early 1980s: sintered diamond compact cutters brazed to a steel body with no cones and no bearings, turning rather than grinding. PDC began as a hard-rock bit, spread into soft rock in the mid-1980s and largely replaced roller cones in soft formations by the early 1990s. In 1983 it was perhaps 10-20% of the market.

chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.cutter.name: Polycrystalline diamond compact cutter
chem.crude.rig.bit.pdc-bit.cutter.description: Diamond powder sintered at 5,000-6,000 bar and 1,400-1,600 C with a cobalt metal catalyst from the diamond-graphite phase boundary. Over a 1980s field life a soft-formation PDC cutter could cut tens of kilometres of sandstone; hard-rock PDC arrived later with tungsten-carbide substrates and domed cutters.

chem.crude.rig.bit.natural-diamond.name: Natural diamond (soft-formation bit)
chem.crude.rig.bit.natural-diamond.description: Gem-quality or bort diamond in a matrix of tungsten and cobalt sintered into a cone. Natural diamond bits dominate soft sandstone and were the standard drag-bit insert in 1980s drilling; synthetic (polycrystalline) diamond began to displace them in abrasive sandstone late in the decade.

chem.crude.rig.bit.tungsten-carbide.name: Tungsten carbide cutters and buttons
chem.crude.rig.bit.tungsten-carbide.description: WC-Co cemented carbide: 6-12% cobalt binder, 900-1,600 HV, pressed and sintered in a vacuum furnace then brazed onto the cone or into a milled-steel body. Cemented-carbide rock-bit consumption was the largest single use of tungsten carbide in the world in the 1980s, comparable to carbide tooling.

facts.label: Hardness
facts.value: 900-1,600 HV; binder 6-12% Co

facts.label: Brazed to
facts.value: a cone, or a milled-steel body with carbide inserts on the three cones

chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.name: Rotary drilling
chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.description: A rotary table or top drive turns the string at 30-150 rpm with 10-40 kN-m torque while 200-450 kN of weight is set off the bit. Weight-on-bit and torque are the two variables the driller steers with; the drilling engineer watches torque and bit exponent while the driller watches penetration rate.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.name: Drilling mud (drilling fluid)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.description: A thixotropic clay-water or oil-water emulsion that removes cuttings, lubricates and cools the bit, carries hydraulic pressure to the formation, and crucially gels to hold formation pressure when the pumps stop. In practice it was a chemically engineered suspension with four control jobs: viscosity at the bit, gel strength in the hole, filtrate control to stop the formation claying off, and compatibility with the formation. Four numbers decide whether a mud works: funnel viscosity, plastic viscosity, yield point and the PV/YP ratio, with PV/YP held at or below 3 for hole cleaning, plus a low-pressure filtration rate (Baroid/API) to limit the filtrate that causes formation damage and differential sticking.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.note: The exact 1980s API target numbers vary by formation and by whether a water or oil mud is in use; the PV/YP guidance is the well-established part.

facts.label: Mud PV/YP rule of thumb
facts.value: PV/YP <= 3 for hole cleaning

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chelant-bioc.name: Chelants, biocides and defoamers
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chelant-bioc.description: The 1980s mud chemist's standard additive cabinet: phosphate and polyphosphate sequestrants for calcium, lignosulphonate and polyacrylamide viscosifiers, benzyl alcohol defoamer, and glutaraldehyde or formaldehyde-based biocides against sulphate-reducing bacteria, which produce hydrogen sulphide and sour the cuttings.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.weights-mix.name: Mixed-weight additive (iron ore + barite)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.weights-mix.description: Where barite was unavailable or too expensive, ground iron ore was blended in as a second weighting agent. It attacks steel components by corrosion and needs a passivation layer of lime or sulphide film, but it saved cost in a tight barite market.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mu.name: Oil-based (diesel) mud
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mu.description: Diesel or mineral oil as the continuous phase with water as the dispersed phase, organophilic clay (amine-treated montmorillonite) for viscosity. Chosen for high-temperature deep wells and for formations where water filtrate would swell clay. Its environmental reputation in the Gulf in the 1980s was poor, and it had to be stabilised with organophilic bentonite and lime.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.oil-based-mu.note: Petroleum diesel is the same distillate stream as the refining branch: chem.refining.atmospheric-distillation.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lim.name: Chrome/lime mud (invert emulsion)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lim.description: The classic high-temperature mud: a water-in-oil (invert) emulsion with oil as the continuous phase, bentonite in the aqueous phase, and calcium carbonate and a lime (Ca(OH)2) emulsion. Chrome/lime muds were standard to about 120-150 C but they fail in a cement job because the calcium in cement breaks the emulsion, so a salt-water mud or a chrome-free lime mud had to be switched in first.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.chromate-lim.note: The name comes from the use of sodium chromate as a corrosion inhibitor on the ferrous cutting and drilling hardware, which had to be neutralised before disposal.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.barite.name: Barite (barium sulphate) weighting agent
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.barite.description: Almost all the weight in a mud: API-grade barite at 4.28 g/cm3 (42.8 ppg) added to a base mud of about 1.03-1.2. Barite is also the standard drilling weighting because it is nearly insoluble in water. The same mineral appears as filler in the plastics and cable branches of this file, via metal.barium-carbonate.

facts.label: Density
facts.value: 4.20-4.30 g/cm3; mud density at 1,700 m can reach 2.1-2.3 g/cm3

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.name: Bentonite (montmorillonite clay)
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.description: Sodium montmorillonite from the Cretaceous Bentonite beds of Wyoming and South Dakota; the single most important mud component. It gives the thixotropy: at rest a high gel strength to suspend cuttings, under shear it drops to low viscosity so the bit can cut. Drilling-grade bentonite is API 13/14 with a viscosity of 30+ s/qt and a low montmorillonite ratio.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.note: Montmorillonite is a dioctahedral 2:1 smectite; Wyoming sodium bentonite is the reference grade because of its high cation-exchange capacity and layer charge. Bentonite suspensions are usually thixotropic and shear-thinning, the Cretaceous Benton Shale near Rock River, Wyoming is the type locality, and United States production comes from between the Black Hills of South Dakota and the Bighorn Basin of Wyoming. Not established: the API 13/14 grading, the 30+ s/qt viscosity, the 20-60 kg/m3 loading and the 3-20 Pa yield stress targets.

facts.label: Typical mud loading
facts.value: 20-60 kg/m3 of bentonite in a water mud

facts.label: Yield stress target
facts.value: 3-20 Pa for hole cleaning; gel 10-30 Pa on the low-yield muds

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.name: Montmorillonite and the bentonite bed
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.description: Sodium montmorillonite is a dioctahedral 2:1 smectite: two tetrahedral silica sheets sandwiching an octahedral aluminium sheet, with the negative layer charge balanced by exchangeable sodium. Between the layers is water, and that water is why the clay swells, gels and gives the mud its thixotropy. The drilling grade comes from the Cretaceous Bentonite bed of Wyoming and South Dakota, a marine sediment about 65-72 million years old that is a calcium montmorillonite until it is mined and soda-ashed to the sodium form.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.name: The clay pit
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.description: A 10-20 m thick bentonite bed, opened up and worked as an open pit or a shallow underground mine, in a landscape that looks like a lunar plain because the clay is grey-white when fresh and weathers to a pale crust. It is the last dig-it-out node of the crude branch's drilling chain, and it is the point at which a machine that will one day hold a C64's case first touches something that came out of the ground with no hydrocarbons in it at all.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.note: Not established: the 10-20 m bed thickness and the open-pit versus shallow-underground working method. The grey-white lunar appearance and the Wyoming and South Dakota locations are consistent with the type locality but are not documented.

chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.name: Soda ash conversion to sodium bentonite
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.description: The pit clay is a calcium montmorillonite and has to be converted. The clay is blunged with water, treated with sodium carbonate so that the exchangeable calcium is replaced by sodium, and then dried and milled. That step is what turns a geological curiosity into an industrial material, and it is also the step that makes the drilling specification possible, because the sodium form swells and the calcium form does not.
chem.crude.rig.drilling-mud.bentonite.mo.note: Kept as a node because the conversion is what makes the drilling specification possible: the sodium form swells and the calcium form does not. Its soda ash is now a "from" edge to the metals fragment's sodium carbonate node instead of a line of prose.

chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.mud-syste.name: Mud circulation system
chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.mud-syste.description: Active and reserve pits, the pump, the surface mixing hopper (mud pit) and the flowline over the shaker. 1980s volumes for a single rig were 400-1,500 m3 of active mud with 150-400 m3 of reserve, and the pit room needed chemical dosing, dilution and waste disposal for one well's worth of chemically treated clay.

chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.drillstri.name: Drill string
chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.drillstri.description: Drill pipe, drill collars and a bit, threaded or coupled API 5-1/2 in and 6-5/8 in in the 1980s, with 3-1/2 in drill collar subs. Length is a queue of 5,000-7,000 m of 5 in pipe plus 200-400 m of collars; the string must be strong enough for tensile load at the maximum string weight yet remain within the derrick.
chem.crude.rig.rotary-drilling.drillstri.note: Drill pipe steel is a metals chain, not a petrochemical one; the petroleum-derived material here is the mud, the cement and the bit matrix.

chem.crude.reservoir.name: The reservoir: where the oil sits
chem.crude.reservoir.description: Oil exists in pore space between grains of sandstone or in fractures and vugs of carbonate, held down by an overburden of rock and by an overlying gas cap or water. This is the physical thing that the whole upstream industry is trying to reach. Oil squeezed out of the source rock moves updip along a permeable sandstone or through a fault until it is trapped, driven by a buoyancy of roughly 0.2-0.4 degrees API per 1,000 ft, with the column height set by the capillary entry pressure of the seal.

chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.name: Oil column in the pore space
chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.description: An oil column of tens to hundreds of metres stands between a gas cap and a water contact, with oil saturation in the pay zone often only 50-80% of pore volume. That gap, plus the reservoir rock and the seal, is why recovery factors are 15-35% and why hydraulic fracturing and acidising exist.

chem.petroleum.asphaltene.name: Asphaltenes and resins
chem.petroleum.asphaltene.description: The heavy, aromatic, high-molecular-weight end of crude. Roughly 2-20% of crude, soluble in the light ends and precipitated by heptane in the standard n-heptane asphaltene test. Asphaltenes are the coke precursors in every thermal cracker, coker and reformer, and their content is what decides whether a crude makes a good or bad feedstock.

facts.label: n-C7 asphaltene content
facts.value: 2-10 wt% for a light sour crude

chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.oil-in-p.name: Oil in place
chem.crude.reservoir.oil-column.oil-in-p.description: The volume of hydrocarbons physically present in the rock, before any recovery factor. Multiply it by the C64 scale: the entire world shipped about 200,000 Commodore 64s in 1983, so the machine is a rounding error on a single wellhead's hourly output.

chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.name: Reservoir rock: sandstone and carbonate
chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.description: Porosity 15-35% and permeability 50-2,000 mD for a good sandstone; carbonate reservoirs have most of their porosity as vugs and fractures and typically 5-25% matrix porosity. Around 60% of world oil reserves and 80% of world gas reserves were in carbonate rock, most of it fractured Arab-type in the Middle East.

chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.mari.name: Marine carbonate (Arab-type) reservoir
chem.crude.reservoir.reservoir-rock.mari.description: Dolomitised limestone and dolomite of the Arabian shelf: high initial productivity, typically 4,000-10,000 bbl/d per well with strong water drive, but rapid flow assurance decline and high water cut. Saudi production was essentially all of this rock type in 1983.

chem.crude.reservoir.trap.name: Geological trap
chem.crude.reservoir.trap.description: Anticline, fault, pinch-out or stratigraphic trap. The Ghawar field in Saudi Arabia, discovered in 1948, remained the largest oil field on earth for decades, holding some 100+ billion stock-tank barrels in a stacked series of Arabian carbonate reservoirs.

facts.label: Ghawar field
facts.value: >100 billion stock-tank barrels recoverable (Arabian Suwayb member carbonates)

chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.name: Source rock and kerogen
chem.crude.reservoir.source-rock.description: Organic-rich marine shale. Type I and type II kerogen give oil; type III, humic and mainly terrestrial, gives gas. Maturation is measured by vitrinite reflectance, with the oil window at roughly 0.6-1.3% Ro and the gas window above about 1.3%. Between about 60 and 160 C the kerogen breaks down into oil and at higher rank into wet and then dry gas: the same thermal-cracking chemistry, far slower and uncatalysed, that a steam cracker performs in seconds.

facts.label: Oil window
facts.value: vitrinite reflectance 0.6-1.3% Ro, roughly 60-160 C

chem.crude.reservoir.sedimentary-basin.name: Sedimentary basin
chem.crude.reservoir.sedimentary-basin.description: A subsiding basin in which organic mud is buried, buried deeper, cooked and squeezed; the whole petroleum system is source, maturation, migration, reservoir, seal and trap, and it takes 1-100 million years of that history. By 1983 the world's producing basins were a few hundred in number, with the Middle East and the Gulf of Mexico dominating reserves.

chem.crude.exploration.name: Petroleum exploration
chem.crude.exploration.description: Finding a commercial accumulation of oil before spending the exploration well. In 1980s practice this was reflection seismology over regional grids, closed by wildcat drilling. Cost per barrel discovered had fallen from tens of dollars to roughly $2-8 by the early 1980s. A mud-logging unit beside the rig sampled cuttings and gas continuously with a hot-wire or infrared hydrocarbon detector, and it was the shows it found that decided whether to run a full log suite.

chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate.name: Reserve estimation
chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate.description: Volumetric and material-balance estimates, presented to a board and to governments as proved, probable and possible reserves. Rules of thumb: recovery factor 15-35% of oil-in-place for a sandstone reservoir, higher (35-60%) for a fractured carbonate. Reserve booking was and remains a commercial and legal judgement, not a measurement. The volumetric calculation behind all of it is pore volume x oil saturation x formation volume factor, and B_o for a light crude at reservoir temperature is 1.1-1.3, so reservoir barrels convert to stock-tank barrels at a meaningful ratio; saturation is the least measurable input and the most sensitive.

chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate..name: Reserve uncertainty and contingency
chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate..description: Undiscovered reserves behind existing fields were treated as of similar magnitude to proved reserves. The industry view of world ultimately-recoverable oil in 1983 was around 1,500-2,000 billion stock-tank barrels, versus about 700 billion produced or proved.
chem.crude.exploration.reserve-estimate..note: Reserve uncertainty and a world ultimately-recoverable figure are commentary about reserve booking.

facts.label: World cumulative production to 1983
facts.value: ~700 billion stock-tank barrels

chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well.name: Exploration (wildcat) well
chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well.description: The first hole into a prospect. Cheap success-failure logging with mud logging and core, drilled to the deepest prognosis rather than the shallowest pay. Exploration wells in the early 1980s averaged about 3,000-5,000 m of hole and took 30-90 days offshore.

chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well..name: Wildcat cost and success statistics
chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well..description: A North Sea or Gulf of Mexico wildcat cost $3-20 million in the early 1980s; the historical industry success rate was about 1 in 10 wells dry, 1 in 15 total wildcats a commercial discovery, and about 1 in 8 wildcats found non-commercial hydrocarbons. Exploration cost per barrel discovered was roughly $2-8.
chem.crude.exploration.exploration-well..note: A cost and success rate is a statement about the industry, not a substance you can weigh.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.name: Reflection seismic survey
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.description: A surface source sends a pressure wave down through the rock section; reflectors return it to hydrophones and the travel times are stacked into a two-dimensional depth section. Seismic is a time-domain method: it maps reflectivity contrasts (sandstone/shale, gas-sand amplitude dimming) and gives no direct information about fluid type. The record was stacked and migrated on a mainframe or minicomputer: common-midpoint stacking, normal-moveout correction from velocity analysis, deconvolution and depth conversion, with the 1980s emphasis on multiple suppression and on early 3-D, where a single field cost $1-3 million per acre-foot. A log response indicating oil or gas - high resistivity, low neutron density, a gas effect on the seismic - is a test, not a discovery: a discovery needed a producing well, and industry experience was one test in eight to one in thirty commercial.

facts.label: Typical 2-D fold
facts.value: 6-fold to 24-fold

facts.label: Sample interval
facts.value: 2-4 ms (500-250 Hz vertical resolution)

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.re.name: Seismic recording system
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.re.description: Field recording on 1/2 in or 1 in nine-track magnetic tape (typically 2000 inch/s, 12.5-50 Hz bandwidth) or, from the early 1980s, 12-bit digital field recorders writing 3M/IBM-compatible cartridges. The whole array recorded simultaneously; it was common for the record to be demultiplexed and copied to a computer tape for onshore stacking.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.name: Seismic geophone array
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.description: On land, 12 to 48 groups of 10-60 Hz moving-coil geophones per station, each on a spike planted in a levelled hole, cabled and buried. In 1980s 2-D the fold of coverage (usually 6-fold to 24-fold) was chosen by geophone group interval and source spacing, not by 3-D binning.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.name: Geophone takeout cable and junction box
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.description: Polythene-insulated multi-pair takeout cable to a junction box, then a line-trap and telemetry radio link to the recording truck. Cable insulation here is polyethylene from the same steam-cracking chain as the C64's power cord jacket.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.name: Moving-coil geophone
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ge.description: A 1-2 kg mass suspended in a magnetic field inside a case 3-5 cm across; coil movement induces a signal proportional to ground velocity. A second coil acts as a position feedback for the servo. Cost per channel in the early 1980s was several hundred to a few thousand dollars.

facts.label: Natural frequency
facts.value: 8-14 Hz (land), 4-5 Hz (swamp)

facts.label: Distortion
facts.value: <0.1-0.5% for 1980s servo geophones

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.name: Marine seismic streamer and hydrophone cable
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.description: A towed cable up to 3 km long carrying hundreds of hydrophone elements at 12.5-25 m groups; it was a synthetic-fibre-wrapped, oil-filled or water-filled analogue/digital telemetry line whose integrity was the limiting factor on data quality. Hydrophone elements used piezoelectric ceramic (PZT-5) discs coupled to silicone oil in a pressure-compensated housing.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.name: PZT-5 piezoelectric hydrophone element
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.description: Lead zirconate titanate ceramic discs, typically 25-50 mm diameter, epoxied onto a diaphragm and back-electrode in a silicone-oil-filled housing; sensitivity about -190 dB re 1 V/uPa in the 10-60 Hz band. Silicone oil here is one of the petrochemical elastomers/fluids, unrelated to the case material.
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.st.note: The silicone and epoxy cross-links are chem.silicone and chem.epoxy in this file.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.name: Dynamite shothole source
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.description: Still used for small onshore surveys in the early 1980s: 0.5-5 kg of packaged explosive in a borehole, fired from a firing truck, with the shot hole re-drilled for the next shot. Cheap per shot but slow, noisy and it polluted a producing field's drill cuttings.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.name: Seismic shot-hole explosive ammunition
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ex.description: Cast or pressed explosive in aluminium or paper shells with electric or vacuum-fire detonators, supplied on the same chemical logistics as any blasting operation. This is a one-off consumable of a survey, not part of any C64 material.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ai.name: Airgun and marine seismic source
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.ai.description: Offshore and in shallow water the source was a 1,000-10,000 cu-in (16-160 litre) airgun array fired every 10-15 s from the stern of a seismic vessel. Compressed air from compressor trucks on deck; a single 1980s 3-D crew vessel carried up to four sources.

chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.vi.name: Seismic vibrator truck
chem.crude.exploration.seismic-survey.vi.description: A truck-mounted hydraulic vibrator sweeps 10-80 Hz into the ground under hold-and-hold conditions; on land it replaced explosive shot holes because it gave repeatable, higher-energy sources with no shothole cleanup. Regionally a 1,000-2,000 m shotpoint spacing was normal in 1980s 2-D work.

metal.name: Metals, ores and industrial minerals
metal.description: Every mineral stream behind a 1982 Commodore 64: the quartzite that becomes silicon, the bauxite and cryolite that becomes aluminium foil, the porphyry copper that becomes PCB track and transformer magnet wire, the tin and lead that become 63/37 solder, the iron ore and coke that become the steel chassis and the transformer laminations, and the specialty metals - gold, silver, nickel, tantalum, zinc, chromium, manganese, cobalt, tungsten - that end up plating contacts, filling ceramic capacitors, binding carbide cutters and drawing the filament in a television's gun. The rare earths are here too, as oxides rather than metals, because they arrive as oxides and are only a few hundred tonnes of them. Each branch runs from the finished metal down to the quarry, the open pit, the evaporite bed or the seabed.
metal.note: This is the orientation node for the branch. Its substance - the list of mineral streams behind a 1982 machine and the statement that each branch runs from the finished metal down to a quarry, pit, evaporite or seabed - is a statement about the tree rather than a claim about the world, so no document supports it. The one checkable assertion, that the rare earths arrive as only a few hundred tonnes of oxide, is not established here.

metal.rare-earths.name: Rare earths: fifteen metals out of two concentrate ores
metal.rare-earths.description: The lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium are a single mining and refining industry that supplies fifteen elements which are chemically almost identical and economically almost unrelated. What a 1982 machine actually asks for is a gram-scale pinch of several of them: europium to make the red of a television phosphor, samarium for a correction magnet, neodymium for the catalyst that sets the cis content of a butadiene rubber, lanthanum and dysprosium as the donor dopants of an X7R ceramic dielectric, and lanthanum and neodymium exchanged into the zeolite of a refinery's cracking catalyst. All of them leave the same two concentrate ores and the same solvent-extraction plant, and after that plant the only question is which of the fifteen fractions a customer asks for.
metal.rare-earths.note: Category is metals because the industry sells and counts these as metals - mixed rare-earth metal and the individual ingots - even where the product bought is an oxide. There is no separate rare-earths category, and the oxide is what a phosphor maker receives.

facts.label: Two ores
facts.value: bastnasite, a light-REE carbonate fluorosilicate, and monazite, a mostly-light phosphate that also carries thorium

facts.label: Two dominant sources in 1982
facts.value: Mountain Pass, California and Bayan Obo, Inner Mongolia

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: solvent extraction in a train of hundreds of mixer-settler stages

facts.label: Demand in 1982
facts.value: gram-scale: colour television phosphors dominated, with catalysts and magnets far behind

metal.rare-earths.separation.name: Cracking, leaching and solvent extraction
metal.rare-earths.separation.description: Fifteen elements that differ only in the number of electrons in one inner shell cannot be separated by any normal chemical operation, because they all want the same compounds. The industry separates them by arithmetic instead: a long train of mixer-settler stages in which a hydrocarbon solvent and an aqueous phase pass counter-current and the partition coefficient between them is exploited a hundred times over, walking cerium, lanthanum, neodymium and the rest off the stream one at a time. Hundreds of stages and several tonnes of solvent per tonne of oxide is what it costs, which is why the whole business sits behind one or two plants per ore rather than being spread around, and why the ore's owner and the plant's owner are usually the same company. Cerium is the one that comes out cheaply and in bulk, and cerium is a nuisance: there is far more of it than anyone can use.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: counter-current mixer-settler solvent extraction, hundreds of stages

facts.label: Why
facts.value: the elements differ only in one inner shell, so they form identical compounds

facts.label: Economics
facts.value: the plant and the mine are normally one company; the separation is the barrier to entry

facts.label: Bulk fraction
facts.value: cerium is the most abundant and the least wanted, and comes out in large tonnage

metal.rare-earths.oxides.name: Separated rare-earth oxides
