metal.rare-earths.oxides.description: The output of the separation plant is a set of individual oxides rather than a mixture: europium oxide for the red activator in a colour television phosphor, samarium oxide for the samarium-cobalt magnet, neodymium oxide for the lanthanide rubber catalyst and for the cracking-catalyst zeolite, lanthanum and dysprosium oxides ground to sub-micron as the donor dopants of a ceramic dielectric, and yttrium oxide as both a dopant and a stabiliser. Grades are quoted by purity - 99.9% or 99.99% for the phosphor and magnet grades - and the price differences between them are large enough that the tonnages are shaped by which grade happens to be wanted, not by how much of the element there is in the ground.

facts.label: Grades sold
facts.value: 99.9% and 99.99% oxide for phosphor, magnet and catalyst uses

facts.label: Particle size matters
facts.value: MLCC dopant oxides are ground and sieved to sub-micron

facts.label: Price
facts.value: europium, samarium and dysprosium cost orders of magnitude more per kilogram than cerium

metal.rare-earths.monazite.name: Monazite concentrate and the beach-sand placer
metal.rare-earths.monazite.description: Monazite, (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4, is a heavy placer mineral from the beach sands that carry ilmenite, zircon, rutile and xenotime with it - the Kerala and Queensland and Cape Breton sands, worked by a dredge and a floating concentrator with shaking tables, spirals, a magnet and an electrostatic separator. It holds 20-30% rare-earth oxides and, because thorium's chemistry is so close to the rare earths', 5-30% ThO2 as well. That thorium is the practical difficulty and the reason monazite had been worked mainly for its heavy minerals: it follows the rare earths through the whole separation chemistry and has to be parked in a radioactive residue. Monazite is mined for thorium, for the heavy minerals and, in a few places, for the rare earths themselves. It is also an impurity that a coltan refinery has to filter off its fluoride solution.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: (Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4 with 5-30% ThO2

facts.label: Occurrence
facts.value: heavy placer concentrates from a beach sand, alongside ilmenite, zircon, rutile and xenotime

facts.label: The thorium problem
facts.value: thorium's chemistry follows the rare earths through the whole circuit and reports in the residue

metal.rare-earths.monazite.caustic-bake.name: Caustic soda bake to split the rare earths from the thorium
metal.rare-earths.monazite.caustic-bake.description: Monazite is a refractory phosphate, so the industrial split between the rare earths and the thorium is a matter of finding a lye that will dissolve one and not the other. A 50% caustic soda solution is mixed with the sand and taken to about 140-150 C for several hours; the phosphate is broken down and the rare-earth elements go into solution as hydroxides, while thorium and uranium stay behind as comparatively insoluble hydroxides in the residue, where they concentrate into a radioactive waste that has to be stored. The pregnant liquor is then diluted, filtered and taken to the separation plant. An acid digestion at 150-200 C does the same job more cheaply on some ores and worse on others, because it dissolves the thorium too and puts the separation problem downstream.
metal.rare-earths.monazite.caustic-bake.note: The caustic bake and its selectivity against thorium are well documented in monazite processing; which route a given 1982 plant used is not established.

facts.label: Bake
facts.value: about 50% NaOH at 140-150 C for several hours

facts.label: Split
facts.value: rare earths dissolve as hydroxides; thorium and uranium stay in the residue

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: nitric or sulfuric acid digestion at 150-200 C, which takes the thorium into solution as well

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: the thorium residue is a radioactive waste that has to be stored, not sold

metal.monazite.beach.name: The heavy-mineral beach and its dredge
metal.monazite.beach.description: A beach on the east coast of Queensland or on the Malabar coast of Kerala where the wave has concentrated ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite and xenotime into a dark, 1-10% heavy-mineral band a metre or two thick in the sand. It is worked by a cutter-suction dredge or a walking dredge on a barge, which pumps the sand onto a floating concentrator with shaking tables, spirals, a magnetic separator and an electrostatic separator. This is the shared geological endpoint of a surprising amount of this file: the titanium dioxide, the coltan, the thorium residue, the rare earths and the zircon all came out of a band like this one, which is why a capacitor's tantalum and a television's red phosphor can be argued about at the same beach.

facts.label: Band
facts.value: 0.5-5 m of heavy-mineral sand at 1-10% HM

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: cutter-suction dredge or a walking dredge on a barge

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: gravity tables and spirals, then magnet and electrostatic separation

metal.rare-earths.bastnasite.name: Bastnasite concentrate and the Mountain Pass carbonatite
metal.rare-earths.bastnasite.description: Bastnasite - usually written bastnaesite in commercial and metallurgical use, and bastnäsite in mineralogy - is (Ce,La)CO3F, a light-brown carbonate fluorosilicate carrying 6-9% rare-earth oxides. It was found in 1878 at Bastnas in Sweden and worked in quantity from 1949, but the ore that supplied the western industry in 1982 was a carbonatite in the Clark Mountains in California. It is an open pit in a 1.4-billion-year-old carbonatite intrusion, 8-12% rare-earth oxides in bastnasite with calcite, barite and dolomite as gangue, and it is dredged, floated and sent to its own separation plant on the same site. Mountain Pass is the clearest single example in this tree of an ore mined for an element nobody can see in it: barium is the gangue, iron is what comes out of the separation circuit, and the rare earths are what it is for. Production rose steeply through the 1960s to supply europium for the red of colour television. The other giant, Bayan Obo in Inner Mongolia, is different in kind: it is an iron-ore mine first, with monazite and bastnasite in the ore and the rare earths and niobium recovered as by-products, its concentrate travelling 150 km to the separation works at Baotou.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: (Ce,La)CO3F, a carbonate fluorosilicate

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 6-9% REO; the Mountain Pass carbonatite carries 8-12% REO

facts.label: Gangue
facts.value: calcite, barite and dolomite

facts.label: Bayan Obo
facts.value: an iron-ore mine whose rare earths and niobium are by-products; ore processed at Baotou 150 km away

facts.label: What it is mined for
facts.value: europium for colour television red expanded Mountain Pass production steeply in the 1960s

metal.cobalt.name: Cobalt: the carbide binder, the ferrite dopant and the magnet alloy
metal.cobalt.description: Cobalt is the element nobody thinks of and cannot do without. In a 1982 C64 and its peripherals it is the metal that holds tungsten carbide together in a drill cone, an end mill and a stamping die; the grain-boundary dopant that makes NiZn ferrite behave; the balance element in the iron-nickel-cobalt lid sealed onto a memory chip's ceramic package; a few percent of an Alnico correction magnet; and, at the top of the price range, half of a samarium-cobalt magnet. The mass in any one machine is a few grams. What is worth tracing is where it comes from, because cobalt is almost never mined for itself: it is overwhelmingly a by-product reporting out of somebody else's circuit, most often a copper-cobalt orebody or a nickel refinery, so the cobalt supply chain is largely a set of attachments to the copper and nickel branches.
metal.cobalt.note: The market was not short in 1982, which is the opposite of the usual assumption. The genuine disruption was the Shaba invasions of 1977 and 1978 in Zaire, which stopped the Katanga copper mines; the price went from about $5.58/lb in 1977 to about $25/lb in 1980 and then fell back as Zaire's stockpiles came down and nickel-derived supply grew. Even the Shaba shock was milder than expected, because cobalt is a rare metal, its pigment is toxic enough that a formulator could substitute, and the industry had established effective recycling. Which plants contributed how much cobalt in a particular year is not established here.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: grey-white, hard and brittle, density 8.83 g/cm3, melting point 1495 C

facts.label: Supply character
facts.value: almost entirely a by-product of copper and of nickel; primary cobalt deposits are rare

facts.label: Late-1970s concentration
facts.value: a contemporary industry survey put Zaire at 53% of world output, with Zambia 9%, Australia 7%, New Caledonia 6% and Morocco 6%

facts.label: Price
facts.value: $5.58/lb in 1977, $25/lb in 1980, about $12.50/lb in May 1982, about $5/lb by 1983-84

facts.label: Share of the market
facts.value: superalloys and cemented carbides have historically taken the largest share

metal.cobalt.oxide.name: Cobalt(II) oxide, the additive grade
metal.cobalt.oxide.description: The oxide a component maker actually buys is neither the ore nor the metal but a calcined powder, and in 1982 electronics the grade in question was a few percent of a zinc oxide varistor disc and a trace in a ferrite body. Heating cobalt metal in oxygen gives the blue-black spinel Co3O4, which is the oxide most of the industry actually trades; the green rocksalt CoO underneath it is a different substance with a different stability range, oxidising back to Co3O4 at 600-700 C and reappearing only when the temperature goes above 900 C. That is why the calcining route is described as reducing to the metal by way of Co3O4, and why a supplier's 'cobalt monoxide' and 'cobalt oxide' can be the same powder. The varistor is why this matters - a few percent of cobalt lets a zinc oxide disc hold a wide voltage range without failing, by making the grain boundaries and the grain interiors drift to their breakdown voltages at different rates.
metal.cobalt.oxide.note: The CoO/Co3O4 equilibrium is textbook inorganic chemistry; which specific oxide a 1982 varistor or ferrite supplier used is not established, so the node records the substance rather than a claim about a particular part.

facts.label: The traded oxide
facts.value: blue-black spinel Co3O4, from heating cobalt metal in oxygen

facts.label: The two oxides
facts.value: CoO oxidises to Co3O4 at 600-700 C, and Co3O4 loses oxygen above 900 C to give CoO again

facts.label: Varistor use
facts.value: a few percent in a ZnO disc, to spread the grain-boundary and grain-interior breakdown voltages

metal.cobalt.electrolytic.name: Electrolytic refining to 99.8% cathode
metal.cobalt.electrolytic.description: Almost all cobalt metal on the market is won by electrolysis, and that is a deliberate choice about purity rather than about cost. The cobalt hydroxide or the crude metal is dissolved in sulfuric acid to make a cobalt sulphate solution; that solution is fed to an insoluble anode and a cobalt starter cathode, and metal grows on the cathode at a controlled current density while the impurities that are not plating out stay in the bath. The result is a cobalt cathode of about 99.8% - the grade trade calls Falconbridge cathode - and it is the standard feed for the tungsten-carbide industry, because a carbide's cobalt binder has to be fine, uniform and free of the copper, iron and lead that would poison the sintering. Electrolytic cobalt is also how the high-purity metal for superalloys and for the samarium-cobalt magnets was made.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: cobalt sulphate solution, insoluble anode, cobalt starter cathode

facts.label: Product
facts.value: about 99.8% cobalt cathode

facts.label: Other grades
facts.value: about 99.6% from Zambia, 99.3% ingot from the Soviet Union

facts.label: Why the grade matters
facts.value: the WC binder must be fine and free of copper, iron and lead or the carbide will not sinter

metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl.name: Dicobalt octacarbonyl, Co2(CO)8
metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl.description: The cobalt in a Mond residue is a genuine industrial source, and an unusual one: the residue left after the nickel has been volatilised as Ni(CO)4 still contains the cobalt as Co2(CO)8, and the two carbonyls are separated by exploiting the fact that dicobalt octacarbonyl is solid and will crystallise out while nickel carbonyl boils off at 43 C. In the classical route the residue is treated with copper at about 200 C under hydrogen to reduce both carbonyls, and then re-carbonylated to re-form Co2(CO)8, which is filtered and decomposed to metal. The consequence for the wider market is that every tonne of nickel refined by the carbonyl process is a tonne of cobalt that did not have to be mined, which is why the two nickel carbonyl plants at Sudbury and Kokkola were influential in the cobalt market well beyond their own output.
metal.nickel.cobalt-carbonyl.note: The chemistry and the plants are well documented. How much cobalt came from this route in 1982 is not established, and the market that year was falling rather than short: about $12.50/lb in May, against $25/lb in 1980 and about $5/lb by 1983-84.

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: Co2(CO)8 is solid and crystallises; Ni(CO)4 boils at 43 C and distils off

facts.label: Process
facts.value: reduction with copper under hydrogen at about 200 C, then carbonylation, then decomposition to metal

facts.label: Market effect
facts.value: nickel carbonyl plants are a by-product source of cobalt, so nickel capacity sets part of the cobalt supply

metal.cobalt.ammoniacal-leach.name: The Sherritt-Gordon ammonia pressure leach
metal.cobalt.ammoniacal-leach.description: The second big route takes cobalt out of a nickel refinery rather than out of an orebody, and it exists because the nickel circuit was already there. Nickel concentrate or matte is leached with ammonia and ammonium sulphate in horizontal autoclaves under air at elevated pressure, which dissolves the nickel, cobalt and copper as metal-ammine complexes while the sulphide sulphur is oxidised and leaves as ammonium sulphate - a saleable fertiliser, which is what made the process pay. Cobalt is then separated from nickel on the fact that the cobalt ammine is far more stable: it is held in solution while the nickel is thrown down, and the cobalt stream is finished separately to metal. Because the feed is somebody else's concentrate, every tonne of cobalt this route makes is a tonne that did not have to be mined.
metal.cobalt.ammoniacal-leach.note: The ammonia pressure leach is a mature Sherritt-Gordon process by 1982 and is applied to sulphide concentrate as well as to laterite-derived precipitate; the share of world cobalt it supplied in 1982 is not asserted here.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: nickel concentrate or matte, and lateritic mixed sulphide precipitate

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: ammonia and ammonium sulphate, air, elevated pressure, horizontal autoclaves

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: the cobalt ammine is much more stable than the nickel ammine, so cobalt is held and nickel is thrown down

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: ammonium sulphate fertiliser, which is what made the process economic

metal.cobalt.ore.name: Cobalt ore: heterogenite, carrollite and asbolane
metal.cobalt.ore.description: Most cobalt never appears as a cobalt mineral at all. In the Copperbelt - the Shaba and Nkana strata of Zaire and Zambia - it sits in the sulphide ores as carrollite, Cu(Co,Ni)2S4, and it is recovered by flotation alongside the copper sulphides, so its output tracks the copper mine's. Where the deposit weathers, the same cobalt is oxidised to heterogenite, CoO(OH), a black manganese-rich oxide in the near-surface ore, and it is the oxide that the later hydrometallurgical flowsheets treat. A third source is asbolane, (Ni,Co)2-xMn4+(O,OH)4.nH2O, the cobalt-nickel-manganese oxide that forms in New Caledonian laterite. Grades are low: laterites run 0.1-1.5% Co, and the oxide zones are mined at a few percent.

facts.label: Copperbelt sulphide
facts.value: carrollite Cu(Co,Ni)2S4, floated with the copper sulphides

facts.label: Oxide zone
facts.value: heterogenite CoO(OH), the near-surface weathering product

facts.label: Laterite
facts.value: asbolane (Ni,Co)2-xMn4+(O,OH)4.nH2O, New Caledonia

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: 0.1-1.5% Co in laterite; the oxide zones are worked at a few percent

metal.cobalt.ore.hydromet.name: Leach the copper-cobalt oxide ore
metal.cobalt.ore.hydromet.description: The oxide ores of the Copperbelt are not smelted for their cobalt: they are leached. The ore is crushed and agitated in a sulfuric acid solution, which dissolves the cobalt and copper as sulphates while the iron stays in the residue as hydroxide, and the pregnant liquor is then taken to a solvent-extraction circuit that pulls the cobalt and copper apart from each other. What comes out of that circuit is a cobalt sulphate solution and, from it, a cobalt hydroxide intermediate that is shipped to a refinery. This is why the cobalt in a 1982 tungsten-carbide drill cone is a chemical-plant product rather than a smelter product, and why the Copperbelt's cobalt followed the fortunes of its acid plants and its export routes.
metal.cobalt.ore.hydromet.note: The sulfate-leach and solvent-extraction flowsheet for Copperbelt oxide ore is well established; which particular plant or circuit served a given carbide maker in 1982 is not established.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: sulfuric acid; cobalt and copper dissolve as sulphates, iron stays in the residue

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: solvent extraction splits cobalt from copper

facts.label: Intermediate
facts.value: cobalt hydroxide concentrate, shipped to a refinery

metal.tungsten.name: Tungsten: filaments, carbide and alloying element
metal.tungsten.description: Very little tungsten is inside a 1982 C64, and almost all of what there is sits in capital equipment and consumables rather than in the machine: the heater filament in a television's electron gun, the cemented-carbide cutters that drill the mainboard and route the glass-epoxy laminate, the carbide dies that draw the power-supply transformer's magnet wire, the tungsten-rhenium needles of a wafer probe card, and a percent or two of it in the simple tooling and stamping steels. What it is: the highest-melting-point of all metals at 3422 C, boiling at 5930 C, density 19.25 g/cm3 - a metal that is essentially never found as native metal, because wolframite and scheelite carry it at 0.3-2.5% WO3 and it has to be chemically opened before it can be reduced. It is not in the case mould: SKD61 and H13 are chromium-molybdenum-vanadium steels with no tungsten in them at all, and the alloying element in that family is molybdenum.

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: 3422 C - the highest of any metal; boils at 5930 C

facts.label: Density
facts.value: 19.25 g/cm3, about 1.7 times lead

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 0.3-2.5 wt% WO3 in the run-of-mine ore; about 60% WO3 in a concentrate

facts.label: End-use split
facts.value: cemented carbide 60-70%, steels and other alloys 20-30%, the rest in compounds

facts.label: Abundance
facts.value: about 1.5 ppm of the earth's crust, the 58th most abundant element

facts.label: Not in the case mould
facts.value: SKD61 / H13 is 5Cr-5Mo-1V-0.4C with no tungsten; the W-bearing steels are the W1/SKS3 tooling class and the high-speed steels, up to 18% W

metal.tungsten.carbide.name: Tungsten carbide and the WC-Co cemented carbide
metal.tungsten.carbide.description: Tungsten carbide, WC, is made by heating tungsten powder with carbon above 2000 C, and pressed and sintered on its own it is brittle and useless. What the industry actually buys is the composite: 6-12% finely divided cobalt powder mixed with WC grains of 0.5-30 microns, pressed and vacuum-sintered at 1400-1600 C, then ground and lapped to shape. The molten cobalt wets the carbide grains and holds them in a continuous binder, which is why the two metals are inseparable inside one object - a rock bit cone is a tungsten product and a cobalt product at once. By the 1980s cemented carbide was the largest single use of tungsten, ahead of filament, and oil-well drill cones were among its largest markets, so the bit on the rig producing the crude is a tungsten product just as much as the end mill cutting a C64 mainboard is.
metal.tungsten.carbide.note: Drilling and metalworking tooling together took the majority of cemented carbide; rock bits were the single largest application in the 1980s.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 6-12% cobalt binder, 900-1600 HV

facts.label: Making
facts.value: WC from tungsten powder and carbon above 2000 C; pressed and vacuum-sintered at 1400-1600 C

facts.label: Grain size
facts.value: 0.5-30 microns of WC in the sintered body

facts.label: Share of tungsten use
facts.value: cemented carbide takes 60-70% of world tungsten consumption

metal.tungsten.reduction.name: Reduce the trioxide to tungsten powder
metal.tungsten.reduction.description: WO3 + 3 H2 gives W + 3 H2O. Hydrogen is the reducing agent because carbon would give tungsten carbide, which is a different and also valuable product rather than the metal anyone wants here; the reaction is carried out on a boat of fine powder in a hydrogen tube furnace at 500-1000 C. What comes out is not yet a usable metal: it is a porous mass of interlocking crystallites a few microns across that can be crushed but not drawn. Tungsten is brittle at room temperature - its ductile-to-brittle transition sits near 200 C - so no amount of powder metallurgy alone gives a workable solid, and the grain boundary chemistry of the powder has to be fixed before the metal can be made at all.

facts.label: Why hydrogen
facts.value: carbon reduction makes WC rather than W

facts.label: Product form
facts.value: a porous sintered mass of micronscale crystallites, not a workable metal

metal.tungsten.powder.name: Doped tungsten powder
metal.tungsten.powder.description: Undoped tungsten powder has almost no grain boundary strength, and a filament drawn from it sags as it heats and burns out where the sag is greatest. The fix, worked out in the 1920s and universal by 1982, is to add a few tenths of a percent of potassium as potassium hydroxide or potassium carbonate, with a little alumina alongside, during the reduction itself: the potassium ends up as finely dispersed potassium bubbles along the grain boundaries, and it is those bubbles that pin the boundaries so the wire can be drawn to 0.04 mm without slumping. Alumina refines the grain as well. The doped compact is pressed and sintered, then hot-worked, and the final filament metal is 99.9-99.95% pure with the potassium content controlled to control the grain.

facts.label: Doping
facts.value: 0.1-1 wt% potassium as KOH or K2CO3, plus 0.1-0.5% Al2O3

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: dispersed potassium bubbles pin the grain boundaries - non-sag tungsten

facts.label: Filament purity
facts.value: 99.9-99.95%, with potassium controlled to control the grain size

metal.tungsten.wire.name: Drawn tungsten wire
metal.tungsten.wire.description: The compact is swaged, then rolled, then drawn through carbide or diamond dies in a long series of steps, with a hydrogen anneal between them, because tungsten will not work cold: the ductile-to-brittle transition is close to room temperature and cold tungsten cracks rather than draws. A domestic television's heater ends up as wire 0.04-0.08 mm in diameter and 60-150 mm long, folded into a flat zig-zag under the cathode cup and run off 6.3 V; at that diameter a 30 cm length weighs about a hundredth of a gram and is the largest single reason a colour tube of that generation failed. The same carbide that draws this wire draws the enamelled magnet wire on the power-supply transformer, and the same wire stock makes the probe-card needles that touch every bond pad on a 6510 die.
metal.tungsten.wire.note: Not established: the 0.04-0.08 mm filament diameter, the 60-150 mm length, the 6.3 V heater, the 0.01 g mass for 30 cm, and a ductile-to-brittle transition near room temperature. The tungsten reference states only that tungsten can be worked by forging, drawing, rolling or extruding, and that polycrystalline tungsten is intrinsically brittle.

facts.label: Filament
facts.value: 0.04-0.08 mm diameter, 60-150 mm long, 6.3 V heater

facts.label: Working
facts.value: swaged, rolled and drawn with a hydrogen anneal between every reduction step

facts.label: Why anneal
facts.value: the ductile-to-brittle transition sits near room temperature

metal.tungsten.apt.name: Ammonium paratungstate (APT)
metal.tungsten.apt.description: The intermediate every other tungsten product starts from. The concentrate is digested with sodium hydroxide or with soda ash at about 900-1000 C, which brings the tungsten into solution as sodium tungstate while the calcium, iron and fluorine stay behind as insoluble residues that are filtered off; ammonium chloride then precipitates ammonium paratungstate. APT is a stable, dry, freely soluble white solid, and that is the whole point of it: it can be shipped a long way without absorbing moisture or picking up anything from a wooden crate, so APT rather than concentrate is what crosses an ocean. Calcining it at 500-600 C drives off the ammonia and leaves yellow tungsten trioxide, the one stable oxide and the universal feedstock for the metal.
metal.tungsten.apt.note: Soda ash is the alternative to caustic soda; the two routes were both in commercial use in 1982 and the choice is largely a question of what the works already had.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: (NH4)10H2W12O42, the standard traded intermediate

facts.label: Decomposition
facts.value: about 900-1000 C with NaOH or Na2CO3 to a sodium tungstate solution

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: APT crystallised out with NH4Cl from the tungstate liquor

facts.label: Calcination
facts.value: 500-600 C to yellow WO3

metal.tungsten.ore.name: Wolframite and scheelite ore
metal.tungsten.ore.description: The two ores are chemically different and are opened differently, which is why the mine and the mill are designed separately. Wolframite, (Fe,Mn)WO4, a solid solution of ferberite FeWO4 and huebnerite MnWO4, is a dense black mineral of specific gravity 7.1-7.9 that sits in the quartz veins of a granite cupola with cassiterite, topaz and native bismuth; being that heavy and weakly magnetic it concentrates on a shaking table and on a magnetic separator. Scheelite, CaWO4, is the calcium equivalent - too light and too non-magnetic for gravity, so it is froth-floated, and it is the ore of the Climax and Pine Creek skarns in Colorado and Montana and of the Felbertauern in Austria. Neither commonly exceeds about 1.5% WO3, so a tungsten mine is a large mill for a small product and it is usually a by-product operation. Molybdenum and tungsten share the greisen hydrothermal environment, so scheelite and molybdenite MoS2 are sometimes intergrown in one vein.

facts.label: Wolframite
facts.value: (Fe,Mn)WO4: ferberite FeWO4 solid solution with huebnerite MnWO4; specific gravity 7.1-7.9, weakly magnetic

facts.label: Scheelite
facts.value: CaWO4; floated rather than gravity-concentrated

facts.label: Typical host rock
facts.value: quartz vein in a granite cupola, with cassiterite, topaz and wolframite

facts.label: Companion metal
facts.value: scheelite CaWO4 and molybdenite MoS2 intergrown in the same greisen vein

metal.tungsten.ore.mine.name: Tungsten mine and concentrator
metal.tungsten.ore.mine.description: Wolframite is dense and refractory, so the ore is mined, crushed and gravity-concentrated or floated to a 60-70% WO3 concentrate, which is roughly a hundredfold upgrade on a 0.6% head grade. Because the ore is so often a by-product of a tin or molybdenum mine rather than the main product of its own, tungsten supply followed the fortunes of tin mining for most of the twentieth century, and the price spiked hard whenever the tin market wobbled. The supply map changed abruptly around 1980: China had been a minor producer whose entire output went to its own steel industry, and from 1980 its production rose sharply on an export surge, while South Korea's Sangdong was the other new large source. Korea and China were becoming the dominant suppliers just as the electronics industry started buying filament wire.
metal.tungsten.ore.mine.note: The pre-1980 supply geography and the general by-product character of tungsten mining are well established; the exact 1982 split between China, Korea, Zaire, Bolivia and Austria is not asserted here.
inputs: greasy and xanthate collectors for flotation

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 60-70% WO3, roughly a 100x upgrade

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: underground stoping and hand sorting, plus alluvial alluvial placers on the Malay Archipelago tin belt

facts.label: Supply shift
facts.value: China's output rose sharply from 1980 on an export surge, alongside South Korea

metal.barium.name: Barium titanate: the ceramic capacitor dielectric
metal.barium.description: The disk and multilayer ceramic capacitors on a 1982 C64 mainboard are barium titanate - BaTiO3 - and barium titanate is an industrial material made from barite, the same heavy white mineral that makes the drilling mud. The chain is barite to barium sulphide to barium carbonate to barium titanate, and then a 1000-1400 C calcination and a ceramic pressing. It is the most complete oxide-mineral chain in this file: a sulphate ore, a carbothermal reduction, a carbonate, a perovskite, and a dielectric constant of several thousand.

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~1000-5000 for X7R barium titanate; ~10,000 for the pure material near its Curie point

facts.label: Barite
facts.value: BaSO4, 90-98% in commercial grades; 53% Ba

facts.label: China's share
facts.value: China supplied the majority of world barite in 1982

facts.label: Also used for
facts.value: the glass frit of the ferrite coating, the ferrite body itself, and the barium ferrite magnet

metal.barium.titanate.name: Barium titanate powder (BaTiO3)
metal.barium.titanate.description: The solid-state reaction of barium carbonate with titanium dioxide: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2. It happens in a calcination at 1100-1350 C, in a rotary kiln or a batch furnace, and the outcome is a powder of perovskite-structured grains - a cubic cell with the titanium atom at the centre of an octahedron of six oxygens and the barium in the twelve-fold site between them. It has to be de-aerated and it must be calcined in an atmosphere that keeps the titanium from being reduced to the +3 state, because a reduced titanate is a semiconductor and a lossy dielectric. This is a real problem in the ceramic industry and the reason the calciner is sealed and the oxygen partial pressure controlled. The bulk material is then ball-milled to sub-micron before the powder is pressed or cast into a film.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: perovskite, ABO3, a cubic cell with Ti in an octahedron of O6 and Ba in the 12-fold site

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ball-milled to 0.1-1 um for the dielectric; coarse powder for the low-end grades

facts.label: Reducing atmosphere
facts.value: must be avoided: Ti4+ reduced to Ti3+ turns the material semiconducting and lossy

metal.barium-titanate-capacitor.name: The ceramic capacitor and its dielectric classes
metal.barium-titanate-capacitor.description: The finished use. A 1982 C64 mainboard carries perhaps 30-60 ceramic capacitors, mostly small discs and a few multilayer blocks. The disc is a pressed or cast barium titanate body, sintered at 1250-1350 C, silver-coated on both faces and fired to make the electrodes, and dipped in an epoxy or phenolic encapsulant. The multilayer capacitor stacks hundreds of microns-thick dielectric layers with internal nickel or palladium electrodes, screen-printed and co-fired - a technology that was genuinely new in 1982 and was the reason a 10 nF 50 V part started to fit in a 1.6 mm-tall package. The dielectric classes are named by their temperature coefficient: X7R and Z5U for the general-purpose 1980s parts, Y5V for the high-capacitance low-stability ones.
metal.barium-titanate-capacitor.note: The class nomenclature and the sintering temperatures are standard; the count of ceramic capacitors on a C64 mainboard is an estimate and belongs to the passives agent.

facts.label: Multilayer
facts.value: 1-10 um dielectric layers, Ni or Pd internal electrodes, co-fired at 1200-1350 C in a reducing atmosphere, then re-oxidised

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: silver for discs (fired at 700-900 C); base-metal nickel for multilayer

metal.dielectric-grading.name: Grade the barium titanate powder into a dielectric class
metal.dielectric-grading.description: The same powder cannot make a Y5V capacitor and an X7R one. Y5V is made from a fine, uniform, high-surface-area powder near the Curie point, where the dielectric constant is enormous and wildly temperature-dependent - a huge capacitance that changes by a factor of five over the working range. X7R is made from a coarser powder with barium zirconate or barium strontium titanate added, which flattens the temperature curve at the cost of the peak. So the capacitor 'class' is really a powder specification, and the class marking on the part is a statement about the ball mill that ground it.
metal.dielectric-grading.note: Medium confidence; the class-to-chemistry mapping is standard and the recipes are proprietary.

facts.label: Y5V
facts.value: fine powder near the Curie point, K of several thousand, very high temperature coefficient

facts.label: X7R
facts.value: coarser powder with solid solution, K of 1000-4000, +/-15% over -55 to +125 C

facts.label: Additives
facts.value: Ba(Zr,Ti)O3, Ba(Sr,Ti)O3, and rare-earth dopants for the high-capacitance grades

metal.dielectric-grading.mlc.name: Co-fire the internal electrodes in a low-oxygen atmosphere
metal.dielectric-grading.mlc.description: A multilayer capacitor's internal electrode is nickel or palladium, printed as a paste and co-fired with the ceramic. That will not work in air - the ceramic would reduce and become a lossy semiconductor - so the whole stack is fired in a low-oxygen atmosphere at 1200-1350 C in hydrogen or in a nitrogen-hydrogen mix, and then re-oxidised afterwards so the barium titanate goes back to being an insulator. The oxygen partial pressure is controlled to a few millibars. It is the most metallurgically demanding step in the whole electronics supply chain that nobody ever sees, and it is a barium carbonate problem.
metal.dielectric-grading.mlc.note: Medium confidence; the co-firing atmosphere is standard practice but the exact pO2 is proprietary.

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: nickel or palladium paste, screen-printed

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: low pO2, a few millibars, in H2 or N2/H2

facts.label: Reoxidation
facts.value: a separate anneal afterwards to restore the insulator

metal.titanium-dioxide.name: Titanium dioxide from rutile sand
metal.titanium-dioxide.description: The titanium dioxide half of the equation, and it comes from a beach sand. Ilmenite, a titanium-iron oxide, is dredged from the heavy-mineral beach sands of the Cap York coast in Queensland, of Kerala in India, of the Mozambique coast and of the Richards Bay area of South Africa; it is separated from the zircon and the rutile by gravity and electrostatic separation; and it is then either chlorinated with coke and chlorine at 900-1000 C to give TiCl4, which is oxidised in a flame to give the pigment TiO2, or sulfided and digested to give synthetic rutile and then the pigment. Rutile, the TiO2 mineral itself, is also separated directly from the sand and is the higher-grade feed for ceramic-grade titanium dioxide. The pigment industry is by far the biggest user of titanium dioxide in 1982, and barium titanate is a small, very high-value user of the same commodity.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: ilmenite at 42-60% TiO2, and rutile at 90-95% TiO2, both from beach placer sands

facts.label: Chloride process
facts.value: ilmenite + coke + Cl2 at 900-1000 C -> TiCl4, then flame oxidation at 1200-1400 C -> TiO2 + Cl2

facts.label: Sulfate process
facts.value: ilmenite + concentrated H2SO4 -> titanyl sulphate, then hydrolysis and calcination

facts.label: Ceramic grade
facts.value: needs high purity and low iron; much of the pigment grade is too impure for a dielectric

metal.ilmenite-sand.name: Heavy mineral beach sand and the dredge
metal.ilmenite-sand.description: The leaf: a beach or dune sand a few metres thick carrying 1-10% heavy minerals - ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite, tourmaline - in a strip along the shoreline. A concentrator dredges a cutter suction pump from the shallow water, washes and upgrades on a shaking table and a spiral, then on gravity and electrostatic separators, recovering 200,000-300,000 t of ilmenite a year from a single operation. So the barium in a 1982 disk capacitor, having gone through a rotary kiln and a hydrogen sulphide stream, ends up in a titanium atom that came out of a Queensland beach.

facts.label: Sand grade
facts.value: 1-10% heavy minerals in a quartz sand

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: cutter-suction dredging of a beach or an offshore bar, with a gravity and electrostatic concentrator onshore

facts.label: Products
facts.value: ilmenite, zircon, rutile, monazite (and in Kerala, the monazite for thorium and rare earths)

metal.barite.reduction.name: Barite to barium sulphide, then barium carbonate
metal.barite.reduction.description: The chemical reduction of barite. Barite plus coke at 900-1100 C in a rotary kiln gives barium sulphide: BaSO4 + 4C -> BaS + 4CO. That reaction needs about 1100 C to proceed at a useful rate, and the kiln is a long steel tube, 2-3 m diameter and 30-50 m long, rotating at 0.5-1 rpm, heated by a gas or oil burner at one end. The barium sulphide is leached out of the cooled cake with water, giving a solution of BaS, and that solution is carbonated with carbon dioxide - from a coke oven, from the sinter plant, from anywhere - and barium carbonate precipitates: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S. So the barium carbonate is made from a sulphate ore, a coke-oven gas and a stream of hydrogen sulphide, and the H2S is either burned to sulphur or sent to a Claus plant.

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: BaSO4 + 4C -> BaS + 4CO at 900-1100 C

facts.label: Kiln
facts.value: rotary, 2-3 m diameter, 30-50 m long, 0.5-1 rpm

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: the cake is leached with water, hot, and the BaS solution is clarified

facts.label: Carbonation
facts.value: BaS + CO2 + H2O -> BaCO3 + H2S, at room temperature

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~90% on the reduction, 95%+ on the carbonation

facts.label: Barium carbonate purity
facts.value: 99.0-99.5% for ceramic grade; iron is the impurity to watch

metal.hydrogen-sulfide.name: Hydrogen sulphide from the carbonation
metal.hydrogen-sulfide.description: The barium carbonate process makes hydrogen sulphide as a by-product, roughly 0.2 t of H2S per tonne of barium carbonate, and H2S is an acutely toxic gas that a 1982 barium plant either burned in a flare or sent to a Claus plant for elemental sulphur. It is also, if you are unlucky, a gas that kills by olfactory paralysis: at high concentration you cannot smell it, which is why a barium works had an H2S alarm on the roof and why the workers carried a supplied-air respirator. It is the least well-known hazard in this tree and a real one.
metal.hydrogen-sulfide.note: Medium confidence on the H2S yield; the hazard mechanism is textbook.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: roughly 0.15-0.3 t of H2S per tonne of BaCO3

facts.label: Control
facts.value: flared or sent to a Claus plant, with continuous monitoring

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: H2S paralyzes the sense of smell at high concentration

metal.barium-carbonate.name: Ceramic-grade barium carbonate
metal.barium-carbonate.description: A fine white powder, 99%+ BaCO3, and the actual commodity that the barium titanate maker buys. Its iron and sulphur contents are the specification that matters, and both come back from the reduction step. It is also used directly - in the glass frit of the ferrite coat, in the barium ferrite magnet, in the dielectric of the lower-value ceramic capacitor grades, and in the ferrite itself.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.0-99.5% BaCO3 for ceramic grade

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: BaTiO3, glass frit, ferrite, barium ferrite magnets

metal.barium-carbonate.calcination.name: Calcine the carbonate to a reactive powder
metal.barium-carbonate.calcination.description: The barium carbonate that comes out of the carbonation tank is 99.0-99.5% pure but coarse and dense, and barium titanate needs a reactive powder. So the carbonate is calcined at 1000-1200 C to break it down to the oxide and then re-carbonated lightly, or it is ground extremely fine. Either way it is a chemical-material step rather than a smelting one, and it is where a lot of the ceramic-grade versus technical-grade distinction is made.
metal.barium-carbonate.calcination.note: Medium confidence; the calcination step is standard but the specific practice varies.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: to raise the reactivity of the carbonate for the solid-state reaction with TiO2

metal.barium-carbonate.contamination.name: Iron and sulphur in the ceramic grade
metal.barium-carbonate.contamination.description: The ceramic-grade barium carbonate specification is essentially a statement about two impurities. Iron, carried through from the barite and from the flue of the reduction kiln, if it survives into barium titanate, acts as an acceptor and shifts the Curie point and the dielectric constant and hurts the loss - so iron has to be below a few hundred ppm. Sulphur, carried from the reduction and not removed by the carbonation, sits at the grain boundary of the fired ceramic and hurts the breakdown voltage. Both of them are the same answer as in the ferrite branch: wash, precipitate, and calcine in a controlled atmosphere. It is a recurring theme in ceramics that the last hundred ppm is the whole specification.
metal.barium-carbonate.contamination.note: Medium confidence; the impurity mechanisms in barium titanate ceramics are standard in the ceramics literature.

facts.label: Iron
facts.value: below a few hundred ppm; an acceptor dopant that degrades the dielectric

facts.label: Sulphur
facts.value: must be removed by the carbonation and the calcine; it degrades the breakdown voltage

metal.barite.name: Barite (BaSO4) ore, 90-98%
metal.barite.description: Barite is a very heavy, very white, chemically inert mineral - specific gravity 4.5 - which occurs as veins, as replacement bodies in limestone, and as a residual clay. It has two completely separate markets. The drilling-mud market is by far the biggest and takes barite that has simply been crushed and graded to 200 mesh, because all it needs is density and a low quartz content. The chemical-grade market, which is where the barium titanate comes from, needs the barite to be low in iron and low in silica, because those impurities end up in the ceramic. In 1982 the chemical-grade barite was a small, carefully selected part of the output, and China and Morocco were the dominant suppliers.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 90-98% BaSO4 for drilling grade; chemical grade requires Fe2O3 <0.5% and SiO2 <1-2%

facts.label: Ba content
facts.value: 58.8% by mass

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: underground or surface; sometimes a byproduct of lead-zinc and of fluorspar

metal.barite.drilling-mud.name: Drilling grade barite and its mud
metal.barite.drilling-mud.description: The larger half of the barite market, and the reason a chemical-grade barite supplier has to be selective. Drilling mud needs a barite that is dense, grindable to a very fine size, low in soluble salts and above all low in cadmium and other toxic heavy metals, because the drill cuttings go into a mud pit and the barite is not recovered. In 1982 the drilling grade specification was a gravity of at least 4.2 and a particle distribution such that 90% passed 45 um. A 1982 rig's mud for a deep well used 100-300 tonnes of barite per kilometre.
metal.barite.drilling-mud.note: Medium confidence; the mud consumption figure is representative rather than a specific well.

facts.label: Specification
facts.value: specific gravity above 4.2, 90% below 45 um, low soluble salts

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 100-300 t of barite per km of hole in a deep well

metal.barite.mine.name: Barite vein and replacement mine
metal.barite.mine.description: Barite is mined as a primary vein mineral - a gangue mineral of many lead-zinc hydrothermal deposits - or as a replacement of limestone. The processing is simple: crush, wash off the clay, and either float or just size and sell. A barite plant of the 1980s was a jaw crusher, a log washer and a deslimer, and the quality specification was almost entirely about the Fe2O3. The chemical-grade plants did a rougher job: a flotation and an acid leach to take the iron down.
metal.barite.mine.note: Medium confidence on the chemical-grade processing route; it varies a lot by deposit.

facts.label: Processing
facts.value: crush to 25 mm, log wash, deslime, size to 200 mesh for drilling grade

facts.label: Chemical grade
facts.value: flotation plus an acid leach to bring Fe2O3 below 0.5%

metal.barite.mud-system.name: Barite, bentonite and lime: the drilling mud system
metal.barite.mud-system.description: A drilling mud is not one material; it is a designed composite. The barite is the weight - it is the only cheap, abundant mineral dense enough to hold back formation pressure at a density of 1.5-2.0. The bentonite is the viscosity and the filtration control, and it works because its sodium montmorillonite swells in water to several times its dry volume. The lime and the lime-soil inhibitors control the calcium contamination that comes up with the cement and that would flocculate the bentonite. So the barite branch of this tree converges with the bentonite branch of the steel branch, and both converge on the drilling of the oil and gas wells that produce the crude oil the plastics agent starts from.
metal.barite.mud-system.note: Medium confidence; the mud chemistry is standard drilling engineering.

facts.label: Weight
facts.value: barite takes the mud to 1.5-2.0 specific gravity

facts.label: Viscosity
facts.value: bentonite, swollen to several times its dry volume

facts.label: Calcium control
facts.value: lime and inhibitors, because calcium flocculates the clay

metal.lime.name: Lime (CaO) and calcium
metal.lime.description: Lime is one of the most-used industrial chemicals there is, and this tree touches it in four places: the Bayer plant uses it to desilicate and to causticise, the blast furnace uses limestone directly as flux, the PCB fabricator regenerates ferric chloride etchant and neutralises with it, and the metallurgical silicon and tin circuits use lime as a flux and a scavenger. Lime is roasted limestone; limestone is quarried rock.
metal.lime.note: Documented: calcination of calcium carbonate in a lime kiln above 900 C gives quicklime, and adding water gives slaked lime. Not established: the 1000-1100 C kiln temperature, the roughly 44% loss on ignition and 56% CaO yield, the 65% mass gain on slaking, and the coke/coal-fines/anthracite fuel list.

facts.label: Kiln temperature
facts.value: 1000-1100 C in a vertical or horizontal lime kiln

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2

facts.label: Loss on ignition
facts.value: ~44% by weight; a 100 t kiln yields roughly 56 t of CaO

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: coke, coal fines or anthracite depending on local availability

facts.label: Slaking
facts.value: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 is exothermic and adds about 65% to the mass

metal.lime.scavenger.name: Lime as a slag flux in tin, lead and silicon smelting
metal.lime.scavenger.description: Beyond alumina and iron, lime shows up as a cheap flux wherever a siliceous slag has to stay liquid and the impurity has to be dumped: tin smelting adds lime to pull silica and some tungsten into the slag, the lead sinter and blast furnace charge roughly 15-25% limestone, and calcium compounds are added to the silicon furnace feed to mop up alumina. It is the general-purpose garbage collector of the metals industry.
metal.lime.scavenger.note: Snelter lime practice is very smelter-specific; medium confidence.

facts.label: Lead sinter
facts.value: order 15-25% limestone in the sinter mix

metal.lime.pcb-etch.name: Regenerate ferric chloride etchant with lime
metal.lime.pcb-etch.description: At the board fab the copper etchant is ferric chloride: CuCl2 + FeCl3 -> CuCl + FeCl2, and the ferric is regenerated by blowing air through the spent bath, which is where a great deal of the chlorine chemistry of PCB etching comes from. Lime then raises the pH and drops the copper out as copper hydroxide so the iron can be reclaimed, and lime also neutralises the acid process streams downstream of the etcher. The board's own etch chemistry belongs to the board subsystem; what matters here is that the reagent traces back to a limestone quarry.

facts.label: Regeneration
facts.value: FeCl2 + air/Cl2 -> FeCl3; then CuCl2 + Ca(OH)2 -> Cu(OH)2 + CaCl2

metal.lime.blast-flux.name: Flux the blast furnace slag with limestone and lime
metal.lime.blast-flux.description: The furnace needs its slag liquid at 1450 C, and calcium is how you get there: CaO absorbs silica into a calcium silicate slag whose liquidus is around 1300-1400 C, so the slag runs off the tuyeres before the iron does. The burden carries roughly 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal, deliberately paired with a silica content of about 0.4-0.6 mass units of SiO2 per unit of CaO.
metal.lime.blast-flux.note: Typical burden practice; specific works ran tighter ratios.

facts.label: Burden rate
facts.value: order 0.25-0.35 t limestone per t hot metal

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: slag basicity CaO/SiO2 of roughly 1.0-1.3

metal.lime.bayer-uses.name: Causticise and desilicate the Bayer liquor
metal.lime.bayer-uses.description: Two unrelated jobs in one plant. Lime added during digestion converts reactive silica (kaolinite) into an insoluble calcium silicate, which would otherwise lock up alumina permanently - the single most important reason a high-silica bauxite is unprocessable. Lime also drives the causticisation step, converting the sodium carbonate that accumulates in the Bayer liquor back into caustic, and it helps precipitate iron and titanium as hydroxides. Dosage was order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite digested.
metal.lime.bayer-uses.note: Dosage range varies with ore; medium confidence.

facts.label: Dosage
facts.value: order 5-20 kg CaO per tonne of bauxite

facts.label: Desilication reaction
facts.value: kaolinite + lime -> calcium silicate hydrate, permanently wasted

facts.label: Causticisation
facts.value: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3

metal.lime.pre-desilication.name: Pre-desilicate the ore by attrition washing
metal.lime.pre-desilication.description: By 1982 the more elegant answer to high-silica bauxite had arrived and it needs no lime at all: wash the ore. An attrition scrub and a desliming step take out the kaolinite clay before the ore ever meets the caustic, and a gibbsitic ore washed this way can digest without lime at all. The cost of the process is a lot of water and a lot of clay tailings - and the tailings are the same red mud, just produced earlier and with less soda in it. So the industry moved from a chemistry problem to a solids-handling problem, which is a recurring theme in aluminium refining.
metal.lime.pre-desilication.note: Medium confidence; the adoption rate was highly ore-dependent.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: attrition scrub followed by desliming at about 40-60 um

facts.label: Removes
facts.value: typically 1-4% of the mass as clay, which was 10-40% of the reactive silica

facts.label: Trade
facts.value: less lime and less caustic consumed, more water and more tailings

metal.lime.causticisation.name: Causticise the carbonate back to caustic soda
metal.lime.causticisation.description: The Bayer liquor's sodium carbonate is converted back to caustic with lime: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3, and the calcium carbonate drops out as a filter cake that is a by-product of every tonne of alumina. The cycle is the industry's real control loop, because the caustic that leaves in the red mud is replaced by buying new caustic or by buying lime and causticising it, and the choice is mostly about what lime is available near the refinery. It is also why a bauxite refinery is nearly always built next to a limestone quarry.
metal.lime.causticisation.note: Medium confidence; the reversibility of the causticisation is the textbook caveat.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> 2NaOH + CaCO3

facts.label: Reactor
facts.value: a stirred causticiser with a settler and a filter

facts.label: Caveat
facts.value: this reaction is reversible; it only goes far enough because the carbonate is continuously removed and the liquor stays dilute

metal.lime.slaking.name: Slaking: quicklime to hydrated lime
metal.lime.slaking.description: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, releasing about 65% more mass and enough heat to boil water. Slaking is done in a pan with a rotating rake, or in a ball mill in the paper industry, and the product is a fine white powder or a milk. It is done at the steelworks, at the water treatment plant and at the board fab's causticisation circuit. The safety point that every plant's training programme is about is that a lump of quicklime dropped into a drum of water will split the drum.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, +64% by mass, strongly exothermic

facts.label: Solubility
facts.value: about 1.7 g/L at 20 C - enough to be caustic, not enough to be a base

metal.lime.cement.name: Lime in Portland cement
metal.lime.cement.description: By far the largest single use of lime in the world, and the reason the business had a global price: about 90% of all lime produced goes into cement, and cement is the second-largest industrial material after steel. The route is the one already in this branch - limestone, kiln, CaO - and then the clinker: 75-80% limestone with 20-25% clay or shale in a rotary kiln at 1450 C, and the resulting clinker ground with 3-5% gypsum. A C64's case was painted, not cemented, but the cement industry is the reason lime is cheap, and it is a legitimate side door out of this branch.

facts.label: Lime share of lime demand
facts.value: ~90% goes into cement

facts.label: Clinker
facts.value: 75-80% limestone, 20-25% clay, fired at 1450 C in a rotary kiln

facts.label: Gypsum
facts.value: 3-5% added at the cement mill to control the set

metal.lime.kiln.name: Shaft and rotary lime kilns
metal.lime.kiln.description: Limestone plus coke or coal in a vertical shaft 20-40 m tall, or on a rotary kiln, at 1000-1100 C. The vertical kiln - a stack of alternating layers of 250 kg limestone and 40 kg coke in a 2.5-4 m shaft, fired from the bottom - makes the good lime, because the counter-current gas gives a soft, well-calcined product; the rotary kiln makes it faster and is what a captive lime plant at a steelworks or a Bayer refinery used. A 300 t/day shaft kiln is a small plant by industrial standards and there were thousands of them.

facts.label: Shaft kiln
facts.value: 20-40 m tall, 2.5-4 m diameter, 250 kg limestone per 40 kg coke

facts.label: Rotary kiln
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long, inclined, 100-1000 t/day

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: ~110-130 kg coke or coal per tonne of CaO, or ~80 kg in a rotary kiln with a preheater

metal.lime.kiln-gas.name: The lime kiln gas and its CO2
metal.lime.kiln-gas.description: A lime kiln makes carbon dioxide as its main product, roughly 0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, and in 1982 that gas was usually burnt or dumped because there was nowhere to put it. Its two real uses were the Solvay tower, which is built beside its lime kilns, and - much later - the emerging practice of feeding kiln gas to a nearby chemical plant. So the limestone quarry behind a C64's case carries a hidden carbon footprint that did not become an engineering problem until the 1990s.
metal.lime.kiln-gas.note: Medium confidence; the stoichiometric yield is certain, the 1982 disposition is a generalisation.

facts.label: CO2 yield
facts.value: ~0.44 t of CO2 per tonne of CaO, plus the fuel

facts.label: 1982 fate
facts.value: burnt for heat, or vented; the sequestration era had not arrived

metal.lime.rotary-kiln.name: The rotary kiln and the preheater
metal.lime.rotary-kiln.description: A 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long rotary kiln, inclined a few degrees, turning 1-3 rpm, heated by a burner at the lower discharge end with coal, coke or gas, and fitted at the upper end with a preheater or a flash dryer for the limestone. The rotary kiln makes worse lime than the shaft kiln - the residence time varies through the bed and the lime is over- and under-burnt - but it makes it faster and it copes with a variable feed, so a captive plant at a steelworks or an alumina refinery used one. A 2000 t/day rotary lime kiln is the sort of thing that sits next to a coke-oven battery.
metal.lime.rotary-kiln.note: Medium confidence; the fuel figure assumes a preheater, which is where most of the saving is.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 m diameter, 40-60 m long, 100-1000 t/day

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: pulverised coal, coke, anthracite or gas, at about 80 kg per tonne of CaO with a preheater

metal.lime.kiln-clinker.name: Overburnt lime and the clinker problem
metal.lime.kiln-clinker.description: If a lime kiln burns a stone too hot for too long, the lime grains sinter together into hard 'clinker' and the lime is unusable: it slakes too slowly and lumps in the mixer. Overburnt lime is a real fraction of the output of a poor kiln and it has to be screened out or ground. The same failure happens in a captive lime kiln feeding a blast furnace, where the operator is watching the furnace's slag chemistry and the lime plant's temperature curve at the same time. It is a small thing and it is a good illustration that lime is a feed, not a commodity.
metal.lime.kiln-clinker.note: Medium confidence; the mechanism is standard.

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: overburning: local temperature above about 1200 C for too long

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: the grains sinter; the lime slakes slowly and lumps in the mixer

metal.lime.shaft-kiln.name: The counter-current shaft kiln
metal.lime.shaft-kiln.description: Because limestone goes in at the top at ambient temperature and lime comes out at the bottom at 1000 C, the shaft has to be a heat exchanger as well as a kiln, and that is why a shaft kiln makes a better lime than a rotary one. The gases go up, the stone goes down, and the last of the fuel burns out in the upper third. Below the burn zone the calcination is isothermal, so the lime is not over-heated and does not shrink the kiln's yield.
metal.lime.shaft-kiln.note: Zone layout is standard practice; medium confidence on the yield range.

facts.label: Zones
facts.value: drying, preheating, calcination, burning, cooling

facts.label: Burn zone
facts.value: the upper third of the shaft

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 80-90% of theoretical lime

metal.bentonite.name: Bentonite binder from a clay pit
metal.bentonite.description: A sodium bentonite with a high swelling capacity, mined from a montmorillonite clay bed and used as the binder that makes a pellet roll up instead of shatter. In 1982 the world bentonite market was dominated by Wyoming and by Italy and the Balkan sources, and it was also the drilling mud of the oil industry, so the two applications competed for the same tonnage. The particular clay a pelletiser wants is a sodium montmorillonite, which is a specific alteration product of volcanic ash - the leaf of this little branch is a bentonite bed in a Tertiary volcanic sequence.
metal.bentonite.note: Pellet binder levels are standard; the specific source geology is medium confidence.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: sodium montmorillonite, high swelling capacity

facts.label: Dose
facts.value: 2-3% of the pellet mass

metal.barite.rock.name: Barite vein in limestone or as a hydrothermal gangue
metal.barite.rock.description: The leaf: white bladed or massive barite filling a fracture, or replacing a fossiliferous limestone bed. The barite has essentially no use as a rock - it is only ever interesting where it happens to be 90% or better and low in iron.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: hydrothermal vein or replacement body in carbonate rock

metal.ferrite.name: Ferrite: transformer and choke cores
metal.ferrite.description: The C64's power supply transformer, the filter chokes, the RF modulator coil and the ferrite beads on the board are all ceramic magnetic materials, not metal. A power ferrite is a spinel - either MnO.Fe2O3.ZnO or NiO.Fe2O3.ZnO - pressed as a powder and fired to 1200-1300 C, which is powder metallurgy in the truest sense: the magnetisation is not in the metal particles, it is in the magnetic domain walls of a ceramic. This is the branch where the metals tree stops being about metal and starts being about oxide chemistry, and the raw materials are iron oxide, manganese carbonate, zinc oxide and nickel oxide.

facts.label: MnZn power ferrite
facts.value: ~50% Fe2O3, 20-30% MnO, 10-20% ZnO; sintered at 1200-1300 C in air

facts.label: NiZn ferrite
facts.value: ~50-55% Fe2O3, 10-30% NiO, balance ZnO; useful to about 100 MHz

facts.label: Two families
facts.value: MnZn for 10 kHz to 1 MHz and high flux; NiZn for 1 to 200 MHz and low loss at high frequency

metal.ferrite.radio.name: Radio-frequency and rod ferrite
metal.ferrite.radio.description: A third shape family: ferrite rod and toroid for antenna and RF applications, pressed with an anisotropic die so the ferrite is oriented in the pressing direction. An isotropic pressed ferrite has half the usable permeability along the pressing axis as across it, because the pores are flattened; a ferrite maker who wants an antenna rod presses it in a die that aligns the grains. This is the ferrite in a portable radio's antenna, and it is the same powder as the transformer core, pressed in a different die.
metal.ferrite.radio.note: Low confidence on the anisotropy ratio; the effect is real and well known but the number varies with the pressing pressure.

facts.label: Anisotropy
facts.value: pressed ferrite has about half the through-thickness permeability of the in-plane value

facts.label: Use
facts.value: antenna rods, ferrite beads on cable, EMI cores

metal.ferrite.radio.aniso-die.name: The anisotropic pressing die
metal.ferrite.radio.aniso-die.description: A ferrite pressed in an ordinary die has its pores flattened in the pressing direction, and flattened pores cut the permeability in that direction roughly in half - so a plain-pressed ferrite rod is a poor antenna core along its length. To avoid that, a rod core is pressed in a die with a fine central punch, so the powder is displaced radially and the pores and the grains align across the rod instead of along it. The same die idea is behind the toroid's oriented product and behind ferrite for read heads. It is a small piece of die engineering with a large effect, and it is why ferrite die makers were a specialist trade in the 1980s.
metal.ferrite.radio.aniso-die.note: Low confidence on the specific die geometry; the anisotropy effect is well established but the tool design is proprietary.

facts.label: Die
facts.value: a fine central punch displacing the powder radially rather than axially

metal.ferrite.hard.name: Hard ferrites and permanent magnet materials
metal.ferrite.hard.description: The same pressed-and-fired powder metallurgy as the power ferrite, but with no permeability requirement and a coercive force instead. Barium and strontium hexaferrite, BaFe12O19 and SrFe12O19, are sintered into magnet blocks for small motors and, in this tree, for the permanent magnets inside a magnetic ore separator. None of it is in the C64; it is here because the ore concentrator that feeds the blast furnace is full of ferrite magnets, and because the separator is the one place the barium branch and the ferrite branch meet.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: SrFe12O19 or BaFe12O19, sintered; remanence about 0.3-0.4 T

facts.label: C64 use
facts.value: none; the magnets are in the concentrator and in small motors

metal.ferrite.strontium-ferrite.name: Strontium ferrite magnet
metal.ferrite.strontium-ferrite.description: SrFe12O19 pressed and fired like a power ferrite, then cooled through the Curie point in a magnetic field so the hexferrite grains line up. It is brittle, it is an oxide, and its key property is that it does not need any rare earth at all - which is exactly why barium and strontium ferrite are the standard cheap magnet, and why the two-share-the-mill argument makes this branch's economics obvious.
metal.ferrite.strontium-ferrite.note: Medium confidence on the remanence figures; these are typical class values.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: SrFe12O19 (strontium hexferrite)

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: above the Curie point, then field-cooled

facts.label: Remanence
facts.value: ~0.35-0.45 T; roughly a third of a Nd-Fe-B magnet

metal.strontium-carbonate.name: Strontium carbonate
metal.strontium-carbonate.description: The only geologically interesting part: strontium is the rarest of the three alkaline-earth metals used in ferrites and ceramics, because it has no ore of its own that anyone uses. Strontium sulfate (celestine) is mined in Spain, Mexico and Iran, and almost all of it is converted to strontium carbonate. A C64 contains no strontium, so this is a dead end, but it is a real example of a mineral that exists only to make a ceramic.
metal.strontium-carbonate.note: Strontium supply is a genuine constraint on hard-ferrite production; medium confidence on the source countries' relative shares in 1982.

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: celestine, SrSO4

facts.label: Main sources
facts.value: Spain, Mexico, Iran, China

metal.ferrite.manufacture.name: Ferrite powder metallurgy from blend to fired core
metal.ferrite.manufacture.description: Five steps, all of them inherited from the ceramic industry, none of them changed since the 1950s. Blend: the oxides are mixed wet in a ball mill or a vibrating mill to a few tenths of a percent. Calcine or pre-sinter: the blend is heated in air to about 900-1100 C, which drives off the moisture and the carbonate carbon dioxide and starts forming the spinel; the material comes out as a hard, sintered cake. Granulate: the cake is crushed and screened, and about 1-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or polyethylene binder is added with a little water so the powder will press. Press: a dry press - a 100-250 tonne hydraulic press - forms the shape at 100-200 MPa, with the tool steel die giving the final dimensions. Fire: the pressed part is sintered in air at 1200-1350 C, and the part shrinks about 1% linearly, which is why the die is made oversize and why every ferrite part in the world is ground afterwards. Finish: the fired part is ground on a double-disc or planetary grinder to final dimension, because the press cannot hold the tolerance.
metal.ferrite.manufacture.note: The firing schedule - the temperature, the ramp, and the oxygen partial pressure - is where the entire performance of a ferrite lives, and it is the most closely guarded secret in the industry. The 1980s practice was a sinter belt furnace with a controlled atmosphere over several hours; the tight-oxygen and fast-fire schedules came later.

facts.label: Calcination
facts.value: ~940 C in air for a typical MnZn blend

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1200-1300 C in air for MnZn; 1150-1250 C for NiZn

facts.label: Pressing
facts.value: 100-200 MPa in a 100-250 t dry press; shrinkage ~1% linear

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 0.5-2% PVA or PVA-polyethylene glycol

facts.label: Green density
facts.value: ~2.0-2.2 g/cm3 for MnZn, against ~5.0 fired

metal.ferrite.quality.name: Control the firing atmosphere and the schedule
metal.ferrite.quality.description: The most closely guarded part of the whole ferrite industry is the firing curve: the ramp rate, the hold times, and the oxygen partial pressure through a 12-30 hour cycle. Too fast through the Curie point and the grain boundaries form in the wrong order and the core is lossy; too oxidising and Mn2+ becomes Mn3+ and the losses double; too reducing and the Fe becomes FeO and the permeability collapses. The kiln in 1982 was a tunnel kiln or a continuous belt with a controlled-atmosphere section and a dewpoint-controlled atmosphere, and the recipe was the plant's only real asset.
metal.ferrite.quality.note: The mechanism is well established; the specific schedules are proprietary and are not reproduced here.

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 12-30 h through a tunnel or continuous belt kiln

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: dewpoint-controlled; the oxygen partial pressure through the Curie point is the critical variable

facts.label: Oxidation states
facts.value: Mn2+/Mn3+ and Fe2+/Fe3+ ratio set the loss

metal.ferrite.grinding.name: Grinding the fired part to size
metal.ferrite.grinding.description: Because the fired part cannot be held to a useful dimension by pressing, it is lapped and ground. An E core is face-ground and the bore is ground; a toroid is OD and ID ground. In 1982 this was a double-disc or a planetary grinder with a diamond wheel, and it was expensive enough that a great many ferrite parts were still sold with a loose dimension tolerance and machined by the customer. The final steps are the coating: a thin epoxy or phenolic coat, or a dry lacquer coat and bake, which holds the core together, insulates it from the winding, and gives it a corrosion-resistant surface.
metal.ferrite.grinding.note: Medium confidence on the cost trade-off; it depends entirely on the part size and the volume.

facts.label: Grinding
facts.value: double-disc or planetary, diamond wheel, to about +/-0.1 mm

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: epoxy or phenolic coat and bake at 150-200 C, or a dry coat

facts.label: 1982 economics
facts.value: for small E cores it was often cheaper to sell an oversize core and let the transformer builder grind it

metal.ferrite.sintering.name: Firing at 1200-1300 C and the shrinkage
metal.ferrite.sintering.description: The pressed part is fired on a belt or in a tunnel kiln in air, and in the last stage of the sintering it goes through the Curie temperature - about 200-250 C for MnZn - which is a magnetic transition, and above it the permeability of the material is irrelevant because it is paramagnetic. That is why a fire that goes too fast or spends too little time above the Curie point produces a core with poor low-frequency properties even though its density looks fine. During firing the part shrinks about 1% linearly, so a 20 mm E core comes out of a 20.2 mm die, and the finished dimension has to be set by grinding.

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1200-1300 C in air for MnZn

facts.label: Shrinkage
facts.value: ~1% linear, 3% by volume

facts.label: Curie temperature
facts.value: 200-250 C for MnZn

facts.label: Hold
facts.value: 30 min to several hours above 1000 C, atmosphere and ramp critical

metal.ferrite.pressing.name: Dry pressing in a tool steel die
metal.ferrite.pressing.description: The pressed shape is the finished shape - an E, an EE, a toroid, a drum core - and the tool is a hardened steel die in a 100-250 tonne press. Ferrite presses in 1982 were 100-250 t, usually with a single or double action upper punch, and the cycle time for a small E core was 0.3-2 s. The part is pressed dry, which is why the powder has to be granulated first: free powder flows, granulated powder fills a die uniformly. The tooling is the same tool steel as an extrusion die, so the SKD61/H13 branch serves the ferrite industry too.
metal.ferrite.pressing.note: Medium confidence on die life; abrasive wear of the powder is highly formulation-dependent.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: 100-250 t, cycle 0.3-2 s per part

facts.label: Green density tolerance
facts.value: +/-2%, which is what sets the finished permeability tolerance

facts.label: Die life
facts.value: order 100,000-1,000,000 shots depending on the abrasive behaviour of the powder

metal.ferrite.calcination.name: Calcination and the spinel formation
metal.ferrite.calcination.description: The chemical heart of the branch. Below the calcination temperature the blend is a mechanical mixture; by 900-1100 C the oxides have reacted and the cubic spinel lattice - which has three cation sites and eight for every 32 oxygen atoms - has formed, with the zinc on the tetrahedral sites, the manganese on the octahedral sites and the iron distributed across both. That distribution is why MnZn has a high permeability: Mn2+ and Fe2+ on opposing sublattices give an antiparallel but nearly equal spin arrangement, so the magnetisation can be tipped by a small field. It is an oxide chemistry result, and it is why a C64's transformer is ceramic and not iron.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 900-1100 C in air

facts.label: Product
facts.value: partly formed MnZn or NiZn spinel, still porous and crushable

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: cubic spinel, AB2O4; 8 formula units per unit cell

metal.ferrite.mixing.name: Wet mixing and the ceramic ball mill
metal.ferrite.mixing.description: The oxide blend is mixed wet in a rubber-lined ball mill or a vibrating mill, because water is the only way to get all three oxides into intimate contact within half a percent. A 1982 MnZn blend ran in a 1-3 m vibratory mill at 25-50 Hz, or in a ball mill with a few hundred kilos of zirconia or rubber-lined steel balls. The wet slip is then dried on a spray dryer or a rotary dryer to a granulated powder with the right moisture and the right particle size. The whole discipline of the ceramic industry is really about this step, and the blending tolerances of the finished core are set here.
metal.ferrite.mixing.note: Medium confidence; the process is standard ceramic practice.

facts.label: Mill
facts.value: 1-3 m vibratory mill at 25-50 Hz, or a rubber-lined ball mill

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: better than +/-0.2 wt% on each oxide

facts.label: Drying
facts.value: spray dryer for a granulated free-flowing powder

metal.ferrite.granulation.name: Granulation and the binder
metal.ferrite.granulation.description: Free powder flows; a pressed ferrite part needs the powder to fill the die uniformly, so the powder is granulated with 0.5-2% of a polyvinyl alcohol or a PVA-polyethylene glycol binder and 8-12% water, on a spray granulator or a pan granulator, into 100-400 um granules. The granule has to survive being filled at a few grams per stroke and being pressed at 200 MPa, which is a tough mechanical requirement for a granule of ceramic powder.
metal.ferrite.granulation.note: Medium confidence; granulation practice is proprietary and varies between manufacturers.

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 0.5-2% PVA or PVA-PEG

facts.label: Water
facts.value: 8-12% of the green granule

metal.ferrite.raw-materials.name: Ferrite raw materials: the oxide blend
metal.ferrite.raw-materials.description: The three powders that get blended, and each one has its own industrial route. The iron oxide is either mill scale from the aluminium or the steel mill - washed, dried and milled, and the cheapest source - or a precipitated oxide made by acid leaching hematite. The manganese is manganese carbonate, a chemical precipitate from a manganese sulphate solution. The zinc is zinc oxide, made by roasting zinc ore or by burning zinc metal. The blend has to be accurate to about 0.2% in each component, because the magnetic properties are extremely sensitive to it, and by the 1980s the oxide suppliers were selling pre-blended 'master mixes' to the smaller ferrite makers precisely because the blending was the hard part.

facts.label: Fe2O3
facts.value: mill scale (5-30% Fe2O3, the rest magnetite/FeO, needs magnetic separation) or a precipitated high-purity oxide

facts.label: MnCO3
facts.value: precipitated from manganese sulphate solution; 1-2% Fe is the usual impurity

facts.label: ZnO
facts.value: from the zinc smelter, 99.0-99.7% ZnO

facts.label: Blend tolerance
facts.value: better than +/-0.2 wt% on each oxide for a good power ferrite

metal.ferrite.mix-house.name: The mix house and the recipe book
metal.ferrite.mix-house.description: The place where a ferrite formula is actually executed. A blend of perhaps 300 kg of oxide is weighed into a mixer - a ribbon blender or a ball mill - to 0.1 kg, sampled, analysed, and then the result is used to correct the next batch. The correction logic is where the manufacturer differs: some makers blend to the analysis and some blend to the recipe, and the argument between them is an old one. The mix house also holds the master recipes, and the confidentiality around them is a matter of pride rather than of deep mystery. A 1980s small ferrite factory had one mix house, one kiln line and one grinding room, and made a few hundred tonnes a year.
metal.ferrite.mix-house.note: Medium confidence; the mix-house practice is standard but proprietary in detail.

facts.label: Batch
facts.value: 100-500 kg of oxide per blend

facts.label: Correction
facts.value: blend-to-analysis or blend-to-recipe; the industry splits on this

facts.label: Small factory output
facts.value: a few hundred tonnes a year

metal.nickel.nickel-oxide.name: Nickel oxide (NiO)
metal.nickel.nickel-oxide.description: The commercially traded intermediate. The pregnant solvent is stripped of ammonia and boiled, basic nickel carbonate NiCO3.2Ni(OH)2.4H2O drops out, it is filtered and washed, and it is calcined at 400-600 C to green-black nickel oxide at 99.0-99.5% Ni. In 1982 the overwhelming majority of nickel oxide went to ferronickel smelting; pure nickel oxide was a smaller but growing market for stainless steel and for plating.
metal.nickel.nickel-oxide.note: The later hydrometallurgical routes (Murrin Murrin, using a sulphate/chloride pressure leach) came after 1982; medium confidence.

metal.zinc.oxide.name: Zinc oxide sinter: the smelter's intermediate
metal.zinc.oxide.description: The dead-roast sinter is the actual feed to the leach circuit, and its specification is a compromise between the roast and the leach. It wants to be as completely roasted as possible so that the zinc is all in the oxide, but it also wants to be porous enough for the sulphuric acid to reach it, which is what the sintering stage of the roaster-sinter plant is for. Between 5 and 10% of the zinc stays locked up in the silicate matrix and is lost in the leach residue, which is the second big reason a zinc plant's recovery is not higher than it is.
metal.zinc.oxide.note: Medium confidence; the sinter quality figures are typical rather than specification values.

facts.label: Zinc soluble
facts.value: 90-95%; the rest is locked in the silicate

facts.label: Loss
facts.value: 1-3% of the zinc reports to the leach residue
