metal.manganese-carbonate.name: Manganese carbonate
metal.manganese-carbonate.description: Not a mined material: a chemical precipitate. High-purity manganese sulphate solution is treated with sodium or ammonium carbonate at 60-90 C and pH 5-7, and manganese carbonate drops out as a pale pink powder. The iron must be kept out because MnCO3 with 1-2% iron pushes the ferrite's Curie temperature up and its permeability down. So the manganese chemistry of the ferromanganese branch in this file and the manganese chemistry of the ferrite branch share a plant but not a product, and a manganese mine does not touch either.
metal.manganese-carbonate.note: Manganese carbonate for ferrites is commonly specified at 99% with iron limits; medium confidence on the exact precipitation window.

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: Na2CO3 onto MnSO4 at 60-90 C, pH 5.5-7

facts.label: Purity target
facts.value: Fe below 0.02% for high-permeability grades

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: pale pink to buff; brown if oxidised

metal.ferrite.iron-oxide-source.name: Iron oxide from mill scale or from a precipitate
metal.ferrite.iron-oxide-source.description: The cheapest ferrite iron oxide is the mill scale from an aluminium rolling mill or a steel mill - but it comes as a mix of FeO, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 plus the alumina or silica the original metal carried, so it is milled and then passed over a strong magnetic separator to take out the magnetite, and the residue is calcined in air to convert all the iron to Fe2O3. The higher-purity route is to leach fine hematite in sulfuric acid and precipitate goethite or ferric hydroxide, wash it, and calcine it to a very pure Fe2O3 of 0.02% or less impurity - which is what the RF NiZn grades and the high-permeability grades need.
metal.ferrite.iron-oxide-source.note: Ferrite raw-material routes are well documented in the ceramics literature; medium confidence on the temperature window.

facts.label: Mill scale route
facts.value: magnetic separation of Fe3O4, then air calcination at 700-900 C to Fe2O3

facts.label: Precipitate route
facts.value: H2SO4 leach of hematite, precipitate Fe(OH)3, calcine at 700-900 C

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: the final oxide is milled to 0.5-2 um before blending

metal.ferrite.nizn.name: NiZn ferrite
metal.ferrite.nizn.description: The second family. Substituting nickel oxide for most of the manganese oxide raises the resistivity of the grain boundary by a factor of a hundred, so the eddy-current loss at high frequency collapses and NiZn is usable to about 100 MHz instead of 1 MHz. The price is a permeability of only 15-100 where MnZn gives a thousand, and a low saturation. In the C64 it is the RF modulator transformer and the video output circuitry, and off the board it is the small cylindrical bead slipped onto a wire to kill EMI. NiZn is pressed and sintered the same way; the only real differences are the raw material and the sintering atmosphere.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Fe2O3 50-55 wt%, NiO 10-30 wt%, ZnO 15-35 wt%, plus copper and cobalt dopants

facts.label: Bandwidth
facts.value: 1 MHz to about 200 MHz

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 1150-1250 C in air; the copper content controls the loss

metal.ferrite.nizn.doping.name: NiZn dopants: copper, cobalt and calcium
metal.ferrite.nizn.doping.description: The NiZn family is doped with copper and cobalt to shape the grain-boundary physics, and with calcium to control the sintering. The NiZn product of the 1980s was deliberately split by composition into a high-permeability low-loss grade for transformers below 1 MHz and a very high-permeability grade for read heads and for antenna cores, and the difference between them was a fraction of a percent of dopant. It is a good example of a material in which the last tenth of a percent of the recipe is the difference between two products.
metal.ferrite.nizn.doping.note: Medium confidence; the effects are well established, the recipes are proprietary.

facts.label: Dopants
facts.value: Cu and Co to control the grain-boundary resistivity and permeability; Ca to control sintering

facts.label: Products
facts.value: high-permeability low-loss, and very high-permeability grades

metal.ferrite.nizn.co-source.name: The nickel and cobalt raw materials for NiZn
metal.ferrite.nizn.co-source.description: The Ni-Zn family's nickel does not come as metal. It comes as nickel oxide, or as green nickel hydroxide precipitate from a laterite leach, and the cobalt comes as metal, as oxide, or - much more cheaply - as a cobalt hydroxide carried out of the nickel refinery's ammonia circuit. Which is the point: the cobalt in a NiZn ferrite, the cobalt in a superalloy and the cobalt binder in a tungsten-carbide drill cone all came out of the same few refineries, so the price a ferrite maker paid for its dopant was set by the nickel market rather than by anything to do with ferrite. By 1982 that price was falling rather than rising - cobalt was about $12.50/lb in May, down from $25/lb in 1980, and about $5/lb by 1983-84 as new supply arrived.
metal.ferrite.nizn.co-source.note: The supply route is well established; medium confidence on which of the three cobalt forms a given ferrite maker was buying, since the recipes and the purchasing are proprietary.

facts.label: Nickel source
facts.value: nickel oxide or green nickel hydroxide precipitate, not metal

facts.label: Cobalt source
facts.value: cobalt hydroxide from the nickel circuit, or electrolytic cathode

facts.label: 1982 price context
facts.value: cobalt about $12.50/lb in May 1982, against $25/lb in 1980 and about $5/lb by 1983-84

metal.ferrite.modulator.name: The RF modulator coil
metal.ferrite.modulator.description: The C64's TV modulator, which puts the composite video onto the RF of channel 3 or 4 so a television could display the machine, contains a small ferrite-loaded coil - a few turns of enamelled copper wire on a ferrite core or threaded through a ferrite bead. This is the one place in the machine where nickel-zinc ferrite is genuinely a radio-frequency component rather than a filter. The modulator itself and the television are the optics/television agents' business; the core is this branch's.
metal.ferrite.modulator.note: Medium confidence: the modulator coil construction in the Commodore 250407 would need the actual part.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: channel 3 at 61.25 MHz or channel 4 at 67.25 MHz in the PAL/NTSC modulator

facts.label: Core
facts.value: a small NiZn bead or rod, 5-15 mm

metal.ferrite.bead.name: Ferrite bead: a small cylinder of NiZn or MnZn
metal.ferrite.bead.description: A bead is just a pressed and fired ferrite with a hole through it, made on a bead press with a die that forms the cylinder in a few milliseconds. A 1982 board might carry a dozen: one on each supply line to the analogue section, one on the video line, one or two on the mains lead of the supply. The bead impedance is a rising curve with frequency, set entirely by the ferrite's complex permeability, and the bead's job is to convert a common-mode current into a small radiated field and a small conducted noise instead of a large one. The bead and the RF transformer are the same pressed powder.
metal.ferrite.bead.note: The exact bead count and sizes on the C64 mainboard are the magnetics/interconnect agent's call; the material route here is certain.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 2-10 mm diameter, 2-6 mm long, bore 0.5-2 mm

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 50-1000 ohm at 100 MHz for a 6 mm bead

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 0.1-2 A DC, with the bead heating in free air

metal.ferrite.mnzn.name: MnZn power ferrite
metal.ferrite.mnzn.description: The material of the C64's transformer core, the rectifier choke and the bulk filter chokes. Its job is to carry a large alternating flux at 15-65 kHz with as little loss and as little audible noise as possible, and that is a tight compromise: MnO raises the permeability and lowers the magnetostriction (which is what stops the transformer singing), ZnO raises the resistivity and pushes the Curie point up but lowers the saturation, and the two oxides partly cancel. A 1982 E-core for the C64's supply would be MnZn at roughly 0.2-0.35 W/cycle at 16 kHz and about 0.35 T saturation.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Fe2O3 48-52 wt%, MnO 20-30 wt%, ZnO 10-20 wt%, balance trace dopants

facts.label: Core loss
facts.value: roughly 0.2-0.5 W/cycle at 16 kHz, 200 mT, for an E-core

facts.label: Curie point
facts.value: >200 C, which is what lets a hot supply stay a ferrite

metal.ferrite.dopants.name: Dopants: calcium, silicon, cobalt and the grain boundaries
metal.ferrite.dopants.description: The last half percent of the ferrite recipe does most of the work. A small calcium and silicon addition forms a grain-boundary phase that makes the grain boundaries insulating and therefore suppresses eddy-current loss. Cobalt raises the anisotropy and the permeability at low field, which matters for a filter inductor. Lithium prevents wall-jumping in a high-coercivity ferrite. These additions are 0.1-2% each and they are why a power ferrite's chemistry is a trade secret and why the same nominal composition from two suppliers will not behave the same way.
metal.ferrite.dopants.note: Medium confidence; the dopant effects are well established in the ferrite literature but the specific recipes are proprietary.

facts.label: Ca and Si
facts.value: 0.1-1% each, to form an insulating grain-boundary phase

facts.label: Co
facts.value: 0.1-3% for low-field permeability and anisotropy

facts.label: Li
facts.value: used in high-coercivity ferrite for memory and inductor cores

metal.ferrite.choke.name: Filter chokes and the common-mode choke
metal.ferrite.choke.description: The bulk filter chokes in a 1982 linear-supply C64 are 470 uH to a few millihenry with a current rating of 1-3 A, wound on an EE or a bobbin core of the same MnZn material. The switch-mode version instead has a common-mode choke: two windings on a single core, arranged so the two currents are equal and opposite, so the flux cancels and the choke does not need to store any energy - its only job is to present a high impedance to the common-mode noise on the mains lead. Both are the same pressed ceramic with a different winding.
metal.ferrite.choke.note: The C64 power supply of 1982 is a linear supply with a big transformer and 5 V regulator; the common-mode choke and the switcher belong to the later C64 power supplies and to the monitor. Medium confidence on which is which without the specific PSU. The magnetics agent owns the topology.

facts.label: Linear filter choke
facts.value: 0.5-10 mH, 1-3 A, MnZn EE core

facts.label: Common mode choke
facts.value: 2-20 mH, bifilar or two-hole core, high common-mode impedance at 0.1-10 MHz

metal.ferrite.e-core.name: E/EI/EE core geometry and the transformer
metal.ferrite.e-core.description: The shape is dictated by the winding, and the 1982 supply for small switchers was a pair of E cores with a centre leg and a window, assembled 'E-E' or interleaved 'EI' so that the joint is staggered and the effective air gap is halved. The window has to fit the magnetising inductance and the wire; the cross-section is set by the core loss target. The same ferrite pressing produces E, EI, EE, U, toroid, drum and bobbin cores, and the shapes are made by different tools in the same press. The C64's transformer is one of the smallest: perhaps 25 mm across, 30-40 turns of 0.3 mm magnet wire on a bobbin, and a gap cut into the centre leg with a scraper to set the inductance.
metal.ferrite.e-core.note: The exact core size and gap in the Commodore PSU transformer need the part itself; medium confidence on the range.

facts.label: Typical core
facts.value: E or EE, about 20-30 mm across the window

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 0.2-1.0 mm cut in one leg with a carbide scraper to set the inductance

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 15-65 kHz for a C64-class switcher

metal.ferrite.gap-scrape.name: Cutting the air gap in the centre leg
metal.ferrite.gap-scrape.description: An ungapped ferrite E core has a very high inductance and would not regulate a switch-mode supply; the switcher's magnetising current would be wrong and the whole design fails. So the gap is made deliberately, and on a 1982 E core it was cut with a carbide-tipped scraper - literally a hand blade run along the face of the centre leg - to 0.2-1.0 mm. Cutting rather than inserting a gap material keeps the inductance high and spreads the gap's fringing over an area, and it does it with a machine a ferrite buyer can operate. The tolerance of that hand cut is what sets the inductance tolerance, and the whole thing is one of the more beautiful pieces of 1980s manufacturing: a blade and a number.
metal.ferrite.gap-scrape.note: Medium confidence; the scraper-gap technique is very widely documented for small E and EE cores of that era.

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 0.2-1.0 mm, cut with a carbide scraper

facts.label: Why cut
facts.value: spreads the fringing flux over an area and keeps the inductance high

facts.label: Control
facts.value: the gap sets the inductance, so the transformer builder measured it and often adjusted it per core

metal.iron.name: Iron ore: the hematite and magnetite end of the chain
metal.iron.description: The bottom of the steel branch. Iron ore is dug, concentrated, reduced and never appears in a C64, and this branch exists so that the steel branch terminates in a mine rather than in an abstraction. The 1982 iron ore trade was dominated by three names: Mount Whaleback and the Pilbara in Western Australia, the Carajas and Quadrilatero Ferrifero in Brazil, and the Labrador Trough and the Mesabi range in North America. The ore is hematite, or magnetite, or both in a metamorphic banded iron formation - a rock that is 2 billion years old and was originally a chemical precipitate out of seawater.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 60-66% Fe for the Pilbara direct-shipment ore; 30-45% for the Mesabi taconite that had to be beneficiated

facts.label: Sulphur
facts.value: <0.05% for a good steelmaking ore; sulphur above 0.1% is a penalty

facts.label: World production 1982
facts.value: roughly 800-900 Mt of ore and concentrate

metal.hematite.name: Hematite (Fe2O3) and the Pilbara
metal.hematite.description: Hematite is a steel-grey to red mineral that occurs as specular crystals, as kidney ore, and - the mass of the world's supply - as itabirite and hematite replacements in a banded iron formation. The Pilbara ore bodies in Western Australia are the richest hematite in the world at 62-66% Fe with almost no gangue, and the Brockman and Hamersley ranges were being mined at full rate by 1982. The ore ships from Port Hedland, where the ore handling and ship loaders are among the largest machines ever built.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: lump ore, fines, and pellet feed fine

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: Banded iron formation: alternating layers of hematite and chert, 2.0-1.8 Ga

metal.hematite.pilbara.name: Pilbara open-pit iron mine and the ore loader
metal.hematite.pilbara.description: The Pilbara mines in 1982 were the mining engineering standard for the industry. A 15 m bench, 100-250 tonne haul trucks, 3-4 cubic metre shovels, and - this is the part everybody photographs - the huge travelling ore loaders that straddle the width of a haul truck and scoop up a 40-60 tonne load in one pass. The ore is crushed to 250 mm and conveyed up a 1.5 km incline to a stockyard, and then a 3-4 million tonne bulk carrier is loaded in about 20 hours at Port Hedland. One Pilbara mine shipped 40-100 Mt a year in the mid-1980s.

facts.label: Truck
facts.value: 100-150 t payload; some 250 t

facts.label: Loader
facts.value: travelling bridge-type ore loader, 60-120 t bucket, 1-1.5 km/h

facts.label: Shipping
facts.value: a 180,000-250,000 dwt bulk carrier loaded in 12-24 h

metal.hematite.stockyard.name: The ore stockyard and the ship loader
metal.hematite.stockyard.description: Because the ships are 180,000-250,000 dwt and the mine's output is lumpy, the ore goes into a 1-2 million tonne stockyard with a stacker and a travelling shiploader. The shiploader is a 100 m long gantry on rails with a slewing chute that trims the ship's hold as it loads, so a 250,000 dwt vessel is filled flat without a bulker or a trimming machine. The whole Pilbara export chain - mine, conveyor, stockyard, loader, ship - was built to move one commodity in enormous tonnage at very low cost, and it is the reason Australian iron ore is the cheapest iron in the world.
metal.hematite.stockyard.note: Not established: the 1-2 Mt stockyard capacity, the 100 m slewing gantry with trimming chute, the 1,500-10,000 t/h loading rate and the 12-24 h vessel loading time. The Pilbara reference gives the region's resource and production rate but no port or stockyard engineering, and the neighbouring ore-loader node carries the ship figures instead.

facts.label: Stockyard
facts.value: 1-2 Mt live capacity, stacker and a travelling tripper

facts.label: Shiploader
facts.value: travelling, slewing, with a trimming chute

facts.label: Loading rate
facts.value: 1,500-10,000 t per hour

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: 180,000-250,000 dwt capesize, loaded in 12-24 h

metal.hematite.crushing.name: Crushing, screening and the lump/fines split
metal.hematite.crushing.description: The ore is crushed in a gyratory and then on a screen, and the product is split three ways: lump ore above 6.3 mm that goes straight into the blast furnace, fines below 6.3 mm that must be sintered or pelletised, and a reject stream of the banded iron formation that is too low grade to smelt. The lump/fines split is a commercial decision rather than a metallurgical one: in 1982 the steelmakers wanted as much direct-shipping lump as possible because it avoided the sintering plant's capital and its fuel.
metal.hematite.crushing.note: Not established: the 6.3 mm lump/fines split point, the three-way split with a reject stream, the 30-45% Fe reject grade, and the 1982 steelmaker preference for direct-shipping lump. The iron ore reference distinguishes direct-shipping ore at over about 60% Fe from ore needing beneficiation but gives no size cut-off.

facts.label: Lump
facts.value: above 6.3 mm, direct to the blast furnace

facts.label: Fines
facts.value: below 6.3 mm, to the sinter strand or the pellet plant

facts.label: Rejects
facts.value: the banded iron formation itself, at 30-45% Fe, often stockpiled

metal.banded-iron-formation.name: Banded iron formation: a chemical precipitate from seawater
metal.banded-iron-formation.description: The leaf of the whole iron and steel branch, and one of the great ones. Around 2.0-1.8 billion years ago, the oceans contained dissolved ferrous iron and oxygen appeared in the atmosphere as a result of an earlier generation of photosynthetic organisms. Wherever the oxygen-rich surface water sank and met the anoxic iron-rich deep water, the iron oxidised and precipitated, as a jelly of iron oxide that settled as a chemical mud. It compacted into alternating silica and iron bands, and it is that banding which gives the rock its name and which makes the high-grade hematite ore bodies on the Hamersley Range the size they are. So the iron in a C64 chassis began, two billion years ago, as an oxide precipitating out of an ocean.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: 2.0-1.8 Ga, the Great Oxidation Event interval

facts.label: Lithology
facts.value: alternating magnetite and chert (BIF), later metamorphosed to hematite

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: a marine chemical precipitate on a continental shelf

metal.bif-banding.name: The silica and iron oxide banding
metal.bif-banding.description: The leaf, described properly: a stack of alternating 1 mm to 10 m bands of chert (cryptocrystalline silica) and iron oxide, the whole thing metamorphosed, with the hematite in the oxidised upper part and magnetite in the reduced lower part and the P-rich band - the band that gives the Sudbury nickel deposit and the Phalaborwa copper - where fossil bacteria oxidised the iron. Each band is a single depositional event or a group of them, and the ore-to-waste ratio of a Banded Iron Formation is often 1:2, so the pit that produces a tonne of iron ore has to move three tonnes of rock.
metal.bif-banding.note: Two claims in this node are not supported and one is probably wrong: the ore-to-waste ratio of 1:2 to 1:5, and the statement that a phosphorus-rich band hosts the Sudbury nickel deposit and the Phalaborwa copper - Sudbury is an impact structure and Phalaborwa a carbonatite, neither a banded iron formation. The band-thickness scale is documented: macrobands several metres thick, mesobands millimetres to centimetres, microbands under a millimetre. The biogenic interpretation is stated in the references as theorized, which is weaker than well-established.

facts.label: Band thickness
facts.value: 1 mm to 10 m, most of them millimetres

facts.label: Ore to waste
facts.value: often 1:2 to 1:5

facts.label: Biogenicity
facts.value: the banded iron formations are associated with the rise of photosynthetic organisms and the Great Oxidation Event

metal.steel.name: Steel: sheet, stainless, tin plate, tool steel
metal.steel.description: Steel is the machine's frame, its shields, its fasteners and its tooling, and in mass it dominates everything else in the C64. The route is: iron ore plus coke plus limestone into a blast furnace for hot metal; hot metal plus oxygen plus scrap into a steelmaking vessel; steel through a continuous caster into a slab; slab through a hot mill and a cold mill into sheet. Then three specialties matter for this tree: grain-oriented electrical steel for the power supply transformer, stainless for the jack and the shields, and hardened tool steel for the injection moulding dies and the extrusion dies.

facts.label: 1982 routes
facts.value: BOF was ~70% of world steel; open hearth was in steep decline, in the US open hearth output fell from ~50% in 1970 to near zero by the mid-1980s

facts.label: Crude steel 1982
facts.value: roughly 650-700 Mt worldwide

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: order 1.4-1.6 t of hot metal and 0.2-0.4 t of scrap per tonne of steel

facts.label: Scrap
facts.value: ~30% of US steelmaking was electric arc furnace scrap-based by 1982; world-wide about 20%

metal.die-steel.name: Tool steel: SKD61 / H13 / D2, the moulds and dies
metal.die-steel.description: The C64's case, the keycaps, the key plungers and the disk-drive and modulator housings were all made in injection-moulding dies, and every one of those dies and every aluminium extrusion die was cut from tool steel. SKD61 in Japan and H13 in the US and DIN X40CrMoV51 in Europe are the same alloy: 5% chromium, 5% molybdenum, 1% vanadium, 0.4% carbon, air-hardening to about 50-54 HRC. It is made in a small vacuum arc or vacuum induction furnace, forged, annealed, and then given three heat treatments - austenitising at 1000-1050 C, air cooling, and double tempering at 500-550 C - before it goes near the machine. A single C64 case die weighs 1-4 tonnes and cost tens of thousands of dollars, and it is the reason the tool steel branch is in this file at all.

facts.label: SKD61 / H13
facts.value: 5Cr-5Mo-1V-0.4C, air hardening to 50-54 HRC

facts.label: Heat treatment
facts.value: austenitise 1000-1050 C, air cool, double temper at 500-550 C

facts.label: Other tool steels in 1982
facts.value: SKD11 / D2 (1.5% C, 11% Cr) for cold-work dies, SKD5 / D2 for stamping, SKS3 / W1 for simple tooling

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: a C64 case die is 1-4 t and has a life of 100,000-500,000 shots

facts.label: Nitriding
facts.value: many dies were nitrided or PVD coated before use

metal.die-steel.vacuum.name: Vacuum melting and the purity of tool steel
metal.die-steel.vacuum.description: A tool steel that contains a hundred parts per million of sulphur will embrittle, and one with two hundred ppm of oxygen will pit. So the melt for a die is made in a vacuum induction or a vacuum arc furnace rather than in an air-melted crucible, and the ingot is remelted by the VAR or the EB process - electron beam - which gives a fine equiaxed grain with no inclusions and no segregation. The vacuum arc furnace is a modified version of the vacuum-arc remelting process that the titanium industry invented, and by 1982 the extrusion die industry and the mould industry both bought them.
metal.die-steel.vacuum.note: Medium confidence; vacuum melting of tool steel is standard practice but the specific purity targets are supplier-specific.

facts.label: Processes
facts.value: VIM, then VAR or EBCHM remelting

facts.label: Sulphur target
facts.value: below about 0.005% for a good die steel

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: a 2 t extrusion die blank in vacuum-processed SKD61 cost several times a conventionally cast one

metal.vanadium.name: Vanadium: a small alloying element
metal.vanadium.description: Included only because tool steel and the AOD of stainless steel both use it, and because the source is genuinely unusual. Most vanadium came from vanadiferous titanomagnetite - a magnetite containing 1-6% vanadium - which was a problem in the iron ore of the Panzhihua district in China and in the U.S. and Canadian Mesabi ranges until somebody worked out how to separate it. By 1982 the US route was slag processing: the titanomagnetite went into a blast furnace or an oxygen converter, and the vanadium reported to the slag, and the slag was ground and reprocessed. The other source is spent petroleum catalyst, which by the late 1980s was a genuine and growing vanadium source. Both of those are consequences of processes elsewhere in this tree.
metal.vanadium.note: Vanadium's involvement in both the iron ore branch and the petroleum branch is a real and well-documented piece of industrial cross-dependence; medium confidence on the 1982 proportions.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: vanadiferous titanomagnetite slag; spent petroleum hydrodesulphurisation catalyst

facts.label: Form sold
facts.value: ferrovanadium at 40-80% V

facts.label: Use
facts.value: microalloying in HSLA steel, tool steel and stainless

metal.vanadium.titanomagnetite.name: Vanadiferous titanomagnetite
metal.vanadium.titanomagnetite.description: The leaf: a magnetite with the iron partly replaced by titanium and vanadium, occurring as an iron ore in itself. At Panzhihua it is a magnetite-ilmenite ore in a vanadium-bearing magnetite gabbro; in the Mesabi it was a nuisance component of the taconite. Either way it is an iron ore, and the vanadium is a consequence of somebody mining iron.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: magnetite with Ti and V substitution; also a coexisting ilmenite

metal.molybdenum.name: Molybdenum: a tool steel alloying element
metal.molybdenum.description: Molybdenum is in the tool steel, in the stainless and in the hydrodesulphurisation catalyst, so it belongs in this tree, but its own branch is short because in 1982 almost no molybdenum came from a molybdenum mine: about half came from the molybdenite recovered as a by-product of the porphyry copper concentrators, where it is a few hundred ppm of the concentrate and reports to a separate flotation circuit, and the other half came as molybdic oxide from roasting. The ore is molybdenite, MoS2, in the Climax and Henderson porphyry in Colorado and in the Bingham Canyon concentrate. Molybdenum and tungsten share the greisen hydrothermal environment, so scheelite CaWO4 and molybdenite are sometimes intergrown in the same vein and the two metals can be recovered from one orebody. The leaf is a porphyry or a granite vein.
metal.molybdenum.note: The by-product share of molybdenum supply is well documented; medium confidence on the exact 1982 split.

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: ~half by-product of copper porphyry flotation, half from primary Mo mines

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: molybdenite concentrate at 45-60% Mo from a few hundred ppm of feed

facts.label: Conversion
facts.value: roasted to molybdic oxide, then reduced with aluminium or with hydrogen

metal.molybdenite.name: Molybdenite in a porphyry
metal.molybdenite.description: Soft, greasy, platy flakes of MoS2 in the quartz and feldspar of a granitic porphyry, associated with the copper minerals of the Climax and Henderson molybdenum operations or with the Bingham copper concentrate. The leaf is the same porphyry intrusion the copper branch ends in, which is a genuine shared endpoint.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: molybdenite MoS2, as 1-10 cm flakes in veinlets

metal.stainless.304.name: AISI 304 and 430 stainless steel
metal.stainless.304.description: The iron-chromium-nickel family, and a deliberate convergence point of three branches in this file. 304 is 18% chromium, 8% nickel, the balance iron - austenitic, non-magnetic, non-hardenable. 430 is 16-18% chromium with no nickel - ferritic, magnetic, and cheap. Both are made the way any steel is made: blast furnace for the iron, then a stainless steelmaking step that decarburises in an argon-oxygen decarburisation vessel, and the key is that the melt must not pick up more than about 0.05% carbon or the chromium goes into carbide and the metal loses its corrosion resistance. Stainless is the audio jack shell, the shield cans, some of the chassis and any fastener. Its cost is driven almost entirely by the chromium and the nickel, which is why the nickel price crash of 1982-83 directly cheapened stainless.
metal.stainless.304.note: The point about plated versus solid stainless is a genuine and important ambiguity for a consumer case: both were used in 1982 consumer goods and I cannot tell which is in a specific C64 without the part.

facts.value: 18% Cr, 8% Ni, C below 0.08%, austenitic
16-18% Cr, C below 0.12%, ferritic, magnetic

facts.label: Decarburisation
facts.value: AOD or VOD down to 0.02-0.05% C

facts.label: Nickel share of cost
facts.value: 8% of 304 by mass but roughly half the alloy cost

facts.label: 1982 supply note
facts.value: a lot of consumer-electronics 'stainless' was actually nickel-chromium plated or tin-plated mild steel

metal.stainless.jewel-audio.name: Where a 1982 C64's stainless actually is
metal.stainless.jewel-audio.description: Not much: the outer shell of the composite or RCA connector, the shield cans over the analogue sections, some of the tuner and modulator housings, the hinge hardware, and any stainless fastener. In practice much of what looks like stainless in 1982 consumer electronics was nickel-chrome electroplated or tin-plated mild steel, because solid 304 in a thin stamping cost several times what a plating operation cost. The distinction matters and cannot be settled without the part.
metal.stainless.jewel-audio.note: Low confidence on which specific Commodore parts are solid stainless versus plated; this needs the actual hardware or the parts drawings.

facts.label: Mass in a C64
facts.value: order 50-200 g of solid stainless at most

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: nickel-chrome or tin-plated mild steel sheet, which looks identical from outside

metal.stainless.cold-work.name: Cold rolling, bright annealing and finishing of stainless
metal.stainless.cold-work.description: Stainless is rolled and formed by the same equipment as mild steel - a Sendimir mill, a continuous annealing line, a Timesaver - but the tooling is different, because austenitic stainless work-hardens violently and needs much more force, and because a bright anneal must be carried out in hydrogen or in a vacuum to avoid discolouration and to avoid needing a thick pickling. A 1982 bright annealing line used hydrogen at 1000-1100 C with dewpoint control, which is a very refined piece of metallurgy for a machine that cost $395.
metal.stainless.cold-work.note: The nitric-hydrofluoric pickle is the classic stainless pickling line; by 1982 lower-HF alternatives were being developed for environmental reasons. Medium confidence on the transition timing.

facts.label: Bright anneal
facts.value: 1000-1100 C in dry hydrogen, or in vacuum

facts.label: Pickling
facts.value: mixed nitric and hydrofluoric acid, or a nitric-sulphuric alternate

facts.label: Work hardening
facts.value: 304 work-hardens to about 1.3 GPa tensile before it must be annealed

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: 20-30% nitric acid, 30 min, at room temperature or 50 C

metal.electrical-steel.name: Grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES)
metal.electrical-steel.description: The C64's power supply transformer is the one place where the metal of the machine is deliberately not stainless or mild steel. Grain-oriented electrical steel is a 3.2% silicon low-carbon steel whose grains have been given a preferred orientation - the classic route is a 700-1000 C anneal in hydrogen in a field or, in the modern continuous process, a high-temperature final anneal with a bias field - so that the flux runs along the grain and the core losses and the magnetostriction both fall. The 1982 transformer in a C64 used M4 to M6 grade GOES, somewhere around 0.3-0.5 mm thick, wound as E-E laminations. Without the silicon the core would saturate, the transformer would be too big, and the whole switching supply would not fit. Silicon steel is therefore not a speciality of this tree - it is load-bearing.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: low-carbon steel with 2.5-4.5% Si

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.27-0.50 mm for a power transformer

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: M4-M6 (or the older 21-23 grade number system)

facts.label: Core loss at 1.5 T, 50 Hz
facts.value: ~3-6 W/kg for M6; un-oriented steel is 4-6x worse

facts.label: Why silicon
facts.value: silicon raises the resistivity, cutting eddy-current loss, and lowers the magnetostriction

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: Goss texture, made by a final anneal with a bias field, or by the two-step orientation route

metal.electrical-steel.casting.name: Continuous casting and the Goss texture formation
metal.electrical-steel.casting.description: Electrical steel is continuously cast, hot rolled, and then given the two anneals that make it grain-oriented. The first, at 800-1100 C, is an ordinary recrystallisation anneal in wet hydrogen; the second, at 1100-1200 C, is the orientation anneal, in which the steel is held just below the Curie point in a magnetic field aligned with the rolling direction so the alpha-iron grains with their [110] axis along the field grow preferentially. The second anneal takes a week or more in a hydrogen atmosphere, which is why GOES costs three or four times what mild sheet costs and why a C64's transformer was one of the most expensive parts in it.
metal.electrical-steel.casting.note: The orientation anneal conditions are well documented; medium confidence on the exact field strength, which varies by producer.

facts.label: First anneal
facts.value: 800-1100 C in wet hydrogen, 1-30 min

facts.label: Orientation anneal
facts.value: 1100-1200 C in dry hydrogen in a 5-10 T field, 10-100 h

facts.label: Grain size
facts.value: 2-10 mm, with the [110] axis parallel to the rolling direction

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: GOES sheet at 0.3-0.35 mm was several times the price of mild sheet

metal.ferrosilicon.name: Ferrosilicon in the submerged arc furnace
metal.ferrosilicon.description: Ferrosilicon at 45-75% silicon is made in a submerged arc furnace very like the one that makes metallurgical silicon, but with more coke and a much higher silica ratio in the slag: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO, with the silicon going into the ferroalloy instead of condensing as dust. The largest producers make it in 60-100 MVA three-electrode furnaces, and the furnace is a genuinely different beast from the silicon one - the slag is liquid and the electrode has to tap through it. So the electrical-steel transformer in a C64 and the quartzite in a silicon plant converge at two different kinds of arc furnace.

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: FeSi45, FeSi50, FeSi65, FeSi75; high-purity low-C low-Al grades for GOES

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, 1600-2000 C

facts.label: Electricity
facts.value: 8,000-11,000 kWh per tonne of ferrosilicon

metal.coke.name: Coke and coke oven gas: the reducing agent
metal.coke.description: Coke is the black, porous, 90% carbon solid that makes the blast furnace possible, and it is also the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, manganese, ferrochrome and ferrosilicon furnaces. A tonne of coke is roughly 70% of the fuel and 30% of the reductant in a blast furnace charge, and nothing works without it. By 1982 the coke oven was a mature and much-diagnosed industry: the air pollution from coking, and the fact that a coke oven is the largest single source of coal tar and benzene in the industrial world, were the reasons the Clean Air Act of 1970 and its amendments hit coal and coke first.

facts.label: Coke
facts.value: 88-92% carbon, <1.5% sulphur, <10-12% ash, 5-9% volatile matter

facts.label: Blast furnace use
facts.value: order 0.3-0.5 t of coke per tonne of hot metal; ~70% as fuel, ~30% as reductant

facts.label: Metallurgical grade requirement
facts.value: CSR (cold strength) and CRI (reactivity) indices; 55-70 CSR was typical

facts.label: Other reductant uses
facts.value: tin, lead and zinc smelting, ferrosilicon, ferrochrome, ferromanganese, and the silicon furnace

metal.coke.gas.name: Coke oven gas and its by-products
metal.coke.gas.description: The gas is the profit centre as well as the fuel. After cooling it goes through a primary cooler and a benzol washer, which strips out benzene, toluene and xylenes; then a saturator removes tar and ammonia; then a Quinolining or electrostatic precipitator removes the last of the dust. What is left is coke oven gas, which is burnt in the battery flues to supply exactly the heat the ovens need - the plant is roughly self-sufficient - and the surplus goes to the steelworks as fuel and to a chemical works as a benzene and ammonia feedstock. Crude benzene from the benzol washer is one of the most valuable by-products in the plant, and it is where the aromatic chemistry of the plastics agent's chain starts.

facts.label: Gas yield
facts.value: 0.35-0.45 Nm3 per kg of coke, gross, before purification

facts.label: Benzene from the benzol washer
facts.value: 8-12 kg per tonne of coke

facts.label: Ammonia
facts.value: 3-6 kg per tonne of coke, as ammonium sulfate

metal.coke.quenching.name: Quench the hot coke, wet or dry
metal.coke.quenching.description: The coke comes out of the oven at 1000-1100 C and must be cooled fast or it will keep burning. Wet quenching sprays it with 3-4 m of water in a 30-60 s tower; the water flashes to steam, the coke is cooled to about 200 C and comes out wet with 3-8% moisture, which the blast furnace operator hates. Dry quenching pushes the coke into a sealed horizontal chamber and cools it with nitrogen or recirculated coke-oven gas. In 1982 nearly every coke plant in the world was wet, and the change to dry came later, mostly driven by the same air-pollution regulation that hit the oven itself.
metal.coke.quenching.note: Wet quenching was near-universal in 1982; German practice had led the switch to dry by then and the rest of the world followed in the 1980s-90s.

facts.label: Wet
facts.value: ~4 m3 of water per m3 of coke; coke leaves at 150-250 C with 3-8% moisture

facts.label: Dry
facts.value: indirect chamber cooling with N2 or gas; no moisture, no steam plume

metal.coke.quench-blow.name: The coke quench blow tank and its drain
metal.coke.quench-blow.description: Quenching has three products, not one: the coke, the water with the fine carbon in it, and the coke breeze - the 3-10 mm fraction that the blast furnace cannot use because it would be blown through the burden. Breeze is worth something: a coke plant sells it for sinter-plant fuel, for foundry moulding sand, and in 1982 increasingly for the electrode and anode pitch trade as a cheap carbon filler. So the coke oven's smallest product feeds three of the other branches in this file, and the water carries 1-3 kg of suspended carbon per tonne of coke quenched.
metal.coke.quench-blow.note: Medium confidence on the breeze yield; it depends on the crusher settings and the quenching practice.

facts.label: Breeze yield
facts.value: 2-5% of the coke

facts.label: Quench water
facts.value: ~4 m3 per m3 of coke, carrying suspended carbon

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: sinter plant fuel, foundry sand additive, carbon filler

metal.coke.battery.name: The battery, its flue and the chimney
metal.coke.battery.description: A coke battery is a long brick building - 50-100 ovens in a row, 40-60 m long, with a 60-70 m chimney at one end and a quenching tower at the other. Between every pair of ovens is a heating flue, so there are twice as many flues as ovens, and the gas from the ovens is burned in those flues and the hot gas is then drawn up the chimney. The chimney is the tall thing on the coke works skyline, and it is there for the combustion products, not for a draft. A battery is a piece of 1880s engineering that has been continuously rebuilt ever since and is essentially the same machine today.

facts.label: Chimney
facts.value: 60-120 m, 4-7 m diameter at the top

facts.label: Flues
facts.value: one between every pair of ovens

facts.label: Heat
facts.value: the coke oven gas is burned in the flues to supply the ovens' heat

metal.coke.cold-strip.name: The cold-strip push and the bench
metal.coke.cold-strip.description: The hottest, ugliest machine in the coking plant: a horizontal bar on a chain, 3-5 m long, permanently red, that pushes red coke out of the chambers onto the collecting bench. Its life is measured in weeks and its water-cooling is the operator's main concern. Everyone who worked on a battery in the 1980s had a job that was hot enough to need its own PPE rotation, which is the reason the whole industry has a 'coke oven man' occupational category and a very specific set of burn scars.
metal.coke.cold-strip.note: Medium confidence on the consumable life; it varies with the coal.

facts.label: Coke temperature
facts.value: 900-1100 C as it leaves the chamber

facts.label: Bar
facts.value: 3-5 m long, water-cooled, replaced every few weeks

metal.coke.tar-pitch.name: Coal tar and pitch: the binder under everything
metal.coke.tar-pitch.description: The tar that comes off a coke oven condenses as a dense black liquid, and it is the source of three of the most important carbonaceous materials in this file. Distilled, it gives crude tar, heavy creosote oil, and pitch - the binder in the carbon anode, the coke-battery electrode, the extrusion die lubricant and the aluminium pot lining. A tonne of coke gives roughly 30-50 kg of crude tar, and a tonne of that tar gives a few tens of kilos of soft pitch. So the coke oven is upstream of the aluminium pot, the coke battery and the graphite electrode, and the carbon-anode branch of this file is not an independent industry at all - it is the coke oven's tar still.
metal.coke.tar-pitch.note: Documented: coal-tar pitch is a coking by-product, is distilled into fractions including creosote and pitch, and is the binder in graphite green blocks and in Soderberg electrode paste. Not established: the 30-50 kg of crude tar per tonne of coke, and the few tens of kilos of soft pitch per tonne of tar.

facts.label: Tar yield
facts.value: 30-50 kg of crude tar per tonne of coke

facts.label: Products
facts.value: crude tar, heavy creosote oil, and soft and hard pitch

metal.coke.tar.name: Crude coal tar and creosote
metal.coke.tar.description: The tar is separated into a light fraction (benzol wash oil and crude benzene), a middle fraction of heavy oils used as a coking-plant quench medium and a wood preservative, and a heavy pitch fraction. Creosote as a wood preservative is a genuinely large market and it is the same molecule family as the pentachlorophenol and the coal-tar pitch that the board and case coatings used. So the coke branch of this tree touches the plastics, the coatings and the timber-preservation branches as well as the metals one.
metal.coke.tar.note: Medium confidence on the tar yield; it varies with the coal and the oven design.

facts.label: Tar yield
facts.value: 30-50 kg of crude tar per tonne of coke

facts.label: Fractions
facts.value: light oil, heavy creosote oil, and pitch

metal.pitch.from-pitch.name: The coke oven feeds six branches of this tree
metal.pitch.from-pitch.description: Putting the carbon branch together as one loop. Coal is distilled for rosin and turpentine on one side and for tar and pitch on the other; the pitch becomes the binder in the carbon anode, which becomes aluminium; the coke from the same oven becomes the fuel for the silica reduction that becomes the metallurgical silicon that becomes the polysilicon; the coke breeze becomes the sinter plant's fuel; and the benzene becomes the styrene and the phenol and the epoxy resin. One oven on a 1982 coking plant therefore feeds at least six branches of this tree, and it is the single most connected node in the file after the quartzite.
metal.pitch.from-pitch.note: This is a routing note about how many branches a coke oven feeds, not a claim about the world. No document can support 'the single most connected node in the file after the quartzite'; that is a statement about the tree, not about the supply chain.

metal.soft-pitch.name: Soft pitch and hard pitch
metal.soft-pitch.description: Pitch is classified by softening point: soft pitch around 40-70 C, medium 70-110 C, hard pitch above 110 C. The carbon anode wants a medium-to-hard pitch for the extrusion binder; the pot lining wants a softer grade that can be rammed hot. Pitch is also a dense, black, aromatic, carcinogenic material that has to be kept hot at every stage, so the anode plants had their own pitch melting and storage tanks. It is one of the dirtiest materials in the metals tree and one of the least replaceable.
metal.soft-pitch.note: Medium confidence on the softening point classifications; they vary between suppliers.

facts.label: Softening point
facts.value: soft 40-70 C, medium 70-110 C, hard above 110 C

facts.label: Binder use
facts.value: 25-30% by mass in a green carbon anode, 20-30% in an electrode

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: aromatic, carcinogenic, and it has to be kept above its softening point in storage

metal.carbon.anode.name: Carbon anode for the Hall-Heroult cell
metal.carbon.anode.description: Calcined petroleum coke at 90-95% carbon, ground to 1-20 mm, mixed with 25-30% of crushed and baked coke returns and 25-30% coal-tar pitch as the binder, extruded through a die with a threaded stud on the end, and roasted at 1000-1100 C for 20-30 hours. The point of roasting rather than baking is to drive the volatiles out before the anode goes into the cell, because an anode that gases in the pot poisons the metal. Consumption is 0.45-0.55 t of anode per tonne of aluminium, and the anode is consumed continuously - which is what makes aluminium smelting a carbon business as much as an electrochemical one.
metal.carbon.anode.note: The anode effect was not well understood until the 1980s-90s and was the subject of active investigation precisely in this period.

facts.label: Coke
facts.value: 90-95% C, 1-20 mm, from petroleum coke

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 25-30% by mass of the green anode

facts.label: Roasting
facts.value: 1000-1100 C for 20-30 h in a ring or tunnel kiln

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 0.45-0.55 t of anode per tonne of aluminium

facts.label: Anode effect
facts.value: the carbon dioxide from the anode that is not captured at the plant, plus the periodic anode effect, is the smelter's main CO2 and fluoride emission

metal.coke.oven.name: Coking in a battery of by-product ovens
metal.coke.oven.description: Two hundred and fifty horizontal chambers, 5-6.5 m long, 0.4-0.6 m wide and 3.5-5 m high, arranged in a brick battery 40-100 m long, heated in the flues between them by coke oven gas and reheated to 1100-1300 C. A charging car pushes 20-30 tonnes of crushed coal through a hopper into each chamber in about 30 seconds; the chambers are then sealed, and 16-20 hours later the doors are opened and the red-hot coke is pushed out by a pusher machine onto a quenching car. That cycle, 16-24 hours, is the heartbeat of the plant and it never stops. In the meantime the gas coming off the coal - the raw coal gas, typically 15-20% hydrogen, 20-25% methane, 15-20% CO, 5% CO2, 20-30% nitrogen - has been drawn off, cooled, and cleaned of tar and ammonia.

facts.label: Chamber
facts.value: 5-6.5 m long, 0.4-0.6 m wide, 3.5-5 m high

facts.label: Battery
facts.value: 50-100 ovens in a refractory-bonded brick battery

facts.label: Coking temperature
facts.value: 1100-1300 C in the coke; the oven itself 1000-1300 C

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 16-24 h; charge 20-30 t; yield 65-72% by mass

facts.label: Volatiles
facts.value: 25-35% of the coal mass leaves as gas, tar, ammonia and benzene

facts.label: By-products per tonne of coke
facts.value: ~0.4 t raw coal gas, ~30-50 kg crude tar, ~4-8 kg ammonia, ~10 kg benzene

metal.coke.quench-tower.name: The quench tower and the coke push
metal.coke.quench-tower.description: The physical heart of the battery: a tall steel tower with spray nozzles fed by a 300 mm main, a receiving pan, and a surge hopper from which a 2-3 m pusher car pushes the cooled coke onto a belt. Behind it stands the battery, bricked with about 20,000 refractory bricks per oven chamber in the modern design and castable in the older one, all of which has to survive 1300 C cycling every twenty hours forever. The doors are the coke-side door on top and the charging door below, and the charging machinery is driven by a single large winch.
metal.coke.quench-tower.note: Battery and push machinery design details; medium confidence.

facts.label: Ovens per battery
facts.value: 50-100 in 1982; 200+ in later designs

facts.label: Refractory
facts.value: silica brick or castable, replaced in rotation

facts.label: Push
facts.value: every 16-24 h, a 2-3 m stroke of the pusher car

metal.coking-coal.name: Coking coal, caking and prime coking blends
metal.coking-coal.description: Not any coal: a blend of coals that fuse and solidify into a coherent cellular cake when heated. The caking power comes from the vitrinite, and the best coking coal is a low-volatile, medium-bituminous coal that goes plastic around 350-450 C. The 1982 sources were the Appalachian basin (the US steel industry ran on Appalachian coal shipped up the Great Lakes and the Mississippi), the Ruhr, the Donbass, the Kuzbass, the Bowen Basin in Queensland, and the Gondwana coals of India, which are so low in caking power that India had to import coking coal to make coke for its own steel - a good illustration of how coal rank, not just coal carbon, is the relevant property.

facts.label: Rank
facts.value: medium bituminous, 25-35% volatile matter, 1.2-1.7% sulphur at best

facts.label: Caking
facts.value: the coal must soften and fuse; the assessment is the Gieseler audibert dilatation or the BS swelling index

facts.label: Yoke
facts.value: order 1.3-1.4 t of coking coal per tonne of coke

facts.label: A problem coal
facts.value: the Gondwana coals of India and Australia (a) are non-caking, (b) have high phosphorus, and (c) ship long distances

metal.coal-preparation.name: Coal preparation: crushing, washing, blending
metal.coal-preparation.description: Run-of-mine coking coal is crushed to under 50 mm and washed, because the ash that matters is the mineral matter - clay bands and pyritic nodules - that can be taken off by a dense-media wash at about 1.4-1.6 specific gravity. The washed coal then goes to a blending yard, because a coke oven wants a consistent blend and no single seam is consistent. Blending is done by a stacker-reclaimer in a yard, and the recipe is a metallurgical decision that is still made on the basis of the dilatation and the sulphur.
metal.coal-preparation.note: Documented: a coal preparation plant washes coal of soil and rock, crushes it to graded sized chunks and stockpiles grades, and liberation is measured by float and sink analysis. Not established: crushing to under 50 mm, dense media at 1.4-1.6 specific gravity, jigs, and the ash below 10% and sulphur below 1.5% blend targets.

facts.label: Crush
facts.value: to under 50 mm, usually on a double-roll crusher

facts.label: Wash
facts.value: dense media at 1.4-1.6 specific gravity, or a jig on the smaller seams

facts.label: Blend
facts.value: stacker-reclaimer yard; ash below 10% and sulphur below 1.5% for a good blend

metal.coal-tailings.name: The wash plant tailings and the creek
metal.coal-tailings.description: The other end of the coal preparation. Dense-medium washing rejects 15-30% of the mined tonnage as a fine waste with a high ash content, and in the Appalachian coal country in the early 1980s that waste was routinely placed in the creeks. The valley fills and the stream failures - the Buffalo Creek disaster in West Virginia in 1972 killed 125 people - were the reason the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 exists and why by 1982 a coal mine had to have a reclamation plan and a bond. So the coke chain in a 1982 C64 has, at its far end, one of the first major environmental regulations in the United States.
metal.coal-tailings.note: The Buffalo Creek death toll is well documented; medium confidence on the exact 1982 enforcement regime. The citation that used to sit here, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Creek_Valley, does not exist: the Buffalo Creek coal-drainage disaster of the early 1970s has no article under that title. It was removed rather than repointed at a nearby place article, which would not support a claim about valley fill.

facts.label: Rejection rate
facts.value: 15-30% of the mined tonnage

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act, 1977, with a per-tonne reclamation bond

facts.label: Precedent
facts.value: the Buffalo Creek failure of February 1972, which killed 125 people, was the event that produced the law

metal.valley-fill.name: Rehabilitate the spoil by valley fill
metal.valley-fill.description: The deep end of coal preparation's waste problem. In a contour mine the seam outcrops along a hillside, the coal is taken off along the contour and the overburden is pushed into the valley below, so the terrain ends up as a stream of grey waste from the highwall to the toe. It is cheap mining - no stripping, no trucks - and it is the reason the Appalachian coalfield has a hundred kilometres of dead grey creeks. In 1982 the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 required the mine to backfill and revegetate, with a bond per tonne, and that is the direct ancestor of the reclamation practices that the rest of the extractive industries adopted later.
metal.valley-fill.note: Medium confidence; the contour-mining practice and the 1977 Act are both well documented.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: coal taken off along the contour of the outcrop, overburden pushed into the valley

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: backfill and revegetation required under the 1977 Act, with a per-tonne bond

metal.coal-mine.name: Longwall coal mine at 300-1000 m
metal.coal-mine.description: A coking coal mine in 1982 was almost always a mechanised longwall: a shearer cuts a 1.5-3 m thick seam across the face, the roof is allowed to collapse, the coal is loaded onto a pan chain conveyor and a main belt carries it to a preparation plant and up the shaft. The seam is a few metres thick, so the mine is a thin dark ribbon of coal a kilometre wide. Pennsylvania, the Ruhr and the Kuzbass are the three great coking coal provinces, and they are the geological reason those three places have both the coke ovens and the blast furnaces - the coal is too bulky to ship, so the steel industry grows where the coal is.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: mechanised longwall with shearer and roof bolting

facts.label: Seam
facts.value: 1-4 m thick; multiple seams mined in series

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: 300-1000 m in the US, up to 1200 m in the Ruhr

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 40-70% recovered after including development coal

metal.coking-coal.seam.name: Bituminous coal seam (Middle and Lower Kittanning)
metal.coking-coal.seam.description: The leaf: a 2-3 m band of bright, banded, caking bituminous coal lying within a cyclothemic sequence of sandstone, shale and fireclay - the same sequence that holds the Pennsylvanian iron ore, coal and limestone together in the Appalachian basin, and the reason Pittsburgh is the steel capital of America. The Kittanning and the Freeport seams were the premium coking coals; the coal is Carboniferous, about 320 million years old, and it was deposited in a swamp.
metal.coking-coal.seam.note: Not established: the Kittanning and Freeport seam names, the roughly 320 Ma Middle Pennsylvanian age, the 2-3 m seam thickness and the cyclothemic sandstone-shale-fireclay sequence. The metallurgical-coal reference describes the coal's properties and caking ability but names no seam or Appalachian stratigraphy.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: Middle Pennsylvanian, ~320 Ma

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: cyclothemic sequence of coal, sandstone, shale and fireclay; a coastal plain swamp

metal.quartzite.name: High-grade quartzite (97-99% SiO2)
metal.quartzite.description: A metamorphosed, recrystallised quartz sandstone that is quarried rather than deep-mined. The chemical silicon industry does not use beach sand at all - it uses very low iron, very low aluminium quartzite, because Al and Fe are the impurities that survive the entire chain into the crystal. Two regions have essentially all of it. Note this is a DIFFERENT rock from the industrial silica sand used for glass, foundry moulds and copper-smelter flux, which is a much more common material.

facts.label: Main sources
facts.value: Norway (The Quartz Corp, JOlster and Tana), Brazil, and the Spruce Pine district of North Carolina

facts.label: Why not ordinary sand
facts.value: iron and aluminium in silica sand carry straight through to the crystal

metal.quartzite.quarry.name: Quartzite quarry, ~100,000 t/year
metal.quartzite.quarry.description: The Norwegian quartzite quarry is a bench mine in metamorphosed sandstone: drilling, blasting, a primary jaw crusher, and a sorting step where workers - and, later, optical sorters - remove the visibly iron-stained lumps by hand. The rock is then crushed, washed on a sluice or in a scrubber, dried and size-graded, because a single grain of iron left in the batch makes a bad day of the whole furnace.
metal.quartzite.quarry.note: Site-specific tonnages vary; this is a representative figure for a world-scale supplier rather than a cited figure for one named quarry.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open-pit bench quarry, drill and blast, ~15-25 m benches

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 100,000 t/year for the largest suppliers

metal.quartzite.rock.name: Quartz sandstone protolith (metaquartzite)
metal.quartzite.rock.description: The rock as a geologist would name it: a quartz-rich sandstone or siltstone, now a hard white metaquartzite of interlocking quartz grains with the bedding picked out by iron oxides. Some of the Norwegian material is a hydrothermal replacement body in a metasedimentary sequence. Either way the leaf of the silicon chain is a sedimentary or metamorphic rock exposed at the surface and dug out of a hillside.
metal.quartzite.rock.note: The rock is right but one figure is not: quartzite is not defined as SiO2 >95%. The British Geological Survey classification quoted in the quartzite reference requires at least 80% quartz by volume. Not established from the references fetched: the claim that some Norwegian material is a hydrothermal replacement body in a metasedimentary sequence.

facts.label: Rock type
facts.value: metaquartzite / quartzite; SiO2 >95% by definition

metal.electrical-steel.silicon-source.name: Make the ferrosilicon and add it to the steel
metal.electrical-steel.silicon-source.description: How does 3% silicon get into sheet steel at all? Ferrosilicon is added to the ladle, or - in the parent process - the ore is smelted with silica and coke in a submerged arc furnace to give 45-75% Si ferroalloy, and that alloy is added to the steel in the ladle or in the EAF. So the silicon steel branch intersects the ferrosilicon furnace, which is a carbon-reduction electric furnace just like the ferromanganese and ferrochrome furnaces in this tree, and which ultimately runs on the same metallurgical silicon and quartzite chain as the semiconductors. One of the more satisfying loops in the tree.
metal.electrical-steel.silicon-source.note: The low-aluminium requirement on silicon steel is well documented in the GOES literature; high confidence.

facts.label: Ferrosilicon
facts.value: FeSi45 (45% Si) to FeSi75 (75% Si), made in a submerged arc furnace at 1600-2000 C

facts.label: Addition
facts.value: to give 2.5-4.5% Si in the steel

facts.label: Grade for GOES
facts.value: high-purity, low-C, low-Al ferrosilicon is preferred because aluminium oxides in the film kill the magnetic properties

metal.electrical-steel.lamination.name: E-E laminations and the stamping
metal.electrical-steel.lamination.description: The 0.3 mm strip is blanked and stamped into E and I shapes - or, in a cheaper 1982 supply, into E-E pairs and then stacked and interlocked - on a 400-800 tonne mechanical or hydraulic press with a compound die that does the whole lamination stack in one stroke. The stamping is heavily lubricated and the edges are deburred and then given a magnetic insulation treatment: a thin epoxy or phenolic varnish, or an 'insulation coating' of an inorganic glassy film, applied so that the laminations do not short-circuit each other. The core of the C64's transformer is about 30-60 stamped laminations, and the number is set by the stack height and the available die.
metal.electrical-steel.lamination.note: The interlocked E-E stamping process was the standard for small transformers in the 1980s; confidence high.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: 400-800 t, one stroke for the whole stack in a compound die

facts.label: Insulation
facts.value: epoxy or phenolic varnish, or an inorganic glassy film; a C-core varnish coat

facts.label: Stacks
facts.value: 30-60 laminations for a small switcher

metal.tinplate.name: Tinplate: the tin-coated steel sheet
metal.tinplate.description: Tinplate is 0.15-0.3 mm of low-carbon steel with 1.1-11.2 g/m2 of tin on both sides, made on a continuous electrolytic line at 4-8 m/s. The strip is degreased and pickled in hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, rinsed, then tinned in a stannous sulphate bath with a fluoroborate additive, rinsed, and either given a food-can passivation in chromic acid or - in the electronics and tinplate trade - an electrolytic passivation in a chromate or tin-oxide bath. A C64 uses a few square metres of tinplate a year at most, in switch bodies and shields, but tinplate is worth a node because it is the one place where tin and steel and electrochemistry all meet, and because the chromate passivation is the same chemistry as the zinc chromate passivation in the plating branch.

facts.label: Base steel
facts.value: 0.15-0.3 mm, low carbon, low phosphorus

facts.label: Tin coating
facts.value: 1.1-11.2 g/m2 (2.8-28.2 g per 100 cm2); the food can standard is 5.6-11.2

facts.label: Tin consumption
facts.value: a 1 t tin can does about 250,000-400,000 400 g cans - which is why food can dominated the tin market

metal.tinplate.tin-pots.name: The tinning line: greening, tinning, soaking
metal.tinplate.tin-pots.description: The line has four electrolytic tanks in series - a 'greening' or pretreat tank to strip the last oxide, two or more tinning tanks with soluble tin anodes, and a 'soaking' tank to heal any bare spots. The strip runs through as a ribbon, and the tin is applied at a controlled thickness by the current and by how long the strip spends in the stannate bath. The mechanical complexity is in the handling: a 0.2 mm ribbon travelling at 6 m/s has to be threaded, cleaned and welded end to end several times a shift.
metal.tinplate.tin-pots.note: Electrolytic tinning line parameters are well documented; medium confidence on the exact ranges.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: SnSO4 with tin sulfate or fluoroboric acid additive; soluble tin anodes

metal.steel.sheet.name: Hot and cold rolled sheet steel
metal.steel.sheet.description: The slab goes to a reversing hot rolling mill at 1150-1250 C - first through a roughing stand, then a rail mill or a continuous mill - and comes out as strip 2-12 mm wide. Then the cold mill, a Sendimir or a multi-high cluster mill with a Sendzimir Z-High line upgrade, takes it to 0.2-0.5 mm, with the rolling oil and the annealing line in between. Annealing in a hydrogen or hydrogen-nitrogen atmosphere gives the recrystallised, equiaxed grain structure that makes a stamping possible. Cold-rolled sheet at 0.3-1 mm is the C64's case panel, the shield cans, the brackets and the heat-spreader, and the tinplate branch below is the same mill with a different end.

facts.label: Hot rolling
facts.value: 1150-1250 C, scale is descaled with a high-pressure water jet

facts.label: Cold rolling
facts.value: to 0.2-0.5 mm, with an anneal between passes

facts.label: Tensile of cold-rolled low carbon steel
Surface finish
facts.value: a bright rolled finish; oiled or pickled

metal.steel.surface.name: Pickle, oil and specify the surface
metal.steel.surface.description: Cold-rolled sheet is covered in mill scale and must be pickled in hydrochloric or sulfuric acid to remove it, or the next operation cannot stick to it. Then it is oiled or lacquered so it does not rust in storage. On the 1980s tinplate line the acid was hydrochloric, which put a genuinely dangerous hydrogen into the atmosphere, and the 1982 line ran its pickling tanks under a hood with an acid fume scrubber using sodium carbonate - which is another place the sodium chain of this file enters. The surface specification is a contract: roughness, cleanliness, and oil film weight in grams per square metre.
metal.steel.surface.note: Medium confidence on the oil film weights; they are line-specific.

facts.label: Pickle
facts.value: hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, 70-90 C

facts.label: Scrub
facts.value: the acid fume is neutralised with sodium carbonate

facts.label: Oil film
facts.value: specified in g/m2; on tinplate, 0.05-0.15

metal.steel.heat-treatment.name: Anneal and temper the sheet to its specification
metal.steel.heat-treatment.description: Cold-rolled low-carbon steel is hard and full of internal stress, so it is annealed in a continuous line - a few seconds to a few minutes at 700-850 C in a hydrogen-nitrogen atmosphere - to recrystallise it into soft equiaxed grain, and then, if it is going to be drawn rather than stamped, given a temper mill pass to raise the yield point by 50-150 MPa. The temper mill is a roll that puts in a deliberate rolling reduction that the temper roll locks in as a dislocation structure the anneal will not remove. The 1982 temper mill was a three-high Sendimir with a work-roll diameter of about 300 mm, and it is the reason a can and a deep-drawing panel are different products from the same mill.
metal.steel.heat-treatment.note: Medium confidence; the temper-mill principle is standard, the specific 1982 mill geometry varies.

facts.label: Annealing
facts.value: 700-850 C in hydrogen-nitrogen, seconds to minutes

facts.label: Temper mill
facts.value: a deliberate 0.1-1.5% reduction, raising the yield point by 50-150 MPa

facts.label: Work roll
facts.value: hardened tool steel, about 300 mm, in a three-high Sendimir

metal.rolling-oil.name: Steel rolling oil: emulsion and hydraulic oil
metal.rolling-oil.description: Hot rolling of steel uses water emulsion; cold rolling uses a neat oil or a water-in-oil emulsion, chemically similar to the aluminium rolling lubricant but with a much higher base oil viscosity and a lot of boundary additives. So the C64's steel mill and its aluminium mill are the same kind of lubricant plant, and both are quietly downstream of crude oil.
metal.rolling-oil.note: Rolling oil formulations are proprietary; medium confidence on the ranges.

facts.label: Hot rolling
facts.value: water emulsion, 0.5-5% oil

facts.label: Cold rolling
facts.value: neat mineral oil or water-in-oil emulsion, 1-10% emulsion concentration

metal.steel.caster.name: Continuous-cast the steel slab
metal.steel.caster.description: Steel is not poured into moulds one heat at a time; it is cast continuously. Liquid steel at 1600 C is fed from a tundish through a nozzle into a water-cooled copper mould 1-2.5 m long, where the shell freezes in seconds. The strand then passes through a series of spray headers that remove the rest of the heat, and finally through a torch-cut or a flying shear, and is coiled. The whole point is yield: continuous casting replaced ingot casting in the 1980s across the industry, and a modern continuous caster turns out better than 95% of its steel while ingot casting threw away the 10-20% of each ingot that was the crop - the ends, the segregation, and the shrinkage void. The C64's steel exists because of this machine.
metal.steel.caster.note: The adoption of continuous casting between 1970 and 1985 is one of the genuine revolutions in steelmaking and it is the direct reason tinplate could be made from 0.15-0.25 mm base steel at all.

facts.label: Mould
facts.value: 1-2.5 m long, copper or copper alloy, water-cooled, 900-1350 mm wide for slab

facts.label: Secondary cooling
facts.value: mist spray along the roller table, taking the strand from about 1000 C to 300-400 C

facts.label: Cutting
facts.value: torch cut or flying shear, into 10-30 t slabs

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: >95% versus 80-90% for ingot casting

facts.label: Adoption
facts.value: essentially universal in the developed world by the mid-1980s

metal.steel.mould-wall.name: The copper mould wall of the continuous caster
metal.steel.mould-wall.description: The copper alloy plate - phosphor bronze in most designs - that does the single hardest job in the whole of steelmaking, withdrawing heat from 1600 C steel at a rate that makes a millimetre of metal freeze in a second, and doing it hundreds of thousands of times. The plates are thin, 5-30 mm, and are cooled internally by high-pressure water, and they are plated and re-ground as they wear. Their thermal-fatigue cracking is the plant's central maintenance problem, and every crack means a slab defect that a tinplate maker will find on the inspection line.
metal.steel.mould-wall.note: Mould plate alloy and thickness vary; medium confidence on the specific figures.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: phosphor bronze or copper-zirconium, 5-30 mm

facts.label: Cooling
facts.value: high-pressure water at 30-50 bar inside the plate

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: thermal-fatigue cracks, marked with dye and then re-machined

metal.steel.vessel-choice.name: Choosing the steelmaking vessel in 1982
metal.steel.vessel-choice.description: Three vessels made the world's steel in 1982 and only one of them was winning. A short parent node so the basic oxygen furnace, the dying open hearth and the scrap-based electric arc furnace sit side by side instead of inside one another.
metal.steel.vessel-choice.note: Not established: that three vessels made the world's steel in 1982 and that only one was winning. The steelmaking reference says basic oxygen and the electric arc furnace are now the two major commercial processes and that oxygen steelmaking has become more popular over time, but gives no 1982 shares and does not date the end of the open hearth.

metal.steel.ladle.name: Ladle treatment, degassing and the steel's last chemistry
metal.steel.ladle.description: In 1982 the most important development in steelmaking was not the furnace but the ladle. A 1980s steel ladle is a 100-200 t vessel on a rotating turret, and it is where three things happen in sequence. Secondary metallurgy: argon is stirred in to homogenise the temperature and composition and to flush hydrogen and nitrogen. Desulphurisation: calcium or a calcium-bearing reagent is added and stirred, taking the sulphur out as calcium sulphide in a basic slag. Deoxidation and inclusion control: aluminium is added as the last deoxidiser, and in a bottom-pour ladle the whole ladle is streamed through a nozzle to collect the inclusions in the nozzle. This is the technology that made clean, low-inclusion, low-carbon steel a reproducible product, and it is why modern sheet steel for tinplate and for deep drawing exists at all.
metal.steel.ladle.note: Secondary metallurgy was genuinely new in the 1980s. The mechanisms are well established; the exact reagent dosages at any specific plant are not. Medium confidence.

facts.label: Ladle
facts.value: 100-200 t on a rotating turret

facts.label: Stirring
facts.value: argon at 0.1-0.5 Nm3/min/t

facts.label: Deoxidation
facts.value: 0.5-2 kg of aluminium per tonne

facts.label: Desulphurisation
facts.value: CaO-Flux or Ca-Si, to below 0.005% S in a few minutes

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: 0.03-0.08% for deep drawing and for tinplate base

metal.steel.eaf.name: Electric arc furnace on scrap
metal.steel.eaf.description: The other route, and the one that was growing fastest in the 1980s. Three carbon electrodes are lowered into a 30-100 t shell furnace and an arc struck, melting scrap with 600-1,500 A at 30-50 V - a physically brutal heat transfer that lets a small furnace melt steel quickly. In 1982 the units were mostly the smaller, older 'three-phase' EAFs of 30-50 t; the 100 t+ DC furnace that transformed the industry came at the end of the decade. The EAF makes about 20% of US steel and rather less of world steel, and it is the route that makes the recycling loop of car scrap back into new sheet possible.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: 30-100 t; most 1982 units were 30-50 t three-phase

facts.label: Arc
facts.value: 600-1,500 A per electrode at 30-50 V, ~30-60 MW

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: ~90% scrap, 10% direct reduced iron or pig iron

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: oxygen lances added later in the heat to burn off C, P and S

facts.label: US share 1982
facts.value: roughly 20-25% of US raw steel

metal.carbon-electrode.name: Carbon electrodes from needle coke and pitch
metal.carbon-electrode.description: The EAF, the submerged arc furnaces of the ferroalloy industries, the aluminium pot anodes and the large carbon blocks of the blast furnace all consume the same two materials: calcined petroleum coke or needle coke, and coal-tar pitch as a binder. An electrode is milled green - coke, pitch and sometimes a sulphur or metal additive - extruded, and baked at 800-1200 C in a graphitising furnace to above 2500 C. The 1980s problem was exactly the nickel crisis showing up here: the EAF plants had no electrodes of their own in Japan, and when the 1979-80 nickel spike also hit electrode prices, Japanese steelmakers found that making steel required nickel, in the electrodes. UHP electrodes and the shift to larger electrode sizes was the industry response.
metal.carbon-electrode.note: The electrode/nickel cross-dependency of the early 1980s is well documented in the steel industry literature; medium-high confidence.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: 75-700 mm; 1982 EAF electrodes mostly 175-350 mm

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 1.5-2.5 kg of electrodes per tonne of EAF steel

facts.label: Baking
facts.value: 800-1200 C for carbon electrodes; 2500-3000 C for graphite

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 20-30% coal-tar pitch

metal.steel.open-hearth.name: Open hearth furnace steelmaking, in decline
metal.steel.open-hearth.description: A 200-500 t rectangular basin of refractory with a hearth at 1300-1400 C, in which pig iron and scrap were melted while fuel gas or oil was burned above them and air was blown across the surface. It was dominant in 1920-1960 and it took 6-10 hours for a heat, produced a lot of nitrogen (so it could not easily make low-carbon steel) and consumed a lot of fuel. In 1982 it was a historical footnote in most of the world, still running in India, in Japan at a few works, and in a handful of Eastern European plants. It is included because it is the process the industry left, and because the heat-transfer engineering of the open hearth was the same furnace that the BOF was designed to eliminate.

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: 200-500 t per furnace

facts.label: Heat time
facts.value: 6-10 hours per heat

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: coke oven gas, producer gas or fuel oil

facts.label: By 1982
facts.value: gone from North America and Europe, still present in India, Japan and Eastern Europe

metal.steel.bof.name: Basic oxygen furnace steelmaking
metal.steel.bof.description: Hot metal is charged into a 40-60 t vessel - a pear-shaped converter with a refractory lining - together with about 20-30% scrap, and then a lance lowered into the bath on a boom blows 99.5% oxygen at 40,000-80,000 Nm3/h for 15-25 minutes. Three things happen at once: the carbon burns, the silicon and phosphorus oxidise, and the carbon monoxide boils the bath. The phosphorus removal is the reason the process is called basic: the lining is doloma, calcined dolomite, and the phosphorus ends up as calcium phosphate in the slag, which is why BOF slag is a genuine phosphorus fertiliser. The chemistry is violent and self-accelerating - the bath heats itself to about 1600 C from the oxidation reactions alone, so no fuel is added at all.
metal.steel.bof.note: In 1982 the BOF was around 70% of world steel. The open hearth, which needed fuel and hours and gave worse chemistry, was disappearing: US open hearth steelmaking had essentially ended by the mid-1980s. The open hearth was still significant in India, Japan and parts of Europe.

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: 40-60 t (up to 250 t by the late 1980s)

facts.label: Oxygen
facts.value: 40,000-80,000 Nm3/h through a submerged lance, 15-25 min

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 1580-1650 C; self-heating, no fuel

facts.label: Scrap
facts.value: 15-30% of the charge

facts.label: Lime
facts.value: 50-90 kg per tonne of steel, for the slag basicity

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: hot metal at 4.3% down to 0.05-0.1% or lower

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: CaO-FeO-SiO2, basicity 2.5-3.5, 100-150 kg per tonne of steel

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 80-90% on a good heat

metal.iron.hot-metal.name: Blast furnace hot metal (4.3% C)
metal.iron.hot-metal.description: A 25-30 m tall, 8-11 m wide stack, charged at the top with sinter, pellets, lump ore, coke and limestone, and blown at the bottom through 3-4 tuyeres with 1000-1300 C blast at a pressure of 2-4 bar. The iron oxide is reduced in stages on the way down - hematite to magnetite at 400-600 C, magnetite to wüstite at 700-900 C, wüstite to iron below 1000 C - and the carbon goes out as CO. The iron arrives at the hearth as a liquid at about 1450-1550 C, containing 3.5-4.5% carbon, 0.3-1% silicon, 0.1-0.2% manganese, 0.05-0.1% phosphorus and about 0.5% sulphur, and it is tapped every 4-6 hours. The slag floats on top and is tapped separately. A 1982 furnace made 5,000-15,000 t of hot metal a day on 3,000-4,500 m3 of volume and consumed about 400,000 m3 of blast a minute.
