metal.iron.hot-metal.note: The blast furnace has changed very little in the last fifty years: the great technical changes were the pellet plant and the oxygen enrichment of the blast, both of which were complete before 1982.

facts.label: Hot metal temperature
facts.value: 1450-1550 C at the tap

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: CaO-SiO2-Al2O3, 30-35% by mass, tapped at ~1500 C

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 5,000-15,000 t/day of hot metal

facts.label: Coke rate
facts.value: 0.3-0.5 t of coke per tonne of hot metal

facts.label: Tuyere zone
facts.value: the only place a furnace can fail catastrophically; a tuyere burn-through means 500 t of hot metal on the floor

metal.iron.burden-shaft.name: The furnace stack, throat and bustle pipe
metal.iron.burden-shaft.description: The 20-30 m stack is lined with 1,000-2,000 mm of refractory and carries the burden down through a rotating throat seal into a stock column. The burden rests on a 'ledge' in the wall where the gas changes from upward to horizontal flow - the place every blast furnace operator watches, because if the burden descends too fast the gas gets through and the furnace races. At the bottom, the bustle pipe wraps the furnace and delivers the blast through the tuyeres, with the hot blast stoves - Cowper stoves, 8-12 per furnace, each 8-12 m tall - heating the air to 1000-1300 C on the gas from the previous cycle. A 1982 furnace is a machine about 25 m tall and 9 m wide with a 3,500 m3 working volume, and it holds about 100 tonnes of burden in flight at any moment.

facts.label: Height
facts.value: 25-30 m to the top of the stack

facts.label: Hot blast stoves
facts.value: 8-12 Cowper stoves per furnace, 1000-1300 C

facts.label: Refractory
facts.value: carbon-impregnated brick in the hearth and bosh; the hearth stave cooling is the critical maintenance

metal.iron.copper-cooler.name: Copper stave hearth cooling
metal.iron.copper-cooler.description: The stave coolers that protect the hearth from 1500 C molten iron are made of copper or copper alloy with a water passage cast into them, because copper conducts heat far better than cast iron. They are a copper industry product, and they are one of the more elegant cross-links in this tree: the blast furnace cannot survive without a copper casting technology. On a modern furnace the stave is cast as a composite with a cast-iron backing and a copper water-cooled front, and about 400-900 staves are fitted.
metal.iron.copper-cooler.note: Not established: the 400-900 staves per furnace, the cast-iron-backed composite construction, and failure by fatigue at the waterway. The blast furnace reference confirms water-cooled copper jackets are used in lead blast furnace walls, which is a different vessel from an iron furnace hearth.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: copper or copper-iron composite with an internal cooling waterway

facts.label: Count
facts.value: 400-900 staves per furnace

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: years to decades; they fail by fatigue at the waterway

metal.iron.burden.name: Blast furnace burden: sinter, pellets, lump ore, coke and flux
metal.iron.burden.description: The furnace eats a precisely weighed blend, batched in 1-3 t bins and dumped in a rotating order around the bell-less throat so the burden descends evenly. Sinter is 55-65% Fe and 8-12% gangue; pellets are 62-66% Fe and are nearly always the majority of the iron-bearing burden in a modern furnace because they are uniform and permeable; lump ore is 45-60% Fe and is in retreat. The blend is sized and ground so it is permeable enough for the gas to reach the burden and rigid enough not to collapse into the raceways.
metal.iron.burden.note: Documented: the burden is ore, coke and limestone flux charged at the top, and the descending column must be porous enough for the flue gas to pass upward; slag forms when the ore's silica reacts with the calcined limestone. Not established: any of the five figures - sinter 55-65% Fe and basicity 1.0-1.6, pellets 62-66% Fe and 9-16 mm, coke 30-90 mm and a 0.3-0.5 t/t coke rate, and 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal.

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 55-65% Fe, basicity 1.0-1.6

facts.label: Coke
facts.value: 30-90 mm, with a coke rate of 0.3-0.5 t/t

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: 0.25-0.35 t of limestone per tonne of hot metal

facts.label: Gangue
facts.value: the SiO2 and Al2O3 of the ore is the slag former, hence the silica/alkali balance

metal.pellet.name: Pelletising the concentrate on a disc or a pelletiser
metal.pellet.description: Very fine concentrate - under 45 um - is mixed with 5-8% bentonite binder and 0.5-1% limestone, moistened, and fed to a rotating disc pelletiser or a drum pelletiser where 3-10 mm green pellets are rolled up by capillary action. The green pellets are then fired on a travelling grate at 1200-1350 C in an oxidising atmosphere, which sinters the surface, gives the pellet its compressive strength and, if the furnace is properly controlled, magnetises it - the hematite becomes magnetite, which means the pellet can itself be recovered magnetically, and its reduction in the blast furnace is faster. Pelletising is what made the 1970s and 1980s post-and-tensile steel possible and it is the reason Brazil and Canada have a modern steel industry at all.

facts.label: Pellet
facts.value: 9-16 mm, compressive strength 200-300 daN per pellet

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 2-3% bentonite; the pellet must survive handling from the pellet plant to the furnace

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: pellet capacity became the binding constraint on a new blast furnace's size

metal.sinter.name: Sinter the fine ore on a travelling grate
metal.sinter.description: Fine iron ore cannot be charged into a blast furnace - it would be blown away or it would pack. So it is sintered: mixed with 8-12% returning sinter fines, 5-7% coke and 10-20% lime, moistened to 6-8%, spread in a 0.7-1.0 m bed on a travelling grate, and ignited. At 1200-1400 C the bed self-fuses into a porous 100-150 mm cake. A modern sinter strand produces 3,000-6,000 t of sinter an hour and consumes about 1 GJ of fuel per tonne. It is the same machine as the lead sinter and the manganese sinter, and it emits a great deal of dust.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 1200-1400 C in the flame front

facts.label: Output
facts.value: 3,000-6,000 t/h per sinter strand

facts.label: Return fines
facts.value: 10-25% of the sinter produced is crushed and recycled

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: coke breeze or anthracite, ~60-90 MJ per tonne of sinter

facts.label: Gas cleaning
facts.value: cyclones and an electrostatic precipitator; the sinter plant was the biggest single dust emission at a steelworks

metal.coke-breeze.name: Coke breeze: the sinter fuel
metal.coke-breeze.description: The 3-10 mm fraction of coke, screened out at the coke plant, that would be too small for the blast furnace. A steelworks' sinter plant is therefore a consumer of its own coke plant's fines - a neat example of an internal recycling loop in the iron and carbon chain that closes from the coke oven's quench, through the sinter plant, back into the blast furnace's burn.
metal.coke-breeze.note: The coke reference defines coke breeze as the fraction under 10 mm, so the upper bound is right. Not established: the 3 mm lower bound and the 8-12% of the sinter mix share.

facts.label: Use
facts.value: 8-12% of the sinter mix as the fuel

metal.tantalum.name: Tantalum powder for electrolytic capacitors
metal.tantalum.description: A 1982 C64 has a handful of tantalum capacitors on the mainboard, in the analogue filter section, and tantalum beads in small packages. Each one is a sintered porous tantalum anode with a tantalum oxide dielectric and a solid manganese dioxide or a liquid electrolyte. The tantalum metal is won from columbite-tantalite, a refractory oxide ore, through a hydrofluoric-acid digestion that is one of the most corrosive industrial processes in existence. In 1982-83 there was a real tantalum supply crisis - the Congo and Brazil supply, the Botswana and Zimbabwe expansions, the US stockpile, and a price that doubled - and it is the one place in this tree where a commodity shock from a mining country touched a home computer.

facts.label: Metal purity
facts.value: 99.9%+; capacitor powder is made from very high-purity metal

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: columbite-tantalite (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 at 10-40% Ta2O5

facts.label: Market 1982-83
facts.value: a genuine supply disruption in 1982-83; the price roughly doubled and the electronics industry began substituting niobium

facts.label: Capacitor grade
facts.value: capacitor-grade powder, 99.9%+ Ta, particle size controlled by milling and by sodium reduction

metal.tantalum.separation.name: Separation of tantalum from niobium: K2TaF7
metal.tantalum.separation.description: From the fluoride solution the tantalum is selectively precipitated as potassium heptafluorotantalate, K2TaF7, by adding potassium chloride and hydrofluoric acid at 70-90 C - and this is the step that separates it from niobium, because K2TaF7 is far less soluble than K2NbF7. The K2TaF7 crystals are filtered, washed and dried. Then the metal is won from it in one of two ways. The potassium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with liquid potassium metal, or with sodium, at 700-800 C, giving a coarse tantalum powder. The aluminium reduction: K2TaF7 is reduced with aluminium in an induction furnace, and the charge is self-separating by particle size - the tantalum comes out as the finer powder and the aluminium-fluoride slag on top. The capacitor industry wanted the sodium-reduction powder specifically, because it could be made much finer.
metal.tantalum.separation.note: The sodium reduction of K2TaF7 at 700-800 C is the standard capacitor-grade route and is still the industrial norm; the aluminium reduction is for bulk metal.

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: K2TaF7 from the fluoride solution by KCl at 70-90 C; niobium stays in solution

facts.label: Potassium/sodium reduction
facts.value: K2TaF7 + 7Na -> Ta + 7NaF at 700-800 C; the standard capacitor-grade route

facts.label: Aluminium reduction
facts.value: K2TaF7 + 5Al -> Ta + 5AlF3, at 700-900 C in an induction furnace

facts.label: Product form
facts.value: tantalum powder; capacitor grade needs a controlled particle size and a high surface area

metal.tantalum.kcl-cycle.name: Recycling the potassium and fluorine
metal.tantalum.kcl-cycle.description: The potassium in K2TaF7 and the fluorine in it both come back. The mother liquor from the precipitation is evaporated and the potassium is recycled, and the fluoride is recovered from the aluminium fluoride slag in the metal reduction by hydrolysing it to fluoride and re-fluorinating. A modern tantalum plant's fluorine and potassium consumption is a small fraction of its theoretical requirement because of this loop, and the 1980s plants were learning it. It is a small detail that says something about how tight the tantalum business economics were - and the answer is that they were tight enough to make the 1982-83 supply crisis severe.
metal.tantalum.kcl-cycle.note: Low confidence on the 1982s recovery efficiencies; the flowsheet is standard but the plant data is proprietary.

facts.label: Streams
facts.value: KCl from the mother liquor; fluoride from the AlF3 slag

metal.tantalum.powder.name: Tantalum powder
metal.tantalum.powder.description: The anode of a tantalum capacitor is a pressed and sintered tantalum pellet of porous sintered tantalum powder, sintered at 1200-1400 C under vacuum, then anodised - electrolytically grown Ta2O5 - to a formation voltage of about 2-4 times the working voltage. The dielectric is the anodised oxide itself, which is why a tantalum capacitor is a bipolar electrolytic part with no liquid. The powder must be pure and must be milled and classified so the particle size is right for the pellet's porosity: a sintered pellet has to have a tortuous pore path, or it will short.
metal.tantalum.powder.note: The silver-electrode variant (that is, a silver counter-electrode) only became commercial around the turn of the 1990s; in 1982 nearly all molded tantalum capacitors used a manganese dioxide or silver-paste counter-electrode, so this node is a convergence of the tantalum and manganese branches.

facts.label: Pellet
facts.value: pressed and vacuum-sintered at 1200-1400 C, porosity ~30-50%

facts.label: Anodisation
facts.value: Ta2O5 grown electrolytically to 2-4x the working voltage, in phosphoric or nitric acid

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: classified to about 1-8 um for the pellet

facts.label: Counter-electrode
facts.value: MnO2 from manganese nitrate, or a solid silver electrolyte (a later 1980s development)

facts.label: In 1982
facts.value: tantalum bead and molded chip packages were on the mainboard; wet slug parts were being displaced by these

metal.tantalum.hf-digest.name: Hydrofluoric acid digestion at 100-200 C
metal.tantalum.hf-digest.description: The concentrate is digested in a mixture of hydrofluoric acid, nitric acid and hydrochloric acid at 100-200 C in a Teflon-lined or Monel vessel with a condenser to keep the HF in the loop. Ta2O5 and Nb2O5 both dissolve as pentafluorides, while iron, tin, thorium and most of the rare earths stay as insoluble fluorides or oxides and are filtered off. Thorium in particular is a problem: it is a radioactive alpha emitter that comes with the coltan and has to be separated and disposed of carefully. The mixed HF/HNO3/HCl digestion was the industry standard for decades; the Bayer process digest, using anhydrous HF with calcium fluoride at 150-200 C, arrived later.
metal.tantalum.hf-digest.note: The Bayer-process alternative digest came into commercial use in the 1980s and 1990s; the acid digestion below is the 1982 norm.

facts.label: Medium
facts.value: HF/HNO3/HCl, or HF with CaF2 (the Bayer process digest)

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: Monel or Teflon-lined, with a reflux condenser - HF attacks glass

facts.label: Refractory waste
facts.value: 5-15% of the mass leaves as insoluble fluoride sludge; the hardest waste stream in the industry

metal.tantalum.digest-vessel.name: The fluoride digestion vessel
metal.tantalum.digest-vessel.description: The digestor is the most aggressively corrosive piece of equipment in the metals tree. Anhydrous hydrofluoric acid at 100-200 C attacks glass, attacks most metals, and attacks concrete; so the vessel is Monel, nickel, or Teflon-lined, with the condenser and the piping also in Monel, and there is a continuous fluoride leak problem because HF is off-gassing from a boiling slurry. The industry answer through the 1980s was the Monel plant, with a steam stripping system to recover the HF and a caustic scrubber on the vent, and it was the single largest reason the industry needed a process chemist rather than a metallurgist.
metal.tantalum.digest-vessel.note: Medium confidence; the materials of construction for HF service are well established in chemical engineering handbooks.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: Monel, nickel, or PTFE-lined steel

facts.label: Why
facts.value: anhydrous HF at 100-200 C attacks glass, most metals and concrete

facts.label: Fluoride recovery
facts.value: steam stripping of the offgas, then a caustic scrubber

metal.nickel-monel.name: Monel: nickel with copper
metal.nickel-monel.description: The alloy that made the fluorine chemistry of the 1980s possible: 60-70% nickel with 30% copper, and sometimes molybdenum, made in the same vacuum-melted, cast-and-rolled route as any nickel alloy. Monel resists hydrofluoric acid better than almost anything because the nickel fluoride film that forms is protective while aluminium fluoride and steel fluoride are not. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor was separated in a vessel made of a nickel alloy that came out of the nickel branch of this same file, and the aluminium capacitor in the power supply is made with an acid that would destroy it.
metal.nickel-monel.note: Medium confidence; Monel's composition is well documented and the mechanism is the standard explanation.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 60-70% Ni, 25-35% Cu, sometimes 1-5% Mo

facts.label: Why it survives HF
facts.value: the nickel fluoride film is protective; aluminium and iron fluorides are not

metal.tantalum.thorium.name: Thorium in the coltan: a radioactive by-product
metal.tantalum.thorium.description: Columbite-tantalite carries thorium and uranium in solid solution, typically 0.01-0.5% Th as ThO2, and because thorium's chemistry is so close to the rare earths it follows them through the whole fluoride circuit and reports with the rare-earth product. It is an alpha emitter, so the refinery's thorium residue is a radioactive waste that has to be stored, and in 1982 the disposal arrangements in most producing countries were informal. The leaf is a radioactive waste site, which is a legitimate if slightly grim terminus for a branch of the metals tree.
metal.tantalum.thorium.note: The thorium content of coltan is well documented; medium confidence on the 1982 commercial handling arrangements.

facts.label: Thorium content
facts.value: 0.01-0.5% Th as ThO2 in coltan concentrate

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: follows the rare earths through the fluoride circuit

facts.label: 1982 handling
facts.value: thorium nitrate sold as a 'fertile material' for a thorium fuel cycle that never arrived; the rest was stored

metal.hydrofluoric-acid.name: Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar
metal.hydrofluoric-acid.description: The corrosive reagent. Fluorspar plus sulfuric acid gives hydrogen fluoride in a kiln at 200-300 C; fluorspar plus concentrated sulfuric acid in a rotary kiln gives anhydrous HF directly, and the anhydrous route is what makes water-free fluorinations possible. HF is the reagent for silicon to trichlorosilane, tantalum to K2TaF7, glass etching, uranium hexafluoride, and the fluorochemical industry generally.

facts.label: Wet route
facts.value: CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2HF at 200-300 C

facts.label: Anhydrous HF
facts.value: fluorspar + concentrated H2SO4 in a rotary kiln at 200-250 C

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: HF causes deep burns and systemic hypocalcaemia; anhydrous HF handling required nickel or Monel equipment

metal.columbite.name: Columbite-tantalite concentrate
metal.columbite.description: A hard, black, sub-conchoidal mineral - (Fe,Mn)(Nb,Ta)2O6 - that in practice is never a pure species but a solid solution, and that is the whole problem of the tantalum industry: tantalum and niobium are chemically almost identical and always occur together, with the tantalum content ranging from a few percent to more than 50% of the total. The separation is the entire industry. The main 1982 sources were the Greenbushes and Wodgina pegmatites in Western Australia, the Cat Creek and Oarkopper operations in Brazil, and the columbite-tantalite concentrates from the Congo, Nigeria and Zimbabwe. Tantalum-bearing tin slags from Malaysia and Brazil were a secondary source.

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 20-60% Ta2O5 in the tantalum-rich fraction; lower for ordinary columbite

facts.label: Host
facts.value: granitic pegmatite; the Greenbushes pegmatite is a lithium-tantalum-columbite body

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: the ore is chemically a refractory oxide locked in a silicate rock

metal.columbite.concentrator.name: Coltan concentrator: gravity, magnet and electrostatic
metal.columbite.concentrator.description: The coltan upgrade in a small operation is a classic three-stage gravity and magnetic plant: a shaking table or a jig throws away the quartz and mica, a magnetic separator takes off the magnetite and ilmenite, and a second gravity stage with a dense-medium separator makes a 20-30% Ta2O5 concentrate from a 0.05-0.1% pegmatite. Electrostatic separation takes out the zircon. The mass yield is under 1%, so the concentrator's job is mostly to throw away 99.5% of the rock, which is why a coltan operation is a small, cheap, labour-intensive plant sitting next to the pit rather than a large mill.
metal.columbite.concentrator.note: Recovery figures for artisanal coltan operations vary enormously; medium confidence.

facts.label: Stages
facts.value: jig or shaking table, magnetic separator, dense medium, electrostatic

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: 0.05-0.1% Ta2O5 pegmatite

facts.label: Concentrate
facts.value: 20-30% Ta2O5, at 60-80% recovery

metal.columbite.tailings.name: Coltan tailings
metal.columbite.tailings.description: A coltan concentrator throws away over 99% of the mass it treats, and in the artisanal operations of the 1970s and 1980s that was put into the creek bed without any attempt at settling, and the creek carried it away. The ecological consequence of that was small compared to what followed - the coltan rush of 2000-2008 - but the mining itself was the problem and the tantalum industry spent most of the 1980s designing a better process and a better tailings facility precisely because it was planning for exactly the kind of scrutiny it eventually got. A node whose importance is only visible in hindsight.
metal.columbite.tailings.note: Low confidence; the 1980s artisanal tailings practice is poorly documented; this is reasoned from the mass balance rather than from a source.

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: over 99% of the feed mass, as a fine quartz-mica-feldspar slurry

metal.columbite.mine.name: Pegmatite open pit with sluicing
metal.columbite.mine.description: The tantalum ore is in a pegmatite dyke, a very coarse-grained granite intrusion, and the extraction in the small operations is almost artisanal: the dyke is blasted, the rock is crushed and hand-sorted, and the heavy tantalum minerals are concentrated on a sluice or a jig. The Greenbushes operation, at the time one of the largest, mined a 3 km pegmatite by open pit with a 200,000 t/year plant. So the tantalum in a 1982 C64's capacitors very plausibly came out of an Australian open cut in a pegmatite, hand-sorted and sluiced.
metal.columbite.mine.note: Greenbushes was already a tin mine before it was a tantalum mine and then a lithium mine - a genuinely rare example of one pit changing commodities. Medium confidence on the production figures for 1982.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open pit, drill and blast, coarse crushing, hand sorting, gravity concentration, or a dense-medium plant

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: coltan at 20-30% Ta2O5 from a 0.05-0.1% Ta2O5 pegmatite

facts.label: Predecessor technology
facts.value: cassiterite and wolframite were the original 1940s products of these same operations

metal.columbite.pegmatite.name: Granitic pegmatite dyke
metal.columbite.pegmatite.description: The leaf: a coarse-grained, quartz-feldspar-mica rock so coarse that individual crystals are centimetres across, with the tantalum-bearing minerals in small pockets of rare-metal enrichment. Pegmatites are the last-crystallising fraction of a granite magma, so they are the natural home of every incompatible element - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, rare earths. There is no more apt end point for the tantalum chain than a dyke of crystals bigger than your fist.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: granitic pegmatite: quartz, albite, potassium feldspar, mica, with coltan pockets

facts.label: Grain size
facts.value: commonly 1-100 mm crystals

metal.pegmatite-crystals.name: The crystals and the rare-metal pockets
metal.pegmatite-crystals.description: The leaf of the tantalum branch. A pegmatite is the last thing a granite magma crystallises, and because it is water-rich and volatile-rich it can hold elements that have no business being in a granite at all - lithium, tantalum, niobium, beryllium, tin, the rare earths - at hundreds of times their normal concentration. Those elements concentrate in the last pockets to crystallise, and a pocket 30 cm across can hold a few kilos of coltan worth more than the whole pegmatite around it. So the tantalum in a 1982 capacitor came out of small pockets in a last-stage granite pocket, hand-sorted out of a rock whose crystals are bigger than your fist, in a pegmatite that is less than 0.1% tantalum.

facts.label: Enrichment
facts.value: volatile elements concentrate in the final crystallising pockets, at 100-1000x background

facts.label: Pocket size
facts.value: cm to tens of cm, holding grams to kilograms of coltan

facts.label: Host
facts.value: a granitic pegmatite dyke

metal.silver.name: Silver: contacts, solder paste, brazing
metal.silver.description: Silver is the most electrically conductive of any element, and it is used in a C64 where the contact has to carry current at low force: the contacts of the rocker switches and of many of the keyboard switches, the silver-bearing solder and brazing alloys for the heat sinks and chassis joints, the silver-filled epoxy and silver ink of the keyboard membrane, and the silver that comes out of the lead and copper refineries as a by-product. Most of the world's silver is mined as a by-product - of lead, of copper, of zinc - and only about a fifth comes from a primary silver mine.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.9% (2N) minimum; 99.99% (4N) for contacts

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: native silver, argentite Ag2S, at 100-2000 g/t; the great districts were Freiberg, Potosi, Guanajuato, Cobalt, Broken Hill

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: ~75% of silver production is a by-product of lead, zinc and copper refining

metal.silver.refining.name: Refine the silver to 99.9-99.99%
metal.silver.refining.description: Most silver never gets a refinery of its own. It is separated inside the lead smelter and refinery, or the copper anode slime, and refined there. The copper route: the slime is dissolved in nitric acid or in an aqua-regia type circuit, silver precipitates as silver chloride which is then reduced with copper and melted, and gold is recovered separately. The lead route: the Parkes process and the cupellation furnace described in the lead branch deliver silver at 96-99%, and it is electrorefined in a small silver tankhouse with a silver anode and a silver cathode in a nitric acid or a copper nitrate electrolyte at 2-4 V. In 1982 perhaps 60% of the world's refined silver was made at a handful of silver refineries and the rest was by-product metal refined alongside lead and copper.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: nitric acid with a little silver nitrate, or copper nitrate

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.9% cathode; 99.99% by re-electrorefining

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: order 300-600 kWh per tonne of silver

metal.silver.electrorefining.name: Electrolyse the silver and the dore loop
metal.silver.electrorefining.description: The silver from the Parkes cupellation or from the anode slime is cast as anodes and dissolved in a nitric acid electrolyte with a little silver nitrate, at 2-4 V with a pure silver cathode. The electrolyte's job is to hold the silver as the nitrate while the gold and the base metals either stay in the anode mud or fall out as slime. A small refinery might have 20-40 cells and make 5-20 t a month. The silver cathode is then melted and cast, and the whole cycle - cupell, electrorefine, cast, cupell again - can run three times to get five nines.
metal.silver.electrorefining.note: Medium confidence on the cell counts and the energy figure; the process itself is standard.

facts.label: Cells
facts.value: 20-40 per small refinery

facts.label: Passes
facts.value: 2-3 electrorefining passes for 99.99%

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 300-600 kWh per tonne of silver

metal.silver.borax-flux.name: Fire assay with borax and litharge
metal.silver.borax-flux.description: A refinery that also assays needs a cupellation furnace and a borax flux, because silver is assayed by cupellation: the sample is mixed with borax and litharge, cupelled, and the silver bead that is left is weighed. So the assay and the refining process are the same process, which is why a small refinery has a cupel furnace whether or not it refines. It is also why the assayer's skill and the refiner's skill are the same skill, and why the price of silver has always been set by a weighing scale on a furnace roof.
metal.silver.borax-flux.note: Medium confidence; cupellation as an assay method is well documented.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: cupellation with a borax-litharge flux, weighing the silver bead

facts.label: Fusion assay
facts.value: the alternative, for ores where the silver reports to the lead button

metal.silver.contact-powder.name: Silver contact powder: Ag-SnO2 and Ag-graphite
metal.silver.contact-powder.description: A switch contact is not silver metal. It is a powder metallurgy composite: 80-95% silver powder mixed with 5-15% of a refractory oxide - tin oxide, cadmium oxide or graphite - pressed at 200-400 MPa and sintered at 700-950 C. The oxide breaks up the silver grain boundaries and suppresses the metal transfer that otherwise builds up on a small, low-force contact, at the price of some conductivity. Silver-graphite is the same idea for sliding contacts, and silver-graphite in a rotary encoder or a potentiometer is the single most common use of silver powder in electronics.
metal.silver.contact-powder.note: The cadmium oxide contact alloy was being phased out on toxicity grounds through the 1980s; medium confidence on the timing of that shift.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 80-95% Ag, 5-15% SnO2 or CdO or graphite

facts.label: Sintering
facts.value: 700-950 C in a hydrogen atmosphere

facts.label: 1982 competition
facts.value: Ag-SnO2 and the gold-plated contact were already displacing Ag-CdO on cost and toxicity grounds

metal.silver.ingot.name: Silver ingot, 99.9%, and silver contact material
metal.silver.ingot.description: A 99.9% ingot is the standard commodity grade, cast as 0.5-1 kg bars or as a 15-30 kg or 1000 troy ounce bar. For the contacts of the C64's switches and keys the relevant alloy is not pure silver but a silver-cadmium-oxide or silver-tin-oxide electrical contact material - a silver matrix with 5-15% of a refractory oxide that reduces the contact resistance rise caused by metal transfer, at the cost of a bit of conductivity. Silver-graphite is a related and very common sliding contact material: 50-95% silver in graphite, sintered and infiltrated, used where the contact has to rub.
metal.silver.ingot.note: The exact contact alloy in Commodore's keyboard switches is not something I can confirm; Ag-SnO2 and Ag-CdO were both standard contact materials in the 1980s. Medium confidence.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.9% (2N) commodity; 99.99% (4N) for contacts

facts.label: Contact alloys
facts.value: Ag-CdO, Ag-SnO2, Ag-graphite; typically 80-95% Ag

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: silver's conductivity is 63 MS/m; the oxide suppresses arc erosion and metal transfer

facts.label: 1950s-1980s note
facts.value: silver contacts were being displaced in low-voltage, low-current applications by silver-plated base metals and by gold

metal.silver.ore.name: Silver ore and the by-product sources
metal.silver.ore.description: Silver behaves chemically like lead, so it substitutes for it in galena, and the world's most productive silver mines are really lead mines. The primary ores are native silver, argentite Ag2S, pyrargyrite Ag3SbS3 and stephanite Ag5SbS4 - the last two are why silver is also a lead-bysulphide metallurgy problem. The Cordillera Real of Potosi in Bolivia and Zacatecas in Mexico were the great producers, and Cobalt in Ontario is the historical outlier where silver was the target. Silver at 500-1000 g/t is a very good ore and at 5-50 g/t it is a credit.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 100-2000 g/t Ag in primary veins; 20-200 g/t as a lead-zinc credit

facts.label: Minerals
facts.value: native Ag, argentite Ag2S, pyrargyrite Ag3SbS3, stephanite, and solid solution in galena

metal.silver.mill.name: Silver mill: crushing, grinding and flotation
metal.silver.mill.description: Ore at 300-1500 g/t is crushed to 10-25 mm, ground in a ball mill to 50-100 um, and floated with a xanthate or a thio compound collector at pH 8-10. Silver sulphides float with the lead and zinc sulphides they are intergrown with, so the circuit produces a bulk concentrate that the smelter treats as a lead concentrate. The recovery is 60-85% and the tailings are the reason the Zacatecas and Guanajuato districts look the way they do - a very large volume of finely ground rock in long, engineered tailings impoundments.
metal.silver.mill.note: Silver flotation is not well served by generic numbers because the mineralogy is so varied; medium confidence.

metal.silver.concentrate-shipping.name: Why silver concentrate goes to a lead smelter
metal.silver.concentrate-shipping.description: A silver concentrate is not a product anybody wants to buy; it is a concentrate to ship to a lead smelter 500 km away, because the only economical way to separate silver from lead is the Parkes process, and that needs a lead smelter. So the silver chain leaves the mine, joins the lead chain inside a smelter that may be in a different country, and comes back out at 99.9%. This is the practical meaning of silver being a by-product metal, and it is why the silver price has so little to do with the silver mines.

metal.lead.blast-furnace.name: Lead blast furnace reduction to crude lead
metal.lead.blast-furnace.description: A lead blast furnace looks like an iron blast furnace but is only 4-7 m tall, because lead reduces so easily. Self-fluxing sinter, coke and limestone are charged at the top; a blast of 200-350 C air is blown in at the hearth; the PbO is reduced to lead by CO at 1000-1100 C and the metal runs out. The sinter, coke and limestone charge comes down a shaft that is deliberately kept chilled so the metallic lead freezes before it goes further down - if it melted it would run into the tuyeres. Two outputs: crude lead bullion at 950-1050 C at the bottom, and a slag carrying off the iron and silica.

facts.label: Furnace height
facts.value: 4.7-7.5 m (much shorter than an iron furnace)

facts.label: Blast
facts.value: 200-350 C, wet or filtered

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: PbO + C -> Pb + CO, at 1000-1100 C

facts.label: Chilling
facts.value: the shaft is cooled by sprays so the lead freezes as a sponge above the tuyeres

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: CaO-FeO-SiO2, 15-20% of the sinter charge, sometimes tapped separately

metal.lead.ingot.name: Refined lead ingot, 99.99%
metal.lead.ingot.description: Cast into 25 kg pigs or into 500 kg slabs. About two thirds of all the lead refined in the world was never made into a product in the refinery - it went straight into an alloy, most of it lead-acid battery plate and cable sheath. The solder industry took a small fraction, on the order of five to ten percent, and in 1982 that fraction was the entire basis of the electronics solder business. This is a deliberate convergence node: the blast furnace branch, the Parkes desilverisation branch and the solder branch all meet here.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) standard; 99.999% 'five nines' was available for special applications

facts.label: End use split
facts.value: batteries about 60%, cable sheath about 15%, solder about 5-10%

metal.lead.cupellation-lead.name: Cupellation of the silver dross to silver and gold
metal.lead.cupellation-lead.description: The dross from the Parkes process is mixed with lead and flux and cast into a 30-50 kg charge, which is placed in a cupellation furnace at 1000-1150 C and blown with air. The lead oxidises to litharge, PbO, which melts at 888 C and is absorbed by the porous cupel, while the silver and gold do not oxidise and stay on the surface. When all the lead is gone the silver is 96-99% pure and the gold is 30-50% of it; the gold is then cupelled again, or electrorefined, to 99.9%. So every lead bullion makes a small pile of very pure silver - a deliberate convergence of the lead and silver branches.
metal.lead.cupellation-lead.note: Points to metal.silver.ingot and metal.gold.ingot in the same tree.

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: 30-50 kg of dross with litharge and flux

facts.label: Products
facts.value: silver at 96-99%, gold dore at 30-50% Au

metal.lead.bullion.name: Crude lead bullion with silver and gold
metal.lead.bullion.description: Tapped at 950-1050 C, the bullion is about 95-98% lead with 1-3% silver, a little gold, and copper, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. Silver at 1-3% is not a trace - it is often the difference between a viable mine and a marginal one, and the Parkes process that recovers it is the reason lead smelters have a refinery at all. By 1982 crude lead was increasingly sold as a low-grade bullion to the refinery and the smelter/ refinery was one continuous plant.
metal.lead.bullion.note: Documented: the blast furnace yields lead bullion that goes to drossing, the crude bullion contains significant copper, and the Parkes process separates silver or gold from lead. Not established: the 95-98% Pb / 1-3% Ag / 10-100 g/t Au assay, the 250-800 g/t silver equivalent, and the 950-1050 C tap temperature.

facts.label: Wealth in the bullion
facts.value: order 250-800 g/t Ag equivalent

metal.lead.copper-drossing.name: Hot-dross the copper out of the lead bullion
metal.lead.copper-drossing.description: Before the Parkes zinc drossing, the bullion is hot-drossed for copper. The blast-furnace bullion comes out at 950-1050 C holding copper, which is insoluble in lead at that temperature and forms a separate copper matte that floats on top; the refinery skims it off, cools it, and recovers the copper and its precious metals by further processing. It is the same physical principle as the zinc drossing - a metal that mixes preferentially with another - and it is done first because the copper dross would otherwise interfere with the silver dross.
metal.lead.copper-drossing.note: Medium confidence; the sequence is standard and the copper figures are typical.

facts.label: Order
facts.value: hot copper drossing at 950-1050 C, then the Parkes zinc drossing at 400-500 C

facts.label: Bullion copper
facts.value: 0.2-1.5%, dropping to 0.02-0.06% after hot drossing

metal.lead.dross-smelting.name: Retorting the Parkes dross to recover the zinc
metal.lead.dross-smelting.description: After the silver has been skimmed off as dross, the dross itself has to be processed, and it is done in a cast-iron retort: the dross is mixed with charcoal and a little limestone, charged into a retort at 800-950 C, and the zinc distils out - it boils at 907 C - into a condenser where it is collected as a crude zinc metal. The silver and gold stay in the retort. A dross retort holds 100-500 kg and takes 8-20 hours, and a refinery had six to a dozen of them. The recovered zinc is dirty and goes back into the next drossing cycle, which is why the Parkes process consumes no net zinc even though it uses some every time round.
metal.lead.dross-smelting.note: Medium confidence; the retort practice is well described in the historical and metallurgical literature.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 800-950 C, above the 907 C boiling point of zinc inside the retort

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: 100-500 kg of dross with charcoal and limestone

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 8-20 h per retort

facts.label: Zinc balance
facts.value: the recovered zinc is returned to the drossing cycle, so net zinc consumption is small

metal.lead.dross-retort.name: The dross retort and its condenser
metal.lead.dross-retort.description: A cast-iron or steel tube, 1.5-3 m long, charged at one end and heated in a coke-fired setting, with a condenser of iron pipes at the cool end into which the zinc vapour condenses and runs out as a crude metal. The retort has to be skimmed of oxide and it is a batch process, so a refinery ran a bank of them in shifts. It is an object that is essentially unchanged since the 1850s, which makes it one of the oldest continuous processes in this file.
metal.lead.dross-retort.note: Medium confidence; the retort geometry is standard historical practice.

facts.label: Retort
facts.value: 1.5-3 m long cast iron, fired in a coke setting

facts.label: Condenser
facts.value: iron pipe condenser, crude zinc metal collecting in a pot

metal.lead.parkes.name: Parkes process: zinc drossing and desilverisation
metal.lead.parkes.description: The genius step, invented in 1850 and still standard in 1982. The molten bullion is stirred with a few tenths of a percent of zinc, which has a much stronger chemical affinity for silver than lead does, so a zinc-silver intermetallic (AgZn2, Ag2Zn5) migrates to the zinc 'dross' floating on top. The dross is skimmed, and the now-silver-poor lead is treated again with fresh zinc until it is down to 10-30 g/t silver. The dross is then distilled in a retort: zinc boils at 907 C and is condensed, and the silver and gold stay behind, to be cupelled. The zinc is a sacrificial reagent and goes back into the alloy.
metal.lead.parkes.note: The Parkes process is essentially unchanged since 1850 and is still in use today; that is unusual enough to be worth stating.

facts.label: Zinc addition
facts.value: 0.2-0.8% of the bullion mass

facts.label: Cycles
facts.value: 3-5 drossing and skimming stages

facts.label: Desilverised lead
facts.value: 10-30 g/t Ag (the 'corroding' grade)

facts.label: Retort distillation
facts.value: zinc distilled off at 800-950 C and condensed

facts.label: Second reagent
facts.value: the Parkes process is sometimes followed by the Harris 'throat' blow, which adds 0.1% Na and 0.06% Mg for copper and for the last of the silver

metal.lead.vacuum-degassing.name: Vacuum-degass and dross the lead bullion
metal.lead.vacuum-degassing.description: The modern version of both processes in one machine: a 6-10 m tall cylindrical steel vacuum vessel with an internal fractionating column. Molten lead is sprayed into the vacuum; the volatiles - hydrogen, oxygen, zinc, and the remaining silver on its way out - distil out and are fractionated, so the silver comes off as a separate metal rather than as a dross. It replaces two steps with one, cuts the labour, and gives 99.99% lead with under 5 g/t silver. It was the technology that spread through the lead industry in the 1980s, and it is a good marker for what was changing in smelting and what was not.
metal.lead.vacuum-degassing.note: The drossing tower was a genuine 1980s innovation in lead refining; medium confidence on the precise vacuum figures.

facts.label: Vacuum
facts.value: 0.1-1 mbar

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: lead at 700-850 C in a tall vessel

metal.lead.betts.name: Betts process: electrolytic refining
metal.lead.betts.description: The rival to the Parkes process, and the answer for the last fraction of a gram of bismuth. Anodes of impure lead are dissolved in a caustic soda solution containing sodium plumbite (Na2PbO3), and pure lead plates onto the cathode. The chemistry is unusual - the anode dissolves as plumbite and the deposit forms by the reaction of plumbite with metal, which is why the bath has to be kept in a narrow alkaline window. Cost is high, energy is high, so it was used only as a finishing step on top of the Parkes route, and in the 1980s it was being displaced by the Betterton-Krastchkow continuous drossing tower.
metal.lead.betts.note: The decline of the Betts process in the 1980s is well documented; medium confidence on the specific replacement technologies used by any given smelter.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: Na2PbO3 in caustic soda at 35-45 C

facts.label: 1982s position
facts.value: falling out of favour in favour of continuous drossing towers

metal.silver.amalgamation.name: Mercury amalgamation of small silver operations
metal.silver.amalgamation.description: Before cyanide, silver was recovered by amalgamating the crushed ore with mercury: 4Au + 8Hg -> 4AuHg4 and 4Ag + 4Hg -> 4Ag2Hg, then squeezing the amalgam in a heated press and retorting the sponge at 500-700 C to drive the mercury off and recover the metal. The process left 10-100 grams of mercury per tonne of ore behind in the tailings, and it is one of the largest anthropogenic mercury dispersals in history. In 1982 it was in decline in the large mines and still widespread in artisanal operations; in the small artisanal miners' union of Guanajuato it outlived the century.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Ag + Hg -> amalgam; retort at 500-700 C recovers the metal

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: 10-500 g of Hg per tonne of ore, most of it lost

facts.label: 1982 status
facts.value: declining in industry, persisting in artisanal mining

metal.mercury-source.name: Mercury: cinnabar from Idrija and Almaden
metal.mercury-source.description: Amalgamation consumes mercury and does not give it back, so a silver mine that amalgamated needed a mercury supply. Cinnabar, HgS, the vermilion pigment mineral, came from Idrija in Slovenia - the largest mercury mine in the world for 500 years - and from Almaden in Spain, and from the New Idria and New Almaden mines in California. The leaf is a mercury deposit, which is itself a strange one: cinnabar forms in shallow hydrothermal systems, and the Spanish and Yugoslav mines are in exactly the kind of fractured carbonate and volcanic rocks that the precious-metal branches of this file have already been through.
metal.mercury-source.note: The Idrija and Almaden mercury mines are well documented; medium confidence on the 1982 production split.

facts.label: Mineral
facts.value: cinnabar HgS, scarlet, with metacinnabar (black cubic)

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: epithermal and structurally controlled, in carbonate and volcanic host rocks

facts.label: 1982 supply note
facts.value: Idrija was still producing; the Idrija mercury plant closed in 1995

metal.cinnabar.bed.name: The cinnabar vein
metal.cinnabar.bed.description: The leaf: a scarlet vein of cinnabar in brecciated limestone, sometimes 10 m wide, worked by open pit and by fire-setting underground since Roman times. It is the only mercury ore that has ever mattered commercially, and it is a beautiful and rather grim example of a metal that exists in one mineral, in one setting, in a few places on Earth.

facts.label: Host
facts.value: brecciated and faulted carbonate rock, with clay and chalcedony

metal.silver.mine-mexican.name: The Zacatecas-Potosi silver vein mines
metal.silver.mine-mexican.description: Mines like the Fresnillo, the Zacatecas and the San Luis Potosi: an underground operation on steeply dipping epithermal quartz veins carrying native silver, argentite and the antimony sulphides, worked in the Spanish colonial era by water-driven mills, mercury amalgamation and patio amalgamation, and by 1982 by mechanised narrow-vein mining and flotation. The Fresnillo mine is a silver mine that also happens to be the world's largest producer of antimony, which is a neat illustration of the interpenetration of these branches.
metal.silver.mine-mexican.note: Amalgamation was still in use for small operations in the 1980s; the mid-1980s saw a strong shift to cyanide. Medium confidence.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: underground narrow-vein, sublevel or conventional stoping; flotation of the antimony sulphides

facts.label: Dating
facts.value: Zacatecas was producing silver from 1548

metal.gold.name: Gold: plating, bonding wire, contacts
metal.gold.description: A C64 contains perhaps 0.2-1 g of gold. It is the flash on the edge-connector fingers, the plating on the IC leads, the ball or wedge bond from the die pad to the package, and the contacts in the 'jewel' switch mechanisms. Gold is the only metal that does not tarnish and does not form an insulating oxide, which is the entire reason it is used where an electrical contact has to survive years untouched. All of that gold is refined to 99.99% from an ore averaging a few grams per tonne, and in 1982 essentially all of it came out of a cyanide leach.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) minimum for plating; 99.9995% (5N) for bonding wire

facts.label: Ore grade
facts.value: 0.5-8 g/t for open-pit and heap leach operations; underground veins run 5-30 g/t

facts.label: Leachant
facts.value: 0.01-0.05% NaCN in solution (100-500 mg/L)

facts.label: 1982 route
facts.value: cyanide leaching and carbon adsorption, plus amalgamation and gravity in older small operations

metal.gold.ingot.name: Refined gold anode, 99.99%, and the plated flash
metal.gold.ingot.description: The gold that reaches the electronics industry is 99.99% minimum, as a rolled sheet or an anode, and it is used in three ways. Flash plating for connector fingers and IC leads: the gold is dissolved in a cyanide gold bath - typically a gold cyanide, potassium cyanide, gold hydroxide bath at 0.5-2 g/L gold - and deposited on the nickel underplate at 0.1-1 A/dm2 for a few seconds, giving 0.05-0.25 um. Wire bonding: 15-50 um pure gold wire, drawn through diamond dies like copper, is welded from the die pad to the package lead with a thermosonic bonder. And sputtering: thin film resistors and the gold metallisation on some hybrid ICs were gold, sputtered from a cathode.
metal.gold.ingot.note: The thickness and bath figures are textbook ranges; I cannot confirm the specific plating specification on Commodore's connectors in 1982.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.99% (4N); bonding wire is 99.999% (5N)

facts.label: Flash thickness
facts.value: 0.05-0.25 um on connector fingers and leads

facts.label: Wire gauge
facts.value: 15-50 um (0.6-2 mil) gold bonding wire

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: gold cyanide / potassium cyanide with a gold hydroxide addition, 0.5-2 g/L Au

metal.gold.wire-bonding.name: Gold wire bonding of the die
metal.gold.wire-bonding.description: Each die has to be electrically connected to the package. The 1982 method was wire bonding: a 25 um gold or aluminium wire is threaded through a ceramic or carbide capillary, the tip is melted by a discharge or by a heated work holder, and the first weld is made to the die's aluminium pad. The wire is then run out and the second weld is made to the package bond pad, and the wire is cut. A 40-pin chip has 80 of these welds per package, each under a milligram of gold, and the whole thing happens a thousand times a minute. Aluminium bonding wire was already displacing gold on most logic parts by 1982 for cost reasons, but gold remained the default for anything requiring a conductive epoxy or a eutectic die attach.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 20-50 um gold or aluminium

facts.label: Methods
facts.value: thermasonic (ultrasonic plus heat), the 1980s default for gold

facts.label: Bonds per package
facts.value: order 80 for a 40-pin DIP

facts.label: Gold per bond
facts.value: order 0.05-0.3 mg

facts.label: Intermetallic
facts.value: Au-Al intermetallics form in the bond; the purple plague is AuAl2

metal.gold.contact-jewel.name: Gold-plated contacts: the edge connector and the switches
metal.gold.contact-jewel.description: Two very different gold contacts in the C64. The 62-way edge connector at the rear has gold-flashed fingers - a 35 um copper-alloy finger with 0.1-0.5 um of gold and a nickel underplate, inserted in the board by a wipe in the card guides. The keyboard and the rocker switches use either gold-plated copper-alloy leaf springs or, in the better keys, solid silver or silver-alloy contacts. The gold flash on the edge connector is the only place where gold must survive thousands of insertions, and it does so because the nickel underplate stops the copper from diffusing into the gold and the gold itself never oxidises.
metal.gold.contact-jewel.note: The gold flash thickness and the contact material choice on the actual Commodore keyboard I cannot confirm; these are the standard ranges. Medium confidence on the specifics, high on the metallurgy.

facts.label: Edge connector
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 um gold flash on 1-3 um nickel over a copper-alloy finger

facts.label: Insertion life
facts.value: 50,000-100,000 insertion cycles is a normal target for a gold-flashed card edge

facts.label: Why gold
facts.value: no oxide, no tarnish; noble metal does not form a resistive film

facts.label: Jewel switches
facts.value: some high-end switches used solid gold-alloy leaf springs, but 1982 consumer keyboards mostly used silver-plated or nickel-plated springs

metal.gold.cyanide-synthesis.name: Sodium cyanide from natural gas
metal.gold.cyanide-synthesis.description: Cyanide is an industrial chemical, not a mined material, and its feedstock is the same natural gas that makes hydrogen cyanide for acrylonitrile. The Andrussow process is the cheap one: natural gas plus ammonia plus oxygen over a platinum-rhodium catalyst at 900-1000 C gives hydrogen cyanide, which is absorbed in caustic to give sodium cyanide. So the cyanide that leaches the gold that plates the connector comes out of an ammonia-and-air reactor fed with methane.
metal.gold.cyanide-synthesis.note: Also a very high confidence node: sodium cyanide manufacture from HCN is exactly this reaction.

facts.label: Andrussow reaction
facts.value: CH4 + NH3 + 1.5 O2 -> HCN + 3H2O at 900-1000 C over Pt-Rh

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: HCN + NaOH -> NaCN + H2O

facts.label: Form sold
facts.value: solid briquettes or flakes of 80-85% NaCN; bulk solution at mines

metal.gold.cyanide-leach.name: Cyanide leaching of gold ore at pH 10-11
metal.gold.cyanide-leach.description: The reaction is 4Au + 8NaCN + O2 + 2H2O -> 4Na[Au(CN)2] + 4NaOH, and it needs three things: cyanide, lime to hold the pH at 10-11 so the cyanide does not protonate into deadly hydrogen cyanide gas, and dissolved oxygen. The pulp - ground ore plus lime, at 25-50% solids by mass - is agitated in an aerated pachuca tank or a Dorr agitator for 12-48 hours. The design variables are all about cyanide consumption, most of which is not gold dissolving but the cyanide reacting with the copper, iron and zinc minerals in the ore. In 1982 the plant that won was the one that kept the concentration as low as possible and the oxygen pressure as high as possible, which is the lesson of the 1986 Carbonin/Small's Pouso Bello mine disaster in Brazil, where 5-6 tonnes of cyanide went into the environment through a tailings dam failure and poisoned a river.

facts.label: NaCN
facts.value: 0.01-0.05% (100-500 mg/L), matched to the ore

facts.label: pH
facts.value: 10.0-11.0, held with lime or soda ash

facts.label: Solids
facts.value: 20-50% by mass

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 60-95% depending on the ore; refractory carbonaceous ores much less

metal.gold.miller.name: Miller chlorination and the Aubure process
metal.gold.miller.description: The refinery end. Gold doré - typically 90-95% gold with 5-10% silver - is fluxed with borax and litharge and blown with chlorine gas in an MRL (Mineral Resources Limited) chlorinator, heated by a propane torch, for 1-3 hours. The chlorine dissolves the gold as AuCl3 and the silver as AgCl, and the silver chloride precipitates as a crust. The gold is then stripped of the silver by the Aubure process - a hot parting - which reduces the silver chloride with wet wood chips and wet clay, a piece of technology that had not changed since the Middle Ages: the organic matter reduces the AgCl to metallic silver. What is left is gold at 99.5-99.9%, which is then electrorefined to 99.99% or cast directly into an anode.

facts.label: Chlorinator
facts.value: MRL/Merrill type, 350-1000 kg of doré per charge, propane-heated to 1000-1200 C

facts.label: Chlorine
facts.value: a continuous stream through a hollow lance into a molten salt flux

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 1-3 h per charge

facts.label: Parting
facts.value: Aubure: AgCl reduced by wood chips and clay

metal.gold.dore-melting.name: Melt the dore bars
metal.gold.dore-melting.description: Before the gold can be chlorinated it has to be melted, and the doré - whatever mixture of gold and silver the refinery is holding - is melted with a little borax and litharge in a clay or graphite crucible to 1000-1200 C and poured into a dore ingot weighing 20-50 kg. The litharge is what makes the dore pour cleanly, because it fluxes the oxide skin; it also means a little lead comes along, which is harmless because the next step takes it out. The dore is weighed and assayed, and that assay is the number on which the refinery is paid for the month's production.
metal.gold.dore-melting.note: Medium confidence; dore melting practice is standard and was unchanged from the 19th century.

facts.label: Charge
facts.value: 20-50 kg of doré with borax and litharge

facts.label: Flux
facts.value: borax plus litharge; the lead is removed in the chlorination step

metal.gold.electrorefining.name: Electrorefine the gold to 99.99%
metal.gold.electrorefining.description: The Doré is cast into anodes and dissolved in an aqueous solution of gold chloride in hydrochloric acid at 50-60 C. The electrolyte is the Wohlwill process electrolyte, with a little silver nitrate added to make the silver chloride stay solid and drop out. Gold plates onto a pure gold or platinum cathode at 99.99% and the whole refinery runs at 2-5 V with a very high current efficiency. Every gold refinery in the world in 1982 used the Wohlwill process and it is essentially unchanged today.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: AuCl3 in HCl, with 5-20 g/L AgNO3 added

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% (4N) cathode, 99.9995% (5N) possible

metal.gold.cip.name: Carbon-in-pulp and activated carbon adsorption
metal.gold.cip.description: Gold is present in the pregnant solution as the cyanide complex at only about 1 mg/L, far too dilute to precipitate or to recover directly. The industry fix is adsorption onto activated carbon: the slurry after leaching goes through a bank of 4-8 tall columns of 1.5-3 mm coconut-shell carbon, which takes up the gold. In carbon-in-pulp the carbon is instead added directly to the leach tanks and separated by a static or centrifugal screen. The carbon is then stripped in a hot caustic solution - with a few parts in a million of cyanide and, from the late 1970s, acetonitrile, which is what makes the strip efficient - and the gold is electrowon off a lead or stainless cathode, or smelted.

facts.label: Pregnant solution
facts.value: typically 0.5-5 mg/L Au in cyanide

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: 0.6-1.6 mm activated coconut or coal carbon, 5-10 kg/m3 of carbon

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 1,000-6,000 g Au per tonne of carbon

facts.label: Elution
facts.value: 1-2% NaOH at 90-120 C, with 100-500 ppm CN-; acetonitrile used from the late 1970s

facts.label: Stripped solution
facts.value: 20-200 mg/L Au, electrowon to a 99.5% melt

facts.label: Carbon loss
facts.value: carbon is regenerated by acid and steam at 700-1000 C and reused

metal.activated-carbon.name: Activated carbon from coconut shell
metal.activated-carbon.description: The adsorbent is a botanical product, not a mineral: coconut or palm-kernel shell, or coal, carbonised at 500-900 C and steam-activated at 800-1000 C until the pore volume is about half the material's bulk volume. The pore structure is what holds the gold cyanide. So the carbon in the carbon-in-pulp column is a plantation or coal-mill product, and by the 1980s activated carbon was becoming an industrial commodity in its own right.
metal.activated-carbon.note: The 1980s activated carbon industry shifted toward coal and later petroleum coke because coconut shell became scarce and expensive; medium confidence on the timing.

facts.label: Activation
facts.value: steam at 800-1000 C

facts.label: Surface area
facts.value: 700-1200 m2/g for the best grades

facts.label: Feedstock
facts.value: coconut shell, wood, hard coal, and in 1982 increasingly petroleum coke

metal.activated-carbon.coal.name: Hard coal and petroleum coke as activated carbon feed
metal.activated-carbon.coal.description: By 1982 the industry was moving off coconut shell, which had become scarce and expensive as the plastics and activated-carbon markets grew, onto hard coal and - as the process matured - onto delayed petroleum coke, which has the right isotropic pore structure and essentially no ash. The activation is the same: carbonise, then blow steam at 800-1000 C to burn out the carbon and open the pores, giving a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. So the carbon in a carbon-in-pulp gold plant in the 1980s was often made from the same coke as the aluminium anode and the coke battery electrode, which is one of the more unexpected places this tree's carbon converges.
metal.activated-carbon.coal.note: The shift to petroleum-coke feed for activated carbon was a genuine 1980s trend; medium confidence on the timing.

facts.label: Feedstocks
facts.value: coconut shell, hard coal, and increasingly petroleum coke

facts.label: Surface area
facts.value: 700-1200 m2/g for the best grades

facts.label: Ash
facts.value: coke-derived carbon is essentially ash-free, which is why gold plants wanted it

metal.steam-activation.name: Activate the carbon with steam at 800-1000 C
metal.steam-activation.description: The step that makes charcoal into activated carbon. A bed of coke or coal is held at 800-1000 C while steam and carbon dioxide are passed over it, and the gas burns the carbon away, opening a pore structure with a surface area of 700-1200 m2/g. The rate of the burn is the whole process: too fast and the structure collapses, too slow and the pores are too small to admit the gold cyanide complex. The gold is adsorbed as the ion-pair Au(CN)2- at the carbon surface, so the carbon's chemistry is an ion-exchange chemistry rather than a physical adsorption, which is why the carbon has to be chemically clean and why it has to be regenerated before its capacity falls too far.
metal.steam-activation.note: Medium confidence on the mechanism being ion exchange rather than purely physical; it is the standard description but the mechanism is genuinely not fully settled.

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 800-1000 C with steam and carbon dioxide

facts.label: Adsorption
facts.value: the Au(CN)2- ion pair, i.e. an ion-exchange mechanism

metal.gold.pachuca.name: Pachuca tank and the Dorr agitator
metal.gold.pachuca.description: The 1982 standard leach vessel was either a Pachuca tank - a tall cylindrical tank with a cone at the bottom and a compressed-air rising pipe that boils the pulp like a carbonated drink - or a Dorr agitator, a vertical tank with a rotating central shaft and radial arms and baffles. A typical circuit was 4-8 tanks of 30-60 m diameter in series, 6 m deep, with the air line serving as both the agitator and the oxygen supply. Life before the mid-1980s the industry moved to Dorr thickeners and to the large rectangular Dorr-Oliver leach tanks.
metal.gold.pachuca.note: Air consumption figures are class values from mineral processing textbooks; medium confidence.

facts.label: Tank
facts.value: 30-60 m diameter, 5-8 m deep, 4-8 in series

facts.label: Air
facts.value: 0.3-1.5 Nm3 per m3 of slurry per minute

metal.gold.ore.name: Low-grade gold ore (0.5-5 g/t)
metal.gold.ore.description: Gold at a few parts per million is not visible and not dense in a hand specimen - it is in the ore as discrete grains, often only microns across, or in tellurides. Most of it is in quartz veins, often with sulfides. The 1982 world had two completely different industries: the deep underground Witwatersrand, where a 15 cm face of reef at 10-40 g/t gave 100,000 tonnes a day through mills, and the Carlin trend and the Nevada heap leaches, where 0.5-2 g/t in oxide rock was stacked in 10 m heaps and leached in place. The heap leach was a genuine 1970s invention and by 1982 it had become a third of Nevada's production.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 0.5-8 g/t open pit and heap leach; 5-30 g/t underground vein

facts.label: Host
facts.value: quartz veins (lode gold), disseminated in carbonate and jasperoid (Carlin-type), and reef conglomerate (Witwatersrand)

facts.label: Precious-metal credits
facts.value: typically 1-3% of the ore's gross value is silver

metal.gold.wits-mine.name: Witwatersrand underground gold mining
metal.gold.wits-mine.description: The other end of the industry. A 15 cm to 3 m band of gold-bearing conglomerate called 'the reef' lies at 1000-6000 m below the Witwatersrand, and from 1886 to 1982 the industry sank shafts and drove long decline haulages and ventilation and cooling galleries into it. Ventilation was the limiting factor: rock at 3000 m is at 40-50 C because of the geothermal gradient and because the rock is 3-6 C warmer than surface, so a mine 4 km deep needed refrigeration and a shaft fan development that took hours to boost air through the raises. Each shift broke perhaps 30,000 tonnes of reef in the mine and treated 100,000 tonnes in the plant, so the metallurgy was crushing a very hard quartzite and recovering maybe 60-70% of a 10-40 g/t ore.
metal.gold.wits-mine.note: Documented: gold mining in the buried parts of the Witwatersrand Supergroup is carried out at depths of 4 km below the surface. Not established: the 1000-6000 m depth range as a mine-by-mine figure, the 40-50 C rock temperature at 3000 m, the 3 C per 100 m gradient, the 20,000-40,000 t broken per shift, the longwall stoping with hydraulic sand fill, and the 60-70% recovery from a 10-40 g/t ore.

facts.label: Mine production
facts.value: order 20,000-40,000 t of ore broken per shift

facts.label: Rock temperature
facts.value: geothermal gradient of ~3 C per 100 m, giving 40-50 C at depth

facts.label: Mining method
facts.value: long-wall stopes, stepped, backfilled with a sand-and-cement fill from a hydraulic stope

metal.gold.reef.name: Witwatersrand gold reef conglomerate
metal.gold.reef.description: The leaf: a 2.9 billion year old quartzite with rounded pebbles of quartz and jasper in a fine matrix - a fossil beach. The gold is in the matrix, as discrete grains a few microns across, and the deepest part of the deposit has the highest grade because it is the oldest and the most distal. It is one of the largest gold concentrations ever formed and it is a sediment.
metal.gold.reef.note: Documented: gold sits in the conglomerate strata called banket, in layers the miners call reefs, where it occurs in streaks rather than uniformly, associated with pyrite and uraninite. One claim here is contradicted: the reference says the gold-bearing conglomerates occur chiefly in the upper, younger layers of the Supergroup, not in the deepest part, and the Supergroup is dated from about 2.97 Ga with the gold-bearing units among the younger members. Not established: the 2.9 Ga age as the age of the reef itself and the 5-40 g/t Far West Deep grade.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: quartzite with quartz and jasper pebbles, 2.9 Ga

facts.label: Gold
facts.value: fine grains in the matrix, 5-40 g/t in the Far West Deep

metal.gold.uraninite.name: The uraninite in the Witwatersrand reef
metal.gold.uraninite.description: The gold reef is also the world's largest gold-uranium conglomerate, and the same reef that was being mined for gold was being mined for uranium by a separate set of shafts from the 1950s onwards. The uraninite is present as discrete grains on the carbon seams, and it recovers in the gold plant's gravity circuits and in the tailings retreatment plants. So the uranium in the C64's power supply - in a 1982 it might have been a South African or Canadian utility's grid, but the fuel cycle is the same one - began in the same bed as the gold on the edge connectors. It is the single best example in this tree of one layer of rock supplying two unrelated metals.
metal.gold.uraninite.note: Medium confidence on the uranium grade figures; the co-occurrence of gold and uranium in the Witwatersrand is very well established but the grade varies enormously between reefs.

facts.label: Uranium grade
facts.value: roughly 0.5-3 kg of U per tonne of reef in the uranium-bearing zones

facts.label: Form
facts.value: uraninite grains on the carbon seams, released by weathering

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: with the gold, in the gravity and flotation circuits and later in tailings retreatment

metal.gold.heap-leach.name: Heap leaching with cyanide, 10 m pads
metal.gold.heap-leach.description: Run-of-mine ore, after a cyanide spray test, is crushed to a few centimetres and stacked in 100,000-tonne heaps on an impermeable pad. It is flooded with 0.02-0.05% NaCN solution, allowed to percolate for 30-60 days, and then drained and sprayed again. The pregnant solution is sent through a carbon bed and then an electrowinning cell. A heap-leach pad is a piece of civil engineering first and a chemical plant second: the entire economics depend on the liner holding and the pad draining properly, and the cyanide inventory on a large heap is the largest single cyanide hazard in mining. After the leach the cyanide is destroyed with lime and ferrous sulphate and the pad is detoxified before closure.

facts.label: Solution
facts.value: 0.02-0.05% NaCN (200-500 mg/L), with lime to pH 10-11

facts.label: Heap
facts.value: 50,000-400,000 t, 6-12 m high, irrigated for 30-60 days

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 50-75% for a well-oxidised ore

facts.label: Detoxification
facts.value: lime plus ferrous sulphate to convert CN- to cyanate

metal.chromium.name: Chromium: stainless, ferrochrome, hard chrome
metal.chromium.description: Chromium does three separate jobs: it makes stainless steel stainless, it is the alloying element in the NiCr film resistors on the board, and as hexavalent chromium it is the hard chrome plating on switch contacts, the keyboard frame hinges and the RF shielding. The plating chemistry is the one with a body of regulation attached to it, and the ferrochrome industry is a South African monopoly that gave apartheid-era South Africa its nickname 'Chrome City'.

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: chromite FeCr2O4, 30-45% Cr2O3

facts.label: Refined form
facts.value: ferrochrome, 60-70% Cr, and chromium metal

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: ~95% of world ferrochrome capacity was in South Africa in the early 1980s

facts.label: Electrolytic chromium
facts.value: a few thousand tonnes a year of 99.9% metal, for plating chemistry and sputtering targets

metal.chromate-passivation.name: Chromate conversion coating
metal.chromate-passivation.description: A nitric acid or chromic acid bath - most often a sodium dichromate bath in 1982 - converts a zinc, tin or cadmium surface to a chromium oxide-hydroxide film a few hundred nanometres thick. Yellow is dichromate, olive is chromic acid, and the black 'iridium' used on some zinc die castings is a different chromate chemistry altogether. This is where the electronics industry met hexavalent chromium: not only in the plating baths but on every chromate-passivated steel part, on every tin-plated part that went through a passivation tank, and in the anode foil formation treatment. It is the reason the OSHA hexavalent chromium standard, published in 1971, was one of the first such rules in the United States, and it is a deliberate convergence point of the zinc, tin, aluminium-foil and chromium branches.
metal.chromate-passivation.note: This node is the third of chromium's three markets - ferrochrome into stainless steel, electrolytic metal into the plating bath, and chromate conversion on the plated surface - so it is deliberately given two parents, the chromium branch and metal.zinc.electroplate.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: sodium dichromate plus nitric acid, 5-30 s at room temperature

facts.label: Film
facts.value: ~0.1-0.5 um of mixed chromium oxide-hydroxide

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) in the film, which is why the dried chromate coating itself is not toxic

facts.label: Applicable to
facts.value: zinc electroplate, tinplate, cadmium, and aluminium anode foil formation treatments

metal.chromium.metal.name: Electrolytic chromium metal from chrome alum
metal.chromium.metal.description: Pure chromium metal - for the chromium plating chemistry and for chromium sputtering targets - is made the opposite way to ferrochrome: hydrometallurgically. Chromite is roasted with soda ash to a water-soluble sodium chromate, the chromate is leached, the hexavalent chromium is reduced to trivalent in an acid solution, and the metal is electrowon onto a lead cathode to 99.9%. It is a short, small industry - a few thousand tonnes a year of a metal worth a great deal. The chrome alum the world consumed came largely from chemical processing plants, and the sulphur dioxide from the roast was a nuisance that pre-1950 plants simply released. The same hydrometallurgical route also produced the sodium chromate that went into the chromate conversion coatings of the zinc and tin plating branches.
metal.chromium.metal.note: The hydrometallurgical chromium route is well documented; medium confidence on the exact 1982 process parameters.

facts.label: Roast
facts.value: 500-700 C with soda ash, to water-soluble sodium chromate

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: sodium metabisulphite to Cr(III) as chrome alum

facts.label: Electrowinning
facts.value: lead cathode, low voltage, to 99.9% Cr

metal.chromium.metal.cell.name: Chromium electrowinning cell and the diaphragm
metal.chromium.metal.cell.description: Chromium is electrowon from a trivalent chromium sulphate solution at 5-8 V with a lead or lead-alloy cathode, in cells separated by a diaphragm - traditionally asbestos cloth, later a synthetic fibre - because the anodic chlorine would otherwise oxidise the trivalent chromium back and the two would meet and precipitate. The product is 99.9% chromium at 80-90% current efficiency. The cell room is the most noxious part of the whole chromium industry: hexavalent chromium in the feed, acidic mist, and an operator who must be in a respirator.
metal.chromium.metal.cell.note: Low confidence on the cellroom details; this part of the industry is poorly documented outside the chrome plating literature, where the figures for chromium metal electrowinning are not commonly given.

facts.label: Cathode
facts.value: lead or lead alloy

facts.label: Diaphragm
facts.value: asbestos cloth, later synthetic fibre

metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm.name: The diaphragm and the asbestos inheritance
metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm.description: The cell needs the anodic chlorine kept away from the trivalent chromium in the catholyte, and the membrane that does that was, until the 1980s, asbestos cloth - the same asbestos as the chlor-alkali diaphragm cells. So the chromium and chlor-alkali industries of the early twentieth century share a materials problem that was only being dealt with in the 1980s, in both cases by a conversion programme driven by worker exposure rather than by metallurgy. The 1982 answer was a synthetic fibre diaphragm, which worked and cost more.
metal.chromium.cell.diaphragm.note: Low confidence on the specific 1982 chromium cell diaphragm practice; the asbestos overlap with chlor-alkali is real, but the chromium side of it is inferred.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: asbestos cloth, replaced by synthetic fibre and PTFE-lined designs through the 1980s

metal.hex-chrome-plating.name: Hexavalent chromium electroplating bath
metal.hex-chrome-plating.description: The classic chromiumic acid bath: CrO3 at 50-250 g/L in dilute sulfuric acid at 100-250 g/L, run at 45-60 C, 3-7 V, 15-60 A/dm2, with a lead-lead dioxide anode. A special steel anode is used and the bath is extremely hard to waste-treat: the chromium has to get from Cr(VI) down to Cr(III) before it can be precipitated. Cr(VI) is acutely and cumulatively toxic with a demonstrated carcinogenicity, and the 1971 OSHA standard for airborne hexavalent chromium was one of the first such rules in the United States. A C64's hard chrome on the switch contacts, the case hinges and the shield-contact points would have been plated in a plant subject to it.
metal.hex-chrome-plating.note: Hexavalent chromium plating is essentially unchanged since the 1980s except for the trivalent and hex-free alternatives developed after 2000; high confidence on the chemistry.

facts.label: Voltage and current
facts.value: 3-7 V, 15-60 A/dm2 for hard chrome

facts.label: Anode
facts.value: lead-lead dioxide; 5-15% Sn-Pb alloy

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: an automatic catalyst based on sulphate, in the 1980s

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: OSHA standard on airborne hexavalent chromium, 1971

metal.chromium.aod.name: Argon-oxygen decarburisation and the stainless vessel
metal.chromium.aod.description: The step that makes stainless steel possible. A 300-450 tonne ladle is fitted with a lance that injects a mixture of argon and oxygen under the steel surface. The argon stirs the melt and dilutes the carbon, the oxygen burns carbon to carbon monoxide, and because the gas is argon rather than air the melt does not pick up nitrogen - and nitrogen is exactly what stops 304 from being fully austenitic. At the end the gas is switched to pure oxygen and then back to argon to dilute the carbon without oxidising the chromium. The whole cycle takes 40-90 minutes and takes carbon from about 0.6% down to 0.03%, and it is why a stainless melt shop looks like nothing else in the steel industry. A deliberate convergence point of the chromium, nickel, ferrochrome and steel branches.

facts.label: Ladle
facts.value: 300-450 t, with a submerged lance

facts.label: Gas
facts.value: ~78% Ar / 22% O2 initially, rising to pure O2, then back to Ar

facts.label: Chromium loss
facts.value: some chromia goes to the bath, recovered from ferrochrome dust

metal.chromium.aod.lance.name: The AOD lance and its tuyere block
metal.chromium.aod.lance.description: The lance is a 10-25 cm carbon-molybdenum or refractory tube lowered into the metal on a mast, and it carries both the argon and the oxygen. Around it sits a refractory tuyere block in the ladle lining with a single small hole through which the gas is injected into the melt, so the gas is introduced a few hundred millimetres below the surface and the stirring is far more effective than a surface lance. The lance itself is a consumable: the oxygen attacks the tip, and a lance lasts one heat or a few hours, so there is a pile of spent lances outside every AOD vessel.
metal.chromium.aod.lance.note: Medium confidence; the lance geometry and injection depth are standard practice.

facts.label: Lance
facts.value: 10-25 cm diameter, carbon-molybdenum, a consumable

facts.label: Injection depth
facts.value: 200-500 mm below the metal surface

facts.label: Argon flow
facts.value: 0.1-0.5 Nm3 per minute per tonne of steel

metal.refractory-ladle.name: The refractory ladle lining
metal.refractory-ladle.description: The AOD vessel is lined with magnesia or with magnesia-carbon, and the slag at pH 5 or higher eats a basic lining - which is why a stainless ladle lining is more expensive and more carefully maintained than a mild steel one. The lining is a consumable of its own, replaced every few hundred heats. So the chromium branch reaches the bottom not only in an ore body but in a sea of magnesia sand, and the magnesia is from seawater or from a magnesite mine.
metal.refractory-ladle.note: Medium confidence; the magnesia supply chain is well documented but is not part of this subsystem's requested scope.

facts.label: Lining
facts.value: magnesia or magnesia-carbon brick, 200-300 mm

facts.label: Feedstock
facts.value: dead-burnt magnesite (MgCO3) or seawater magnesia (Mg(OH)2)

metal.chromium.stainless-use.name: Where the chromium ends up in a 1982 C64
