metal.chromium.stainless-use.description: AISI 304 in the audio jack shell, the shield cans and any stainless fastener or bracket; 430 where a magnetic ferritic grade was wanted. Chromium at 18% is above the roughly 11% needed for the surface to passivate, which is the whole trick: chromium forms a self-healing chromium oxide film about 2 nm thick, and that film is why stainless does not corrode. The passivation step in nitric acid is what removes the free iron that welding and machining leave on the surface, and without it the stainless rusts.
metal.chromium.stainless-use.note: The passivation chemistry is standard; whether Commodore's specific parts were passivated in manufacture is medium confidence.

facts.label: Cr in 304
facts.value: 18%, well above the ~11% passivation threshold

facts.label: Passive film
facts.value: ~1-5 nm of chromium(III) oxide

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: 20-30% nitric acid, room temperature or 50 C, 30 min

metal.ferrochrome.name: High-carbon ferrochrome, 60-70% Cr
metal.ferrochrome.description: Chromite ore and coke are charged into a submerged arc furnace at 1400-1600 C with a chromite self-fluxing slag, and the result is an alloy of 60-70% chromium, 1-3% silicon and 5-8% carbon. It consumes about 500-700 kWh per tonne of ferrochrome - a fifth of aluminium's energy per tonne but on a much smaller tonnage. In the 1980s the industry was the classic vertically integrated single-industry town: the chromite mine, the power station with its 400 MW supply contract, and the smelter were all owned by the same company in the same town. The 1982-85 US and European voluntary export restraints on ferrochrome were aimed squarely at the market power of one country, and it is why ferrochrome is one of the very few metals where the 1982 price environment is a real story.
metal.ferrochrome.note: Explicit correction of the brief's framing of chromium: the chromite-to-ferrochrome branch is dominated by South Africa, not by any American or European mine, and the 1982-85 export restraint is the period's defining event in it.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 25-105 MVA, three electrodes, 1400-1600 C

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: 60-70% Cr, 1-3% Si, 5-8% C, balance iron

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 500-700 kWh per tonne of ferrochrome

facts.label: 1982-85 trade measure
facts.value: the United States and the European Community imposed voluntary export restraints on ferrochrome

metal.ferrochrome.slag.name: The self-fluxing chromite slag
metal.ferrochrome.slag.description: A ferrochrome furnace is self-fluxing, which means the ore's own silica is balanced by the ore's own magnesia and there is nothing to add - the chromite is 16% MgO and 20% SiO2 and the ratio of the two is already about right for a liquid slag at 1500 C. That is why the smelter does not need lime, and it is also why the ore is smelted as it is rather than being beneficiated: a ferrochrome plant is a furnace and a power station, and the beneficiation happens in the ore dressing only if the ore is too fine to charge.
metal.ferrochrome.slag.note: Medium confidence on the exact oxide balance; the self-fluxing character of chromite is well established.

facts.label: Slag basicity
facts.value: MgO/SiO2 about 0.8-1.0, so no lime is needed

metal.chromite.name: Chromite ore (FeCr2O4), 38-46% Cr2O3
metal.chromite.description: A hard, black, opaque spinel - FeO plus chromium oxide in a cubic lattice - that occurs not as veins but as layer after layer in the lower part of the Bushveld Complex and the Transvaal Group. It is unusually resistant to both chemical attack and heat, which is why chromite is also found in beach placer sands in Oregon and California, and it is effectively the only chromium ore of commercial scale. The Bushveld chromite pits run 200 m deep on a 1-6 m seam, which is one of the more extreme geometries in mining. This is a convergence node for the ferrochrome furnace, the AOD vessel and the chromium metal plant.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 38-46% Cr2O3 for smelter-grade chromite

facts.label: Occurrence
facts.value: layered in the Lower Zone of the Bushveld Complex and the Transvaal Group

facts.label: Other sources
facts.value: Kemi in Finland, the Appalachian and Oregon beach sands, Kazakhstan and Zimbabwe

metal.chromite.mine.name: Layer-seam chromite open pit, 200 m deep
metal.chromite.mine.description: The Bushveld chromite mines are among the deepest and most geometrically awkward open pits in the world. A 1-6 m chromitite layer is covered by 100-200 m of layered norite, and the pit must be advanced strip by strip along the seam, so the benches are narrow and the truck travels a long way for every tonne. The waste is platinum-group ore, so the chromite mines and the platinum mines are the same mines, and their combined revenue is what made the region what it is. The ore is crushed to about 100 mm and shipped to a smelter, sometimes 400 km away.
metal.chromite.mine.note: Documented: chromite forms in layered intrusions as layers from 1 cm to 1 m thick, laterally up to 70 km, and the Bushveld is the type example with chromitite layers and PGM reefs. Not established: the 0.5-6 m seam, the 100-200 m norite cover, the 150-300 m pit depth, the crushing to about 100 mm and the 400 km haul - so the claim that these are among the deepest and most awkward open pits in the world is unsupported.

facts.label: Seam thickness
facts.value: 0.5-6 m chromitite layer

facts.label: Cover
facts.value: 100-200 m of layered norite and pyroxenite

facts.label: Co-product
facts.value: the waste rock is platinum-group ore

metal.chromite.bench.name: Following a seam: the narrow-bench problem
metal.chromite.bench.description: A normal open pit advances in benches 15 m high and 100-200 m wide, with haul roads on every bench. A chromite seam is 1-6 m thick, so the pit has to advance along the seam instead, and the benches are 100-200 m high with a 5-10 m working width and a haul road cut into the wall. The consequence is a bench width of a few tens of metres where a truck needs twenty, so the ore is either hauled a long way or handled by a shovel that strips the ore off the face and tips it down to a loading point on the bench floor. That is why the Bushveld pits look nothing like an iron ore pit even though they move similar tonnages, and it is a nice demonstration that mining cost is a function of geometry before it is a function of the rock.
metal.chromite.bench.note: Medium confidence; the geometry argument is sound and the specific figures are representative of the Bushveld pits.

facts.label: Bench
facts.value: 100-200 m high with a 5-10 m working width

facts.label: Advance
facts.value: along the seam, not across it

facts.label: Truck requirement
facts.value: order 20 m of road width, more than the seam provides

metal.chromite.layered.name: Layered norite of the Bushveld Complex
metal.chromite.layered.description: The leaf: a 2 km thick layered mafic intrusion with a spectacularly regular magmatic stratification - a metre-scale layering of plagioclase and pyroxene laid down by a magma chamber over about a million years - with the chromite concentrating into a single thin seam at one horizon. It is the single most chromium-rich geological structure on Earth.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: layered norite, pyroxenite and anorthosite with a chromitite seam

facts.label: Age
facts.value: about 2.05 billion years

metal.chromite.merensky.name: The Merensky Reef: the same layer as the chrome
metal.chromite.merensky.description: Just below the chromitite seams of the Bushveld Complex lies a 0.4-1 m layer of pyroxenite carrying 3-8 g/t of platinum-group metals - the Merensky Reef - and it is the reason the chromite is mined as it is. The waste from a chromite pit is a platinum ore, so the two industries are financially intertwined, and the chromite pits were dug by companies that made their real money on platinum. So a chrome-bearing steel for the key plungers of a computer came out of a pit whose main product was a catalyst for a chemical that is not in this tree at all.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: 3-8 g/t of platinum-group metals

facts.label: Relationship
facts.value: lies directly beneath the chromitite seams

metal.manganese.name: Manganese: the steel deoxidiser
metal.manganese.description: Manganese has no visible place in a C64, but without it the steel the case and the shielding are made from would have inclusions and blowholes in it. Almost all manganese ore is used to make ferromanganese, which is added to the steelmaking furnace as a deoxidiser and desulphuriser and as an alloying element. It is a branch included because the steel branch cannot honestly stop without it.

facts.label: Refined form
facts.value: ferromanganese, most commonly high-carbon at 6-8% C

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: pyrolusite MnO2 at 30-50% Mn; the 'manganese nodules' on the abyssal plains held most of the world's reserve

metal.manganese.ladle-charging.name: Charge the ferromanganese into the steel ladle
metal.manganese.ladle-charging.description: A ladle of steel is a bad place to drop a lump of ferromanganese, because the lump floats, the reaction is violent and the steel is left with unreacted alloy inclusions. So the FeMn is added in sized lumps and, increasingly in the 1980s, in cored wire - a steel tube filled with powdered ferromanganese and flux, fed into the ladle on a lance and dissolved by the passage of the steel through it. Cored-wire charging was a genuine 1980s development in secondary metallurgy and it improved the yield of the manganese, because it puts the metal into the steel rather than onto it.
metal.manganese.ladle-charging.note: Medium confidence; cored-wire charging of ferroalloys is well documented in secondary-metallurgy practice.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sized lumps, or cored wire on a ladle lance

facts.label: Why
facts.value: a lump floats and reacts only at the surface; cored wire dissolves below the surface and gives a higher yield

facts.label: Typical addition
facts.value: order 1 kg of FeMn per tonne of steel

metal.ferromanganese.name: High-carbon ferromanganese, Mn 65-80%, C 6-8%
metal.ferromanganese.description: Made in a submerged arc furnace, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, at 1400-1600 C with the electrode tips submerged in the slag. The charge is sintered manganese ore, coke, limestone and often a good deal of iron ore, because the aim is an alloy of about 70% manganese at 6-8% carbon, and manganese is expensive enough that the industry buys more ore than stoichiometry requires in order to reach the assay. The manganese comes out as a carbide, Mn7C3, not as the metal, which is why the alloy has a carbon content at all. CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: high-carbon ferromanganese is 6-8% C, not 13-15%; medium-carbon is 1-4% and low-carbon is under 0.5%, so 13-15% is not a real grade.
metal.ferromanganese.note: Correction to the brief: 6-8% C for high-carbon ferromanganese, not 13-15%. Confidence high on the grades; the furnace size range is a class figure.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 25-100 MVA, three electrodes, 1400-1600 C

facts.label: Medium and low carbon
facts.value: C 1-4% and C below 0.5%

facts.label: Phase
facts.value: manganese is present as carbide, mostly Mn7C3

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: roughly 1.0-1.5 kg of FeMn per tonne of steel made

metal.manganese.smelter-electricity.name: Why a ferroalloy smelter is built beside its power station
metal.manganese.smelter-electricity.description: A 100 MVA submerged arc furnace draws about 80-90 MW continuously and cannot be stopped without destroying the furnace. So it needs a long-term supply contract and, in most cases, its own generating plant or a dedicated hydro or coal share. In the 1980s several ferroalloy industries - Norway's ferrochrome and ferrosilicon, South Africa's ferrochrome, Norway and Quebec's ferrosilicon - were built around cheap hydropower, and the industry's geography is essentially a map of where the cheap electricity was. It is the same fact as the aluminium smelter's, and the reason the same two or three countries dominated both.
metal.manganese.smelter-electricity.note: The energy figures are consistent across the ferroalloy literature; medium confidence on the exact values by product.

facts.label: Furnace load
facts.value: 80-90 MW continuous for a 100 MVA unit

facts.label: Energy per tonne
facts.value: 3,000-6,000 kWh for ferromanganese; 8,000-11,000 for ferrosilicon; 500-700 for ferrochrome

metal.manganese.furnace-lining.name: The submerged arc furnace and its refractory
metal.manganese.furnace-lining.description: A ferromanganese furnace is 25-100 MVA with three electrodes 1.5-2.0 m in diameter, and the difference from a silicon furnace is the slag: the ferromanganese process makes a large volume of a liquid, low-basicity slag, so the furnace is a slag vessel with an electrode in it. The shell is steel with a refractory lining of magnesite or magnesite-carbon, and the lining is eroded by the slag at 1500 C faster than in a silicon furnace. Carbon pastes, electrode paste made of the same coke-and-pitch as the aluminium anode, are rammed into holes in the roof around each electrode. So a ferromanganese plant is a coke-and-pitch shop as much as a manganese shop, which is the same convergence as the ferrochrome and ferrosilicon branches.
metal.manganese.furnace-lining.note: Medium confidence; the ferromanganese furnace design is well described in ferroalloy practice.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: 25-100 MVA, three electrodes 1.5-2.0 m diameter, 1400-1600 C

facts.label: Lining
facts.value: magnesite or magnesite-carbon, eroded by the low-basicity slag

facts.label: Electrode paste
facts.value: rammed into roof holes, made of coke and pitch

metal.graphite.electrode.name: Graphite and carbon electrodes
metal.graphite.electrode.description: The EAF electrodes, the submerged arc furnace electrodes of the ferrosilicon, ferrochrome and ferromanganese industries, the aluminium pot anodes, the silicon furnace electrodes and the large carbon blocks of a blast furnace hearth all consume the same two feedstocks: calcined petroleum or needle coke, and coal-tar pitch as the binder. A 'graphite' electrode is green-milled from petroleum coke, extruded, and baked above 2500 C; a 'carbon' electrode stops at 800-1200 C. Pitch coke dominates for the graphite grades because it gives the higher density and the lower ash.
metal.graphite.electrode.note: Pitch coke is the highest-grade carbon feedstock and is itself a coke-oven by-product; see metal.coke in this file for the oven that makes the tar.

facts.label: Graphite grade
facts.value: baked at 2500-3000 C, ash <1%, density ~2.2 g/cm3

facts.label: Carbon grade
facts.value: baked at 800-1200 C, ash 2-5%, density ~1.6-1.8 g/cm3

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: 20-30% coal-tar pitch

facts.label: Diameters in 1982
facts.value: 75-350 mm for electrodes; 400-1000 mm for pot anodes and hearth blocks

metal.manganese.deoxidiser.name: Deoxidation and desulphurisation in the steel ladle
metal.manganese.deoxidiser.description: Where the alloy is actually used. During tapping, ferromanganese is added to the steel. Manganese has a higher oxygen affinity than iron, so it combines with the dissolved oxygen to form MnO inclusions - which is the point: the oxygen is now safely tied up in an oxide the steelmaker can float out instead of being trapped as a gas bubble or an oxide stringer. Manganese also lowers the sulphur by forming MnS. The cost is that every kilo of manganese added becomes an inclusion unless the steel is properly deoxidised and the slag properly cleaned, which is why the amount is carefully calculated and why clean, low-inclusion steel is a specific technical achievement.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Mn + [O] -> MnO, and Mn + [S] -> MnS

facts.label: Dosage
facts.value: roughly 1.0-1.5 kg of FeMn per tonne of steel

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: during tapping or in the ladle, before the degasser

metal.manganese.inclusion-removal.name: Removing the inclusions: degassing and filtration
metal.manganese.inclusion-removal.description: A modern low-sulphur steel has few MnS inclusions but a lot of fine Al2O3, and that is a different problem: fine alumina does not float out, so it has to be filtered. A 1980s plate mill that wanted clean, formable sheet for deep drawing or for tinplating ran a ladle through a vacuum degasser to flush hydrogen and nitrogen and then through a ceramic foam filter in the ladle, or poured through a tundish filter. This is the technology that made the C64's chassis panel and the tinplate base material reproducible rather than lucky.
metal.manganese.inclusion-removal.note: The filtration step is a genuine 1980s development; medium confidence on the specific purity targets.

facts.label: Vacuum
facts.value: <10 mbar, 10-25 min, with argon stirring

facts.label: Filter
facts.value: ceramic foam, 0.4-1.0 mm pore, in the ladle or the tundish

facts.label: Target
facts.value: total oxygen below 20 ppm and sulphur below 0.005% for ultra-clean steel

metal.manganese.melt-deoxidation.name: Aluminium and silicon deoxidation
metal.manganese.melt-deoxidation.description: The last step in the ladle is the one that actually decides the steel's quality. Manganese ties up the bulk of the dissolved oxygen as MnO inclusions, and then a calculated addition of aluminium - 0.5-2 kg per tonne - ties up the rest as Al2O3. Those inclusions have to go, and in a well-run plant they are floated out in the ladle or removed later by degassing and filtering. Manganese is what makes the aluminium deoxidation work: without manganese in solution, aluminium would oxidise preferentially as Al2O3 straight out of the bath and never reach the steel.
metal.manganese.melt-deoxidation.note: Medium confidence; the sequence is standard practice in aluminium-killed steel.

facts.label: Sequence
facts.value: Si, then Mn, then Al - the order matters

facts.label: Aluminium
facts.value: 0.5-2 kg per tonne, for a final soluble oxygen of 2-5 ppm

facts.label: Result
facts.value: fine Al2O3 inclusions dispersed in a MnS-bearing matrix

metal.manganese.sintering.name: Sintering the manganese ore
metal.manganese.sintering.description: Manganese ore is very fine and very friable, so it cannot be blown into a submerged arc furnace as a powder; it is sintered first, on a travelling grate exactly like the lead sinter, to make a 30-50 mm porous cake. The sinter belt at a manganese works is a zinc-works sinter plant or a lead-works sinter plant wearing different clothes, which makes it a nice example of a single machine serving three of the branches in this file.
metal.manganese.sintering.note: Medium confidence on the sinter temperature range; the process itself is standard.

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: travelling-grate sinter strand, 1100-1300 C in the burn zone

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 30-50 mm cake

metal.manganese.ore.name: Pyrolusite and manganiferous ore, 25-50% Mn
metal.manganese.ore.description: Manganese ore is almost never a clean manganese mineral. The Groote Eylandt and South African supergene ores are a hard, black, sooty mass of MnO2 cryptocrystalline material - wad and psilomelane - interbedded with iron formation. Grade is 25-50% Mn, and low-grade ore needs beneficiation: the South African ores were washed and jigged to reject the iron, and Groote Eylandt is washed in a scrubber and on a sluice. Silica and phosphorus are the two impurities that destroy value. This is a convergence node: the ferromanganese furnace, the ferrite branch's manganese carbonate and the steel deoxidiser all hang off it.

facts.label: Forms
facts.value: hard lumps (metallurgical), fines, sinter feed, and nodule fines

facts.label: Supply 1982
facts.value: South Africa and Australia were the dominant sources; the Groote Eylandt mine had been shipping since 1969

metal.manganese.nodule.name: Abyssal manganese nodule dredge
metal.manganese.nodule.description: The other, entirely different source: polymetallic nodules lying in thousands of square kilometres of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone and the Peru Basin at 4,000-6,000 m depth, containing 30% Mn, 2% Ni, 1% Cu and 25% Fe. Collecting them means a 10,000-tonne ship dragging a pipe across the seabed for 20,000 hours a year. It was never commercial in 1982 - technology trials were running but no mine was producing - and the incentive that eventually made it real was nickel, not manganese. This node is here because the 1980s seabed mining industry was built by exactly the people looking at the ore as a nickel resource, and by 1982 the C64's nickel supply chain and this geological curiosity were the same corporate conversation.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: hydraulic collector on a dragline with a riser to a ship, or a riserless system

facts.label: 1982 status
facts.value: technology demonstration only; no commercial production until decades later

metal.collector.name: The hydraulic collector head
metal.collector.description: The machine the whole idea rests on: a manifold of suction nozzles, 10-30 m across, towed along the seabed at 1-3 knots, that lifts the nodules into a riser pipe and up to a ship 4,000-6,000 m above. The 1970s trials worked at the point where the ocean is deepest to learn whether nodules survive being lifted - the attrition of the nodules on the way up turned out to be a genuine engineering problem - and the riserless concepts that would have solved it were still on paper. It is a beautiful illustration of how much of deep-sea mining is really a fluid mechanics problem.
metal.collector.note: Low confidence on the specific dimensions; the general design is standard and the detail is prototype-specific.

facts.label: Collector
facts.value: 10-30 m manifold of suction nozzles, towed at 1-3 knots

facts.label: Riser
facts.value: several thousand metres of pipe to a surface ship

metal.manganese.nodule-tech.name: Why the 1970s nodule trials were abandoned
metal.manganese.nodule-tech.description: By 1982 seabed nodule mining was a real programme with real money behind it, and the money is the interesting part. The incentive was not manganese - the grades were assumed recoverable but nobody had proved it at scale. The incentive was nickel and cobalt, because the strategic metal studies of the 1970s and early 1980s concluded that the West had too little nickel and too little cobalt and that the seabed was the answer. The trials - the French Nodule, the American DOMES and NOAA work, the Japanese and the German programmes - put a collector on the bottom and brought up tonnages. Nothing commercial resulted before the 2000s, largely on legal grounds, but the 1982 assessment was optimistic, and that is a genuine piece of the 1982 story rather than hindsight.
metal.manganese.nodule-tech.note: Low confidence on the specific programme details and outcomes. The strategic argument of the period is well understood; the individual trials are not.

facts.label: Programmes
facts.value: Nodule (France), DOMES and NOAA (United States), and Japanese and German programmes

facts.label: Incentive
facts.value: strategic-mine concern about nickel and cobalt supply, not about manganese

facts.label: 1982 outcome
facts.value: no commercial production; trials demonstrated recovery at the collector only

metal.manganese.nodule-rock.name: Manganese oxide concretions on pelagic clay
metal.manganese.nodule-rock.description: The leaf: millimetre-to-centimetre potato-shaped concretions of Mn-Fe oxide lying unattached in a soft abyssal red clay. The metal has precipitated out of seawater around a nucleus, slowly, over millions of years. It is the most extraordinary leaf in this tree: the manganese in a C64's steel is, in principle, available from the floor of an ocean.
metal.manganese.nodule-rock.note: Documented: manganese nodules are concretions of iron and manganese oxides on the sea floor built in concentric layers around a nucleus, and the largest deposits lie on abyssal plains at 4,000-6,000 m. Not established: the 1-10 mm per million year growth rate, and the host described specifically as abyssal red clay.

facts.label: Host
facts.value: pelagic abyssal red clay, thousands of metres down

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: 1-10 mm per million years

metal.abyssal-clay.name: The abyssal red clay beneath the nodules
metal.abyssal-clay.description: The true bottom of the manganese branch: a soft, red, pelagic clay that covers the abyssal plains at 4,000-6,000 m and that took the better part of 100 million years to accumulate, one centimetre at a time. The nodules sit on top of it. So the deepest leaf in this tree is a handful of dark potatoes on a carpet of red mud at the bottom of the Pacific, and the entire industrial-manganese question of whether to mine it is a question about that carpet.
metal.abyssal-clay.note: Medium confidence on the sedimentation rate range.

facts.label: Sedimentation rate
facts.value: order 0.1-1 cm per million years

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: abyssal pelagic clay, far from any land-derived sediment

metal.manganese.laterite-mine.name: Supergene manganese mining in the Kalahari
metal.manganese.laterite-mine.description: The Transvaal and the northern Cape were the world's largest producers in 1982 by a wide margin, and the operation was surface mining on a 5-20 m ore layer over a 100 m thick band of black manganese-bearing sandstone. Drag hoists, belt conveyors, and a scrubber-and-jig beneficiation plant, then a sinter belt. The ore is a black, hard, siliceous rock and it is dug out of a 30 m face.
metal.manganese.laterite-mine.note: The Kalahari field was opened in the 1970s and by 1982 was the dominant world source of metallurgical manganese ore; medium confidence on bench details.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: open pit, shovel and dragline, 5-20 m ore benches

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: scrub and jig to reject iron; 30-40% Mn product

metal.manganese.washing-plant.name: Scrubber, sluice and jig beneficiation
metal.manganese.washing-plant.description: Groote Eylandt and the South African operations do not smelt the raw lump: they wash it. The ore is dumped on a heap, a high-pressure water monitor scrubs off the fines and the clay, and the coarse goes over a sluice and a jig where the density difference between the manganese minerals (4.5-5.1) and the iron formation (5.0-5.3 but with a very different mineralogy) and the waste gangue separates the product. That is why a 30% Mn ore can make a 40% Mn product at low cost: the operation is a placer operation with a shovel in it.
metal.manganese.washing-plant.note: The scrubbing and jigging flowsheet is well documented for Groote Eylandt; medium confidence on the exact recoveries.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: scrubbing with water monitors, sluice boxes and jigs

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 30-40% Mn, and the fines go to the sinter belt

metal.manganese.oxide-phase.name: The oxide and carbonate phases of the ore
metal.manganese.oxide-phase.description: The leaf of the manganese branch's rock: the manganese in a supergene ore is not one mineral but four. Pyrolusite MnO2 is the black, soft, fibrous one; psilomelane is a barium-bearing cryptocrystalline mixture; braunite Mn2O3 is the hard brown one; and rhodochrosite MnCO3 is the pink carbonate in the primary zone. The refractory braunite is the one the smelter hates, because it takes three times the reductant and gives a high slag. Which phase a shipment is made of determines whether it goes to a ferromanganese furnace or to a chemical plant, and the assay is a chemical analysis, not a visual test.

facts.label: Pyrolusite
facts.value: MnO2, black and soft, easily reduced

facts.label: Braunite
facts.value: Mn2O3, hard and refractory, expensive to reduce

facts.label: Rhodochrosite
facts.value: MnCO3, pink, in the primary carbonate zone

metal.nickel.name: Nickel: connector plating, alloys, stainless
metal.nickel.description: Nickel is small in mass and enormous in function. In a C64 it is the plating on the connector shells and the gold-plated edge connector fingers' underlayer, the constantan and nichrome of the thin-film resistors on the board, the Invar of the composite-video circuit's chroma delay, and the bulk of AISI 304 and 430 stainless in the audio jack and the shield cans. 1982 was the year nickel was in a price crisis - the 1982-83 LME collapse, following the Escondida-adjacent and the Sherritt expansions of the late 1970s, took nickel from about $4/lb in 1980 to under $1.30/lb by 1983.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.8% cathode nickel; 99.9% for plating and for 304 stainless

facts.label: 1982 price context
facts.value: the LME nickel price collapsed from over $4/lb in early 1980 to under $1.50/lb by 1983 - a factor of three in three years

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: sulphide at 1-3% Ni (Sudbury, Thompson, Ranko Inlet) or laterite at 1.5-3% Ni (Cuba, Philippines, New Caledonia, Queensland)

metal.nickel.ingot.name: Electrolytic or cathode nickel, 99.9%
metal.nickel.ingot.description: Nickel metal arrives at the user as a cathode or a briquette: 99.8% for ferronickel-grade stainless, 99.9% for stainless and for plating. For a plating line the metal arrives as matte or as a soluble anode, but in 1982 the majority of nickel plating anodes were still the insoluble carbon steel anode, with the nickel actually coming from the electrolyte as nickel sulphate made from nickel oxide. This is a deliberate convergence node: the laterite branch, the Mond branch, the plating branch and the stainless branch all meet here.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.8% cathode, 99.9% for plating and stainless

facts.label: 1982 supply route
facts.value: mostly ferronickel-derived; electrolytic and carbonyl nickel were the premium products

metal.nickel.electroplating.name: Nickel electroplating and the gold underplate
metal.nickel.electroplating.description: The single most important metallurgical fact about nickel in a 1982 C64: gold plating does not sit on copper. It sits on a nickel underplate of 1-3 um, and the reason is electrochemistry - gold will not plate directly onto copper because the copper dissolves faster than the gold deposits, and a gold-copper diffusion couple makes a brittle, corrosion-prone joint. So the connector fingers and the IC leads get nickel and then a thin gold flash, or electroless nickel - a nickel-phosphorus deposit from a hypophosphite bath - followed by gold. The electroless route was standard in the semiconductor industry of the era and was how the die-attached gold on a hybrid IC was built.
metal.nickel.electroplating.note: The Watts bath composition is textbook; the specific underplate thicknesses on Commodore's connectors in 1982 are not something I can confirm. Medium confidence on the specific figures, high on the mechanism.

facts.label: Watts bath
facts.value: nickel sulphate plus nickel chloride plus boric acid, 50-60 C, pH 4.0-4.5

facts.label: Voltage and current
facts.value: 3-8 V, 2-8 A/dm2; 15-60 s for a flash

facts.label: Underplate
facts.value: 1-3 um of nickel under 0.05-0.25 um of gold

facts.label: Electroless nickel
facts.value: Ni-P from nickel sulphate and sodium hypophosphite, 3-8% phosphorus, at 85-95 C

metal.nickel.sherritt-gordon.name: Sherritt-Gordon ammonia leach and hydrogen reduction
metal.nickel.sherritt-gordon.description: The process that unlocked the laterites in the 1970s and 1980s. The slurry is leached at atmospheric pressure with concentrated ammonia and oxygen at 50-70 C: nickel and copper form soluble ammine complexes while the iron precipitates as hematite. The pregnant liquor is heated in a pressure autoclave with hydrogen and more ammonia, and the nickel comes out of solution as a metal powder while the copper stays in solution as the ammine, so the two separate in one vessel. The powder is filtered, washed and dried in a rotary vacuum dryer. This is genuinely a 1980s technology - the first commercial laterite plant, at Browns River in Queensland, started in 1974 and Sherritt licensed the process to the Cubans and the Japanese in the second half of the decade.

facts.label: Ammonia leach
facts.value: 50-70 C, atmospheric pressure, concentrated NH3, aerated

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: Ni2+ and Cu2+ as [Ni(NH3)6]2+ and [Cu(NH3)4]2+; Fe precipitates as hematite

facts.label: Hydrogen reduction
facts.value: 150-200 C, 20-35 bar H2, in a stirred autoclave

facts.label: Product
facts.value: nickel powder 99%+

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: copper stays in solution and is electrowon separately

facts.label: First commercial plant
facts.value: Browns River, Queensland, 1974

metal.ferronickel.name: Ferronickel, the laterite iron-nickel alloy
metal.ferronickel.description: The dominant way nickel actually became metal in 1982. Dried laterite and quartzite are fed with coke into a large submerged arc furnace, 30-60 MW, three electrodes, running at 1350-1500 C. The laterite's iron is already present as hematite, so the whole charge reduces together and the product is not nickel metal but an alloy of about 60-75% Ni and 25-40% Fe, plus a slag of magnesium, silicon and aluminium oxides. The ferronickel is tapped and either refined in the same operation to pure nickel or - more commonly in the 1980s - sold straight to a stainless steel mill as a charge, which is why the whole ferronickel industry is really a stainless steel industry.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: submerged arc, 30-60 MW, three electrodes, 1350-1500 C

facts.label: Product
facts.value: ferronickel, 60-75% Ni / 25-40% Fe

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 1.5-2.5 t of dried laterite per tonne of Ni in the alloy

facts.label: Charge drying
facts.value: suspension or rotary dryer to reduce the 30-45% moisture of laterite to below 1-2% before the furnace

metal.nickel.mond.name: Mond carbonyl refining (nickel from 99.9 to 99.999)
metal.nickel.mond.description: Ludwig Mond's 1890s process, still used in the 1980s for the last nines. Nickel carbonyl Ni(CO)4 is formed at 50-60 C in a saturator, distilled off as a colourless liquid boiling at 43 C, and decomposed in a decomposer column at 200-230 C onto 99.99% nickel pellets. The trick is that the carbonyl of cobalt is much less volatile and iron forms a non-volatile carbonyl, so the distillation separates the three metals in one operation - the same volatility trick as the trichlorosilane column in the silicon branch. Cobalt is recovered from the residue as Co2(CO)8.

facts.label: Carbonyl
facts.value: Ni(CO)4, liquid, boils 43 C at atmospheric pressure

facts.label: Decomposer
facts.value: 200-230 C, produces high-purity nickel pellets

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.99% nickel - the Mondcarbonyl process still supplies the very pure nickel used in plating chemistry

facts.label: Safety
facts.value: extremely toxic; the vapour is the reason Mond refineries had continuous air monitoring from the 1970s

metal.nickel.mond.safety.name: Why nickel carbonyl is the deadliest room in metals
metal.nickel.mond.safety.description: Nickel tetracarbonyl is a colourless, volatile liquid that boils at 43 C and is lethal by inhalation at concentrations far below anything that can be smelled. A Mond refinery therefore runs on a rule that no one enters a carbonyl area without a respirator, that the vapour is continuously monitored at the floor and at breathing height, and that the whole plant is vented through a high-temperature incinerator that destroys the carbonyl before releasing it. The 1980s occupational-hygiene literature on nickel carbonyl is a case study in how a process can be kept running at all when the material is that toxic, and the number of fatal poisonings in nickel refineries over the century is a reminder that this is one of the most dangerous processes in the metals industry.
metal.nickel.mond.safety.note: The exposure limit varies by jurisdiction; medium confidence on the specific 1982 figures.

facts.label: Boiling point
facts.value: 43 C at atmospheric pressure

facts.label: Exposure limit
facts.value: of the order of 0.1 ppm as an 8-hour TWA in most jurisdictions by the 1980s

facts.label: Control
facts.value: closed process, continuous air monitoring, and high-temperature incineration of the offgas

metal.nickel.electrowinning.name: Nickel electrowinning from a pure sulphide circuit
metal.nickel.electrowinning.description: Where the ore is sulphide rather than laterite, Sherritt's original ammonia-pressure process dissolves the concentrate in ammoniacal ammonium sulphate at 160-190 F (70-90 C) with oxygen, and then electrowins the nickel directly out of the pregnant liquor onto titanium cathodes in diaphragm cells at a very low voltage, about 0.5-1.0 V, because hydrogen evolution competes and the current efficiency is only 70-85%. This is the Sherritt-Gordon route as it was licensed in 1969-1972, and it is why the company is called after two towns in Manitoba. The cathodes are stripped, briquetted and remelted.
metal.nickel.electrowinning.note: The 160-190 F optimum is from Sherritt's own published leach chemistry for sulphide concentrates; medium confidence on the current efficiency range.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: ammoniacal ammonium sulphate, 70-90 C, aerated

facts.label: Cathode
facts.value: titanium starter sheets, stripped and briquetted

metal.nickel.sulphide-concentrate.name: Nickel sulphide concentrate (Sudbury)
metal.nickel.sulphide-concentrate.description: The Sudbury basin of Ontario was the world's nickel capital and it is a genuinely strange deposit: an impact structure full of shock-melted, metal-rich breccia at the base of a 1.8 billion year old impact crater, with pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8 and millerite NiS. The INCO operation mined both underground and, from 1962, from the open pit at the south end of the basin, and roasted the ore in fluidised beds to make 'fines' - a nickel-copper matte rather than a concentrate - before smelting. The tree therefore continues down through the Sudbury ore to a shocked sulphide breccia in an impact melt sheet, which is as geologically interesting an endpoint as this tree has.

facts.label: Minerals
facts.value: pentlandite (Fe,Ni)9S8, millerite NiS, pyrrhotite

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: a 1.85 billion year old meteorite impact structure; the ore sits in and below the melt sheet

facts.label: Route
facts.value: fluidised-bed roasting to sinter fines, then smelting to a matte, then converting

metal.nickel.impact-melt.name: Impact melt sheet at the base of the Sudbury crater
metal.nickel.impact-melt.description: The leaf: a foot-thick to 20 m layer of rock melted and shock-altered by the impact, in which the nickel and copper sulphides were disseminated as droplets. It is a metamorphic and melt rock, not an igneous intrusion, and it is a band about 60 km long and 20 km wide across northern Ontario. The mining is ordinary room-and-pillar or open-pit on a sheet that lies only a few hundred metres below the Huronian cover.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: impact melt and suevite breccia, disseminated Ni-Cu sulphide

metal.nickel.autoclave.name: The ammonia-hydrogen autoclave
metal.nickel.autoclave.description: A 10-15 m long, 3-5 m diameter, titanium or 316L-lined pressure vessel in a 6-10 stage cascade. In each stage the liquor is contacted with hydrogen and stirred, and the nickel comes out onto the walls and the cooling surfaces. The whole chemistry depends on the fact that ammonia complexes nickel and copper so strongly that hydrogen alone cannot reduce them at atmospheric pressure; the autoclave gives the extra pressure to push the equilibrium over. Removing the ammonia and boiling the slurry then precipitates basic nickel carbonate, which is calcined to nickel oxide.
metal.nickel.autoclave.note: Sherritt's own patents cover the details; medium confidence on the vessel dimensions.

facts.label: Vessel
facts.value: 3-5 m diameter, 10-15 m long, 6-10 stages

facts.label: Material
facts.value: carbon steel with titanium or stainless lining

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: a cobalt-nickel or iron-based slurry catalyst seeds the deposition

metal.nickel.laterite.name: Nickel laterite (garnierite ore)
metal.nickel.laterite.description: A soft, earthy, red-brown clay-and-laterite ore, really a weathering product of ultramafic rock: olivine and pyroxene in a serpentinised peridotite are altered from scratch, and nickel substitutes for magnesium in the clay lattice, giving garnierite. There is no nickel mineral to concentrate; the whole ore body is the ore. The great deposits in 1982 were the Cuban Moa and Nicaro operations - where the ore was shipped to the United States and Japan for the nickel limit of the United States Defense Production Act of 1981 made government stockpiling a political event - the Philippines' Surigao and Bacojo operations, the New Caledonian laterite, and the Queensland laterite. Laterite is mined in the open pit in soft, wet ground with a bucket-wheel excavator or a walking dragline, and often leached in place.

facts.label: Assay
facts.value: 1.5-3.0% Ni, 15-40% Fe, low silica (<2%) for the best, high-silica (>20%) for the Chinese and Indonesian shales

facts.label: Ore type
facts.value: limonite (high-Fe, low-Mg), saprolite, or smectitic (high-silica) - only the limonite-rich low-silica ore is worth the pressure leach

facts.label: Depth of weathering
facts.value: 5-100 m of overburden before reaching the saprolite

metal.nickel.drying.name: Dry the laterite before smelting
metal.nickel.drying.description: A laterite arrives at 30-45% moisture and the submerged arc furnace cannot take it wet, because the water costs more steam than the reaction releases. So the dewatered ore is dried in a rotary dryer or - in the Cuban and Philippine operations of the 1980s - in a suspension dryer with the hot flue gas, to below 1-2% moisture, and the drier's exhaust is the source of the dust and the fuel consumption that dominated the cost. Some plants solved the problem differently: the Queensland operations calcined and reduced the ore on the pad and then shipped a nickel oxide, which moved the water problem upstream to the leach.
metal.nickel.drying.note: Medium confidence; the alternative routes are well documented for specific operations.

facts.label: Feed moisture
facts.value: 30-45% from the washing plant

facts.label: Product moisture
facts.value: below 1-2%

facts.label: Alternatives
facts.value: rotary dryer, or a suspension dryer, or on-pad reduction and shipping a nickel oxide

metal.nickel.laterite-mine.name: Bucket-wheel excavator laterite mine
metal.nickel.laterite-mine.description: The soft, wet, deeply weathered ore is the ideal bucket-wheel material. A walking or rail-mounted bucket-wheel excavator with a 20-40 m boom cuts the overburden and the ore bench itself, dropping it onto a belt conveyor, and the ore goes to a long washing and screening plant rather than to a crusher. The Philippine and Cuban operations had bucket-wheel excavators with booms over 50 m by the early 1980s. The ore arrives at the plant as a slurry, which is why the pressure leach of the 1980s was designed for a pumped pulp and not for a dry concentrate.
metal.nickel.laterite-mine.note: Boom lengths and bucket volumes are machine-class figures, not specific to any named mine; medium confidence.

facts.label: Boom length
facts.value: 20-60 m; the largest bucket-wheel excavators of the era

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 0.3-0.6 m3 per bucket at 0.6-1.5 s cycle

facts.label: Conveying
facts.value: belt conveyor from the excavator directly to the washing plant

metal.nickel.ore-washing.name: The laterite washing and screening plant
metal.nickel.ore-washing.description: The laterite arrives from a bucket-wheel excavator as a slurry, and it goes through a log washer, a scrubber, a screen tower and a series of hydrocyclones, and the -0.5 mm fraction is rejected outright as low-grade clay. The coarse fraction is dewatered on a screen and stacked in a concrete bin. In the Cuban and Philippine operations the stacked ore was then leached in place on a pad, in the Queensland operations it was dried in a rotary dryer and shipped to a furnace. The whole plant exists because the ore is a soft, wet, variable, low-grade bulk material, and the plants are mostly about handling water.
metal.nickel.ore-washing.note: Medium confidence; the flowsheet is well documented for Cuban and Philippine operations.

facts.label: Rejection
facts.value: the -0.5 mm clay fraction is discarded, and it is often 20-40% of the feed

facts.label: Dewatering
facts.value: screens, cyclones, and a large thickener

facts.label: Moisture in the dried ore
facts.value: reduced to below 1-2% before any furnace

metal.nickel.limonite-garnierite.name: Limonite and garnierite: the two nickel minerals
metal.nickel.limonite-garnierite.description: The leaf of the nickel branch, and it is a mineral solution rather than a mineral. There is no nickel mineral in a laterite. Nickel substitutes for magnesium in the smectite and kaolinite clays - the mineral is garnierite, which is really a mixture - and it substitutes for iron in the goethite of the limonite, so a limonite laterite's nickel is spread through amorphous iron oxide at a few percent. The two grades of laterite that matter commercially are the high-iron limonite ore and the low-silica saprolite ore, and the difference between them is the grade of the nickel-bearing lattice, which is why the pressure leach was developed for one and not the other.

facts.label: Garnierite
facts.value: (Ni,Mg)3Si2O5(OH)4, nickel substituting for magnesium in a smectite

facts.label: Limonite
facts.value: nickel substituting for iron in amorphous goethite, FeO(OH)

facts.label: Two commercial ores
facts.value: high-iron limonite ore and low-silica saprolite ore

metal.nickel.peridotite.name: Serpentinised peridotite
metal.nickel.peridotite.description: The leaf: an ultramafic igneous rock, mostly olivine, now largely converted to serpentine, that has been chemically weathered for tens of millions of years in a warm wet climate. The nickel is in the clay and in the limonite, not in a crystal. Cuba, New Caledonia and the Philippines all have large serpentinite bodies, and that is why the island arcs of the Pacific are the nickel map.

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: serpentinised peridotite / dunite, weathered to garnierite-bearing laterite

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: tropical weathering profile, tens of metres thick, on an ultramafic body

metal.zinc.name: Zinc: die-cast alloy, plating, brass, varistor
metal.zinc.description: Zinc is the fourth non-ferrous metal and the most recycled one. In a 1982 C64 it appears as a die-cast zinc alloy for the case-mounted parts and the key plungers, as a plating on steel for EMI shields and chassis fasteners, as brass (copper-zinc) for the bus-bar and connector bodies, and as zinc oxide in the varistor that clamps the supply spikes off the mains input. The smelting industry in 1982 was in the middle of its biggest change in a century: the roast-leach-electrowin zinc-iron plant was replacing the horizontal retort furnace.

facts.label: Refined grade
facts.value: 99.995% (SHG), the standard grade for galvanising and die casting

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: sphalerite ZnS at 3-20% Zn; the ore is often mined as a lead-zinc deposit

facts.label: Chain
facts.value: ~100 t of 6% Zn ore -> ~18 t of 55% Zn concentrate -> ~5 t of zinc metal in the concentrate

metal.zinc.electrowinning.name: Electrowinning of zinc on aluminium cathodes
metal.zinc.electrowinning.description: Zinc is one of the few metals won by electrolysis out of an aqueous solution at industrial scale. The reason is that zinc is more negative than hydrogen and would just deposit hydrogen from water if it were not for the high hydrogen overvoltage on aluminium; each cathode is an aluminium plate of 1-2 m2 and 10-25 mm thick, and the scraper at the top of the cycle knocks off a 5-25 kg slab. The slabs are melted in a small induction furnace and cast into 25 kg ingots at 99.995%. The energy is 3,000-3,500 kWh per tonne of zinc - high, but the purity and the by-product recovery make the route worth it for ores that cannot be smelted. This is the convergence point of the roast, leach, purification and ingot branches.
metal.zinc.electrowinning.note: The zinc-iron plant was the dominant new-build technology through the 1980s; the Imperial Smelting zinc-iron process and the roast-leach-electrowin are the same family.

facts.label: Current density
facts.value: 500-1200 A/m2 of cathode

facts.label: Cathode
facts.value: 1-2 m2 of aluminium plate, 10-25 mm thick

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 24-72 h, then strip; plates weigh 5-25 kg of zinc each

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 3000-3500 kWh per tonne of zinc

facts.label: Product
facts.value: 99.992-99.995% zinc, cast into 25 kg ingots

metal.zinc.electrowinning-cell.name: The single-deck electrolysis cell
metal.zinc.electrowinning-cell.description: The 1980s zinc tankhouse cell was a plain open-top concrete or rubber-lined steel box, 3-6 m long, 1.5-2.5 m wide, 2-3 m deep, with an aluminium cathode every 15-25 mm and a lead anode between them. The electrolyte is fed in at one end and pulled out at the other; the plates go in, run for 24-72 hours, come out, get scraped, and go to the melting furnace. A modern plant with 300,000-400,000 m2 of cathode area is a building the size of a football pitch. This is one of the least mechanised and most manually-intensive electrolysis plants in the industry, because the plate handling has never lent itself to automation.
metal.zinc.electrowinning-cell.note: Medium confidence; the cell layout is standard but varies between plants.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: 3-6 m long, 1.5-2.5 m wide, 2-3 m deep, 2-5 V

facts.label: Electrode pitch
facts.value: 15-25 mm between an anode and a cathode

metal.zinc.stripping.name: Strip the cathodes and melt the SHG ingot
metal.zinc.stripping.description: At the end of the cycle each cathode is lifted out, tipped against a steel plate that shears the zinc slab off, and the slabs are charged to a 100-500 kg induction furnace. The furnace has to be held at 450-470 C and under a cover flux because zinc oxidises readily and every gram of oxide is a loss. Two refinements came in during the 1980s: induction furnaces with better stirring and better control, and the move to a single large furnace rather than a fleet of small ones, which cut the oxide loss and the labour.
metal.zinc.stripping.note: The oxide loss figure is a rule of thumb; medium confidence.

facts.label: Melting
facts.value: 450-470 C in an induction furnace under a cover flux

facts.label: Slab
facts.value: 5-25 kg per cathode

facts.label: Loss
facts.value: 1-3% of the metal is lost as oxide and dross

metal.zinc.ingot.name: Special high grade zinc ingot, 99.995%
metal.zinc.ingot.description: Twenty-five kilogram ingots, or the 500 kg minimum-content ingot that the bigger plants preferred by 1982. Special high grade at 99.995% was the grade specified by the galvanising industry and by die-casters, because both are very sensitive to lead, cadmium and iron. Two thirds of world zinc goes into galvanising and roughly a sixth into die casting. The four markets below are the whole of the demand: galvanising, die casting, electroplating with a chromate passivate, and brass. An ingot that misses any of the four impurity limits is unsellable, which is why the smelter spends its margin on the assay rather than on the metal.

facts.label: End use
facts.value: ~65% galvanising, ~15-20% die casting, ~10% brass, rest chemicals

metal.zinc-oxide-varistor.name: Zinc oxide varistor: the mains spike clamp
metal.zinc-oxide-varistor.description: The C64's power supply faces the mains directly. A zinc oxide varistor disc - ZnO powder pressed and sintered between two fired electrodes - sits across the input, and its resistance is astronomically high until the mains edge is exceeded, at which point it conducts and clamps the surge. ZnO is essentially a doped semiconductor ceramic: zinc oxide powder mixed with a few mol percent of the oxides of bismuth, cobalt, nickel, manganese and antimony, calcined, granulated with a binder, dry-pressed at 100-200 MPa, fired at 1100-1300 C, and cooled under a reducing atmosphere so the grain boundaries become the non-stoichiometry that gives the voltage knee. So the surge protection on the input filter is a zinc metallurgy product - and, incidentally, the same powder metallurgy as the ferrites.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: ZnO with 0.5-2 mol% each of Bi2O3, CoO, MnO and other dopants

facts.label: Clamp voltage
facts.value: ~240 V for a mains disc, ~700 V for a DC-side disc

facts.label: Energy handling
facts.value: 10 J to over 1 kJ per disc, set by diameter

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1100-1300 C, then a controlled-atmosphere cool

metal.zinc-oxide-powder.name: Zinc oxide powder
metal.zinc-oxide-powder.description: Zinc oxide for ceramics was, in 1982, made by burning high-purity zinc in air, by calcining high-purity zinc carbonate, or - for the highest grades - by the vapour-phase oxidation of high-purity zinc metal, which gives spherical sub-micron particles with a very tight size distribution. A varistor powder needs high-purity ZnO because any foreign phase at the grain boundary changes the voltage knee. So the varistor in the C64's power supply starts with 99.99% zinc.
metal.zinc-oxide-powder.note: The exact powder route for a given varistor is proprietary; medium confidence. The atmospheric oxidation of zinc metal is the bottom of this branch and is a certainty.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: combustion or calcination; vapour-phase oxidation for the best powder

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: sub-micron for the vapour route

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 2Zn + O2 -> 2ZnO at 400-600 C

metal.zinc.brass.name: Brass (Cu-Zn)
metal.zinc.brass.description: Zinc's largest engineering use is as the alloying element in brass and bronze. Brass is 60-95% copper with zinc, and the connector bodies, bus bars, shield cans and some switch frames in a C64 are brass, often brass plated with tin or nickel. Brass is melted and cast from cathode copper and zinc ingots in a small reverberatory or induction furnace, then extruded or rolled and machined. It is included because roughly a third of the world's refined zinc goes into brass, and because it is a genuine convergence of the copper and zinc branches.

facts.label: Common grades
facts.value: C26000 cartridge brass (70/30), C36000 free-machining brass (62/38 with 0.5% Pb)

facts.label: Zinc share
facts.value: brass takes roughly a third of refined zinc

facts.label: Famous problem
facts.value: dezincification of alpha brasses in seawater; the cartridge brass avoids it

metal.zinc.electroplate.name: Electrolytic zinc plating of steel
metal.zinc.electroplate.description: For small plated parts - chassis fasteners, brackets, EMI shields - zinc is electroplated rather than dipped. An alkaline cyanide bath, a non-cyanide acid chloride bath, or in the barrel a simple sulphate. The deposit is sacrificial: even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes preferentially and protects the steel underneath. A chromate passivation on top gives the characteristic yellow or olive colour and much better corrosion resistance, and by 1982 chromate was already being restricted because of hexavalent chromium.
metal.zinc.electroplate.note: Trivalent chromium passivation arrived in the 1990s-2000s; hexavalent chromate was the 1982 norm.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: alkaline cyanide zincate, or acid chloride, or sulphate

facts.label: Deposit
facts.value: 5-25 um for passivated decorative and EMI shielding work

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: yellow or olive chromate conversion coating

metal.zinc.die-cast.name: Zamak die-cast alloy and the pressure die-caster
metal.zinc.die-cast.description: Zinc's most interesting product for this tree. A zinc alloy with 4% aluminium and a little copper - Zamak 3 is Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5, Zamak 5 with 5% aluminium for better die-castability - is injected into a steel die at 380-430 C under 20-150 MPa by a cold-chamber machine with 200-800 tonnes of clamping force. It fills the thinnest sections any metal can fill - 0.8 mm walls, and details you could not machine - and it holds a fine surface as cast. The 1982 pressure die-caster was a 350-800 tonne machine, and the seconds per shot multiplied by the shots an hour is the number that set the cost of a key plunger or a case bracket.
metal.zinc.die-cast.note: Zinc die casting lost share to aluminium and to engineering polymers during the 1980s-90s, and the alloy names (Zamak, ZA, ZA-8) are supplier-dependent. High confidence on the chemistry and the process, medium on the specific alloy for any Commodore part.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: Zamak 3: Zn 96 / Al 4 / Cu 0.5; Zamak 5: Zn 95 / Al 5 / Cu 0.5

facts.label: Clamp force
facts.value: 200-800 t on a 1982 machine

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 1-5 s per shot; 400-700 shots per hour on a small machine

facts.label: Minimum wall
facts.value: 0.8-1.0 mm, tighter than aluminium

metal.zinc.ingot-furnace.name: Zinc alloy melting furnace
metal.zinc.ingot-furnace.description: The die-caster does not melt its own alloy from primary metal; it buys 10-25 kg alloy ingots of a certified composition and melts them in a thermostatically controlled holding furnace - typically a 100-500 kg crucible furnace with an immersed resistance heater and a lead bath to keep the alloy away from air. A crucible furnace full of molten zinc is the classic source of metal-fume fever among die-casters, because zinc oxide fume is generated wherever the surface is disturbed.
metal.zinc.ingot-furnace.note: Furnace design varies widely; medium confidence on capacities.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: 100-500 kg crucible, resistance or oil-heated, 380-430 C, held under a cover flux

facts.label: Occupational hazard
facts.value: zinc oxide fume from disturbed surfaces; metal-fume fever

metal.zinc.galvanising.name: Hot-dip galvanising of steel strip
metal.zinc.galvanising.description: Steel sheet, strip or fabric is pickled in hydrochloric acid, fluxed in an ammonium chloride-zinc chloride bath, and dipped in a kettle of molten zinc at 450-470 C. The zinc wets the steel, forms an iron-zinc intermetallic, and the kettle surface is skimmed of dross by a wiper roll. Every galvanising line in the world consumed thousands of tonnes of zinc a year this way, and a big continuous strip line used 50-300 t a day. The C64 itself is not galvanised, but its chassis and any sheet-metal bracket, and much of the world around it, was.
metal.zinc.galvanising.note: Zinc-aluminium and zinc-nickel coated sheet for automotive was a 1980s development, not a 1982 consumer-electronics one.

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: 45-85 g/m2 for sheet; 300-600 g/m2 for fabric

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: a continuous strip line uses 50-300 t of zinc a day, of which the dross is a real loss

facts.label: Coating form
facts.value: pure zinc for general use; Zn-Al alloy for high-drip lines; Zn-Ni for automotive sheet

metal.zinc.dross-recovery.name: Recover the zinc from the galvanising dross
metal.zinc.dross-recovery.description: The iron-rich dross and the bottom ash skinned off a galvanising kettle are picked out, and the metal is recovered in a specialised horizontal crucible furnace, where the dross is heated with a flux and the iron drops out as Fe-Zn hard zinc. The remaining zinc is pumped out. A galvanising line therefore recovers most of its zinc, and in 1982 the galvanising industry was also the main secondary source of zinc, second only to galvanised scrap.
metal.zinc.dross-recovery.note: Recovery efficiency varies with dross age; medium confidence.

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 70-90% of the dross metal is recovered

metal.zinc.anode-mb.name: Lead-silver anode in the tankhouse
metal.zinc.anode-mb.description: The insoluble anode is a lead alloy - 99% Pb with 0.5-1% Ag, cast as 10-40 mm thick plates - which works because when it does corrode slowly, the lead dioxide layer that forms is a perfectly good anode surface. Silver is added because it slows the corrosion. So the zinc tankhouse is structurally a lead operation: it consumes lead anodes at a rate of a few kilograms per tonne of zinc, which is one of the more elegant hidden cross-links between the lead and zinc branches in this file.

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 2-5 kg of lead alloy anode per tonne of zinc

metal.zinc.leach-purify.name: Acid leach and purification of the zinc sulphate solution
metal.zinc.leach-purify.description: The dead-roast sinter is leached in spent electrolyte diluted with water, at pH about 4.5 and 40-60 C, in a series of leaching tanks. Then the solution must be purified, because almost every impurity that reaches the cell either consumes current or plates out on the cathode as a short circuit. Iron is removed by air oxidising the pH up to 5.2 so it precipitates as jarosite or goethite - a step that consumes zinc as well and is where most of the zinc plants' zinc loss is. Then copper, cadmium and cobalt are removed by adding zinc dust, which by cementation throws those metals out of solution. Chloride is kept down by jarosite precipitation. Every one of these is a chemistry rather than a metallurgy, and every one of them costs zinc.
metal.zinc.leach-purify.note: The zinc loss in iron removal is the single biggest reason zinc plants' recoveries sit at 85-92% rather than higher; medium confidence on the exact figure range.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: spent electrolyte + water, pH 4.5, 40-60 C

facts.label: Iron removal
facts.value: air oxidisation to pH 5.2, precipitating jarosite or goethite; costs 3-8 kg Zn per tonne of Zn

facts.label: Cementation
facts.value: zinc dust removes Cu, Cd and Co down to mg/L

facts.label: Chloride
facts.value: kept below about 500 mg/L; chloride drives anode corrosion

facts.label: Ajar residue
facts.value: the iron precipitate is a residue stream of 1-3 t per tonne of zinc

metal.zinc.iron-removal.name: Iron removal by the jarosite and goethite routes
metal.zinc.iron-removal.description: The purification chemistry in one process. The leach liquor's pH is raised with limestone and the iron is oxidised with air in a bank of aeration tanks at 90-100 C. Whether the precipitate is jarosite (the older route, at pH 5.2 with sodium sulphate added, at 90-100 C over 10-20 hours) or goethite (the newer route, at 80-95 C with less retention time) decides how much zinc the residue holds and how much sulphate the plant makes. Every zinc plant in 1982 had made a choice between these two, and the choice is the single biggest determinant of its cost.
metal.zinc.iron-removal.note: The jarosite versus goethite split is a real and well-documented 1980s process choice; medium confidence on the specific temperature windows.

facts.label: Jarosite
facts.value: pH 5.2, 90-100 C, 10-20 h, needs added sulphate

facts.label: Goethite
facts.value: 80-95 C, shorter retention, no added sulphate

facts.label: Neutralising reagent
facts.value: limestone, from the same quarry as the blast furnace flux

metal.zinc.jarosite-residue.name: Jarosite residue and the zinc it costs
metal.zinc.jarosite-residue.description: The iron precipitation step that makes the zinc plant's chemistry work is also its biggest single loss. Oxidising the iron out at pH 5.2 throws down jarosite or goethite, and both of them carry zinc in their lattice - typically 4-10% Zn. At 1-3 tonnes of residue per tonne of zinc made, and 5-10% of the contained zinc never recovered, the iron removal step is where a zinc plant loses a million dollars a year. It is also a waste stream: acidic, iron-rich, and in the 1980s dumped in a lined pond. This is the residue the modern jarosite and goethite processes are designed to shrink.
metal.zinc.jarosite-residue.note: The 5-10% zinc loss figure is a rule of thumb; medium confidence.

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: 1-3 t of residue per tonne of zinc

facts.label: Zinc lost
facts.value: 4-10% of the contained zinc in the residue

facts.label: Overall plant recovery
facts.value: 85-92%, limited mostly by this step

metal.zinc.dust.name: Zinc dust for cementation
metal.zinc.dust.description: The purification step uses zinc metal itself, atomised from a small kettle, as the reagent that throws out copper, cadmium and cobalt. The cemented metals - a black sludge heavy with copper and cadmium - is filtered off and shipped to a cadmium refinery, which is where the world's cadmium came from in 1982. So the zinc plant's purification residue is a cadmium ore in all but name.
metal.zinc.dust.note: Dust consumption depends on the impurity load; medium confidence on the range.

facts.label: Dust size
facts.value: atomised, 75-150 um

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 3-10 kg of zinc dust per tonne of zinc

metal.cadmium-residue.name: Copper-cadmium residue
metal.cadmium-residue.description: A 1980s cadmium plant roasted the residue in a retort at 600-800 C: the cadmium volatilised off (it boils at 767 C) and was condensed in a condenser, giving 99.9% cadmium metal, while the copper stayed behind. This is the only major industrial source of cadmium, and it is a zinc by-product. It matters here only as a consequence of zinc refining; a C64 has no cadmium.
metal.cadmium-residue.note: Cadmium is included as a consequence of the zinc chain; medium confidence on retort detail.

facts.label: Retort
facts.value: 600-800 C, cadmium distilled and condensed

metal.zinc.roasting.name: Roasting of sphalerite to zinc oxide
metal.zinc.roasting.description: The concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed or on a sinter strand, 850-1000 C, with the result 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. The 1980s plant that grew out of this is the roaster-sinter plant, in which the hot ZnO and Fe2O3 sinter together into a porous 'dead roast sinter' that is a much better feed for an acid leach than a fine powder. The SO2 at 8-12% goes to the acid plant. This roasting step is where a zinc smelter became a sulfuric acid producer of the same order as a copper smelter, and where the sinter plant's dust catch and its dewpoint control - keep the gas above about 150 C or the zinc and lead fume plasters the plant - became a real engineering discipline.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2

facts.label: SO2 to acid
facts.value: 8-12%, captured; a zinc plant makes 3-5 t of 100% acid per tonne of zinc

facts.label: Dewpoint control
facts.value: offgas held above roughly 150 C to keep zinc and lead oxides out of the gas

facts.label: By-products
facts.value: cadmium and lead fume captured from the roaster gas; mercury in the fume is a modern problem, largely uncontrolled in 1982

metal.zinc.fume-catch.name: Catch the cadmium and lead in the roaster gas
metal.zinc.fume-catch.description: The roaster gas carries a fine zinc oxide fume and, in the vapour phase, the cadmium and the lead. Economically the cadmium is the point: the fume goes to a baghouse, and the cadmium is recovered in a separate cadmium plant. The lead in the same gas is a nuisance and an occupational hazard, and in 1982 the zinc plants of North America were beginning to worry about it for exactly the reason they would later worry about it in the environmental context. The dust is one of the more awkward solid wastes in metallurgy because it is both valuable and toxic.
metal.zinc.fume-catch.note: The cadmium recovery route is well documented; medium confidence on the 1982 collection efficiency.

facts.label: Collection
facts.value: baghouse or electrostatic precipitator after a cooling tower

facts.label: Fume
facts.value: ZnO with Cd, Pb and Cl compounds

facts.label: Cadmium recovery
facts.value: the fume goes to a cadmium distilling plant

metal.zinc.roaster.name: Fluidised-bed roaster
metal.zinc.roaster.description: Concentrate is fed into a bed of 1-3 m of the roast itself on a distributor of tuyeres, held at 850-950 C by the fluidising air, and the bed overflows continuously into a hot cyclone and then a sintering conveyor where the last 100-150 C of roast and the sintering happen together. The whole thing was invented at the Balotelawezwa plant in South Africa and Canadian Calumet in the 1960s and was standard new-plant practice by 1982. An older plant would instead have used a multiple-hearth roaster or a sinter strand and produced a fine, un-sintered ZnO.
metal.zinc.roaster.note: Roaster design details vary; medium confidence.

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 50-60% Zn, 6-10% Zn soluble, rest in the silicate matrix

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: flotation concentrate, 4-12% moisture

metal.sphalerite.name: Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate, 50-60% Zn
metal.sphalerite.description: Sphalerite is one of the few ores that is not visually recognisable: it is a black to honey-brown cubic crystal whose colour depends on the iron substituting in the lattice, so the industry grades it in grades of iron - a 4% iron concentrate looks black and a 12% iron concentrate looks ruby red-brown. Concentration is by flotation with an amine or xanthate collector. The great districts were the Red Dog and the Sullivan mine in British Columbia, Broken Hill, the Cerro Rico of Potosi, the Rammelsberg of Goslar, and the Appalachian and Midwestern US zinc districts such as the Bartlesville and the Tennessee mines.

facts.label: Mining
facts.value: usually underground room-and-pillar or long-hole stoping in a stratiform or replacement body

facts.label: Beneficiation
facts.value: differential flotation or bulk float with amine collectors

metal.sphalerite.mine.name: Underground zinc-lead mine
metal.sphalerite.mine.description: The Red Dog and Sullivan type deposit: a massive sulphide body in a sedimentary basin, mined underground from a ramp or a shaft, with the ore hoisted in a friction hoist or a skip, and the mill right at the portal. Broken Hill's Broken Hill Proprietary was the other archetype, an open pit above a very large primary orebody that was mined for sixty years. Where the zinc and lead are in separate veins, gravity and flotation split them: galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 do separate well on a dense-medium separator.
metal.sphalerite.mine.note: Documented: roughly half the world's sphalerite lead and zinc comes from sediment-hosted massive sulphide deposits - stratiform Pb-Zn sulphides hosted by shales, carbonates and siltstones - with combined grades typically 10-20%, and Red Dog, Sullivan, Mount Isa and Broken Hill are the named mines. Not established: galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 specific gravity, the dense-media or differential gravity split between them, and the friction-hoist and mill-at-the-portal detail.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: underground room-and-pillar or long-hole stoping; open pit for large primary bodies

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: dense-media / differential gravity for galena vs sphalerite, then flotation

metal.sphalerite.host.name: The host basin and its caprock
metal.sphalerite.host.description: The final leaf of the zinc chain is not a rock but a structure: a sedimentary basin with a metal-bearing horizon in it. The Red Dog deposit is a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin on the Tukarakka Peninsula; Broken Hill is a metamorphosed, deformed massive sulphide in a sequence of Proterozoic metasediments. In both cases the orebody sits at a specific stratigraphic level, and the mine is a series of ramps and stopes chasing a bedding-parallel body a few metres thick. So the zinc in a C64's die-cast key plunger came out of a bed that happens to lie a kilometre beneath a river delta.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: sediment-hosted massive sulphide at a specific horizon in a basin

facts.label: Ore thickness
facts.value: 5-25 m of ore under hundreds of metres of host rock

metal.sphalerite.mill.name: Zinc concentrator: differential flotation
metal.sphalerite.mill.description: The ore is crushed to 10-25 mm, ground to 50-100 um in a ball or autogenous mill, and floated in stages. The classic circuit is differential: copper and lead sulphides are floated first with a stronger collector and a higher pH, and then the sphalerite is floated from the tailings with a weaker collector at a lower pH, with copper sulphate added as an activator because sphalerite does not float on its own. That gives a 50-60% Zn concentrate at 85-92% recovery. The Red Dog and Sullivan concentrators were among the largest in the world and are the reason those two mines could be mines at all.
metal.sphalerite.mill.note: Medium confidence on the specific additive dosages; the circuit configuration is standard.

facts.label: Circuit
facts.value: Cu-Pb bulk float first, then Zn float from the tailings

facts.label: Activator
facts.value: copper sulphate, 0.1-1 kg/t

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: 85-92% to a 50-60% Zn concentrate

metal.sphalerite.dms.name: Dense-media separation of galena from sphalerite
metal.sphalerite.dms.description: Galena at 7.6 and sphalerite at 4.1 are separable on a shaking table or, much faster, in a dense-medium separator using a ferrosilicon or magnetite suspension at a cut density of about 3.0-3.5. The lead concentrate and the zinc concentrate are thereby split before flotation, which lets the flotation plant be small. Dense-medium separation of a polymetallic ore is one of the great quiet successes of twentieth-century mineral processing.
metal.sphalerite.dms.note: The cut densities and throughputs are class values; medium confidence.

facts.label: Medium
facts.value: ferrosilicon or magnetite in water at 2.5-3.5 specific gravity

facts.label: Cut density
facts.value: 3.0-3.5 separates galena from sphalerite

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: 100-500 t/h on a modern separator

metal.dms.fe-silicon.name: Ferrosilicon powder for dense-media separation
metal.dms.fe-silicon.description: The liquid in a dense-medium separator is ferrosilicon - an alloy of iron and silicon made in exactly the submerged arc furnace described in the electrical-steel and metallurgical-silicon branches of this file. So a 1982 concentrator that separated galena from sphalerite by density was running a slurry of metallurgical silicon, and the silicon branch of this tree reaches a zinc concentrator as well as a power transformer. Silicon really does end up everywhere: 60-90% of all ferrosilicon production goes into the steel and aluminium branches, but the rest goes into heavy-media separation, and it is the sharpest possible illustration of why a tree like this has cross-links.
metal.dms.fe-silicon.note: Medium confidence on the consumption rate; it varies greatly with the ore.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: 15-30% Si, ground to under 100 um

facts.label: Source
facts.value: ferrosilicon, made in a submerged arc furnace

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.2-1 kg of ferrosilicon per tonne of ore processed

metal.sphalerite.massive-sulphide.name: Massive sulphide in a sedimentary basin
metal.sphalerite.massive-sulphide.description: The leaf: a lens-shaped body of fine-grained sulphide - sphalerite, galena, pyrite, with chalcopyrite and arsenopyrite - conformable with the bedding of a marine shale or carbonate, and sitting at a specific stratigraphic horizon. The Red Dog deposit is exactly this: a Devonian shale-hosted lens in the Buckland River basin. The ore is not in a vein you can see from the surface; it is a stratigraphic layer you have to know is there.

facts.label: Setting
facts.value: sediment-hosted massive sulphide lens in fine-grained clastic sediment

metal.solder.name: 63/37 Sn-Pb solder: wire, bar, paste
metal.solder.description: The alloy that makes electronics manufacturable. 63% tin, 37% lead is a true eutectic, so it melts and freezes at one temperature, 183 C, with no mushy interval - which means a joint goes from solid to liquid in milliseconds and the reflow time window can be measured in seconds. That property is why a decade of copper thicknesses and lead-free anxiety has not displaced it from the bench. A C64 has roughly 3,500 through-hole joints; at about 30 mg of solder per joint that is around 100 g of alloy per machine, in wire fed from spools and in a few kilos of bar in the wave-solder tank.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 63% Sn, 37% Pb by weight

facts.label: Liquidus and solidus
facts.value: 183 C exactly - a eutectic

facts.label: Tensile strength
facts.value: 30-45 kg/mm2 annealed

facts.label: Forms
facts.value: solid-core wire 0.3-1.0 mm, cast bar, and paste

metal.solder.waste.name: The solder factory's own waste streams
metal.solder.waste.description: A solder pot, a dross heap, a flux residue stream, a wash-water drain and a baghouse for the flux fumes. The dross goes to a reclaimer or to a hazardous-waste disposal contract; the baghouse dust is lead oxide and rosin and is genuinely hazardous; and the wash water goes to the drain with the lead in it. In 1982 this was the least regulated part of the whole electronics industry, and it is the reason the United States' lead exposure limits for electronics workers - which were set at a time when electronics was not a regulated industry - exist at all. The waste stream is a leaf of this tree and a genuinely uncomfortable one.

facts.label: Fractions
facts.value: flux-cork dross, baghouse dust off the flux fume, wash-water and spent degreasing solvent

metal.solder.waste-baghouse.name: The flux fume baghouse and its dust
metal.solder.waste-baghouse.description: The wave-solder hood has an extraction duct and a baghouse, because the fume is an aerosol of lead oxide and of rosin-acid degradation products. The dust is 30-60% lead oxide and it is collected as a hazardous waste. A big 1982 line threw away tens of kilograms a week. The control measure was local exhaust ventilation with a capture hood about 100 mm from the wave, and the compliance measure was an area respirator, which was why electronics assembly was one of the more heavily respirated occupations of the period.
metal.solder.waste-baghouse.note: Medium confidence on the dust composition; the lead oxide figure is representative.

facts.label: Dust
facts.value: 30-60% lead oxide with rosin-acid residues

facts.label: Capture
facts.value: local exhaust at about 100 mm from the wave, plus a baghouse

metal.solder.cleaning.name: Cleaning the flux residue off the board
metal.solder.cleaning.description: A rosin-fluxed board is covered in a sticky, slightly acidic film of flux decomposition products that will corrode the copper and will not accept a conformal coating. In 1982 it was removed in an aqueous machine - a conveyor with spray bars and drying ovens - often followed by a trichloroethane or perchloroethylene vapour degreaser. The cleaning water left the factory through the drain with the lead in it, which is the other half of the 1982 leaded-solder problem and the reason the electronics industry spent the late 1980s arguing about what to do about it.
metal.solder.cleaning.note: The water consumption and the solvent choice are representative; medium confidence.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: aqueous wash with detergents, then trichloroethane or perchloroethylene vapour degrease

facts.label: Water
facts.value: 50-200 litres per board on a heavy-duty line

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: the wash water carried lead and tin; the varnish and resin types were the difficult ones

metal.solder.waste-water.name: The solder wash-water waste stream
