Not established: the 1000-1150 C steam or dry-oxygen furnace, the hour-and-a-half cycle, the roughly 1000-1500 angstrom gate oxide of a 1982 NMOS process, and the 0.1% of wafer thickness consumed.

facts.label: Gate oxide
facts.value: ~1000-1500 A in a 1982 NMOS process

facts.label: Wet vs dry
facts.value: dry O2 for the thin gate oxide, wet steam for the thicker field oxide

metal.silica.czochralski.crucible.name: Fused quartz growth crucible
metal.silica.czochralski.crucible.description: The crucible the melt sits in is made from the same silicon chain one step further down, from high-purity quartz fused in vacuum or wet hydrogen to knock out the alkali that would poison a p-type wafer. It is expensive, fragile, and replaced every few hundred pulls.
metal.silica.czochralski.crucible.note: Crucible life varied enormously with melt temperature discipline; treat as order of magnitude.

facts.label: Fusing temperature
facts.value: ~2000 C in vacuum or wet H2

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: a few hundred growth runs in 1980s practice

metal.silica.polysilicon.name: Polysilicon ingot and rod, 9N
metal.silica.polysilicon.description: Shiny grey metalloid deposited as a polycrystalline boule on electrically heated silicon seed rods and then sawn into chunks. The chunks are the cathode-grade feedstock that the crystal puller charges. In 1982 the world outside Japan consumed polysilicon as an expensive specialty chemical, not as a commodity. The 6510 is an NMOS part, so its 1982 die uses aluminium gate metal and thermally grown oxide rather than a polysilicon gate; this branch is the industry feedstock route behind that, and it is where the energy and the boron problem lived.

facts.label: Typical purity
facts.value: 9N (99.9999999%); 6N-7N was typical of the 1982 era

facts.label: Form
facts.value: sawn rod segments, 5-30 kg per chunk in 1980s practice

facts.label: Energy for the whole route
facts.value: 100-200 kWh per kg of polysilicon

metal.silica.tcs.name: Trichlorosilane (HSiCl3), 11N
metal.silica.tcs.description: Colourless fuming liquid, the money molecule of the whole silicon industry. Made by chlorinating impure silicon with hydrogen chloride in a fluidised bed, then purified to 11 nines purely by fractional distillation, because every one of the metal impurities that matter happens to be a chloride with a different boiling point from HSiCl3.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 11N (99.999999999%) after distillation

metal.silica.tcs.fluid-bed-chlorination.name: Fluid-bed chlorination of silicon at ~300 C
metal.silica.tcs.fluid-bed-chlorination.description: Metallurgical silicon is fluidised with nitrogen and metered HCl gas at 290-320 C. Silicon converts to trichlorosilane with hydrogen off; a large fraction of the feed instead goes to silicon tetrachloride, because the oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals push the stoichiometry. The bed is a tall stainless vessel with a distributor plate, and the reaction is exothermic enough that cooling coils matter.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: Si + 3HCl -> HSiCl3 + H2, with Si + 4HCl -> SiCl4 + 2H2 as the side reaction

facts.label: Feed requirement
facts.value: ~99% Si with boron below ~20 ppm

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: historically copper or copper chloride; most modern plants run catalyst-free

metal.hydrochloric-acid.name: Hydrochloric acid (commercial 32-37%)
metal.hydrochloric-acid.description: The hydrochloric acid that chlorinates metallurgical silicon. Industrial acid is made by burning hydrogen in chlorine, both products of the chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, so the silicon plant's feedstock chain runs back through a 1970s chlor-alkali plant and, behind that, a salt mine or a solar salt pan. The same acid is used for galvanising pickling, for the stainless pickling line, for the tinplate line, and for regenerating ferric chloride etchant at the board fab.
metal.hydrochloric-acid.note: Contradicted on the azeotrope. Hydrochloric acid as a binary mixture of HCl and water has a constant-boiling azeotrope at 20.2% HCl and 108.6 C, so the 32-37% figure is a commercial sale concentration, not the azeotrope this node calls it. The route is documented - hydrogen and chlorine are combined in an HCl burner and the gas absorbed in deionised water, and the acid is also obtained by absorbing by-product hydrogen chloride. Not established: the 10-30 t of acid per tonne of polysilicon plant output.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl

facts.label: Commercial strength
facts.value: commercial acid is sold at about 32-37% w/w; that is a sale grade, NOT the azeotrope. The HCl-water azeotrope is 20.2% HCl, constant-boiling at 108.6 C.

facts.label: Typical silicon-plant demand
facts.value: order 10-30 t of acid per tonne of polysilicon plant output

metal.hydrochloric-acid.synthesis.name: HCl synthesis and absorption
metal.hydrochloric-acid.synthesis.description: Chlorine and hydrogen are fed to a steel burner with a plug of graphite or a water film that quenches the flame - a free gas-phase hydrogen-chlorine reaction is not something you leave unattended. The hot HCl gas is then absorbed in a water scrubber to make the azeotrope, and the acid is pumped out to wherever it is going: the fluidised bed, the pickle line, the tankhouse.

facts.label: Flame temperature
facts.value: >2000 C, quenched below 400 C within milliseconds

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: water scrubber, adiabatic, controlled by a weak-acid bleed

metal.silica.tcs.sicl4-recycle.name: Silicon tetrachloride by-product and recycling
metal.silica.tcs.sicl4-recycle.description: Roughly half to two thirds of the silicon fed to a fluidised-bed chlorinator leaves as SiCl4 instead of HSiCl3, because oxygen in the oxide layer and the trace metals conspire. SiCl4 boils at 57.6 C and separates easily; it was largely dumped in the 1970s and later re-admitted as a chlorinating agent. The stoichiometric route that lets a plant recycle SiCl4 back into HSiCl3 by adding hydrogen and more silicon is the reason modern plants get the yields they do.
metal.silica.tcs.sicl4-recycle.note: The fraction and its fate vary strongly between plants and years; high confidence in the chemistry, medium on the 1982 commercial split.

facts.label: 1980s practice
facts.value: a large fraction of by-product SiCl4 was sold as a solvent or to fumed-silica makers; full recycle came later

metal.silica.mgsi.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
metal.silica.mgsi.description: The commodity-grade output of a submerged arc furnace: a grey-black brittle lump material about the density of bone. In 1982 a Japanese or Taiwanese silicon plant bought it as if it were ore. The specification that matters is not the silicon but the boron - anything above roughly 20 ppm boron cannot reach electronics grade, which is why the silicon furnace takes a low-ash petroleum coke and not the 10-12% ash coke the steel industry uses.

facts.label: Why not steel coke
facts.value: coke ash carries boron and phosphorus above the electronics budget

metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace.name: Submerged-arc furnace reduction at 1800-2000 C
metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace.description: A three-phase submerged arc furnace drops quartz, coal and woodchips down between graphite electrodes into a molten carbide bath at 1800-2000 C, and carbothermic reduction strips the oxygen off silica. Chemical silicon came to dominate this furnace by the late 1970s because the copper-clad electrode could then be pushed to a much higher current density. The off-gas, silicon monoxide at 400-1000 C, carries the energy away and is what lets the furnace run near-thermoneutral on the electrode side.
metal.silica.submerged-arc-furnace.note: The off-gas silicon monoxide chemistry was well understood by the 1980s and was the basis of several recovery processes that were still being commercialised then.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO

facts.label: Furnace size
facts.value: 25-75 MVA, 3-6 electrodes, 150-400 t/day of silicon

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: graphite or UHP carbon, consumed at ~1-1.5 t per t of silicon

facts.label: Off-gas
facts.value: SiO-rich gas leaving at 400-1000 C, cleaned in cyclones and baghouses

facts.label: Power
facts.value: order 11,000-13,000 kWh per tonne of silicon from the arc furnace alone

metal.silica.reducer.name: Carbothermal reductant: coke and woodchips
metal.silica.reducer.description: The silicon furnace burns roughly one tonne of high-ash-reduction carbon per three tonnes of silicon, and the recipe is a tight compromise: too much ash and you get slag, too much volatile and the furnace fumes. Producers blend low-ash petroleum coke or anthracite with a proportion of woodchips, because the wood brings in hydrogen and potassium that volatilise out and are quietly useful, and because the porosity of the burnt wood helps the charge breathe. The same class of carbon, at different purity, is the reductant in the tin, lead, zinc, ferrosilicon, ferromanganese and ferrochrome branches of this file.
metal.silica.reducer.note: The consumption ratio varies with furnace design and recovery; treat as order of magnitude.

facts.label: Ash target
facts.value: <1% for the reducer, versus the 10-12% typical of foundry coke

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: order 0.9-1.1 t of carbon per t of silicon

metal.silica.petcoke.name: Calcined petroleum coke for silicon
metal.silica.petcoke.description: Delayed-coker green coke calcined in a rotary or shaft kiln to 2200-2800 C and quenched. The silicon grade is chosen for low ash, low vanadium and low sulphur, which is a narrow slice of the coke market - needle coke and sponge coke are the mainstream products and both carry more vanadium than the silicon furnace wants.

metal.silica.tcs.distillation.name: Fractional distillation of HSiCl3
metal.silica.tcs.distillation.description: Tall, stainless, pressure-rated columns that separate trichlorosilane from its neighbours purely on volatility. The separation is the entire purification strategy: nothing clever happens chemically, the same material is simply re-fractionated until the boron is gone.
metal.silica.tcs.distillation.note: The boron cuts are the hard part: BCl3 boils close to trichlorosilane and boron has a low distribution coefficient, so 1980s plants used tall columns and many theoretical plates.

metal.silica.polysilicon.deposition.name: Siemens deposition on UHF-heated rods
metal.silica.polysilicon.deposition.description: Trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow over silicon rods held just below their melting point by radio-frequency induction, and silicon atoms drop out as polycrystalline growth. Rod temperature is the whole ballgame: too cold and you get powder, too hot and you get liquid droplets that fall into the bed. Two temperature measurement methods were in use - an optical pyrometer sighted on a blackened patch of rod, and a movable thermocouple in the gas stream - and calibrating that pyrometer was a plant secret worth millions.

facts.label: Induction frequency
facts.value: 200-500 kHz historically, multi-MHz later

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 100-200 kWh per kg of polysilicon across the whole chlorosilane route

facts.label: Deposition rate
facts.value: single-digit micrometres per hour per rod in 1980s reactors

metal.silica.polysilicon.flaking.name: Crushing, flaking and acid etching of the rod
metal.silica.polysilicon.flaking.description: The deposited rod is sawn with a slurry-impregnated circular saw, then the pieces are fractured and leached in hot hydrochloric-nitric acid to strip near-surface contamination from the seed end. What the puller wants is small pieces with clean fracture faces, because every surface is a chance to recontaminate. Rod ends were also ground back and reused as seed.
metal.silica.polysilicon.flaking.note: The etch chemistry varied plant to plant and was rarely published; described here from general practice.

facts.label: Chunk size
facts.value: 5-30 kg per sawn rod segment in 1980s practice

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: a hot HCl/HF polish removes the saw damage and the surface boron before the chunk is charged to the puller

metal.silica.polysilicon.doping.name: Doped vs undoped polysilicon
metal.silica.polysilicon.doping.description: Two grades were produced side by side in the same plant. UNdoped polysilicon went to the crystal puller for Czochralski ingots. Heavily doped material - p-type with boron or phosphorus, n-type with phosphorus or arsenic - went to subcollector plugs, to doped polysilicon films in later processes, and, most importantly, to the heavily doped epi and subcollector wafers that the NMOS logic was built on. In 1982 the dopant was dosed into the trichlorosilane stream as phosphine or the corresponding trichloride.
metal.silica.polysilicon.doping.note: Not established: which dopant gas a given 1982 Taiwanese polysilicon plant used; the specific pairing is medium confidence.

facts.label: Target resistivity
facts.value: 0.005-0.02 ohm-cm for a doped polysilicon film; subcollector 0.1 ohm-cm

facts.label: Dopant sources
facts.value: PH3 for both polarities in older practice; AsH3 for n-type

c64.joystick.name: Joystick controller
c64.joystick.description: The self-centring 4-way joystick Commodore bundled with the C64 and sold with most of its software: a moulded gate plate held neutral by four springs, four miniature microswitches underneath it, a steel shaft with a ball top, a plastic knob, and a coiled cable to one of the DE-9 control ports. Five moving electrical contacts and one mechanical centring mechanism, in a shell of black ABS.
c64.joystick.note: The C64's bundled joystick is a plain 2-button 4-way unit; the 3-button version came later and was supplied separately or with the C64C. Commodore also sold a version with a fire button on the shaft and a third button on the knob top; Commodore 4611 and its successors are cited for these in the retro literature, but no Commodore part number is established for the specific 1982 bundle.

facts.label: Directions
facts.value: 4-way + fire (2-button in the 1982 bundle)

facts.label: Centring
facts.value: 4 torsion/coil springs, not a positional detent

facts.label: Switches
facts.value: 4 miniature microswitches

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: coiled, terminating in a DE-9 male plug

c64.joystick.cable.name: Coiled cable and DE-9 plug
c64.joystick.cable.description: A coiled cable of seven or nine conductors leaving the chassis bottom, terminating in a DE-9 male plug that looks mechanically identical to the socket it plugs into but has male pins. The plug's contacts are gold-flashed brass, made the same way and by the same stamping and plating route as the socket contacts on the machine.
c64.joystick.cable.note: The coiled cable was traditionally PVC-insulated stranded copper; some units shipped with a straight lead. The number of conductors varies between joystick models and the C64 bundle's count is not established.

facts.label: Conductors
facts.value: 9 (5 signals + common + fire + spares)

facts.label: Plug
facts.value: DE-9 male, gold-flashed brass contacts

c64.joystick.cable.plug.name: DE-9 male plug contacts
c64.joystick.cable.plug.description: Stamped brass pins, gold-flashed over nickel, moulded into a thermoplastic D-shell that keys to the socket's D-shape. Because the D-shell is polarised, the plug physically cannot be inserted backwards - the same mechanical trick as the moulded keyway on a D-sub generally.
c64.joystick.cable.plug.note: Not established: which metal and plating a 1982 joystick's DE-9 plug used. The D-shell polarisation is inherent to the DE-9 form factor, but nothing consulted states the pin alloy or plating for an aftermarket joystick.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.name: Stranded conductor
c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.description: Fine-stranded copper, tinned, for flexibility. Seven or nine of them, depending on the joystick model - the C64 reads five signals plus the common and the fire button.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.tinnin.name: Tinning of the conductor
c64.joystick.cable.plug.conductor.tinnin.description: The stranded conductor is tinned so the crimp barrel grips cleanly and the joint is solderable. Tin from cassiterite, in a peripheral cable a few centimetres from the machine.

c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly.name: Cable assembly and strain relief
c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly.description: The conductors are crimped into the DE-9 pins and the cable is clamped by a moulded strain relief at the shell, so bending the cable does not work the pin out of the crimp. Strain relief is the single cheapest thing that decides whether a peripheral cable survives five years of use.
c64.joystick.cable.plug.cable-assembly.note: Not established: the crimped strain-relief construction and the claim that strain relief decides cable life. Plausible connector practice, but no document consulted describes a joystick cable assembly.

c64.joystick.knob.name: ABS knob and top button
c64.joystick.knob.description: The moulded handle on the top of the shaft. On a 2-button unit it is a plain grip knob; on a 3-button unit a fire switch is moulded into the shaft and a third button into the knob's top, sprung against the shaft and actuated by a rod inside it. Black ABS, textured on the grip faces.
c64.joystick.knob.note: A soft overmould on the grip was a quality feature on some 1980s sticks and absent on the cheap bundled ones; I cannot say which the C64 bundle shipped with.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, sometimes with a soft TPE or rubber overmould

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: injection moulded, ~10^4-10^5 shots per tool

c64.joystick.knob.abs.name: ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene)
c64.joystick.knob.abs.description: The workhorse thermoplastic of consumer electronics housings in 1982: injection mouldable to a hard gloss surface, tough enough for a hand-held knob, and cheap. The same material as the keycaps, and largely the same hydrocarbon feedstock.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.note: The three monomers are traced once, under the keycap ABS; this knob is the same copolymer.

facts.label: Melt flow
facts.value: chosen grade ~5-15 g/10 min for housings

facts.label: Mould temperature
facts.value: ~230-260 C melt, 40-80 C tool

c64.joystick.knob.abs.fire-button.name: Fire button on shaft and knob
c64.joystick.knob.abs.fire-button.description: On 3-button sticks a fire switch is moulded into the shaft itself and a third button into the knob top, actuated by a rod inside the shaft. Each is a miniature microswitch of the same family as the direction switches.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.name: Injection moulding of the knob
c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.description: The knob is a two-shot or single-shot ABS moulding, often with a moulded-in texture or a soft overmould. It has to be comfortable and it has to stay on the shaft for decades.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.note: Not established: whether the knob was two-shot or single-shot moulded, and whether it carried a moulded-in texture or soft overmould. Most 1980s joystick knobs were single-shot ABS; no document consulted describes it.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.tool.name: Knob mould tool
c64.joystick.knob.abs.moulding.tool.description: A hardened steel cavity tool, polished so the knob has a gloss finish. Thousands of knobs per tool life; the polish is the difference between a shiny knob and a matt one.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.name: Pigments and fillers in the ABS knob
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.description: The knob is black because of a pigment - usually a carbon black or an iron oxide - dispersed in the ABS before moulding, and it is stiffened with glass or mineral filler. Where a lighter colour was wanted the whitener was rutile titanium dioxide from ilmenite, which is the same titanium chain as the barium titanate capacitor powder.
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.note: The colourant is dispersed into the polymer in a compounding extruder before the moulding, not added at the press, so a black joystick knob contains a few per cent of carbon black and an antioxidant package. Titanium dioxide for a lighter colour comes from ilmenite sand, the same titanium chain as the barium titanate capacitor powder.

facts.label: Black pigment
facts.value: carbon black or iron oxide

facts.label: White pigment
facts.value: titanium dioxide from ilmenite

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.name: Pigment dispersion in the ABS
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.description: The colourant is dispersed into the polymer in a compounding extruder before the moulding, not added at the press. A black joystick knob therefore contains a few per cent of carbon black and an antioxidant package.

c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.name: Titanium dioxide whitener
c64.joystick.knob.abs.filler.pigment-dis.description: Where a lighter colour was used, the whitener was rutile TiO2 from ilmenite - the same titanium chain as the barium titanate powder.

c64.joystick.shaft.name: Steel shaft and ball top
c64.joystick.shaft.description: A cross-section steel shaft pressed into the gate, rising through the chassis with a moulded ball or ball-and-paddle top at the user end. The ball is the most-comforted part of the design and is also the part that wears smooth or cracks in old machines.
c64.joystick.shaft.note: Not established: which steel, the cold-drawn square section, and the 6 mm by 35 mm dimensions. The corrosion-at-the-bushing failure mode is well attested across the vintage joystick genre but is not a sourced measurement. The blast-furnace burden belongs to the metals file.

facts.label: Shaft
facts.value: ~6 mm square steel section, pressed into the gate

facts.label: Top
facts.value: moulded ball or ball-and-paddle, ~20 mm diameter

c64.joystick.shaft.steel.name: Cold-drawn steel bar
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.description: Mild or low-alloy steel, cold-drawn to a square section and cut to length. The gate's press fit is what locates the shaft; the steel is unplated except where it passes through the chassis, where corrosion is a genuine failure mode on a machine stored in a damp shed. The steel begins as sintered hematite-magnetite pellets and lump ore charged with coke and limestone, and the bulk of world steel in 1982 was made that way, so rust and pitting on a forty-year-old joystick shaft is this ore still trying to get out.
c64.joystick.shaft.steel.note: The frozen-shaft failure is well documented across the vintage joystick genre; the steel chain itself belongs to the metals file.

facts.label: Section
facts.value: ~6 mm square, ~35 mm long

facts.label: Corrosion
facts.value: the shaft rimes in place in the bushing, freezing the stick

facts.label: Ores
facts.value: hematite Fe2O3 and magnetite Fe3O4

facts.label: Route
facts.value: blast furnace -> basic oxygen furnace -> continuous cast bar

facts.label: Burden
facts.value: sinter or pellet ore, coke and limestone

c64.joystick.microswitches.name: Four miniature microswitches
c64.joystick.microswitches.description: Four sealed miniature switches under the gate, one per direction. Each is a plastic case with a plunger and a fixed leaf plus a sprung leaf, gold-plated so the contact resistance stays low through millions of actuations. The plunger is depressed by a rib on the gate as it slides.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: ~10 mA at 5-12 V DC; 10^5-10^6 actuations

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: gold-plated on brass or phosphor bronze

facts.label: Case
facts.value: moulded thermoset or thermoplastic body, sealed or dust-covered

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.name: Switch case polymer
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case.description: A small moulded case in a filled thermoset or a glass-filled nylon, chosen so the case survives being dropped off a desk with the stick still in hand - which, for a joystick sold with a computer, was a frequent event.

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..name: Through-hole mounting and solder lugs
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..description: The switches are pushed into holes in the joystick's printed board and their pins soldered from underneath. Positioning them on that board is what sets how far the gate has to travel before a direction registers - the mechanical timing of the whole joystick.
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..note: Not established: that the microswitches were mounted in holes in a small printed board with through-hole pins soldered from underneath, and that board layout set the gate travel. On many 1980s joysticks the four microswitches were wired directly to the DE-9 with no local board at all.

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..name: Glass-filled nylon case
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..description: A glass-filled nylon case gives a microswitch enough stiffness to keep its contact force with a thin wall, and enough toughness to survive being dropped. It is the standard material for that class of switch through the 1980s.
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..note: Glass-filled nylon is documented as increasing structural and impact strength and rigidity, with thermoplastic glass-filled composites quoted at 25-30 % glass fibre. Not established: glass-filled nylon as the standard microswitch case material through the 1980s, and that this is the case material in a 1982 joystick.

c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..name: Nylon-6-6 resin
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..description: The base polymer of the glass-filled nylon case, made from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid. Caprolactam is the route to nylon 6, a different grade. A single C64 contains nylon in its switch housings, its joystick bushings and its microswitch cases.
c64.joystick.microswitches.plastic-case..note: The chemistry is documented: nylon-6,6 is the condensation polymer of a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid, and nylon 6 is a different molecule made by ring-opening polymerisation of caprolactam. Not established: hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid as the specific pair - the sources give the general ABAB structure without naming the monomers for 6,6 - and the claim about nylon appearing in a single C64's switch housings, bushings and microswitch cases.

c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.name: Sprung leaf contact
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.description: Inside each switch a formed leaf is bowed against a fixed contact; pressing the plunger straightens the leaf onto it. The contacts are gold-plated over nickel because a joystick switch is a low-current, high-cycle signal contact where a stable millivolt-level resistance matters, and because the leaf is wiped clean on every actuation.
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.note: The sprung-leaf mechanism and the gold-over-nickel contact plating are standard practice for this switch class. Not established: the 0.1-0.5 um gold thickness and the 50-150 g operating force, neither of which appears in any document consulted for this machine.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: gold over nickel, ~0.1-0.5 um gold

facts.label: Operating force
facts.value: ~50-150 g on the plunger

c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.name: Gold plating of the microswitch leaf
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.description: The contact is gold-plated over nickel so its resistance stays at the millivolt level through millions of cycles. Gold leaf contacts in this class of switch were a real reliability advantage over the silver and nickel contacts used in cheaper equivalents.
c64.joystick.microswitches.leaves.gold-p.note: Not established: that these particular switch contacts were gold-plated over nickel. Gold plating is a real low-level-contact practice, but no document consulted identifies the plating in a 1982 joystick's microswitches.

c64.joystick.gate.name: 4-way direction gate
c64.joystick.gate.description: A cross-shaped sliding gate that physically interlocks so only one of the four directions can be closed at a time - the same gating trick as a keyboard's 3-key rollover prevention. The gate rides on four ribs and is held centred by four springs, so it is self-centring and has no detented 'gate 2' half-way position.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: moulded glass-filled nylon or PBT gate on an ABS chassis

facts.label: Gating
facts.value: one direction at a time; diagonals blocked

facts.label: Return
facts.value: four coil or torsion springs on the gate ribs

c64.joystick.gate.friction.name: Bushing and friction washer
c64.joystick.gate.friction.description: The shaft is supported by a plastic bushing or a nylon washer in the chassis, and a felt or fibre friction pad under the gate sets the feel. Friction pads compress and shed debris with age, which is the second classic cause of a stiff or drifting stick.
c64.joystick.gate.friction.note: Friction pads are standard in this class of joystick; pad dimensions for the C64's unit are not established.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.name: Friction pad
c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.description: A small felt or fibre pad under the gate that sets the lateral friction. Felt pads need almost no oil, dry-run cleanly, and shed a black dust that eventually gums the gate if the stick is never cleaned.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.wool.name: Wool felt
c64.joystick.gate.friction.felt-pad.wool.description: Pressed wool felt sets the lateral friction of the gate. Unlike an oiled pad it needs no lubricant, which matters because an oiled pad in a 1982 joystick attracts dust and eventually gums.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.name: Nylon bushing in the chassis
c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.description: A moulded nylon bushing in the ABS chassis that the steel shaft runs in. Nylon is used because it is self-lubricating and will not gall the shaft; a metal bushing would seize onto the shaft as it rimes.

c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.name: Lubricated nylon 6,6 bushing resin
c64.joystick.gate.friction.nylon-bushing.description: A lubricated or unfilled nylon grade, chosen for low friction against steel. The base polymer is nylon 6,6 from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid; caprolactam is the route to nylon 6, a different grade. The joystick contains nylon in this bushing, in its microswitch cases and in its gate.

c64.joystick.gate.spring.name: Centring springs
c64.joystick.gate.spring.description: Four small compression or torsion springs push the gate back to neutral from every direction. They are the part that wears out: once the springs weaken, the stick stays pushed, which is the most common repair on a vintage joystick and the reason 'joystick centering' appears in every retro repair guide.
c64.joystick.gate.spring.note: That centring springs are the wear item and the common repair is widely attested in repair guides, but no document consulted is an acceptable source for that. Not established: music-wire or stainless spring wire as the material.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: music-wire or stainless spring wire

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: the limiting part; springs lose tension and occasionally snap

c64.joystick.gate.spring.replacement.name: Why springs are the failure point
c64.joystick.gate.spring.replacement.description: Gate springs carry the whole centring duty and are cycled by every direction press. Once one is weakened the stick sits off-centre and the machine reads a direction the user is not pressing - the most common single joystick fault of the era.
c64.joystick.gate.spring.replacement.note: The failure mode is plausible and repeatedly reported, but 'the most common single joystick fault of the era' is an unsourced ranking. No primary or encyclopaedic source consulted quantifies joystick fault frequency.

c64.joystick.gate.spring.wire.name: Centring spring wire
c64.joystick.gate.spring.wire.description: Drawn music-wire or stainless spring wire, coiled and closed. Centring springs are the cheapest consumable in the whole joystick and the one that is always replaced rather than repaired.
c64.joystick.gate.spring.wire.note: Not established: music-wire or stainless spring wire as the material, and that these springs are always replaced rather than repaired.

c64.extras.name: Finishing and bundled extras
c64.extras.description: Three branches that hang off the machine rather than being part of it: how legends and colours were printed onto moulded plastic, how one keyboard key becomes a bit in the matrix, and the joystick that shipped in the box in some markets. None of them is needed to trace the machine's own supply line - they are the finishing and the bundled accessories, gathered here so they are not mistaken for part of the board.
c64.extras.note: A grouping rather than a plant. Its three children are real things: decoration is a set of processes, the keyboard switches are parts, the joystick is a part. Two of the three are not interconnect goods, so the branch sits with the machine rather than with the interconnects it happens to be stored beside. Not established: which joystick shipped in the box in which market - Commodore's own documentation does not state a standard bundled joystick, so the three-child grouping is a convenience rather than a documented shipping configuration.

c64.keyboard-switches.name: Keyboard matrix switches and domes
c64.keyboard-switches.description: How one keystroke on a C64 becomes a 1 in memory: 63 rubber domes on a rigid printed circuit board, scanned by CIA #1 as an 8 x 8 matrix. The domes are carbon-loaded rubber pills that short two plated pads when a keycap's plunger drives them closed, and the scanned result is simply a pair of row and column lines being connected.
c64.keyboard-switches.note: The C64 keyboard is not a flexible membrane with silver-ink traces. It is a rubber-dome keyboard on a rigid printed circuit board with plated conductive pads, and the domes themselves are the conductive element. Earlier VIC-20-generation Commodore keyboards also used rigid boards but with bare, unplated copper pads, which oxidise - the reason some early C64 keyboards need cleaning while later ones do not. Commodore did use silver-filled ink pads on some other keyboards and peripherals of the period, so that construction is worth carrying, but it is not the breadbin C64.

facts.label: Keys
facts.value: 63 (including 5 cursor keys); matrix directly covers 64 of 66 positions

facts.label: Matrix
facts.value: 8 columns driven on CIA #1 port A, 8 rows read on port B

facts.label: Domed keys
facts.value: 61 of the 63; SHIFT LOCK is wired on the same line as LSHIFT

facts.label: Out-of-matrix
facts.value: RESTORE (wired to NMI) and SHIFT LOCK

facts.label: Key travel
facts.value: ~2-2.5 mm before the dome closes

facts.label: Operating force
facts.value: ~40-70 g typical

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.name: Flat ribbon cable to the mainboard
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.description: A flat multi-conductor ribbon leaves the keyboard board, loops through the case, and terminates at the pin header on the front-left edge of the mainboard. The ribbon is crimped into an insulation-displacement connector on the keyboard end in later designs, and soldered directly to the header on the mainboard end.
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.note: The mainboard end is confirmed: the 250407 parts list has CN1 as 'Header w/LKG Sil 2.54 CTR 20 Pin', a 20-pin locking silicon header on a 2.54 mm pitch, which is what the ribbon plugs into. Not established: the 0.5-1.27 mm conductor pitch, the PVC jacket, the insulation-displacement crimp at the keyboard end, and the fatigue-fracture-at-the-header failure mode - none of that appears in the primary documentation.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: flat flexible cable, PVC-jacketed, 0.5-1.27 mm pitch

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: conductor fatigue fracture at the header - the single most common C64 keyboard fault

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.name: PET/PVC flat flexible cable
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.description: Parallel copper conductors laminated between polyester film layers with a PVC jacket. The jacket and the film are all hydrocarbon polymers, so this cable is chemically the same family as the switch housings and the case.
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.note: The mainboard end is a 20-pin 2.54 mm locking header per the primary parts list. Not established: parallel copper conductors laminated between polyester film with a PVC jacket, the 0.5-1.27 mm conductor pitch, and the insulation-displacement crimp. The 1992 manual does not describe the cable.

facts.label: Jacket
facts.value: PVC or flat polyester (PET)

c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.name: PVC jacket
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.description: The ribbon's outer jacket is extruded PVC, the cheapest flexible insulation available. Vinyl chloride is made by oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine, and the chlorine comes from salt - rock salt mined or solution-mined - while the ethylene comes from a steam cracker. So the ribbon cable ends at both rock salt and crude oil.
c64.keyboard-switches.ribbon.film.pvc.note: Vinyl chloride comes from oxychlorinating ethylene with chlorine, and the chlorine comes from brine electrolysis, so the ribbon jacket touches both an oil field and a salt field. The vinyl chloride monomer node is chem.pvc.vcm.

facts.label: Vinyl chloride route
facts.value: ethylene + chlorine -> EDC -> VCM, oxychlorination

facts.label: Chlorine
facts.value: from rock salt / brine electrolysis

c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.name: SHIFT LOCK and RESTORE, the two off-matrix keys
c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.description: Two of the 66 keys are not in the scanned 8x8 matrix. SHIFT LOCK is wired in parallel with LSHIFT on the same wire, so the firmware cannot tell the two apart and pressing SHIFT LOCK simply holds the shift bit down. RESTORE is on a completely different wire, straight to the 6510 NMI pin, so pressing it halts the CPU with no firmware involvement at all - a hardware reset, not a key.
c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.note: Documented on the C64 wiki keyboard page. Key count cross-checked against the C64 Service Manual ("KEYS 66 Keys total, 2 Cursor control keys, 4 Function keys") and against c64.keyboard, whose facts give 66 total with 8x8 = 64 scanned and 2 off-matrix. SHIFT LOCK is a latching dome arrangement (the dome is deformed or a second contact is added) rather than a scanner-visible key.

facts.label: SHIFT LOCK
facts.value: wired to the same wire as LSHIFT

facts.label: RESTORE
facts.value: wired to NMI, outside the matrix entirely

c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.latchin.name: Latching dome for SHIFT LOCK
c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.latchin.description: A dome that latches: pressing it collapses it and it stays collapsed, requiring a second, firmer press (or a press on a neighbouring key) to release. Mechanically it is a deformation of the rubber dome itself rather than a separate switch, which is why no space in the matrix is spent on it. The latch works because the rubber is shaped so that under a light press it collapses past its own elastic limit and stays collapsed, which makes it a mechanical latch rather than an electrical one - and is why the firmware has no idea a separate key exists.
c64.keyboard-switches.shift-lock.latchin.note: Not established: the latching-dome mechanism itself. The service manual confirms that RESTORE and the off-matrix keys exist and that depressing RESTORE triggers U20 to generate a non-maskable interrupt, but nothing consulted describes how the SHIFT LOCK key latches, or that its matrix position is not scanned.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.name: Keycap and plunger mechanism
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.description: A double-shot moulded keycap on a cross-shaped plastic stem. The stem sits in a plunger barrel and carries either a coil spring back up (the common later C64 keycap) or, on the earliest VIC-20-derived keyboards, nothing at all - those rely purely on the rubber dome for their return and feel markedly sluggish.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: double-shot moulded ABS or ABS/PC, legend printed or moulded

facts.label: Plunger
facts.value: moulded plastic cross stem in a barrel

facts.label: Return
facts.value: coil spring in later keycaps; absent on the earliest keyboards

facts.label: Travel
facts.value: ~2 mm before the dome closes

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.name: Coil return spring
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.description: A small stainless or music-wire spring inside the plunger barrel returning the key to its rest position and setting the initial (pre-dome) force. Without it the user bottoms out on the dome itself, which is why the earliest keyboards feel hard and inconsistent.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.note: Music wire (high-carbon steel) or stainless; the spring wire is wound on a small coil-winder in the millions.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.name: Spring coiling machine
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.description: A cam-controlled coiler winds a coil spring from wire, sets its free length and closes the ends, tens of thousands per hour. Every keycap plunger spring on the keyboard was made on a machine of this type.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.note: Not established: that the keycap plunger springs were made on cam-controlled coil-winders at tens of thousands per hour. This is a general statement about spring manufacturing, not about this keyboard.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.name: Tool steel cam and dies
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.coil.description: The coiler tool is hardened tool steel, and the coiler is a Camweld or similar automatic machine. Ferrous tooling, so iron ore again.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.musi.name: Music wire (patented steel)
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.spring.musi.description: A high-carbon steel wire, patented and drawn to a fine diameter, with a very high tensile strength - which is what lets a millimetre-thick coil inside a keycap return thousands of times without taking a set.

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: ~0.6-0.9 % (music wire)

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Double-shot moulding of the top legends
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: The legends on the TOP of the keycap - letters, numbers and symbols - are moulded into the plastic, not printed on it. The cap is injection-moulded twice in one tool cycle: first in the dark brown-grey base colour, then a second shot of a contrasting lighter colour is injected into a slightly larger cavity, covering everything except the legend characters, which are left as uncoated islands of the first shot. Nothing is printed on the top face, so the legend cannot wear off - which is why a forty-year-old cap still reads cleanly, and why the mould line and the islands are visible when a cap is pulled off its stem. This covers the cap top only: the graphics characters on the front wall are a different process (c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend), and the two are told apart at a glance by whether the character wears.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.note: The top face of the cap is double-shot, white legends on a very dark brown; the PETSCII legends on the front face are printed separately. Keyboard Wiki (themk.org): The alphanumeric keys are double-shot white on a very dark brown. Deskthority thread 8102: With the exception of the spacebar, they are all double shot injection molded keycaps. Neither the Commodore C64/C64C Service Manual nor The Anatomy of the Commodore 64 discusses keycap printing. The 1988 C64C is different: the same Keyboard Wiki page records All legends ... pad-printed on top of the keys for that machine.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: the cap top only - letters, numbers and symbols

facts.label: Shots
facts.value: two injection mouldings, co-moulded in the same tool cycle

facts.label: Legend
facts.value: island of the base-colour shot, not a printed decal

facts.label: Wear
facts.value: none - a moulded legend outlives the printed front characters

facts.label: Exception
facts.value: the spacebar is reported not to be double-shot; all other caps are

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Second-shot colour
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: The outer shot is pigmented with an organic or inorganic colourant at high loading. The light legends on the dark brown-grey caps - and, on some sets, the orange or grey function-key caps - are all achievable with pigmented ABS; the moulding must be run at high enough pressure that the two shots fuse rather than delaminate.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Iron oxide pigments
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: Synthetic iron oxides, made by oxidising iron scrap or precipitating from an iron solution, were the standard browns, reds and blacks of the period and are still used. They begin at iron ore and end up in the keycap, which makes the keycap a surprisingly direct consumer of the iron chain.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.name: Colourant in the second shot
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot.description: The second-shot colour is a pigment dispersed in the ABS matrix at high loading. Organic pigments give brighter colours and cost more; inorganic iron oxides give the earthier browns, reds and blacks. The moulder buys a masterbatch rather than raw pigment, so the colour arrives as a compounded material.

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.name: ABS copolymer (three monomers)
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene: a styrene-acrylonitrile matrix rubberised with polybutadiene. It is tough, dimensionally stable, chemically scratch-resistant and - crucially for legends - it takes paint and plating well. Almost every C64 keycap is ABS or ABS/PC.

facts.label: Components
facts.value: acrylonitrile + butadiene + styrene

facts.label: Why ABS
facts.value: impact strength plus the ability to hold a printed legend

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.name: Sohlo ammoxidation of propylene
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.description: The acrylonitrile monomer is made by the Sohlo process: propylene, ammonia and oxygen are passed over a bismuth-antimony or bismuth-molybdenum catalyst to give acrylonitrile selectively. Propylene itself comes from steam cracking of naphtha, so the keycap of a C64 is roughly one and a half hydrocarbon molecules away from crude oil.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: Sohlo ammoxidation, ~425-500 C, fixed bed

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~70-80 % selectivity on propylene

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.name: Bismuth-antimony catalyst
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.description: The ammoxidation catalyst is a bismuth molybdate or bismuth-antimony promoted silica. Bismuth came from bismuthinite, a comparatively rare ore worked chiefly in Bolivia and China, and it was a real bottleneck for acrylonitrile capacity in the 1980s.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.acrylon.note: Bismuth supply was genuinely tight in the early 1980s and the ammoxidation catalyst industry was a significant consumer; the size of that demand is not quantified.

facts.label: Ore
facts.value: bismuthinite, Bi2S3

c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.name: Polybutadiene rubber phase
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.description: The elastic phase that makes ABS impact-resistant, made by polymerising butadiene derived from refinery butadiene, which itself comes from steam cracking propylene. This is the hydrocarbon tree: propylene to butadiene to the rubber in the keycap's grip surface.
c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.abs.butadie.note: Not established: that a polybutadiene phase is what makes these keycaps impact-resistant, and the propylene-to-butadiene cracker route. The butadiene polymer chain belongs to the chemicals file; this node asserts its presence in the keycap without evidence.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.name: Carbon-loaded rubber domes
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.description: Each key position has a small moulded rubber pill, domed upwards, whose underside carries a conductive carbon-loaded contact that bridges two pads when the dome is crushed. Because carbon is loaded into the rubber as a filler rather than plated on, the dome is its own contact - it wears slightly with use and it is the consumable part of the switch.

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: carbon black or graphite powder in a silicone or neoprene elastomer

facts.label: Activation force
facts.value: ~150-250 g on the dome alone, plus the keycap spring

facts.label: Life
facts.value: ~millions of actuations, but the conductive face tarnishes with skin oil and dust

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.name: Compression moulding of the dome sheet
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.description: The domes are moulded as a continuous sheet on a heated platen press: uncured compound is placed in a multi-cavity tool, pressed, cured, and the sheet released as one piece with every key's dome attached. Domes therefore arrive as a single printed-circuit-sized rubber sheet that has to be aligned to the pads by hand.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.note: Compression-moulded dome sheets were standard; whether the C64's came as a sheet or pre-applied to a carrier film is not established.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: ~150-180 C, minutes, for silicone; ~100-140 C for neoprene

facts.label: Sheet
facts.value: one sheet per keyboard, 61-63 domes

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.name: Steel dome tool
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.description: A machined or spark-eroded steel tool with one hemispherical cavity per key. It has to be replaced as the dome geometry is re-specified, and its surface finish is what the dome's mating face is polished against.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.name: Spark-erosion machining of the dome cavity
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.description: A fine copper electrode is brought within micrometres of the workpiece in a dielectric bath and pulses of a few microseconds melt a microscopic crater per pulse. Spark erosion is how a one-micron hemispherical cavity gets cut in hardened tool steel without any mechanical stress on the surface.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.note: Spark erosion as a process is real, but not established: that it was used to cut one-micron hemispherical cavities in hardened tool steel for these dome tools, the micrometre gap, the microsecond pulse, and the copper electrode. Graphite is the electrode material actually cited elsewhere in the tree for dome tooling.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.name: Graphite tool electrode
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.too.description: Graphite is the standard spark-erosion electrode: it is conductive, machinable to a fine tip, and wears slowly by re-graphitising. Machined graphite is made from petroleum coke calcined at ~3000 C.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.pla.name: Heated platen press
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.moulding.pla.description: A hydraulic flat-bed press with heated platens holds a multi-cavity dome tool against the compound long enough to cure the elastomer. Small presses of this type did the whole dome sheet for a keyboard in one shot.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.name: Carbon-filled elastomer compound
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.description: Carbon black is compounded into the elastomer at a few tens of per cent by weight. The particles form a percolation network so the dome conducts along its own bulk, and the higher the loading the lower the resistance - but too much loading makes the dome brittle. This is the same black powder that goes into resistor films and pot tracks.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition.note: Not established: the 20-60 phr carbon black loading and the contact resistance of tens to hundreds of ohms. Both are quantitative figures for a specific conductive-elastomer compound, and neither appears in any document consulted. The percolation mechanism is plausible but unsourced here.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: roughly 20-60 phr carbon black

facts.label: Contact resistance
facts.value: typically tens to hundreds of ohms - enough to trip a CMOS input, far too much for a logic 'low'

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Carbon black filler (petroleum-derived)
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: The same furnace-black feedstock used in the resistors, compounded into the elastomer. The dome's conductivity and its wear rate are both set by the grade and loading of this powder. A high-structure furnace black gives a stronger percolation network at lower loading, so a dome can be made conductive with less filler and stay soft; the grade choice is the difference between a responsive key and a stiff one.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..note: Not established: that a high-structure furnace black gives a stronger percolation network at lower loading, and that this is what distinguishes a responsive key from a stiff one. No carbon-black grade comparison is available in the sources consulted.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Silicone or neoprene elastomer
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: The dome body. Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane) was favoured for its high compression set and wide temperature range; neoprene (polychloroprene) for oil and abrasion resistance. Both are thermoset elastomers, vulcanised in the mould rather than injection-moulded as thermoplastics, which is why they are compression-moulded sheet.
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..note: Which elastomer the C64's dome sheet used is not established; both were standard.

c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..name: Silicone dome compound
c64.keyboard-switches.domes.composition..description: Silicone rubber is built on a silicon-oxygen backbone and is filled with reinforcing silica. It stays elastic over a wide temperature range and does not take up much oil, which is why a silicone dome does not swell and seize.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.name: 8 x 8 keyboard matrix
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.description: Eight column lines snake around the board and eight row lines snake around the other way, each pair of crossing traces forming one key. Pressing a key connects its column to its row; the firmware walks the matrix by writing a pattern to CIA #1's port A and reading port B. Because one row line can touch eight different columns, a single conducting bridge is the entire 'switch'.

facts.label: Scan
facts.value: write column pattern to $DC00, read rows from $DC01

facts.label: Latency
facts.value: one scan per ~1/60 s frame unless idle

facts.label: Ghosting
facts.value: 3-key combinations can produce an extra false key - the classic matrix ghosting problem

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-e.name: Glass-epoxy laminate (FR-4)
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-e.description: Woven glass-fibre cloth impregnated with epoxy and pressed into a sheet. The standard printed-circuit laminate since the 1960s, replacing the older phenolic paper board. The keyboard board is a trivial two-layer FR-4 part, but it goes through the same copper foil lamination and hole-drilling lines as a mainboard.
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb-glass-e.note: FR-4 as the standard printed-circuit laminate is uncontroversial. Not established: that the keyboard board is specifically two-layer FR-4, and that it went through the same copper-foil lamination and drilling lines as the mainboard. The keyboard is normally a separate assembly on its own line.

c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.name: Epoxy resin of the laminate
c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.description: The epoxy that binds the glass cloth is derived from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin, both of which are petrochemical. A two-layer keyboard PCB is thus a woven silica sheet glued with a fossil-derived resin and clad in copper.
c64.keyboard-switches.pcb-resin.note: Not established: that this laminate's epoxy is derived from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin. That is the standard chemistry for the epoxy family, but no document consulted ties a particular 1982 keyboard PCB to it.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.name: Rigid keyboard PCB with plated pads
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.description: A glass-epoxy laminate board, drilled and plated through in the usual way, carrying the matrix traces as copper and terminating each key position in a pair of plated pads. On the breadbin keyboard the pads are plated metal; on the earlier VIC-20-derived boards they were bare copper, and bare copper oxidises into a high-resistance film - the reason those keyboards need periodic cleaning and later ones generally do not.
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.note: The bare-copper-pad claim comes from a restoration account of an early VIC-20-derived C64 keyboard whose activation pads are not protected from oxidation the way later keyboards are. The laminate is chem.glass-fiber plus chem.epoxy, and the traces are metal.copper.foil.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: rigid FR-4, not a flex membrane

facts.label: Pads
facts.value: plated through-hole pads on breadbin boards; bare copper on earliest

facts.label: Mounting
facts.value: standoffs and screws into the case, not clips

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.name: Plating of the key pads
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.description: The exposed pads are plated - gold over nickel on later keyboards - so the carbon contact of the rubber dome has a low-resistance, non-oxidising surface to bridge onto. Where the plating is absent or has worn through, the bare copper oxidises and the key needs cleaning.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.name: Gold flash on the key pads
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.pad-pla.description: A thin gold flash over nickel on the key pads. Gold does not oxidise, so the dome keeps making contact for decades; where the flash is thin or gone, the key stops working until cleaned.

c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.name: Electrodeposited copper foil
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.description: The matrix traces are copper, deposited on the laminate by an electroplating line using acid copper sulphate solution and an insoluble anode. The same copper foil process as the mainboard, at a much thinner gauge.
c64.keyboard-switches.matrix.pcb.copper-.note: Not established: acid copper sulphate electrodeposition on an insoluble anode for this board, and the 35 um (1 oz) foil thickness. Foil gauge is a boardhouse specification, not something a reference document states.

facts.label: Foil thickness
facts.value: ~35 um (1 oz)

c64.decor.name: Decorating the case and the keycaps
c64.decor.description: Getting colour and type onto moulded plastic in 1982 meant printing it, not moulding colour into it. Commodore pad printed the sixty-six keycap legends in two colours and printed the rainbow Commodore badge on the bezel with the same two-colour tampo press; the shiny bars of the badge used ink loaded with atomised aluminium flake. Screen printing went onto flat panels and labels elsewhere in the machine but could not hold the fine leather grain of the bezel, which is exactly why pad printing won on the case. The case itself was single-colour: the beige-brown is pigment let down into the resin at the compounding line, not a coating sprayed or printed onto the part.
c64.decor.note: Not established: that Commodore pad-printed the sixty-six keycap legends and the rainbow badge in two colours, and that the bright badge bars carried metallised flake. Neither the service manual nor the parts lists record a decorating route.

facts.label: Legends
facts.value: two-colour pad printing (tampo), one character per cap top

facts.label: Badge
facts.value: pad printed in colour, with metallised flake in the bright bars

facts.label: Case colour route
facts.value: pigment in the resin at compounding, not painted on

facts.label: Screen printing
facts.value: flat panels and labels only; will not hold the bezel grain

c64.decor.prepress.name: Prepress: artwork to film and plate
c64.decor.prepress.description: Every legend and every logo started as artwork, composed mechanically or photographically in 1982, then copied onto black-and-white film by a process camera; the film was used to expose a plate, either a photopolymer or an electrotyped copper one. Text was set in hot metal or phototype, and the Commodore rainbow artwork was assembled from hand-painted separations.
c64.decor.prepress.note: Not established: which of the two plate routes Commodore used, and how the rainbow separations were made. The camera-to-film-to-plate sequence is a printing-industry convention rather than a documented Commodore practice.

facts.label: Text setting
facts.value: hot metal or phototypesetting, later CRT phototype

facts.label: Copy
facts.value: process camera onto ortho film

facts.label: Plates
facts.value: photopolymer, or electrotyped copper

c64.decor.prepress.film.name: Ortho photographic film (negative)
c64.decor.prepress.film.description: The black-and-white film that carries the image to the plate. It is a cellulose or polyester film coated with a silver-halide emulsion; exposed in a process camera or a contact frame, then developed and fixed in a chemical line.
c64.decor.prepress.film.note: Not established: the film type and gauge carried on a Commodore prepress line. The material is described here as a class of product, not a recorded part.

c64.decor.prepress.silver-halide.name: Silver halide emulsion
c64.decor.prepress.silver-halide.description: Silver bromide or silver iodide crystals suspended in gelatin. The silver comes from silver ore, and most photographic silver of the era was recovered as a byproduct of lead and copper refining rather than mined for itself.
c64.decor.prepress.silver-halide.note: That the light-sensitive constituent of a photographic emulsion is a silver halide is established: Daguerre redirected his efforts toward the light-sensitive silver halides, and sodium thiosulphate was found to be a solvent of silver halides and to fix silver-halide-based photographs. Not established: that the crystals here are specifically silver bromide or silver iodide suspended in gelatin, and that most photographic silver of the era was recovered as a byproduct of lead and copper refining rather than mined for itself.

c64.decor.prepress.film-base.name: Film base (cellulose triacetate or polyester)
c64.decor.prepress.film-base.description: A flexible transparent film on which the emulsion is cast. Cellulose triacetate was the standard photographic film base, made from acetic anhydride and cellulose; polyester (PET) film base became common later for its dimensional stability.
c64.decor.prepress.film-base.note: Not established: whether a 1982 Commodore legend negative was on cellulose triacetate or on polyester film, and the base thickness.

c64.decor.prepress.cellulose.name: Cellulose (for triacetate)
c64.decor.prepress.cellulose.description: Dissolved from wood pulp and regenerated into fibre. The film route is a small, high-purity use of cellulose compared with paper, but it is the same feedstock: a tree.

c64.decor.prepress.acetic-acid.name: Acetic acid and acetic anhydride
c64.decor.prepress.acetic-acid.description: Made by catalytic oxidation of ethanol, or by the carbonylation of methanol. Methanol comes from synthesis gas, which comes from natural-gas reforming.
c64.decor.prepress.acetic-acid.note: The methanol carbonylation route is established and was the dominant one: rhodium-catalysed methanol carbonylation became the dominant method of acetic acid production, with the first plant on that catalyst built in 1970. Not established: the 150-200 C figure, the ethanol-oxidation alternative, and that the acetic anhydride for a cellulose triacetate base came from this route. Cellulose triacetate film base is made from acetic anhydride, which is made from methanol by carbonylation. So the negative that carries a keycap legend is partly wood and partly natural gas, which is as far as this trail usefully goes.

facts.label: Carbonylation
facts.value: methanol + CO to acetic acid, rhodium catalyst, 150-200 C

c64.decor.metallised.name: Metallised and pearlescent ink
c64.decor.metallised.description: The shiny bars in the Commodore rainbow badge are metallised ink: pigment-grade aluminium flake suspended in a binder and printed, then optionally burnished between heated polished rollers so the flakes lie flat and mirror rather than scatter. The same effect could be had from a hot foil, pressed from vacuum-metallised polyester or aluminium film with a type plate, but on a textured ABS case the foil needs a rougher surface or a soft die, which is why flake ink won.
c64.decor.metallised.note: Not established: that the Commodore rainbow badge was printed in metallised flake ink, and that the print was burnished. The comparison against hot foil stamping is a general decorating argument, not a record of what Commodore did.

facts.label: Flake
facts.value: atomised aluminium, about 5-15 um

facts.label: Alternative route
facts.value: hot foil stamping, 150-250 C die; lost to flake ink on a textured case

facts.label: Appearance
facts.value: burnished flake reads as a flat mirror-like metallic that shifts with viewing angle

c64.decor.metallised.binders.name: Metallised ink binder
c64.decor.metallised.binders.description: A drying ink binder that holds the flakes flat and lets them reflect. Formulated so the flake lies parallel to the surface; this is what produces the flat metallic look rather than a sparkly one.

c64.decor.metallised.flake.name: Atomised aluminium flake
c64.decor.metallised.flake.description: Molten aluminium atomised with air into 5-15 um flakes, then washed, sieved by size and coated with an oxidation-inhibiting lacquer so they do not go grey. The same atomisation principle as the aluminium in the EMI shield, at a different scale: the flake is pigment, the foil is sheet.
c64.decor.metallised.flake.note: Not established: the flake size range and the passivation route on a 1982 Commodore ink. Atomised aluminium flake pigment is an old and well documented material; the specific grading applied here is not.

facts.label: Atomisation
facts.value: air-blast or mechanical, about 1400 C melt

facts.label: Flake size
facts.value: 5-15 um, sieved

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: lacquer or chromate wash to stop further oxidation

c64.decor.screen-printing.name: Screen printing
c64.decor.screen-printing.description: Silk screening through a mesh, used on Commodore parts where the surface is flat enough: printed panels, cartridge labels and some case markings. It cannot print the grain-textured bezel reliably, which is exactly why pad printing won on the case and on the keycaps.
c64.decor.screen-printing.note: Retained because Commodore did screen-print product panels and cartridge labels, but nothing on the breadbin case or keycaps went through a screen.

facts.label: Mesh
facts.value: nylon monofilament or stainless steel wire, 100-200 mesh

c64.decor.screen-print.ink.name: Screen-printing ink (one-part epoxy)
c64.decor.screen-print.ink.description: A one-component epoxy or polyester ink with a latent hardener, screen-printed through the stencil and then heat-cured. Epoxy ink is unusually durable on plastics and is what screen-printed Commodore product panels and keycap overlays used.
c64.decor.screen-print.ink.note: One-part epoxy inks cure at 120-150 C for 5-20 minutes, or flash to UV if the formulation is UV-curable. Epoxy ink is unusually durable on plastics and is what screen-printed Commodore product panels used; the epoxy chain from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin is documented under the other-polymers branch of the case.

c64.decor.screen-print.squeegee.name: Squeegee blade
c64.decor.screen-print.squeegee.description: A rubber or neoprene blade in a wooden or aluminium holder that forces ink through the stencil and wipes the surface. The durometer of the blade is the operator's variable: hard for fine detail, soft for heavy coverage.

c64.decor.screen-print.neoprene.name: Neoprene squeegee rubber
c64.decor.screen-print.neoprene.description: Polychloroprene, chosen because it resists the solvents in screen ink and wears well. It is the same chloroprene rubber used for cable jackets and gaskets, again pointing back to the C4 cracker cut.
c64.decor.screen-print.neoprene.note: Neoprene, also polychloroprene, is established as a family of synthetic rubbers produced by polymerisation of chloroprene, which exhibits good chemical stability and maintains flexibility over a wide temperature range. Not established: that it was chosen specifically for solvent resistance against screen inks, and the same chloroprene compound being used for cable jackets and gaskets.

c64.decor.screen-print.emulsion.name: Screen emulsion (PVA or diazo)
c64.decor.screen-print.emulsion.description: The photosensitive coating that becomes the stencil. Diazo emulsions, standard in 1982, are washed out with water after exposure; PVA emulsion requires a separate exposure through the base and is more solvent-resistant. The stencil is exposed through a film positive and then washed.
c64.decor.screen-print.emulsion.note: Not established: whether the stencils were diazo or PVA emulsions, and the stencil thickness. Screen printing as such is documented; the specific chemistry on a Commodore line is not.

facts.label: Common type (1982)
facts.value: diazo resin emulsion on mesh

facts.label: Stencil
facts.value: ~0.05-0.1 mm thick

c64.decor.screen-print.mesh.name: Screen mesh (nylon monofilament or stainless wire)
c64.decor.screen-print.mesh.description: A woven mesh stretched and glued to an aluminium frame. Nylon is used where solvent or epoxy inks would attack a wire screen; stainless wire is used where long life under abrasive inks matters. Both are woven from a drawn filament or wire on a loom.
c64.decor.screen-print.mesh.note: In part in conflict: the source says the most popular mesh in general use is made of polyester, with special-use mesh materials of nylon and stainless steel available to the screen-printer. That nylon and stainless are the special-case materials here is therefore the right shape of claim, but the 100-200 mesh count, the 50-80 um drawn filament and the aluminium frame are not established. The nylon is hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid again - the same PA6,6 that goes into connector latches, drawn down to 50-80 um for the mesh.

facts.label: Count
facts.value: ~100-200 mesh for fine legends, coarser for solid areas

c64.decor.pad-printing.name: Pad printing the legends and badge
c64.decor.pad-printing.description: The workhorse decorating process on this machine. A soft silicone rubber pad is pressed onto a flat metal cliche carrying the image in wet ink, picks the ink up on its raised relief, then deforms against the curved or textured plastic part and transfers the image. One pad, one colour, one station; two stations give the two-colour keycap legends. It is chosen over screen printing precisely because the parts are curved, crowned and leather-grained, none of which a flat screen will lie against.
c64.decor.pad-printing.note: Registration is the skill of the job: on a two-colour legend the second impression has to land exactly on top of the first, shifted symbols and all, so every printed part is checked for legibility, registration and offset before it goes into the machine, under a fixed lamp. A shift of half a character width is a reject, which is one reason the legends look so consistent on surviving machines. UV-curing ink was available by 1982 and needed no drying time, but solvent drying was still the volume route.

facts.label: Stations
facts.value: 1-2 (single or two-colour)

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: hundreds to thousands of impressions per hour

facts.label: Surface tolerance
facts.value: curved, crowned and textured parts, unlike screen printing

facts.label: Inspection
facts.value: 100% visual under a fixed lamp; registration to a fraction of a character width

c64.decor.uv-curing.name: UV curing of ink
c64.decor.uv-curing.description: A mercury or metal-halide lamp floods the printed part in under a second and the photo-initiator in the ink polymerises it in place. It was the big printing-technology change of the late 1970s and early 1980s: instant cure, no solvent, no oven, and a harder, more abrasion-resistant print.
c64.decor.uv-curing.note: Two elements are established: the photoinitiator is what absorbs the light and starts the reaction, which controls the cure rate and depth of cure; and medium-pressure mercury-vapor lamps have historically been the industry standard for curing products with ultraviolet light. Not established: the 80-120 W/cm lamp rating, the sub-second cure, that the photo-initiator was a benzophenone or an imidazole ketone, and that UV was established on Commodore keycaps by 1982 while solvent drying was still the volume route. By 1982 UV curing was established in screen and pad printing on plastics but not yet universal; solvent drying was still the volume route. Its big advantage for a decorating shop is that a printed keycap can be stacked immediately with no drying time.

facts.label: Lamp
facts.value: medium-pressure mercury, 80-120 W/cm

facts.label: Cure time
facts.value: sub-second per exposure

facts.label: Photo-initiator
facts.value: a benzophenone or imidazole ketone

c64.decor.pad-print.ink.name: Pad-printing ink (solvent or UV)
c64.decor.pad-print.ink.description: A free-flowing, low-viscosity ink that will transfer off a soft pad and then dry on a plastic part. In 1982 most pad inks were solvent-based (glycol ether / xylene / ester solvent with an alkyd or acrylic resin and a pigment); UV-curing pad inks existed and were gaining ground, and were faster but needed a lamp.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink.note: Not established: the solvent system, the resin and the viscosity of Commodore pad-printing ink, and whether the volume route in 1982 was solvent or UV. The general pad-printing mechanism is documented.

facts.label: Viscosity
facts.value: very low, ~10-40 s Zahn cup

facts.label: Drying
facts.value: air dry (minutes), heat (seconds), or UV (instant)

c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent.name: Ink solvent (glycol ether / ester blend)
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent.description: The volatile carrier that gives pad ink its low viscosity. Common 1980s pad-ink solvents were propylene glycol ethers, dibutyl phthalate or xylene blends. It flashes off the pad quickly enough to give a sharp print and slowly enough that the impression can be placed.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-solvent.note: Solvent-based pad ink is largely gone from consumer goods today because of VOC regulation; UV-curing pad ink, which needs no solvent at all, is the modern replacement and was already available in 1982.

c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment.name: Legend and logo pigments
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment.description: The legend white is almost always titanium dioxide in an alkyd binder; the rainbow logo uses a set of saturated organic pigments - phthalocyanine blue, quinacridone magenta, azo yellow - and sometimes a metallised flake for the bright bars.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-pigment.note: Not established: which pigments were in the Commodore keycap and badge inks. The pigment supply chain converges on the same handful of chemical plants as the case masterbatch and the box ink; its use in these inks is not.

c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin.name: Ink binder resin (alkyd or acrylic)
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin.description: The film-forming part of the ink: an alkyd built from drying-oil fatty acids and a polyacid (the same chemistry as the printing ink vehicle on the box), or an acrylic copolymer. It is chosen for adhesion to ABS, which is notoriously hard to print on without a surface treatment.
c64.decor.pad-print.ink-resin.note: ABS has a low surface energy and low surface tension (~38-39 dynes/cm, against ~72 for water), which is why printing ink on it needs a good wetting binder or a plasma/corona treatment - and why the legends on a forty-year-old cap can be abraded off but not easily peeled.

c64.decor.pad-print.cliche.name: Cliche (printing plate)
c64.decor.pad-print.cliche.description: The flat copper or nickel electrotype that carries the image, sunk into a plate table and flooded with ink. The traditional route photographs the artwork onto a sensitised copper plate, electroplates it up to about 1 mm and then grinds and polishes the surface back so that only the image stands proud; the photopolymer plate is the same object made from a photosensitive polymer film on a steel backing, exposed through the artwork film and washed out in relief, which needs no electroplating step and suits short runs. A flat pad-print cliche is a simpler object than a litho plate because there is no water damping - it is essentially a stencil on a copper block - which is why pad printing was chosen for short runs as well as long ones.
c64.decor.pad-print.cliche.note: That the plate carrying the image in pad printing is called a cliche is established by the process description, which names the cliche as the element the image is transferred from via the silicone pad. Not established: which of the two routes Commodore used, and it does not change what the cliche is - a copper electrotype with a ground-back relief, or a photopolymer plate on a steel backing. The electrotype is the older route and the one a print shop could repair; the photopolymer plate is cheaper per plate and better on fine detail, which matters for a 66-character legend set.

facts.label: Plate
facts.value: copper or nickel electrotype, or a photopolymer plate on a steel backing

facts.label: Image relief
facts.value: about 0.05-0.2 mm on an electrotype, 0.1-0.5 mm on a photopolymer

facts.label: Electrodeposit
facts.value: about 1 mm, ground and polished back to the relief

c64.decor.pad-print.electroplating.name: Copper electrotyping the plate
c64.decor.pad-print.electroplating.description: The sensitised copper plate is electroplated in an acid copper bath to build a thick deposit on the image, then the surface is ground and polished back so only the image stands proud. It is an old, slow process, but it gives an image hard enough to print millions of impressions.
c64.decor.pad-print.electroplating.note: Not established: that Commodore printing plates were copper electrotypes, and the deposit thickness and bath conditions. Electrotyping is an old process but no Commodore record of it has been found.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: acidified copper sulphate with an additive

c64.decor.pad-print.pad.name: Silicone rubber printing pad
c64.decor.pad-print.pad.description: A soft, solvent-resistant, low-surface-energy pad, almost always silicone rubber, cut or cast with the relief to pick up and transfer the image. It is the consumable that has to be replaced every few thousand impressions, and pad hardness relative to the detail size is the operator's main variable.

facts.label: Hardness
facts.value: Shore A 30-70 depending on the image

facts.label: Life
facts.value: thousands to tens of thousands of impressions

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: two-part cast pad with a hardened steel or aluminium backing

c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound.name: Two-part silicone pad compound
c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound.description: A polydimethylsiloxane casting system cured at room temperature with a tin catalyst, or an addition-cure platinum system.
