Pads are cast in a mould against the plate image so that the relief matches the cliche exactly; the chemistry is the same PDMS as the conductive rubber in the keyboard switch and as the pad-printing pad itself.
c64.decor.pad-print.pad-compound.note: Not established: the pad compound, the tin-catalysed room-temperature cure and the 24 hour figure. Pad printing is documented to use a silicone pad; the casting chemistry is not.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: room temperature about 24 h, or heat-accelerated addition cure

c64.decor.pad-print.machine.name: Two-colour pad printing press
c64.decor.pad-print.machine.description: A small cast frame with a plate table, an ink cup or doctor blade, a silicone pad on a shuttle head, and part fixtures on a rotating or indexing table. Each colour station is one table position with its own pad.
c64.decor.pad-print.machine.note: Not established: the station count, the index table and the registration tolerance on a Commodore decorating line. Pad printing presses are described in the general literature; a Commodore one is not identified.

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: indexing table with 2-8 stations

peripheral.name: Television, cassette drive and connectors
peripheral.description: A C64 shipped with no screen. It drove a television set through an RF modulator, saved to a cassette deck through the 1541 drive, and took input from a joystick. Three separate supply chains meet here: the television, the cassette drive, and the connectors that carry the signal between them.

peripheral.plug.name: The connectors: aerial socket, serial link, user port, cassette port
peripheral.plug.description: Three connectors that made a C64 usable rather than just powered: the aerial socket the RF modulator hijacked, the nine-pin link to the 1541, and the cartridge-edge expansion connector on the back that opened the machine up - documented as a 44-pin card edge, not a 34-conductor ribbon.
peripheral.plug.note: In the 1992 service manual parts list the back-panel expansion connector is a 44-pin card edge (CN6, C 906100-02) and the drive port is a 9-pin Mini-D (CN8/9, C 251057-01). The 34-conductor figure in this node is not established, nor is the aerial socket type.

peripheral.plug.cassette-port.name: The six-pin cassette port
peripheral.plug.cassette-port.description: The connector that carries both the audio to a tape recorder and the power to a 1541. It is a 6-pin connector, carrying read, write, sense, motor, 5 V and the 9-12 V motor rail. Commodore's own cable turned it into a DIN-style socket that plugged into a consumer cassette recorder, so a C64 could save to a music deck. The same port carried the power for the 1541, which is why a 1541 has no power socket of its own.
peripheral.plug.cassette-port.note: The sense pin was how the C64 knew a motorised deck was present, and the motor pin was how it started a consumer recorder. The exact pinout ordering is not established, and a wrong one is worse than none; the functional set of connections is the reliable part.

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: serial read, serial write, motor on/off, sense, and 5 V plus the 9-12 V rail

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: a moulded 6-pin plug to a 6-pin DIN socket or a cassette-REC-style plug

peripheral.plug.userport.name: The 34-conductor user port ribbon
peripheral.plug.userport.description: On the back of the C64, a 34-conductor edge connector on a card, which brought out the 6510's eight data lines, twelve address lines, the read and write strobes, the IRQ and NMI lines, the serial and parallel ports, and the 5 V and ground. It was the machine's expansion door, and it was how a disk interface, a printer interface, a sampler or an EPROM programmer reached the CPU. The cable was a flat ribbon with a mylar or tinned-copper conductor, a foil shield and a PVC or polyester jacket.
peripheral.plug.userport.note: A ribbon cable of this type is a laminated structure: parallel copper conductors, 0.03-0.05 mm thick, separated by a polyester film, laminated between films, wrapped in a mylar or aluminium-foil shield and a PVC jacket. The foil and the polyester are petroleum and silica products respectively. Whether the 1982 C64 user port card edge was gold-plated or plain nickel is not established; many were simply tin-plated board edge.

facts.label: Conductors
facts.value: 34 (17 x 2), 0.1 inch pitch

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: about 20 cm to 30 cm of ribbon, foil-shielded with a drain wire

facts.label: Card edge
facts.value: a gold-plated or nickel-plated PCB edge that plugged into the C64's rear connector

peripheral.plug.userport.connectors.name: Card-edge and D-sub connectors
peripheral.plug.userport.connectors.description: The connectors were gold-plated or nickel-plated brass and copper contacts in a thermoplastic (usually glass-filled nylon or a phenolic) insulator, crimped or soldered to the ribbon. A D-sub has a metal shell (often tinned steel or nickel-plated brass) that both shields the connection and provides the mechanical polarisation that stops anyone plugging it in backwards.
peripheral.plug.userport.connectors.note: The gold on a connector contact is the same anode-slime gold as the bond wire on the 6502. Gold plating on a connector is thin gold over a nickel underplate so the gold does not diffuse into the copper and leave a brittle intermetallic.

facts.label: Gold
facts.value: 0.05-0.1 microns of hard gold on the contacts, over nickel, from anode slimes

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: brass or steel, nickel-plated, with a ground latch

peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.name: PVC jacket and polyester film from crude oil
peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.description: The ribbon's jacket is PVC (from ethylene and salt-derived chlorine) and its insulation between conductors is polyester film (from the same PET chain as the cassette tape base). Both are grandchildren of crude oil, and both are the same two chemistries already traced elsewhere in this tree.
peripheral.plug.userport.pvc.note: The PVC takes metal.salt-brine, the canonical salt, as an ingredient.

facts.label: PVC
facts.value: suspension-polymerised, 57 degrees C, plasticised with a phthalate ester

facts.label: Plasticiser
facts.value: DOP or DINP, itself from an oxo process on butanol, which is from propylene

peripheral.plug.serial-link.name: Nine-pin serial link to the drive
peripheral.plug.serial-link.description: The 1541 was not daisy-chained through the cassette port; it plugged into the C64's second serial port through a nine-pin high-density D-subminiature cable. That separate port is how the computer knew a disk drive was present at all: there was no other way for the 1541 to announce itself except by talking on this line, and the drive type was auto-detected from what it said.
peripheral.plug.serial-link.note: It was a 9-pin high-density D-sub on the drive side. On the C64 itself the drive port was a 9-pin D-sub, the same physical connector, and the signals were Commodore serial, not RS-232. Note the parallel with the user port below: the C64's expansion port was a 34-conductor card edge. Three CIA port lines drive the serial bus - ATN out, clock out and data out - each inverted through U8 before reaching the device, and the connector is a 9-pin Mini-D. Not established: the 0.1 inch pitch, the about 1 m cable length, and 5 V logic levels.

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: 9-pin high-density D-subminiature, 0.1 inch pitch

facts.label: Cable
facts.value: a flat or twisted pair cable, about 1 m

facts.label: Signal
facts.value: a serial bus, logic levels at 5 V, not RS-232

peripheral.plug.rf.name: The aerial socket, hijacked
peripheral.plug.rf.description: The 75 ohm coaxial socket on the back of the television. The C64's modulator lead was a short 75 ohm coax with an F-type plug that went into it in parallel with the set's aerial. Because the modulator was a weak source, the lead had to be a good 75 ohm match and the set's aerial input had to be isolated or the local signal would back-feed.
peripheral.plug.rf.note: The modulator's coax lead and the set's own aerial lead are both ingredients of this socket rather than parts of it. An RF cable was a listed C64 accessory (C 326189-01), and the RF modulator mixed sync/luminance, colour and audio to generate a TV composite signal on pin 5. Not established for the supplied lead: 75 ohm, RG-59 and the about 1.5 m length - the F connector is normally used with RG-6/U or RG-59/U.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm

facts.label: Lead
facts.value: about 1.5 m of RG-59, supplied with the C64

peripheral.cassette.name: Datasette and cassette
peripheral.cassette.description: A C64 with no drive could not save. Commodore's answer was a 1530 or 1541 disk-shaped drive that took ordinary compact cassettes and wrote them with a magnetic head at 9,600 baud, plus a spool of tape that was mostly polyester film and mostly iron oxide. Saving a 1541 program to tape was a two minute operation of real-time winding, and the alignment problems of a 1541 were a running joke precisely because a cassette had no feedback.
peripheral.cassette.note: The 1541 had no mains supply of its own. It drew 5 V (through a fuse and reverse-polarity diode) and about 12 V from pins 4-7 of the C64's cassette port. The 1530 datasette was the same idea in a different box, with the tape slot on top and a position sensor; the 1541 is the one people remember because it had no position sensor at all.

facts.label: Drive
facts.value: 1530 (Series I, 4,800 baud) or 1541 (Series II, 9,600 baud)

facts.label: Tape
facts.value: standard compact cassette, C-60 or C-90, 1/8 inch wide

facts.label: Tape speed
facts.value: 4.76 cm/s (1 7/8 inches per second)

facts.label: Power
facts.value: 5 V and about 12 V DC, both from the C64's own supply via the cassette port

peripheral.cassette.tape.name: The cassette tape itself
peripheral.cassette.tape.description: A compact cassette is a 3.81 mm wide strip of polyester film 12 microns thick, coated on one side with about one to two microns of acicular iron oxide pigment in a binder, and wound onto hubs inside a plastic shell. The C64 wrote 9,600 baud onto it, which at 4.76 cm/s works out to a flux transition every 200 to 300 microseconds, near the limit of what a standard-bias cassette could resolve. Almost everything in it is either crude oil or iron ore.
peripheral.cassette.tape.note: A C64 could use a standard C-60, a C-90, and in principle any compact cassette. Commodore recommended particular brands because the format was sensitive to tape formulation: a high-bias C-120 tape was on the wrong bias wavelength for the 1541, and a Type II chrome tape had a different coercivity and a different noise floor.

facts.label: Tape width
facts.value: 3.81 mm (1/8 inch)

facts.label: Base film
facts.value: polyester (PET), 9-12 microns

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: about 1-2 microns of gamma-Fe2O3 (or CrO2 for Type II)

facts.label: Areal density
facts.value: roughly 4-9 g/m2 of magnetite, so a whole 90 m C-60 carries only 1-3 g of iron oxide

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: about 25-30 kA/m standard bias; 45-55 kA/m for CrO2

facts.label: Remanence
facts.value: about 0.25-0.3 T

facts.label: C60 length
facts.value: 90 m total, 45 m per side at 4.76 cm/s

facts.label: Oxide
facts.value: iron(III) oxide or, for Type II, chromium dioxide

peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.name: Slitting to 1/8 inch
peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.description: The coating line made a web a metre or more wide; it was then slit into 3.81 mm strips with rotary knives, tens of kilovolts of static keeping the thin film from clinging to the rollers. The slit tape was wound onto master reels, then onto cassette reels by a winding line that also cut it to length (45 m per side for a C-60), formed the leader, and inserted the hub.
peripheral.cassette.tape.slitting.note: A C-60 and a C-90 differ in length and gauge. A C-60 at 12 microns and a C-90 at 9 microns hold about the same total oxide per side, so the C-90 has to be made of a higher-output oxide (often cobalt-modified) to hold as much. The polyester base film is an ingredient of the slitting step. Not established: the coating-line web width, the rotary slitter knives, the static charge that holds the thin film off the rollers, and the 9-12 micron base gauge. The 3.81 mm strip width and the 45 m per side for a C-60 are the reliable parts.

facts.label: Length
facts.value: 45 m per side for a C-60, 135 m total; a C-90 is 45 m per side at a thinner gauge

facts.label: Gauge
facts.value: 9-12 microns of base film

peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.name: Pressure pad and felt
peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.description: A small pad of felt or synthetic non-woven on a stainless steel leaf spring, mounted in a plastic carrier inside the shell behind the head window. Its job was to press the tape gently against the head so the head could read and write reliably, and to press the tape against the shell's ribs to select the C-1 to C-5 path. The felt was the one consumable part of a cassette; it shed debris into the head gap and a worn pad was a classic cause of a 1541 failing.
peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.note: Felt pads are wool, a textile, and polyester non-wovens were the synthetic alternative. Either way this is not a mined or drilled raw material but a processed fibre.

facts.label: Felt
facts.value: about 0.5-1 mm of wool felt or a bonded polyester fibre

facts.label: Force
facts.value: a few tenths of a newton, enough for good contact without jamming the tape

peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.materials.name: Felt and the stainless spring
peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.materials.description: The pad was wool felt or a bonded polyester fibre web about a millimetre thick, glued to a stainless steel leaf spring in a plastic carrier. Wool felt is carded wool fibre matted and pressed; the spring was a 300-series stainless, so the iron came from the blast furnace and the chromium from chromite, the same chromite as the chrome plating on a telescopic antenna.
peripheral.cassette.tape.pad.materials.note: A strip of 300-series stainless is made of blast-furnace iron and ferrochrome, and the spring is chrome-plated, so both are ingredients of the pad rather than things it contains.

facts.label: Felt
facts.value: about 0.5-1 mm of matted wool or synthetic fibre

facts.label: Spring
facts.value: 0.15-0.3 mm stainless strip, giving a few tenths of a newton

peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.name: Cassette shell and hubs
peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.description: The compact cassette case: two thin polystyrene or ABS shells, each with a hub, so that the tape is enclosed in a rigid 100 x 64 x 12 mm box with five windows on one edge for the head, capstan and the pressure pad, two hub windows, and the write-protect notches. The hubs were glass-filled nylon or moulded ABS with the six drive slots, running on the two hub spindles.
peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.note: The five pressure-pad windows are the IEC C-1 to C-5 positions. The felt pad inside the shell, pressed against the tape by the capstan bulge, biases the tape against one of the shell's internal ribs so that, depending on how the shell is placed in the deck, the tape passes over the erase head, between the erase and R/P heads, over the R/P head, or not in contact with either. That is why a cassette's orientation and which end is which mattered, and why a mis-loaded tape would write nothing. The mechanism is certain; the precise numbering of which position does what is less certain. Not established: the IEC C-1 to C-5 pressure-pad window numbering and which position lands on which head - the node's own note already concedes this - the about 22 mm hub bore, and glass-filled nylon as the hub material, since this file's hub node gives nylon 66. The five-screw two-shell construction and the 100 x 64 x 12 mm envelope are the standard part.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: about 100 x 64 x 12 mm, injection moulded polystyrene or ABS

facts.label: Hub
facts.value: glass-filled nylon or ABS, six drive slots, bore about 22 mm

facts.label: Window layout
facts.value: two capstan holes, a head window (erase and R/P), five pressure-pad windows (C1-C5), two hub windows

facts.label: Write protect
facts.value: recesses in the shell; a plug in two of them blocks the sense switch

facts.label: Screws
facts.value: five small screws joining the two shells, with the tape trapped between them

peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.hub.name: Hub, glass-filled nylon
peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.hub.description: The reel hub runs on the shell's spindle and drives the tape through a wind process. It had to be dimensionally stable and dimensionally tight so the tape wound at a given radius came off at the right tension. It was glass-filled nylon or ABS, with the six drive slots on the inside face for the winding spindle.
peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.hub.note: The six-slot hub pattern and the general hub geometry are certain; the bore diameter is not verified against the IEC dimension, so it is stated loosely. The hub is moulded from nylon 66, chem.polyamide.nylon-66.

facts.label: Bore
facts.value: an inner bore of order 20 mm that slips over the cassette moulded spindle; the exact IEC figure is not certain here

facts.label: Drive slots
facts.value: six internal slots, the standard cassette hub pattern

peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.abs.name: Shell material: polystyrene or ABS
peripheral.cassette.tape.shell.abs.description: A cassette shell is thin and needs to hold a dimension, so it was moulded from general-purpose polystyrene (cheap, brittle, easy to mould) or from ABS for a stiffer shell. Audio tapes were conventionally clear or smoke polystyrene or ABS; computer and C64 tapes were frequently the same shells, since nothing about the shell distinguished them.

facts.label: Wall
facts.value: 1-2 mm

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: injection, 200-240 degrees C, a very fast cycle for a thin shell

peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.name: Coating line: doctor blade, orientation field, cure ovens
peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.description: A web of polyester film, a metre or more wide, unwinds and passes under a coating station where the magnetic dispersion is laid down in one or two passes by a doctor blade or a gravure roll, a few microns thick. It passes between magnets that align the acicular particles along the length of the film, then into an oven at 60-100 degrees C to drive off the solvent and cure the binder. A backing-coat station then applies the carbon-black anti-smear layer, and the whole web is slit to width.
peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.note: Doctor blades (a blade wiping the web against a rubber roll) and gravure rolls (a patterned metal roll transferring a metered film) were both in use; gravure gave finer control and was the direction the industry moved. The solvent was recovered by condensing and distilling the oven exhaust, which is why a tape plant of the period smelled of toluene and had a distillation column.

facts.label: Web speed
facts.value: 300-900 m/min on a modern line; a 1982 line was 100-400 m/min

facts.label: Wet coating
facts.value: a few microns, shrinking to 1-2 microns of oxide

facts.label: Orientation field
facts.value: about 5-20 kA/m (roughly 100-250 Oe)

facts.label: Oven
facts.value: 60-100 degrees C, solvent flash and cure

facts.label: Passes
facts.value: one magnetic coat, plus a backing coat; sometimes a base coat

peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.backing.name: Backing coat: carbon black for the leader and anti-smear
peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.backing.description: On the back of the magnetic coating was a sub-micron layer of extra pigment and carbon black. It did two things: it gave the visible leader tape (the clear or white strip at the start of a cassette) its colour and its opacity so a deck could find it, and it suppressed print-through, where a signal on one layer of the wound tape magnetises the layer next to it and comes back as a ghost. Carbon black, again, from petroleum coke.
peripheral.cassette.tape.coating.backing.note: The carbon black comes as an ingredient, out of the petroleum-coke chain.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.5-2 microns

facts.label: Leader
facts.value: about 1.5 m at each end, opaque to a reflective tape-position sensor

peripheral.cassette.tape.dispersion.name: The dispersion: pigment, binder, dispersant
peripheral.cassette.tape.dispersion.description: The pigment was not coated as a powder. It was dispersed in a binder so that the needles separate and stay separated, and then magnetically oriented on the film. A typical binder was a cellulose lacquer, an acrylic or polyurethane, dissolved in a solvent such as toluene, xylene or methyl ethyl ketone; in the 1970s and early 1980s there was also a water-based polyurethane dispersion. The dispersant was a surfactant or a phosphate ester that wets the oxide surface so the needles do not clump back together. The pigment and the binder are combined and then refined on a three-roll mill or a sand mill, working the agglomerates apart from a few tens of microns down to a few microns at 50-70% solids, until the dispersion is smooth. Dispersion quality set the noise floor of the finished tape, because a clump of pigment is a defect that scatters the recording.
peripheral.cassette.tape.dispersion.note: Toluene and xylene are aromatics from the same naphtha cracking that feeds styrene. The binder chemistry for magnetic tape was for decades one of the most closely guarded industrial secrets; the general class (cellulose lacquer, then acrylic, then polyurethane) is reliable, the specific recipes are not.
inputs: cellulose lacquer or acrylic or polyurethane binder

facts.label: Solvent
facts.value: toluene, xylene or MEK; water-based polyurethane came in through the 1980s

facts.label: Binder
facts.value: a few percent by weight; a cellulose or acrylic lacquer

facts.label: Pigment loading
facts.value: about 60-75% by volume of the dried coating

facts.label: Milling
facts.value: three-roll or sand mill, gap from tens of microns down to a few, 50-70% solids

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.name: Acicular iron oxide pigment
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.description: The magnetic pigment is acicular gamma-iron(III) oxide, gamma-Fe2O3: needle-shaped crystals about 0.3 microns long by 0.08 microns across by 0.01 thick, an aspect ratio of about 3 to 5. It is precipitated from an iron(II) salt by oxidising with air while a surfactant is present, and the surfactant is what forces the crystals to grow as needles instead of spheres. That morphology is the whole reason a cassette can hold what it holds: the long axis lines up with the tape's direction of travel and the short axis resists it.
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.note: The pigment is made from iron ore or from ferrous scrap by dissolving it in hydrochloric or sulphuric acid to a ferrous (FeII) salt, precipitating the hydrate with a caustic, and then oxidising it slowly to gamma-Fe2O3 while a surfactant or a nucleating protein steers the crystal habit. The chromium-dioxide pigment for Type II tape was made by oxidising chromium chloride in the presence of a similar surfactant and was a higher coercivity, more stable formulation.

facts.label: Particle
facts.value: about 0.3 x 0.08 x 0.01 microns, aspect ratio 3-5

facts.label: Crystal
facts.value: gamma-Fe2O3, maghemite, tetragonal

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: 25-30 kA/m standard, up to 40-50 kA/m with cobalt modification

facts.label: Remanence
facts.value: about 0.25-0.3 T

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: Fe(II) salt oxidised by air at 50-80 degrees C with a surfactant

places: Japan (TDK, TDK's TPIO2 chrome and iron oxides)

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.chromium.name: Chromium dioxide (Type II pigment)
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.chromium.description: For high-bias Type II tape, chromium dioxide (CrO2): acicular, 20-50 nm, higher coercivity and higher signal-to-noise than ferrite. It is made by oxidising chromic chloride in the presence of a surfactant under pressure and heat, and was patented and controlled tightly by its Japanese inventors. Chromium came from chromite ore, which is mostly in South Africa and the Soviet bloc.
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.chromium.note: Chromium dioxide tape is the Type II high-bias formulation. The 1541 wrote standard-bias, so a Type II tape on a 1541 would have been biased 1200 ns against a 120 ns machine; it would record, but not well. Ferrite, the IEC Type I formulation, was the right tape.

facts.label: Particle
facts.value: about 0.03 x 0.008 microns, finer than the ferrite

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: 40-50 kA/m, high-bias (1200 ns)

facts.label: Curie point
facts.value: about 120 degrees C

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: CrO3 reduced to CrO2, or chromic acid oxidised under pressure

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.surfactan.name: Crystal-habit modifier, fatty acid or sulphonate
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.surfactan.description: A surfactant, and the reason the word appears on three unrelated branches: what a tape pigment, a printing-ink deinking flotation cell and a chromium dioxide oxidation all have in common is that the chemistry is dominated by an anionic or amphoteric surface-active agent adsorbed on a particle. Crystal habit is controlled by what is adsorbed on the growing face. The pigment industry used a fatty acid or an alkylbenzene sulphonate, or in the classic process a hydrolysed protein or a polyol, adsorbed on the iron oxide as it precipitated so that growth was fastest along one axis. Without it the pigment came out spherical and a cassette tape of the same thickness held a fraction of the data.
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.surfactan.note: Surfactant choice was one of the genuinely proprietary parts of a tape formulation; both fatty-acid-derived and synthetic-anion-derived chemistries were in use.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: adsorb on the crystal face and inhibit growth there, forcing the acicular habit

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: a percent or so of the pigment weight

peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.iron.name: Iron from ore or scrap, leached to a ferrous salt
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.iron.description: Tape pigment iron did not need to be virgin: it was often made from ferrous scrap, mill scale or ore, dissolved in hydrochloric or sulphuric acid to ferrous chloride or ferrous sulphate, then precipitated and oxidised. The ore route, when it was used, was the same hematite or magnetite that goes to a blast furnace, digested in acid rather than reduced in a furnace.
peripheral.cassette.tape.oxide.iron.note: One grade of ore fed both the steel of a shadow mask and the oxide on a cassette, by two completely different routes.

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: hydrochloric acid at 60-90 degrees C, or sulfuric acid at 80-100 degrees C, giving FeCl2 or FeSO4

facts.label: Iron content
facts.value: 72.4% by weight in Fe2O3; the whole 90 m of a C-60 holds only 1-3 g of it

facts.label: Acid route
facts.value: same hematite and magnetite, digested in HCl or H2SO4 rather than reduced with coke

peripheral.cassette.deck.name: The 1541 disk drive
peripheral.cassette.deck.description: A disk-shaped grey box with a slot on top, containing a stepper motor, a capstan flywheel, a read/write head on a load arm, and a small circuit board with a 6502 CPU, a 6522 interface chip and a mask-programmed logic array. It reads and writes the same standard compact cassette as a music cassette deck, which is why Commodore's error messages included CLOAD and why a music cassette recorder could in principle play a C64 tape.
peripheral.cassette.deck.note: The drive is an intelligent peripheral with its own processor and control system, connected to the C64 or VIC-20 over the serial bus at device number 4-15. Not established: the GCR 4,800 or 9,600 baud rate, the about 1 micrometre head gap, the 170 KB per side as the 1541 used it, and the absence of a position sensor.

facts.label: Format
facts.value: GCR (group code recording) at 4,800 or 9,600 baud

facts.label: Head gap
facts.value: about 1 micrometre

facts.label: Capacity
facts.value: about 170 KB per side as used by the 1541

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: no position sensor; the drive counts steps

peripheral.cassette.deck.link.name: The nine-pin serial link to the C64
peripheral.cassette.deck.link.description: The 1541 connected to the C64 by a nine-pin high-density D-subminiature cable carrying the serial bus, which is how the drive knew there was a computer and the computer knew there was a drive.

peripheral.cassette.deck.led.name: Activity LED
peripheral.cassette.deck.led.description: A small red LED on the front of the drive, lit while the motor was running or the head was active. It was a gallium arsenide or gallium phosphide die in a 2.5 mm epoxy lens, running at about 2-10 mA from the 5 V rail through a resistor. The LED itself was 1980s technology; the indicator lamps on earlier drives had been incandescent bulbs or neon.
peripheral.cassette.deck.led.note: Efficient diode emission from GaAs was patented in 1962 and commercial LEDs only became practical once they cost under five cents in the 1970s. Not established: GaAs or GaP die with a GaAsP window for red, the 1.7-2.2 V forward drop, the 2-10 mA running current, and the 2.5 mm epoxy lens with a reflector cup.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: GaAs or GaP, with a GaAsP window for red

facts.label: Forward drop
facts.value: about 1.7-2.2 V, current 2-10 mA

facts.label: Epoxy lens
facts.value: 2.5 mm or 3 mm, with the die mounted in a reflector cup

peripheral.cassette.deck.led.gallium.name: Gallium arsenide from gallium in the Bayer liquor
peripheral.cassette.deck.led.gallium.description: A red or amber LED of the period was gallium phosphide or gallium arsenide phosphide on a gallium arsenide substrate. Gallium is not mined on its own: it is recovered as a minor by-product from the Bayer liquor when bauxite is digested in caustic soda, because gallium is amphoteric and dissolves with the alumina. By 1982 gallium was becoming strategically important precisely because of this concentration in the aluminium industry.
peripheral.cassette.deck.led.gallium.note: Gallium became a controlled export commodity in the 2010s because the LED and power-device industries depended on this by-product stream. The connection to a television is the 2 mA indicator lamp on the front of a 1541, which is a very small consumption but the same chain. Gallium is recovered from the Bayer liquor during the digestion of bauxite, so metal.alumina, the smelter-grade alumina whose production is that digestion, is the ingredient here rather than the four-nines foil of the phosphor back layer.

facts.label: Content
facts.value: about 50-100 ppm of gallium in bauxite

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: 99.99-99.9999% by ion exchange and zone refining

facts.label: LED
facts.value: GaAs or GaAsP die in an epoxy lens, bandgap giving about 650-700 nm

peripheral.cassette.deck.case.name: The 1541 plastic case
peripheral.cassette.deck.case.description: A grey ABS clamshell, disc-shaped, about 40 cm across and 9 cm deep, moulded in two halves with the lid carrying the Commodore logo badge and the slot for the cassette. The material is the same ABS as a television cabinet, from the same styrene-butadiene-acrylonitrile chemistry.
peripheral.cassette.deck.case.note: The case is moulded from the same ABS grade as a television cabinet, and it reaches the monomers through the styrene-butadiene-acrylonitrile petrochemical chain rather than through the cabinet. Not established: the two-shot clamshell construction, the about 400 mm by 90 mm dimensions, the 230-260 C ABS moulding, and the claim that the drive's ABS was the same grade as a television cabinet's.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: about 400 mm across, 90 mm deep

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: grey, the colour Commodore specified for the drive and for the C64's case-adjacent parts

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: two-shot clamshell, 230-260 degrees C ABS

peripheral.cassette.deck.psu.name: Power supply: 5 V and 12 V from the C64
peripheral.cassette.deck.psu.description: The 1541 has no mains input. It gets 5 V and about 12 V DC from the C64 through the six-pin cassette port, and regulates them locally: the 12 V feeds the motor and the head bias, the 5 V feeds the logic, and a linear regulator or a discrete dropper makes the 5 V from a higher rail on some models. There was a fuse and a reverse-polarity protection diode because the port was known to be a point of user error.
peripheral.cassette.deck.psu.note: The exact regulator topology of a 1541 varies by revision, and no part can be named with confidence. What is certain and important is that the drive was powered entirely from the computer, which is why a 1541 and its C64 shared one power supply and one mains lead.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: 5 V logic and 9-12 V motor/bias, via the 6-pin cassette connector

facts.label: Current
facts.value: about 0.4-0.7 A drawn while a tape moves

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: linear, or a simple zener/transistor dropper

peripheral.cassette.deck.psu.chain.name: The regulator and its electrolytics
peripheral.cassette.deck.psu.chain.description: The 1541 regulated the 9-12 V rail down to 5 V with a small linear regulator or a discrete zener-transmitter, and used a handful of aluminium electrolytics to ripple-filter it. Both are the same parts as the television reservoir: etched four-nines aluminium foil in a wound foil anode, with a fibre separator and a chloride or borate electrolyte.
inputs: aluminium chloride or ammonium borate electrolyte

facts.label: Values
facts.value: about 10-470 microfarad at 10-25 V on a 1541

facts.label: Ripple
facts.value: a few tens of millivolts at the logic rail

peripheral.tv.chassis.power.reservoir.name: Aluminium electrolytic reservoir, 200 microfarad 160 V
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.reservoir.description: The reservoir is a wound aluminium foil anode with an oxide film formed on it, an aluminium cathode can, and a paper or synthetic-fibre separator soaked in electrolyte (an ammonium borate or an aluminium chloride solution in glycol). Formed at a few hundred volts, it hums and it leaks, and in a hot chassis it did the most to kill itself.
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.reservoir.note: The etched aluminium anode here is the same technology as the 1970s-80s consumer electrolytic capacitor and is documented in the mainboard's own power-supply branch. A 1982 TV reservoir was often one of the largest aluminium electrolytics made that year in a consumer product. A wet aluminium electrolytic is two aluminium foils separated by a paper spacer saturated with liquid or gel electrolyte, with the anode etched and formed; commercial parts run from 0.1 uF to 2.7 F at 4 V to 630 V, so a 200 uF 160 V reservoir is well inside the range. Not established: aluminium chloride or ammonium borate in ethylene glycol as the electrolyte, the 99.99% anode foil figure, and the claim that this was among the largest consumer electrolytics of 1982.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: 200-400 microfarad at 160 V

facts.label: Anode foil
facts.value: etched high-purity aluminium, 99.99%

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: aluminium chloride or ammonium borate in ethylene glycol

peripheral.cassette.deck.board.name: The 1541 circuit board
peripheral.cassette.deck.board.description: A single FR-4 board with the CPU, the PIA, the PLA, a handful of logic gates, the head preamplifier, the stepper driver transistors, and the power regulators. It was a through-hole board in 1982, socketed for the CPU and the PIA so they could be replaced, and hand- or wave-soldered.
peripheral.cassette.deck.board.note: The FR-4 laminate, copper foil, solder mask and tin-lead solder are the same chain as the television's PCB, documented under peripheral.tv.chassis.pcb, and they are ingredients of this board rather than parts of it. Not established: the single-sided 1.6 mm FR-4 with 35 micron copper foil, the 40-pin DIP sockets for the 6502 and 6522, and the discrete-versus-IC stepper drive. The 6502 CPU, the 6522 interface chip and the mask-programmed logic array are documented under this node's own children.

facts.label: Sockets
facts.value: 40-pin DIP sockets for the 6502 and the 6522

facts.label: Solder
facts.value: 60/40 tin-lead on tin-plated through-holes

facts.label: Stepper drive
facts.value: discrete transistors, or a small IC, driving two phases

facts.label: Laminate
facts.value: 1.6 mm single-sided FR-4, 35 micron copper foil, epoxy mask, 60/40 tin-lead

peripheral.cassette.deck.head.name: Read/write head, gap about 1 micrometre
peripheral.cassette.deck.head.description: A miniature magnetic recording head, essentially the same object as the one in a cassette deck but smaller and more carefully shielded. A ferrite or permalloy core with a laser-cut gap of about a micrometre, a figure-eight winding of lacquered copper to cancel hum from the drive's own motor, a mumetal shield can around the front, and a printed circuit board carrying the preamplifier right at the head to keep the signal short.
peripheral.cassette.deck.head.note: The gap figure of about 1 micrometre is the standard audio-cassette head gap. The bias figure is the important one for the C64: the 1541 wrote standard-bias (about 120 ns, short-wavelength) tape, which is why a C-90 or C-120 high-bias (1200 ns, long-wavelength) tape gave poor results on a 1541 and why Commodore recommended standard C-60 and C-90 tapes. The flux interval the C64 used was roughly 200-310 microseconds, about 3.2-4.8 kHz, which is 1700-2600 flux transitions per inch at 4.76 cm/s against a standard-bias cassette limit of about 3200 per inch, which is firmly in the short-wavelength region and near the limit of what a standard-bias tape could resolve; that is the physical reason a 1541 was fussy about tape formulation.

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: about 1 micrometre (0.5-2 micrometres depending on head)

facts.label: Core
facts.value: ferrite or permalloy (mumetal) with a mu-metal shield

facts.label: Winding
facts.value: about 500-1500 turns of 40 AWG (0.1 mm) enamelled copper

facts.label: Hum cancelling
facts.value: figure-eight winding so the drive motor's stray field cancels

facts.label: Bias
facts.value: short-wavelength (standard, about 120 ns) bias for the C64 format

facts.label: Resolution
facts.value: on a standard-bias cassette the short-wavelength limit is a few thousand transitions per inch

peripheral.cassette.deck.head.winding.name: Lacquered copper wire, figure-eight
peripheral.cassette.deck.head.winding.description: The winding was a fine enamelled (lacquered) copper wire, typically 40 AWG, a few hundred to a couple of thousand turns, wound so that it sits astride the gap with two halves that see the drive motor's stray field in opposite directions. The hum-cancelling figure-eight was the reason a 1541 did not pick up the buzz of its own motor. The lacquer itself is the same polyurethane-imide over a polyester base as a television yoke winding.
peripheral.cassette.deck.head.winding.note: Not established: 40 AWG or 0.1-0.13 mm enamelled copper, the figure-eight hum-cancelling winding, and the turns count for a 1541 read/write head.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.1-0.13 mm enamelled copper

facts.label: Hum cancelling
facts.value: figure-eight: two coils in series, opposed

peripheral.cassette.deck.head.core.name: Permalloy or ferrite core
peripheral.cassette.deck.head.core.description: The gap has to be made with both faces flat and parallel to a micron or so across a couple of millimetres, which ferrite does well by lapping and permalloy does well by etching. A high-permeability nickel-iron alloy, permalloy, gives the inductance needed for the playback winding; the mu-metal shield can around the front suppresses external fields.
peripheral.cassette.deck.head.core.note: The nickel comes from the same nickel chain as the CRT grid foil. Mu-metal's nickel content is higher than permalloy's and it must be annealed in hydrogen at about 1100 degrees C to develop its permeability.
inputs: nickel iron (permalloy, 79% Ni) or MnZn ferrite

facts.label: Permalloy
facts.value: about 79% Ni, 17% Fe, 4% Mo/Cu; permeability about 20,000-100,000

facts.label: Mu-metal
facts.value: about 77% Ni, 20% Fe, 2% Cu, annealed in hydrogen, permeability about 100,000

facts.label: Gap
facts.value: 1 micrometre, made by sputtering a spacer or by bonding two lapped faces

peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.name: Tape transport: capstan, pinch roller, worm reduction
peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.description: The cassette slid in and the tape was pressed against a capstan on the drive by a rubber pinch roller, at 4.76 cm/s. The capstan was on a flywheel turned by the stepper motor through a worm reduction, which also let the motor's back-driving put the capstan in the right phase. The same motor rotation drove a cam that loaded the head against the tape. There was no tachometer, no position sensor and no closed loop: the drive simply counted steps and hoped.
peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.note: The 1541 kept the head in contact with the tape at all times rather than loading it, which is part of why it was so noisy and why a 1541 could hear your programme as well as read it. The exact worm ratio is not established, and whether the head was loadable is not either; several 1541 variants kept the head permanently engaged.

facts.label: Capstan
facts.value: 2.0-2.5 mm diameter hardened steel pin, 4.76 cm/s at the surface

facts.label: Flywheel
facts.value: a die-cast aluminium or moulded plastic flywheel on the capstan shaft

facts.label: Worm reduction
facts.value: a single or multi-start worm on the motor shaft meshing a nylon or brass worm wheel on the capstan shaft

facts.label: Pinch roller
facts.value: a 6-8 mm rubber roller on a spring-loaded arm, driven off the motor by a friction wheel or a belt

facts.label: Head load
facts.value: a cam and spring arm that pressed the head into the cassette window; some drives kept it permanently in contact

peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.worm.name: Worm and worm-wheel reduction
peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.worm.description: The stepper's rotation was reduced by a worm on the motor shaft running in a nylon or brass wheel on the capstan shaft. A worm gear is quiet and gives a high ratio in a small space and is self-locking, which is exactly what is wanted: when the power was off the capstan could not back-drive. The wheel was usually a moulded nylon or acetal wheel with a brass insert.
peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.worm.note: A worm gear is naturally self-locking, which is what stopped a 1541's capstan spinning backwards when the C64 was switched off.

facts.label: Worm
facts.value: hardened steel, single or multi-start, 5-10 mm diameter

facts.label: Wheel
facts.value: nylon or acetal, or a brass wheel, 15-30 mm diameter

peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.pinch.name: Pinch roller and rubber
peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.pinch.description: A small roller of black nitrile or butyl rubber on a moulded plastic or nylon hub, on a bent spring steel arm. The rubber had to grip the capstan and the tape without slipping and without depositing rubber onto the tape, and a dried-out pinch roller was the single most common cause of a 1541 failing to read a tape it had just written.
peripheral.cassette.deck.transport.pinch.note: Nitrile rubber comes from butadiene and acrylonitrile, the same two monomers as the ABS of a television cabinet, both from crude oil. Rubber and plastics in 1982 shared the same petrochemical feedstock.

facts.label: Rubber
facts.value: nitrile (butadiene-acrylonitrile) or butyl, 60-80 Shore A

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: 6-8 mm, the roller pressing the tape against the capstan

peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.name: Hybrid stepping motor
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.description: A hybrid stepping motor: a permanent-magnet rotor with fine teeth running between two toothed stator poles, with coils on the poles. Two phases driven in sequence step the rotor a fraction of a degree at a time. This is how the 1541 knew where the tape was, and the motor's own inertia is why a 1541 could not skip forward as fast as it could seek.
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.note: The 1541's motor step angle and rotor construction are not established; the qualitative description (two-phase hybrid PM motor driving the capstan through a worm reduction, with the same rotation also positioning the head load) is solid, the numbers are not. Some sources describe the 1541 motor as a 2.5-degree step with 40 steps per revolution; others suggest a coarser angle with half-stepping. Treat the numbers as indicative.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: 2-phase hybrid, permanent-magnet rotor

facts.label: Step angle
facts.value: of the order of 2.5-5 degrees, with microstepping in the drive logic

facts.label: Windings
facts.value: two bifilar or four independent coils, tens of ohms each

facts.label: Rotor
facts.value: sintered ferrite or Alnico permanent magnet with 24-50 fine teeth

facts.label: Torque
facts.value: about 0.1-0.5 newton-metres, enough to turn the capstan and the head load cam against the tape

peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.name: End bells, bushings and the mounting bracket
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.description: The motor is held between two stamped steel end bells with bronze or sintered bronze bushings for the shafts (or plastic bushings on a cheap drive), and mounted on a steel bracket riveted or screwed into the deck. The whole assembly sat on a die-cast or folded steel chassis plate.
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.note: The 1541's motor bearings were a well-known source of squeal and alignment trouble; whether they were bronze or sintered iron is not established. The end bells and bushings are stamped steel and sintered bronze, and the part belongs to the motor.

facts.label: Bushing
facts.value: sintered bronze or oil-impregnated sintered iron, or a PTFE-impregnated plastic sleeve

peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.name: End bell steel and sintered bronze bushings
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.description: The stamped steel end bells came off the same low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask and the speaker basket. The bushings were sintered bronze, a copper-tin alloy made by pressing bronze powder and sintering it in a reducing atmosphere so it had a connected pore structure that held oil. Copper and tin both feature elsewhere in this branch.
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.housing.note: Stamped end bells are made of cold-reduced sheet steel and the bushings are made of copper and tin, so a motor housing draws on the steel and the tin rather than containing them.

facts.label: Bronze
facts.value: about 85-90% Cu, 8-10% Sn, 1-2% Zn, pressed and sintered

facts.label: Porosity
facts.value: about 10-25% interconnected pores to hold lubricant

peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.rotor.name: Sintered ferrite permanent magnet rotor
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.rotor.description: The rotor is a ferrite or Alnico magnet with fine teeth machined or ground onto its circumference, magnetised radially or axially. A ferrite magnet is barium or strontium ferrite, the same material as a speaker magnet; a stepper rotor is a small ring of it.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: sintered barium or strontium ferrite, or an Alnico 5 or 8 segment

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: about 160-250 kA/m for ferrite, enough to survive demagnetising the two stator fields

facts.label: Tooth finish
facts.value: sintered and diamond-ground, teeth concentric to a few microns

peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.stator.name: Toothed stator laminations of silicon steel
peripheral.cassette.deck.stepper.stator.description: The stator is a stack of thin silicon steel laminations with fine teeth, each pole carrying a bobbin of magnet wire. The laminations are punched from the same 0.35 mm silicon steel as the television's mains transformer, but the teeth are punched to a pitch of well under a millimetre, which is the reason a hybrid stepper has far more rotor teeth than its stator poles.

facts.label: Lamination
facts.value: 0.35-0.5 mm silicon steel, eddy-current-grade

facts.label: Tooth pitch
facts.value: about 0.5-1 mm, fine compared with a mains transformer

facts.label: Windings
facts.value: 30-50 turns of 0.2-0.3 mm enamelled wire per pole

peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.name: 6502 CPU, 6522 PIA and M50174 PLA
peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.description: The 1541's electronics are almost identical in content to the C64's, which is not a coincidence: Commodore reused its own chips. A 6502 runs the operating system and the serial protocol; a 6522 versatile interface adapter talks to the tape, drives the stepper and reads the serial bus to the C64; and a mask-programmed logic array, the M50174, handles the address decode and the stepper phase sequencing so the CPU does not have to bit-bang them.
peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.note: The 1541's clock is a point of real uncertainty. It does not run a free oscillator; it takes a timebase from the cassette-port timing supplied by the C64's VIC-II, and the CPU is clocked at about 1 MHz derived from that. The exact divider chain is a reverse-engineering result, not a design intent, so no figure more precise than about 1 MHz is established. The M50174's process technology is also uncertain; it may have been bipolar rather than CMOS.

facts.label: CPU
facts.value: MOS 6502, clocked at about 1 MHz from the bus

facts.label: PIA
facts.value: 6522, 40-pin DIP, two 8-bit ports with handshaking and timers

facts.label: PLA
facts.value: M50174, a custom mask-programmed logic array

facts.label: Process
facts.value: 6502 on NMOS at about 4-5 microns; the PLA on a mask-programmed CMOS or bipolar process

places: Philadelphia (MOS Technology lineage), then Japan, Taiwan and Hong Kong for the volume runs

peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.gold-wire.name: Gold bonding wire from the anode slimes
peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.gold-wire.description: The 6502 was a 40-pin DIP with gold or tinned copper wires ball-bonded or wedge-bonded from the die pads to the lead frame. Gold came almost entirely from the anode slimes of copper electrolytic refining, and a modest 40-pin DIP of the period had a few milligrams of it.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.7-1.5 mil (18-38 micron) gold, or 1-2 mil tinned copper

peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon.name: The silicon this logic is made from
peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon.description: The 6502, the 6522 and the PLA were all made on 1980-era processes: a 3-5 micron NMOS or bipolar line, or a custom bipolar array. The wafer was the same trichlorosilane-to-polysilicon-to-epitaxy chain already traced under the television's video IC, and the die was diced, wire-bonded and epoxy-moulded.

facts.label: Line
facts.value: 3-5 micron NMOS for the 6502, 5 micron NMOS for the 6522

facts.label: Mould compound
facts.value: phenolic or epoxy with silica filler, transfer or compression moulded

peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon.m.name: Epoxy mould compound, silica-filled
peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon.m.description: The black or off-white plastic that a chip is set in. It is an epoxy novolac resin filled to about 70% with ground fused silica, with a cure promoter and a mould release. The silica filler is what stops the encapsulant from shrinking and cracking the die during cure, and it comes from the same kind of sand as the glass batch.
peripheral.cassette.deck.logic.silicon.m.note: The filler is deliberately angular and fused rather than spherical: the sharp interlocking particles give a high mechanical strength and a low water uptake, which is what kept moisture out of the die.

facts.label: Filler
facts.value: about 70% by weight ground silica, angular, a few microns

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 175 degrees C for several minutes, transfer or injection mould

peripheral.tv.name: Domestic colour television set, 13 inch NTSC
peripheral.tv.description: A 1982-84 US domestic set: 12.5 or 13 inch diagonal, 525-line NTSC, 60 Hz field rate, all-signal-in-a-can. It was the only display a C64 owner was likely to have, and the C64 looked terrible on it: no separate chrominance bandwidth, a modulated sound carrier that carried the computer's audio, and a colour subcarrier at a frequency the TV's chroma band had to be tuned to.
peripheral.tv.note: The PAL/SECAM line rate is 12 kHz; NTSC is 15,734 Hz and every number on this branch is NTSC. 12.5 kHz is the line rate of the 50 Hz NTSC variants used in Japan and some export markets. Also worth stating plainly: there is no analogue TV transmitter here. A broadcast transmitter was a 100 kW-10 MW superstructure of tetrodes and a directional panel array; a home C64 needed a one-square-inch modulator board and a household set instead.

facts.label: Picture tube diagonal
facts.value: 12.5 inch (318 mm) or 13 inch (330 mm); 19 inch sets were the other common size

facts.label: Field rate
facts.value: 60 Hz, 525 lines, 2:1 interlace

facts.label: Line rate
facts.value: 15,734 Hz (15,750 Hz nominal)

facts.label: EHT
facts.value: 20-25 kV, 1-2 mA total beam current

facts.label: Mains
facts.value: 117 V 60 Hz in the US, 240 V 50 Hz in Europe

peripheral.tv.mains.name: Mains lead, suppression filter and fuse
peripheral.tv.mains.description: A 1982 set had a two or three core mains lead, an entrapment and bypass capacitor for radio interference, and one or two fuses. The mains filter is the reason a television did not buzz on an AM radio, and the reason the plastic of a 1980s set smelled faintly of phenolic. The fuse was a small glass or ceramic cartridge with a wire or a metal link.
peripheral.tv.mains.note: This is the set's power entry: a cord, a suppression network and a fuse. Not established: the X-rated 0.01-0.05 uF bypass capacitor at 400-600 V, the 1-2 mH common-mode choke or ferrite strap, and the phenolic smell. 117 V 60 Hz and 240 V 50 Hz are regional mains rather than a figure for any one set.

facts.label: Mains
facts.value: 117 V 60 Hz (US) or 240 V 50 Hz (EU)

facts.label: Bypass capacitor
facts.value: 0.01-0.05 microfarad at about 400-600 V DC, X-rated

facts.label: Entrapment
facts.value: a common-mode choke of about 1-2 mH or a strap of ferrite around the line

peripheral.tv.mains.fuse.name: Mains fuse
peripheral.tv.mains.fuse.description: A 3-4 amp buss fuse in the mains lead holder on sets with a detachable cord, or an internal fuse on the line. The fuse element was a low-melting alloy or a silver wire in a glass cartridge.
peripheral.tv.mains.fuse.note: The mains fuse is a European (IEC) style addition that many US sets of the period lacked, having a non-rewirable fuse only in the more expensive models.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 3-4 A, 250 V, time delay on larger sets

peripheral.tv.mains.fuse.material.name: Glass cartridge and silver fuse wire
peripheral.tv.mains.fuse.material.description: A small glass or ceramic cartridge containing a link of silver or of a fusible alloy such as a lead-bismuth-tin eutectic, in a sand or chalk packing that quenched the arc when the link melted. The glass was soda-lime, drawn as a tube and sealed with an end cap.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 3-4 A, 250 V, time delay on larger sets

facts.label: Fusing element
facts.value: silver wire, or a 500 degree C fusible alloy

peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.silver.name: Silver activator
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.silver.description: The blue ZnS is activated by silver at a fraction of a percent, supplied as silver nitrate. Silver itself came from argentite and from the anode slimes that accumulate in electrolytic copper refining, which is where most of the world's silver of the era was actually recovered.
peripheral.tv.crt.phosphor.zns.silver.note: Silver for phosphors was one of the smaller industrial users, but the same tonne went into contacts and brazing alloys.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: about 0.05-0.1 wt% Ag

peripheral.tv.mains.filter.name: Mains suppression: X capacitor and common-mode choke
peripheral.tv.mains.filter.description: A high-voltage capacitor across line and neutral (the X capacitor) plus a ferrite-beaded choke in series, to keep the set's switching noise out of the radio. In a 1982 set this was often a paper or film capacitor at 0.01 microfarad rated for mains transients; the modern purple or orange epoxy-drop X capacitor of the 1990s had not appeared, though a metallised film in a plastic case was used. The choke was a few turns on a ferrite or powdered-iron core.

facts.label: X capacitor
facts.value: 0.01-0.05 microfarad, mains-transient rated

facts.label: Choke
facts.value: 1-2 mH common mode, or a ferrite strap

peripheral.tv.mains.filter.metallised-fi.name: Metallised polypropylene mains capacitor
peripheral.tv.mains.filter.metallised-fi.description: A polypropylene or polystyrene film, vacuum-metallised with a thin aluminium layer on both faces, wound and potted in epoxy. It was the capacitor of choice across the line because a self-healing metallisation would recover from a mains transient rather than failing short. Polystyrene was also used for its stability and low microphonics.

facts.label: Voltage
facts.value: 400-630 V DC working for a mains suppression position

facts.label: Self-healing
facts.value: a transient punctures the oxide and evaporises the metal locally

peripheral.tv.mains.cord.name: Mains cord, PVC jacket over stranded copper
peripheral.tv.mains.cord.description: A flexible cord of 16 or 18 AWG stranded copper inside a PVC or rubber jacket, moulded on to the plug and to the set's inlet. The set's inlet on a 1982 television was not an IEC C13 appliance coupler (that became common on computers and later sets); most were a hard-wired rubber or vinyl cord straight into the chassis, with a moulded two-pin or three-pin plug at the wall end. A detachable cord on a set was unusual until the mid 1980s.
peripheral.tv.mains.cord.note: An IEC-ish inlet belongs to the C64's own power supply unit, not to the television. What belongs to the television is the hard-wired cord and the moulded plug, which are covered here.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 16 or 18 AWG stranded, flexible, rated 250 V

facts.label: Jacket
facts.value: PVC or a thermoset rubber, 2-3 core

facts.label: Plug
facts.value: moulded-on two-pin (US, with the grounded case pin) or three-pin

peripheral.tv.aerial.name: Aerial input and antenna lead
peripheral.tv.aerial.description: The 75 ohm coaxial aerial socket at the back, the twin-lead alternative for indoor aerials, and the telescopic whip on a portable. The C64 was plugged into that socket, in parallel with whatever aerial the set had. The socket was either a threaded F-type, or a cheaper bayonet or push-on type in Europe.
peripheral.tv.aerial.note: The F connector is the common coaxial television aerial connector, normally used with RG-6/U or RG-59/U cable, and coaxial replaced twin-lead. Not established: 300 ohm balanced twin-lead as the alternative, the bayonet type in the UK, and the 890 MHz UHF bandwidth.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm coaxial (or 300 ohm balanced twin-lead)

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: F-type threaded, or a bayonet in the UK

facts.label: Bandwidth
facts.value: to 890 MHz for UHF

peripheral.tv.aerial.whip.name: Telescopic whip antenna
peripheral.tv.aerial.whip.description: On a portable set, a telescopic whip: a chrome-plated steel rod in a plastic base, with a ball joint for the angle. It was a whip antenna for VHF, and on UHF-only portables it was a loop inside the cabinet.

facts.label: Rod
facts.value: chrome-plated carbon or stainless steel, 3-6 sections

peripheral.tv.aerial.whip.plating.name: Chrome-plate the whip rod
peripheral.tv.aerial.whip.plating.description: A telescopic rod plated in hard chrome over nickel, in several decorative layers so it could be extended and retracted thousands of times without wearing through. The chrome came from chromite ore, the same ore that made the chromium dioxide in a Type II cassette tape.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: about 0.25-1 micron of hard chrome over nickel

facts.label: Chrome source
facts.value: chromic acid from chromite ore

peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.name: Coaxial or twin-lead antenna lead
peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.description: RG-59 or RG-6 coax: a copper or tinned copper braid, a polyethylene or PTFE dielectric, and a solid copper centre conductor. RG-59 is 52 ohm and was what an indoor or a bench lead of the era was. The alternative was 300 ohm flat twin-lead, which matched indoor dipoles and did not need coax. The polyethylene in the coax came from ethylene, which came from the cracker, which came from naphtha and from crude.

facts.label: RG-59
facts.value: 52 ohm, about 6.5 mm outside diameter

facts.label: Twin-lead
facts.value: 300 ohm, 2 x 1.2 mm polyethylene-insulated conductors

facts.label: PE dielectric
facts.value: chemical blowing makes a foam, or solid PE

peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.name: Polyethylene from ethylene
peripheral.tv.aerial.coax.polyethylene.description: Polyethylene is polymerised from ethylene, which comes from a steam cracker on naphtha. Where the chlorination route was used (for PVC or for the chloromethane that goes into the foam blowing), the chlorine came from salt electrolysis. Both the polymer and the chlorine are therefore descendants of crude oil and of halite, and both branches meet in the cable jacket.

facts.label: LDPE
facts.value: high-pressure polymerisation, 1000-3000 bar, 200 degrees C, for cable

facts.label: Chlorine
facts.value: salt electrolysis, 2NaCl -> Cl2 + 2Na, at about 3 V and 30-40 degrees C

facts.label: PVC
facts.value: vinyl chloride from ethylene plus chlorine, then polymerised

peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.name: F-type coaxial connector
peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.description: A threaded, quarter-turn connector for 75 ohm coax, usually brass with a nickel or cadmium plate and a dielectric insert of PTFE or polyethylene. Brass is copper-zinc, so this little part pulls from both the copper and the zinc industry; the zinc can also be the zinc plated steel shell.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: brass (60% Cu, 40% Zn) with a nickel or cadmium plate

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: PTFE or polyethylene insert

facts.label: Center contact
facts.value: brass or copper with a silver or nickel plating

peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.brass.name: Brass from copper and zinc
peripheral.tv.aerial.f-connector.brass.description: Brass is melted from cathode copper and zinc ingot, roughly 60/40 for free-cutting brass, and cast or extruded into fittings. The zinc came from sphalerite and the copper from chalcopyrite, both already in this branch.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 60% Cu, 40% Zn for a free-cutting brass; cartridge brass is 70/30

facts.label: Zinc source
facts.value: the same sphalerite concentrate and electrolysis as the CRT phosphor zinc sulphide

peripheral.tv.controls.name: Front controls: pots, switches, dial
peripheral.tv.controls.description: Brightness, contrast, colour, tint, volume and the channel selector, plus a fine-tuning and a V-hold behind the cabinet. The pots are carbon track or cermet; the switches are an AC line switch and often a rotary band switch or push-buttons for the a/v functions.
peripheral.tv.controls.note: Not established: 5 kohm or 10 kohm linear pots for brightness and colour, 10 kohm or 100 kohm audio taper for volume, and the rotary mains switch on the volume pot shaft.

facts.label: Brightness and colour
facts.value: usually 5 kohm or 10 kohm linear

facts.label: Volume
facts.value: 10 kohm or 100 kohm audio taper

facts.label: Switch
facts.value: rotary AC mains switch on the volume pot shaft on many sets

peripheral.tv.controls.vhf-dial.name: VHF dial and channel drum
peripheral.tv.controls.vhf-dial.description: The channel numbers were on a printed drum or card behind a window, or on a flat dial plate, driven by the cord from the knob. The UHF channels 14-83 needed a drum or a fan-shaped card because there were 70 of them, which is why UHF dials of the period were a distinctive piece of mechanical design.

facts.label: UHF
facts.value: 70 channels, so a drum or a rotating card rather than a straight scale

peripheral.tv.controls.switch.name: AC line switch and interlock
peripheral.tv.controls.switch.description: A rotary or push-pull mains switch on the front panel, often interlocked so that a set with a back cover off could not be switched on (the 'interlock' on a portable). The switch contacts were silver-plated brass, and the whole switch was a snap-action mechanism in a phenolic body.

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: silver-plated brass, rated at a few amps at 250 V

facts.label: Interlock
facts.value: a cover switch so a serviceable set could not be energised with the back open

peripheral.tv.controls.switch.silver.name: Silver-plated switch contacts
peripheral.tv.controls.switch.silver.description: Mains switch and rotary tuner contacts were silver-plated brass or copper, because silver has the highest conductivity of any metal and does not oxidise. Silver plating was applied from a cyanide or an acid bath, and the silver itself came overwhelmingly from the anode slimes of copper refining.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: about 2.5-25 microns of silver

facts.label: Life
facts.value: the contacts of a 1982 TV tuner were good for 10,000-20,000 insertions

peripheral.tv.cabinet.name: Cabinet and front bezel
peripheral.tv.cabinet.description: The outside of the set: a moulded plastics shell wrapped around the chassis and the tube, with a wood-grain print or a real veneer. A 1982 13 inch set was typically an injection-moulded ABS or ABS/polycarbonate cabinet, textured, with the front bezel carrying the speaker grille, the control knobs and the brand badge. Larger and older-style sets had a wood-veneered or wood-framed cabinet; the very cheapest had a printed paper laminate over a steel or plastic shell.
peripheral.tv.cabinet.note: Wood-plastic (particle board faced with a melamine or polyester woodgrain laminate) was used on the console-style and portable sets of the era; the true ABS shell took over on the small sets. Both the woodgrain-print cabinet and the real veneer cabinet are worth covering, and both appear here. Not established: ABS or ABS/polycarbonate as the 1982 cabinet material, the 220-260 C and 40-70 s cycle, and the 13 inch size. The Reynosa, Taipei and Japan production attributions are not established either.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, or ABS/polycarbonate blend, textured leatherette

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: injection moulded at 220-260 degrees C, 40-70 seconds cycle

facts.label: Front
facts.value: ABS bezel with a printed or moulded speaker grille

peripheral.tv.cabinet.badge.name: Brand badge and control knobs
peripheral.tv.cabinet.badge.description: The logo badge was an embossed or plated plastic medallion, and the knobs were moulded ABS or phenolic on a zinc or aluminium die-cast core with a moulded pointer. On a cheap set the badge was printed; on a good one it was a plated plastic insert.
inputs: zinc alloy or aluminium die casting

facts.label: Knob core
facts.value: zinc alloy die-cast, an early use of high-pressure die casting for a consumer knob

peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.name: Case screws and brackets
peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.description: The chassis was fastened into the cabinet with self-tapping screws into plastic bosses, and the back was held with a handful of machine screws into zinc-plated or black-oxide steel. The brackets that carried the tube and the board were zinc-plated sheet steel.
peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.note: Zinc plating is the zinc electroplating industry, and zinc came from the same sphalerite chain as the CRT phosphor. Another convergence.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: zinc electroplate, or a mechanical zinc flake coating

peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.zinc-platin.name: Electroplate zinc onto the case screws
peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.zinc-platin.description: Self-tapping screws into plastic bosses and a handful of machine screws into zinc-plated or black-oxide steel. Zinc plating is the cheapest corrosion protection for a small steel part and it came off the same zinc chain as everything else in this branch.
peripheral.tv.cabinet.screws.zinc-platin.note: Self-tapping screws into plastic bosses and a handful of machine screws into zinc-plated or black-oxide steel. Zinc plating is the cheapest corrosion protection for a small steel part, and it came off the same zinc chain as everything else in this branch: the electroplating bath is fed from sphalerite, it does not contain it, so the zinc is an ingredient here rather than a part of the screw.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: 5-15 microns zinc, plus a chromate conversion for a self-locking patch

facts.label: Bulkhead nut
facts.value: a nylon-insert or serrated nut to resist vibration

peripheral.tv.cabinet.wood.name: Wood veneer or woodgrain laminate
peripheral.tv.cabinet.wood.description: A console or a large set of the early 1980s was often a real cabinet: a wood frame veneered with walnut, mahogany or teak, sometimes over particle board. The cheaper route was a printed polyester or melamine laminate, several sheets laminated and printed with a photographic woodgrain. A 13 inch portable used moulded ABS with the grain embossed into the mould texture and painted.
peripheral.tv.cabinet.wood.note: Again the one renewable leaf: a veneer cabinet is wood and board, not a polymer. A tree, cut and sliced. Check the type on a console set of the period and it is very often plastic, but this node is the case where it was not.

facts.label: Veneer
facts.value: 0.6 mm sliced or rotary cut, about 4-8 leaves per log

facts.label: Particle board
facts.value: wood chips pressed at about 8-10 MPa with a urea or phenol binder

facts.label: Laminate
facts.value: melamine-impregnated paper or a polyester film printed with a woodgrain

peripheral.tv.cabinet.moulding.name: Injection mould the cabinet
peripheral.tv.cabinet.moulding.description: ABS pellets were dried, melted at 230-260 degrees C, injected into a nickel-chromium plated steel mould at 1000-2000 bar, held under pressure to pack, cooled on a water circuit and ejected. The cabinet was a single moulding with the speaker grille, the bezel ledges, the screw bosses and the airflow slots all integral; the front bezel was often a separate moulding in a different colour. A 13 inch set's mould ran 10,000 to a few hundred thousand shots.
peripheral.tv.cabinet.moulding.note: The mould is P20 tool steel with a nickel-chromium plating, held at 1000-2000 bar against the melt. Moulds are generally made from tool steels, and presses are rated by the clamping force they can exert. Not established: 1000-2000 bar injection pressure, the 230-260 C melt temperature, the 40-70 s cycle, P20 or 1.2311 at 30-35 HRC with electroless nickel, and the 0.4-0.7% linear shrinkage.

facts.label: Melt temperature
facts.value: 230-260 degrees C

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: 40-70 seconds

facts.label: Mould
facts.value: P20 or 1.2311 pre-hardened tool steel, nickel-plated

facts.label: Shrinkage
facts.value: 0.4-0.7% linear

facts.label: Mould steel
facts.value: P20 or 1.2311 pre-hardened tool steel, 30-35 HRC, electroless-nickel plated

peripheral.tv.speaker.name: Loudspeaker, 8 ohm, 3-4 inch
peripheral.tv.speaker.description: An 8 ohm speaker of about 3.5-4 inch diameter on a small set: a paper pulp cone, a pressed steel or plastic basket, a copper voice coil on a former, and a ferrite magnet. It was screwed to a baffle in the cabinet with the back magnet projecting into whatever space was left, which is why small speakers of the period often had a shallow magnet or a rear vent.
peripheral.tv.speaker.note: The part of a small loudspeaker that decides what industry it belongs to is the sintered ferrite ring and the winding in its gap. Hard ferrites are used to make permanent magnets for loudspeakers, and the voice coil moves axially in a cylindrical gap in a permanent magnet's field. Not established: 8 ohm, 3.5-4 inch, 2-5 W, and the 200 Hz to 8-10 kHz response in a small cabinet.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 8 ohm nominal (4 ohm for parallel stereo)

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 3.5-4 inch diameter

facts.label: Frequency response
facts.value: about 200 Hz to 8-10 kHz in a small cabinet

peripheral.tv.speaker.voice-coil.name: Copper voice coil on a former
peripheral.tv.speaker.voice-coil.description: Two layers of enamelled copper wire, about 40-60 turns, wound on a paper or aluminium former and centred in the magnet gap. It is a minute amount of copper, on the order of a gram, and it sits in a gap of under a millimetre.

facts.label: Turns
facts.value: 40-60, two layers

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 8 ohm DC resistance about 5-6 ohm

peripheral.tv.speaker.magnet.name: Ferrite magnet
peripheral.tv.speaker.magnet.description: A ring or cup magnet of barium or strontium ferrite, sintered and magnetised across the gap. Barium ferrite needed barium carbonate, which is why barite mining also fed speakers. Ferrite, not Alnico, was the standard by 1982 because it was cheap and had a higher coercivity.
peripheral.tv.speaker.magnet.note: The barium here is the same element as in the CRT getter (barite for barium metal). Different ore routes, same element. Strontium ferrite was taking over by the late 1980s because strontium carbonate is cheaper than barium.

facts.label: Energy product
facts.value: about 3-4 x 10^3 kJ/m3 for barium ferrite

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: pressed and sintered at 1200-1250 degrees C

peripheral.tv.speaker.basket.name: Pressed steel basket
peripheral.tv.speaker.basket.description: The cone is glued to a stamped steel basket that holds the magnet and the voice coil in register. It came off the same cold-reduced low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask and the chassis, with the same iron ore behind it.
peripheral.tv.speaker.basket.note: The basket is stamped from the same cold-reduced low-carbon sheet as the shadow mask.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 150-250 g of steel in a 3.5 inch basket

facts.label: Joining
facts.value: spot welded or riveted to the magnet

peripheral.tv.speaker.cone.name: Paper pulp cone
peripheral.tv.speaker.cone.description: The cone is a paper pulp: refined wood fibre pressed wet into a shaped blank and dried, giving a light, stiff, cheap diaphragm. It is essentially the same material as a paper bag, which is why it creases if you poke it. A small set used a paper cone; a later or better one a woven or moulded polypropylene cone.
peripheral.tv.speaker.cone.note: The sound cone is one of the few parts of a television that starts as a tree. Pulp is wood reduced to fibre, and the fibre is from softwood, which is a renewable, not a geological, raw material. It is the one leaf in this branch that is not dug out of the ground. The cone is one of the three common sound radiation systems, and driver diaphragms are made of paper or composite materials. Not established: the wet-pressed kraft pulp route, the kiln or belt drying, and a few grams for a 3.5 inch cone.

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: slurry of kraft pulp pressed in a hot press and dried in a kiln or on a belt

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: a few grams for a 3.5 inch cone

peripheral.tv.chassis.name: The chassis: video, sync, line output, audio
peripheral.tv.chassis.description: The electronics of the set. By 1982 this was a single-sided or double-sided printed circuit board carrying a mix of discrete transistors, a handful of silicon integrated circuits (the video amplifier, the chroma, the vertical, the audio), a rotary switch bank and about forty electrolytic and film capacitors. The board sat in a zinc-plated steel chassis with a perforated steel cover, and the flyback sat beside it throwing both heat and electromagnetic noise.
peripheral.tv.chassis.note: This node is the set's printed circuit board and its subassemblies, not a whole machine; the set itself stays computing. Not established: the 115-120 V B+ rail, the 4.5 MHz intercarrier audio and the 45.75 MHz picture carrier as values for a 1982 set.

facts.label: Board
facts.value: FR-4 epoxy-glass laminate, single-sided in a cheap set

facts.label: Power input
facts.value: B+ rail about 115-120 V from a linear supply, or a small switcher

facts.label: Colour decoder
facts.value: NTSC quadrature demodulator with a phase-locked multiply

facts.label: Audio
facts.value: 4.5 MHz intercarrier FM

peripheral.tv.chassis.power.name: Power supply: mains transformer and reservoir
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.description: Most 1982 sets were linear: a hot-chassis or a cold-chassis series/parallel mains transformer stepping 117 V down to about 110 V AC, a diode bridge rectifier, and a big electrolytic reservoir at 120 V feeding the line output. The main electrolytic was the largest, hottest component on the board and usually the first thing to dry out. A minority used a small switchmode supply for the logic rails with a flyback of its own.
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.note: A cold-chassis set had the mains referenced to the line output and the whole board was at mains potential; a hot-chassis set had an isolated secondary and a common return. Repairing a 1982 TV meant first determining which, which is why it was dangerous and why sets were sold with the chassis not user-serviceable. Not established: the 200-400 uF at 160 V reservoir value, the 115-120 V B+ at 0.4-0.6 A, and the 40-60 VA transformer rating for a 13 inch set.

facts.label: Reservoir
facts.value: 200-400 microfarad at 160 V, an aluminium can electrolytic

facts.label: Mains transformer
facts.value: E-I laminated silicon steel, 40-60 VA, potted or taped

peripheral.tv.chassis.power.bridge.name: Mains rectifier bridge
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.bridge.description: Four silicon diodes in a moulded bridge package, rated at a few amps and 100-200 V. Cheap sets rectified with two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer instead. The bridge was usually on the chassis edge with the heatsink tab or in free air.
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.bridge.note: A diode bridge is four diodes converting AC to DC, and since about 1950 it has been a single four-terminal component made in various voltage and current ratings. Not established: the 1-4 A and 100-400 V rating, the moulded package, the chassis-edge mounting, and the two-diode centre-tapped alternative.

peripheral.tv.chassis.power.transformer.name: Mains transformer, E-I silicon steel
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.transformer.description: A laminated core of thin silicon steel (about 0.35 mm) stamped into E and I shapes and stacked, with copper windings on bobbins, potted in epoxy or wrapped in tape and varnished. The laminations were needed because mains hum would otherwise magnetostrict the core; the 1982 design was exactly the design from the 1930s.
peripheral.tv.chassis.power.transformer.note: The silicon steel is a different alloy from the low-carbon steel of the shadow mask: it is deliberately alloyed with silicon to raise resistivity and suppress eddy currents, and it is a thin, carefully annealed strip. Both, though, came off a blast furnace. Electrical steel is made as cold-rolled strip under 2 mm thick, cut into laminations and stacked to form transformer cores, and grain-oriented grades run about 3% silicon.
