peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batc.description: Where the funnel batch leaned on lead and alkali for its expansion match, the panel batch deliberately excluded sodium and potassium and got its properties from silica, alumina and boric oxide plus a small amount of barium to suppress solarisation under the phosphor firing. It is the same silica sand as the funnel, but a batch designed to be unfriendly to sodium.
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.panel-glass.batc.note: The alumina in a panel batch is refractory-grade alumina from the Bayer process, not the four-nines rolled foil used behind the phosphor; metal.alumina, the canonical alumina in this tree, is the ingredient it takes.
inputs: antimony or arsenic as a fining agent

facts.label: Na2O + K2O
facts.value: held below about 1% for an alkali-free panel glass

facts.label: Melt
facts.value: same 1380-1500 degrees C tank furnace as the funnel

facts.label: Solarisation
facts.value: the phosphor firing at 430-450 degrees C can darken a glass with too much alkali; barium and antimony suppressed it

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln.name: Continuous belt kiln
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln.description: A continuous refractory belt kiln, with a jig that aligns the printed panel rim to the funnel flange as the two travel through the firing zone where the frit melts and fuses. The seal is judged visually, by how far the heated frit bulges past its own edge. The tube is then helium leak tested on a separate manifold before it ever goes near the vacuum pumps, and that test is a gauge on a manifold rather than part of the kiln.
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.seal-kiln.note: Ion-pump or penning-gauge helium leak testing at that sensitivity was standard practice; the exact acceptance spec varies by plant, which is why the confidence here is low. The node is the kiln: the leak test used to share the title with it, and two different objects do not belong in one name.

facts.label: Zone temperature
facts.value: 430-460 degrees C peak

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: tens of minutes

facts.label: Leak criterion
facts.value: 10^-7 mbar l/s helium

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.name: Funnel glass batch, melted at 1400 degrees C
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.description: Funnel glass is a borosilicate with low alkali, formulated so that its thermal expansion matches the panel. The batch is silica sand, boric acid, soda ash, limestone and a little red lead or litharge as a fining agent, melted for tens of hours in a regenerative gas-fired tank furnace and then drawn into tubing.

facts.label: Melt temperature
facts.value: 1380-1500 degrees C

facts.label: Annealing
facts.value: lehr cooling 450 down to 20 degrees C over 10-20 hours

peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.bor.name: Boric acid
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.bor.description: Borates lower the glass's expansion coefficient and its melting point, which is exactly what a funnel that must survive a 25 kV implosion needs. Most borax for the western hemisphere came from borate ores in southern California and from Turkey.
peripheral.tv.crt.panel.funnel-glass.bor.note: No canonical borate node exists anywhere in the tree yet, so this chain stays here; the colemanite diggings and the acid digestion are as deep as it goes.

peripheral.why-rf.name: Why a television set was mandatory
peripheral.why-rf.description: The VIC-II chip outputs a 1 MHz-ish analogue composite signal on its own pin: luma, blanking and a colour subcarrier, but no RF. In 1982 there was no agreed analogue video standard between a computer and a monitor, no DE-15 or VGA, and no DVI. Commodore's answer was a small RF modulator, a printed board with one video modulator oscillator and a VHF converter, whose output was injected into the aerial socket of an ordinary television. The TV then had to be tuned to channel 3 (61.75 MHz in the US) or channel 4, and the picture was in colour only if the TV had a colour decoder for that subcarrier frequency.
peripheral.why-rf.note: The modulator board is usually treated as part of the C64, not as a peripheral, so it lives here as the hinge of this branch. Output power figures vary between sources; treat them as order-of-magnitude. A TV modulator injected at the aerial socket needs a floating (isolated) aerial input or the local TV signal will back-feed and wash out the computer picture, which is why sets with an isolated aerial socket were prized. The modulator itself is documented in the mainboard as mb.rf-modulator.
inputs: composite video from the VIC-II pin

facts.label: Output impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm, unbalanced

facts.label: Output power
facts.value: roughly 0.5-1 mW (a few hundred microwatts to 1 milliwatt)

facts.label: Colour subcarrier
facts.value: 3.58 MHz (NTSC) / 4.43 MHz (PAL)

facts.label: Default channel
facts.value: channel 3 US, switchable to 4

peripheral.why-rf.modern-comparison.name: Later video connectors: the 1702 DIN and the C128 RGBI
peripheral.why-rf.modern-comparison.description: Commodore's own 1702 monitor took a composite luma-and-blank input over a 5-pin DIN, and in 1985-86 Commodore adopted the DE-9 connector used by the C128's RGBI monitors, which carried separate red, green and blue analogue signals on pins 5, 6, 7 with no modulation at all. There was still no standard, which is why the C128 ended up with a proprietary DIN-8 video connector rather than a DE-15.
peripheral.why-rf.modern-comparison.note: The 1702 and the C128 RGBI monitors are real objects but they are not upstream of a 1982 C64, so they do not belong on a supply line.

peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm.name: Signal-level margin between a modulator and a transmitter
peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm.description: A broadcast TV station transmitted tens of kilowatts; a C64 modulator put out about a milliwatt. The set had to be tuned by hand, and reception quality was a function of the modulator's output impedance matching the aerial input. Anyone who ever moved the TV or unplugged the aerial lead knows how marginal this was.
peripheral.why-rf.tv-loses-75-ohm.note: Quantitative comparison of received signal levels is reconstructed from general receiver-sensitivity reasoning rather than from a measurement of a specific 1.1902-type modulator.

c64.packaging.name: Retail packaging: printed box, foam, polybag, manual
c64.packaging.description: A breadbin C64 shipped in a corrugated board box printed lithographically with Commodore's rainbow graphics, with the machine cradled in two moulded polystyrene end blocks and wrapped in a polyethylene bag, plus the user's manual and a warranty card. Boxes went to a corrugated master carton on a timber skid for shipping to warehouses.
c64.packaging.note: Internal packaging varied by region, by production run and by whether the machine was sold boxed or shipped in bulk to a distributor, so 'the C64 box' is really several packages: an early plain brown box with a rainbow stripe, later 'rainbow' graphics, and machined-in plain boxes. The user's manual is documented as Commodore part 320974 in the service-manual parts list. Not verified: the exact internal foam arrangement for every region.

facts.label: Box
facts.value: corrugated board, lithographically printed, rainbow graphics

facts.label: Internal protection
facts.value: moulded expanded polystyrene end blocks, chlorinated blowing agent

facts.label: Bag
facts.value: plain polyethylene sleeve over the machine

facts.label: Paperwork
facts.value: user's manual (Commodore part 320974) and a warranty/registration card

facts.label: Bulk shipping
facts.value: corrugated master carton banded on a timber skid

c64.packaging.packaging-line.name: Pack-out and case packing
c64.packaging.packaging-line.description: At the end of the case-moulding and assembly plant, machines are bagged, placed in the foam blocks, dropped into the printed box with the manual and the warranty card, and the box is closed, labelled and case-packed. This was semi-automatic and was the labour-heavy step that determined where a home computer was finally assembled.
c64.packaging.packaging-line.note: Not established: the operations, the operator count and where pack-out was done. A C64 box, foam end blocks and a printed manual are documented by the parts list; the pack-out line that combined them is not.

facts.label: Operations
facts.value: bag, foam, box, insert paper, close, label, case-pack

facts.label: Labour
facts.value: a few operators per line; the constraint on Commodore's throughput

c64.packaging.master-carton.name: Shipping master carton and skid
c64.packaging.master-carton.description: Retail boxes were packed into corrugated master cartons, several to a carton, and banded on a timber skid for palletised shipping from the Hong Kong or Taiwan assembly plant to a regional warehouse. Skids - not euro-pallets - were the norm for export shipping of this period.
c64.packaging.master-carton.note: Not established: the master carton size, the number of machines per carton, and that the load was skidded rather than palletised. The general period practice is described in the packaging literature, not in a Commodore record.

facts.label: Master carton
facts.value: double-wall corrugated, usually printed stencilled with contents and count

facts.label: Skid
facts.value: sawn timber skid with a bearers, no deckboards

facts.label: Strapping
facts.value: steel or polypropylene band around the carton

c64.packaging.carton-board.name: Master-carton board
c64.packaging.carton-board.description: Heavier double-wall corrugated, usually a recycled medium and recycled liners, with the shipping marks stencilled or flexo-printed rather than litho-printed.
c64.packaging.carton-board.note: Not established: that the master carton was double-wall recycled board with stencilled marks. Single-wall construction and starch bonding of corrugated board are documented; the shipping carton specification is not.

c64.packaging.strapping.name: Strapping (steel or polypropylene)
c64.packaging.strapping.description: Steel band with a stamped seal, or the polypropylene strapping that had largely displaced it by the 1980s because it does not rust, does not cut the carton and is lighter to ship back as waste.
c64.packaging.strapping.note: Not established: whether the export cartons were banded with steel or with polypropylene, and the band specification.

c64.packaging.skids.name: Timber skid
c64.packaging.skids.description: A wooden skid: three or more bearers with a top deck, or a bare skid with the cartons loaded straight onto it. Skids are made from rough-sawn softwood offcuts, which is why they are the cheapest way to make a heavy load forkable.
c64.packaging.skids.note: Not established: the skid construction on Commodore export shipments. Nothing in the parts list or the corporate record describes the export pack.

c64.packaging.timber.name: Rough-sawn softwood
c64.packaging.timber.description: Kiln-dried or green softwood, band-sawn to bearers and deckboards. The sawmill waste that cannot be pulped into paper - knots, ends, slabs - is exactly what a skid is made of, which is a neat closure of the wood chain.
c64.packaging.timber.note: Not established: the species, the moisture condition and the section sizes of the export skid.

facts.label: Species
facts.value: pine, spruce or fir

facts.label: Moisture
facts.value: green or kiln-dried, depending on the shipping leg

c64.packaging.warranty-card.name: Warranty and registration card
c64.packaging.warranty-card.description: A small printed card with the warranty terms and a serial-number registration slip. It is the same litho process as the manual on a heavier board stock, and it is the only part of the package with a legal function.
c64.packaging.warranty-card.note: Not established: that a warranty and registration card was packed with a 1982 C64, and its board stock and print. The service manual parts list records only the users manual.

facts.label: Stock
facts.value: 250-350 gsm coated or uncoated board

facts.label: Print
facts.value: one or two colours offset

c64.packaging.manual.name: User's manual (fold-in-fold booklet)
c64.packaging.manual.description: The Commodore 64 user's manual, part 320974 in the service-manual parts list, is a cheap but well-made fold-in-fold booklet: a single sheet of coated wood-pulp paper printed in colour on both sides, folded twice with a 16-page section glued into the middle crease. The result opens flat and costs almost nothing to assemble, and the construction is the same as a road atlas. A long sheet is printed with the page imposition for the 16-page booklet and the centre section is glued with PVA or hot-melt.
c64.packaging.manual.note: The manual is established as a shipped accessory: the parts list carries Users Manual, Commodore part 320974. Not established: the fold-in-fold construction, the 16-page glued centre section, the 60-100 gsm coated stock, the CMYK plus spot printing and the 320974 attribution to the service-manual parts list beyond the part number itself.

facts.label: Stock
facts.value: coated wood-pulp paper, about 60-100 gsm, colour both sides

facts.label: Binding
facts.value: 16-page fold-in-fold, glued on the centre spread

facts.label: Imposition
facts.value: 16 pages on one sheet, folded twice

c64.packaging.manual.printing.name: Colour offset printing of the manual
c64.packaging.manual.printing.description: Sheet-fed offset litho in four colours (CMYK), plus spot colours for the Commodore rainbow and the red 'RESTORE' key highlights. The manual's diagrams and BASIC listings were set in hot-metal or phototypeset, then printed from plates.
c64.packaging.manual.printing.note: Not established: the press type, the colour count and the spot colours on the C64 manual. The manual as a part is documented; how it was printed is not.

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: process CMYK plus spot colours

facts.label: Prepress
facts.value: phototypesetting and photographic copy for the diagrams

c64.packaging.manual.paper.name: Coated printing paper
c64.packaging.manual.paper.description: Wood-pulp paper filled and coated with clay (kaolin) and a binder, then calendered, so the ink sits on the surface and the colours are bright and sharp. It is the same stock as a supermarket leaflet.
c64.packaging.manual.paper.note: Not established: the grammage, the coating and the furnish of the stock the C64 manual was printed on.

facts.label: Gramnage
facts.value: 60-100 gsm coated

facts.label: Coating
facts.value: kaolin/clay + starch or PVA binder

facts.label: Fibre
facts.value: mostly softwood mechanical and kraft pulp

c64.packaging.polybag.name: Polyethylene sleeve over the machine
c64.packaging.polybag.description: A plain polyethylene bag over the boxed machine, to stop the moulded case and the printed manual from rubbing and to keep dust out during transit. It is a low-cost LDPE sleeve, blown as a tube on the same film-blowing line used for all commodity packaging film.
c64.packaging.polybag.note: Not established: that a 1982 C64 was shipped in a polyethylene sleeve, and the film gauge. The parts list records no bag.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: LDPE, ~40-80 um

facts.label: Use
facts.value: dust and abrasion protection during distribution

c64.packaging.film-blowing.name: Film blowing and bag making
c64.packaging.film-blowing.description: LDPE pellets are blown as a thin tube through a die and a bubble, cooled in an air ring, collapsed and wound; the tube is then cut and heat-sealed into a bag. Film blowing is high-volume and very cheap - the bag is cents, not dollars.
c64.packaging.film-blowing.note: Not established: the film gauge and line speed. Film blowing is a documented process; that it made this bag is not.

facts.label: Line speed
facts.value: 100+ m/min of collapsed tube

c64.packaging.foam-caps.name: Moulded polystyrene end blocks
c64.packaging.foam-caps.description: Two white expanded-polystyrene blocks that cradle the ends of the machine so the case cannot be crushed in the box and cannot slide. They are moulded to the machine's outline in a steam-heated block mould, then cut down to size.
c64.packaging.foam-caps.note: EPS blocks were the standard protection for beige consumer electronics through the 1980s. Their disadvantage - they cannot be recycled with paper and they shatter into Styrofoam - is exactly why they vanished from Commodore's later packaging in favour of pulp and cardboard trays.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: expanded polystyrene (EPS), bead foam

facts.label: Density
facts.value: about 15-30 kg/m3 for packaging foam

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: chlorinated hydrocarbon (CFC-11 or dichloromethane), about 5-7% into the bead

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: steam-heated block mould, 100-140 C, cut to size on a band saw or hot wire

c64.packaging.eps.name: Expanded polystyrene (EPS)
c64.packaging.eps.description: Small beads of polystyrene, each already blown up with a blowing agent, heated and expanded again in a mould so the beads fuse into a solid block shaped to the part. The polymer is the same styrene feedstock as the ABS and the SAN; only the physical form is different. The documented blowing agent is pentane, an aliphatic hydrocarbon permeating the bead before expansion; chlorinated blowing agents were also used and were being eliminated from foam through the 1980s and 1990s.
c64.packaging.eps.note: Corrected: this node previously stated the 1982 blowing agent was CFC-11 or dichloromethane, with pentane arriving only after the 1987 Montreal Protocol. The documented history runs the other way: pentane-blown beads were patented in 1949, and the 1987 bans removed CFC from foam rather than introducing pentane. Which agent the C64 packing foam actually used is not established; no Commodore document records the formulation.

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: pentane is the commonly used blowing agent, absorbed into the bead and expanded by heat and steam; chlorinated agents were earlier and were phased out of foam through the 1980s and 1990s

facts.label: Pentane-bead process
facts.value: developed before 1949 by F. Stastny and patented by BASF and Stastny in 1949; first public demonstration 1952

facts.label: Regulation
facts.value: US municipal bans on CFC foam containers began 1987, which removed CFC from foam rather than introducing pentane, the documented agent from 1949

facts.label: Which agent in this package
facts.value: not established; no Commodore document records the packing foam formulation

c64.packaging.eps-moulding.name: Block moulding in a steam-heated mould
c64.packaging.eps-moulding.description: Beads are blown into a heated aluminium mould and the steam expands them to fill it; the mould is then cooled and the block ejected. A block mould makes a slab that is later cut on a band saw or hot wire into the end blocks. The mould is a heat exchanger - the steam lines run through it.
c64.packaging.eps-moulding.note: Not established: the mould temperature, the cycle time and that the C64 end blocks were cut from a block mould.

facts.label: Mould
facts.value: steam-heated aluminium, 100-140 C; cycle about 1-3 minutes

c64.packaging.eps-expansion.name: Bead expansion (bead expander)
c64.packaging.eps-expansion.description: Beads are fed into a steam-heated expander where they expand, are held at temperature to sinter them into a cake, and are then cooled and dried in a silo. The expander is the machine that sets the final foam density.
c64.packaging.eps-expansion.note: Not established: the expansion ratio and the expander used on the Commodore packing line.

facts.label: Expansion ratio
facts.value: about 50-100x by volume

c64.packaging.eps-beads.name: EPS beads (expanded in a bead expander)
c64.packaging.eps-beads.description: Styrene is suspension-polymerised in water to small beads, then a blowing agent is dissolved into them under pressure; on heating the agent flashes and expands each bead, and the beads are chilled and sieved by size.
c64.packaging.eps-beads.note: Not established, and in conflict: that the blowing agent in 1982 EPS was CFC-11 or dichloromethane. Expanded polystyrene beads made with a pentane blowing agent were patented in 1949, so the chlorinated agent was not the only route and may not have been the one used here. Bead sizes and the steam conditions are also unverified.

facts.label: Bead size
facts.value: raw about 0.5-1 mm; expanded 2-6 mm

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: pentane or another aliphatic hydrocarbon; chlorinated agents such as CFC-11 were also used. The agent in this package is not established.

facts.label: Expansion
facts.value: about 100-140 C steam at 1-2 bar

c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent.name: Chlorinated blowing agent (CFC-11 / dichloromethane)
c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent.description: Trichlorofluoromethane, or methylene chloride in the European trade. Both are excellent blowing agents: low boiling point, no flammability risk in the bead, and chemically inert enough to survive the polymerisation. They are also chlorinated, which is the whole problem - they destroy stratospheric ozone, so they were phased out of packaging foam through the 1990s and replaced by pentane and by butane.
c64.packaging.chlorinated-blowing-agent.note: Not established: that a chlorinated blowing agent was used in C64 packing foam. Both agents boiling points and the Montreal Protocol phase-out are documented chemistry; their use in this package is not recorded.

facts.label: Why chosen then
facts.value: non-flammable, cheap, and already produced in bulk as a refrigerant

c64.packaging.retail-box.name: Retail corrugated box
c64.packaging.retail-box.description: A regular slotted container or a tuck-end box in single-wall corrugated board, printed on a sheet-fed or web offset press in up to four or six colours plus the rainbow gradient, then creased, cut, folded and glued. It is a commodity: the board is a mill product and the printing is a printshop product, not a Commodore product. The board gives the box its edge crush strength for the couple of Newtons of stacking force a pallet of them actually sees.
c64.packaging.retail-box.note: Not established: the flute grade, the colour count and the converting route for the C64 retail box. A printed corrugated retail box is a documented product class; this one is not specified anywhere.

facts.label: Board grade
facts.value: B-flute (about 2.5 mm) or C-flute (about 4 mm) single wall

facts.label: Printing
facts.value: flexo or offset litho, 2-6 colours

facts.label: Converting
facts.value: slotter-creater then folder-gluer; hundreds to thousands of boxes an hour

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: PVA or hot-melt, starch for heavy board

c64.packaging.parts-tray.name: Moulded parts tray
c64.packaging.parts-tray.description: Inside the box, below or beside the machine, the power cord, the A/V lead and the paperwork were either tied together in the foam or held in a separate moulded tray. Where a tray was used it was expanded polystyrene, or on later runs a folded pulp tray.
c64.packaging.parts-tray.note: The exact internal arrangement of the C64 box varied by region, production run and whether the machine was sold boxed or shipped in bulk to a distributor, and no particular arrangement has been verified for every region. A tray or folded pulp cradle for the loose items existed as a standard 1980s arrangement.

facts.label: Materials used
facts.value: expanded polystyrene block, or moulded pulp

facts.label: Contents
facts.value: mains cord, A/V lead, manual, warranty card

c64.packaging.box-printing.name: Box printing (offset litho) and the rainbow graphics
c64.packaging.box-printing.description: The printed sheet is run on an offset litho press - sheet-fed for short runs, web-fed for long - in a small number of process colours, with the Commodore rainbow reproduced as a multi-stop gradient from duotone overprints at varying screen densities or, on later short runs, a spray unit. A thin aqueous varnish is often applied over the top for scuff resistance. Flexographic printing on corrugate with rubber or photopolymer plates became the normal route for high-run corrugated print during this period and later; for a mid-run consumer box in the early 1980s, sheet-fed offset on a liner was still common.
c64.packaging.box-printing.note: The offset mechanism is established: the inked image is transferred from a plate to a rubber blanket and then to the printing surface, with a water roller applying a water-based film to the non-image areas. Not established: that the Commodore rainbow on the box was run on an offset press at all, that it was reproduced as a duotone gradient from overprints at varying screen densities or on a spray unit, the three-to-six process colour count, and the aqueous varnish. The number of separations and the duotone-versus-spray choice vary by printing run and region; the visual effect, a rainbow gradient band, is consistent across the packaging.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: sheet-fed offset or rotary web offset

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: typically 3-6 process colours; the rainbow needs extra separations or a duotone gradient

facts.label: Surface
facts.value: uncoated kraft board, often with a thin aqueous varnish

c64.packaging.offset-litho.name: Offset lithographic printing
c64.packaging.offset-litho.description: The image is on a flat plate, wetted with dampening solution so the image areas reject ink, and printed by a rubber blanket onto paper. Litho gives fine detail and consistent colour on uncoated board, at the cost of a plate-making step per colour.

facts.label: Process colours
facts.value: cyan, magenta, yellow, black (CMYK)

facts.label: Press
facts.value: sheet-fed or web-fed

c64.packaging.litho-press.name: Offset press (sheet-fed or web)
c64.packaging.litho-press.description: A printing press: plate cylinders, blanket cylinders, inking units, and either a sheet feed with a delivery stacker or a web unwind and rewind with a folder. For a corrugated box liner, the press is the capital equipment a converter owns.
c64.packaging.litho-press.note: Not established: the press type, the unit count and the frame. Offset printing is documented; the machine that printed Commodore packaging is not identified.

facts.label: Units
facts.value: 2-6 inking units for up to 6 colours

c64.packaging.litho-ink.name: Offset printing ink
c64.packaging.litho-ink.description: A pigment dispersed in a drying-oil-based vehicle (linseed/soy alkyd) with resin, wax and a drier. Water-based offset inks became the norm for corrugated in the 1990s; oil-based inks were standard in 1982.

facts.label: Vehicle
facts.value: linseed or soy alkyd resin

facts.label: Pigments
facts.value: titanium dioxide white, phthalocyanine blues, phthalochromate yellows

c64.packaging.ink-pigment.name: Ink pigments (organic and inorganic)
c64.packaging.ink-pigment.description: In 1982 most packaging colourants were still inorganic: iron oxides, chrome yellow, ultramarine. The bright synthetic organic pigments (phthalocyanines, azo yellows) were used for the saturated rainbow, and the titanium dioxide white for the light areas.
c64.packaging.ink-pigment.note: Not established: the pigment set in 1982 Commodore packaging inks. The named pigments are all documented materials; their use on these boxes is not.

c64.packaging.soy-oil.name: Soy or linseed oil (ink vehicle base)
c64.packaging.soy-oil.description: A vegetable oil pressed from a crop. It oxidises (dries) on the printed sheet, which is what 'drying ink' means. In 1982 soybean oil was becoming the preferred ink vehicle because of the 1970s linseed-oil shortages.
c64.packaging.soy-oil.note: Not established: that soybean oil was the ink vehicle on C64 packaging in 1982, and that the 1970s linseed shortage drove the switch. Alkyd vehicles are documented; the crop on Commodore packaging is not.

c64.packaging.ink-resin.name: Alkyd ink vehicle
c64.packaging.ink-resin.description: Built from vegetable oil (linseed or soybean) fatty acids condensed with a polyol and a phthalic or maleic anhydride, then crosslinked by oxidative polymerisation on the press. So the ink vehicle on the box traces back to a phthalic anhydride plant, the same chemistry as the pigment in the case.

facts.label: Vehicle
facts.value: linseed or soy alkyd resin

c64.packaging.litho-plate.name: Lithographic printing plate
c64.packaging.litho-plate.description: A thin aluminium or copper plate, grained and treated, with a photopolymer or metal-image layer carrying the separations. The classic long-run offset plate is an aluminium sheet electro-grained and anodised; short runs use photopolymer plates directly.
c64.packaging.litho-plate.note: Not established: whether the plates were grained aluminium offset plates or photopolymer plates on the C64 packaging runs.

facts.label: Plate
facts.value: aluminium (offset), copper (letterpress), or photopolymer

c64.packaging.box-board.name: Corrugated board (liner + medium)
c64.packaging.box-board.description: Two kraft liners glued to a fluted medium, corrugated between two rotating fluted rolls with heat and starch glue and then glued to the liners. The flute is a beam, which is the whole reason a pizza box folds and a used sheet does not, and it is why a C64 box is B or C flute single wall rather than anything heavier. Medium paper is run onto the corrugator at 200-400 m/min and the sheet is then cut and creased.
c64.packaging.box-board.note: Reusing office paper makes poor medium; box fibre is preferred because the flute is only as strong as the paper in it.

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: liner / fluted medium / liner, single wall

facts.label: Typical flute
facts.value: B (about 2.5 mm) or C (about 4 mm)

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: starch or dextrin, hot-water resistant grade

facts.label: Machine speed
facts.value: about 200-400 m/min

c64.packaging.starch-adhesive.name: Starch corrugating adhesive
c64.packaging.starch-adhesive.description: The glue holding the flutes and the liners is a corn- or tapioca-starch dextrin, cooked on the corrugator and applied hot. It is the standard adhesive in corrugated board and the reason the board is not a fire hazard in the way solvent glues would be.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: starch / dextrin, hot-water resistant grade for the liners

c64.packaging.corn-starch.name: Corn (maize) starch
c64.packaging.corn-starch.description: Starch is wet-milled from maize: the kernels are steeped in warm water to soften the germ, ground, and the starch is separated by gravity or centrifugally and dried. Every corrugated box is glued with a plant, not a petrochemical.
c64.packaging.corn-starch.note: Not established: that the corrugating adhesive was a maize or tapioca starch dextrin. Starch is the documented corrugating adhesive; the source crop is not recorded.

c64.packaging.maize.name: Maize crop
c64.packaging.maize.description: A cereal grain grown in enormous tonnages in the US corn belt and in Europe, China and Brazil; the harvested cobs are shelled and the kernels go to wet milling. This is the agricultural end of the adhesive chain.
c64.packaging.maize.note: Not established: any Commodore figure for maize tonnage or origin. The adhesive chain is documented to the level of plant starch.

c64.packaging.corrugated-medium.name: Fluted medium (recycled)
c64.packaging.corrugated-medium.description: The wavy centre of the board is usually made from 100% recycled paper, because the flute does not need virgin-fibre strength. Old corrugated boxes are collected, pulped (the recycled / OCF route), and run onto a corrugating machine.
c64.packaging.corrugated-medium.note: Not established: that the fluted medium was 100% recycled. Recycled medium is common practice but the fibre blend on this board is not recorded.

c64.packaging.wastepaper.name: Recovered paper (OCC / mixed waste)
c64.packaging.wastepaper.description: Collected corrugated and box board, baled, repulped in a hydrapulper and screened. The deinking stage is needed for printed waste; unprinted OCC is repulped as it is. The fibre in a C64 box's fluted medium is therefore almost certainly several previous boxes.
c64.packaging.wastepaper.note: That old corrugated containers are the characteristic post-consumer waste stream for board fibre is established: post-consumer waste is discarded after consumer use, such as old corrugated containers (OCC), magazines, and newspapers. Not established: the 500 kg bale weight, the specific grade used for C64 board, and that the fibre in this box is several previous boxes.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: OCC (old corrugated container) or mixed waste paper

facts.label: Baling
facts.value: hydraulic baler to ~500 kg bales

c64.packaging.deinking.name: Repulping and deinking
c64.packaging.deinking.description: Bales are dropped into a hydrapulper, torn up into fibre, screened, and deinked with a flotation cell and surfactant to remove printing inks. A high proportion of the world's corrugated medium fibre is recovered in exactly this way.
c64.packaging.deinking.note: That deinking is the named industrial process for removing printing ink from paper fibres to make deinked pulp is established. Not established: the hydrapulper and flotation-cell sequence, the caustic and surfactant charges, and that a high proportion of the world's corrugated medium fibre is recovered this way.

c64.packaging.kraft-liner.name: Kraft liner (topside and underside)
c64.packaging.kraft-liner.description: Unbleached paper made from long-fibre softwood pulp, typically 120-200 gsm. Kraft paper is also known as brown paper: the brown is the colour of the unbleached grade, not the consequence of a lignin-preserving cook, because the kraft cook in fact removes most of the lignin present in the wood.
c64.packaging.kraft-liner.note: In part in conflict. That unbleached kraft is the strong, cheap liner grade is established, and so is the reason it is strong: kraft pulping removes most of the lignin present originally in the wood, and the low lignin matters because the hydrophobic nature of lignin interferes with the hydrogen bonds between cellulose fibres. That is the opposite of the explanation given here, which is that the brown colour comes from the kraft cook keeping the lignin. The brown colour of kraft paper is established as the colour of the unbleached grade itself, kraft paper also being known as brown paper; the mechanism by which it is brown is not settled by the source.

facts.label: Fibre
facts.value: long-fibre softwood (spruce, pine)

c64.packaging.kraft-pulp.name: Kraft pulp
c64.packaging.kraft-pulp.description: Wood chips are steamed, cooked in a kraft digester with sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide, washed, and bleached only lightly. The kraft cook is a delignifying cook: it removes most of the lignin originally present in the wood, and the surviving cellulose is what makes kraft pulp stronger than sulfite or mechanical pulp. Kraft pulp is darker than other wood pulps and is normally left unbleached for sack and liner grades.
c64.packaging.kraft-pulp.note: That kraft pulp is produced by the kraft process and that the process yields stronger pulp than sulfite or mechanical pulping is established. In part in conflict: the source says kraft pulping removes most of the lignin present originally in the wood, whereas the description here says the brown colour is retained kraft lignin. Not established: the sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide charges, the 160-180 C cook, the one to three hour duration and the 45-50% yield.

facts.label: Cook
facts.value: kraft/sulfate cook at 160-180 C

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: ~45-50% of wood weight

c64.packaging.kraft-process.name: Kraft grade versus bleached
c64.packaging.kraft-process.description: Unbleached kraft keeps its brown colour and is the cheapest strong liner; kraft paper is also known as brown paper. The colour is a property of the unbleached grade rather than of retained lignin, since the kraft cook removes most of the wood's lignin. A bleached or semi-bleached top liner costs more and is used where the print needs a white background. Commodore's boxes are brown board with printing on top, so the brown liner is exactly right.
c64.packaging.kraft-process.note: That unbleached kraft is cheaper than a bleached top liner is established in general terms by kraft paper also being known as brown paper, and produced from the kraft process. Not established: that the pulp is brown before it reaches the paper machine because the cook keeps the lignin, since the source says kraft pulping removes most of the lignin; the bleaching chemistries; or that Commodore's boxes were brown board with printing on top. Chlorine bleaching of pulp was standard in 1982 and has since been largely displaced by chlorine-free processes for environmental reasons - a clear 1980s-versus-modern difference in the same plant.

facts.label: Bleaching
facts.value: chlorine, chlorine dioxide or oxygen/peroxide delignification

c64.packaging.digestion.name: Kraft cooking (digestion)
c64.packaging.digestion.description: Chips are cooked in a spherical or continuous digester with white liquor (sodium hydroxide + sodium sulfide + sodium carbonate) at 160-180 C. The alkali dissolves the lignin; the sulfide keeps the dissolved lignin in solution so the fibres do not darken.
c64.packaging.digestion.note: Not established: the cook temperature, the duration and the white-liquor composition, and that the digester sat next to a Commodore packaging supplier rather than a paper mill.

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 1-3 hours

facts.label: Chemical recovery
facts.value: black liquor is evaporated and burnt to regenerate the chemicals

c64.packaging.wood-chips.name: Wood chips from sawmill waste
c64.packaging.wood-chips.description: Roundwood is debarked and chipped into 20-30 mm chips in a disc chipper, ready for the digester. The chips are the whole reason the paper mill sits next to a forest: you cannot make paper without wood fibre.
c64.packaging.wood-chips.note: Not established: the chipper type, the chip size and that sawmill waste was the source.

c64.packaging.forest-stand.name: Standing softwood in a managed plantation
c64.packaging.forest-stand.description: Managed conifer plantations - spruce, pine or southern pine - felled on a rotation and replanted, where the fibre chain for a box begins. A box is wood, and the wood is a tree that was grown, cut and chipped.
c64.packaging.forest-stand.note: Not established: the species, the rotation length or the plantation source of the fibre.

c64.packaging.log.name: Roundwood logs
c64.packaging.log.description: Trunk sections felled and delimbed, usually conifer in northern Europe and North America. Softwood is preferred for kraft because its long fibres give paper strength; hardwoods go into hardwood kraft or into mechanical pulp.
c64.packaging.log.note: Not established: the species mix, the origin and the logging route for the fibre.

c64.cables.name: Supplied cables: RF lead, A/V lead, mains cord
c64.cables.description: Three cables shipped with or sold alongside a breadbin C64, plus the optional TV switch box. The RF cable carries the modulator's VHF output from the machine's phono socket to a television's aerial input, so it is a 75-ohm coaxial. The A/V lead carries luma, chroma, composite and audio to a monitor through an 8-pin DIN. The mains cord is a two- or three-core PVC-jacketed cord with a moulded plug that feeds the external power supply.
c64.cables.note: The breadbin's RF modulator sits on the motherboard (Astec or Mitsumi depending on production run) and its output leaves through the machine's own phono socket. The supplied RF cable is therefore a coax lead with a phono plug at the C64 end and a television-plug at the TV end. Early boards used a 5-pin video socket; later ones an 8-pin DIN, which changes the A/V cable but not the RF cable.

facts.label: RF cable
facts.value: Commodore part 326189-01, 75-ohm coax, phono to TV aerial plug

facts.label: A/V socket
facts.value: 8-pin DIN at CN5 on the motherboard; 5-pin on early sets

facts.label: Switch box
facts.value: Commodore part 904778-01, an RF splitter accessory

c64.cables.switch-box.name: TV RF switch box
c64.cables.switch-box.description: Commodore part 904778-01, an external box that let the C64's RF output share a television aerial socket with a real antenna, switching between them. It is an accessory rather than a cable, but it is the same moulded-plastic-and-coax family and shares the cable supply chain.
c64.cables.switch-box.note: The service-manual parts list gives this number; its exact internals are not documented in the sources available here, so the internal switch and connectors are described generically rather than specifically.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: switch between computer RF and TV aerial

c64.cables.power-cord.name: Mains power cord
c64.cables.power-cord.description: A detachable mains lead for the external power supply: two or three PVC-insulated copper conductors, twisted together on a planetary twister so the cord resists unwinding, then jacketed in a second extrusion over the twisted bundle. Each conductor is passed through a die and coated with rigid or semi-rigid PVC at a few hundred volts' worth of insulation, with the colour added by pigment masterbatch. At the supply end there is a moulded figure-8 or IEC C8 inlet; at the wall end a moulded mains plug whose cord body is the part that actually fails, because it is unbolted from the prongs and slides off the cable.
c64.cables.power-cord.note: Not established: the conductor count, the insulation wall, the twist rate, the stranding class and the current rating of the C64 mains lead. The service manual lists a detachable power supply but does not specify the cord. The shipped-accessories list is Users Manual, Power Supply, RF Cable and Switch Box, with the power supply a single part, 251053-02, so a detachable lead is not recorded as an accessory in its own right.

facts.label: Conductors
facts.value: 2 (continental Europe) or 3 (North America, with earth)

facts.label: Insulation
facts.value: PVC per conductor, about 0.6-0.8 mm wall; line speed tens of m/min

facts.label: Outer jacket
facts.value: flexible PVC, about 2.5-3 mm wall

facts.label: Cord twist
facts.value: planetary or bunch twisting, tens of twists per metre

facts.label: Stranding
facts.value: class 2 or 5 flexible, 0.5-0.75 mm2

facts.label: Current rating
facts.value: 2.5-10 A, well over the C64's about 15 W draw

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: figure-8 (C7) or IEC C8 inlet on the power supply

c64.cables.power-cord.mains-plug.name: Moulded mains plug
c64.cables.power-cord.mains-plug.description: A plug with a thermoplastic cord body wrapped around the cable entry to take the bending strain, and two or three brass prongs riveted or crimped in. The cord body is the part that actually fails: the plug is unbolted from the prongs and slides off the cable.
c64.cables.power-cord.mains-plug.note: Not established: the prong material and plating, the cord body polymer and the rating on the plug Commodore shipped.

facts.label: Prongs
facts.value: brass, plated; nickel-plated as well on the North American 3-pin plug

facts.label: Cord body
facts.value: PVC or polypropylene overmoulded grip

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: the cord body tears at its root after years of being yanked from the wall

c64.cables.power-cord.cord-body.name: Cord body / strain-relief grip
c64.cables.power-cord.cord-body.description: Moulded in PVC or polypropylene and over-moulded onto the jacket. It is deliberately flexible so the cable can swivel, which is also why a moulded cord body eventually tears at its root after years of being yanked out of a wall socket by the wire.
c64.cables.power-cord.cord-body.note: Not established: the cord body polymer and whether it was overmoulded onto the jacket.

c64.cables.power-cord.conductors.name: Flexible stranded copper conductors
c64.cables.power-cord.conductors.description: Fine-strand flexible copper, made by bunching many small wires in a roving machine and twisting them. Flexible stranding is what lets a mains lead bend without breaking the strands, and class 2 or 5 stranding at 0.5-0.75 mm2 is what a 2.5-10 A cord of this period used.
c64.cables.power-cord.conductors.note: Not established: the stranding class, the conductor cross-section and that the lead was bunched on a roving machine.

facts.label: Stranding
facts.value: class 2 or 5 flexible, 0.5-0.75 mm2 conductors

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: bunching and twisting (stranding) machine

c64.cables.av-cable.name: A/V cable to a 1701/1702 monitor
c64.cables.av-cable.description: A monitor lead carrying luma, chroma, composite video, audio in and out, and +5V/ground, in an 8-pin DIN connector at each end. It was often bundled with the monitor rather than sold with the computer, which is why many C64 owners improvised with a phono lead for composite only.
c64.cables.av-cable.note: The monitor lead was often bundled with the monitor rather than sold with the computer, which is why many C64 owners improvised with a phono lead for composite only.

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: 8-pin DIN (CN5); early machines used a 5-pin socket

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: luma, chroma, composite, audio out, audio in, +5 V, ground

c64.cables.av-cable.wires.name: Cable conductors and insulation
c64.cables.av-cable.wires.description: Stranded tinned copper conductors with PVC insulation, colour-coded to the DIN pinout, with the audio lines twisted or shielded to keep the 1 MHz clock out of the speaker. The wire gauge is not recorded in the sources available here.

c64.cables.av-cable.din.name: DIN connector and cable
c64.cables.av-cable.din.description: A moulded DIN plug with a metal shell and a screw-on or clip-on backshell that clamps the cable and provides strain relief. The shell is nickel-plated steel or brass, and the interior is filled with a phenolic or thermoplastic insert holding the female contacts.
c64.cables.av-cable.din.note: DIN connectors on this machine are established from the parts lists: CN4 6 Pin Din 903361-01, and on the later 250407-04 CN5 8 Pin Din 325573-01, against CN5 5 Pin Din 903362-01 on the earliest. Not established: that the shell is nickel-plated steel or brass, that the insert is phenolic or thermoplastic, or that the C64's monitor ecosystem was deliberately European. The DIN plug is a European standard (DIN 41512) and is one of the few connectors where the C64's whole monitor ecosystem was deliberately European.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: nickel-plated steel or brass

facts.label: Insert
facts.value: phenolic or thermoplastic, holding the contacts

c64.cables.rf-cable.name: RF cable (phono plug to TV plug)
c64.cables.rf-cable.description: A 75-ohm coaxial lead. Its job is to get a 1 MHz video signal, sitting on a VHF carrier, into a television's analogue aerial input without picking up half the room on the way. Impedance matching and a decent screen are what keep the picture from ghosting.
c64.cables.rf-cable.note: That a 75-ohm shielded coaxial lead was a shipped accessory is established: the service manual lists RF Cable, Commodore part 326189-01, in the accessories. The structure of coax is established in general terms. Not established: that this lead ran from a moulded phono plug at the computer to a coaxial television plug, its length, or that it was bundled with the monitor rather than sold with the computer.

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm

facts.label: C64 end
facts.value: moulded phono (RCA) plug

facts.label: TV end
facts.value: coaxial television plug (the old round type)

c64.cables.rf-cable.strain-relief.name: Strain-relief boot
c64.cables.rf-cable.strain-relief.description: A moulded rubber or PVC boot at each cable end where it enters the plug body, taking the bending load so the conductor does not fatigue at the termination. Cheap to add, and the difference between a lead that survives ten years and one that breaks at the root.
c64.cables.rf-cable.strain-relief.note: Not established: that the C64 RF lead had moulded strain-relief boots at both ends, and their form.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: PVC or vulcanised rubber

facts.label: Form
facts.value: moulded-in taper or a slid-on sleeve

c64.cables.rf-cable.plug.name: Moulded phono plug and TV plug
c64.cables.rf-cable.plug.description: Both ends are moulded: a phono (RCA) plug with a nickel-plated centre pin in a moulded barrel at the C64 end, and a television coaxial plug at the other. The pin is electroplated rather than bare so it survives being shoved into and out of the television a thousand times; nickel is the classic choice for a connector contact because its contact resistance stays low and it does not corrode in a socket. Brass is the standard pin material because it machines well, springs enough to take a wipe and does not rust.
c64.cables.rf-cable.plug.note: Not established: the pin material and plating, the barrel construction and the plating thickness on the C64 RF lead.

facts.label: Phono pin
facts.value: nickel-plated brass, about 3 mm

facts.label: Barrel
facts.value: knurled, pressed or screwed onto the jacket

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: sulfate or sulfamate nickel with a brightening additive, 2-10 um

c64.cables.rf-cable.coax.name: 75-ohm coaxial cable
c64.cables.rf-cable.coax.description: The cable itself: a centre conductor, a dielectric, a braided screen and an outer PVC jacket, assembled in that order. The braid is what does the shielding; the jacket is only there to survive being dragged under a TV cabinet for twenty years. A consumer lead of this type was often thin-wall 75-ohm coax rather than a strict RG designation, and the important properties are 75 ohms and full-coverage screen.
c64.cables.rf-cable.coax.note: A 70%-covered braid leaks RF, and that leakage is why a badly-made RF cable puts a visible ghost on the picture. Anything not fully shielded is worth replacing rather than adjusting.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: solid or stranded centre conductor, PE or PTFE dielectric, braided tinned-copper screen, PVC jacket

facts.label: Typical class
facts.value: RG-59 / RG-6 style 75 ohm

c64.cables.rf-cable.polymer-extrusion.name: Cable extrusion line
c64.cables.rf-cable.polymer-extrusion.description: A vertical or horizontal line where conductor is drawn through a die, dielectric tube is extruded or foamed around it, braid is laid on from a rotating carrier, and the jacket is extruded and cooled in a trough. Cable extrusion is one of the few polymer processes that is genuinely continuous and high-speed.
c64.cables.rf-cable.polymer-extrusion.note: Not established: the line speed, the number of passes and the spark test on the cable that shipped with the C64.

facts.label: Line speed
facts.value: tens to hundreds of m/min

facts.label: Steps
facts.value: conductor -> dielectric -> braid -> jacket, often on separate lines

facts.label: Spark testing
facts.value: each length passes a high-voltage spark tester

c64.cables.rf-cable.braid.name: Braided screen (tinned copper)
c64.cables.rf-cable.braid.description: A flat bundle of tinned copper wires woven over the dielectric by a braiding machine, usually with a second pass to push coverage from ~70% toward 90%. Tinning reduces oxidation and makes the braid easier to terminate.
c64.cables.rf-cable.braid.note: That a woven copper braid serves as the concentric conducting shield in coaxial cable is established. Not established: that this braid was tinned, the 70-95% coverage figures, the second pass, and the maypole versus tubular braider. Coverage is the number that matters: a 70%-covered braid leaks RF, and that leakage is why a badly-made RF cable puts a visible ghost on the picture.

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: ~70-95%; more passes = better shield

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: maypole (flat) or tubular braider

c64.cables.rf-cable.jacket.name: Coaxial cable PVC jacket
c64.cables.rf-cable.jacket.description: A lead-compounded PVC jacket, flexible grade with a plasticiser so the cable stays bendable. It has nothing to do with the signal; its job is abrasion and handling. The plasticiser is what makes the lead supple instead of stiff and brittle, and the phthalate ester it is made from comes off the same phthalic anhydride plant as the pigment in the case.
c64.cables.rf-cable.jacket.note: Not established: the jacket grade and wall thickness on the C64 RF lead, and which plasticiser was used.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: flexible (plasticised) PVC

facts.label: Wall
facts.value: about 0.7-1.0 mm

c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser.name: Plasticiser in flexible PVC
c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser.description: Cable PVC is not rigid: it is compounded with a plasticiser such as dioctyl phthalate (DOP) or trimellitates, dropped into an extruder at 5-10% and mixed before extrusion. The plasticiser is what makes the lead supple instead of stiff and brittle.
c64.cables.rf-cable.plasticiser.note: Not established: that a phthalate plasticiser was used in the C64 RF cable jacket, and the loading.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 5-15% by weight

facts.label: Common plasticisers
facts.value: DOP (DEHP), DINP, trimellitate esters

c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric.name: Dielectric (polyethylene or PTFE)
c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric.description: The insulating foam between conductor and braid. Polyethylene is the volume material for consumer coax, often gas-injected or foam-injected to lower the dielectric constant and hold 75 ohm with a bigger centre conductor. PTFE (Teflon) is the low-loss, low-noise alternative used where a very clean signal or a tight bend radius matters.
c64.cables.rf-cable.dielectric.note: That the insulating material between the centre conductor and the shield is the dielectric is established. Not established: that polyethylene was the volume choice for consumer coax, that it was gas- or foam-injected, and that PTFE was the premium choice. Foamed polyethylene is worth noting because it is the same polymer as the plastic bags in the packaging: chain-grafted or chemical-blowing-agent foam, blown in the extrusion line.

facts.label: Volume choice
facts.value: polyethylene, often foamed

facts.label: Premium choice
facts.value: PTFE for low loss and low dielectric constant

facts.label: Extrusion
facts.value: pre-extruded dielectric tube, then conductor drawn in

c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe.name: Low-density polyethylene (the volume dielectric)
c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe.description: The bulk of consumer coax dielectric is LDPE made by high-pressure or low-pressure polymerisation of ethylene. LDPE is branched and low-density, which is exactly what you want here: the branching lowers the dielectric constant so the coaxial geometry lands on 75 ohm with a reasonable centre-conductor size.
c64.cables.rf-cable.ldpe.note: That LDPE is the branched low-density form of polyethylene is established: the article heads its structure section with the branched structure of LDPE, and identifies branching as one of the features that distinguishes polyethylene grades. Not established: that the branching is what allows a 75 ohm coaxial geometry with a reasonable centre conductor, the 2.2-2.35 dielectric constant and the 0.91-0.93 g/cm3 density.

c64.cables.rf-cable.centre-conductor.name: Centre conductor (copper, or copper-clad steel)
c64.cables.rf-cable.centre-conductor.description: The signal-carrying core. Consumer coax uses solid bare copper or, to save money, copper-clad steel. At RF frequencies a copper-clad-steel core is perfectly adequate over a metre of cable, and the copper wire rod for it comes from the same electrolytic refinery as the winding wire and the contact metal elsewhere in the machine.
c64.cables.rf-cable.centre-conductor.note: That the signal-carrying core of a coaxial cable is the inner centre conductor is established. Not established: that consumer coax of this period used copper-clad steel to save money, that a copper-clad-steel core is adequate over a metre at RF, or that the rod for it came from the same refinery as the machine's other conductors. Cable plants buy cathode and draw rod in-house; drawing anneals and work-hardens the copper in the same step.

c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire.name: Copper wire rod and drawing
c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire.description: Copper cathodes are melted, cast into wire rod, then drawn through a series of dies to the finished diameter. A cable plant buys rod and draws it in-house; drawing anneals and work-hardens the copper in the same step.
c64.cables.rf-cable.copper-wire.note: Not established: the purity grade, the die material and whether the C64 cable plant drew wire in house.

facts.label: Copper purity
facts.value: E-C grade 99.9%+, from electrolytic refining

facts.label: Drawing
facts.value: wet or dry, through carbide or diamond dies

c64.mains.name: C64 mains side: cord, plug, switch, fuse
c64.mains.description: Everything between the wall socket and the transformer primary: the three-conductor line cord and its moulded plug, the rocker switch, the line fuse, the X-rated suppression capacitor and the protective-earth bonding. The brick's case is entirely plastic, so the earth conductor never bonds to an enclosure - it terminates on the interwinding screen inside the transformer, and that is the whole of the earthing arrangement.
c64.mains.note: The reported 120 mA / 200 mA primary fuse ratings are consistent with a 15-30 W supply and the recommendation of a fuse at about 125% of the calculated input current, so they are plausible rather than confirmed from the factory documentation.

facts.label: Cord
facts.value: three conductors in the North American build (line, neutral, protective earth); two conductors in some markets

facts.label: Primary fuse
facts.value: reported as 120 mA or 200 mA depending on the mains voltage and build

facts.label: Thermal protection
facts.value: a thermal fuse in series with one end of the primary winding, documented on the 251053-02

facts.label: Switch
facts.value: rocker or slider, in-line with the line conductor

c64.mains.approvals.name: Safety approvals and standards
c64.mains.approvals.description: The brick is certified as a component rather than as an appliance. In the United States that is UL 478, Power Supply Units, with the file number moulded into the case - 13J5 with 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER' on the 3-83 build. In Canada it is CSA, in Singapore the NLS scheme, and in West Germany VDE. Each is a recognised component mark; the finished C64 was then certified separately under whichever national scheme applied to the appliance.
c64.mains.approvals.note: UL 478 was the correct US standard in 1982-84 and has since been withdrawn in favour of UL 62368-1, which replaced the shock-hazard model with a hazard-based energy model; the test voltages and limits quoted in this tree are the 1980s values and will not appear in the current standard.

facts.label: US
facts.value: UL 478, file 13J5

facts.label: Canada
facts.value: CSA

facts.label: Singapore
facts.value: NLS

facts.label: Europe
facts.value: VDE; the appliance-level standard was IEC 65 / BS 415 / EN 41003

c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.name: Routine production tests
c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.description: Beyond the type tests, every unit gets a dielectric withstand test between the primary and the secondaries, an earth-continuity test, and a functional test with a load on both outputs. The dielectric withstand is the test that actually keeps people alive, because the failure it detects - a foil short, a pinched wire, a solder splash across the bobbin - is the fault that puts mains on a 5 V rail.
c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.note: Not established: that this specific three-test set (dielectric withstand, earth continuity, loaded functional test) was applied to every unit of this supply, or the 1500-2500 V / 1 s withstand level, the <= 0.1 ohm earth-continuity limit, or the burn-in loading. The dielectric withstand test itself is a documented production test; its levels are set by the applicable product standard, not stated here.

facts.label: Dielectric withstand
facts.value: 1500-2500 V AC for about 1 s, leakage current monitored

facts.label: Functional
facts.value: both outputs loaded and measured, case temperature observed

facts.label: Where the dielectric withstand lives
facts.value: the brick's own assembly branch carries the hi-pot, earth-continuity and burn-in tests; this node is the standards view of the same three

c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.aql.name: Lot sampling and the critical-component control plan
c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.aql.description: Listing does not mean every unit is tested at every test. Instead the manufacturer submits a control plan: the dielectric withstand and earth continuity are 100% tests because they are the safety-critical ones, while the routine functional and leakage-current checks are sampled at an agreed quality level - typically one in three to one in thirty, with any failure escalating the lot to 100%. Critical components (the transformer, the switch, the fuse, the line capacitor, the cord set) come only from named manufacturers and are subject to incoming inspection.
c64.mains.approvals.normal-tests.aql.note: The AQL concept and the critical/major/minor defect split are standard (ANSI/ASQ Z1.4), but not established: this control plan. No document states that dielectric withstand and earth continuity were 100% tests while functional and leakage were sampled, nor the AQL 2.5 or 6.5 levels, nor that critical parts came from a named-vendor list with certificate of conformance.

facts.label: Safety tests
facts.value: 100% dielectric withstand, 100% earth continuity

facts.label: Functional tests
facts.value: sampled, typically AQL 2.5 or 6.5

facts.label: Critical parts
facts.value: from a named-vendor list only, with certificate-of-conformance required

facts.label: Lot size
facts.value: typically one shift, one line, one component lot

facts.label: Reject number
facts.value: from the original sample plan, not re-derived

c64.mains.approvals.safety-file.name: The safety file
c64.mains.approvals.safety-file.description: Listing is not just a test. The applicant submits a design file: schematic, printed-board artwork, bill of materials, critical-components list, the transformer's winding instruction and insulation system drawing, the enclosure material specifications, and the test report. The follow-up inspection checks that production still matches the file, and it is the reason a safe transformer cannot simply be substituted with a cheaper one after manufacture.
c64.mains.approvals.safety-file.note: Not established: the contents of the design file submitted for this supply - schematic, PCB artwork, BOM, transformer winding instruction and insulation-system drawing, enclosure material specification - and the periodic follow-up factory inspection that checks production still matches. UL is documented as certifying products against its own standards; the file-and-follow-up regime is not documented in the sources consulted.

facts.label: Critical parts
facts.value: the transformer, the line capacitor, the switch, the fuse holder, the cord set and the enclosure flammability

facts.label: Follow-up
facts.value: periodic factory inspection of the listed factory

facts.label: Relationship to the listing
facts.value: the design file is what the applicant submits to obtain the listing; the brick's own final-test branch carries the type tests themselves

c64.mains.earthing.name: Protective earth bonding
c64.mains.earthing.description: The brick is entirely moulded ABS with no metal chassis, so there is nothing external to bond earth to. The earth conductor runs from the plug, into the epoxy-filled case, and terminates on the aluminium or copper screen buried between the transformer's primary and secondary windings. The earthing path therefore closes and opens entirely inside one potted block, and the C64 itself has an unconnected earth: the supply behaves like a Class II appliance even though it carries an earth conductor.
c64.mains.earthing.note: A two-conductor cord with no earth at all would have been perfectly acceptable for a doubly-insulated Class II appliance of this size, and some Commodore builds do use a two-wire cord. Carrying an earth into an all-plastic supply is belt-and-braces: it protects against the earth pin being energised by a primary-secondary fault inside the transformer, which is precisely what the interwinding screen does.

facts.label: Case
facts.value: all-plastic ABS, no metal enclosure

facts.label: Bond point
facts.value: the interwinding screen inside the transformer

facts.label: Continuity test
facts.value: <= 0.1 ohm from the cord earth pin to the bonded screen

c64.mains.line-capacitor.name: X-rated line filter capacitor
c64.mains.line-capacitor.description: A small polypropylene film capacitor connected across line and neutral to shunt radio-frequency noise that the switching action of the rectifier diodes and the regulator would otherwise inject back onto the supply. It is rated X - that is, for use between line and neutral - which in 1980s practice meant a recognised 250 V AC across-the-line capacitor with a defined failure mode.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.note: Not established from a teardown photograph: that a specific Commodore brick contains an X-rated capacitor, although they are a standard fit in any listed appliance of this era and enthusiasts repairing original bricks commonly replace a RIFA suppression capacitor. The physics of the circuit requires it, but its presence in this specific assembly is inferred rather than documented. On the RIFA point specifically: RIFA was the dominant European supplier of X-rated metallised film capacitors in the 1980s, and parts from that era are now treated as a fire hazard in their own right - decades-old metallised-film suppression capacitors that have been sitting unused can draw leakage current, heat and in the worst cases short, which is why they are replaced on sight rather than tested. The failure was a design weakness, not a manufacturing defect.

facts.label: Voltage class
facts.value: X2 (rated for line-to-neutral) or X1

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: metallised polypropylene or metallised polyester

facts.label: Safety approval
facts.value: VDE, UL and CSA component recognition; the mark is printed on the body

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Film winding and vacuum metallisation
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: The film web is wound on a rotating vacuum-chamber drum while a wire feed head traverses it, laying down an aluminium layer 20-50 nm thick by resistive evaporation. At the same time a nucleation solution is dosed in to promote columnar crystal growth, so the metal grains follow the drum direction and the resulting capacitor has a low-loss, self-healing electrode. The web is slit to width and the capacitor is wound from slits onto a core.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.note: The un-metallised capacitor film is made on a separate line by a similar drum winder with a die and a chill roll; the metallising line normally sits downstream of the film line in the same plant.

facts.label: Evaporation rate
facts.value: ~1-3 nm per second, drum 300-800 mm diameter

facts.label: Slit width
facts.value: 5-30 mm for small parts

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Cast film production
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: Polypropylene is extruded through a flat die onto a chilled cast roll, then stretched and heat-set so it is strong in both directions, then slit into webs 20-60 um wide. A plain film is wound on the same type of machine as the metallised film, so the two steps are usually separate plants.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.note: Not established: the cast-film route for capacitor film - extrusion through a flat die onto a chilled cast roll at 200-250 C, heat-setting, and slitting to 20-60 um webs - or the 20-40 um starting gauge. Polypropylene film is documented as extruded and, for biaxially oriented film, stretched in both directions; capacitor-grade machine-direction-oriented cast film on a chill roll is not documented.

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: machine-direction orientation is typical for capacitor film

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Metallised polypropylene film capacitor
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: A 6-12 um polypropylene film is metallised with vapour-deposited aluminium to form the electrodes, then wound with a polypropylene or paper separator. Because the metallisation is only 20-50 nm thick it self-heals when a dielectric breakdown occurs: the arc evaporates the local metal, the arc is extinguished, and the damaged area is electrically isolated.
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.note: Self-healing metallised film is why these capacitors are chosen for snubber and suppression duty: a transient across the line does not destroy the part.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: polypropylene or polyester, ~6-12 um

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: vapour-deposited aluminium, ~20-50 nm

facts.label: Self-healing
facts.value: clears a dielectric fault by evaporating the electrode around it

c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.name: Polypropylene film
c64.mains.line-capacitor.metallised-film.description: Made by polymerising propylene from a steam cracker in a slurry or gas-phase process; the resulting isotactic polypropylene is extruded into a thin film, biaxially oriented for tear strength, and wound onto a core. It is the normal dielectric for a suppression capacitor because it does not soften or shrink with temperature the way polyester does.

facts.label: Monomer
facts.value: propylene from the steam cracker

facts.label: Cracking conditions
facts.value: propylene from a steam cracker at 800-900 C and 0.5-2 s residence, then purified by selective hydrogenation and distillation

c64.mains.fuses.name: Primary fuse and thermal fuse
c64.mains.fuses.description: Two serial protections on the mains side. The primary fuse is a small cartridge type rated at roughly 120 mA (115 V) or 200 mA (230 V), sized at about 125% of the running input current so the transformer draws its inrush without nuisance failure. The second, documented in the 251053-02, is a thermal fuse in series with one end of the primary: a fusible alloy element that opens irreversibly if the transformer overheats.
c64.mains.fuses.note: The 3 A fuse in the 9 V AC conductor exists so a short on the output cable cannot damage the transformer before the brick is ever plugged into a C64; the 5 A slow fuse in the rectifier conductor is sized for the charging surge of the 4700 uF reservoir capacitor.

facts.label: Primary fuse rating
facts.value: reported 120 mA / 200 mA, depending on build and mains voltage

facts.label: Secondary fuses
facts.value: 3 A in the 9 V AC conductor, 5 A slow-blow in the rectifier conductor of the 902503-02

facts.label: Thermal fuse
facts.value: in series with one end of the primary winding on the 251053-02

c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.name: Thermal fuse
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.description: A one-shot temperature fuse: a fusible alloy link, often a fine wire of a low-melting alloy such as a bismuth-lead-tin-indium eutectic, bonded to the transformer or mounted in thermal contact with it. At its trip temperature - typically 100-130 C - the link melts and opens the circuit permanently. It cannot be reset, which is intentional: the fault that overheated the transformer is not allowed to be repeated.
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.note: The 13-83 teardown explicitly shows a thermal fuse between one end of the primary winding and the other line-in terminal.

facts.label: Trip temperature
facts.value: ~100-130 C typical

facts.label: Fusible alloy
facts.value: a low-melting eutectic, melting at a controlled temperature

facts.label: Fuse alloy
facts.value: often a small helical coil to make the melt more sensitive to a temperature ramp

c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.name: Low-melting fusible alloy
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.description: An eutectic or near-eutectic mixture chosen so that it melts sharply at one temperature. A common mains fuse alloy is 50% tin, 50% lead melting at 180 C; a common thermal-fuse alloy is a bismuth-lead-tin-indium low-melting eutectic below 100 C. The alloy is cast or extruded into a strip or wire in air, then plated to keep it from oxidising.

facts.label: Example
facts.value: 50Sn/50Pb melts at 183 C; Bi-Pb-Sn-In systems melt at 70-120 C

facts.label: Sensitivity
facts.value: a thin section melts at a lower power because its surface-to-volume ratio is high

c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.bismu.name: Bismuth and its ore
c64.mains.fuses.thermal-fuse.alloy.bismu.description: Bismuth is recovered commercially as a by-product of lead and copper refining, from anode slimes and from the residues of the Wohlwill process, and as a minor component of some tin and tungsten ores. Native bismuth and bismuthinite occur too, but refinery by-product is the industrial source.

facts.label: Content
facts.value: typically 0.01-0.1% of refinery residues

c64.mains.fuses.ceramic-wirewound.name: Ceramic wirewound fuse
c64.mains.fuses.ceramic-wirewound.description: A slow-acting fuse for the high inrush of the reservoir capacitor: a length of resistance wire wound on a ceramic bobbin, shunted by a strip of fusible alloy that runs beside it. The strip carries the current normally; the winding heats up when the fuse is overloaded and melts the strip, so the fuse tolerates a brief surge that would blow a straight element.
c64.mains.fuses.ceramic-wirewound.note: The distinction between the two secondary fuses was made by inspection: the fast-acting one is a straight piece of fusible wire while the slow one contains a visible spiral or spring.

facts.label: Element
facts.value: resistance wire in parallel with a fusible alloy strip

facts.label: Characteristic
facts.value: time-delay (slow-blow); identified in the teardown by a small spiral inside the cartridge

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 A 250 V in the rectifier conductor of the 902503-02

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.name: Glass cartridge fuse
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.description: A fuse element of pure tin or a tin alloy, historically a lead-antimony or tin-lead alloy, held between two metal end caps inside a glass tube. The glass is there so a failure is visible: the element melts, an arc forms, the tube fills with metal vapour and the arc is quenched as the pressure collapses, and the tube blackens.

facts.label: Element
facts.value: tin or tin-lead alloy, ~0.1-0.5 mm

facts.label: Voltage rating
facts.value: 250 V for the sizes used here

facts.label: Breaking capacity
facts.value: ~35-100 A for a small cartridge fuse

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Soda-lime tube glass
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: The fuse tube is a drawn borosilicate or soda-lime glass tube, chosen because it is dimensionally stable, easy to seal and does not outgas. Glass tubing is made by melting the batch and drawing the softened gather between rollers, so the wall thickness and diameter stay within a few microns along the length.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 70-74% SiO2, ~13% Na2O, ~10% CaO, with alumina and magnesia

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Glass batch and silica sand
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: The batch is a few hundred kilograms of silica sand, soda ash, limestone and cullet melted in a regenerative furnace at 1400-1500 C. The silica sand, dug from high-silica deposits, is the leaf of the glass chain.

facts.label: Batch
facts.value: ~70% silica sand, ~15% soda ash, ~10% limestone, ~5% cullet

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Regenerative furnace and cowper
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: A glass furnace cannot simply burn gas, because glassmelting needs far more heat than combustion can deliver at that temperature. The answer is regeneration: a Cowper regenerator beside the furnace stores the heat of the exhaust in a refractory mass, then blows the air through it on the next firing. The two 1980s designs were the regenerative box furnace and the unit-regenerator furnace.
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.note: Not established: the Cowper regenerator beside a glass furnace, the 1400-1500 C working temperature, the 600-1000 C preheated air, or the 20-40% waste-heat recovery figure. No encyclopaedic source describes the regenerative box or unit-regenerator glass tank; the general principle that combustion cannot supply enough heat at glass-melting temperature is not itself in doubt, but nothing corroborates the figures.

facts.label: Fuel
facts.value: natural gas or oil, preheated to 600-1000 C by the regenerator

facts.label: Waste-heat recovery
facts.value: ~20-40% of the fuel energy returned to the air blast

c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.name: Refractory lining and checker plates
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.description: The furnace and regenerator are lined with refractory brick, and the regenerator's internal mass is a stack of checker plates of silica or chrome-magnesite. Refractory brick is made by pressing or hand-moulding a graded mineral aggregate with a clay binder and firing it in a tunnel or car kiln; the grading, not the chemistry, is what gives a lining its thermal-shock resistance.
c64.mains.fuses.glass-cartridge.tube-gla.note: Beryllium oxide had even higher conductivity but was withdrawn from general use in the 1980s because of its toxicity.

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: 1400-1500 C for silica brick; 1600-1750 C for magnesia

facts.label: Silica brick
facts.value: ~94-98% SiO2, use limited to about 1500 C

facts.label: Magnesia brick
facts.value: 85-95% MgO, used to ~1700 C

c64.mains.switch.name: Rocker switch
c64.mains.switch.description: A mains switch in the line conductor, mounted in the case wall so the rocker is the only part exposed. It is a snap-action mechanism: a spring-loaded plunger forces a moving contact against a fixed one with a definite wiping motion as it passes through centre, which both makes the circuit and scrapes oxide off the contact faces.
c64.mains.switch.note: Not established for the brick's own switch: its rating, contact alloy, endurance figure, or the snap-action wiping mechanism. The C64's own supply switch is a documented, numbered part - the 1992 service manual parts list gives SW1 as "Rocker Switch DPDT 904500-01" on the connector panel "(Power, ON, OFF) 251095-01", and the circuit theory states that the filtered 5 V rail "is then controlled by on/off switch S1" - but that is the machine's switch, not the brick's, and the double-pole configuration corroborates only the note that the machine's switch interrupts both supplies.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: ~6 A at 250 V AC for a small rocker

facts.label: Contact alloy
facts.value: silver or a silver-nickel brazed contact on a brass carrier

facts.label: Endurance
facts.value: ~10,000 operations typical for a 1980s rocker

c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler.name: Glass-reinforced switch body
c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler.description: Glass fibre is added to the switch body at 20-30% by weight and the compound is compression moulded. The glass reduces creepage and raises the distortion temperature, which is what keeps the moulding from softening near a hot transformer.
