c64.mains.switch.actuator.filler.note: Not established: 20-30% glass content by weight in 3-6 mm strands, or the ~150-200 C distortion temperature. E-glass is documented as an alumino-borosilicate glass with less than 1% alkali oxides used for glass-reinforced plastics, and glass fibre reinforcement of nylon 66 is documented, but no source gives the glass fraction, the strand length or a distortion temperature for a glass-filled phenolic.

facts.label: Glass content
facts.value: 20-30% by weight, chopped 3-6 mm strands

facts.label: Distortion temperature
facts.value: ~150-200 C for a glass-filled phenolic

c64.mains.switch.actuator.name: Rocker actuator and case
c64.mains.switch.actuator.description: The external rocker is moulded in a glass-filled thermoset or a self-extinguishing thermoplastic and clips over a phenolic or nylon body carrying the fixed contacts. The case must be rated for the insulation class and have the flammability rating appropriate to an appliance, and the actuator must not be able to be jammed in the on position.
c64.mains.switch.actuator.note: Not established: the UL 94 V-0 rating, the nylon 66 or phenolic case material, or the ~4 mm creepage between line and neutral terminals. Nylon 66 and glass-reinforced grades of it are documented as injection-moulded and as capable of being made fire retardant, but no source ties those facts to a mains switch actuator or gives the creepage figure.

facts.label: Case material
facts.value: phenolic or nylon 66, UL 94 V-0

facts.label: Creepage
facts.value: ~4 mm between line and neutral terminals, set by the moulding

c64.mains.switch.contacts.name: Silver-alloy contacts and arc erosion
c64.mains.switch.contacts.description: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of any metal and, unlike copper, its oxide is still conductive, so a silver contact keeps working even when it blackens. Contacts are riveted or welded to brass carriers so the spring force is set by the carrier rather than by the contact material. Every make operation evaporates a microscopic amount of metal as an arc; the contact is sized so that tens of thousands of makes erode it only slightly, and so that a failed contact fails open rather than welded shut.
c64.mains.switch.contacts.note: Not established, and partly contradicted: the reason given for preferring silver - that its oxide is still electrically conductive. The conductivity ranking is documented ("The electrical conductivity of silver is the highest of all metals, greater even than copper") and silver's blackening is documented ("silver tarnishes in air to form the black silver sulfide"), but the silver article describes an amphoteric oxide, not a conducting one, so the load-bearing claim is unsupported. Also unestablished: Ag-SnO2 contact practice in 1980s mains switches, the ~1-3 N contact force and the erosion rate.

facts.label: Contact material
facts.value: Ag, Ag-SnO2 or Ag-Ni, on a brass or phosphor-bronze carrier

facts.label: Contact force
facts.value: ~1-3 N, giving a low and stable contact resistance

facts.label: Erosion rate
facts.value: ~0.01-0.1 mm per 10,000 operations in the worst case

c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver.name: Copper and silver ores
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver.description: The moving and fixed blades are brass or phosphor bronze (copper with tin), and the contact faces are silver. Copper comes from sulphide concentrate and silver from argentiferous lead ores or from cyanide leaching of low-grade residues.

facts.label: Phosphor bronze
facts.value: ~90% Cu with 4-10% Sn, the standard spring carrier alloy

c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..name: Silver refining from lead residues
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..description: Argentiferous lead concentrates are roasted and smelted, and the silver reports to the lead bullion, from which it is recovered by Parkes' process: the bullion is cooled so copper crystallises out and is skimmed, then zinc is added, which scavenges the silver and gold into a zinc crust that is skimmed off and distilled. The crude silver is cupelled and electrolytically refined to 99.9% or better.
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..note: Silver for electrical contacts has always been by-product metal, so its price is set by the lead and zinc smelters rather than by silver mines; most of the 1982 supply came from Mexico, Peru and the Soviet bloc.

facts.label: Parkes process
facts.value: zinc added at 1-2% of the bullion mass, crust skimmed at 600-700 C

facts.label: Refining
facts.value: Moebius or Balbach-Thum electrolysis, silver nitrate electrolyte

c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..name: Cupellation
c64.mains.switch.contacts.copper-silver..description: An ancient refining step that survives into the 1980s for precious metals: the metal is melted with a lead oxide flux and blown with air, which oxidises the lead and the base metals to litharge that floats off, while the silver and gold stay as metal. Agricola described it in the 16th century and it is still the standard way to remove base metal from silver dross.

facts.label: Litharge
facts.value: PbO, the oxidised lead, absorbed into the bone ash cupel

c64.psu.name: Commodore 64 external 'brick' power supply
c64.psu.description: A sealed black ABS box roughly 150 x 100 x 60 mm that sits under the C64 and converts wall mains into 5 V DC for the logic plus unfiltered ~9 V AC for the cassette motor, the RF modulator, the VIC-II's CAN +5 V rail, the SID's +12 V doubler and the 50/60 Hz time-of-day clock. It is a linear supply: an iron-core transformer, two rectifier diodes, one 4700 uF electrolytic, one three-terminal 5 V regulator and a folded aluminium heatsink, all buried under a minty-green epoxy pour from 1983 on.
c64.psu.note: Part-number correction: the external supply is ASSY 120407; 250407 is the C64 *motherboard* (the version in this tree's spine file). Regulator silicon changed three times in three years: a discrete 2N3055/2N3792 pass transistor in the earliest 'repairable' silver-label boxes, a plain 7805-class three-pin regulator in the potted 1983-84 units, and a Sanken SI-3052P in the later 902503-02. Diodes are 400GI or 1N5400, not 1N4001, in most builds.

facts.label: Input
facts.value: 117 V 50/60 Hz, 40-46 VA (North American 902503-02 / 251053-02 builds)

facts.label: 5 V DC output
facts.value: 7.5-8.5 W rated (1.5-1.7 A), unregulated 5 V AC rail separate

facts.label: 9 V AC output
facts.value: 6.7-9.0 VA, unfiltered sine, galvanically separate winding

facts.label: Output connector
facts.value: 6-pin round DIN (4-pin on some builds)

facts.label: Approvals seen on case
facts.value: UL 13J5 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER', CSA, NLS, 'SHOCK HAZARD DO NOT OPEN'

facts.label: Made in
facts.value: Singapore (251053-02); transformer marked 'MP' (Miles-Platts, UK)

c64.psu.assembly.name: Brick assembly and final test
c64.psu.assembly.description: The order of operations is visible in the potted builds: the transformer is soldered to by the diodes and fuses at its own pins, the small board is populated, the LED and connector are fitted, the assembly is dropped into the case, epoxy is poured, the halves are screwed together, and the finished unit is then hi-pot tested, earth-continuity tested and burned in on load. Testing after potting is what lets a potted brick be safe and unrepairable at the same time.
c64.psu.assembly.note: Order confirmed in part: the 902503-02 teardown states that "The diodes and fuses are soldered directly to the transformer 'pins'" and that "The rest of the components are mounted on a small printed circuit board (PCB)". Not established: the epoxy potting and close-and-test sequence, because the same teardown states that this part number "is not 'potted' and can be opened and inspected" - potting applies to the later sealed bricks, not to the unit documented here. Also unestablished: the 2-8 h burn-in and the <= 0.1 ohm earth-continuity figure.

facts.label: Order
facts.value: transformer wiring first, then board, then connector, then pot, then close and test

facts.label: Documents required
facts.value: the safety file: schematic, PCB artwork, BOM, transformer winding instruction, insulation system drawing, critical-components list and test instructions

facts.label: Earth continuity
facts.value: <= 0.1 ohm from the cord earth pin to the bonded point; in this all-plastic brick the earth stops at the transformer, so it is a continuity check on one bond

facts.label: Burn-in
facts.value: 2-8 h at rated load, 1.5 A on the 5 V rail plus up to 1 A on the 9 V AC winding, logging case temperature, output voltage and ripple

c64.psu.assembly.approval.name: UL 478 / IEC 65 listing
c64.psu.assembly.approval.description: The brick is certified as a component, not as a consumer appliance: UL 478 'Power Supply Units' in the United States, the equivalent IEC/EN 41003 and IEC 65 (BS 415 in the UK, VDE in West Germany) in Europe, plus CSA in Canada and Singapore's NLS scheme. Getting on the list required submitting the transformer winding instruction and the critical parts list, because those are the two things that cannot be verified by testing a finished unit.
c64.psu.assembly.approval.note: UL 478 was the correct standard in 1982-84; it has since been withdrawn and replaced by UL 62368-1, which moved from a shock-hazard model to a hazard-based energy model. That change is why the old test voltages and limits quoted here no longer appear in current standards.

facts.label: US standard
facts.value: UL 478, Power Supply Units

facts.label: File number seen
facts.value: 13J5, moulded into the case, with 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER'

facts.label: Other marks seen
facts.value: CSA, NLS (Singapore), and on European units VDE

c64.psu.assembly.approval.isolation-cree.name: Isolation, creepage and clearance
c64.psu.assembly.approval.isolation-cree.description: The physical rules that make the layout safe: a primary-to-secondary creepage of about 6.4 mm and clearance of 3.2 mm for a 250 V basic insulation, the earthed foil between the windings, and the bobbin and terminal block designed so that a wire cannot fall across the isolation barrier. Every one of those dimensions is on the drawing and is checked at the follow-up inspection.
c64.psu.assembly.approval.isolation-cree.note: Exact creepage and clearance figures depend on the pollution degree, the insulation type and the applicable standard edition; the values above are the order of magnitude for basic insulation at these voltages, not a substitute for the standard's tables.

facts.label: Pinhole test
facts.value: a 0.5-1.0 mm hole in the earth screen is allowed to be probed without breakdown

c64.psu.assembly.hipot.name: Hi-pot dielectric withstand test
c64.psu.assembly.hipot.description: 1-1.5 kV AC is applied between the primary and the joined secondaries for about one second, with the leakage current monitored and the test set tripping on either a flashover or an excess leakage current. It finds a pinhole in the enamel, a missing layer of insulation paper, or a solder splash bridging the bobbin.

facts.label: Trip current
facts.value: typically 5 mA for a basic-insulation product

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 50/60 Hz, or 0.1-0.5 Hz on modern electronic test sets

c64.psu.nameplate.name: Rating label and moulded markings
c64.psu.nameplate.description: The safety-critical data: input volts and frequency, VA input, 5 V DC watts, 9 V AC VA, the approval marks and the warning text. On the 3-83 build the text is moulded into the case; on the 13-83 it is printed on the underside, duplicated on a top label and given a date on a metallised sticker. Every approval scheme requires this data to be legible without opening the unit.

facts.label: 3-83 build
facts.value: 117 V 50/60 Hz 40 VA in; 5 V DC 7.5 W and 9 V AC 6.7 VA out; UL 13J5; 'FOR USE WITH COMMODORE COMPUTER'

facts.label: 13-83 build
facts.value: 117 V 50/60 Hz 46 W in; 5 V DC 8.5 W and 9 V AC 9 VA out; CSA and NLS marks; 'SHOCK HAZARD DO NOT OPEN' in English and French

c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.name: Metallised polyester label
c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.description: A 25 um metallised polyester film printed with one or two hit spot colours and applied with an acrylic adhesive. Metallised polyester is used because it is tear-resistant, solvent-resistant and survives the polyester solvents in the potting epoxy, unlike paper.
c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.note: Not established: that the rating label on this supply is a 25 um metallised polyester film with a pressure-sensitive acrylic adhesive, that it is printed in one or two spot colours, or that paper was excluded because it does not survive the potting epoxy's solvents. Metallised BOPP and vacuum-deposited aluminium are documented as such, but no source describes a mains rating label.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: 25 um metallised BOPP or polyester

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: acrylic, applied by pressure-sensitive transfer

c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp.name: Metallised BOPP film
c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp.description: Biaxially oriented polypropylene film, stretched in both directions so the molecules line up to give high tensile strength and tear resistance in any direction, then vacuum-metallised with aluminium. The printing inks are solvent-based dyes and pigment pastes that are dried and overlaminated.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 20-40 um before metallisation

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: ~0.1 um of vapour-deposited aluminium

c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp..name: Biaxial orientation
c64.psu.nameplate.metallised-label.bopp..description: A cast polypropylene or cast polyethylene film is stretched in the machine direction, cooled, then stretched again in the transverse direction and heat-set. The two stretching steps line the polymer chains up in both directions, so the film has high tensile strength and tear resistance whatever the pull direction - which is exactly why a torn BOPP label ends in a straight line rather than a ragged one.

facts.label: Stretch ratios
facts.value: ~3-5x machine direction, ~4-10x transverse for a label film

facts.label: Set temperature
facts.value: 110-140 C to freeze the orientation

c64.psu.power-led.name: Power indicator LED
c64.psu.power-led.description: Not present on every brick. Where fitted it is a 3 mm red LED in a small nylon bezel, fed from the 5 V rail through a 330 Ohm to 1 kOhm resistor so that the constant ~7 mA is well inside the LED's safe operating current, and the resistor - not the LED - is what limits the current when the rail is at 5.4 V.
c64.psu.power-led.note: Confirmed only on some replacement bricks; not verified inside an original Commodore brick, and the 251053-02 teardown photo descriptions do not mention one. The 3-83/13-83 case markings list only 'power supply', no indicator, which suggests the indicator is on later units only.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: 3 mm diffused red LED, ~1.6-2.0 V forward drop

facts.label: Series resistor
facts.value: 330 Ohm - 1 kOhm carbon film

c64.psu.connector.name: 6-pin DIN output connector
c64.psu.connector.description: A moulded round DIN socket on the case face carrying the two 5 V conductors, the two 9 V AC conductors and, in the six-pin version, the second 9 V AC leg. Later builds reduced it to four pins. The C64's mainboard has the mating plug, and the two ends of the 5 V pair are deliberately larger-diameter so the plug cannot be inserted backwards.
c64.psu.connector.note: The 902503-02 schematic labels the output as 5 V DC 7.5A; 7.5 W (1.5 A) is the correct figure and the 'A' is a long-standing typo on Commodore's own drawing.

facts.label: Pins
facts.value: 6 on the 120407-era and 251053-02 builds; 4 on some later revisions

facts.label: Assignment (902503-02)
facts.value: pin 2 = 0 V return, pin 5 = +5 V, pins 6 and 7 = the two 9 V AC legs

facts.label: Housing
facts.value: nylon or phenolic shell over brass pins

c64.psu.connector.nylon-shell.name: Connector nylon shell and brass pins
c64.psu.connector.nylon-shell.description: The shell is moulded from a glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF) with a chamfered keyway that defines the pin polarisation; the pins are brass, often nickel-plated for wear, and are a press-fit or riveted into the shell. The 5 V pins are larger so that the plug is keyed by power, not by numbering.
c64.psu.connector.nylon-shell.note: Not established: PA66-GF30 or phenolic at UL 94 V-0, brass pins 0.8-1.0 mm nickel-plated, the chamfered keyway, or the 180 degree circular DIN pitch. The 1992 service manual identifies the machine-side connector as CN7 and gives its pin functions, but the moulded shell, its glass-filled nylon and its keying are not documented in any source consulted.

facts.label: Shell material
facts.value: PA66-GF30 or phenolic, UL 94 V-0

facts.label: Pins
facts.value: brass, 0.8-1.0 mm, nickel-plated

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: circular DIN, 180 degrees between pins

c64.psu.case.name: Black ABS enclosure
c64.psu.case.description: A two-half injection-moulded case in black ABS, ~150 x 100 x 60 mm, with a tongue-and-groove seam, ribbing on the sides for stiffness, four case screws and one larger screw holding the cable clamp. On the potted builds the seam is a line of epoxy. Some units have the rating text moulded into the plastic; others have it printed on the underside and on a metallised label.
c64.psu.case.note: ABS is used because it is tough, chemically inert to the epoxy and the PVC of the cord, and injection moulds to a good surface for the moulded-in lettering. It burns readily - which is why the flammability rating and the 94-HB test are part of the approval, not decoration.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene), natural or black

facts.label: Flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB is the normal requirement for a PSU enclosure; V-2 or V-0 is required if it is a subassembly of a listed appliance

facts.label: Markings
facts.value: moulded into the casing on the 3-83 build; printed on the underside with a metalised date sticker on the 13-83

facts.label: UL 94 HB
facts.value: burning rate <= 1 mm/s over the first 100 mm on a 125 x 13 x 13 mm bar conditioned 48 h at 23 C / 50% RH

facts.label: UL 94 V-0
facts.value: flame out within 10 s and no glowing after 30 s, no drips

c64.psu.case.screws.name: Case screws
c64.psu.case.screws.description: Cross-recessed pan-head self-tapping screws into moulded bosses in the plastic, and in a mains appliance they must be short enough that they cannot reach the primary wiring - a specific check in the safety audit.
c64.psu.case.screws.note: Not established: the 3.5 x 10 mm pan-head cross-recess zinc-plated fastener, or the specific safety rule that no screw may be long enough to reach a live part. Screw geometry and plating are common practice but no source consulted states either the size or the rule for this case.

facts.label: Fastener
facts.value: 3.5 x 10 mm pan-head cross recess, zinc-plated steel

facts.label: Safety rule
facts.value: no screw long enough to contact a live part

c64.psu.potting.name: Epoxy potting pour
c64.psu.potting.description: From mid-1983 Commodore filled the case with a two-part epoxy so the whole assembly became one solid block: transformer, board, fuses, leads, the lot, in a minty-green or cool-grey mass. It made the unit tamper-proof and un-serviceable, and it turned out to be the primary cause of failure because the heat of the linear regulator could no longer escape.
c64.psu.potting.note: The epoxy is also an insulator thermally as well as electrically: it fills the natural convection paths around the heatsink and the transformer, so internal temperatures run 20-40 C above what the same parts see in an open case.

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: minty green (3-83) or cool grey (13-83), both indicating different epoxy batches

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: the case is filled to within a few mm of the lid, leaving only the connector, cord and switch exposed

facts.label: Repairability
facts.value: effectively zero - extraction breaks the PCB and the transformer terminals

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: DGEBA (bisphenol A diglycidyl ether), epoxide value 0.52-0.57 mol/100 g

facts.label: Hardener
facts.value: triethylene tetramine (DETA) or an anhydride

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 24 h at 25 C or 2-4 h at 80 C

facts.label: Thermal conductivity
facts.value: 0.2-0.4 W/m.K unfilled; 1-3 W/m.K silica-filled

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: DGEBA (bisphenol A diglycidyl ether, epoxide value 0.52-0.57 mol/100 g) with triethylene tetramine or an anhydride hardener; 24 h at 25 C or 2-4 h at 80 C

c64.psu.board.name: Small regulator PCB, 'PNE-5'
c64.psu.board.description: A single-sided glass-epoxy board about 40 x 30 mm carrying the regulator, the two electrolytics, the tantalum and two resistors, with the identification 'PNE-5' etched into the copper on the earlier build and no marking at all on the later one. It is held in place only by the epoxy that floods the whole case, which is why de-potting usually breaks it.

facts.label: Marking
facts.value: 'PNE-5' etched into the copper on the 3-83 build; unmarked on the 13-83

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: FR-4 glass-epoxy, ~1.6 mm, single sided

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: single-sided, no plated-through holes, tracks and pads in 35 um copper

facts.label: Substrate detail
facts.value: FR-4 glass-epoxy, Tg ~135-150 C at the usual ~18-20% resin loading, UL 94 V-0; prepreg and foil pressed at 160-200 C and 1-3 MPa for 30-60 min

c64.psu.aux-caps.name: Tantalum and small electrolytic capacitors
c64.psu.aux-caps.description: Secondary filtering: a 0.22 uF 35 V tantalum and a 47 uF 10 V electrolytic on the 5 V output for stability and for the load transients the VIC-II produces when it banks memory. The tantalum is polar and fails short, so it is the more dramatic failure of the pair.

facts.label: Tantalum
facts.value: 0.22 uF / 35 V, epoxy-dipped bead or drop

facts.label: Electrolytic
facts.value: 47 uF / 10 V radial

facts.label: Resistors
facts.value: 100 Ohm and 22 Ohm carbon-film, embedded in the epoxy pour

c64.psu.bulk-cap.name: 4700 uF 16 V aluminium electrolytic
c64.psu.bulk-cap.description: The single reservoir capacitor on the rectifier output. It is the part that has killed the most C64s: as the electrolyte dries out the ripple current is no longer smoothed, the series regulator loses headroom and starts pumping 100/120 Hz ripple onto the 5 V rail, and eventually the cap leaks current into the regulator's ground reference and pushes the output up past 5.5 V. Replacements are still sold as the C64 'fix' four decades later.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.note: Two capacitors in parallel have lower ESR than either alone, which is why both the replacement-PSU literature and the datasheets push for two. Failure is not dramatic: capacitance drifts down, ESR climbs, ripple appears, and eventually the leakage current rises far enough to upset the regulator.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: 4700 uF / 16 V radial (2200 uF in some builds; 2200 uF / 16 V on the C64 mainboard itself)

facts.label: Lifetime
facts.value: rated 2000 h at 85 C; real service life 10-20 years at 40 C ambient

c64.psu.bulk-cap.winding.name: Winding and impregnating the cell
c64.psu.bulk-cap.winding.description: The anode foil (etched) and the cathode (bare aluminium foil, or the can itself in later types) are separated by the separator and wound on a mandrel into a compact roll, the leads are brought out, and the roll is impregnated under vacuum at 1-10 mbar with the electrolyte so the pores fill completely. Air left in the roll is the single biggest cause of high ESR. The can is then closed with a rubber bung pressed against the leads and a silicone or bitumen fill, and the leads are rolled down to set the dimensions.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.winding.note: Modern high-CV parts use a laser-drilled solid can as the cathode, eliminating the cathode foil and reducing ESR and inductance further.

facts.label: Vacuum impregnation
facts.value: ~1-10 mbar before electrolyte is admitted

facts.label: Squeeze
facts.value: rolled to expel electrolyte and set the dimensions

facts.label: Can seal
facts.value: rubber bung pressed against the leads, then a silicone or bitumen fill

c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.name: Cell separator
c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.description: A porous dielectric sheet between the anode and the cathode foil, keeping them apart without shorting. Low-voltage parts in 1980-82 used cellulose (paper) separators, which is the direct cause of the decades-later failure: paper is hygroscopic and absorbs electrolyte, and the carbonisation of that paper when leakage current rises shorts the cell.

facts.label: 1980-82 default
facts.value: cellulose kraft separator

facts.label: Later default
facts.value: polypropylene or polyethylene, and aluminium oxide-filled separators

c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.cellulose.name: Cellulose paper separator
c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.cellulose.description: A thin kraft paper sheet made on a Fourdrinier or twin-wire machine from long-fibre softwood pulp cooked at 160-180 C in sodium hydroxide; the lignin is washed out into a black liquor that is burned for process heat, roughly 1.2-1.5 t per tonne of pulp, and the pulp is bleached with chlorine or hypochlorite before an acid wash. The paper absorbs electrolyte and swells, and on ageing it chars and shorts.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.cellulose.note: Not established: the 160-180 C sodium-hydroxide cook, the 2-6 h cycle, the 1.2-1.5 t of black liquor per tonne of pulp, the chlorine or hypochlorite bleach and acid wash, and the 10-20 um sheet gauge. Kraft pulp being stronger than other pulps, darker, and bleachable, and sack kraft being made from softwood with high tear resistance, are documented; the capacitor-grade electrical paper specification and its manufacture are not.

facts.label: Cooking
facts.value: 160-180 C in sodium hydroxide, 2-6 h

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: ~1.2-1.5 t black liquor per tonne of pulp, burned for process heat

facts.label: Bleaching
facts.value: chlorine or hypochlorite, then acid wash

facts.label: Sheet thickness
facts.value: 10-20 um kraft

c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.polypropylene.name: Polypropylene separator
c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.polypropylene.description: A microporous isotactic polypropylene film, 12-25 um thick and about 35-45% porous, made by extruding a film and stretching it or by solvent extraction so that the electrolyte fills the voids while the sheet still keeps the electrodes apart. It replaced paper because it absorbs no electrolyte and, when it overheats, softens instead of carbonising into a conductive bridge.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.separator.polypropylene.note: Not established: the 12-25 um microporous isotactic polypropylene separator, the 35-45% porosity, and the stretch or solvent-extraction routes. The available source on aluminium electrolytics describes a paper spacer and does not mention a polypropylene separator; the claim that it replaced paper in service is likewise undocumented.

facts.label: Making the porous film
facts.value: extruded and stretched, or solvent-extracted; the monomer is propylene from a steam cracker at 800-900 C and 0.5-2 s residence

c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte.name: Electrolytic electrolyte
c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte.description: An aqueous solution of an ammonium or amine salt - ammonium pentaborate was the classic low-voltage recipe - that forms the counter-electrode ion layer against the oxide. In an aluminium electrolytic the cathode reaction deposits a hydrated aluminium oxide or tin layer from the metal ion, and the leakage current is exactly that reaction rate.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.electrolyte.note: Partly contradicted. The documented low-voltage electrolyte systems are glycol/borax - "Electrolytes based on ethylene glycol and boric acid" - plus almost-anhydrous organic solvents (DMF, DMA, gamma-butyrolactone) and water-rich low-ESR systems; ammonium pentaborate as "the classic low-voltage recipe" is not among them, and the pH 4.5-7.0 range and the I = kCV leakage relation are not stated. What is documented is that the electrolyte supplies oxygen for self-healing, that service life is limited by electrolyte loss, and that organic-solvent systems give low leakage and long life.

facts.label: Typical system
facts.value: ammonium pentaborate / ammonium chloride, or an amine salt

facts.label: Leakage current
facts.value: I = kC V, roughly 2x the CV product rated current at 25 C

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.name: Aluminium anode foil
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.description: The anode is a 12-20 um aluminium foil that has been chemically etched in a hot chlorate or permanganate bath to roughen the surface into a high-area sponge. Because capacitance is proportional to real surface area, the etch multiplies the effective area by 30-100x and is the entire reason a 4700 uF part fits in a 25 mm can. The foil gauge, the rolling lubricant and the last work-hardening pass matter as much as the etch: at 12 um the metal is barely thicker than the oxide skin on it, so a single pinhole becomes a short. The stock foil and its rolling chain are the shared metal.aluminum.foil line, from the rolling ingot down to the slitter.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.note: Mechanism documented, figures conflict. The 12-20 um anode gauge and the 30-100x surface gain are not corroborated and are contradicted by the best available source, which gives the anode foil as "~ 20-100 um made of aluminum with a high purity of at least 99.99%" and states that "the surface area can be increased by a factor of approximately 200 with respect to a smooth surface". The 0.5-2 um pore size, the NaClO3/HCl or KMnO4 etch at 70-80 C, the kerosene/paraffin lubricant and the 80-140 MPa tensile strength are not established.

facts.label: Foil thickness
facts.value: 12-20 um for the anode; 6-9 um for the cathode

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: NaClO3/HCl or KMnO4 at 70-80 C for 10-60 min

facts.label: Surface gain
facts.value: 30-100x the geometrical area; pore size 0.5-2 um

facts.label: Route
facts.value: ingot -> hot roll 6 mm -> cold roll -> 12-20 um

facts.label: Lubricant
facts.value: kerosene or paraffin for the final pass

facts.label: Tensile strength at 12 um
facts.value: ~80-140 MPa, work-hardened

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.formation.name: Electrolytic formation of the anode oxide
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.formation.description: The wound wet cell is energised from a DC source at a voltage ramped up to the rated working voltage. At the anode the aluminium oxidises to a dense amorphous alumina film only a few nanometres thick - the dielectric. Raising the voltage thickens the film; raising the temperature thickens it faster but also lets it dissolve, which is why forming is done hot and forming voltage is always lower than the operating voltage.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.formation.note: Mechanism documented, figures conflict. Documented: dielectric thickness is proportional to forming voltage, and "due to standardized safety margins the actual forming voltage of electrolytic capacitors is higher than the rated voltage of the component"; amorphous oxide has "a dielectric ratio of ~ 1.4 nm/V". That gives roughly 14 nm at a 10 V rating, not the 2-5 nm claimed here at 16 V. Not established: the 1.1-1.3x ramp, the 1-4 h ramp time, the 80-95 C formation temperature and the ~8-10 dielectric constant.

facts.label: Forming voltage
facts.value: ~1.1-1.3x the rated voltage, ramped over 1-4 h

facts.label: Film thickness
facts.value: 2-5 nm of amorphous Al2O3 at 16 V rating

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~8-10 for amorphous alumina

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.name: Chemical etching of the anode foil
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.description: The foil is threaded continuously through an etch tank at 70-80 C. Sodium chlorate with hydrochloric acid, or potassium permanganate, dissolves aluminium faster where the surface is already rough, so the etch runs away into a deep microscopic pore structure rather than eating away uniformly. The etched foil is rinsed, dried and cut to length.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.note: Not established: sodium chlorate with hydrochloric acid or potassium permanganate as the etchant, the 70-80 C tank temperature, the 10-60 min dwell, and the runaway-into-pore-structure mechanism. What is documented is generic: the anode is "etched (roughened) in an electrochemical process to increase the effective electrode surface". The specific etch chemistry and its process conditions have no source here.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: NaClO3 + HCl, or KMnO4 in an alkaline bath

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 10-60 min depending on the required pore depth

c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.perman.name: Potassium permanganate etchant
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.perman.description: An alkaline potassium permanganate bath oxidises the aluminium surface; the loose MnO2 sludge is removed by brushing or a nitric acid dip. The alternative chlorate chemistry was being phased out for safety and environmental reasons through the 1980s because chlorate/dioxide is toxic.
c64.psu.bulk-cap.alu-foil.etching.perman.note: Not established: that an alkaline potassium permanganate bath at ~2-6% plus NaOH was used to etch capacitor foil, that the loose MnO2 sludge is brushed off or nitric-acid dipped, and that the chlorate route was being phased out through the 1980s. Potassium permanganate is documented as a strong oxidising agent and sodium chlorate's main commercial use as chlorine dioxide feed, but neither article mentions aluminium foil etching for capacitors.

facts.label: Concentration
facts.value: ~2-6% KMnO4 plus NaOH

c64.psu.heatsink.name: Folded aluminium heatsink
c64.psu.heatsink.description: A thin aluminium plate folded into a U so that one leg clamps under the case and the other presents an area against the regulator. There are no fins: the design relies on the natural convection of a brick sitting under a desk. It is the reason the case runs at 60-70 C and the epoxy never fully cools. The sheet is commercial-purity aluminium folded on a press brake and tapped for the regulator screw, usually left mill finish or painted, occasionally black anodised.
c64.psu.heatsink.note: Modern practice would use an extruded finned profile in 6063 aluminium; a folded sheet U gives only 0.02-0.04 m2 of surface, an order of magnitude less than the fins a switching supply would use for the same power.

facts.label: Geometry
facts.value: flat sheet folded into a U, ~1-2 mm thick, no fins

facts.label: Dissipation
facts.value: 3-8 W at a 35-45 C rise above ambient

facts.label: Surface finish
facts.value: mill finish, painted, or black anodised (sulphuric acid bath at 20 C, 1-2 V at 0.5-1 A/dm2, 5-25 um film sealed in boiling water); on a folded sheet with no fins the emissivity gain is marginal

facts.label: Stock
facts.value: commercial-purity aluminium sheet, 1050 or 3003 and 99.0-99.7% Al, off a rolling ingot from a Hall-Heroult pot running at 950-970 C in molten cryolite on roughly 13,000-15,000 kWh per tonne

c64.psu.heatsink.forming.name: Sheet folding and tapping
c64.psu.heatsink.forming.description: Strip or sheet is blanked, then folded on a press brake to a U; the mounting hole is punched or drilled and tapped with a thread-forming tap. Aluminium's low modulus means the fold must be given a generous inside radius or the sheet tears, and the tapped hole must be at least 1.5 diameters from the bend.
c64.psu.heatsink.forming.note: Not established: the >= 1.5 t inside bend radius, the 1.5-diameter minimum distance from bend to tapped hole, and the M3/M4 roll-tapped thread. No encyclopaedic source covers press-brake bend-radius or thread-forming-tap practice; the general statements about aluminium's low modulus are common engineering knowledge but are not cited here.

facts.label: Fold radius
facts.value: >=1.5 t inside radius

facts.label: Thread
facts.value: M3 or M4 roll-tapped (form tap) to avoid chipping the threads

c64.psu.regulator.name: 5 V linear voltage regulator
c64.psu.regulator.description: The pass element that turns roughly 8-10 V of pulsating DC into 5.00 V. Three different implementations appear in C64 bricks inside two years, and the choice of which one determines how much heat has to be removed. At full load the drop across the pass device is 3-5 V at 1.5 A, so 4.5-7.5 W has to go into the heatsink - which is why these supplies run hot and why the electrolytics above them cook.
c64.psu.regulator.note: The failure mode that destroyed C64s is the pass device shorting the input to the output, putting ~8-10 V on a rail designed for 5 V. Unloaded 5.3 V is normal; 5.4 V is the number to worry about; below 4.6 V the machine will not boot.

facts.label: Dissipation
facts.value: ~3 W at 8 V in / 1 A out; ~8 W at 10.4 V in / 1.4 A out

facts.label: Efficiency
facts.value: ~40-50% for the whole brick, dominated by the series pass

c64.psu.regulator.mounting.name: Bolting the regulator to the heatsink
c64.psu.regulator.mounting.description: The regulator tab or TO-3 can is bolted to the folded aluminium plate with a thin layer of thermal compound - in 1982 typically a zinc-oxide paste in a silicone or hydrocarbon base, or sometimes simply a piece of thin copper foil. The thermal interface matters more than the compound brand: dry metal-to-metal contact is roughly ten times worse than a properly filled joint.
c64.psu.regulator.mounting.note: The 251053-02 teardown shows the heatsink as a 'featureless aluminium plate bent into a U-shape' with a drilled and tapped hole for the regulator screw; a drill bit slipped into the soft aluminium and had to be drilled out from several angles, which is a good illustration of how thin and soft the sink actually is.

facts.label: Torque
facts.value: ~0.3-0.5 Nm on an M3 screw for a TO-3; overtightening cracks the can

facts.label: Interface
facts.value: 0.05-0.1 mm thermal grease, or a thin copper shim

facts.label: Isolator
facts.value: mica or silicone-rubber washer under a TO-3 collector tab

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.name: Discrete 2N3055 / 2N3792 series-pass regulator
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.description: The earliest 'repairable' silver-label brick used a discrete design: an NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can bolted to a heatsink as the series pass, a smaller driver transistor, a zener or low-current regulator as the reference, wirewound resistors in the emitter and base for current limiting, and a thermal shutdown in contact with the heatsink. It is the arrangement the 902503-02's monolithic regulator replaced.
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.note: No verified transcription of the 120407 discrete-regulator schematic is available (lemon64's forum is behind a bot challenge). The topology and part families described here are the standard 1982 discrete 5 V linear supply of this size; the exact part numbers are unconfirmed for this specific assembly.

facts.label: Pass transistor
facts.value: 2N3055 (15 A / 60 V, TO-3) or 2N3792 (1.5 A class NPN, TO-3)

facts.label: Vbe multiplier error amp
facts.value: two-transistor error amplifier sensing the output through a divider

facts.label: Emitter ballast
facts.value: wirewound resistor to force a minimum standing current and to limit current sharing

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.therm.name: Thermal shutdown
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.therm.description: A temperature-sensitive element in contact with the heatsink - a thermistor or a bimetallic thermal switch - that shorts or removes the driver bias when the sink passes roughly 90-110 C, so the supply folds back rather than destroying itself. Commodore's bricks more often relied on a thermal fuse in the primary and on the epoxy pot for heat retention, which is the root of their reputation.
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.therm.note: The 251053-02 teardowns document a thermal fuse in series with the primary winding, but no thermal shutdown switch inside the regulator board is documented.

facts.label: Trip temperature
facts.value: ~95-110 C typical for a thermal switch

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: bimetal opens a contact, or an SCR crowbar latches a short

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.therm.name: NTC thermistor
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.therm.description: A bead or disc of semiconducting metal oxide whose resistance falls steeply with temperature (10 kOhm at 25 C, ~1 kOhm at 100 C for the standard 10K curve). Glued or bolted to the heatsink and shunting the driver bias, it gives a soft, non-resetting protection that must cool before it re-conducts.

facts.label: Resistance
facts.value: 10 kOhm at 25 C, B = 3435 K curve

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ferric oxide or manganese oxide semiconducting ceramic

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.emitt.name: Emitter ballast resistors
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.emitt.description: One to three wirewound resistors in series with the pass transistor's emitter. Their purpose is to develop a signal proportional to output current for current limiting and to force a standing current through the pass transistor so its hFE and therefore the loop gain do not collapse at light load. Wirewound rather than film because the dissipation is fractional watts but the temperature rise has to stay small.
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.emitt.note: Ballast resistors were largely abandoned in integrated regulators because the current-limit loop senses the emitter directly through a pin.

facts.label: Values
facts.value: 0.1-1 Ohm, 1-3 W wirewound, manganin or constantan

facts.label: Temperature coefficient
facts.value: chosen near zero for manganin, positive for constantan

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.emitt.name: Manganin wire
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.emitt.description: A copper-manganese-nickel alloy (typically 86% Cu, 12% Mn, 2% Ni) whose resistivity barely changes with temperature. A spiral-wound wirewound resistor is made by winding manganin or constantan wire onto a ceramic or plastic former and baking it under high tension so the winding stress-relaxes and stays against the form.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: ~86 Cu / 12 Mn / 2 Ni (manganin) or ~60 Cu / 40 Ni (constantan)

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: <10 ppm/K for manganin

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.refer.name: Voltage reference
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.refer.description: In a 1982 discrete supply the reference is either a 5.1-6.2 V zener diode biased from a constant-current source, or a low-current three-terminal regulator such as a TL431 or a small 7805 in a TO-92 used purely as a reference. The zener route needs a stable bias current; the temperature coefficient of an ordinary zener is poor, which shows up as output drift with case temperature.
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.refer.note: Modern practice is a bandgap reference inside the regulator IC, giving ±0.5% over temperature; the zener plus Vbe-multiplier arrangement of 1982 gave ±3-5% and drifted with case temperature.

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: ~0.1%/C for an uncompensated zener vs ~0.005%/C for a bandgap reference

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.drive.name: Driver / error-amplifier transistor
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.drive.description: A small-signal NPN whose job is to supply the ~0.7 V of base drive plus the feedback signal the pass transistor needs. In a 1982 discrete supply this is typically a TO-92 part with hFE around 100-400, or one half of a matched pair. Its collector dissipation is small but its junction temperature is close to the pass transistor's, so it shares the same heatsink metal.
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.drive.note: The C64 mainboard itself uses 2N3904 and 2N4401 in TO-92 packages for its audio and cassette motor drives (Q1-Q8 in the 326298 parts list), so the same parts bins would have supplied the brick.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: TO-92 small-signal NPN, e.g. 2N3904 / BC547 class

facts.label: Base drive
facts.value: ~0.6-0.8 V above the pass emitter, set by the Vbe multiplier

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.name: 2N3055 / 2N3792 power NPN
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.description: A triple-diffused planar NPN power transistor in a TO-3 can: a bolted metal header with an isolation disc, the die brazed or soldered to the header, one or two emitter bonds, and a hermetic can with a glass-sealed pin feedthrough. The 2N3055 is grossly oversized for a 1.5 A load (15 A, 60 V, 115 W dissipation capability), which is exactly why it was chosen: it could not fail thermally even when the circuit was badly designed.
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.note: Modern practice for a 1.5 A rail is an 8-20 A TO-220 or a DPAK/LDO with an active current limit; the 2N3055 in a TO-3 is expensive and a thermal mismatch, but it was the safest thing an engineer could buy off the shelf in 1982.

facts.label: 2N3055
facts.value: NPN, 15 A Ic, 60 V Vceo, Pc 115 W with a good heat sink

facts.label: 2N3792
facts.value: NPN power transistor, roughly 1.5 A / 60 V class, TO-3

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: triple-diffused planar (collector-base, base-emitter, collector-emitter diffusions)

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-3 can, 40-60 g of nickel-plated copper, mica or thin mica-fibre washer under the can

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.name: Emitter wire bonds
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.description: Two to four 100-200 um aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the emitter metallisation to the emitter lead to carry the full emitter current; the collector current flows through the die's back contact straight into the header. Ultrasonic wedge bonding at 50-250 g per wire was the universal method - ball bonding was for fine-pitch.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 100-200 um aluminium, 99.99% Al + small Mg

facts.label: Force
facts.value: 50-250 g ultrasonic

facts.label: Bonds
facts.value: 2-4 in parallel on the emitter for a 15 A device

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.name: Die attach and hermetic TO-3 sealing
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.description: The die is brazed to the header in a hydrogen atmosphere at 700-800 C with an active-metal braze, or soldered with a 50Pb-50Sn or AuSn preform at 220-300 C; the header is then nickel-plated. The can is crimped or cold-welded onto the header with an annular glass or ceramic feedthrough insulator; mica or a thin mica-fibre washer goes between the can and the heatsink to isolate the collector while conducting heat.

facts.label: Brazing
facts.value: Ni-B or Au-Ag, 700-800 C, dry H2

facts.label: Feedthrough
facts.value: glass ring or BeO disc, 20-30 um seal gap

facts.label: Can
facts.value: nickel-plated low-carbon steel, cold-welded (soft solder) or crimped (hard solder)

c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.name: Triple-diffused planar process
c64.psu.regulator.variant-discrete.pass-.description: Three sequential dopings - collector-base, base-emitter, and a deep collector-emitter - through a photolithographically masked oxide. The heavy collector-emitter diffusion carries the load current while the shallow, tightly controlled base-emitter diffusion sets the gain and the breakdown voltage. This is the process that made 15 A transistors possible at all.

facts.label: Diffusions
facts.value: collector-base, base-emitter, collector-emitter (P, B, B, P)

facts.label: Base-emitter depth
facts.value: ~1-2 um; collector-emitter ~20-40 um

facts.label: Die
facts.value: typically 100 x 100 mm wafer, diced into 6 x 6 mm TO-3 dice

c64.psu.regulator.variant-si3052p.name: Sanken SI-3052P integrated regulator
c64.psu.regulator.variant-si3052p.description: The regulator in the later 902503-02, which many hobbyists misidentify as a transistor because it is moulded in a TO-3P-looking package. It is a 5 V / 2 A linear regulator with an internal error amplifier and a foldback current limit that kicks in at about 2.4 A. The datasheet explicitly warns that the output must not be raised by inserting a resistor in the ground pin - and Commodore inserted a 300 Ohm resistor in the ground pin anyway, to make up for the drop in the output cable.
c64.psu.regulator.variant-si3052p.note: The ground-lift trick raises the output a few tens of millivolts to compensate for the resistive drop of a metre of thin output wire, but it also corrupts the regulator's ground reference and interferes with its current-limit behaviour - the datasheet says so in Note 3. Modifying this circuit is the standard modern replacement and is well documented.

facts.label: Maker
facts.value: Sanken Electric (the 'SK' in the part number is Sanken's logo)

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 V fixed, 2 A

facts.label: Current limit
facts.value: ~2.4 A foldback

facts.label: Ground-lift resistor
facts.value: 300 Ohm nominal (some builds 30 Ohm) from the regulator ground pin to the output return

c64.psu.regulator.variant-si3052p.stabil.name: Output stability capacitor
c64.psu.regulator.variant-si3052p.stabil.description: A small electrolytic or tantalum directly across the regulator's input and output pins. The datasheet requires it for loop stability; a 2.2 uF 16 V tantalum appears on some 902503-02 builds and the 3-83 version has the holes for it but does not populate it, which suggests it was a late cost change.

facts.label: Value
facts.value: 2.2 uF 16 V tantalum (populated on some builds, holes only on others)

c64.psu.regulator.variant-7805.name: 7805-class three-pin regulator
c64.psu.regulator.variant-7805.description: The simplest form: a monolithic regulator containing the reference, error amplifier, current limit and the pass transistor, in a TO-220 or TO-3P-like plastic body with a tab bolted to the heatsink. In the 251053-02 brick it is a three-legged part with rectangular legs, screwed straight into the folded aluminium plate under a blob of epoxy.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 5 V, 1.5 A continuous for a 7805 in a TO-220 with a small copper tab

facts.label: Current limit
facts.value: internally ~2.2 A thermal-limited foldback

facts.label: Mounting
facts.value: single bolt through the tab into the heatsink plate

c64.psu.rectifier.name: Rectifier diodes, 400GI / 1N5400
c64.psu.rectifier.description: Two or four stud-less axial rectifier diodes convert the 18 V centre-tapped secondary into pulsating DC. The 902503-02 uses two General Electric 400GI silicon rectifiers in a full-wave centre-tapped configuration, which saves the two extra dice of a bridge; other builds use four 1N5400s or a moulded bridge. The diodes are soldered directly onto the transformer pins.
c64.psu.rectifier.note: The 400GI is a slow-recovery rectifier with a large forward drop for its rating; hobbyists have observed it running well outside its current specification, and it is a recurring failure item. The correct part for the job is a 1N5400.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: GE 400GI (as marked on the 902503-02) or 1N5400, 3 A class

facts.label: Configuration
facts.value: full-wave centre-tapped (2 diodes) on the 902503-02; some builds use a 4-diode bridge

facts.label: Vf at 1 A
facts.value: ~0.9-1.1 V for a 1N5400; the 400GI is noticeably slower and hotter

c64.psu.rectifier.diode.name: Axial rectifier diode
c64.psu.rectifier.diode.description: A single silicon junction in an axial package with a formed lead, cathode band marked with a stripe. Inside: a die a few hundred microns across with a heavy anode metallisation, a glass passivation, and epoxy or a voidless glass body filled with silicone stress-relief gel to survive the power cycling.
c64.psu.rectifier.diode.note: Not established: the 1N5400's ratings as quoted (100 V reverse, 3 A average at 75 C lead temperature), the DO-201AD epoxy-filled axial body, and the practice of marking the cathode with a stripe for the parts used in this supply. The 902503-02 teardown records only that the rectifier diodes "should be marked 1N5400"; no datasheet-level source was consulted.

facts.label: Vceo / Vrrm
facts.value: 50-100 V reverse for a 400GI; 100 V for 1N5400

facts.label: If (av)
facts.value: 3 A at 75 C lead temperature for a 1N5400

facts.label: Body
facts.value: epoxy-filled axial (DO-201AD) or glass-butt

c64.psu.rectifier.bridge-alternative.name: Moulded bridge rectifier alternative
c64.psu.rectifier.bridge-alternative.description: Some builds and most replacement supplies use a packaged bridge: four dice mounted on a common ceramic or moulded body with the terminals formed into the four corners. Commodore's own choice of two discrete diodes over a bridge saved two dice and one package, at the cost of a centre tap on the transformer.

facts.label: Bridge
facts.value: e.g. Varo VMO8, listed in the C64 service manual parts list as CR4 with Commodore stock number 906129-01

c64.psu.rectifier.diode.die.name: Silicon rectifier die
c64.psu.rectifier.diode.die.description: A 100-150 mm wafer ground to a die typically 2 x 2 x 0.3 mm, with a diffused N-type cathode and metallised anode. The same Czochralski silicon as the VIC-II and the 6510; the detailed wafer process belongs to the silicon branch of this tree.

facts.label: Junction depth
facts.value: ~20-40 um phosphorus diffusion

facts.label: Die
facts.value: ~2 x 2 mm after dicing

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO at 1800-2000 C, 97-99% metallurgical grade

facts.label: Upgraded grade
facts.value: 9-11N (99.9999999%) before the single crystal is pulled

facts.label: Feedstock
facts.value: high-purity quartz lump and petroleum coke

c64.psu.rectifier.diode.packaging.name: Die attach, wire bond and axial encapsulation
c64.psu.rectifier.diode.packaging.description: The die is die-attached to the anode lead with silver-loaded glass or a soft solder, one or two aluminium wires are wedge-bonded from the cathode metallisation to the cathode lead, then the whole assembly is transfer-moulded or cast in an epoxy body filled with silicone gel to relieve the thermal cycle between the glass and the leads.
c64.psu.rectifier.diode.packaging.note: Not established: silver-glass die attach at 430 C, the 80Au/20Sn reflow, the 50-150 um aluminium wedge bond, and epoxy or glass-preform encapsulation at 150-175 C for an axial rectifier. Wire bonding and epoxy as technologies are documented, but the specific attach, wire and moulding conditions for an axial diode have no source here.

facts.label: Die attach
facts.value: silver-glass die attach at 430 C, or 80Au/20Sn solder reflow at 220 C

facts.label: Wire bond
facts.value: aluminium, 50-150 um diameter, ultrasonic wedge bond, 50-250 g

facts.label: Encapsulant
facts.value: epoxy or glass preform moulded at 150-175 C

c64.psu.transformer.name: Mains transformer, 40-46 VA
c64.psu.transformer.description: The whole of the supply's energy conversion. One primary on 117 V mains, a centre-tapped ~18 V secondary feeding the 5 V regulator, and a separate ~9 V winding feeding straight out to the C64. The two secondaries are galvanically isolated from each other as well as from the primary - that isolation is what lets the C64 tie their grounds together only at the rectifier. Every wound transformer is proved before it is potted or assembled: a 1500-2500 V AC dielectric withstand between primary and all secondaries, an insulation-resistance check at 500 V DC, a turns-ratio and phasing check between the taps, and a loaded run at nominal line voltage.
c64.psu.transformer.note: The 'MP' mark on the core is most likely Miles-Platts (founded 1971, a UK bobbin and insulation specialist whose own company history lists inch-lamination and metric-lamination bobbins), i.e. the coil former and interwinding materials rather than necessarily the whole assembly.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 40 VA (3-83 build) / 46 W (13-83 build) input at 117 V 60 Hz

facts.label: 9 V winding
facts.value: 9 V AC 9.0 VA, protected by a 3 A fuse in the conductor

facts.label: HV winding
facts.value: 18 V AC centre-tapped, pins 6/7/8 on 902503-02, protected by a 5 A (slow) fuse

facts.label: Maker's mark
facts.value: MP (Miles-Platts, Leicester, UK - bobbins and insulation systems)

facts.label: Dielectric withstand before potting
facts.value: 1500-2500 V AC for 1 s between primary and all secondaries, per UL 478 / IEC 65 practice for unlisted components

facts.label: Insulation resistance
facts.value: >=2 MOhm at 500 V DC

facts.label: Ratio and phasing check
facts.value: secondary voltage within +/-5% of nominal at rated load, and the taps in phase

facts.label: Loaded run
facts.value: at nominal line voltage, checking regulation and temperature rise

c64.psu.transformer.pinboard.name: Transformer pin terminal board
c64.psu.transformer.pinboard.description: A row of brass pins on a small phenolic or nylon board carrying the primary, the interwinding earth, and all the secondary taps. The rectifier diodes and fuses in the 1983-84 bricks are soldered straight onto these pins, which is why the schematic 'terminals' that appear in a teardown are the transformer's own pins rather than a separate board.

facts.label: Pins
facts.value: 8-12 brass pins on 2.54 mm pitch

facts.label: Board material
facts.value: phenolic (paper/phenol formaldehyde) or nylon

facts.label: 902503-02 numbering
facts.value: pins 6/7/8 = centre-tapped 18 V; pins 9/11 = 9 V AC; 10 and 12 = unused spares

c64.psu.transformer.pinboard.phenolic.name: Phenolic laminate board
c64.psu.transformer.pinboard.phenolic.description: Paper or cotton-linen web impregnated with phenol-formaldehyde resin under heat and pressure. Cheap, dimensionally stable and self-extinguishing, which is why it was the default material for transformer terminal boards and fuseholders.

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: phenol-formaldehyde, paper or cotton web

facts.label: UL flammability
facts.value: UL 94 HB at typical resin content

facts.label: Phenol route
facts.value: phenol-formaldehyde at UL 94 HB, phenol from cumene hydroperoxide cleavage in the cumene/propylene-aromatics complex

c64.psu.transformer.winding.name: Enamelled copper winding
c64.psu.transformer.winding.description: The primary, the 18 V centre-tapped secondary and the 9 V output secondary are wound in layers on a moulded bobbin, with a few hundred turns of 0.25-0.4 mm enamelled copper wire. Layer insulation between each pass and interleaved padding between the primary and the secondaries carry the 1000-1500 V RMS of the mains.
c64.psu.transformer.winding.note: Not established: the 0.25-0.4 mm wire, the 500-1200 turns per winding, the 18 V centre-tapped and 9 V secondaries, the layer layout, and the class H 180 C rating by virtue of the enamel. The 902503-02 teardown confirms the winding structure - 9 V AC on pins 9 and 11, and "18V AC with a 'center' tab on pin 6" - but no source documents the wire gauge, turn count or insulation class for this transformer.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 0.25-0.4 mm enamelled copper, roughly 500-1200 turns per winding

facts.label: Insulation class
facts.value: class H, 180 C, by virtue of the enamel

facts.label: Layout
facts.value: layer winding; primary nearest the bobbin or outermost, secondaries separated

c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.name: Polyester varnish impregnation and oven cure
c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.description: The finished assembly is vacuum impregnated with a thermosetting polyester or epoxy varnish so the winding becomes a solid block and cannot move at 50 Hz. Viscous impregnating varnishes were standard by the early 1980s; the alternative is dip-and-bake in an epoxy or a polyurethane.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: vacuum (30-50 mbar) then atmospheric impregnation

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: unsaturated polyester in styrene, or epoxy

c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.name: Impregnating varnish
c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.description: A low-viscosity, high-solids unsaturated polyester resin dissolved in styrene, with an organic peroxide cure catalyst. It cures by crosslinking rather than by solvent loss, so it shrinks very little and fills completely.
c64.psu.transformer.winding.impregnation.note: Not established: 60-70 wt% solids in styrene, the 150 C / 6-10 h cure, the minutes-long gel time at 150 C, and the styrene-from-benzene-and-ethylene route. Vacuum impregnation of a completed winding with an insulating varnish is documented; the unsaturated-polyester-in-styrene formulation, its solids figure and its cure schedule are not.

facts.label: Solids
facts.value: 60-70 wt% in styrene

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 150 C, 6-10 h; gel time minutes at 150 C

facts.label: Monomer
facts.value: styrene from benzene plus ethylene to ethylbenzene and then dehydrogenation; the varnish crosslinks rather than losing solvent

c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.name: Layer winding on a coil winder
c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.description: A single-spindle or two-spindle coil winder turns the bobbin while traversing the wire, and the operator lays interleaved insulation between each layer with a slow-moving 'paper feeder'. Bobbin layers are counter-wound to flatten the coil, and the leads are brought out through the bobbin flange and dressed so they cannot chafe on the core.
c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.note: Not established: single- or twin-spindle coil winding at 1500-4000 rpm, cambered offset layers, the ~50-150 g wire tension, and the paper feeder. No encyclopaedic source describes coil-winding machine practice or counter-wound bobbin layers; this is shop-floor process knowledge with no document behind it here.

facts.label: Machine
facts.value: single- or twin-spindle coil winding machine, 1500-4000 rpm

facts.label: Traverse
facts.value: cambered (offset) layers to give a level coil

facts.label: Tension
facts.value: ~50-150 g on 0.3 mm wire

c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.lead.name: Lead termination and crimped flag terminals
c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.lead.description: The winding leads are soldered or, in the 1983-84 bricks, soldered directly to the transformer's own pins; the line cord and interwinding conductors terminate in tin-plated brass crimp flags. Under the epoxy pour the crimps are the weak link - they can anneal and let go - and the PVC of the line cord is visibly browned right at the pin.
c64.psu.transformer.winding.process.lead.note: Crimping a soldered conductor into a screw terminal is explicitly discouraged by the repair community because the soft solder creeps and the joint goes high-resistance.

facts.label: Terminal
facts.value: tin-plated brass crimp flag or ring, ~6-8 mm2 wire

facts.label: Termination to transformer
facts.value: soldered to the bobbin-terminal pins on most builds

c64.psu.transformer.winding.screen.name: Interwinding earth screen
c64.psu.transformer.winding.screen.description: The protective-earth conductor is bonded to an aluminium or copper foil laid between the primary and the secondary windings - or sometimes to the transformer frame bolt. It does not leave the transformer: the earthing path is closed inside the potted block and never reaches the plastic case or the computer. The foil is plain rolled aluminium or copper, lapped and left uncut so it cannot tear, and it is deliberately insulated from both windings.
c64.psu.transformer.winding.screen.note: Observed on the 902503-02: the protective-earth pin 'somehow connects to the transformer, looks like it goes in the layer between the primary and secondary winding', and does not extend to the output. The brick is all-plastic, so there is nothing to bond earth to on the outside.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: aluminium or copper foil, 0.02-0.05 mm, lapped to a tab

facts.label: Termination
facts.value: crimp ring or soldered to the earth conductor of the line cord

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.name: Layer and interwinding insulation
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.description: Crepe paper or glass-cloth tape between winding layers, a wide kraft or composite tape wrap between the primary and the secondaries, and in the potted builds strips of polyimide (Kapton) film around the whole winding. The 1983-84 bricks visibly used masking tape on the core yoke edges and something like Kapton over the coil to keep the epoxy pour off the windings.

facts.label: Layer insulation
facts.value: crepe paper or muslin/glass cloth, ~0.2 mm

facts.label: Interwinding
facts.value: kraft-paper laminate or glass-cloth tape, 1-3 layers

facts.label: Creepage across windings
facts.value: 2-4 mm, set by the safety standard rather than by physics

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.k.name: Polyimide (Kapton) film
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.k.description: A 12-25 um amber polyimide film used as the barrier between the coil and the epoxy pour and, in later builds, as the layer insulation. Its value is that it does not soften, dissolve or outgas in a hot epoxy cure.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.k.name: Pyromellitic dianhydride monomer
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.k.description: The diacid anhydride half of Kapton is made by air oxidation of pseudocumene to trimellitic acid and then dehydrating it - a petroleum-aromatics chain. The diamine half is 4,4'-oxydianiline or p-phenylenediamine, both aromatics intermediates.

facts.label: Diamine
facts.value: 4,4'-oxydianiline or p-phenylenediamine

facts.label: Polymerisation
facts.value: step-growth in dimethylacetamide at ~200-300 C

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.g.name: Glass-cloth insulation tape
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.g.description: Woven E-glass yarn cloth, ~0.1 mm thick, silane-sized for adhesion, wound in the last layer before the outer tape. Glass has no moisture absorption and much higher dielectric strength than paper, which is why the safety-approved design puts it nearest the primary.

facts.label: Yarn
facts.value: E-glass (borosilicate, ~0.5-1.5% alkali), 204-136 tex

facts.label: Dielectric strength
facts.value: >10 kV/mm in the finished laminate

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.name: Crepe paper insulation
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.description: A lightly crinkled, unbleached kraft paper that stretches to follow the winding contour without bunching. Made on a Fourdrinier machine from a dilute suspension of long-fibre softwood pulp.

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.name: Mechanical wood pulp
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.description: Softwood (spruce/fir) is debarked, chipped, steamed and refined in a disc or refiner mill; the long fibres are ideal for electrical insulation paper because they give high dielectric strength and mechanical strength in the thin sheet.

facts.label: Mill water
facts.value: several tonnes per tonne of pulp, treated with alum, rosin and starch, clarified in a primary settling basin and recirculated

c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.name: Softwood pulp
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.description: The species matters as much as the process: long-fibre softwood pulp from spruce, fir or pine gives the dielectric strength and tear resistance that electrical insulation paper needs, while hardwood pulp from birch or aspen gives opacity and printability and is used in the thinner papers. Softwood is bought as chips or as market pulp.
c64.psu.transformer.winding.insulation.c.note: Not established: the 2-4 mm softwood against 1-2 mm hardwood fibre lengths, the low-conductivity-ash and low-iron electrical grade specification, and the claim that hardwood pulp gives opacity and printability for the thinner papers. Softwood kraft for high-tear-resistance paper is documented; the electrical-grade specification and the species-to-property assignment are not.

facts.label: Fibre length
facts.value: 2-4 mm for softwood, 1-2 mm for hardwood

facts.label: Electrical grade
facts.value: low-conductivity ash and low iron content are specified

c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.name: Moulded nylon bobbin
c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.description: A spool-shaped coil former in glass-filled or unfilled nylon 6 or nylon 6,6, with cheek flanges that locate it on the core leg and a continuous slot that keeps the layer insulation in place. Bobbins were (and still are) a Miles-Platts product line, which fits the 'MP' mark found on this transformer.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: nylon 6 or nylon 6,6, sometimes 30% glass filled

facts.label: Process
facts.value: injection moulding, 2.5-5 mm wall

facts.label: Resin
facts.value: nylon 6 from caprolactam by the Beckmann rearrangement of cyclohexanone, itself from catalytic air oxidation of cyclohexane, which comes from benzene hydrogenation

c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.mould.name: Injection moulding the bobbin
c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.mould.description: Nylon is hygroscopic so the pellets are dried at 80 C for 4-8 h before moulding, then injection moulded at 240-280 C into a multi-cavity tool with hot runners and a mould temperature of 60-90 C. The mould cavity is polished because a flash of loose fibre on the winding slot would be a turn-coat defect.
c64.psu.transformer.winding.bobbin.mould.note: Not established: the 80 C / 4-8 h drying to below 0.1% moisture, the 240-280 C melt, the 60-90 C mould temperature, and the multi-cavity hot-runner tool. Nylon 66 is documented as being injection moulded and as needing to be kept dry because it absorbs moisture, but no source gives the drying schedule or the moulding window for a transformer bobbin.

facts.label: Drying
facts.value: 80 C, 4-8 h to <0.1% moisture

facts.label: Mould temperature
facts.value: 60-90 C, to crystallise the nylon

c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.name: Enamelled magnet wire
c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.description: Bare copper rod drawn down to 0.25-0.4 mm through a series of tungsten-carbide or diamond dies, then coated in two or more passes of a thermosetting enamel - typically polyester-imide (Grade 2 / THEIC) - and baked to cure it. Each coat adds roughly 5-10 um, so a double-grade wire has 25-40% more copper per given window area than bare wire.

facts.label: Wire diameter
facts.value: 0.25-0.4 mm bare, 0.28-0.45 mm with enamel

facts.label: Enamel
facts.value: polyester-imide, 2 coats, ~35-45 um total build

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 160-200 C oven, 5-10 h depending on line speed

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: Grade 2 = ~2x the diameter in insulation for the same wire

facts.label: Copper feedstock
facts.value: blister copper from concentrate of 20-40 wt% Cu, milled from porphyry ore of 0.4-1.0 wt% Cu ground to about 100 um for flotation

c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel.name: Polyester-imide enamel coating
c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel.description: The wire runs continuously through a die-casting oven where a 25-30% solids solution of the modified polyester-imide resin in cresol/xylene is applied, then through a 350-450 C curing oven, and through the same pair again for a second coat. The thermal cure crosslinks the resin to a hard film that resists varnish, oil and coolant.

facts.label: Coats
facts.value: 2 (Grade 2), 3 (Grade 3)

facts.label: Build
facts.value: 35-45 um for Grade 2 at 0.3 mm

facts.label: Cure oven
facts.value: 350-450 C, 20-40 s per coat

c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel..name: Polyester-imide resin
c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel..description: The workhorse magnet-wire enamel of the 1980s. The base is a polycondensation of dimethyl terephthalate (or trimellitic anhydride) with polyols; the imide is introduced with a polyamide of trimellitic anhydride and a diamine such as ethylenediamine, which is what raises the class to H (180 C).
c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.enamel..note: A coal-tar/cresol route to trimellitic anhydride existed and was used into the 1990s; the pseudocumene oxidation route became dominant in the 1980s, which is what makes this enamel a petroleum-aromatics product rather than a coal-tar one. The diamine half of the polyamide is ethylenediamine or a similar short-chain diamine, and it is the imide ring plus that diamine that lifts the insulation class to H.

facts.label: Class
facts.value: H (180 C continuous)

facts.label: Key monomers
facts.value: trimellitic anhydride, terephthalic acid derivatives, diamines

facts.label: Route to the anhydride
facts.value: liquid-phase air oxidation of pseudocumene (1,2,4-trimethylbenzene) over cobalt/manganese acetate at 150-180 C, pseudocumene from catalytic reforming and aromatics extraction of petroleum naphtha

c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.drawing.name: Wire drawing
c64.psu.transformer.winding.wire.drawing.description: A 8 mm copper cathode rod or coil is pickled in sulphuric acid, washed, annealed in a continuous bright-annealing furnace at 500-700 C, then pulled through progressively finer dies with a phosphated soap lubricant. Ten or more die passes take 8 mm to 0.3 mm, and the die temperature is water-cooled to keep the copper from work-hardening to failure.

facts.label: Start
facts.value: 8 mm rod, ~99.99% copper

facts.label: Anneal
facts.value: 500-700 C continuous bright anneal, water-cooled

facts.label: Draw passes
facts.value: 10-15 dies for 8 mm to 0.3 mm

facts.label: Final tensile strength
facts.value: ~350-450 MPa for magnet wire

c64.psu.transformer.core.name: E-I laminated silicon-steel core
c64.psu.transformer.core.description: A stack of punched E and I laminations with interleaved joints, taped along the yoke edges with a single wrap of masking or Kapton tape. For a 40 VA unit at 60 Hz the stack is maybe 25-35 mm tall in 0.35-0.5 mm plate, and it is clamped hard enough that the laminations must be isolated from each other by the oxide scale left on the punched edges.
c64.psu.transformer.core.note: This brick is a laminated-steel design, not a ferrite design: the 251053-02 teardown shows a stack of discrete plates taped along the yoke edges, not a moulded core. Ferrite E/U or E/I cores do appear in later Commodore supplies (the C64C and C16/Plus4 white bricks), where a moulded MnZn core gave a smaller, lighter, lower-loss assembly at several times the material cost and a supply chain in Japan or Germany rather than the local steel mill; that alternative is set out at c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alternative, whose powder metallurgy is the shared metal.ferrite line.

facts.label: Lamination thickness
facts.value: 0.35 mm or 0.5 mm electrical sheet (era range for small power transformers)

facts.label: Material
facts.value: grain-oriented electrical steel, silicon content ~2-3.5 wt%

facts.label: Lamination pitch
facts.value: roughly 20-30 mm; E and I interleaved in a 2:1 or 3:2 sequence

c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alterna.name: MnZn ferrite E-core alternative
c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alterna.description: Later Commodore bricks and the C64C/Plus4 supplies switched to a pressed manganese-zinc ferrite core. Ferrite has much higher resistivity than silicon steel so it can be used as a solid moulded shape with no lamination joints, giving lower core loss at 60 Hz and a much lighter assembly - at several times the material cost, and with a supply chain in Japan or Germany rather than the local steel mill.
c64.psu.transformer.core.ferrite-alterna.note: Not the design in this brick: the 251053-02 teardown is plainly a stack of punched steel laminations. The alternative belongs to later Commodore supplies and is set out here because the comparison is the whole point of the choice - about 10^5 ohm.m against roughly 5x10^-7 ohm.m for silicon steel, at half to a third the saturation induction, so the ferrite core must be physically larger even though it is lighter. Which Commodore part numbers used ferrite could not be verified per part number from a primary source; mark the supply chain as unconfirmed. The oxide blend, the pressing and the firing are the shared metal.ferrite line.

facts.label: Resistivity
facts.value: ~10^5 ohm.m vs ~5x10^-7 ohm.m for silicon steel

facts.label: Saturation
facts.value: ~0.4-0.5 T (much lower than steel, so the core must be bigger)

facts.label: Loss at 50-60 Hz
facts.value: 5-20 kW/m3 at 200 mT

facts.label: Blend
facts.value: Fe2O3 50-60 mol%, MnO 5-15 mol%, ZnO 15-30 mol%, ball-milled 24-48 h to 1-5 um

facts.label: Bind and fire
facts.value: 1-3% PVA binder plus a stearate lubricant, green density ~3.0-3.3 g/cm3, fired at 1100-1250 C for 1-6 h in air or oxygen, 12-18% linear shrinkage

c64.psu.transformer.core.stack.name: Core stack assembly and clamping
c64.psu.transformer.core.stack.description: E and I plates are stacked in alternating layers with the joints staggered so no section of the stack has an unbroken air gap, then clamped end to end by angle plates and bolts or by rivets through the yoke. The joints are the dominant core loss, so the assembler has to keep the interleaving sequence right by hand.

facts.label: Interleave
facts.value: E-I-E-I, joints staggered by half a pitch per layer

facts.label: Clamp
facts.value: steel angle plates and M4 bolts, or pop rivets

c64.psu.transformer.core.stack.clamp-har.name: Clamp bolts and angle plates
c64.psu.transformer.core.stack.clamp-har.description: Mild steel angle plates bolted across the yokes, or two long tie bolts through the core legs, with the axial clamp force chosen so the interlaminar pressure is roughly 3-10 kg/mm2 - enough to stop the stack buzzing at 50 Hz, not so much that the punched edges crack.

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.name: Punched E and I lamination
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.description: One E and one I punched from a strip of grain-oriented electrical steel by a high-speed progression press, roughly 200-600 strokes per minute. The die is a hardened tool-steel stamping die with a compound profile; the strip is fed on a roll and the interlamination burr left by the punch is small enough not to short adjacent plates.
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.note: The steel itself is the shared metal.electrical-steel line: hot-rolled sheet from iron ore, cold rolling to 0.35 mm, a hydrogen magnetic anneal, and the aligned Goss texture. What is uncertain here is whether this brick used it. Oriented electrical steel was several times the price of hot-rolled mild plate and a 40 VA consumer transformer of 1982 could not justify it; the C64 Service Manual parts list calls for a laminated silicon-steel core without specifying an orientation. Treat the grade as unverified and the oxide-isolated stacking as the load-bearing detail.

facts.label: Press rate
facts.value: 200-600 strokes/min (high-speed progression press)

facts.label: Burr height
facts.value: ~10-25 um, sets the shorted-turn loss

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: the E is usually punched with the rolling direction across the yoke so flux runs along the grain

facts.label: Final thickness
facts.value: 0.35 mm (Hi-B) or 0.5 mm

facts.label: Silicon
facts.value: 2.0-3.5 wt%, added to kill eddy currents and raise resistivity

facts.label: Grain texture
facts.value: <100> grain, ~1 mm domain size

facts.label: Coercivity
facts.value: ~0.4-0.5 A/m after the magnetic anneal

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punc.name: High-speed stamping press
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punc.description: A vertical crank or hydraulic press with the compound E+I die in the lower ram and a blanking punch above. In a 1982-era plant the strip ran on a powered roll feed with a pilot pin for registration; the same press also cut the mounting-hole side features and the interleaving key.
