c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punc.note: Not established: the vertical crank or hydraulic press with a compound E+I die in the lower ram, the powered roll feed with pilot-pin registration, and the cutting of the interleaving key and side features in the same stroke. Electrical steel being "cut and converted into 'laminations'" is documented; the press, its feed and its die arrangement are not.

c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punc.name: Hardened tool-steel stamping die
c64.psu.transformer.core.lamination.punc.description: Tungsten-chromium or high-chromium tool steel, hardened and ground, with the compound E and I outline in the same 25-40 mm stroke. Dies lasted millions of hits before the cutting edge rolled and the burr grew past the electrical-steel tolerance.

c64.mainboard.name: Mainboard ASSY 250407
c64.mainboard.description: A single two-layer FR-4 board carrying the whole computer: 1.6 mm of laminate with 35 um of copper on each face, about 1200 unplated component holes, and not one plated-through hole or via anywhere on it. Eight 4164 64 Kbit DRAMs give the 64 KB of main RAM and one 2114L static chip holds 1 KB of screen colour; a 6510 at about 1 MHz, the 6567 VIC-II, the 6581 SID, two 6526 CIAs, a 6532 PPI, a mask-programmed 906114-01 PLA and three mask ROMs - 901226-01 BASIC, 901227-03 KERNAL and the 4 KB 901225-01 character generator - do the rest. Everything is through-hole DIP, so every connection between two parts is a copper trace: where a later revision has a via, this board carries a short single-core jumper wire soldered across the same pads. About 320 components in all: 19 memory, custom-logic and ROM devices, about a dozen 74-series glue parts, a few CMOS parts and a handful of small-signal transistors.
c64.mainboard.note: The 250407 is the long 'breadbin' layout and the U-numbers quoted throughout this tree are its canonical set; they do not line up with the 250425, 250466 or short boards. The via count is the one a validated copy of the 250407 artwork settles: zero, which is why the zero-via claim is stated in the description rather than left as a footnote. This node no longer lists c64.connector-jacks or c64.mains among its children: the plugs belong to the panel they are soldered into, which c64.io-panel carries, and the line cord, plug, switch and fuse live in the external power supply, which is a separate assembly reached from the top of the tree.

facts.value: ASSY 250407, PCB 326498-01, material no. 250406, artwork 251137, schematic 251138

facts.label: Layers / vias

mb.photo.name: Phototooling: how C64 copper artwork became an etched board
mb.photo.description: The chain that turns a board database into a resist image. The 250407 artwork is number 251137. It was drawn on a design workstation, reduced to aperture-table plot files, plotted onto photographic film at a jobbing house, developed, checked on a test coupon, and used as the mask that prints the board's dry-film resist before etching.
mb.photo.note: Modern practice is direct imaging from the CAM data with no film at all. The film phototooling described here is how the board in the machine was actually made. Most of what hangs off this branch is a real artefact - artwork film stock, an electrostatic plotter, magnetic tape, photographic chemistry - so it is kept as a process chain rather than a note. Commentary covers the backannotation workflow and the arrival of laser plotting.

facts.label: Layers plotted
facts.value: 2 copper, plus solder mask and legend

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: vacuum-frame contact exposure of the artwork film onto dry film

mb.photo.panel.name: Panelising the order
mb.photo.panel.description: The board is one part out of a panel of identical boards nested in a sheet large enough for the process equipment. The panel gets tooling holes for registration and for the drill, and the boards are held together by small perforated mouse-bite tabs that are broken out by hand or by a router after the panel is finished. Those tabs leave a characteristic rough edge on the board outline, visible on a 1983 board if you look for it. This is where the layout cost of an order is amortised, and why a two-layer panel in 1983 could hold a surprising number of boards.

mb.photo.mask.name: Printing the artwork onto the resist
mb.photo.mask.description: The artwork film is laid against the exposed dry-film resist on the board and exposed in the vacuum frame. Where the film is clear, the resist hardens and resists the etch; where it is opaque, the resist stays soft and the copper beneath is etched away. This is the moment the phototooling chain finally touches the board, and every solder joint on the finished machine is located by this exposure.
mb.photo.mask.note: Two-sided registration - landing the second side's artwork on the copper to within a fraction of a millimetre, using alignment pins and a register mark - is the hard part of a two-sided board. On this board it matters mainly for the mounting holes and the connector slots; on a via-heavy board it is what decides whether every barrel lands on its own pad. Having no vias makes it a far less critical operation than it would otherwise be, one of the quieter payoffs of the layer-change-by-component-lead strategy.

mb.photo.rephoto.name: Rephotography, the master, and the coupon
mb.photo.rephoto.description: The plotted working film is rephotographed onto a higher-quality film to get a sharper, dimensionally stable master. Before a whole panel is committed, a test coupon is exposed and etched with every line width the panel uses, and the widths are measured under a measuring microscope. This is how a shop proves its process still holds tolerance, and it is the quiet heart of 1980s board making: a cheap, fast way to prove that the narrowest trace the designer asked for is still coming out, before a hundred boards are committed to it.
mb.photo.rephoto.note: Not established: the rephotography step, the test coupon, and the practice of measuring the narrowest trace under a measuring microscope before committing a panel. Board-house procedure of the period is described in trade literature, which is not cited here.

facts.label: Coupon
facts.value: a small test board carrying every line width and pad size on the panel

facts.label: Check
facts.value: measure the narrowest trace on the panel under a measuring microscope

mb.photo.rephoto.master.name: The artwork master
mb.photo.rephoto.master.description: The film treated as the authoritative copy of the design, stored flat and handled by the edges. It is the board's master record, and losing it means paying for the panel again.

mb.photo.develop.name: Developing and fixing the film
mb.photo.develop.description: The exposed film is developed, fixed, washed and dried before it can serve as a mask. The chemistry is ordinary silver-halide photographic processing, run as a short line of tanks.

mb.photo.develop.fixer.name: Fixer (ammonium thiosulfate)
mb.photo.develop.fixer.description: The unexposed silver halide is dissolved away and the image made light-stable, so the film can be handled, stored and re-exposed without latent-image changes.
mb.photo.develop.fixer.note: Thiosulfate chemistry is a sulfur chain, ultimately from sulfur or from sulphur dioxide off sulfide roasting, so it is a different mineral chain from the aromatic one.

mb.photo.develop.developer.name: Photographic developer (hydroquinone)
mb.photo.develop.developer.description: The film emulsion is silver halide; hydroquinone reduces the exposed grains to metallic silver, giving the opaque image that will block the resist. The reducing agent is itself an aromatic chemical made from benzene, so the mask chemistry is a petroleum chain like almost everything else in this branch.

mb.photo.plotter.name: Photoplotting the artwork film
mb.photo.plotter.description: The plot files drive a photoplotter that draws the copper artwork onto a transparent film. In 1983 these machines lived at the fabricator, not the design office, and were the company's most valuable single asset.

mb.photo.plotter.laser.name: Laser plotting, arriving later
mb.photo.plotter.laser.description: An argon-ion or, later, a diode laser writes the film or the photoresist directly. Sharper than corona discharge and faster, but in 1983 it was still being adopted and the electrostatic plotter was not yet history. This is the last piece of 1980s phototooling equipment before direct imaging replaced film entirely in the 1990s - an aside on where the technology was heading, not a step in this board's own process.

mb.photo.plotter.pen.name: Pen plotter
mb.photo.plotter.pen.description: A carriage carrying a light-sensitive pen draws the artwork directly on film or mylar. Simple and reliable, but slow, with real line-width variation, so it was being displaced by the electrostatic plotter through the early 1980s. Still used for check plots and for prototype single-layer boards well into the 1980s.

mb.photo.plotter.film.name: Artwork film stock
mb.photo.plotter.film.description: A high-contrast, dimensionally stable photographic film that the plotter exposes and the shop develops into a finished mask. It must hold its geometry over a store door and be opaque where there is copper. The base is a dimensionally stable polyester, the same polymer family as the dry-film resist carrier used on the board itself.

mb.photo.plotter.electrostatic.name: Electrostatic plotter
mb.photo.plotter.electrostatic.description: The dominant plotting technology of the era. A fine wire or shaped electrode is stepped across the film under computer control and a corona discharge exposes the emulsion wherever copper is wanted. Flatbed machines laid a film flat and exposed quickly, which is why they became the standard for two-sided work. Gerber Scientific commercialised these plotters and the aperture-table format that drove them, so the format the industry still uses is a direct inheritance of this machine.
mb.photo.plotter.electrostatic.note: That vector photoplotters driven by Gerber format data were the dominant plotting technology for PCB artwork of this period is established: Standard Gerber was a numerical control format designed by Gerber Systems Corp to drive their vector photo plotters for the PCB industry in the 1960s and 1970s. Not established: that the exposure was a corona discharge from a stepped wire or shaped electrode, that flatbed machines laid a film flat and so became the standard for two-sided work, the hundreds of beds claim elsewhere in this branch, and that this machine was a Gerber-branded electrostatic plotter. Modern boards use direct imaging, for which Gerber is also the standard image input format, so the format outlived the machine.

mb.photo.cam.name: Data reduction and CAM
mb.photo.cam.description: The database is converted into per-layer plot files. This is where a net becomes copper, a component pin becomes a pad, and the drill hits are separated out; autorouters handled most of the bulk in 1983 and a human cleaned up the critical nets, which is why the copper on a 1983 board looks the way it does. Automated checks for minimum track width, minimum spacing and pad-to-pad clearance ran here too; on a board with no vias the annular-ring check has almost nothing to check, but spacing between fine pads on the IC footprints still matters. Errors at this stage are replicated across a whole panel, which is why the step is done once, carefully, for hundreds of boards.
mb.photo.cam.note: A later twist on the C64 itself: owners of later board revisions found the layouts so tight that home repair needed bodge wires across the copper. That is a board designed to the limit.

mb.photo.cam.apertures.name: Aperture table
mb.photo.cam.apertures.description: Every distinct pad shape and track width is assigned an aperture in a table the plotter reads, so a 1.0 mm round pad and a 0.3 mm track are drawn as repeated simple shapes rather than as free curves. The Gerber format was invented at this time to carry exactly this table, which is why it is still about apertures and flashes rather than geometry, and why it is still the universal interchange format for board artwork today.
mb.photo.cam.apertures.note: On this board the drill programme is trivial to split out from the copper data, precisely because there are no vias: the drill file is only component holes, mounting holes and the connector slots. A via-heavy board of the same era is where plot data and drill data were most often confused, and the result was a hole in the wrong place.

mb.photo.design.name: The board database on the design system
mb.photo.design.description: In 1983 the layout lived on the CAD vendor's own workstation, not in a modern repository. Traces, pads, components and drill data were edited on the machine and periodically written out as plot files on nine-track tape and then on 8-inch floppy disks. Copying it to the jobbing house was a physical act of transporting magnetic media, and a lost tape meant the whole panel waited.

mb.photo.design.backannotation.name: Backannotation from a drawn overlay
mb.photo.design.backannotation.description: The designer taped mylar over the plotted printout, drew routing changes with a special pen, and passed the overlay through a digitizer that read the new lines and apertures back into the database. Some of the most awkward-looking copper on a 1983 board is the residue of this workflow: a routing decision made on a sheet of plastic and converted by an encoder.

mb.photo.design.workstation.name: PCB CAD workstation
mb.photo.design.workstation.description: A dedicated 16-bit microcomputer or small minicomputer with its own storage and a high-resolution monochrome display, often with a pen plotter and a digitizer on the desk. The digitizer mattered as much as the plotter: designers drew and revised artwork on mylar overlays and digitised the changes back into the database. Interactive PCB CAD in the 1980s was a commercial market dominated by a handful of vendors, and the C64 layout predates every open format and tool used today.

mb.photo.design.workstation.storage.name: Plot-file storage media
mb.photo.design.workstation.storage.description: Plot files and library data were written to nine-track tape, then to 8-inch floppy disks. The magnetic oxide on a thin polymer backing is the physical carrier the jobbing house receives. This is the handover point between design and fabrication.

mb.photo.design.workstation.display.name: Monochrome CRT display
mb.photo.design.workstation.display.description: A high-resolution green or white phosphor CRT on which the layout was examined trace by trace. This is a designer's tooling CRT, not the machine's own video output.

mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glas.name: CRT envelope glass
mb.photo.design.workstation.display.glas.description: The bulb is soda-lime glass formed on a glass lathe from the same kind of batch as the reinforcing cloth: silica sand plus limestone plus alkali. A design workstation's screen is a small consumer item, but it is the terminal through which every copper trace of the board was examined.

mb.test.name: Factory test of the C64 mainboard and machine
mb.test.description: How a populated C64 board was proved working before it left the factory. Electrical test on the bare board, then a functional test that boots the machine from a diagnostic ROM in the cartridge port and checks it against a monitor and a test cradle, then burn-in, then final test and packing. The practice was mostly manual, and Commodore's own engineers admitted it was thinner than it should have been.
mb.test.note: There are documented examples of new C64 machines shipping with cut traces, and a software developer's account of opening brand-new machines and finding them. That is the honest backdrop to this branch: it describes what was actually done, not what a modern line would do.

facts.label: Stages
facts.value: bare-board electrical test, functional test, burn-in, final test

facts.label: Test ROM
facts.value: a diagnostic ROM run from the cartridge port

facts.label: Display check
facts.value: the machine's own video output viewed on a test monitor

mb.test.final.name: Final test and packing
mb.test.final.description: A last pass over the complete machine in its case: keyboard, control ports, serial port and a final power-on. Surviving machines are packed with the cord and the manual for shipment, in corrugated board with a printed outer. The packaging branch has its own industrial chemistry under c64.packaging; this node marks only where the tested board leaves the factory.

mb.test.final.ports.name: Control and serial port check
mb.test.final.ports.description: The two control ports and the serial port are exercised with known-good peripherals or loopback plugs. These are the connectors most often left untested on a line that was under pressure, and it is where the documented field failures of this era cluster.

mb.test.burnin.name: Burn-in
mb.test.burnin.description: Finished machines are powered up under load, often at elevated temperature, for an extended period. This was originally to weed out infant-mortality failures in the custom chips, which is exactly where the C64's problems were, and it is why there had to be a diagnostic ROM that could run unattended. Heat is the cheap accelerator of every silicon and soldering defect there is, which is why burn-in exists at all. The ROM is left to run so a machine that fails on its own gives a visible failure, freeing the line from one operator per machine - which is why the dead-test ROM's pattern output mattered as much as its pass-or-fail verdict. Racks were moved in and out of the oven on a schedule, which is a lot of manual handling for what looks like a passive wait.

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: catch early-life failures, especially in the custom chips

facts.label: Method
facts.value: machines run in racks, often warm, sometimes cycling

mb.test.burnin.oven.name: Burn-in oven or rack
mb.test.burnin.oven.description: A room or cabinet holding powered machines on racks, warmed to speed up failure. The heat comes from nichrome resistance elements, an alloy of nickel and chromium that resists oxidation at red heat, so the oven is a consumer of both metals in small but real quantity. It is also one of the largest electricity loads in the plant.
mb.test.burnin.oven.note: Heat is the cheap accelerator of every silicon and soldering defect there is.

mb.test.burnin.oven.rack.name: Burn-in rack
mb.test.burnin.oven.rack.description: A steel frame carrying a shelf of machines, ventilated so the heat is actually reaching them. The rack had to carry a full load of powered machines for hours at temperature, so the frame is structural steel rather than sheet-metal convenience.

mb.test.video.name: CRT display test
mb.test.video.description: The machine's own composite video output is fed to a test monitor and the inspector reads the picture. Nothing instruments this: the pass criterion is that the picture is correct, which means the human being in the loop is doing the measuring. The engineering team said outright that testing colour quality automatically was effectively impossible, and that line workers were told to adjust a colour control until they saw colour. Several thousand machines shipped with garish colours as a result, and the instruction itself was the cause.
mb.test.video.note: The monitor is a small composite set or a colour television; its cathode-ray-tube chain is owned by the peripherals fragment.

facts.label: What is checked
facts.value: a correct picture and sound: colours, borders, sprites, cursor

facts.label: Instruments
facts.value: the human eye, plus a monitor

mb.test.video.monitor.name: Test monitor
mb.test.video.monitor.description: A small composite monochrome monitor, or a colour television, used as the reference picture. Each is a cathode-ray tube: drawn glass envelope, phosphor coating, deflection yoke and a high-voltage supply.

mb.test.functional.name: Functional test with a test ROM
mb.test.functional.description: The populated board is mounted in a test cradle with a power supply and a monitor, and the machine proves itself by running a diagnostic program from the cartridge port. This exercises the real boot path - CPU, ROM, RAM, character ROM, VIC, SID and the I/O chips - all in the configuration they will ship in. Using the cartridge port as the test-vector delivery mechanism is an elegant piece of period engineering: no extra fixture hardware, and it tests the bus the machine actually uses.
mb.test.functional.note: Several cradles were usually in line so inspectors could work in parallel.

facts.label: Test medium
facts.value: a diagnostic ROM in the cartridge port

facts.label: What it proves
facts.value: the machine can reach its own boot ROM and produce a correct picture and sound

mb.test.functional.keyboard.name: Keyboard and ribbon test
mb.test.functional.keyboard.description: Because the keyboard connects to the mainboard through a soldered ribbon on this design, the functional test has to cover that joint: every key is checked, which is a simultaneous test of the connector, the ribbon, the keyboard matrix and the CPU's scanning routine.

mb.test.functional.cradle.name: Test cradle
mb.test.functional.cradle.description: A jig that holds the board on locating pins, presents a regulated 5 V and 12 V, routes the video and audio outputs to a monitor and speaker, and presents the cartridge and edge connectors. The C64's 5 V and 12 V came from its external supply, so the factory had to prove both the board and that supply; testing the power supply itself belongs to the power branch of this tree.

mb.test.functional.cradle.psu.name: Test power supply
mb.test.functional.cradle.psu.description: A regulated supply with a current limit, so a shorted board does not destroy it. This is a bench instrument, not the machine's own power brick.

mb.test.functional.rom.name: Diagnostic and dead-test ROM
mb.test.functional.rom.description: A small EPROM in a cartridge shell which, on power-up, prints a screenful of named tests and runs each one, reporting RAM, ROM and video faults by pattern rather than by instrument. The operator's job is to look at the picture and read the verdict. These test ROMs were so successful that Commodore later sold the same idea to the public as the Dead Test cartridge, which is why they are so well documented today.
mb.test.functional.rom.note: Not established: the cartridge part number, the ROM contents and the identity of the diagnostic ROM. The C64 dead-test screen is associated with the service manual, but the per-page mirror at devili.iki.fi carries circuit-theory pages only and does not reproduce it.

facts.label: Media
facts.value: EPROM in a cartridge shell

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: no instruments needed; the machine tests itself and says so

mb.test.ict.name: In-circuit electrical test
mb.test.ict.description: A bare populated board is checked electrically before it is ever plugged into a machine. The point is to catch a missing component, a shorted pad or a broken trace while it is still trivially fixable. The board is pressed down onto a bed-of-nails fixture whose probes touch every node of interest, so the tester can measure each net without a probe being placed by hand; on a board with no vias and only DIP footprints the fixture is comparatively simple to design and to wire, though it still has to be cut for the artwork, which is why fixtures were an expensive per-part-number investment.
mb.test.ict.note: A modern flying-probe or X-ray system would do this without a custom fixture; in 1983 the bed of nails was the economical choice at volume. The sprung probe pins themselves are the shared node facility.test-equipment.needle-probe.

mb.test.ict.tester.name: The tester itself
mb.test.ict.tester.description: A rack of switching electronics driving the fixture, with a go or no-go readout and a reject bin. It is ordinary 1980s digital test equipment: a small computer, a relay matrix and a display, all built from the same logic families the C64 itself uses.

mb.test.ict.presence.name: Component-presence and seating check
mb.test.ict.presence.description: Checking that the right part is in the right place is a distinct and important test on a board with thirty sockets and a hundred passive parts. A missing, reversed or half-seated socketed IC is the single most common fault on any 1980s logic board. Verifiers that push each socket to confirm its pins are actually in the hole were in use in this era, alongside visual and continuity checks.

mb.test.ict.measure.name: Continuity, resistance and short detection
mb.test.ict.measure.description: The tester looks for opens in the artwork and for shorts between nets that should be isolated, and on some fixtures measures absolute values. On a simple two-layer board with no vias, continuity checking is very nearly the whole job.

mb.assembly.name: Populating, cleaning and finishing the C64 mainboard
mb.assembly.description: What happens between the bare board and the tested machine. Components are inserted, a few hand-fitted wires and jumpers are added, the board is soldered, cleaned, shielded and screwed into the case. On this board the whole operation is through-hole and hand-and-machine insertion: there is no surface-mount reflow anywhere in the C64 mainboard assembly. The connectors, the fuse clips and the keyboard ribbon were all fitted and hand-soldered rather than waved, because a conveyorised wave cannot hold them; the keyboard ribbon in particular is a delicate soldered joint and a classic failure point on surviving machines.
mb.assembly.note: Commodore specifically laid this board out for automated insertion, which cost them their Japanese assembly line and forced production into Hong Kong. The design decision to use DIP sockets rather than soldering the chips directly is a serviceability choice: it made field replacement possible, and it roughly doubled the number of joints on the board. The resistors, their carbon-film elements and the resistor networks are not described here; the passives fragment owns them under mb.passives.resistors.

facts.label: Technology
facts.value: 100 % through-hole; no SMT, no reflow

facts.label: DIP sockets
facts.value: about 30 sockets per board

facts.label: Wire jumpers
facts.value: 2 fitted by hand

facts.label: Component count
facts.value: roughly 80-100 parts per board

mb.assembly.volume.name: Volume and yield reality of the line
mb.assembly.volume.description: Commodore sold on the order of two million C64s a year at the 1983-84 peak, on a production cost that started near 130 dollars and fell as volume rose. Every board here was one of millions per year through the same line, which is the context that explains every process decision in this branch: a two-layer board with no vias and no plated barrels has very few ways to fail, so board yield was high and the cost stayed near a dollar or two.
mb.assembly.volume.note: The 1982-83 units were built at Kentron in Ina, Japan under Commodore Japan Limited, and the boards were made in Hong Kong. Whether Commodore ever had its own in-house printed-circuit-board etching line is not established; the engineering account says the boards were made in Hong Kong, which implies an outside fabricator rather than a Commodore plant.

facts.label: Peak annual output
facts.value: roughly 2-2.5 million units a year around 1984

facts.label: Board cost
facts.value: approx. $1-2

facts.label: Board yield
facts.value: high; a two-layer no-via board has few failure modes

mb.assembly.repair.name: Board-level rework and repair
mb.assembly.repair.description: Bad joints are reworked on the line: the joint is reflowed with an iron, the part is replaced, and a full set of consumable tips is kept to do it. Commodore's own engineering position was famously to ship rather than to hold back, which shows up here as rework being a normal, high-volume operation rather than an exception.
mb.assembly.repair.note: The engineering team's stated culture was that if a product worked it shipped, and that quality control was not coming close enough to where it should have been. That is visible in this subsystem as rework rather than scrap.

mb.assembly.shield.name: EMI shield bonding
mb.assembly.shield.description: The metal shield around the video and audio circuitry is bonded to the board's ground so that the enclosure is actually part of the ground return. Without a real bond the shield picks up the very signals it is there to contain. On this board the bond is a combination: a small tab on the shield soldered to a ground pad, and a plated hole into which a shield screw goes. Either way it is one of the joints most often disturbed by owners, and its condition is worth checking before blaming the video circuit.

mb.assembly.shield.tab.name: The VIC-II heat-sink tab
mb.assembly.shield.tab.description: A metal tab welded inside the shield lid pressed against the top of the video chip package, so the shield doubled as a heat sink for the chip that dissipated about 1.5 W. This was a deliberate design fix for a real heat problem, not a later addition, and it is a neat example of the enclosure, the ground return and the thermal path being one part.
mb.assembly.shield.tab.note: The design history explicitly describes this tab being welded to the shield lid so the enclosure became a heat sink.

facts.label: Heat path
facts.value: about 1.5 W from the VIC-II conducted into the shield lid

mb.assembly.conformal.name: No conformal coating on this board
mb.assembly.conformal.description: A deliberate absence, recorded here so it does not read as an omission. The C64 mainboard was not conformally coated. Conformal coating existed in 1983 for military and automotive work and was increasingly common in commercial electronics, but not for a home computer in a dry indoor case.
mb.assembly.conformal.note: Not established: that the C64 mainboard carried no conformal coating. This is an absence, and the 250407 parts list contains no coating material, but a parts list cannot evidence a process step that was never performed.

mb.assembly.reflow.name: No surface-mount parts and no reflow on this board
mb.assembly.reflow.description: A deliberate absence, recorded here so it does not read as an omission. It is worth being explicit that the C64 mainboard has no surface-mount parts and no reflow step: everything is through-hole, everything is either waved or hand-soldered. Reflow ovens were already known in 1983, but they were used for flat-pack IC packages and for small daughterboards. The analogue RF modulator is one of those daughterboards - a separate small board, covered by the mb.rf-modulator branch of this tree, not part of the main logic board. Any account that reflows the C64 mainboard is describing a different machine.
mb.assembly.reflow.note: Modern boards are dominated by reflow. This one is not. The absence is evidenced by the 250407 bill of materials: across 107 line items and 252 components, every footprint is a through-hole type - DIP, radial, axial, DIP socket, pin header, D-sub, solder jumper - and not one line is a chip resistor or chip capacitor package. That a switch to surface mount began in the 1980s is also established: since the 1980s, surface mount parts have increasingly replaced through-hole components, which dates this board to the end of the era rather than after it.

mb.assembly.jumpers.name: Wire jumpers and configuration links
mb.assembly.jumpers.description: Because the board has no vias, the few places where a connection must cross between the two copper layers with no component to do it are bridged with a short tinned copper wire, hand-fitted into two holes and hand-soldered after wave soldering. These are the E1 and E2 links on the 250407 layout, and there are exactly two of them.
mb.assembly.jumpers.note: These are visible on the bottom of the finished board and are now a small collector's item in their own right. A modern board would put a via or a zero-ohm resistor there instead; none of those were on this board.

facts.label: Count on 250407
facts.value: 2 (references E1, E2 on the artwork)

facts.label: Fitted
facts.value: by hand, after the wave soldering

mb.assembly.jumpers.wire.name: Tinned single-core jumper wire
mb.assembly.jumpers.wire.description: A short length of fine tinned copper wire, cut and formed to the two holes, fitted and soldered by hand. It is the mechanical ancestor of the jumper link on every later board.
mb.assembly.jumpers.wire.note: Modern equivalents are 0-ohm resistors, jumper pins, or just a via.

mb.assembly.sockets.name: DIP sockets as the C64 serviceability choice
mb.assembly.sockets.description: This is the single most underappreciated decision on the board. The C64 sockets its integrated circuits rather than soldering them directly, which means any chip can be swapped in the field - and it means the number of joints roughly doubles, because each socket has two contacts per pin. A home computer with unfield-serviceable ROM or SID chips would generate warranty returns, so Commodore accepted the socket money and the extra joints.
mb.assembly.sockets.note: It is also the reason C64 boards need so much rosin flux and so much cleaning, and the reason a missing, reversed or half-seated socketed IC is the most common fault on any 1980s logic board.

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: field-replaceable ICs

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: roughly doubles the joint count and adds a failure mode of its own

mb.assembly.insertion.name: Component insertion
mb.assembly.insertion.description: Every part goes into the board from the top. Because there are no vias and no bottom-side components, the whole machine is one-sided: one operator can see every joint from the solder side and there is no second-side insertion operation at all. Axial parts are cut to length and formed to a right angle or a left-right offset so they drop into a fixed hole pitch, and radial parts are spread to the board's lead spacing, usually 0.1 or 0.2 in; the forms are set in the machine and are a real cost, because a wrong form is a board that will not insert. Everything the machine could not do - the fuse clips, the connectors, the small-signal parts in awkward places, the wire jumpers - was worked by hand at the line from a traveller's list. Mixed human-and-machine insertion on one board is a recipe for a part inserted twice or missed entirely, so the line had a checking station: a verifier that confirms every part is present and seated before the board goes into the wave.
mb.assembly.insertion.note: Modern practice forms nothing and mounts surface-mount parts; lead-formed axial parts are essentially gone from new consumer hardware.

facts.label: Radial pitch
facts.value: matched to the board hole pitch, often 0.1 in or 0.2 in

facts.label: Lead forming
facts.value: at the component maker or the insertion machine, not by hand on the line

mb.assembly.insertion.fixture.name: Insertion fixture and board handling
mb.assembly.insertion.fixture.description: The board is held in a jig with locating pins while components go in, and the same family of jig carries the board through the wave and into test. Every fixture on the line solves the same problem: the board has to land in exactly one position, every time.

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.name: Insertion engine and its cycle time
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.description: A machine with a magazine per part type picks a part, leads it to the right hole and pushes it in, typically in 0.3-0.6 s per component. On a board of about 90 parts that is roughly half a minute of machine time, which is why insertion engines paid for themselves on volume this high. The bedplate is cast iron or welded steel, because its flatness is the limit on how accurately a lead can be placed in a hole.

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: approx. 0.3-0.6 s per component

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: the machine cannot compensate for a bent lead, so lead forming matters

facts.label: Base
facts.value: cast iron or welded steel bedplate, machined flat

mb.assembly.insertion.engine.magazines.name: Part magazines and vibratory feed
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.magazines.description: Radial magazines shake components down a track to a pick head. Cut, formed axial leads are the hardest part to feed; resistors and capacitors with wide leads feed easily.
mb.assembly.insertion.engine.magazines.note: Failure of vibratory feeding, not of the machine itself, was the usual reason a line stopped on a board full of axial parts.

mb.assembly.insertion.layout.name: Component spacing dictated by the insertion machine
mb.assembly.insertion.layout.description: Component spacing on this board was dictated by the insertion machine rather than by the circuit designer, which is exactly the argument Commodore had with its Japanese plant and lost. The same board could not be hand-inserted efficiently and machine-inserted efficiently at once.
mb.assembly.insertion.layout.note: The IEEE Spectrum account of the C64 design case history states the board was laid out for automated insertion and production was moved to a Hong Kong plant that had the automated tools.

mb.solder.name: Soldering the C64 mainboard
mb.solder.description: Every joint on the C64 mainboard is made with 63/37 tin-lead alloy activated by rosin flux: about 600 in one pass through a wave-soldering machine, the rest by hand afterwards on the connectors, fuse clips, big electrolytics and wire jumpers. This branch follows the machines, the settings and the bench that make those joints; the alloy itself, its wire and its bar, are the shared node metal.solder.
mb.solder.note: The alloy and the wave are established. On the alloy: in electronics assembly, the eutectic alloy with 63% tin and 37% lead (or 60/40, which is almost identical in melting point) has been the alloy of choice; 63/37 melts at 183 deg C and is the only mixture that melts at a point instead of over a range, while 60/40 melts between 183 and 190 deg C; and because a eutectic has the same liquidus and solidus temperature there is no plastic phase, which allows quicker setup as the solder cools, whereas a non-eutectic must remain still through the plastic phase and may crack. On the process: soldering could be done automatically by passing the board over a ripple, or wave, of molten solder in a wave-soldering machine. Not established: that about 600 joints on this board went through the wave in one pass, the 245-255 deg C pot temperature, the 1.5-2.5 m/min wave speed, and the split between waved and hand-soldered joints. The eutectic was the right choice, and the reason is worth stating: at 63/37 the alloy melts and solidifies at one temperature instead of a mushy range, so a joint leaves the wave already set. 60/40, common for hand work, freezes over a range and gives duller, greyer joints. The alloy chain from cassiterite and galena through the ingot to the wire is owned by metal.solder and metal.tin / metal.lead, and the flux by chem.rosin; neither is repeated here. The flux was specified halide-free rather than no-clean: low-solids no-clean fluxes existed but were not the default here, and the goal was a non-ionic flux rather than a skipped cleaning step.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: 63 % Sn / 37 % Pb eutectic, from metal.solder

facts.label: Melting point
facts.value: 183 deg C, a sharp single transition

facts.label: Pot temperature
facts.value: roughly 245-255 deg C

facts.label: Wave speed
facts.value: roughly 1.5-2.5 m/min

facts.label: Joints
facts.value: roughly 600 waved in one pass, the remainder hand-soldered

mb.solder.selective.name: Connectors, fuse clips and heavy joints
mb.solder.selective.description: The parts that cannot simply be taken through the wave in the usual way: the D-sub and DIN connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers and the large electrolytics. The board-mount connectors on this board are right-angle types with solder tails projecting out of the back of the shell, so they were soldered from the underside with the shell already in place - a short working time and a hot iron in a cramped space, which is why so many surviving C64 boards show resoldered connector joints. Inside a shell, solder wicks along a pin and jumps the gap to the next pad, and the bridge cannot be seen happening; the 1983 countermeasures were flux plus a steady iron, then a probe and a rework iron to break the bridge. For genuinely heavy joints the answer was a second iron on the lead to keep it at temperature while the solder melted, so the solder wetted the lead instead of freezing a cold slug around it. Slower per joint, but the only way to get a sound joint onto a big thermal-mass part.
mb.solder.selective.note: Modern lead-free practice would drag a solder bead along the pins to wick off the excess and, failing that, use a solder pot. The prevalence of resoldered connector joints on forty-year-old C64 boards is decent evidence that these joints were marginal from the start.

mb.solder.hand.name: Hand soldering on the line
mb.solder.hand.description: Soldering iron, solder wire and pliers on a bench under a smoke extraction arm. Used for the connectors, the fuse clips, the wire jumpers, the big electrolytics and every joint the inspector rejected. A small minority of joints, but where the line rejects come from too. A small hand-held solder pot or a solder fountain was used for the fuse clips and heavy connector leads where a wave cannot reach.

facts.label: Iron power
facts.value: approx. 25-60 W for fine work

facts.label: Tip temperature
facts.value: approx. 315-380 deg C

facts.label: Tip material
facts.value: oxygen-free copper, often plated so it does not dissolve away

mb.solder.hand.extraction.name: Fume extraction
mb.solder.hand.extraction.description: An arm or hood over the bench draws off the flux smoke. The smoke is resin vapour, not tin vapour, but it is unpleasant and it is the reason every solder bench in 1983 had a hood over it.

mb.solder.hand.iron.name: Soldering iron and tip
mb.solder.hand.iron.description: A nichrome or cartridge heater in a barrel with a replaceable copper tip. The tip has to be kept tinned; a dry tip oxidises and then stops transferring heat at all, which is the real reason beginners conclude solder will not melt on a joint.

mb.solder.reliability.name: Copper-tin intermetallic at the pad
mb.solder.reliability.description: Solder does not merely sit on a pad, it reacts with it. Within seconds of contact, tin and copper fuse at the surface into Cu6Sn5, and a Cu3Sn layer follows as the joint ages. That intermetallic is the actual metallurgical bond holding the joint, and because its growth is limited by diffusion through itself, higher-temperature solders containing silver or gold exist purely to slow the reaction at the pad. Fully intermetallised joints are brittle, which is the origin of solder fatigue and the reason a leaded joint is forgiving in a way a lead-free one is not.
mb.solder.reliability.note: Not established: the Cu6Sn5 then Cu3Sn sequence, the diffusion-limited growth argument and the brittleness claim, from any source read for this node. The intermetallic bond is a standard result in soldering metallurgy but the specific phase sequence here is not cited.

facts.label: First phase
facts.value: Cu6Sn5 at the pad surface within seconds of contact

facts.label: Later phase
facts.value: Cu3Sn grows under the Cu6Sn5 as the joint ages

facts.label: Growth control
facts.value: diffusion-limited through the intermetallic itself

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: brittle, cracks under thermal cycling

mb.solder.profile.name: The wave-soldering profile
mb.solder.profile.description: The machine is set by five numbers together: pot temperature, conveyor speed, preheat temperature, preheat time and flux concentration. Get them wrong in a specific way and you get a specific, diagnosable defect. A joint cools from 250 deg C to 183 deg C in about a second; if the board and the lead start cold the joint solidifies from the outside inward and you get the dull, grainy, poorly wetted fillet a line inspector rejects, which is the entire point of the preheat tunnel. Large thermal-mass leads - the big axial electrolytic, the tabbed regulator - heat far more slowly than the solder around them, so the line runs the conveyor slowly enough that the solder stays molten until the lead is hot, which in turn slows every board on the machine.

facts.label: Pot
facts.value: approx. 245-255 deg C

facts.label: Preheat
facts.value: approx. 110-150 deg C

facts.label: Speed
facts.value: approx. 1.5-2.5 m/min

facts.label: Wave contact
facts.value: roughly 2-4 s

facts.label: Cooling window
facts.value: a joint has about one second from 250 deg C to 183 deg C

mb.solder.profile.defects.name: Joint defects and what causes them
mb.solder.profile.defects.description: The diagnostic vocabulary a line supervisor used in 1983, and it has barely changed since. Dull grainy joints mean a dirty pad or too little preheat. Dry joints and unfilled holes mean a hole too tight for the lead or a wave too slow. Solder balls and spatter mean moisture in the board. Bridging between fine pads means too much flux, a pot too hot, or a wave too shallow. Blowholes in the joint mean damp.

mb.solder.profile.thermalmass.name: Heavy leads set the slowest joint
mb.solder.profile.thermalmass.description: Why the big electrolytics are among the joints most often hand-touched after the wave, and why the instruction to go back and check them existed at all.

mb.solder.profile.thermal.name: Why preheat sets joint quality
mb.solder.profile.thermal.description: The thermal-shock argument for the preheat tunnel, in one place. Starting the joint at 120 deg C lets the alloy flow and wet before it freezes; starting cold does not.

mb.solder.wave.name: Wave-soldering machine
mb.solder.wave.description: A conveyorised machine that drags the underside of the board through a standing wave of molten solder. Components are all inserted from the top so they point the same way, and the wave only ever touches leads and pads. It is why a 1983 line could put hundreds of sound joints on a board for the price of the solder. A single long wave exerts a strong forward drag that tears fine-pitch parts sideways, so any serious machine of this era used a twin-wave or double-peak former: a main wave plus a smaller, faster secondary wave that cuts the drag while still filling holes. That same drag, made worse by lead-free's higher melting point, is what pushed through-hole assembly off wave soldering and onto selective solder a decade later.
mb.solder.wave.note: The machine is bought for its repeatability, not its elegance.

facts.label: Conveyor speed
facts.value: typically 1.5-2.5 m/min

facts.label: Pot temperature
facts.value: approx. 245-255 deg C

facts.label: Preheat
facts.value: approx. 110-150 deg C in a tunnel before the wave

facts.label: Wave contact
facts.value: a few seconds, the length of the wave's contact length

facts.label: Wave form
facts.value: twin-wave or double-peak former, to cut forward drag on fine-pitch parts

mb.solder.wave.cooling.name: Cooling zone
mb.solder.wave.cooling.description: After the wave, boards sit in moving hot air before leaving the machine. Hot air rather than cold, because chilling a freshly soldered joint around a large thermal-mass lead is how you get a cracked solder fillet.

mb.solder.wave.nitrogen.name: Nitrogen blanket over the pot
mb.solder.wave.nitrogen.description: Many machines piped nitrogen over the solder surface to keep the oxide skin thin and stop dross forming. It also stops the skin from insulating the pot from the wave, which makes the wave itself erratic. Cheaper machines ran open to air and simply lived with the dross.

mb.solder.wave.conveyor.name: Conveyor chain and fixtures
mb.solder.wave.conveyor.description: A stainless or phenolic chain carries boards through the machine, held by their edge in fixtures spaced along the chain. Chain pitch and fixture design, not the pump, set the real throughput. The fixtures were often the board's own edge, which is one reason board edge quality was a production concern.

mb.solder.wave.foam.name: Flux foamer
mb.solder.wave.foam.description: Just before the wave, a bank of porous stone immersed in rosin flux bubbles air through it and lays a thin, even, pre-activated film on the board's underside. Foaming gives uniform coverage a spray or brush never does, and it is where the smell of boiling pine on a board line comes from.

mb.solder.wave.foam.stone.name: Sintered porous stone
mb.solder.wave.foam.stone.description: A sintered polyethylene or polyurethane stone whose pore size is chosen to bubble air finely through the flux. It clogs with crystallised flux and has to be soaked out on a schedule.

mb.solder.wave.preheat.name: Preheat tunnel
mb.solder.wave.preheat.description: An oven before the wave that brings the whole board to roughly 120 deg C so the thermal shock of hitting 250 deg C solder is spread out. It also drives off moisture, which would otherwise spit solder out of the holes as the board hits the wave.

mb.solder.wave.preheat.air.name: Recirculating hot-air preheat
mb.solder.wave.preheat.air.description: Preheating is by moving air or radiant tubes, with the zone held below the solder melting point so nothing melts early. Too little preheat gives thermally shocked joints; too much dries the resin and lifts pads off the laminate. A board full of large electrolytics takes a long time to come through, and preheater capacity is usually what sets the conveyor speed for the whole line.

mb.solder.wave.frame.name: Welded machine frame and shell
mb.solder.wave.frame.description: The pot, tunnel and conveyor sit in a welded mild-steel frame that also carries the fume hood and the flux plumbing. The mass of the frame is what keeps the wave flat while the pot runs. The steel is arc- or induction-furnace steel from the same iron ore and coke as every other machine tool on this floor.

mb.crystal.name: Master clock crystal and oscillator
mb.crystal.description: Y1, a hermetically sealed HC-49/U quartz crystal, plus the four glue-logic chips that turn it into the machine's entire timing reference: a colour subcarrier crystal oscillator, a PLL that quadruples it, a divider chain, and a phase/frequency detector that locks the dot clock to the colour clock. Every clock edge in a C64 descends from this one 11 mm metal can.
mb.crystal.note: The C64 master crystal is not a 2 MHz part. On the NTSC breadbin (ASSY 250407) Y1 is 14.31818 MHz, six times the NTSC colour subcarrier, and the 74LS629 / MC4044 PLL multiplies it by four to give an 8.1818 MHz dot clock, which the 74LS193 divides by 7 to 1.16883 MHz and the 74LS74 halves to the 1.022727 MHz Phi 2 CPU clock. The "2 MHz" figure in circulation is the approximate output of that divider, not the crystal. The PAL crystal is 17.734475 MHz, four times the PAL subcarrier; later C64B/C boards used a 16 MHz crystal with a dedicated clock-generator IC.

facts.label: Dot clock
facts.value: 8.1818 MHz NTSC / 7.882 MHz PAL

facts.label: CPU Phi 2
facts.value: 1.022727 MHz NTSC / 0.985248 MHz PAL

facts.label: Package
facts.value: HC-49/U, ~11 x 4.5 x 3.5 mm, 4 leads

facts.label: U31
facts.value: 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator (16-pin DIP)

facts.label: U30
facts.value: 74LS193 4-bit up/down counter

facts.label: U29
facts.value: 74LS74 dual D flip-flop

facts.label: U32
facts.value: MC4044 phase/frequency detector (Motorola CMOS, 14-pin DIP)

mb.crystal.oscillator.name: Oscillator and PLL circuitry
mb.crystal.oscillator.description: The crystal is only the frequency reference. Turning it into the machine's clocks takes a 74LS629 dual VCO crystal oscillator, a Motorola MC4044 phase/frequency detector, a 74LS193 divider, and a 74LS74 flip-flop, with R27 or a trimmer capacitor setting the exact pull.
mb.crystal.oscillator.note: These four are logic ICs rather than passives, but they belong in this branch because without them the quartz is inert. Their fabrication is out of scope for this file.

facts.label: Oscillator topology
facts.value: Pierce (series-mode) in the 74LS629's crystal oscillator half

facts.label: Trim
facts.value: R27 500 ohm cermet trimmer on early boards, capacitive trim on later

facts.label: PLL
facts.value: MC4044 drives the 74LS629's VCO control pin, locking the dot clock to 4x the colour clock

mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.name: PLL: MC4044 into the 74LS629 VCO
mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.description: The 74LS629's second oscillator is a voltage-controlled oscillator. The MC4044 phase/frequency detector compares a divided colour clock against the VIC-II's phase clock and returns a DC control voltage on pin 8, which the 74LS629's frequency-control pin steers. That is the whole of the C64's PLL: a crystal oscillator holding the exact subcarrier frequency, and a tracking VCO running SLOWER than it at 8.1818 MHz, locked to it, for the dot clock.
mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.note: Topology confirmed on the 250407 board: U31 is a 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator, U32 an MC4044 phase/frequency detector whose dc output on pin 8 feeds the frequency-control input, pin 2, of U31. Not established, and contradicted by the same source: the 'x4 multiply' and 'a tracking VCO four times faster' claims. The service manual gives Y1 as 14.31818 MHz producing the colour clock and the second half of U31 as the 8.1818 MHz DOT clock, so the dot clock is the SLOWER of the two - 8.1818/14.31818 is 7/4, and the phase lock is colour clock divided by 14 against dot clock divided by 8.

facts.label: Multiply
facts.value: the dot clock is the lower of the two: 8.1818 MHz against the 14.31818 MHz colour clock, a ratio of 7/4. There is no frequency multiplication; the PLL lock is colour clock /14 against dot clock /8.

facts.label: Divide
facts.value: /7 NTSC, /9 PAL

mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.pal-variant.name: PAL crystal, 17.734475 MHz
mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.pal-variant.description: The PAL machine uses a 17.734475 MHz crystal (four times the 4.433619 MHz PAL subcarrier) in the same circuit, and the 74LS193 divider is switched to divide by nine instead of seven. Later C64B/C boards moved to a 16 MHz crystal and a dedicated clock-generator IC, dropping the discrete VCO.
mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.pal-variant.note: No revision of this machine has a 2 MHz crystal: the colour clock is 14.31818 MHz NTSC and 17.734475 MHz PAL right up to the 16 MHz clock-generator change.

facts.label: PAL Y1
facts.value: 17.734475 MHz = 4 x the 4.433619 MHz PAL subcarrier

facts.label: Divider
facts.value: 74LS193 switched to divide by 9 instead of 7

facts.label: Later boards
facts.value: C64B/C moved to a 16 MHz crystal and a dedicated clock-generator IC

mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.trim-range.name: Why a trim is required at all
mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.trim-range.description: The NTSC colour subcarrier is specified to about 5 parts in 10^7, and an untrimmed crystal and oscillator would wander far more than that over temperature and supply. The trim element (R27 on breadbin boards, a capacitive trim later) lets the whole PLL be pulled onto the exact frequency at the factory and then holds it there.
mb.crystal.oscillator.pll.trim-range.note: The trim element is confirmed: the 250407 parts list has R27 as 'Pot 2K' (a 2 kilohm trimmer; a later board lists R27 as Pot 500Q), and the circuit theory says R27 can be adjusted to obtain exact output frequency. Not established: that the NTSC colour subcarrier is specified to about 5 parts in 10^7, and the account of the trim being locked at the factory.

mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce.name: Pierce oscillator and load capacitors
mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce.description: The crystal acts as a negative-resistance element in a Pierce oscillator with a small load capacitor at its CL and the drive level set by a series resistor. Its frequency is set by the crystal's CL, the load capacitors and the transistor's input capacitance all in series: at 14 MHz with a few tens of picofarads involved, a fraction of a millimetre of stray copper shifts the trim range, which is why the C64 needed an adjustable element here rather than a fixed capacitor. The oscillator is a high-gain positive-feedback amplifier at all frequencies until the crystal's impedance peaks at the design frequency, so the circuit is designed to start on noise and settle; a badly driven crystal never settles, which is the classic symptom of a cracked plate.
mb.crystal.oscillator.pierce.note: The discrete load caps are ceramic (see mb.passives.caps.trim and the C0G timing caps); a Pierce oscillator's frequency is very sensitive to stray capacitance, which is why the C64 needed an adjustable trim.

facts.label: Drive level
facts.value: tens of microwatts (mA-scale drive in the 74LS629)

mb.crystal.y1.name: Y1 quartz crystal, HC-49/U
mb.crystal.y1.description: A plano-convex quartz plate, 0.07 mm thick, with electrodes fired on its two faces, held on supports inside a small metal can filled with argon and sealed by a crimped, resistance-welded cap. The quartz is the oscillator's frequency-setting element: the whole machine's timing accuracy is the accuracy of one cut and lapped slice of Brazilian or synthetic silicon dioxide.
mb.crystal.y1.note: Natural and hydrothermal synthetic quartz are alternatives rather than parent and child, so the two feed routes hang off the crystal separately.

facts.label: Frequency tolerance
facts.value: ~+/-30 to +/-100 ppm over -10 to +60 C

facts.label: Frequency stability
facts.value: roughly +/-0.01 % over 0-50 C for a good AT-cut part

facts.label: Load
facts.value: ~30 pF CL in a Pierce oscillator

facts.label: Fill gas
facts.value: argon or krypton at a few kPa

mb.crystal.y1.case.name: HC-49/U case: crimp, weld and argon fill
mb.crystal.y1.case.description: The plate sits on a pair of wire supports in a crimped and welded nickel can, filled with argon or krypton at a few kPa. The can is drawn from nickel-plated steel or brass, and its small welded lid is what makes the unit hermetic - the reason a 1982 crystal does not drift as the humidity of an attic changes.

facts.label: Case
facts.value: HC-49/U, ~11 x 4.5 x 3.5 mm, four leads

facts.label: Fill gas
facts.value: argon or krypton at a few kPa

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: crimped collar plus a spot-welded / resistance-welded lid

facts.label: Supports
facts.value: spring wire mounts holding the plate at the stress-minimising points

mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.name: Spring-wire supports
mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.description: Two short wires spot-welded to the plate's major faces at the nodal points. Because quartz is piezoelectric, mechanically stressing it shifts its resonant frequency, so the supports must sit where the strain of the vibrating mode is smallest - the whole reason the plate is bevelled and domed.
mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.note: The piezoelectric argument is documented: quartz develops an electric potential on mechanical stress, and the resonant frequency of a quartz crystal oscillator is changed by mechanically loading it. Not established: spot-welded gold or nickel wire supports at the nodal points of the resonating mode, which is the standard crystal-package construction but appears in no source consulted.

facts.label: Position
facts.value: the mechanical nodal points of the resonating mode

facts.label: Material
facts.value: gold or nickel wire, spot-welded to the electrodes

mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.wire.name: Gold or nickel support wire
mb.crystal.y1.case.support-wire.wire.description: Fine wire, 0.1-0.2 mm, spot-welded to the plate electrodes. Gold is preferred where maximum Q is needed; nickel is the cost-driven choice for the volume 1982 HC-49.

mb.crystal.y1.case.argon-fill.name: Argon or krypton fill gas
mb.crystal.y1.case.argon-fill.description: The can is filled with a chemically inert gas before welding. Argon is preferred because it does not react with the electrode and cannot outgas; krypton was used where a slightly more hermetic atmosphere was wanted. The gas also damps acoustic vibration in the plate.
mb.crystal.y1.case.argon-fill.note: Not established: argon or krypton fill gas, the few kPa pressure, the claim that argon cannot outgas, the acoustic damping role, and the later switch to vacuum-filled hybrid cans. No document consulted describes crystal can filling.

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: a few kPa

facts.label: Alternatives
facts.value: vacuum-filled (hybrid) cans became common later

mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.name: Nickel can stock
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.description: HC-49/U cans were drawn from nickel or nickel-plated strip steel, or from brass with a nickel finish. Nickel is used because it matches the thermal expansion of the quartz and the electrode leads closely enough that the mounting stress does not drift the frequency.
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.note: HC-49/U cans were drawn from nickel or nickel-plated strip steel, or from brass with a nickel finish. Nickel matches the thermal expansion of the quartz and the electrode leads closely enough that the mounting stress does not drift the frequency.

mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.name: Welded lid and crimped collar
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.description: The lid is spot-welded or resistance-welded to the collar in an atmosphere of dry hydrogen or forming gas, which keeps the internal oxide clean and lets the fill gas stay inert. Hermeticity is what makes a forty-year-old crystal hold its frequency.
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.note: Not established: spot or resistance welding of the lid in dry hydrogen or forming gas. This is the standard HC-49 hermetic-seal practice, but no source consulted describes it for this crystal, and the manual's circuit theory says nothing about the can.

mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.gas.name: Forming gas for welding
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.weld.gas.description: A mixture of hydrogen and nitrogen used as a cover during the lid weld. Hydrogen also diffuses any internal oxide onto the getters, which is why a well-made can can have a getter mirror at the bottom after opening.

mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.stock.name: Drawn can stock
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.stock.description: The HC-49/U can is deep-drawn from thin nickel-plated strip in a progressive tool, then the crimped collar is rolled and the lid welded on. Both operations happen before the plate goes in - the can is made empty and loaded later.
mb.crystal.y1.case.nickel-can.stock.note: Not established: that the HC-49/U can is deep-drawn from nickel-plated strip in a progressive tool and that the collar is rolled. Nothing in the sources consulted describes the mechanical sequence of can manufacture.

mb.crystal.y1.cutting.name: Cutting the plate and vacuum baking
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.description: The plated blank is cut with a diamond wheel into individual resonator plates, then the plates are vacuum-baked at around 400 C to drive off adsorbed moisture and contaminants. That vacuum bake is what removes the piezoelectric pyroelectric drift and the 'dope' effect - the stress-induced frequency shift as a crystal heats - and it is why a crystal that has been opened is never a good crystal.
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.note: Not established: the 350-400 C vacuum bake for 1-2 hours and its claimed removal of pyroelectric drift and the dope effect. No document consulted describes the post-cut bake or its mechanism. The one nearby documented quartz fact is the alpha-beta transformation at 573 C, well above this bake.

facts.label: Bake
facts.value: ~350-400 C under vacuum for 1-2 h

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: good level frequency stability over temperature

mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.name: Cleaning between steps
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.description: Every step from lapping onward is done washed and clean: a fingerprint on a 0.07 mm plate changes the frequency. Crystal preparation is one of the few wet, cold, dirty-looking processes in electronics.
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.note: Not established: that cleaning from lapping onward is done washed and clean, and that a fingerprint on a 0.07 mm plate shifts the frequency. Sensible contamination control, but unsourced.

mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.deionise.name: Deionised rinse water
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.deionise.description: Every crystal process rinse uses deionised water, because a single dissolved ion on a resonating plate changes the frequency measurably. City water is nowhere good enough.
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.cleanroom.deionise.note: Not established: the specific claim that a single dissolved ion on a resonating plate changes the frequency measurably. Deionised rinse water as the standard is uncontroversial; the quantitative sensitivity assertion is not documented in any source consulted.

mb.crystal.y1.cutting.dicing-saw.name: Diamond dicing saw
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.dicing-saw.description: A thin resin-bonded diamond wheel, ~0.03-0.05 mm thick, cutting the plated blank into resonators. The wheel has to be extremely thin and extremely flat to avoid chipping a 0.07 mm plate.
mb.crystal.y1.cutting.dicing-saw.note: Not established: the 0.03-0.05 mm resin-bonded diamond wheel thickness. Nothing consulted documents dicing saws for resonator plates.

mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.name: Metal electrodes on the blank faces
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.description: Chromium is evaporated or sputtered onto both faces as an adhesion layer, then gold or silver is deposited over it as the conductive electrode, through a shadow mask that defines the electrode area. Chromium-gold is the classic 1980s crystal electrode stack: Cr to bond, Au to conduct.
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.note: Some 1980s HC-49/U crystals used nickel electrodes over chromium for economy; gold-over-chromium was the higher-reliability standard.

facts.label: Adhesion layer
facts.value: Cr or Ti, ~50-100 nm

facts.label: Conductive layer
facts.value: Au (~200-400 nm) or Ag

facts.label: Pattern
facts.value: shadow-mask defined, 6-14 mm2 for a 1982 HC-49

mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.gold-film.name: Gold electrode film
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.gold-film.description: Gold evaporated through a shadow mask to give the electrode its final geometry and conductivity. The mask pattern fixes the electrode area, which together with the plate thickness is what sets the crystal capacitance.
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.gold-film.note: Not established: shadow-mask evaporation, the 200-400 nm gold thickness, and that mask area together with plate thickness sets the crystal capacitance. No source consulted describes crystal electrode metallisation.

mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.gold-film.mask.name: Evaporation shadow mask
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.gold-film.mask.description: A thin metal mask placed above the rotating blank during evaporation so the electrode pattern is defined. The mask is made from a drawn stainless or nickel strip, chemically etched to the electrode shape.

mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.chromium.name: Chromium adhesion layer
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.chromium.description: Chromium is evaporated as the adhesion layer because bare quartz will not hold gold by van der Waals forces alone. Chromium wets both the quartz surface and the gold film, and it is itself a hard, chemically inert metal.
mb.crystal.y1.electrodes.chromium.note: Not established: chromium as the adhesion layer, the 50-100 nm thickness, and the van der Waals argument. Chromium-on-gold adhesion layers are real practice, but no document consulted states this for crystal electrodes.

mb.crystal.y1.supports.name: Mounting and soldering of the crystal
mb.crystal.y1.supports.description: The four HC-49 leads are formed to a right angle and soldered onto the board in a wave-solder pass. The crystal's case sits at the board's natural mechanical frequency well below the circuit's operating frequency, which is deliberate: an HC-49 body has several overtone resonances that would otherwise produce spurious oscillator modes.

mb.crystal.y1.grinding.name: Grinding the lens shape
mb.crystal.y1.grinding.description: The face is bevelled and the outline ground so the finished blank is a lens or plano-convex dome rather than a flat slab. The convexity is deliberate: it makes the crystal's resonant frequency less sensitive to surface damage and to where the mounting points press on it.

facts.label: Final plate thickness
facts.value: ~0.07 mm at the centre, bevelled to ~0.1 mm at the edge

facts.label: Why bevelled
facts.value: so the supports never touch the vibrating centre

mb.crystal.y1.grinding.diamond-wheel.name: Diamond grinding wheel
mb.crystal.y1.grinding.diamond-wheel.description: A resin-bonded diamond wheel, used wet, that bevels the plate edge and cuts the lens curvature. In 1982 diamond abrasive was largely synthetic, made from graphite under a shock wave; natural diamond was reserved for dressing the wheels.

mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.name: Sawing, lapping and X-ray orienting the blank
mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.description: Rough crystal is sawn into blanks, then the cut face is lapped to about 0.15 mm and X-ray diffracted to find its crystallographic orientation. Orientation is everything: only an AT-cut at the right angle gives the flat temperature curve a frequency-stable oscillator needs.

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: X-ray diffractometer; AT-cut ~35 deg to the X axis for 1980s units

mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping.name: Lapping and double-lap polishing
mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping.description: The cut blank is lapped on rotating cast-iron plates with progressively finer abrasives (aluminium oxide, then colloidal silica) down to about 0.15 mm, then double-lapped against a second plate to remove bow and damage left by the saw. Crystal blanks for a 1982 oscillator were lapped on plates run by lapidary and lapping shops, not in the same plant that makes the finished crystal.
mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping.note: Not established: the double-lap sequence, aluminium oxide down to colloidal silica, the 0.15 mm final thickness, and that blanks were lapped by outside lapidary shops. The tree's own source for the parent node is a lapping reference, not a crystal-process source; no document consulted here supports these figures.

facts.label: Final thickness
facts.value: ~0.15 mm before final grinding

facts.label: Abrasives
facts.value: Al2O3 down to colloidal silica

mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping..name: Final lapping abrasive
mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.lapping..description: The last lapping stage uses a colloidal silica slurry, which polishes rather than cuts. Colloidal silica is precipitated from a dilute sodium silicate solution, itself made from silica sand and sodium carbonate.

mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.xray-ori.name: X-ray orientation and AT-cut angle selection
mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.xray-ori.description: A synthetic rough is indexed by X-ray diffraction so its Z axis and X axis are known, then sawn at a chosen angle to the X axis (the 'AT-cut'). The mid-1980s standard for general-purpose oscillators was about 35 degrees; this angle is chosen because it lands the resonance on a flat, temperature-insensitive point in the quartz stiffness-temperature curve.
mb.crystal.y1.blank-preparation.xray-ori.note: Quartz is documented as trigonal alpha-quartz in space group P3221 with a fixed cell, so crystallographic orientation by X-ray is meaningful. Not established: the four-circle diffractometer, the ~35 degree AT-cut as the mid-1980s general-purpose standard, and the claim that this angle flattens the frequency-temperature curve. The 573 C alpha-beta transition is documented but is not the frequency-temperature flatness argument.

facts.label: Instrument
facts.value: four-circle X-ray diffractometer with a goniometer

facts.label: AT-cut angle
facts.value: ~35 degrees

facts.label: Why
facts.value: flattens the frequency-temperature curve

mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.name: Hydrothermal synthetic quartz
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.description: Because natural quartz is limited and variable, industry moved to growing it: an autoclave is charged with silica (often crushed natural quartz) in a hot sodium-hydroxide solution and heated at around 400 C and 150 MPa. Quartz grows on seed crystals hung in the solution, growing the rough in days rather than geological time. This is the source of nearly all quartz crystal blanks made from about the mid-1970s onward.
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.note: This node was moved up out of natural-quartz, where it sat as if natural and synthetic quartz were parent and child; its id retains the old path because ids are stable. By the early 1980s this route, not mined rock crystal, supplied nearly every blank in the industry.

facts.label: Growth pressure
facts.value: ~150 MPa

facts.label: Growth time
facts.value: days to a few weeks

mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.s.name: Quartz sand / crushed quartz feed
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.s.description: The silica feedstock for the autoclave is cleaned quartz sand or lumps of milky quartz. Natural quartz sand is a common beach and dune sand: essentially SiO2, left behind as quartz survives weathering while everything else dissolves and washes away.

mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.a.name: Steel autoclave with seed crystals
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.a.description: A filled, sealed pressure vessel - usually Hastelloy or 17-4PH steel liner - held at high temperature and pressure so an alkaline solution dissolves silica from the feed and re-deposits it on thin zoned seed plates hung in the vessel. Temperature gradients create the supersaturation that drives growth, and the growth zones themselves are what later become the tuned crystal resonators.
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.a.note: Hydrothermal growth in an autoclave is documented, and that by the 1950s it produced synthetic quartz on an industrial scale so that today virtually all quartz crystal used in electronics is synthetic. Not established: the ~400 C and ~150 MPa conditions, the Hastelloy or 17-4PH liner, the NaOH or KOH solvent, the zoned seed plates, and the Rouquay-type process name.

facts.label: Solution
facts.value: NaOH or KOH in water

facts.label: Rouquay-type process
facts.value: industrial standard from the mid-1970s

mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.a.name: Alkali solvent
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.a.description: The growth solution is hot concentrated sodium or potassium hydroxide, which dissolves silica at the elevated temperature while quartz re-deposits on the seeds. The alkali is made by chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, so the crystal ultimately touches rock salt as well as quartz sand.
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.synthetic.a.note: Not established: hot concentrated sodium or potassium hydroxide as the growth solvent, and that the caustic is made by chlor-alkali electrolysis so the crystal chain reaches rock salt. Hydrothermal growth in an autoclave is documented; the alkali solvent and its chlorine link are not, in the sources consulted.

mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.name: Natural rock crystal
mb.crystal.y1.natural-quartz.description: Gem-quality clear quartz for crystal units came historically from the rock-crystal veins of Minas Gerais in Brazil, prized for natural faces that need no lapping and for the very low defect density that makes a low-phase-noise oscillator possible. By the early 1980s this was being displaced by hydrothermal synthetic quartz, which is chemically identical and far more uniform.

mb.passives.name: Mainboard passive components
mb.passives.description: The roughly 250-odd resistors, capacitors, trimmers and networks soldered to a Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 motherboard. No ICs, no connectors: only the two-terminal and adjustable parts that set the bias, timing and filtering of everything else on the board.
mb.passives.note: Population figures are taken from a transcription of the 250407 bill of materials; Commodore shipped several board revisions (250407, 250425, 250466, 250469) and the exact mix of disc vs monolithic ceramic capacitors moved between them.

facts.label: Discrete resistors
facts.value: ~70 axial 1/4 W

facts.label: Thick-film SIP networks
facts.value: 4 (two 8-way 33 ohm, one 8-way 3k3 bussed, one 10-way 3k3 bussed)

facts.label: Trimmers
facts.value: 1 x 500 ohm trimmer potentiometer (R27), 1 x variable capacitor

mb.passives.caps.name: Capacitors
mb.passives.caps.description: The mainboard's decoupling, timing, filtering and coupling capacitors. Overwhelmingly ceramic (0.1 uF bypass plus small timing values), with a smaller tail of aluminium electrolytics for the low-frequency supplies and film polyester for the SID output coupling.

facts.label: Ceramic
facts.value: ~54 x 0.1 uF/50 V plus 15-1800 pF timing caps

facts.label: Electrolytic
facts.value: ~15 x 10 uF/25 V radial + larger 100-2200 uF axial

facts.label: Film
facts.value: a handful of 0.22 uF polyester

mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.name: Capacitor wrap, sleeving and marking
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.description: Not a separate component but the packaging shared across the capacitor families: dipped epoxy for ceramic disc and monolithic parts, printed PVC or polyester sleeving for film caps, cardboard or aluminium sleeves for electrolytics, and printed value/brand markings on all of them.
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.note: The film and foil wrap is covered here for the ceramic and film parts, and under alu-electrolytic.assembly for the electrolytics.

mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.pvc-sl.name: Printed PVC sleeve
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.pvc-sl.description: Film capacitors arrived in a printed plastic sleeve printed with the value, the rating and the maker. Sleeve polymer is the same PVC family as the case and the cable jacket.

mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.name: Capacitor value marking ink
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.description: Values were printed on the sleeve or dipped coat in an oil-based or epoxy ink on an offset or screen coater. The two-digit and three-digit codes (104 for 100 nF, 104K5V) only became an industry standard in the 1970s.

mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.pi.name: Ink pigment
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.pi.description: The value marking pigment is carbon black for dark parts and azo or phthalocyanine colour for bright ones, in a resin vehicle that will not be attacked by the board cleaning solvents.
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.ink.pi.note: The carbon-black furnace that makes this pigment is mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.carbon-film.powder.carbon-black, linked here by id.

mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.epoxy-.name: E dipped conformal coat
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.epoxy-.description: Ceramic and monolithic parts were dip-coated in epoxy or PVC after firing to seal the porous body and to carry the printed marking. A dipped part looks identical to a moulded one, which is why it is hard to tell from a photograph whether a given C64 ceramic is disc or monolithic.

mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.epoxy-.name: Dip-coating line
mb.passives.caps.wrap-and-marking.epoxy-.description: Parts on a wire rack are dipped in an epoxy or PVC solution and withdrawn so the coating tapers at both ends, leaving a characteristic tapered shoulder at the lead exit. A second dip gives the second shoulder.

mb.passives.caps.trim.name: Trimmer and variable capacitors
