mb.passives.caps.trim.description: Small adjustable capacitors used to compensate or trim a circuit. On C64-family boards a trimmer capacitor sits in the crystal oscillator's load network, pulling the frequency exactly onto the NTSC or PAL colour subcarrier; later Commodore boards replaced the earlier adjustable resistor with this capacitor trim.

facts.label: Range
facts.value: a few pF to tens of pF

facts.label: Function
facts.value: crystal load-network trim; swapped in for R27 on later boards

mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.name: Air-gap / film trimmer capacitor
mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.description: Two sets of interdigitated metal plates with an adjustable overlap, separated by air or a thin film. Turning the screw changes the overlap and therefore the capacitance continuously, letting the factory trim the oscillator to the exact subcarrier frequency. The dielectric is air, which is why these parts are stable and non-drifting.
mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.note: The exact trim capacitor reference designator on the 250407 is uncertain to me; the service manual confirms R27 is the adjustable resistor and the later boards use a capacitive trim in the same role.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: interdigitated plates, air or film dielectric

facts.label: Package
facts.value: ~5 x 5 x 4 mm, screw-adjustable

mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-pl.name: Stator and rotor plates
mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-pl.description: The trimmer's rotor is a small disc of alumina ceramic, silver-metallised on one face through a spiral or interdigitated pattern. Turning the screw rotates the disc against a fixed plate, so the overlapping metallised area - and hence the capacitance - changes continuously.
mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-pl.note: Not established: that this is the rotor and stator geometry, the spiral or interdigitated silver pattern, and the continuous overlap-to-capacitance relationship. The service manual lists CT-1 as 'Trimmer 7.7-40pF' but does not describe its construction, and the manual's PLLC replacement notes point to it as a variable.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: alumina ceramic with a silver counter-electrode, air gap

mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-pl.name: Alumina rotor plate material
mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-pl.description: The rotor disc is alumina, polished and metallised with a spiral or interdigitated silver pattern. Alumina is used because it is dimensionally stable, machinable to a fine finish and a good insulator at the trimmer's working voltage.
mb.passives.caps.trim.air-gap.ceramic-pl.note: Not established: alumina as the rotor material, its polish and metallisation, and its role as a good insulator at the trimmer's working voltage. No document consulted describes trimmer rotor plates.

mb.passives.caps.mica.name: Mica capacitor
mb.passives.caps.mica.description: A capacitor built from thin sheets of natural muscovite mica with vacuum-deposited aluminium or silver counter-electrodes. Superb temperature stability and high dielectric strength, too expensive and too fragile for general use, so mica was reserved for precision and high-voltage niches in equipment of the era.
mb.passives.caps.mica.note: Mica was being displaced by film and ceramic in mass-market consumer boards by the 1980s; the sputtered metal-insulator-metal mica construction is a later, higher-reliability form.

mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.name: Vacuum-deposited counter-electrodes
mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.description: Aluminium or silver is evaporated or sputtered through a shadow-mask onto the mica sheets; sheets are stacked with a thin metallised layer between each, bonded under heat and pressure, and the stack is diced into individual capacitors.
mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.note: Vacuum evaporation was the 1982 technique; reactive sputtering of a dielectric was the later MIM form.

facts.label: Deposition
facts.value: vacuum evaporation or sputtering through a shadow mask

mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.alum.name: Aluminium electrode evaporation
mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.alum.description: Aluminium is evaporated rather than sputtered because it is cheap and vapourises at a manageable temperature; it is then left unoxidised under vacuum. Silver electrodes were used where the highest capacitance per unit area was needed.
mb.passives.caps.mica.metallisation.alum.note: Not established: that aluminium rather than silver was evaporated for the C64's mica capacitors, the manageability argument, and the silver electrodes used where maximum capacitance per unit area was needed. No source consulted describes mica capacitor electrode metallisation.

mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.name: Muscovite mica, heat-split into sheets
mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.description: Natural muscovite is mined in large crystal books from pegmatites and delaminated by heating and cementing against a hot plate, so it splits along its perfect basal cleavage into micrometre-thick, optically flat sheets. The crystal's naturally layered atomic structure gives a very uniform, very thin, very stable dielectric when split this way.

facts.label: Split thickness
facts.value: ~1-60 um depending on grade

mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-spl.name: Heat-and-cement splitting and ruby splitting
mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-spl.description: A mica book is mounted on a hot plate; a hot blade of mica is pressed onto it with a cement stick, which drives a wedge along the perfect basal cleavage and peels off a sheet a few microns thick. Repeated, it yields hundreds of optically flat sheets from one crystal, and it is the labour-intensive step that made mica capacitors expensive.
mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-spl.note: Splitting is done by hand against a hot plate; automation did not reach the industry in this period.

facts.label: Split thickness
facts.value: ~1-60 um depending on grade

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: thousands of sheets per cubic foot of rough

mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-spl.name: Hot knife and cement stick
mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.heat-spl.description: A heated mica blade driven by a cement stick along the cleavage plane. The blade has to be hot enough to part the sheets without charring the cement, and both blade and stick are specialist consumables of the splitting trade.

mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.pegmatit.name: Pegmatite host rock
mb.passives.caps.mica.muscovite.pegmatit.description: Mica books grow in the giant granitic pegmatites of the Precambrian shield - Minas Gerais in Brazil, Rajasthan in India, Madagascar, and in the United States the Appalachian and Spruce Pine districts of North Carolina. It is mined in situ and split, not manufactured. The books are followed underground and extracted by hand, selectively enough that the surrounding pegmatite stays intact; Brazilian, Indian and US districts all supply capacitor-grade mica. Mica is traded in sizes - block for the thickest uses, thins for splitting - and grading and splitting, not mining, account for most of the value in the material.

mb.passives.caps.film.name: Film capacitors (polyester / polystyrene)
mb.passives.caps.film.description: Film capacitors use a thin metallised plastic film as the dielectric. Non-polar, stable, and tolerant of voltage and temperature excursions. The C64 uses polyester (Melinex/PET) for coupling and decoupling in the analogue paths; polystyrene appears in the precision timing networks of the same era's equipment.
mb.passives.caps.film.note: Construction and era are documented: metallised aluminium or zinc deposited directly on the plastic film or a separate metal foil; paper and metallised paper almost completely replaced by PET film for low-power DC applications from around 1980; polystyrene used where its near-zero temperature coefficient suits tuned circuits. The board value is now confirmed from the primary parts lists - C20 and C21 are 'Film .22 /tF, 100V, 20%', and the 250425-01 list gives 'Film Rdl .22/iF 100V 20%'. Not established: that the film is polyester (the parts lists say only 'Film'), and the 63 VAC working class.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: biaxially-oriented PET (Melinex) or polystyrene

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: vacuum-deposited aluminium or zinc on the film

facts.label: Value on board
facts.value: 0.22 uF polyester, 63 VAC / 100 V class

mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.name: Polystyrene film capacitor
mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.description: A polystyrene dielectric: exceptionally stable, very low dielectric absorption and low loss, historically the timing capacitor of choice for precision RC oscillators before polystyrene's poor mechanical behaviour pushed it into disfavour. Used in analogue equipment of the era, but not a significant part on the C64 mainboard.
mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.note: Polystyrene parts are not confirmed in the 250407 parts list.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: polystyrene, very low loss, very stable

mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.metall.name: Vacuum metallisation of PS film
mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.metall.description: The same vacuum-deposited aluminium electrode as on the polyester film, but on a more delicate substrate: polystyrene outgasses and embrittles under vacuum heat, so the film has to be baked and the deposition kept cool.

mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.styren.name: Styrene polymerisation to polystyrene
mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.styren.description: Free-radical or ionic polymerisation of styrene, in bulk suspension or emulsion, gives the amorphous thermoplastic. Unmodified polystyrene is brittle and has poor moisture resistance, which is precisely why metalised polystyrene was restricted to sealed precision parts and lost out to polypropylene.
mb.passives.caps.film.polystyrene.styren.note: Not established: brittleness and poor moisture resistance as the reason metallised polystyrene was restricted, and the free-radical or ionic polymerisation route. What is documented is the commercial outcome - polystyrene film could not be made thinner than 10 um and its maximum temperature rating reached only 85 C, so it was largely replaced by polyester; it was valued for high capacitance stability, low dissipation factor, low leakage and a near-zero temperature coefficient.

mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.name: Vacuum-metallised polyester film
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.description: PET pellets are extruded into a cast film, then stretched fast in two perpendicular directions to several times their original length, orienting the polymer chains. That gives a very thin, very uniform, high-tensile dielectric; then a sub-micron metal layer is vacuum-deposited on one or both faces and the metallised film is wound on a core. No separate foil is used - the electrode IS the deposited layer.
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.note: Not established: the 1-6 um film thickness quoted for 1982. The process is documented - biaxial stretching in longitudinal and transverse directions, a vacuum-deposited aluminium metallisation of about 0.03 um on one or both sides, wound onto a mother roll about 1 m wide - and the modern minimum film thickness is quoted as 0.6 um, so a 1982 figure would be thicker, not thinner.

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: ~10-50 nm Al, vacuum deposited

mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.name: PET polymerisation
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.description: The film base is polyethylene terephthalate, made by condensing bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate - itself from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid - in a melt polymeriser at ~250-290 C under vacuum. The terephthalic acid came from paraxylene, which came from the aromatics fraction of a steam cracker or a catalytic reformer.
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.note: Not established: the melt condensation route, the 250-290 C under vacuum, and the bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate intermediate. The one sourced PET fact in hand is the trade names Hostaphan and Mylar and the polyester family classification, which is not a synthesis route.

facts.label: Polymerisation
facts.value: melt condensation at ~270 C under vacuum

facts.label: Monomer route
facts.value: paraxylene -> terephthalic acid; ethylene glycol

mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.name: Para-xylene
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.description: Paraxylene sits in the aromatics complex of a large refinery, separated from a mixed xylene fraction by fractional distillation and adsorption. It is the pivot molecule of the entire polyester industry: 1982 saw PET moving from bottle-grade into film, fibre and capacitor dielectric at once.
mb.passives.caps.film.polyester-metallis.note: Not established: the Urex and Parex adsorption processes, the aromatics-complex location, and the 1982 shift of PET from bottle grade into film and capacitor dielectric. No document consulted covers paraxylene production.

facts.label: Separation
facts.value: Urex and Parex adsorption processes

mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.name: Ceramic disc (monolithic disc) capacitor
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.description: A single fired barium-titanate disc with silver electrodes fired onto its two faces. Enormous capacitance for its size and very cheap, but microphonically noisy, temperature-drifty and physically large, with no self-cancelling inductance. On C64 boards of this era the small 0.1 uF parts were already largely the multilayer form.

facts.label: Electrodes
facts.value: silver paste screen-printed and fired on

facts.label: Breakdown
facts.value: ~2.5 kV per um of effective dielectric thickness (design guideline)

facts.label: Weakness
facts.value: resonant above a few MHz; large body

mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.name: Pressing, sintering and silver-firing
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.description: BaTiO3 powder is pressed into a disc, sintered at 1200-1300 C, then silver electrode paste is screen-printed onto each face and fired at 700-850 C so the silver is glass-bonded to the ceramic. Only two electrodes exist, so the part cannot cancel its own inductance - the structural reason a disc is useless at radio frequencies and a multilayer is not.
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.note: Not established: the 1200-1300 C sinter and the 700-850 C silver electrode fire through the glass frit. What is documented is the construction - the early ceramic disc style was a disc with metallisation on both sides contacted with tinned wires, and the modern disc style is a single-layer disc with a resin coating and through-hole leads. The single-electrode-pair structure is the documented reason a disc has no internal inductance cancellation.

facts.label: Ag electrode fire
facts.value: ~700-850 C through the glass frit

mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.name: Disc body material
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.description: The ceramic body of a high-K disc is a modified barium titanate with a glass phase, on an alumina or steatite base. The dielectric-strength figure of about 2.5 kV per micron of effective thickness is a design guideline for the ceramic, not for the finished part.

mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.name: Steatite or alumina base
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.description: Low-firing ceramic substrates, steatite (magnesium silicate) or alumina, onto which the high-K layer is applied. Steatite is cheap and fires low; alumina is tougher and better at heat.

mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.name: Disc press and sinter
mb.passives.caps.ceramic-disc.press-sint.description: A mechanical or hydraulic press blanks the disc to a controlled thickness; the sinter then densifies it and fires on the silver electrodes.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.name: Tantalum capacitor
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.description: A polarised capacitor built around sintered tantalum powder with an anodic oxide dielectric and a solid electrolyte. Low leakage and very good stability for its size; in the early 1980s tantalum was the default decoupling choice on high-performance professional digital boards.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.note: The breadbin C64 250407 uses aluminium electrolytics and ceramics, NOT tantalum on its logic. Tantalum was standard in the same period's professional and instrumentation designs and appears elsewhere in Commodore hardware of the era. Included for era breadth and for the tantalum supply story; do not read it as mainboard content.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder.name: Columbite ore to capacitor-grade powder
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder.description: Columbite-tantalite ore is digested in hydrofluoric acid in an autoclave at 100-200 C to dissolve the tantalum as a fluorotantalate, the solution is treated with potassium chloride or potassium hydroxide to precipitate K2Ta2O7, and that intermediate is converted to a metallic or oxide powder by sodium reduction, by an aluminium or copper chloride reduction, or by a KCl/KF salt melt. Each step loses yield, which is why an ore shortage shows up in capacitor prices months after the mining news.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder.note: This is the standard industrial route, deliberately compressed: several genuinely distinct flows are described as one node rather than over-claiming which variant a given capacitor maker used.

facts.label: Digestion
facts.value: HF in an autoclave at ~100-200 C

facts.label: Precipitation
facts.value: K2Ta2O7 from KCl/KOH

facts.label: Reduction routes
facts.value: Na reduction, Al or Cu reduction, or KCl/KF salt melt

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..name: Columbite-tantalite ore
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..description: Columbite-tantalite is a solid solution of columbite and tantalite, mined both as placer gravels and as lode pegmatites. Concentrating it needs gravity, magnetic and electrostatic separation followed by an acid-leach circuit, because only a few per cent of the rock is Ta2O5; the concentrate may reach 10-30 % Ta2O5. Because the ore is bulk low-grade rock, mining and concentration - not the chemistry - is where most of the cost of a tantalum capacitor lives. Tantalum-bearing minerals are dense and so concentrate naturally in stream and beach placers below any pegmatite outcrop, and much of the 1980s supply was won by artisanal and semi-industrial alluvial mining in the Kivu highlands, which is exactly why ore supply could be disrupted by regional politics rather than by a mine closure. Historically the ore came from the Congo and from Rwanda-Burundi, which is precisely why Western capacitor supply chains were politically and economically exposed in this period.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.ore-to-powder..note: The DRC ore became a headline conflict-mineral story only from the late 1990s; in 1983-84 the problem was ordinary market tightness and price escalation.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis..name: Capacitor-grade recycling loop
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis..description: Because tantalum metal is expensive, tantalum-bearing scrap - rejected capacitors, anode dust, trimmed pellet scrap - was recovered and returned to the powder supply. This is why a 1983-84 shortage hit prices so hard: recycled powder could not be substituted for virgin powder in a dielectric that had to be defect-free.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis.name: Early-1980s tantalum supply squeeze
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis.description: Capacitor tantalum depends on columbite-tantalite ore, essentially all of it from the Kivu region of Zaire and neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi. A collapse in the electronics market in 1982-83 drained the supply chain's stocks, then demand spiked again in 1984 on the PC and automotive booms. The USGS records a significant spike in tantalum demand in 1984, with US factory sales of tantalum capacitors at an all-time high and escalating prices pushing consumers to substitute aluminium parts and to design tantalum out where they could. It was a real, documented shortage in exactly the C64's production window. The documented engineering response was to reduce tantalum content where possible, substitute aluminium electrolytics, and lengthen qualified lead times - a good example of how a metals shortage propagates into board design decisions within eighteen months.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.supply-crisis.note: The 1984 demand spike and the all-time-high factory-sales figure are verified against USGS Circular OF01-349. No peak capacitor-grade powder price for 1983-84 is stated here because no reliable figure for that grade and year could be sourced. The recycling loop is a real node under the capacitor; this note carries the shortage itself.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.name: Tantalum lead, braze and epoxy seal
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.description: The anode lead is drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the sintered pellet, then the assembly is sealed by an epoxy dip. On wet-slug types the hermetic case is glass or a welded metal can with a Teflon ring seal. The part is then marked with its value, rating and the manufacturer.

facts.label: Anode lead
facts.value: drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the pellet

facts.label: Braze
facts.value: silver or silver-graphite drop for the lead joint; Ta-Au braze on some types

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: epoxy dip for solid types; welded metal can for wet-slug types

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.name: Epoxy dip seal
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.description: Solid tantalum parts were sealed by dipping in epoxy and curing, which protects the brittle MnO2/dielectric stack against handling and moisture. Wet-slug parts instead used a welded metal can with a glass or Teflon seal.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.name: Epoxy resin and bisphenol A
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.description: The standard epoxy of the period: bisphenol A condensed with epichlorohydrin, cured with an amine. Both halves are petrochemical, and bisphenol A was the dominant resin for adhesive, coating, printed-board and capacitor sealants alike.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.packaging.seal.note: Resin-dipped solid tantalum parts are documented. Not established: that the dip sealant was a bisphenol A epoxy cured with an amine, or that bisphenol A dominated capacitor sealants. No source consulted establishes epoxy or bisphenol A.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.name: Anodic Ta2O5 formation and MnO2 solid electrolyte
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.description: The sintered anode is anodised to grow the Ta2O5 dielectric, then coated with manganese dioxide by pyrolysing manganese nitrate: the pellet is dipped into an aqueous nitrate solution and baked at about 250 C to leave the dioxide coat - the classic 1980s solid tantalum part. A sintered silver-paste counter-electrode existed as an alternative construction. Today's conductive-polymer tantalum is a late-1990s development. The anode is anodised at a voltage above its rated working voltage, usually by a factor of 1.5-2, to build a defect-free oxide; the rated voltage of the part is set by that formation step and cannot be adjusted afterwards.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.note: Two divergences from the documented process. The counter-electrode is described as made by pyrolysis of manganese NITRATE, not manganese chloride. And the safety margin between forming voltage and rated voltage for solid MnO2 tantalum is given as typically 2 to 4, not the 1.5-2 quoted here. The anodising step itself is documented: the pellet is submerged in a weak acid, DC is applied, and the total dielectric thickness is set by the final voltage held.

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: Ta2O5 grown anodically

facts.label: Counter-electrode
facts.value: MnO2 from manganese nitrate pyrolysis (standard); sintered Ag paste (alternative)

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: forming voltage sets the working voltage, with a safety margin in oxide thickness of typically 2 to 4 times the rated voltage

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.for.name: Counter-electrode body
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.for.description: Below the manganese dioxide sits the original tantalum anode body and its second termination. The layer stack is metal, dielectric, counter-electrode, then a conductive path to the case - all inside an epoxy dip.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.man.name: Manganese chloride for pyrolysis
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.dielectric.man.description: MnCl2 is vapour-decomposed on the hot tantalum surface in a furnace at several hundred degrees, leaving a conformal MnO2 layer that acts as the solid counter-electrode. The chloride is shipped as a hydrate and is hygroscopic, so it had to be kept dry.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.name: Sintered tantalum anode
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.description: Capacitor-grade tantalum powder is pressed around a tantalum riser wire that becomes the anode connection, and the pellet is vacuum sintered at high temperature so that the powder takes on a sponge-like structure with all particles interconnected. The Ta2O5 dielectric then grows on that internal surface, which is why a gram of powder stores far more capacitance than a gram of film.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.note: Contradicted on the powder figure: capacitor-grade tantalum powder is described as having a typical particle size of 2-10 um, not sub-micron, and the quoted CV/g range of 20k-200k is stated as a ten-fold improvement achieved since the mid-1980s, so 100k-200k uF.C/V per gram cannot be attributed to 1982. The sinter figure is also given as 1200-1800 C, wider than the 1200-1400 C here. The 2-4 m2/g surface area is unsourced.

facts.label: Powder
facts.value: typical particle size 2-10 um; finer grades give higher surface area per unit volume

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: typically 1200-1800 C under vacuum

facts.label: CV product
facts.value: about 20,000 uF.C/V per gram for the earlier material; the roughly ten-fold rise to 200,000 is described as a later achievement and so cannot be attributed to 1982

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.press.name: Anode pressing and sintering
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.press.description: Powder is blended with a binder and pressed around the wire, then debound and sintered in vacuum or flowing hydrogen at 1200-1400 C. The pressed pellet is deliberately porous - roughly half its volume is void - because that void is where the dielectric forms.
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.press.note: Not established: that roughly half the pressed pellet's volume is void. What is documented is that sintering turns the powder into a sponge-like monolithic lattice that is highly porous with a large internal surface area, at 1200-1800 C under vacuum.

mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.name: Drawn tantalum wire
mb.passives.caps.tantalum.anode.wire.description: The anode lead is fine drawn tantalum wire, spot-welded to the sintered pellet, drawn by the same machinery as refractory metals for furnace leads. Whether the anode body is built from reduced metallic powder or from sintered oxide powder, the specification is the same: extremely high purity, sub-micron, high surface area. Impurities here are the defect mechanism that causes tantalum dielectric failures, and every stage from columbite-tantalite concentrate to powder discards most of the feed, which is why a tantalum capacitor carried a high metal cost per cubic centimetre even in 1982.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.name: Aluminium electrolytic capacitor
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.description: The polarised bulk capacitors: about fifteen 10 uF/25 V radial parts decoupling the SID and video analogue rails, plus larger axial 100-2200 uF parts on the rectified supply rails. Value comes from a nanometres-thick anodic oxide on etched aluminium foil soaked in electrolyte - cheap, large capacitance, and the bulk of the board's supply-rail filtering.

facts.label: Radial parts
facts.value: ~15 x 10 uF/25 V, 5 x 5 mm can

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging.name: Ageing and burn-in
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging.description: Finished parts are held at an elevated temperature under DC bias so the oxide re-thickens and the leakage current settles: typically 1-2x the rated voltage at 85-125 C for hours to days. A 1980s capacitor therefore arrives already partly formed, which is why an electrolytic recovered from a two-year-old Commodore machine often measures better than a brand-new one.

facts.label: Burn-in
facts.value: ~1-2x rated voltage at 85-125 C, hours to days

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: reduces initial leakage and stabilises capacitance

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..name: Capacitance and leakage test
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..description: Parts are tested for capacitance, dissipation factor and leakage at rated temperature. Rejection rates in a commodity 10 uF 25 V part were small but non-zero, and every rejected part was a loss of scrap aluminium. A bridge or LCR meter at rated frequency and temperature gives capacitance and dissipation factor, and a DC bias step gives leakage; rejection on leakage is what catches a pinhole in the oxide, the classic failure mode of a fresh electrolytic.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..note: 100 % final measurement of capacitance, leakage current and impedance after post-forming is documented, and the dissipation factor is documented as the datasheet alternative to ESR. Not established: testing at rated temperature specifically, the commodity rejection rate, and that leakage rejection catches a pinhole in the oxide.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..name: Burn-in chamber
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.aging..description: A temperature-controlled rack of trays in which finished parts are held at temperature and bias. A good capacitor plant in 1982 might burn in for hours or days, which is why vintage electrolytics so often arrive already formed.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Crimping, sleeving and end-fill bung
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: Aluminium or tinned-copper alloy terminal tabs are crimped onto the anode and cathode edges of the wound pack. The pack is then sleeved - PVC heat-shrink or a printed cardboard outer - and sealed at the end with a rubber or PVC bung that retains the electrolyte against its expansion over temperature. The paper and foil layers you see when you cut one open are the winding itself.

facts.label: Terminal
facts.value: crimped Al or Cu alloy tab; anode polarity marked on the sleeve

facts.label: Sleeve
facts.value: PVC heat-shrink or printed cardboard outer

facts.label: End seal
facts.value: rubber / PVC end-fill bung

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Aluminium terminal tab
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: A soft aluminium or aluminium-alloy tab, crimped onto the foil edge. Pure aluminium is used because it is the only metal that will not form a galvanic or resistive joint with the foil it must touch.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.note: Terminal welding to lead-out terminals during winding is documented. Not established: crimping, and the claim that pure aluminium is used because it will not form a galvanic or resistive joint with the foil, or the iron and silicon limits of a few tenths of a per cent.

facts.label: Alloy limit
facts.value: Fe and Si above a few tenths of a per cent make the tab hard and prone to sludge in the electrolyte

facts.label: Tab metal
facts.value: capacitor-grade aluminium, purer than structural grade

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: End-fill bung
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: A rubber or PVC disc that fills the end of the sleeve and retains the electrolyte against thermal expansion and the internal pressure generated during burn-in. It is the visible rubber disc at the base of a radial electrolytic.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.name: Silicone rubber bung
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.assemb.description: Heat-cured silicone rubber, chosen because it stays soft and chemically inert in contact with the acid electrolyte for decades. Silicone is a siloxane polymer built on a quartz-derived silicon-oxygen backbone.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.name: Winding on a mandrel and impregnation
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.description: Anode foil, separator and cathode foil are wound together on a rotating mandrel into a compact roll. Electrolyte is then vacuum- or pressure-impregnated into the wound roll, filling every pore and pushing out air, which is what finally gives the part its capacitance.

facts.label: Impregnation
facts.value: vacuum impregnation, repeated 2-4 times to drive out trapped air

facts.label: Slitting
facts.value: cathode foil is slit into two or three ribbons for a multi-section winding

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.name: Winding mandrel
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.description: A polished steel mandrel, often Teflon-coated, on which the foil sandwich is wound. Mandrel diameter and surface finish are set by the smallest foil thickness so the finished pack can be released without creasing.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.windin.note: Automatic winding is documented. Not established: the mandrel material or its Teflon coating, or that mandrel diameter is set by the smallest foil thickness.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.name: Separator (paper or polyolefin)
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.description: A porous, electrolyte-wicking separator keeping the foils apart while letting current through. Bleached kraft paper was still the standard for most 1980s aluminium electrolytics; low-porosity oriented polypropylene or polyethylene sleeves were the premium, longer-life alternative.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.note: Paper was still the volume material in 1982; polypropylene separators had been commercial for years but were not yet dominant.

facts.label: 1982 default
facts.value: bleached kraft paper; PE/PP sleeves for higher-reliability parts

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: the separator is the main leakage path and electrolyte reservoir

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.name: Bleached kraft paper separator
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.description: A very thin, very porous cellulose tissue wound between the foils. It must be wetted completely by the electrolyte but must not contain ions that would raise the leakage current, so it is washed and bleached before use. Kraft paper separators are why the electrolyte is held in place at all.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.separa.note: Not established: the 20-60 um separator thickness quoted here. The standard construction figure for a capacitor rated up to 100 V is 30-75 um, with duplex paper used at higher ratings.

facts.label: Why paper
facts.value: absorbent, cheap, dimensionally stable when wetted

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Working electrolyte
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: The conducting liquid that soaks the separator and carries current between the oxide and the cathode: boric or phosphoric acid dissolved in ethylene glycol, dimethylformamide or dimethyl sulfoxide. The solvent must wet the porous separator without dissolving or attacking the oxide, and the acid concentration sets the oxide's equilibrium thickness.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.note: Not established: dimethyl sulphoxide as a working electrolyte solvent. The documented non-solid systems are borax (ethylene glycol with boric acid) and the organic solvents DMF, DMA and gamma-butyrolactone. The conductivity figure of tens to hundreds of mS/cm is likewise unsourced.

facts.label: Solvents
facts.value: ethylene glycol, DMF, DMSO

facts.label: Acid
facts.value: boric acid / phosphoric acid

facts.label: Conductivity
facts.value: tens to hundreds of mS/cm

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Glycol-ether solvent from petrochemistry
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Ethylene glycol and the glycol ethers used as high-voltage capacitor solvents were derived from ethylene oxide, itself made by oxidising ethylene from a steam cracker. They replaced the glycol-ester electrolytes of the 1950s because they dissolve the anode oxide without attacking it.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.note: Ethylene glycol with boric acid as the standard borax electrolyte, and DMF, DMA and gamma-butyrolactone as the anhydrous organics, are documented. Not established: the glycol-ether route from a steam cracker, and the claim that these replaced glycol-ester electrolytes of the 1950s.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: crude -> steam cracking -> ethylene -> ethylene oxide -> glycol ether

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Ethylene glycol ethers from ethylene oxide
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Ethylene oxide is made by direct oxidation of ethylene over a silver or chromite catalyst, then reacts with an alcohol to give the glycol ether. The solvent chemistry of an aluminium electrolytic is therefore set two or three steps downstream of a steam cracker.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.note: Not established: direct oxidation of ethylene over a silver or chromite catalyst, and the subsequent alcoholysis to the glycol ether. No source consulted establishes ethylene oxide.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Boric acid in the electrolyte
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Boric acid sets the oxide chemistry of the anode and, with phosphoric acid, is the reason an aluminium electrolytic has a usable voltage range at all. Commercially it was made from borax, which is mined from evaporite deposits.

facts.label: Borax source
facts.value: borate minerals in evaporite basins

facts.label: Key deposits
facts.value: California (US), Turkey, Chile - the US borates led world supply in 1982

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.name: Borax (tincalconite) evaporite
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.electr.description: Sodium tetraborate decahydrate occurs in the playas and evaporite deposits of closed desert basins, where boron-bearing volcanic hot springs have fed an evaporating lake for millions of years. It is mined, not synthesised, in the borate districts.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.name: Cathode foil
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.description: Aluminium foil, usually a cheaper alloy and often unetched, serving as the return electrode. It carries no dielectric of its own; its job is simply to collect the return current through the electrolyte.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.name: Cathode foil rolling
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.cathod.description: High-purity aluminium rolled to a few tens of microns, often lightly etched, slit into ribbons for the winding. It uses the same aluminium as the anode but a looser specification, because no dielectric quality depends on it.

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: High-purity anode foil, rolled and etched
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: High-purity aluminium foil, roughened by electrochemical etching so that the surface becomes a mass of microscopic pits, then anodically formed to grow an insulating alumina layer on it. Etching multiplies the effective area of the anode, which is how a hundred microfarads fits into a 5 mm can. The foil is wound with a separate cathode foil and absorbent separator, and the liquid electrolyte is the actual second electrode.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.note: Not established, and contradicted by the standard construction description: the anode foil is quoted as at least 99.99 % pure aluminium and 20-100 um thick, and etching as giving a surface-area increase of up to a factor of 200. The 99.5-99.7 % purity, 12-25 um thickness and x50-x100 area gain quoted here are not supported by any source consulted, and the etch multiplies the anode area, not the cathode's.

facts.label: Foil purity
facts.value: at least 99.99 % Al

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: hot HCl/HNO3, or a sodium chlorate bath

facts.label: Surface area gain
facts.value: up to about x200 relative to a smooth surface, depending on the rated voltage

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: Anode foil from re-melted foil-mill scrap
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: Rolled foil offcuts, edge trim and rejected capacitor-grade foil were re-smelted in a holding furnace and re-rolled into fresh anode foil rather than going back to the general scrap stream. The other half of the loop is primary metal: alumina from bauxite, smelted in a Hall-Heroult cell by dissolving it in molten cryolite and electrolytising at 950-970 C to 99.7 % pure cathodes. That closed loop is why capacitor makers were in effect recycling their own aluminium, and why an aluminium price move showed up in 1982 capacitor prices with a lag.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.note: Cryolite is synthesised from hydrofluoric acid and alumina, and the hydrofluoric acid historically came from fluorspar mined in Mexico, South Africa and China. Prime foil from the primary smelter was still used for the tightest-tolerance parts and I cannot say which proportion applied to Commodore's 1982 supply.

facts.label: Hall-Heroult cell
facts.value: alumina in molten cryolite at ~950-970 C

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 13-16 kWh per kg of aluminium

mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.name: Anodic formation (the real dielectric)
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.description: The etched foil is made the anode in a phosphoric or boric acid bath at 90-200 V DC, growing a barrier-type aluminium oxide layer tens of nanometres thick. The rated working voltage of the finished capacitor is just the voltage the oxide can hold, so higher ratings need a thicker oxide and hence less capacitance for the same area.
mb.passives.caps.alu-electrolytic.anode-.note: Not established: the 90-200 V DC forming voltage quoted for parts rated 6-50 V. What is documented is the relationship - oxide thickness proportional to forming voltage, 14 nm at 10 V and 140 nm at 100 V, amorphous oxide 1.4 nm/V against 1.0 nm/V crystalline - together with the standardised safety margin that puts the forming voltage above the rated voltage.

facts.label: Forming voltage
facts.value: ~90-200 V DC for parts rated 6-50 V

facts.label: Oxide thickness
facts.value: ~10-100 nm; capacitance falls as 1/thickness

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: amorphous Al2O3, partly crystalline

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.name: Monolithic ceramic capacitor (MLCC)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.description: The 0.1 uF bypass and small timing capacitors. Dozens of layers of barium-titanate ceramic with screen-printed metal electrodes buried between them, then fired and terminated. Monolithic construction gives huge capacitance in a tiny body because the electrode area is the whole face of every layer.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.note: The 250407 parts list as transcribed by the replica-board project specifies 0.1 uF 50 V X7R, 0.22 uF Z5U and small C0G parts; Commodore's exact mix of ceramic disc versus monolithic changed between board revisions, and the X7R/Z5U designations are modern restatements of what were then simply 'ceramic'.

facts.label: Dielectric classes
facts.value: X7R / Z5U for the big values, C0G for the small timing caps

facts.label: Size (1982)
facts.value: ~2.5 x 3.2 mm radial blocks and discs

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.name: End terminations (nickel + solderable outer)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.description: After firing, the two exposed end faces are terminated with a conducting band that collects current from the hundreds of buried electrodes. In 1982 this was a fired-on or sputtered nickel layer with a solderable silver or tin outer layer, or a simple dipped solder band. The C64 boards were wave-soldered in tin-lead, so the termination had to wet 63/37 solder.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.terminations.note: The nickel barrier plus a solderable outer layer is well established; which outer-layer option Commodore's capacitor supplier used in 1982 is not.

facts.label: 1982 termination
facts.value: Ni barrier with Ag or Ni-Sn outer layer, or dipped tin-lead solder

facts.label: Modern difference
facts.value: pure sintered Ni-Sn terminations with no precious metal are today's standard

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.name: Firing in a continuous belt kiln
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.description: The blanks go through a continuous belt or pusher kiln under a controlled low oxygen partial pressure, so the ceramic sinters dense and hermetic while the nickel internal electrodes are not oxidised away. Density matters enormously: a porous body lets moisture attack the electrode stack and destroys the insulation resistance. The atmosphere is a forming gas or nitrogen with an oxygen partial pressure held just low enough that nickel does not oxidise and high enough that the organic binder burns off cleanly; getting that window right is the hardest part of base-metal MLCC manufacture.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.note: Not established: the low oxygen partial pressure and forming-gas or nitrogen atmosphere, and the >99.5 % theoretical density figure. What is documented is the order of operations and the temperature - binder burnt out after cutting, then sintering at 1200-1450 C to give the final mainly crystalline structure. The atmosphere requirement is tied to which electrode metal is used and is not stated in the source.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: low pO2 / forming gas or N2

facts.label: Soak
facts.value: hours, to reach >99.5 % theoretical density

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.elements.name: Kiln heating elements
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.elements.description: Silicon-carbide or nichrome elements in a continuous belt kiln held at ~1300 C for hours. Long soaks at high temperature are what drive the ceramic to theoretical density.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.belt-kiln.elements.note: The 1200-1450 C sinter is documented. Not established: that the kiln is heated by silicon-carbide or nichrome elements, or the hours-long soak. No element type or soak time appears in any source consulted.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.name: Dicing into blanks
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.description: The laminated bar is cut with a resin-bonded diamond saw into hundreds or thousands of identical blanks, each one capacitor body. One sintered bar yields thousands of capacitors and one furnace run yields many bars, so the economics only work at that scale - which is why MLCC production had consolidated into a handful of very large Japanese, European and later Taiwanese plants by the early 1980s.

facts.label: Yield per bar
facts.value: 10^3 - 10^4 blanks

facts.label: Saw
facts.value: resin-bonded diamond blade, coolant lubricated

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.blade.name: Resin-bonded diamond blade
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.blade.description: A thin, flat, run-of-the-mill diamond wheel; the same abrasive technology as the crystal grinder but applied to a sintered ceramic bar.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.dicing.blade.note: Cutting the pressed stack into individual components is documented. Not established: that a resin-bonded diamond blade is used, or that this is 'the same abrasive technology as the crystal grinder'.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.name: Stacking, lamination and debinding
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.description: The printed green sheets are stacked offset so every sheet's electrode lands alternately on the two opposed faces, then compressed in a hydraulic laminator and the organic binder burned out slowly. The result is a monolithic bar of hundreds of ceramic layers with the electrodes sealed inside.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.note: Not established: the 10-60 active layer count for a 1982 0.1 uF 50 V part, the lamination pressure in tens of MPa, and the 200-400 C debind ramp. What is documented is that the printed sheets are stacked in the required number of layers, solidified by pressure, and that the binder is burnt out of the stack after cutting.

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: ~10-60 active layers for a 1982 0.1 uF 50 V part

facts.label: Lamination pressure
facts.value: tens of MPa

facts.label: Debinding
facts.value: slow ramp 200-400 C to avoid cracking the stack

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.lam.name: Hydraulic laminator
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.lam.description: A heated hydraulic press that stacks and consolidates hundreds of sheets at once, aligned by registration pins. This is the step that turns a pile of loose printed film into one solid bar.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.stack-laminate.lam.note: Stacking and solidifying by pressure is documented. Not established: a heated hydraulic press, registration pins, or that this is the step that turns loose printed film into a solid bar.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.name: Screen-printing internal electrodes
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.description: A metal paste is printed onto the green sheets to define the buried internal electrodes, the sheets being cut from the rolled foil afterwards. In 1982 the commodity MLCC still used a noble-metal paste: the displacement of palladium-bearing electrodes by cheaper nickel is dated to 1993 by TDK, with copper and nickel arriving later still after a late-1990s surge in noble-metal prices. So the older, expensive palladium-silver electrode was the mainstream choice at this date, not a legacy one.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.note: Not established, and in tension with the source cited: the switch from palladium-bearing to nickel internal electrodes is dated there to 1993 by TDK, with cheaper base metals developing after a late-1990s noble-metal price surge, not to the 1982 commodity part. Screen-printing a metal paste onto the green sheets is documented; the 1982 nickel-versus-palladium-silver balance is not.

facts.label: 1982 internal electrode
facts.value: palladium-silver or similar noble metal for a 1982 part; nickel only from 1993 and later base metals after that

facts.label: Legacy alternative
facts.value: nickel, from 1993 onward

facts.label: Print
facts.value: screen through a photoemulsion mask, offset on high-volume lines

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.name: Base-metal nickel paste
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.description: The internal electrode paste: finely divided nickel in a glass frit and an organic vehicle, screen-printed onto the green sheet and co-fired with the ceramic. Nickel was chosen over silver for cost and over palladium for cost, and it is what let a 0.1 uF 50 V bypass capacitor be sold for a fraction of a cent.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.print-electrodes.n.note: Screen-printing a metal paste that co-fires with the ceramic is documented, and nickel is documented as one of the cheaper base metals later used for internal electrodes. Not established: the sub-micron to 1 um particle size, the low-pO2 co-fire specifically for a nickel electrode, and that nickel was already the dominant 1982 internal electrode - the source dates that change to 1993.

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: sub-micron to ~1 um

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.name: Tape casting to green sheets
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.description: The slip is doctor-bladed onto a moving polyester carrier film to a controlled dry thickness. This single step sets the eventual capacitance density, because capacitance is dielectric thickness divided by the number of electrode layers stacked.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.note: Not established: the 5-20 um green-sheet thickness attributed to early-1980s parts. What is documented is that a thin ceramic foil is cast from a suspension of the powder with a suitable binder, and that dielectric layer thickness fell from 4 um in 1995 to 1 um in 2005 and about 0.5 um by 2010, with the layer thickness limited by the powder grain size.

facts.label: Green sheet thickness
facts.value: ~1-10 um; early-1980s parts often cast 5-20 um

facts.label: Carrier
facts.value: PET (Mylar) belt

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.doctor-b.name: Doctor blade
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.doctor-b.description: A precisely-ground steel or ceramic blade with a controlled edge angle, set to micrometres over the belt. The single most important tool in MLCC making: it sets layer thickness and therefore capacitance density.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.doctor-b.note: Casting a thin ceramic foil from a powder-and-binder suspension to a controlled thickness is documented. Not established: the doctor blade itself - a ground steel or ceramic blade set to micrometres over a moving belt - and its description as the single most important tool in the manufacture.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.belt.name: Moving carrier belt
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.belt.description: The green sheet is carried on a continuous polyester belt and dried in a short oven as the doctor blade lays it down, so the green thickness is set by blade clearance against a moving web rather than by a single-shot cast.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.tape-cast.belt.note: Not established: the continuous polyester carrier belt and the short in-line drying oven. No document consulted describes the tape-casting line layout.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.name: Tape-casting slurry (powder + frit + binder)
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.description: The BaTiO3 powder is blended with a glass frit - an aid to sintering and to dielectric strength at the electrode interface - and an organic binder into a homogeneous, flowable slip. In 1982 this was an acrylic or PVA binder in water, or a cellulose ester in an organic solvent; fully water-based PVA systems became dominant later.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.note: Not established: the glass frit fraction of about 5 % by weight of the ceramic body, and the specific 1982 binder systems. What is documented is that the casting suspension is the powder with a suitable binder.

facts.label: Glass frit
facts.value: ~5 % by weight of the ceramic body

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.glass-frit.name: Glass frit in the slurry
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.glass-frit.description: A few per cent of low-melting glass, added so that on sintering it wets the barium titanate grains, closes the porosity and gives the internal electrode a hermetic interface. Without it the MLCC is not gas-tight and its insulation resistance collapses.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.slurry.glass-frit.note: Not established: the role of the glass frit in wetting the barium titanate grains and closing porosity, the hermetic interface it gives the internal electrode, and the claim that without it the insulation resistance collapses. No document consulted describes the MLCC frit addition.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.name: Barium titanate dielectric powder
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.description: The heart of the MLCC: sub-micron BaTiO3 crystallites, the only powder that has a very high dielectric constant AND survives the high-temperature processing. Chemistry is shifted from pure BaTiO3 by dopants to move the Curie point below room temperature, giving a Class II (X7R/Z5U) part with high capacitance that still decays with temperature.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.note: Not established: the 0.2-1 um particle size attributed to early-1980s X7R powder. What is documented is the class 2 material set and its codes - barium titanate with aluminium silicate, magnesium silicate and aluminium oxide additives, permittivity 200 to 14000, X7R -55 to +125 C at plus or minus 15 %, Z5U +10 to +85 C at +22/-56 % - and a barium titanate Curie temperature of 120-130 C with dielectric constants to 7000, or 15000 over a narrow range. Those are material-class figures; they are not a figure for any particular commercial grade.

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ~0.2-1 um; coarse-grain BaTiO3 was typical of early-1980s X7R

facts.label: Relative permittivity
facts.value: ~3000-10000 near the Curie point

facts.label: X7R
facts.value: -55 to +125 C, capacitance change +/-15 %

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.name: Donor / acceptor doping
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.description: Trivalent donor dopants (La2O3, Dy2O3, Y2O3) or pentavalent acceptors (Nb2O5, Ta2O5, Sb2O5) are added during calcination. Donors leave the ceramic 'depleted' so the grains sit uniformly in the paraelectric phase at room temperature, which gives the stable, moderate-loss X7R curve. Acceptor dopants raise the Curie point so the material stays ferroelectric and gives a much higher, more temperature-sensitive Z5U.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.note: The physics is standard ceramics; the specific dopant-to-Class assignments are my summary and are flagged medium.

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.name: Rare-earth dopant oxides
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.doping.dopa.description: Lanthanum, dysprosium and yttrium oxides, ground and sieved to sub-micron, are the donor dopants that set the temperature coefficient of an X7R dielectric. The sub-micron sieve is the whole difficulty: a barium titanate powder wants its additives soluble or finely dispersed so that no second phase forms, and an oxide bought at the separation plant's standard grade arrives as lumps. These are the most expensive few grams on the bill of materials and they were bought by the kilogram, not the tonne, so the MLCC maker was dependent on the same two plants as the television maker for the same handful of elements.

facts.label: Which oxides
facts.value: lanthanum, dysprosium and yttrium, as donor dopants

facts.label: Particle size
facts.value: ground and sieved to sub-micron, or they will not disperse in the barium titanate

facts.label: Cost position
facts.value: among the most expensive grams in the component, and bought in kilogram quantities

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.name: Solid-state BaTiO3 synthesis
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.description: Barium carbonate and titanium dioxide are ball-milled with the dopants in water to a homogeneous slurry, then calcined in a kiln at about 1050-1200 C. The carbonate decomposes and the perovskite BaTiO3 crystallises. The mass is reground and wet-milled with a dispersant down to the target particle size.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.note: Not established: the 1050-1200 C calcination temperature and the zirconia or nylon wet-milling detail. What is documented is the reaction itself - barium titanate manufactured by heating barium carbonate and titanium dioxide, the reaction proceeding via liquid phase sintering.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: BaCO3 + TiO2 -> BaTiO3 + CO2

facts.label: Milling media
facts.value: zirconia or nylon bead, wet

mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.name: Titanium dioxide (TiO2) feed
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.description: Ceramic-grade TiO2, made by chlorinating ilmenite or rutile to TiCl4 and re-oxidising, or by sulphuric acid digestion. Low-iron pigment-grade material is used so the fired ceramic has good insulation resistance.
mb.passives.caps.mlcc.powder.synthesis.t.note: Barium titanate is documented as made by heating barium carbonate and titanium dioxide, so TiO2 is confirmed as a feed. Not established: the chlorination of ilmenite or rutile to TiCl4 and re-oxidation, the sulphuric acid route, low-iron pigment grade for insulation resistance, and the 1982 ilmenite supply geography.

mb.passives.resistors.name: Resistors
mb.passives.resistors.description: Fixed resistors on the 250407: about seventy 1/4 W axial parts in values from 100 ohm to 1 megohm, plus four thick-film SIP resistor networks and one 500 ohm trimmer. Almost all were 5 percent carbon film; the handful of 1 percent metal film parts sat in the VIC-II colour and timing network.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: axial, 6.3 x 2.3 mm, 0.63 mm lead pitch

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.name: Trim and adjustable resistors
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.description: The single adjustable part on the 250407 is R27, a 500 ohm cermet trimmer potentiometer that biases U31's crystal oscillator so the 14.31818 MHz colour subcarrier lands exactly on NTSC's subcarrier frequency. It is the reason a C64 needs no colour adjustment in normal use but will show colour shimmer when the crystal ages.
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.note: On later C64 boards (the '8710' revision and Commodore's own C64C), this variable resistor was replaced with a trimmer capacitor in the crystal's load network. Both do the same job: pulling the oscillator to exactly the right frequency.

facts.label: Reference
facts.value: R27, 500 ohm linear

facts.label: Case
facts.value: ~9.5 x 4.8 x 4.8 mm, cermet, 3386-style

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: +/-10 % body; the ADJUSTMENT is what matters

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster.name: Adjuster screw and slider
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster.description: A knurled brass or stainless screw drives a moulded slider that rides the wiper along the track. Backing-off epoxy locks the setting once the board is aligned.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..name: Epoxy lock
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..description: After alignment a drop of epoxy is flowed over the adjuster so the setting cannot drift in service. On a machine with no calibration facility this trimmer is effectively a one-time factory adjustment for forty years. It is a deliberate, destructive lock: once the trim is set on the factory line that trimmer is not adjustable again.
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..note: Not established: the epoxy lock and the account of the trimmer as a one-time factory adjustment. That trimmers are for infrequent adjustment during manufacture or repair is documented; the destructive epoxy lock is not, in any source consulted.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..name: Adjuster screw
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..description: A brass or stainless screw, knurled or slotted, driving the slider. Brass is the usual choice because it machines cleanly at small diameters and does not gall against the moulded slider.
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.adjuster..note: Not established: brass or stainless, knurled or slotted, and the anti-galling argument against a moulded slider. Multiturn trimmers use a lead screw and are documented; the material of this adjuster screw is not.

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.name: Cermet resistive element and track
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.description: A thick-film RuO2 resistive track deposited on the top face of an alumina substrate, with a metal-foil wiper that slides along it. Because the element is a printed film rather than a carbon blob, the tracking is smooth and the part does not develop a scratchy potentiometer feel the way a carbon composition pot does. The usable travel is a fraction of the physical length, because the track is designed to put most of its resistance in the middle of the sweep - that is how a 500 ohm trimmer gets a usable 0-500 ohm range out of a single turn of the adjuster screw.
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.note: That a cermet - a ceramic/metal mixture - is a standard potentiometer resistive element is documented, as is ruthenium oxide among the cermet conductors. Not established: the 100 ohm to 1 Mohm per square sheet-resistance range, the specific wiper alloys, and the design intent of concentrating most of the resistance in the middle of the sweep.

facts.label: Element
facts.value: RuO2 cermet, 100 ohm - 1 Mohm/sq

facts.label: Wiper
facts.value: Ni alloy or precious metal, fork or blade

mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.name: Wiper alloy
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.description: A nickel-alloy or precious-metal spring contact rubbing on the RuO2 film. Because the cermet element is hard, the wiper is deliberately the sacrificial element and is made of a soft, wear-resistant alloy.
mb.passives.resistors.trimmers.cermet-el.note: A springy phosphor bronze wiper moving over the resistive element is documented for potentiometers. Not established: nickel-alloy or precious-metal wipers on a cermet trimmer, and the sacrificial-wear design argument.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.name: Thick-film cermet SIP resistor networks
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.description: The four resistor arrays on the 250407: two 8-way isolated 33 ohm packs (series terminators on the DRAM data bus), one 8-way 3k3 bussed pack and one 10-way 3k3 bussed pack. Each is one alumina substrate with several ruthenium-oxide resistive tracks screen-printed and fired together.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.note: A RIFA 481 resistor pack is sometimes quoted for this position. RIFA (British Insulated Callender's Cables, Boxhill, UK) did supply SIP resistor networks to the European electronics trade in the 1980s, but no direct evidence has been found that a RIFA 481 is fitted to a C64 mainboard - treat that specific part number as unverified. A Bourns 4308R-series or equivalent Vishay pack is the functionally correct part.

facts.label: Arrays on board
facts.value: 4 (RP1, RP2 = 33 ohm isolated 8-way; RP3 = 3k3 bussed 8-way; RP4 = 3k3 bussed 10-way)

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 2.54 mm SIP

facts.label: Element rating
facts.value: 0.125 W each

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Epoxy potting and marking
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: The trimmed network is coated in a fire-resistant epoxy or phenolic varnish that also carries the colour code - here a small white dot or body colour denoting the resistance. Glass-filled epoxy was the standard SIP encapsulant.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.note: The on-board network is documented in the primary parts list as a Bourns part - RP1,RP2 '330, 8 Pin (Bourns No. 4308R-102-330)', RP3 '3.3KQ, 8 Pin (Bourns No. 4308R-101-332)', RP4 '3.3KQ, 10 Pin' - which settles the single-in-line pin count but not the encapsulant. Not established: a fire-resistant epoxy or phenolic varnish carrying the colour code, and that glass-filled epoxy was the standard SIP encapsulant.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Lead frame
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: The array's leads are formed from a copper-alloy lead frame, plated in tin or solder, so the package can be inserted on a 2.54 mm pitch and wave-soldered.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.note: The 8-pin and 10-pin single-in-line form factor on a 2.54 mm pitch is documented by the parts list. Not established: that the leads come from a copper-alloy lead frame plated in tin or solder, and that the package is wave-soldered.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.name: Glass-filled epoxy coat
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.description: The whole array is coated in an epoxy loaded with fine glass or silica, which both seals the tracks and gives the package its mechanical rigidity. The colour body is the colourant in that coat.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.en.note: Not established: an epoxy loaded with fine glass or silica as the encapsulant, and that the body colour is the colourant in that coat. The small white dot denoting resistance on these packages is not explained by any source consulted.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Laser trimming of the network
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: An excimer or Nd:YAG laser ablates slots in each printed resistor until a closed-loop bridge calls out the right value. Bulk trimming can be 'slug' or 'v-cut' (pushing a wedge of resistive material aside) rather than ablating material away.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.note: Trimming is documented: the resistance of thick film resistors after manufacture is not highly accurate and is trimmed to value by abrasive or laser trimming. Not established: the excimer and Nd:YAG laser choice, the v-cut or slug bulk-trim alternative, a rate of 10,000 networks per hour, and a tolerance of 0.1 %. The documented history goes the other way on tolerance - thick film resistors started at 5 % and improved to 2 % or 1 %.

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: 10,000+ networks/hour

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Nd:YAG laser crystal
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: Neodymium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet was the standard solid-state laser for resistor trimming: a garnet crystal doped with neodymium, pumped optically and emitting at 1.06 microns. The yttrium-aluminium-garnet host is grown from alumina and yttrium oxide.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.name: Laser trimming system
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.description: A pulsed laser head over a moving substrate with an in-line ohmmeter, cutting and re-measuring thousands of times per second. Excimer lasers were used for fine-resolution cuts on thick films.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.tr.note: Not established: the pulsed laser head with in-line ohmmeter measuring thousands of times per second, and the excimer laser for fine-resolution cuts. The source establishes only that thick film resistors are trimmed by laser among other methods.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.name: Screen printing through a photoemulsion
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.description: A stainless-steel mesh stretched over a frame, coated in photosensitive emulsion, contact-exposed through a film or direct-imaged artwork, developed, and then the paste squeegeed through the open areas onto the substrate. Line width is the resistance knob. Thixotropy is essential to the paste: it must flow under the squeegee and then stand without slumping, or the printed line blurs and the resistance drifts off value, and it comes from the shape of the glass frit particles.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.note: Screen and stencil printing is documented as the thick film deposition method. Not established: the photoemulsion-through-a-film exposure route, the 250-400 mesh, the 10-25 um wet film thickness, and the thixotropy-from-frit-particle-shape argument.

facts.label: Screen mesh
facts.value: ~250-400 mesh for fine resistors

facts.label: Wet film thickness
facts.value: ~10-25 um before drying

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.name: Stainless steel mesh
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.description: The printing screen is a woven stainless-steel or nylon mesh stretched over a frame and photo-imaged. Stainless was standard because it must survive repeated abrasion by the abrasive paste in the paste.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.sc.note: Screen and stencil printing is documented for thick film. Not established: a woven stainless-steel or nylon mesh stretched over a frame and photo-imaged, and the abrasion argument. Note that the printed resistors are inside a sealed package, so the paste never meets the mesh in service.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: RuO2 cermet resistive paste
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: The resistive phase is sub-micron ruthenium dioxide powder blended with a lead-borosilicate glass frit and an organic vehicle (butyl acetate / terpineol) into a thixotropic paste. Its sheet resistance is a known function of powder loading, so a given RuO2 fraction sets a given ohms-per-square.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.note: The paste construction is documented: the resistive ceramic phase is mixed with sintered powdered glass and a carrier liquid so the composite can be screen-printed, and the composite is fused at about 850 C. Ruthenium oxide is listed among the cermet conductors used. Not established: the 0.1-0.5 um RuO2 particle size, the lead-borosilicate glass frit specific to the 1980s, the butyl acetate / terpineol vehicle, and the 10 ohm/sq to 1 Mohm/sq sheet-resistance range.

facts.label: RuO2 powder
facts.value: sub-micron, typically 0.1-0.5 um

facts.label: Glass frit
facts.value: lead-borosilicate in the 1980s

facts.label: Sheet resistance range
facts.value: 10 ohm/sq to 1 Mohm/sq

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Platinum-group ore bearing ruthenium
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: Ruthenium occurs almost only as a minor by-product in platinum and nickel ores (Merensky Reef, Sudbury, Norilsk) rather than in a ruthenium ore of its own. It reaches the resistor paste as ammonium ruthenium chloride after a complex refining sequence.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.note: Coarse chain only; the ammonium ruthenium chloride route is my summary of standard refining practice, not a C64-specific fact.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Merensky Reef and nickel-copper sulphide ores
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: Ruthenium and the other platinum-group metals have no ore of their own. They occur at a few parts per million in the Merensky Reef of the Bushveld Complex and in the Sudbury and Norilsk nickel-copper sulphide ores, so the resistor industry bought ruthenium as a refinery by-product at platinum-group prices.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.name: Ruthenium dioxide powder
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.description: Ruthenium oxide is one of the conductive ceramic phases mixed into a cermet resistor paste, alongside tantalum nitride, lead oxide and others; it is the conductive phase that carries the current, and the glass phase mixed in with it is the insulator that binds the film and gives it its stability. The paste is screen-printed onto a substrate and fused at about 850 C. Ruthenium's scarcity has been a persistent cost driver for cermet resistors.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.ru.note: Ruthenium oxide is documented as one of the ceramic cermet conductors used in thick film resistors. Not established, and doubtful as stated: that RuO2 is the only phase that survives to 900 C without oxidising away (tantalum nitride and nickel chromium are in the same list), and that 'the surrounding glass is what actually carries the current' - glass is the insulator in a cermet, the conductive phase carries the current.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Alumina substrate with printed elements
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A 0.6 mm thick 96 percent alumina bar, pre-fired and metallised. Conductive paste is printed through a photo-plated stainless screen onto the top face only, then the whole bar is fired to fuse the glass frit and mature the resistor.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: ~96 % Al2O3, 0.5-0.8 mm thick

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Tunnel-kiln firing of the printed bar
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A continuous belt or pusher kiln takes the printed substrate through a controlled temperature ramp so the resistors are 'aged' in the firing. Thick-film resistors are typically driven 50 percent above their rating for 15-25 minutes to burn in the grain boundaries and stabilise the value.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: The 850 C firing peak is documented. Not established: driving the resistors at 1.5 times rated power for 15-25 minutes to age them in the firing, which is the substantive claim here.

facts.label: Peak temperature
facts.value: ~850 C for cermet resistors

facts.label: Overload ageing
facts.value: ~15-25 min at 1.5x rated power

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Refractory kiln furniture
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: Alumina setters and shelves carrying the fired substrates through the kiln, themselves made from tabular alumina. Furnace furniture consumption is a real cost line in ceramics, and it comes from the same alumina as the substrate.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Continuous kiln
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A belt or pusher kiln with profiled hot zones, carrying the printed bar through drying, burnout, peak and controlled cooling. The cooling rate matters as much as the peak, because too fast a cool micro-cracks the glass.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: Firing at about 850 C is documented. Not established: the belt or pusher tunnel with profiled hot zones, the drying and burnout stages, and the claim that too fast a cool micro-cracks the glass.

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Thick-film conductor metallisation
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: A base-metal paste of finely divided silver or copper in a glass frit, screen-printed and fired at ~850 C to form the end lands, jumpers and common bus the resistive tracks connect to. Silver-palladium pastes were common in this era; copper pastes needed a nitrogen atmosphere to avoid oxidising.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: The glass-frit conductor paste fired at about 850 C is documented. Not established: that the base metal was silver or silver-palladium with copper pastes needing a nitrogen atmosphere, and the late-1980s dating of nickel-bearing pastes.

facts.label: Firing
facts.value: ~850 C peak

facts.label: Base metal
facts.value: Ag or Ag-Pd (Ni-Pd-Ag common from the late 1980s)

mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.name: Atomised silver powder
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.description: The conductor paste is fine silver flake or powder, not a bulk metal: it has to print as a paste and then fuse into a continuous conductor at 850 C without melting. Domestically mined silver was almost entirely gone by 1982; the metal was bought on the London spot market.
mb.passives.resistors.cermet-networks.su.note: Mined silver was economically a by-product metal by the 1980s, with Mexico, Peru, the US and Canada still significant districts; metal.silver.ingot carries the refining side.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: atomised or electrolytic silver powder / flake, typically 99.9 %

facts.label: Silver ore
facts.value: argentite Ag2S; by 1982 most world silver was a by-product of Pb-Zn and Cu refining

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.name: Discrete axial resistor families
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.description: Three manufacturing routes to a 1/4 W axial resistor coexisted in 1982. The 250407 used overwhelmingly carbon film; carbon composition was still common in cheaper consumer goods; metal film was reserved for precision.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Metal-foil precision resistor
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: An ultra-precise resistor built from rolled, etched metal foil - nickel, a nickel-chromium-iron alloy, or copper - clamped between a rigid steel/ceramic case and a polished die. Changing the roll geometry stretches the foil, so the resistance can be set with a screw to one part in a million.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Included to explain the 'foil' end of the precision-resistor family. No metal-foil parts appear in a Commodore 64; these were calibration standards in the lab and appeared in later high-precision analogue equipment.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Case, die and tension screw
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: The foil roll is sandwiched between a hardened case and a polished die with a slight bow. Turning the adjustment screw changes the roll's circumference, stretching the foil and raising the resistance by a controlled fraction of a part per million.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: The polished die was lapped on cast iron with progressively finer abrasive; a diamond paste finish gives sub-micron flatness.

facts.label: Stability
facts.value: 0.001 %/year and better
