mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Etched metal foil roll
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A strip of pure or alloy foil is rolled to a very tight radius on a mandrel and acid-etched to remove most of it, leaving fine islands of metal in series across the roll. The number of islands, not the sheet resistivity, sets the resistance.

facts.label: Resolution
facts.value: ~1000 islands per inch

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Foil metal
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Pure nickel or a nickel-iron-chromium alloy, chosen for a low temperature coefficient of resistivity and for its mechanical stability under tension.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Selective acid etch
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: The rolled foil is immersed in a ferric-nitrate or nitric-acid etch that removes most of it, leaving a fine grid of metal islands. Resistance is then set by the number of islands in the path, which is why foil resistors have their characteristic very high, very stable resistance values.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Wirewound power resistor
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Resistance wire wound on a ceramic bobbin and vitreously enamelled. Used for the few watts-and-above duties - notably the 7805 regulator's dropping resistor and the video level network. Accurate, stable, but large and inductive.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.note: Wound resistors do not appear in the 250407 BOM I checked; included because they were the standard answer for the same problems in the C64's power supply and peripherals of the same era.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Resistance alloy wire (NiCr / FeCr / CuNi)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Nichrome has the highest resistivity of the common resistance alloys and so minimises the wire length needed; constantan (CuNi) is used where a lower temperature coefficient matters more.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.note: Nichrome is documented as the usual winding wire. Not established: that it has the highest resistivity of the common resistance alloys, and that constantan is chosen where a lower temperature coefficient matters more - no constantan figure appears in the source consulted. Note also that the source gives two different Nichrome compositions, 80 Ni / 20 Cr and 60 Ni / 12 Cr / 26 Fe / 2 Mn, melting at 1350-1420 C.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Vitreous enamel coating
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: The wound wire is coated in a glassy enamel and baked, which is why wirewounds are glassy-bodied. Continuous operation above about 200 C needs cement or silicone instead.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Vitreous enamel
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: A glassy coating on the wound wire, applied as a slurry and baked. The enamel is what makes a wirewound part look like a glass-bodied component and is what lets it run hot without the wire oxidising.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Ceramic bobbin
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: A grooved steatite or alumina former on which a length of enamelled resistance alloy wire is wound. Steatite (magnesium silicate) was the classic low-cost bobbin material.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Steatite bobbin material
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Steatite, a compacted and fired magnesium silicate, was the classic low-cost bobbin and ceramic insulator material: it machines green, fires to a hard white body and is cheap.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.note: That the winding core is ceramic - along with plastic or fibreglass - is documented. Not established: steatite specifically, and its green-machinability and firing behaviour. No source consulted names a magnesium-silicate bobbin for a wirewound resistor.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.name: Talc and soapstone
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.wir.description: Steatite is a mixture of talc with clay. Talc is mined from metamorphosed dolomitic rock and is one of the few minerals still worked in a form close to its natural state.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Metal film resistor (1 % precision)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A NiCr or FeCr film vacuum-deposited onto an alumina substrate, then laser-trimmed to a tight tolerance. Where the VIC-II colour burst and the composite video level had to be set to a few parts in a thousand, a 1 percent metal film part was used instead of a 5 percent carbon film.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: The 250407's parts list is dominated by 5 percent parts; which individual reference designators were 1 percent metal film is not confirmed.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Termination cap and lead
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A crimped steel or aluminium cap grips the lead and makes contact with the film, then the whole assembly is plated in nickel. Metal film parts are always nickel-plated leads, never bare tin.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Not established: the crimped steel or aluminium cap, the nickel plating, or the claim that metal film parts are always nickel-plated and never bare tin. No document consulted describes axial metal film terminations.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Termination cap material
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A nickel-plated steel or aluminium cap, crimped onto the lead and forming the low-resistance joint to the film. Metal film parts are always nickel-plated leads: the plating has to be uniform for the part to be consistent.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Not established: the cap alloy, the crimping, and the requirement that the plating be uniform for consistency. Nothing consulted describes axial metal film end caps.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Laser scribing of the spiral
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: A pulsed ruby or Nd:YAG laser ablates a thin groove across the film, lengthening the resistive path. A closed-loop measuring bridge runs thousands of cuts per second until the value converges. This - not a mechanical wheel - is what buys the 0.1-1 percent tolerance.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: The temperature coefficient is documented exactly: a metal film resistor cut by a helix through a NiCr coating gives 0.5 %, 1 % or 2 % tolerance and a temperature coefficient generally between 50 and 100 ppm/K. Not established: the 0.1-1 % tolerance claimed, the 1000-10000 parts per hour trim rate, and the claim that laser scribing rather than a mechanical wheel is what buys the precision - the source describes the helix cut without saying which tool makes it.

facts.label: Trim rate
facts.value: ~1000-10000 parts/hour

facts.label: Achievable tolerance
facts.value: 0.1-1 %, vs +/-5 % for a cut carbon film

facts.label: TCR
facts.value: +/-50 to +/-100 ppm/degC

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Vacuum deposition bell
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Parts are racked in a vacuum chamber and the resistive film is deposited over the resistive area only, defined by a mask. The documented method for thin film resistors is sputtering; metal film resistors are usually nickel chromium, deposited by vacuum techniques of which sputtering is one. That vacuum deposition was standard for axial resistors in 1982 is reasonable but the exclusion of sputtering is not supported.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Contradicted as stated. The source says thin film resistors are made by sputtering, a method of vacuum deposition, and that metal film resistors are usually coated with nickel chromium by techniques that may include sputtering but need not be limited to it. Nothing supports 'vacuum deposited - not sputtered - was standard for axial resistors in 1982', nor the 50-500 nm film thickness or the 10^-3 to 10^-5 Torr figure.

facts.label: Film thickness
facts.value: ~50-500 nm depending on sheet resistance

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: NiCr resistance alloy
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: 80/20 nickel-chromium, or 75/25 iron-chromium, evaporated or sputtered from a heated wire or boat in a vacuum bell. NiCr is chosen for its bulk resistivity (~1.1 uohm-m) and, critically, for having a near-zero temperature coefficient of resistivity.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Chromite ore and the ferrochrome made from it are metal.chromite and metal.chromium. South Africa supplied the majority of the chrome ore consumed by the Western electronics industry in 1982.

facts.label: Chromium ore
facts.value: chromite FeCr2O4

facts.label: Chrome ore sources
facts.value: Bushveld (South Africa), Stillwater (USA), Kazakhstan

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Flat ceramic substrate (not a tube)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Metal film parts use a flat alumina bar or a flat ceramic tube rather than a tube-with-a-skin, because the uniform flat substrate is what makes laser scribing produce a stable, precise spiral.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Not established: that metal film parts use a flat alumina bar or flat ceramic tube rather than a tube-with-a-skin, and the causal link to stable laser scribing. No source consulted describes axial metal film substrates.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.name: Metal-film substrate material
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.description: Metal film resistors need a very flat and very uniform substrate because the film resistance is set by the length of the deposited track, not by the substrate geometry. Alumina ceramic bar or a flat ceramic tube is used for that flatness.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.met.note: Not established: alumina ceramic bar or flat ceramic tube as the substrate, and the flatness argument. The general need for a smooth uniform substrate follows from the film resistance depending on track length, but no source consulted names the material.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon composition resistor
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A rod of carbon and clay, compression-moulded into a small cylinder with metal end caps. Very cheap and very noisy, with a wide temperature coefficient and drift. Still used in 1982 in low-cost consumer goods and audio gear, but on the C64 itself it was already being displaced by carbon film.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Some very early Commodore boards (VIC-20, early PET) did use composition resistors; the 250407 does not appear to.

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: +/-5 %, commonly +/-10 %

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: +/-2000 ppm/degC (far worse than film)

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Swaged metal end caps and wire leads
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Soft tin or brass caps are pressed over the moulded slug, then a tinned copper wire lead is swaged inside the cap, giving the familiar bulbous ends of a composition resistor.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Lead wire is tin-plated copper drawn from rod, not tinned after the fact.

facts.label: End cap material
facts.value: tin or brass, soft enough to swage

facts.label: End cap ore
facts.value: cassiterite SnO2, 0.1-1 % SnO2 in alluvial workings

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Compression moulding
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The mix is pressed in a matched-metal die at tens of tonnes to fill a slug shaped like a small pill, then baked. End caps of tin or brass are pressed on after cure.

facts.label: Bake
facts.value: ~150-200 C after press

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Matched metal die
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A matched-metal compression die with a cavity shaped like the finished slug. The cavity is chrome plated to survive the abrasive mix and the pressure.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Composition mix (graphite + clay + binder)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A stiffer, higher-carbon paste than the film slurry. Because it is bulk rather than surface-conductive, the resistance is set by the geometry of the moulded rod itself, not by a pattern on its skin.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The mix itself is documented: the resistive element is a mixture of finely powdered carbon and an insulating material, usually ceramic, held together by a resin, with resistance set by the fill-to-carbon ratio and higher carbon giving lower resistance. Not established: that this particular mix used clay rather than another ceramic, or phenolic rather than another resin.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Diluent clay in the composition mix
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A much higher clay fraction than in the film slurry, because a composition resistor has to be a weak conductor in bulk. Kaolin was the traditional diluent, the same mineral as in the film mix.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The substance of the claim is documented: the resistive element is a mixture of finely powdered carbon and an insulating material, usually ceramic, held together by a resin, and the resistance is set by the ratio of the fill material to the carbon. Not established: that the diluent was specifically kaolin.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon film resistor (1/4 W axial)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The bulk of the board's resistors. A thin, discontinuous film of carbon and clay laid on a hollow alumina ceramic tube; carbon loading sets the resistance. Cheap, 5 percent, and tolerant of being bent during manual insertion.

facts.label: Resistance
facts.value: 1 ohm to 10 Mohm, here 100 ohm to 1 Mohm

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: +/-5 % (gold band)

facts.label: Power rating
facts.value: 0.25 W at 70 C

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: +/-200 to +/-1000 ppm/degC by class

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Offset-printed colour-code bands
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The value and tolerance rings are printed on the epoxy body by an offset (rotogravure / dry-offset) coater using inks fired onto the surface. Three bands give significant figures, one multiplier, one tolerance. A 5 percent part gets a gold band; 1 percent gets brown.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Bands are printed AFTER the part is trimmed and moulded - the trim determines the value, the print only reports it.

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: black, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, grey, white; gold, silver

facts.label: Method
facts.value: offset printing, ink cured onto epoxy

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Band ink
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Offset printing inks cured onto the epoxy body. The ink is a pigment in an oil and resin vehicle fired at a few hundred degrees so it will not rub off or solvent-attack during board cleaning.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: That the bands were cheaply printed onto tiny components, and that printing technology later made printed numbers more practical, are both documented. Not established: the offset or rotogravure coater, the pigment-in-oil vehicle, and the cure at a few hundred degrees that keeps the bands from rubbing off or solvent attack.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Moulded epoxy body
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The trimmed resistor is transfer-moulded in epoxy, or coated in a phenolic shell, sealing the film from humidity. Moulding compound is a phenolic or epoxy resin filled with silica flour.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Epoxy moulding of the resistor body
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The resistor is placed in a transfer tool and encapsulated in epoxy resin cured at ~150-175 C for several minutes. Epoxy is chosen because it shrinks little and does not stress the film on cooling.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: transfer-tool encapsulation in epoxy, the 150-175 C cure for several minutes, and the low-shrinkage argument. No document consulted describes how an axial resistor body is moulded. Note that the service manual's own note - 'ALL RESISTORS ARE 1/4 WATT 5% UNLESS OTHERWISE SPECIFIED' - and its separate line 'RESISTORS - All are carbon 1/4 watt, 5% unless noted' establish only the rating and the carbon technology, not the encapsulant.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Value trimming (abrasive wheel)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A diamond wheel cuts a narrow slot through the film from the end of the tube, lengthening the resistive path a few micrometres at a time until the measured resistance hits the middle of the tolerance band. This is why carbon film resistors are called 'film' and why their tolerance is fixed after firing rather than before.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Modern carbon film is still trimmed this way; laser trimming only ever made sense for thin film.

facts.label: Trim resolution
facts.value: sets final tolerance, ~1-5 %

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: abrasive slot, NOT a laser scribing cut

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Abrasive cut-off wheel
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A thin abrasive wheel, run at tens of thousands of revolutions per minute, cuts a slot through the film. Each pass lengthens the resistive path slightly; a few passes reach value.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Abrasive trimming is documented, as is cutting a helix in the film to create the resistive path. Not established: the thin abrasive wheel running at tens of thousands of revolutions per minute, or that each pass lengthens the path slightly.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Aluminium oxide abrasive
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The standard grinding abrasive of the era, made by calcining alumina. Synthetic diamond was used only where the cut had to be finer.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: aluminium oxide as the standard grinding abrasive, or that synthetic diamond was used only where a finer cut was needed. No document consulted describes trim wheel abrasives.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Axial lead termination (electroplate)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A lead is pushed down each end of the tube through the carbon film, and the assembly is barrel-plated in an electroless or electrolytic nickel bath so the film and lead make a low-resistance, solderable joint. In 1982 this was almost always nickel, sometimes with a thin silver flash.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Tinned copper lead wire
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The axial lead is drawn copper wire, cut to length, tinned in a molten tin or tin-lead pot so the resistor dips cleanly in the wave-solder bath. Tinning is what stops the bare copper wire from oxidising between the barrel plating step and the board.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The 0.6 mm tinned lead is documented, though the source states it for low-power wirewound resistors rather than carbon film: wire leads in low power wirewound resistors are usually between 0.6 and 0.8 mm in diameter and tinned for ease of soldering. Not established: the 230-250 C tin pot temperature, and the specific claim about oxidation between barrel plating and the board.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: ~0.6 mm diameter, tinned in a 230-250 C pot

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Electrolytic nickel plating bath
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The lead and film are plated in a sulfamate or a Watts-type nickel bath. A sulfonamide-derived depolarising agent suppresses hydrogen evolution, so the deposit is ductile and the lead does not become brittle - which matters because a brittle lead snaps inside the resistor.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: the sulfamate or pyrophosphate bath, the sulfonamide depolariser, the 30-50 g/L nickel, and the few A/dm2 current density. Plausible plating practice, but no source consulted supports it.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: sulfamate or pyrophosphate, 30-50 g/L nickel

facts.label: Current density
facts.value: a few A/dm2

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Electroplating line (sulfamate / alkaline nickel)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Racks of resistors are plated in a barrel or belt line, then rinsed and dried. Plate thickness is the mechanical anchor that stops the lead being pulled out.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: barrel or belt plating of racks of resistors, and the 2-5 um nickel plate thickness. No document consulted describes axial resistor plating lines.

facts.label: Plate thickness
facts.value: ~2-5 um Ni

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Film deposition on the tube
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The carbon-clay slurry is sprayed or dipped onto the rotating tube in a controlled spiral so the film lands only over the intended resistance length. Patterning the film length, not its thickness, is the primary way the value is dialled in.

facts.label: Cure temperature
facts.value: ~250-280 C, dwell minutes

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: oxidising (air)

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Ceramic tube substrate
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A thin-wall extruded alumina tube, 0.5 mm outside diameter, whose wall carries the film. Hollow construction halves the ceramic mass per resistor, and the tube's inner bore is what the trimmer's abrasive cut reaches.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The Bayer refinery that turns bauxite into this alumina, and its caustic-soda digestion, are metal.alumina and metal.bayer. An earlier local copy of that chain named potassium hydroxide as the 1982 digestant, which is wrong: caustic soda was the mainstream digestant.

facts.label: Tube length
facts.value: ~3.2 mm for 1/4 W

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Tube extrusion and firing
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Plasticised alumina is extruded through a die to a tube, cut to length on a flying saw, and fired in a tunnel kiln. Density is controlled so the film sees a reproducible surface.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Not established: extrusion of plasticised alumina to a tube, the flying saw, and the 1500-1650 C sintering. A carbon film is documented as deposited on an insulating substrate, but the substrate's manufacture is not described in any source consulted.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Resistor slurry (carbon + clay + binder)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Carbon black mixed with china clay as a diluent and a phenolic binder in alcohol to a printable paste. Clay fraction is the coarse knob on resistance; binder keeps the film from flaking off the tube.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: That a carbon film gives lower noise than a carbon composition resistor because of the precise distribution of the pure graphite without binding is documented, and that a carbon film is deposited on an insulating substrate with a helix cut in it. Not established: china clay as the diluent, phenolic binder in alcohol, and the claim that clay fraction is the coarse knob on resistance - the composition-resistor text makes that point for the bulk mix, not for a printed film.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Phenolic binder resin in the slurry
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Phenol-formaldehyde, dissolved in alcohol, holds carbon and clay to the tube and survives the 260 C cure. Cured phenolic also serves as the resistor's opaque body coating, which protects the film from humidity.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: Some 1980s resistor makers switched the body coating to epoxy; the C64's were visually indistinguishable without a microscope.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Kaolin (china clay) diluent
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Hydrated aluminium silicate, crushed and classified to a fine particle size. It is inert and non-conducting, so raising its share raises the sheet resistance of the dried film.
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.note: The kaolinite mineral is metal.bauxite.kaolinite and its feldspar parent is facility.electricity.feldspar; both are linked here by id.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon black (channel/process black)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: Furnace black made by feeding heavy residual oil (or natural gas) into a hot air-cooled furnace so that it impinges and soots on water-cooled steel. Furnace black from petroleum feedstock was the standard conductive phase in resistors by the 1980s.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Petroleum residuum (heavy oil feed)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: The heaviest fraction of an atmospheric or vacuum refinery distillation: a viscous, bituminous, aromatic-rich residue. It was the classical feedstock for furnace black, but from the 1950s onwards natural gas was the cheaper and cleaner alternative, and a carbon-black plant of 1982 could run on either.

mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.name: Carbon black furnace (soot reactor)
mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.car.description: A refractory-lined combustion chamber with a ~1500 C flame and water-cooled steel scraper blades. Feed oil is sprayed across the flame; the resulting soot is scraped off as a mat and pelletised.

facts.label: Grades
facts.value: N550/N660 general purpose for resistors

mb.rf-modulator.name: Commodore RF modulator module (VHF/UHF TV)
mb.rf-modulator.description: The box on the C64 mainboard that turns the VIC-II's separate luma and colour outputs plus the SID's audio into one RF carrier for a television's antenna socket. Commodore published it as schematic 251025 and 251696: a handful of Japanese small-signal transistors, two miniature RF transformers, one trimmer capacitor and about thirty resistors and capacitors, with an RCA phono jack and a ten-way terminal strip on the edge of the board.
mb.rf-modulator.note: Three corrections to the identification. First, 55.25 and 62.25 MHz do not match any broadcast allocation: neither is US channel 3 nor a UK channel. US VHF channel 3 has its picture carrier at 61.25 MHz; the European PAL C64 shipped for UK channel 36, with the vision carrier at 591.25 MHz. Second, the part numbers 474040 and 474041 are not corroborated in any Commodore document; the documented modulator identifiers are the schematic numbers 251025 and 251696 and the part numbers 250469, 326130-01, 51A1-10 and the Mitsumi MD6 series. Third, the standard Commodore modules are discrete through-hole boards with Japanese transistors, not thin-film hybrids.

facts.label: US channel 3 (NTSC)
facts.value: picture carrier 61.25 MHz, chroma 64.25 MHz, sound 67.25 MHz, intercarrier 4.5 MHz

facts.label: US channel 4 (NTSC)
facts.value: picture carrier 67.25 MHz, chroma 70.25 MHz, sound 73.25 MHz, intercarrier 4.5 MHz

facts.label: UK channel 36 (PAL-I, UHF)
facts.value: vision carrier 591.25 MHz, chroma 585.75 MHz, sound 585.25 MHz, intercarrier 5.5 MHz

facts.label: Channel switching
facts.value: an H-L switch (channel 3/4) on NTSC machines; a tuning dial on PAL machines

facts.label: Output impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm, unbalanced

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: the C64's ~9 V unregulated rail, stabilised internally by a zener

facts.label: Terminals
facts.value: 1 +B, 2 sync+luma in, 3 colour in, 4 audio in, 5 composite out, 6 sync+luma out, 7 colour out, 8 intercarrier selector, 9 RF out, 10 channel trimmer

facts.label: Size
facts.value: ~63.6 x 62.6 x 24 mm for the 251025 module

mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain.name: Two composite paths in one module
mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain.description: Because the module has to keep working as a monitor passthrough, it carries two paths: the luma and colour signals are buffered straight through to CN5 so a monitor still gets an unmodified signal, while a separate summed composite is what drives the RF section. This is why S-Video from a breadbin is clean while the RF picture is not - the lossy parts of the chain are only on the RF path.

facts.label: Terminals 6 and 7
facts.value: sync+luma out and colour out, buffered from the inputs

facts.label: Terminal 5
facts.value: composite out, the sum, also fed to CN5 pin 4 on the 5-pin board

mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain..name: NTSC and PAL variants
mb.rf-modulator.quality.composite-chain..description: The earlier 5-pin mainboard mixed sync, luminance and colour into composite on the board itself and fed that to the modulator, whereas the 8-pin boards pass luma and colour separately so the modulator can also provide S-Video. That difference is why the very first modulators are simpler than the later ones, and why the service manual says most modulators are not interchangeable.

facts.label: 5-pin board (326298-01)
facts.value: composite built on the mainboard; the modulator adds audio only

facts.label: 8-pin boards (250407-04, 250425, 250441-01, 250469)
facts.value: the modulator does the mixing and also passes luma and colour to CN5

mb.rf-modulator.assembly.name: Modulator manufacture, alignment and test
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.description: A 1980s RF module was assembled by hand through a small number of components, soldered, then aligned: the channel trimmer is set against a television signal generator or a spectrum analyser, the intercarrier selector link is fitted for the market, the level network is checked on a video monitor, and the unit is burn-in tested with a television running.
mb.rf-modulator.assembly.note: The 1980s practice was to align each module against a television set rather than a calibrated instrument, which explains why modules from different batches did not all land on exactly the same channel and why the rear-panel trimmer dial existed.

facts.label: Soldering
facts.value: 60/40 tin-lead, wave or hand, flux residue cleaned

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: trim the channel capacitor to the exact vision carrier for the market

facts.label: Test
facts.value: modulate a known composite pattern and check picture, sound and intercarrier beat

facts.label: Solder and flux
facts.value: 60/40 tin-lead, 215 C liquidus (183-190 C at the 63/37 eutectic), rosin flux cleaned off with isopropanol or trichloroethane because rosin residue is hygroscopic and slightly conductive when damp

mb.rf-modulator.quality.name: Why the RF picture was poor
mb.rf-modulator.quality.description: The modulator is not the only reason the C64's television picture was soft and cross-talk-ridden, but it removes the last chance to recover quality: the VIC-II's own composite output already mixes luminance and chroma imperfectly, the television's 6 MHz vision channel is a narrow band-pass, the sound is on a separate subcarrier that leaks, and an analogue tuner adds its own noise. Every stage is lossy and they compound.
mb.rf-modulator.quality.note: Empirical tests comparing the original modulator with modern replacements on the same CRT found almost no visible difference, which is the strongest evidence that the modulator was not the main limit - and on S-Video, bypassing the modulator's RF stage entirely, the original's luma and chroma outputs measured slightly better than most replacements.

facts.label: Vision channel width
facts.value: ~5.5 MHz for a 625-line PAL signal in a 6 or 7 MHz slot

facts.label: Composite crosstalk
facts.value: the VIC-II's chroma is not properly band-limited before being added to luminance

facts.label: Set-side limit
facts.value: the analogue tuner's noise figure and AGC dominate at low signal levels

mb.rf-modulator.variants.name: Modulator part numbers and revisions
mb.rf-modulator.variants.description: Commodore changed the modulator repeatedly and warned in the service manual that most modulators are different and the parts are not interchangeable between mainboards. Documented identifiers include 250469 (the short-board C64C), 326130-01, 51A1-10 Rev 2, and Japanese Mitsumi-built modules MD6-UE3603 for PAL and MD6-VA3402 / VA3403 / VA3405 for NTSC.
mb.rf-modulator.variants.note: The part numbers 474040 and 474041 are not found in any Commodore document or parts list. If they are real they are most likely internal drawing or vendor numbers rather than the field-replaceable part numbers listed here.

facts.value: 220 uF 16 V, 10 uF 16 V radial
2 x 4.7 uF 16 V radial

facts.label: Mitsumi MD6-UE3603
facts.value: 470 uF 10 V, 2 x 100 uF 16 V, 10 uF 16 V - the PAL version

facts.label: Mitsumi MD6-VA3402/3403/3405
facts.value: NTSC versions with different electrolytic sets

mb.rf-modulator.variants.toad.name: The 'toad' module nickname
mb.rf-modulator.variants.toad.description: Early Commodore modulators are sometimes described by hobbyists as a toad or a blob: the epoxy-covered module sits on the mainboard with its lead frame splayed out, and from the top it does look like an animal. The nickname is not a Commodore part name - it exists only in the collector community.
mb.rf-modulator.variants.toad.note: No published source uses this nickname for the C64 modulator; it may come from a different platform. The attribution of the nickname to the C64 modulator is uncertain.

mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.name: Mitsumi-built modules
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.description: Mitsumi Electric was a major Japanese supplier of consumer-electronics subassemblies and shipped RF modulator modules to Commodore. The MD6 prefix denotes the module family; the suffix distinguishes NTSC from PAL and the electrolytic set.

facts.label: PAL
facts.value: MD6-UE3603

mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.name: The 1984 C64C video path
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.description: The later C64 boards do not simply carry a better modulator - they changed where the signal is encoded. A dedicated video encoder IC generates the composite and separate luma/chroma outputs from the VIC-II's signals, so the video is encoded once, to a defined standard, outside the modulator; the RF modulator is then reduced to a device that only has to put that composite onto a carrier and add the audio. The contrast with the breadbin is that there the modulator itself was the video encoder as well as the modulator.
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.note: The existence of a dedicated CMOS video encoder on the C64C is well established in the enthusiast literature and C64-Wiki has a page stub for the part, but the device marking and its function in this context are not verified against a primary source. The US and PAL channel frequencies quoted above are standard broadcast allocations and are high confidence; the encoder part number is not.

facts.label: Encoding point
facts.value: moved off the modulator onto a dedicated encoder IC

facts.label: Result
facts.value: composite and S-Video are available regardless of whether the RF modulator is fitted

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: the RF modulator becomes a purely analogue RF carrier generator

mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.name: Video encoder integrated circuit
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.description: A mask-programmed device that takes the VIC-II's luminance and chrominance plus the synchronisation inputs and generates composite video and separate luma and chrominance outputs internally, using on-chip resistor-string DACs for the levels. Building the encoder alongside the VIC-II was what made the S-Video output clean enough to be worth using.
mb.rf-modulator.variants.mitsumi.contras.note: The exact part number and its manufacturer are not verified against a primary source; this is a description of the function rather than of a confirmed device.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: luminance/chrominance to composite and S-Video encoding, with internal level DACs

facts.label: Clock
facts.value: driven from the 14.318 MHz colour clock

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.name: Illustrative hybrid module construction (not Commodore)
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.description: ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY - this is not how any Commodore RF modulator was built. Both Commodore drawings that can be read (schematic 251025 and 251696) show a discrete through-hole board with Japanese small-signal transistors, two miniature RF transformers, a trimmer and about thirty resistors and capacitors, with an RCA phono jack on the module. What follows is the thin-film hybrid construction used by RF modulator modules from Japanese games manufacturers of the same period - a real and common alternative construction of the period, but no Commodore part number has been matched to it. Confidence in every node below is low as a statement about the C64 and high only as a statement about hybrid modules in general.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.note: Read this subtree as a comparison, not as a source. The observable Commodore evidence is the two schematics, both of which show a discrete board; the hybrid construction here is real technology of the period but its presence in a Commodore modulator is unverified and probably wrong for every documented part number.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: 96% alumina or a hermetic ceramic; beryllia for the highest thermal conductivity

facts.label: Resistors
facts.value: thin-film or thick-film deposited and laser-trimmed on the substrate

facts.label: Encapsulant
facts.value: transparent or opaque epoxy, transfer moulded or dipped

facts.label: Leads
facts.value: gold- or nickel-plated DIP or castellated lead frame

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment.name: Substrate alignment and RF screening
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment.description: After assembly the module is screened: an RF sweep is injected at the output terminal and the response curve is checked against a mask. A damaged substrate, a lifted chip termination or a cracked lead frame shows up as a notch in the response, which is why a hybrid modulator's yield is dominated by the ceramic and the assembly rather than by the design.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alignment.note: Screen-on-substrate testing in the bare form was a 1990s technique; a 1982 hybrid was tested only after encapsulation, so a realignment meant re-encapsulating.

facts.label: Test method
facts.value: swept-response substitution with an RF sweep generator and a detector

facts.label: Pass criterion
facts.value: within a mask on insertion loss, return loss and resonance

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.name: Chip inductor and chip capacitor
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.description: In a hybrid RF module the high-value capacitors and the low-value inductors are not screen-printed but chip-bonded: a fired ceramic chip capacitor with metallised terminations is reflowed onto the substrate, and an inductor is a tiny spiral of metallised polyimide on a ceramic chip. The polyimide is photosensitised, plated, etched and diced, so the inductance is set by the artwork rather than by a winding machine.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.note: Chip inductors were a 1990s development for RF modules above about 100 MHz; a 60 MHz television modulator in 1982 used a wound coil, and the chip parts that were used were almost all capacitors.

facts.label: Chip capacitor
facts.value: fired BaTiO3 or tantalum, terminated in fired silver or a solderable metal

facts.label: Chip inductor
facts.value: photosensitised polyimide spiral on alumina, 1-100 nH typical

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.name: Laser trimming of the film resistors
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.description: A laser is pulsed at a deposited resistor while a bridge measures its value, cutting a slot in the film a few microns wide to raise the resistance by a controlled amount. Each pulse changes the value by a known increment and the bridge closes the loop, so a resistor can be trimmed to 0.1% or better in a fraction of a second. Before laser trimming was cheap, the same slot was cut by abrading with a sand jet under a bridge, which was slower and only got to about 5%.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.chip-passi.note: Laser trimming became standard in thick-film hybrid manufacture in the late 1980s; a 1982 module was trimmed by a mechanical probe that cut a slot in the film, or not trimmed at all.

facts.label: Trim resolution
facts.value: ~0.01% per pulse

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.name: Hybrid module assembly and transfer moulding
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.description: The die or chip components are bonded to the substrate, the lead frame is attached, and the whole assembly is transfer moulded in epoxy: a silicone-rubber mould loaded with epoxy powder is vibrated to pack it around the part, the encapsulant is pressed in, and it is cured at 150-175 C. This is the same process used for every integrated circuit in the machine.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.note: For a hybrid the mould is room-temperature or low-temperature cured so that the deposited film and any surface-mounted parts survive; for an IC the epoxy is moulded at full cure temperature.

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 20-60 s per shot for a small mould

facts.label: Curing
facts.value: 150-175 C, several minutes

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.name: Attaching the substrate to the lead frame
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.description: The substrate is aligned to the lead frame to within a few microns, given a thin coat of conductive epoxy - silver-filled epoxy is the usual choice because it cures at only 150-200 C - or a screen-printed solder paste is printed and reflowed, then the assembly is baked so the die attaches without stress. Silver-filled epoxy has no metallurgical bond and can debond with thermal cycling, which is the classic failure mode of a hybrid module.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.note: Not established: the 5-25 um conductive-epoxy and 1-10 um solder alignment figures, the 150-200 C / 1-4 h silver-epoxy cure, and the claim that silver-filled epoxy has no metallurgical bond and debonds on thermal cycling. No source consulted covers hybrid-module substrate-to-lead-frame attachment.

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: 5-25 um for conductive epoxy; 1-10 um for solder attach

facts.label: Curing
facts.value: 150-200 C for 1-4 h for silver epoxy

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.name: Silver-filled conductive epoxy
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.description: Epoxy resin loaded with 50-80% silver flakes. The flakes touch each other to form a percolating conductor while the epoxy gives mechanical strength and cures at a temperature the chip and substrate tolerate. Bulk resistivity is about 0.001-0.01 ohm.cm, two to three orders of magnitude worse than a metal, so it is used for bonding and for conductive fill, never for signal.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.assembly.l.note: Not established: 50-80 wt% silver flake loading, ~5-50 um flakes, and the 0.001-0.01 ohm.cm bulk resistivity, and the gold-filled non-migrating alternative at roughly ten times the cost. Epoxy resins as a family are documented; silver-filled conductive epoxy as a specific composition and its resistivity are not.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 50-80 wt% silver flake, ~5-50 um flakes

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.name: Gold-plated DIP lead frame
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.description: The substrate is attached to a lead frame by reflow or conductive epoxy, and the frame's pins are plated. Gold is used where the RF signal leaves the module, because a nickel or tin surface has poor conductivity at 60 MHz and tarnishes; in cheap modules only the signal pins are gold and the supply pins are tinned.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.lead-frame.note: Hard gold plating came in because gold on soft gold diffused into the bond pads.

facts.label: Frame
facts.value: nickel-iron or copper alloy strip, stamped and formed

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: gold over nickel on signal pins, tin on supply pins

facts.label: Gold thickness
facts.value: ~0.5-2 um hard gold in the 1980s

facts.label: Plating thickness
facts.value: about 0.5-2 um of hard gold over nickel on the signal pins, tin on the supply pins

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.epoxy-enca.name: Epoxy encapsulant as RF seal
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.epoxy-enca.description: A clear or opaque filled epoxy poured or transfer moulded over the finished substrate. In RF modules it does three jobs at once: it excludes moisture and contaminants, it holds the components against vibration, and - because it is a low-loss dielectric with a stable dielectric constant - it fixes the stray capacitance around the tank, which is what stops the carrier drifting with humidity. A conductive epoxy variant is used as a ground plane on the reverse of the substrate.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.epoxy-enca.note: Not established: silica or alumina flour at 40-70% by weight, a 3.5-4.5 dielectric constant, the 15-25 ppm/K filled against 50-70 unfilled CTE, and the specific RF role of fixing stray capacitance around the tank. Epoxy as a thermosetting encapsulant is documented; the filler loading, the electrical figures and the RF rationale are not.

facts.label: Fill
facts.value: silica or alumina flour at 40-70% by weight for low CTE and low moisture uptake

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: ~3.5-4.5, low and stable

facts.label: CTE
facts.value: 15-25 ppm/K filled, versus 50-70 unfilled

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.name: Thin-film and thick-film resistor networks
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.description: A film of nickel-chromium is deposited by vacuum evaporation or sputtering onto the alumina, then patterned by photolithography and etching. Because the sheet resistance of the film is very uniform the as-deposited value is already within a few percent, so a trim brings it to its exact value.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.thin-film-.note: Thick film, a screen-printed ruthenium-oxide paste fired at 800-900 C, was the normal choice for a cheap RF module in 1982; thin film was reserved for precision timing and gain stages.

facts.label: Thin film
facts.value: NiCr sputtered, ~50-500 ohm per square

facts.label: Trim
facts.value: sand-blast trim to 5-10% before laser trimming; laser trim to 0.1-1% became cheap only in the late 1980s

facts.label: TCR
facts.value: 25-100 ppm/K, far better than a thick-film resistor

facts.label: Thick film
facts.value: screen-printed ruthenium-oxide cermet, 10-1000 ohm per square, fired at 800-900 C for 10-30 min; the glass frit content sets the resistance

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.name: Alumina substrate and its ceramic processing
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.description: A thin, smooth, thermally conductive ceramic sheet. Alumina is made by calcining purified aluminium hydroxide, pressing or tape-casting it with an organic binder, sintering at 1500-1700 C, then lapping and laser-cutting the finished sheets to thickness. It is inert, dimensionally stable and easy to metallise.

facts.label: Alumina content
facts.value: 96% standard, 99.5% high-purity

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.25-1.0 mm, lapped and polished

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.name: Magnesium oxide sintering aid
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.description: A few tenths of a percent of magnesium oxide is added to 96% alumina before sintering to stop the ceramic over-shrinking and to fire it at a lower temperature, which is what makes 96% alumina affordable for a hybrid substrate.
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.note: Not established: 0.2-0.5% magnesium oxide as a sintering aid, the ~100-150 C reduction in sintering temperature, and the resulting shrinkage control. The alumina article documents dense alpha-alumina ceramics and high-purity grades but does not mention magnesium oxide as an additive for 96% alumina, nor any sintering temperature.

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: sintering temperature down by ~100-150 C, shrinkage reduced

mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.name: Magnesite ore
mb.rf-modulator.hybrid-module.alumina-su.description: A magnesium carbonate rock mined in Austria, Spain, China and India, calcined at 1400-1700 C to magnesia. In the 1980s most ceramic-grade magnesia was calcined from seawater or from brine, but the rock remains the classic source.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: MgCO3, becoming MgO above ~1400 C

mb.rf-modulator.supply.name: Modulator supply and zener stabiliser
mb.rf-modulator.supply.description: The modulator runs from the C64's ~9 V unregulated DC rail - the same rail that feeds the cassette motor - not from the clean 5 V. Q6 (2SC2120) buffers the feed and a zener with electrolytics sets the working voltage for the analog sections.
mb.rf-modulator.supply.note: Not established: that the modulator is fed from the 9 V unregulated rail, the 2SC2120 buffer, the ~8.2 V zener (HZ-7A1) and the 220 uF / 100 uF / 22 nF reservoir network. The 1992 service manual confirms the modulator exists as a numbered part (M1, Modulator 251696-01; Modulator NTSC 252405-01, on the 250407-04 board with modulator schematic 251696) and confirms the C64's supply rails, but its component-level supply network is not documented in the sources consulted.

facts.label: Input
facts.value: ~9-12 V DC from the C64's unreg 9 V rail, terminal 1 (+B)

facts.label: Zener
facts.value: ~8.2 V class (HZ-7A1 or equivalent in the 251696 drawing)

facts.label: Reservoir
facts.value: 220 uF and 100 uF electrolytics plus a 22 nF decoupling

mb.rf-modulator.supply.zener.name: 8.2 V Zener diode
mb.rf-modulator.supply.zener.description: A heavily doped PN junction reverse-biased into breakdown. The doping is so heavy that the depletion layer is only a few microns wide, which gives the device a very low capacitance and a fast, hard breakdown - ideal for a shunt regulator and for clamping.
mb.rf-modulator.supply.zener.note: The C64 mainboard itself uses 2.7 V (1N4371) and 7.5 V (1N755) zeners in the cassette motor drive, so the same parts bins served the brick, the modulator and the mainboard.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: HZ-7A1 (~6.8-8.2 V) or equivalent

facts.label: Breakdown tolerance
facts.value: +/-5% for an ordinary zener

facts.label: Temperature drift
facts.value: ~+2 mV per volt of nominal per degree C

mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.name: RF output network and 75 ohm match
mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.description: The picture carrier leaves the tank through a tap, is coupled out through a series capacitor, and is matched to the 75 ohm coax of the television's antenna input by a resistive network with a ferrite bead in the supply feed. Getting the match right is what stops the RF from reflecting back into the oscillator and pulling the carrier off channel as the television is tuned.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.note: Most C64 installations put the phono jack on the rear panel of the machine and connect it to the modulator by a short coax or a twisted pair inside the case.

facts.label: Output impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm unbalanced

facts.label: Series match
facts.value: ~82 ohm and ~33 ohm resistors with a blocking capacitor

facts.label: Supply isolation
facts.value: a ferrite bead in the +B feed to the output stage

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: RCA phono jack, mounted on the module in the 251025 drawing

facts.label: Supply isolation bead
facts.value: a ferrite bead on the +B feed, 50-500 ohm at 100 MHz and near zero at DC

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.name: PAL UHF output stage
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.description: At 591 MHz a single transistor oscillator cannot drive a 75 ohm television input through a long lead, so the PAL modulators add a small tuned output stage and, in the later units, an output amplifier with its own bias network. The extra gain is what makes a PAL C64 usable on a European television without a booster.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.note: No schematic for the PAL variant is available, so the topology here is inferred from the service manual's description of the PAL modules and from the general practice of UHF modulators of the period.

facts.label: Gain
facts.value: a few dB of tuned amplification after the oscillator

facts.label: Matching
facts.value: tapped output coil plus a series blocking capacitor into the phono socket

mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.rca-jack.name: RCA phono socket
mb.rf-modulator.rf-output.rca-jack.description: The US-style phono connector that carries the composite antenna signal. The centre pin is often nickel- or gold-plated brass and the outer shell is a turned brass or plated-steel barrel crimped into the body; the body is moulded in a glass-filled thermoplastic.

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: brass, nickel- or gold-plated, 0.8 mm centre pin

facts.label: Impedance
facts.value: 75 ohm characteristic

facts.label: Body
facts.value: glass-filled nylon or polycarbonate

mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.name: Audio intercarrier path
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.description: A separate 4.5 MHz (NTSC) or 5.5 MHz (PAL) oscillator whose amplitude is modulated by the SID's audio output, then added to the picture carrier. Terminal 8 selects between the two: Commodore's drawing notes that terminal 8 shorted to ground is PAL and open is NTSC PAL/US.
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.note: Television sound is transmitted as FM on a subcarrier, and the tuner recovers it by beating the subcarrier against a local oscillator at the same frequency to produce the 6.0 or 5.5 MHz difference that every television's audio detector already handles. Using the standard intercarrier is why the modulator could be so simple - the set needed no second demodulator.

facts.label: Intercarrier
facts.value: 4.5 MHz NTSC, 5.5 MHz PAL

facts.label: Input filter
facts.value: 22 uH choke and a ~10 nF capacitor

facts.label: Audio source
facts.value: the SID's amplified audio, fed from CN5 pin 3

mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.intercarrier.name: Intercarrier selector terminal
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.intercarrier.description: A single link or jumper on terminal 8 that reconfigures the intercarrier oscillator between 4.5 and 5.5 MHz. It is the PAL/NTSC configuration link for the whole module, and it is why one board could serve both markets with a single part change.
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.intercarrier.note: Not established: terminal 8 being shorted to ground for PAL (5.5 MHz) and open for NTSC (4.5 MHz), and its implementation as a link or switch contact in the oscillator bias network. The 1992 service manual confirms two modulator variants exist - schematic 251025 for board 250425-01 and schematic 251696 for board 250407-04, the latter listed as "Modulator NTSC" - which supports the two-market point, but the terminal-8 strapping note is not in any source consulted.

facts.label: Terminal 8
facts.value: shorted to ground = PAL (5.5 MHz); open = NTSC (4.5 MHz)

facts.label: Implementation
facts.value: a link or a switch contact in the oscillator bias network

mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.name: FM modulator network
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.description: The audio signal is fed to the intercarrier oscillator's base through a series resistor and a coupling capacitor, so the oscillator's amplitude follows the audio envelope. A varactor or a reactance modulator would be the higher-fidelity route; amplitude modulation is cheap and adequate because the television's own FM limiter removes most of the distortion.
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.note: Modulation depth is kept low enough to avoid over-modulation and the characteristic buzz of a badly limited FM signal.

facts.label: Series network
facts.value: ~2.2 kOhm and a ~10 nF coupling capacitor into the oscillator base

mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.name: SID audio amplifier transistor
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.description: On the C64 mainboard the SID's pin 27 output is amplified by Q2 before it reaches CN5 pin 3 and the modulator; the modulator's audio input then loads that amplifier. The stage is a common-emitter NPN with a bias divider and an emitter resistor, running from the CAN +5 V rail.
mb.rf-modulator.audio-chain.fm-modulator.note: This stage lives on the mainboard rather than inside the modulator, which is why the modulator's audio input could be a simple high-impedance network. The transistor itself is one of the C64's ordinary small-signal discretes (2N3904, Commodore stock 902658-01), from the same bins as the other board-level amplifiers, not one of the 2SC parts the modulator uses.

facts.label: Device
facts.value: 2N3904 (Commodore stock 902658-01) in the mainboard audio path

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.name: Picture carrier oscillator
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.description: A Clapp or Colpitts oscillator built around Q4 (2SC1730, a VHF transistor with an f_T above 300 MHz) and a miniature RF transformer, with a capacitive divider setting the feedback ratio. Composite video is injected into the oscillator's base network, so the video signal frequency-modulates the carrier directly: the modulation is done by varying the effective tank reactance with the video voltage, not by driving a separate modulator.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.note: Channel setting is a resistor strapping and the channel trimmer, not a switched band. On NTSC machines an H-L switch on the rear panel changes a resistor or opens a contact in that network; on PAL machines there is a tuning dial instead, because the European sets have no fine channel selector - the dial is what makes a Commodore usable on a European television at all.

facts.label: Frequency
facts.value: 61.25 MHz (NTSC ch 3), 67.25 MHz (NTSC ch 4), 591.25 MHz (PAL UK UHF ch 36)

facts.label: Feedback divider
facts.value: ~33.5 pF and 3.3 pF capacitors around the base

facts.label: Deviation
facts.value: +/-4.5 MHz from the carrier, i.e. +/-0.5 MHz of 5.5 MHz peak video

facts.label: Level network
facts.value: ~56 kOhm and 47 ohm series resistors with 30-51 pF capacitors

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.varactor.name: MA57 tuning varactor diode
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.varactor.description: On the earlier 251696 drawing the tuning is done by D3, an MA57: a junction varactor whose capacitance falls as the reverse bias rises. Lifting the tuning out of the tank into a varactor keeps the temperature coefficient and the stray capacitance low. Later drawings use a mechanical trimmer in the same position.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.varactor.note: A junction varactor in a 60 MHz television modulator is unusual - most designs tune with a trimmer - so the MA57 may be a varicap used for a small frequency-modulation or level function rather than for the channel. Its exact role in the 251696 drawing could not be confirmed from the scan.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: MA57 or equivalent (251696 note 2)

facts.label: Function
facts.value: variable reactance in the oscillator tank

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: a screw trimmer capacitor on terminal 10 in the 251025 drawing

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.name: Channel trimmer capacitor
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.description: The channel tuning element brought out to terminal 10 of the module: a small screw-adjusted trimmer in the 1-10 pF range, most often a ceramic plate or disc trimmer with a barium titanate or glass-ceramic dielectric, sometimes a stacked mica trimmer. It sits across the tank and is set once, at the television manufacturer's alignment step, against a sweep generator or a calibrated television signal. It is not one of the multilayer ceramic blocks that appeared later in the decade: a screw-accessible trimmer is what an alignment engineer needs, and a 1-10 pF part with internal electrodes would have been the wrong part for the job.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-tr.note: The 251025 drawing shows two adjustable trimmers in the RF area, one of which is the channel trimmer on terminal 10 and the other in the oscillator's feedback network. Later revisions replaced them with a fixed capacitor plus a resistor strapping for channel 3 or 4, which is why the channel switch exists at all.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: ceramic screw-trimmer or mica trimmer, radial or dip

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.name: Channel and region switching
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.description: Three different ways of reaching the right channel appear across the revisions. The US machines use a two-position H-L switch on the C64's own rear panel, wired to change a component value in the oscillator tank or level network; the switch is a low-voltage contact on the mainboard, not the brick's mains rocker. Some later units bring a variable capacitor or a trimmer out to a dial so the user can tune to their local station. PAL machines use the UHF band, so their oscillator runs at several times the frequency of the NTSC one and the tank, the output matching and an extra tuned output stage are different parts entirely.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.channel-se.note: The C64 Wiki notes that beside the RF jack you often see an H-L switch for channels 3 and 4 (NTSC only) or a control dial for adjusting the oscillator frequency - the two mechanisms correspond to the two markets.

facts.label: NTSC H-L switch
facts.value: switches between 61.25 and 67.25 MHz

facts.label: PAL dial
facts.value: continuous tuning around 591.25 MHz (UK channel 36)

facts.label: Implication
facts.value: one modulator part number could not serve both markets, which is why the service manual lists several

mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.rf-transis.name: 2SC1730 / 2SC2778 VHF transistor
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.rf-transis.description: A VHF small-signal NPN in TO-92, chosen because its unity-gain bandwidth is several times the 60 MHz operating frequency so the oscillator starts easily and stays linear, and because its output capacitance is low enough not to detune the tank.
mb.rf-modulator.rf-oscillator.rf-transis.note: Both are Japanese VHF small-signal types with f_T in the low hundreds of MHz; the exact figures are not verified against a 1982 data book.

facts.label: f_T
facts.value: ~250-350 MHz class

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.name: Video amplifier and clip network
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.description: Three small-signal transistors that take the VIC-II's pin 15 (sync + luminance) and pin 14 (colour), clip them with back-to-back diodes, and provide the two separate buffered outputs that go to the monitor connector as S-Video plus the summed composite that drives the RF section. Commodore called Q1-Q3 2SC1694 or equivalent; the earlier 251696 drawing uses 2SC2405.

facts.label: Q1, Q2, Q3 (251025)
facts.value: 2SC1694 or equivalent; Q4 2SC1730, Q5 2SC460, Q6 2SC2120

facts.label: Q1, Q2 (251696)
facts.value: 2SC2405 or equivalent; Q3, Q4 2SC2778; Q5 2SC2120Y

facts.label: Clamp diodes
facts.value: 1SS119 (251025) or MA151K (251696), back to back on the sync tips

facts.label: Typical network
facts.value: colour in via 68 nF with 1k/33k/43k bias and a 68 ohm emitter; luma in via 2.4 nF and 180 pF with 12k, 100 ohm and 400 ohm

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.clip-diodes.name: 1SS119 / MA151K clip diodes
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.clip-diodes.description: Small-signal switching diodes, typically 50 mA class in a DO-35 glass can, wired back to back across the sync input. They conduct only on the tips of the sync pulses and the colour burst, which clips the signal to the amplitude a television's AGC expects and stops the modulator over-modulating.
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.clip-diodes.note: Not established: the 1SS119 and MA151K designations, the ~0.6-0.7 V forward drop at 1 mA, the DO-35 2 mm package, and the back-to-back sync-clipping topology. The 1992 service manual confirms that the modulator takes the VIC-II's sync/luminance on pin 15 and colour on pin 14 and mixes them with audio, but says nothing about the clipping diodes. No datasheet for either part was consulted.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: 1SS119 (251025) / MA151K (251696) or equivalent

facts.label: Package
facts.value: DO-35 glass, 2 mm diameter

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: 2SC1694 small-signal NPN
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: A TO-92 epoxy-potted silicon NPN with a 100-150 V collector rating, used as a common-emitter amplifier with a collector resistor and an unbypassed emitter resistor. The 2SC-prefix parts were the standard Japanese equivalents of the 2N series, and Commodore specified them as 'or equivalent'.
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.note: Not established: the 2SC1694's 100-150 V collector rating and 50-150 mA class, the TO-92 epoxy-filled package, and Commodore's practice of specifying 2SC-prefix parts as "or equivalent" against 2N3904/2N4401. No datasheet for the 2SC1694 was consulted, so the ratings and package here are unsourced.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-92, epoxy-filled

mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.name: Wafer processing and TO-92 moulding
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.description: The die is a small epitaxial NPN on a 100 mm P-type <111> wafer, sawn with a diamond blade, die-attached with a silver-glass preform, wire-bonded with 50 um aluminium and transfer-moulded in an epoxy-filled TO-92 tool at 150-175 C.
mb.rf-modulator.video-chain.ssc-transist.note: This is one of about forty such transistors in a C64; the silicon branch of this tree carries the full wafer process.

facts.label: Epitaxy
facts.value: 4-6 um N-type epi on a 10-20 ohm.cm P substrate

facts.label: Polycrystalline silicon
facts.value: 9N, grown by Siemens deposition from trichlorosilane at 1000-1150 C over DC-heated filaments, then pulled as a 100-150 mm Czochralski ingot and sawn to ~250-300 um wafers

facts.label: Mould compound
facts.value: black epoxy, usually silica-filled, transfer-moulded in a multi-cavity TO-92 tool at 150-175 C

mb.logic.name: 74-series glue logic
mb.logic.description: The off-the-shelf logic chips on a Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 that are not Commodore's own designs - thirteen positions according to the service-manual parts list, plus an LM556 timer alongside them. They do no arithmetic and no video: they multiplex addresses, latch bytes, decode chip selects, count, generate the video dot clock and invert the cassette port. Ten are 74-series in black epoxy DIP, three are CMOS 4000-series, and the U8 is an older non-Schottky 7406. Individually each was a commodity costing tens of cents.
mb.logic.note: The part list below is taken from the official C64 Service Manual parts list for PCB assembly #250407 and independently corroborated by three hobbyist references (Retrogate's retro.rewind wiki, the C64-Wiki motherboard page, and MonkeySpeak's hardware detail sheet). It is NOT the list that circulates in most '74-series chips in the Commodore 64' compilations (74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125, 74LS181, 74LS14, 74LS04, 74LS00) - those part numbers belong to the Apple II, the VIC-20 and the BBC Micro, not the C64; see the '74-series parts that are NOT on a C64' node below. One widely-copied web page (oldsilicon.com) swaps the 74LS257 and the 74LS373 between U14 and U26; the service manual says U14 = 74LS258 and U26 = 74LS373, which this tree follows, and the 74LS258 node records the discrepancy in its own note. There is also a count discrepancy worth knowing: the frequently quoted 'eleven glue chips' does not reconcile with the parts list. The service manual gives ten packages carrying a 74 prefix - U8, U13, U14, U15, U25, U26, U27, U29, U30, U31 - and three CMOS packages, U16, U28 and U32, which is thirteen positions before the LM556 is counted at all. That is twelve distinct part numbers, because the 74LS257 is fitted twice and the 4066 twice. On the shape of the branch: each chip's `children` are the bipolar process and the DIP package, which is a manufacturing decomposition rather than strict containment, but it is the decomposition every other subsystem in this tree uses for a bought component, and the commodity materials hang off `inputs` so they resolve to the canonical metal.* and chem.* nodes instead of being inlined.

facts.label: 74-series parts fitted
facts.value: 10 packages, 8 distinct part numbers (the 74LS257 is fitted twice)

facts.label: CMOS parts fitted
facts.value: 4 packages, 3 distinct part numbers (4066 x2, MC4044, 74LS629)

facts.label: Distinct part numbers
facts.value: 12 including the adjacent LM556 at U20

facts.label: Package
facts.value: all through-hole epoxy DIP, 14/16/20 pin

mb.logic.economics.name: What a 74LS is made of, and what it cost
mb.logic.economics.description: The whole point of the comparison. A 74LS chip is a few milligrams of silicon, a few milligrams of metal, a third of a gram of epoxy, and a couple of hundred person-minutes of work spread across a fortnight of factory flow time. It sold for a few tens of cents. The 6510 on the same board, a thousand times more transistors on a finer process, cost several dollars. Commodore's entire bill of materials for the electronics was a small fraction of the machine's retail price. The bill of materials for one 74LS04, with the arithmetic: about 3 mg of silicon in a roughly 3.6 mm2 die cut from a 300 um wafer - the '3-5 um' figure usually quoted is the depth of the active junctions, not the mass; 10-30 mg of aluminium on the die from one 1.0-1.5 um level over about half the die area, which is an order of magnitude below the 0.3 g often quoted and is probably a wafer-level inventory figure rather than a per-chip one; under a milligram of gold in total, from about sixteen to twenty 0.5-1.0 mil wire bonds (0.2-0.4 mg) plus the die-attach preform (0.2-0.5 mg of Au-Si); under a milligram of sputtered NiCr; about 100 mg of nickel-iron in the lead frame at roughly 42 percent Ni, most of that mass being the iron half; and 0.3-0.6 g of silica-filled epoxy, three quarters of it fused silica. So the total is roughly half a gram per DIP-14, of which about 100:1 by mass is polymer, and the thirteen glue-chip positions on a C64 together weigh about six grams. The labour figure of roughly 200 person-minutes per finished chip is an order-of-magnitude estimate and worth unpacking, because it is not 200 minutes of one person's attention: it is direct operator and technician time amortised across the whole flow, roughly 20-30 operator touches across the 60-100 front-end steps, plus probe test, assembly, final test and inspection. Flow time is not touch time - a batch of wafers spends a week and a half moving through the fab, almost all of it waiting in a furnace, in a queue or in a cassette under a nitrogen purge, and what costs money is the twenty or thirty separate occasions when somebody has to be present and paying attention, which over a fortnight is a couple of hours. On price: a commodity 74LS gate was priced against a cost of a few tens of cents and a price in the same range, falling year on year as the industry learned; a merchant part's cost is amortised across every customer in the world and over a mask set that runs on a flow making dozens of other part numbers, so Commodore was buying a fraction of the output of a factory that existed whether or not Commodore existed, with a mask set it did not pay for and a design it did not own. The 6510 was the opposite on every count - one mask set, one customer, one buyer, a design that had to be paid for before it shipped a single unit - which is why Commodore's engineers minimised custom silicon and spent money freely on merchant glue, and also why the later C128 could add a second 6510 and a bank-switching PLA without touching the price of the machine.
mb.logic.economics.note: Not established: a primary 1983 distributor price list for 74LS parts, a documented Commodore purchase price for a 6510, or a measured weight for any of these parts. Confidence is low on that basis. The 0.3 g of aluminium often quoted for a 14-pin logic chip is roughly an order of magnitude too high for the metal actually in the die. The mass figures are arithmetic from die dimensions and layer thicknesses and should be right to within a factor of a few; the price figures are order-of-magnitude estimates from the general semiconductor price decline of the era. The broader trend - prices falling roughly 10-30 percent a year in real terms through the early 1980s, faster for commodity logic - is documented in the economic literature and is the basis for the direction even where not the specific prices. Treat every number here as a defensible intuition rather than a measurement.

facts.label: Total mass per DIP-14
facts.value: ~0.4-0.6 g, about 100:1 polymer to die

facts.label: Silicon in the die
facts.value: ~3 mg (3.6 mm2 die x 300 um wafer)

facts.label: Aluminium on the die
facts.value: ~10-30 mg - the often-quoted 0.3 g looks like a wafer-level figure

facts.label: Gold per chip
facts.value: ~0.5-1 mg, from 16-20 wire bonds plus the die-attach preform

facts.label: NiCr per chip
facts.value: < 1 mg

facts.label: Lead frame
facts.value: ~100 mg of 42% Ni iron

facts.label: Epoxy moulding compound
facts.value: ~0.3-0.6 g, ~70-80 wt% fused silica

facts.label: The thirteen glue-chip positions on a C64
facts.value: ~6 g together

facts.label: Direct labour
facts.value: ~100-300 person-minutes per finished device, across ~20-30 operator touches

facts.label: Flow time versus touch time
facts.value: ~1-2 weeks of factory time, of which hours are hands-on

facts.label: Selling price, 1983
facts.value: order 20-60 cents per 74LS (estimate); considerably less on volume contract

facts.label: 6510, same era
facts.value: order a few dollars (estimate)

facts.label: Custom versus merchant cost ratio
facts.value: ~10:1 or more (estimate)

facts.label: Price trend
facts.value: semiconductor prices fell 10-30%/yr in real terms through the early 1980s

mb.logic.sourcing.name: Merchant logic supply to Commodore
mb.logic.sourcing.description: Commodore did not fab logic. It bought merchant 74-series parts from the American and Japanese vendors, and because a machine built in millions cannot wait for a part number to be on allocation, it also ran second sources of its own - internal house-numbered equivalents made at other plants, marked 7701, 7707, 7708, 7711, 8712 and so on. An original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore number, all mixed on the same board, all doing the same job. This branch describes Commodore's procurement rather than a physical process: the vendors are companies, the second-source parts are a real component family, and the distribution chain is a sentence about how parts travelled rather than a thing.
mb.logic.sourcing.note: The vendor list and the second-source practice are well attested by the physical parts on surviving boards and by Commodore's parts lists. Not established: which plants made Commodore's specific lots, so no plant is claimed below as fact.

facts.label: Named suppliers on a 250407
facts.value: TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba, MOS house numbers

facts.label: Purchase route
facts.value: vendor sales, franchised distributor, and broker / open market

mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.name: How the chips physically arrived in 1983
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.description: Nobody at Commodore's Pennsylvania assembly plant picked up a telephone and ordered from Texas Instruments. There was a distribution chain, and where a part sat in that chain decided both its price and whether it was genuine. Buying from the manufacturer's own sales arm or a franchised distributor got you an authorised part with a full warranty and a date code. Buying from a broker or an independent distributor got you the same silicon much cheaper, with no guarantee of origin at all. Three mechanisms made the difference. Allocation: when demand exceeded supply - and in 1982-84 it very often did, because the whole consumer electronics industry was recovering from the 1980-81 recession simultaneously - a manufacturer rationed, a computer maker with a purchase order got whatever share the vendor allocated pro rata, and production had to be scheduled around delivery dates rather than around its own. That is why the price of a commodity 74LS was set by the market's shortage rather than by what it cost to make. Pulls: parts that reached a buyer through anything other than a franchised distributor were, in the trade's language, 'pulled', which could be entirely innocent - a company over-ordered and released surplus, a broker bought at auction - or diverted from a competitor's own allocation. Because a 74LS08 has no serial number, no authentication and no visible origin, nobody could tell the difference; the industry's response through the 1980s and 1990s was a growing formal apparatus for tracking authorised distribution, and the counterfeiting industry grew alongside it. And incoming inspection: every shipment of semiconductors was counted and checked against the bill of materials before the parts went near a board, with non-matching parts quarantined - which is worth noting because the components on a C64 mainboard are not hand-selected, so the board either works with whatever chip arrived in the box or it is reworked, which is a large part of why surviving C64s need a recap and a chip-sorting pass before they will run.
mb.logic.sourcing.distribution.note: The franchised-versus-independent split, and the grey market that grew out of the early-1980s allocation shortages, are industry-level facts rather than properties of any one buyer.

facts.label: Authorised channels
facts.value: direct vendor sales, franchised distributors

facts.label: Unauthorised channels
facts.value: independent distributors, brokers, the open market

facts.label: Why the grey market existed
facts.value: allocation shortages, price gaps, and nobody policing small parts

facts.label: Allocation practice
facts.value: pro rata against a purchase order; 1982-84 was a shortage period

facts.label: Incoming inspection
facts.value: count and quarantine against the bill of materials; not hand-selection

mb.logic.sourcing.second-source.name: Commodore's house-numbered second sources
mb.logic.sourcing.second-source.description: To avoid single-supplier risk Commodore had equivalents of several glue parts made for it and marked with its own house numbers: 7701 and 8701 in place of the PLA family, 7707 for the 7406 hex inverter, 7708 or 7711 for the 74LS139 decoder, and 7712 for the 74LS08 quad AND. These were contracted from other fabs under Commodore's specification. They are functionally equivalent and reliably much worse - the MOS-made decoder and inverter parts are among the most failure-prone components on a C64.
