This node records the practice and the part numbers rather than being one of the parts itself: the four house numbers are four different devices in four different packages, so there is no single object here to put in a box.
mb.logic.sourcing.second-source.note: What this records is the equivalence between Commodore's house numbers and the standard 74-series parts they stand in for, not any single device: the four numbers are four different devices in four different packages.

facts.value: equivalent to the 7406 hex inverter at U8
equivalent to the 74LS139 decoder at U15
equivalent to the 74LS08 quad AND at U27

facts.label: Reliability
facts.value: the MOS house-number parts are notably failure-prone

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.name: The merchant logic vendors
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.description: Five or six companies made the overwhelming majority of the world's 74-series logic in the early 1980s. Between them they ran the same public process to the same design rules, which is why a 74LS08 from any of them was interchangeable. What they did not share was quality: this is the core of the C64's running joke that some boards need three attempts before they work. The companies themselves are the entities here; this framing paragraph is commentary, so the node is a note that keeps them as children.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.note: The observation worth carrying is the one a company list cannot show on its own: the six ran the same public process to the same design rules, so their parts were interchangeable, but not equally well made.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: TI invented the 7400; Fairchild, National and Motorola/Signetics cloned and improved it

facts.label: Interchangeability
facts.value: same pinout and function, different vendor mark

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.japan.name: Hitachi, Toshiba and the Japanese suppliers
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.japan.description: By the mid-1980s Japanese and then Korean vendors had taken a large share of world logic volume, and they were undercutting American silicon hard. C64 boards are also found with Hitachi-branded parts. Commodore bought early and often, and the rising Japanese share was one reason the C64's own bill of materials got cheaper every year of its life.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.japan.note: Low confidence on specific Japanese parts appearing on 1983 C64 boards. The general Japanese penetration of merchant logic through the decade is well documented; a specific Hitachi-branded 74LS in a 250407 is an unverified field report.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.signetics.name: Signetics
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.signetics.description: An early Silicon Valley logic house that second-sourced the 74 series through the 1960s and 1970s, and that had been owned by Philips since 1975. It is not attested by name on surviving ASSY 250407 boards. It appears in this branch only because it shared a licensing and cross-supply arrangement with Motorola from 1969, which is why the two marks appear together in period catalogues and why repair literature treats them as a pair.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.signetics.note: Low confidence, and deliberately so: no source is held for the Philips ownership date or for the 1969 arrangement, and a Signetics-branded part on a C64 mainboard is not verified.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola.name: Motorola
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola.description: The dominant supplier of the 4000-series CMOS parts on this board: the MC4044 phase comparator at U32 and the two MC4066 bilateral switches. The MC prefix on those parts is Motorola's, which is why the C64's glue logic is not entirely a 74-series story. Motorola also ran one of the merchant 74LS lines, and in 1969 it licensed and cross-supplied with Signetics, so the two names turned up in the same catalogue and the same distribution literature of the era.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.motorola.note: Motorola as the MC-prefix supplier of the 4066 and 4044 is high confidence - that is what the MC prefix means. The 1969 licensing and cross-supply arrangement with Signetics is well documented for that era, but no primary source is cited for it here.

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national.name: National Semiconductor
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national.description: A major second-source supplier of 74LS logic throughout the period, and the company that published the 74HC/74HCT databooks that turned high-speed CMOS into a genuine 74-series replacement. It later absorbed much of Fairchild.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.national.note: National as a 74LS supplier is high confidence. Its 74HC databooks (1983) are a well-documented and interesting artefact - the high-speed CMOS family arriving at the same moment as the C64.

facts.label: 74HC introduced
facts.value: 1983 (per the 74-series literature)

facts.label: Position
facts.value: top-tier 74LS supplier

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild.name: Fairchild
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild.description: The company where Faggin invented the silicon-gate technology that made CMOS practical, in 1968, and which shipped the first commercial silicon-gate MOS ICs. Fairchild went bankrupt in 1985 and its remaining operations were absorbed by National and by a French group, so by 1983 a Fairchild-branded 74LS was already a slightly awkward purchase.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.fairchild.note: Fairchild's silicon-gate invention in 1968 and the 1985 bankruptcy are well documented. That Fairchild-branded logic was actually present on C64 boards is field-attested, but no specific board photograph showing it has been verified.

facts.label: Silicon-gate CMOS
facts.value: 1968, Faggin

facts.label: Status in 1983
facts.value: independent but financially distressed

mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti.name: Texas Instruments
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti.description: The company that invented the 7400 series in 1964 and the Schottky TTL in 1964-65, and the largest supplier of the 74LS catalogue. It ran its own fabs (among them Dallas, Sugar Land in Texas, and Niceville in Florida) and also did foundry work for others - the fab-forum business was a real cash generator in the era.
mb.logic.sourcing.makers.ti.note: TI's role and the 7400/74S chronology are high confidence. Specific plant names are given as commonly-cited TI locations rather than verified suppliers of Commodore's lots.

facts.label: Extra business
facts.value: foundry / fab-forum for other semiconductor firms

mb.logic.cmos.name: The CMOS half: 4066, MC4044, 74LS629
mb.logic.cmos.description: Three of the C64's glue chips are CMOS, and they were made on a completely different line from the 74LS parts. Instead of four diffusion cycles and an epitaxial collector, a CMOS line does a p-well and an n-well implant, grows a field oxide between them by LOCOS, grows a hundred-nanometre gate oxide, deposits polysilicon, and uses that same polysilicon as its own mask for the source and drain implant. Roughly ten mask levels, no epitaxy, no gold, no NiCr resistor film, and a static power consumption of nanowatts instead of milliwatts. That combination is why CMOS took the whole logic business within fifteen years.
mb.logic.cmos.note: Describes a 3-5 um n-well/p-well twin-tub CMOS process with LOCOS isolation, self-aligned source/drain and a single aluminium level - the mainstream logic CMOS of 1982-84, and the process behind the RCA/Motorola 4000-series and the early 74HC. TI's Micralign lines, Fairchild's and National's equivalent lines, and the Japanese and Korean fabs all ran something close to this. Two details are period-specific: LOCOS was still the isolation of choice (shallow-trench isolation was arriving but not yet dominant), and the 4000-series parts such as the 4066 and MC4044 were older designs that typically used a simpler, single-well or p-well-only CMOS rather than a full twin-tub. Confidence medium because the exact flow of a given vendor's 4000-series part is proprietary.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: n-well / p-well twin-tub CMOS, LOCOS isolation

facts.label: Minimum feature
facts.value: 3-5 um (same node as the bipolar logic line)

facts.label: Gate
facts.value: polysilicon over ~100 nm thermal oxide, self-aligned S/D

facts.label: Epitaxy
facts.value: none

facts.label: Interconnect
facts.value: single aluminium level

facts.label: Static power
facts.value: nW per gate vs ~2 mW for a 74LS gate

mb.logic.cmos.now.name: What CMOS became
mb.logic.cmos.now.description: The same n-well/p-well/twin-tub idea, shrunk by a factor of thousands. Every design rule changed. The bird's beak - the way LOCOS field oxide grew sideways and swallowed the active area - became a scaling killer, and shallow trench isolation, in which a narrow trench is etched into the substrate and filled with oxide over a nitride liner, gave a much sharper boundary and became universal from the late 1980s onward; STI is itself a direct descendant of the deep-trench-isolation idea that appeared at the high-performance end of the bipolar branch, so the two halves of this tree converged on the same solution. STI in turn gave way to fin-shaped gates and gate-all-around. The gate material changed from polysilicon to metal. The number of copper interconnect layers went from one to a dozen. The light source went from a mercury lamp at 436 nm to an argon-fluoride excimer laser at 193 nm, and then to extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, which needs a vacuum. A 3-5 um logic gate became a nanometre-scale device with billions of its relatives.
mb.logic.cmos.now.note: Shallow trench isolation replaced LOCOS: a narrow trench etched into the substrate and filled with oxide over a nitride liner, giving a much sharper boundary than the bird's beak.

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: LOCOS -> shallow trench -> finFET and gate-all-around

facts.label: Gate material
facts.value: polysilicon -> metal

facts.label: Metallisation
facts.value: 1 aluminium layer -> 10+ copper layers

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: 436 nm mercury lamp -> 193 nm ArF -> 13.5 nm EUV

facts.label: Transistors per die
facts.value: ~10 for a 4066 switch; ~10^10 for a modern GPU

mb.logic.cmos.switch.name: CMOS transmission gate (bilateral switch)
mb.logic.cmos.switch.description: The 4066's four bilateral switches are the canonical CMOS cell: two MOSFETs of opposite polarity in parallel between two nodes, each with its gate driven by one of the two control inputs. When the control is high the pair conducts in both directions; when it is low the pair is off and the terminals float. It is two transistors. That is the whole reason CMOS logic is cheap - there is no junction isolation, no epitaxy, no resistor film and no gold-doped emitter to reproduce for every function, just NMOS and PMOS. It is also why the 4066 could be used as an analogue multiplexer at all: the on-resistance of a few hundred ohms to a few kilohm was low enough to route luma, chroma and audio, where a single bipolar pass transistor would have cost more than the rest of the gate.
mb.logic.cmos.switch.note: The transmission-gate cell is a real object - two MOSFETs of opposite polarity in parallel is what the 4066 is actually made of.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: complementary NMOS + PMOS in parallel = transmission gate

facts.label: Bidirectional
facts.value: yes - unlike an NMOS pass transistor

facts.label: On resistance
facts.value: hundreds of ohms to a few kohm

mb.logic.cmos.litho.name: The photolithography is the same, but the resist is positive
mb.logic.cmos.litho.description: A CMOS line of 1983 reused the same mask aligners, coaters and developers as the bipolar line next door. The one substantive difference is the resist: by the end of the 1970s the NMOS and CMOS lines had already switched to positive resists such as Shipley's AZ-1350, while bipolar logic was still often running negative resists. Positive resists tolerate the small misalignment that LOCOS bird's-beak and oxide steps cause better, which is part of why MOS won.
mb.logic.cmos.litho.note: The positive-resist chemistry - a novolac resin with a photosensitive protecting group, exposure breaking the group off so the exposed resin becomes soluble in alkaline developer, the pattern on the wafer taking the same polarity as the pattern on the mask - is not inlined here; chem.photoresist publishes it and is named in `inputs`. Positive resists went from invention in the 1940s to default in the late 1970s, had won MOS by 1983, and were displacing negative resist on bipolar; within a decade negative resist was gone from production lines entirely.

facts.label: Mask levels
facts.value: ~9-11 (vs ~8 for bipolar logic)

facts.label: Resist
facts.value: positive (AZ-type), the trend already established

facts.label: Adoption
facts.value: NMOS from the late 1970s; all production lines by the early 1990s

mb.logic.cmos.process.name: The twin-tub CMOS flow
mb.logic.cmos.process.description: The order of a CMOS process is dictated by one rule: you can never put anything back into silicon after a high-temperature step, so everything that must survive later furnace work is done first, in descending order of temperature. Wells, then field oxide, then thin gate oxide, then polysilicon, then the self-aligned source/drain implants at a low temperature, then metal.

mb.logic.cmos.process.passivation.name: Passivation, and why CMOS needed less of it
mb.logic.cmos.process.passivation.description: An interlayer oxide and a final nitride cap, opened only at the pads and scribe lanes. A CMOS device is far less sensitive to mobile ions than a bipolar one, because a CMOS gate draws no gate current and its threshold is set electrostatically rather than by charge state; so the passivation job is easier and the nitride does most of the work.
mb.logic.cmos.process.passivation.note: The relative immunity of CMOS to mobile charge is standard device physics; the specific passivation stack comparison is a reasonable generalisation rather than a cited measurement.

mb.logic.cmos.process.contact.name: Contact and aluminium interconnect
mb.logic.cmos.process.contact.description: The field oxide is etched away over the source, drain and gate to expose silicon, then aluminium is deposited and patterned into one single layer of interconnect. Exactly the same metallisation as the bipolar line, exactly the same problems (step coverage over the oxide steps, electromigration under current) and exactly the same solution in this era: one level, because at 3-5 um the cells were big enough to route around with a single layer.
mb.logic.cmos.process.contact.note: Not established: the etch that opens the contact, the single aluminium level, the step-coverage and electromigration problems, or the claim that one level sufficed because the cells were large. Aluminium as the 1980s wiring metal and the later move to copper are documented in general; the level count for a 1983 4000-series part is not.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal.name: Aluminium metallisation
mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal.description: The final mask. A layer of aluminium about 1 micrometre thick is deposited over the whole wafer - sputtered or evaporated - and a mask removes it everywhere except the wires. Those wires connect the transistor terminals, the resistors, and the bonding pads around the edge of the die. One single metal level, no vias, no second layer. This is the single biggest reason a 1983 logic chip was so simple to make: routing was almost free because the cells were small.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.metal.note: That physical vapour deposition was the primary deposition technique until chemical vapour deposition took over in the 1980s is documented. Not established: the 1-1.5 um film thickness, the single-level, no-via constraint, or the comparison that bipolar needed two or three metal layers once it shrank.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: aluminium, ~1-1.5 um

facts.label: Vias
facts.value: none (single level)

mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.name: The self-aligned source and drain
mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.description: With the gate already patterned in polysilicon, the source and drain are implanted straight through the exposed silicon beside it, and the gate itself blocks the implant everywhere it is. No alignment mask is needed: the gate defines the gap between source and drain by its own edge. Two implants, phosphorus for the n-channel source/drain and boron for the p-channel, each masked by the opposite field oxide. This is 'self-aligned', and it is the reason a CMOS transistor's channel length is set by a printed line width and nothing else.
mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.note: That boron and phosphorus are the p- and n-type dopants and that implantation is followed by an activation anneal is documented. Not established: that the source and drain were self-aligned to a polysilicon gate on this part, or the 0.2-0.5 um junction depth. The self-alignment mechanism is not described in the sources available.

facts.label: n+ S/D
facts.value: phosphorus

facts.label: p+ S/D
facts.value: boron

facts.label: Masking
facts.value: the polysilicon gate itself, plus the opposite field oxide

facts.label: Junction depth
facts.value: 0.2-0.5 um (shallower than bipolar)

mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.name: The emitter diffusion - and the gold in it
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.description: The third diffusion. Through a finer mask, a very heavily doped n+ region is driven into the boron base, forming the emitter. Because the n+ emitter is so much more heavily doped than the p base, the emitter-base junction is forward-biased at only 0.7 V and injects enormous current gain - but only as long as the emitter does not punch through the thin base under the reverse bias of the collector. Pushing gold into the emitter diffuses the emitter junction forward slightly, making the junction harder for holes to reverse-inject, which suppresses punch-through and the associated capacitance, and raises the gain. This is the 'gold-doped emitter'.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.note: The gold-doped (Au-doped) polysilicon emitter was a real and important technique of this era, used to raise gain and suppress the emitter-base reverse conductance ('knee'). It was implemented by co-depositing a tiny amount of gold in the emitter polysilicon or dopant glass, then driving it in with the arsenic or phosphorus. Confidence medium: the technique is well documented, but it is not confirmed that a specific 74LS vendor's 1983 process used it; it was common in high-performance bipolar rather than mandatory in low-cost logic. A self-aligned polysilicon emitter - deposit a thin arsenic-doped polysilicon film, pattern it to define the emitter, then push, so the arsenic is confined by the polysilicon walls and the emitter comes out shallower and more uniform - was the other refinement of the era, widespread in analog through the 1980s and 1990s and doubtful on a commodity 74LS. The arsine itself is an ingredient and is named in `inputs`, not inlined as a child; its provenance is worth recording: arsenic occurs as arsenide in copper and lead concentrates, roasting drives it off as arsenic trioxide fume, and the trioxide is reduced and hydrogenated to arsine. Arsenic-bearing copper concentrates were a notorious long-time smelting hazard, which is why arsenic control in copper works is a regulated topic today.

facts.label: Dopant
facts.value: arsenic or phosphorus, n+

facts.label: Rs
facts.value: 10-30 ohm/sq

facts.label: Gold purpose
facts.value: suppress emitter-base reverse leakage and push-through

mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold.name: The gold in the emitter
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold.description: A fraction of a percent of gold, introduced by co-doping the emitter source and driven in with the emitter diffusion. Gold is a deep acceptor-diffusing substitutional impurity in silicon; it behaves in the base like a recombination centre. In the emitter-base junction it forward-shifts the junction for electrons and suppresses hole injection into the emitter, which is what raises gain and kills the reverse gain of the transistor.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.emitter.gold.note: Gold as a recombination centre in silicon is well established physics; its use in Au-doped emitters is a documented period technique. Exact concentration is on the order of a fraction of a percent in the emitter. metal.gold is an ingredient, so it hangs off `inputs`.

mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.anneal.name: The source/drain anneal
mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.anneal.description: After the implant the wafer goes back into a furnace briefly to heal the crystal damage and to activate the dopant atoms into substitutional positions. This is the one remaining high-temperature step, and it is why CMOS still used a furnace in the era when bipolar was moving to implantation.
mb.logic.cmos.process.sd.anneal.note: The activation anneal was around 800-900 C for an hour, or a rapid thermal anneal of a few seconds at 1000 C plus. Medium confidence on the exact numbers.

mb.logic.cmos.process.poly.name: The polysilicon gate
mb.logic.cmos.process.poly.description: A layer of polycrystalline silicon is deposited over the whole wafer, then doped (usually with phosphorus from phosphine, or with POCL3 in a furnace) so that it conducts, then patterned. That patterned polysilicon is the gate. Crucially, it is also used as the mask for the source and drain implant immediately afterwards - so the gate aligns itself, and no extra mask is needed. The self-aligned gate and source/drain, invented at Fairchild in the late 1960s, is the single idea that made CMOS manufacturable at all.
mb.logic.cmos.process.poly.note: The silane feed is SiH4, decomposing on a hot surface at 700-850 C to lay down pure polycrystalline silicon - cleaner and more controllable than trichlorosilane because it carries no chlorine and no corrosive by-products. Trichlorosilane still dominated for boule-grade silicon. A 4000-series part might also deposit a few resistors from this same film: polysilicon resistors cost nothing extra because they are made at the same time as the gate, from the same film, at no extra mask. That the 4066 specifically uses on-chip polysilicon resistors is plausible from its trim and bias requirements but is not verified against a cross-section, and some 4000-series parts use no resistors at all.

facts.label: Deposition
facts.value: LPCVD from silane at ~700-850 C

facts.label: Doping
facts.value: phosphine in the deposition, or POCL3 furnace

facts.label: Key property
facts.value: self-aligns the source/drain implant

facts.label: Silane decomposition
facts.value: SiH4 -> Si + 2H2

mb.logic.cmos.process.gateoxide.name: The gate oxide
mb.logic.cmos.process.gateoxide.description: Inside the active windows the thin gate oxide is grown, by dry oxidation in oxygen at about 1000 C. On a 3-5 um part it is 80-120 nm thick - a few hundred atom layers. This film is the transistor: its thickness sets the threshold voltage and its capacitance sets the drive current, and it is the thinnest and most fragile thing on the chip. At 1983's feature sizes it was still thick by modern standards, which is one reason CMOS of that era was not yet faster than bipolar.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 80-120 nm at 3-5 um

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: dry O2, ~1000 C

facts.label: Why thin
facts.value: oxide thickness sets threshold voltage

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.name: LOCOS isolation
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.description: Locally Oxidised Silicon. Where two transistors must not touch, the field oxide is simply grown. A layer of silicon nitride is deposited and patterned; the wafer is oxidised in steam, so oxide grows everywhere the nitride is absent; the nitride is stripped off in hot phosphoric acid, leaving a thick field oxide behind. It is isolation by oxidising rather than by doping, and it is the reason a CMOS chip looks like a quilt of raised oxide platforms.

facts.label: Mask oxide
facts.value: Si3N4, LPCVD from silane and ammonia

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: wet steam, ~1000 C

facts.label: Nitride strip
facts.value: hot phosphoric acid, ~160 C

facts.label: Known problem
facts.value: the 'bird's beak' - the field oxide grows sideways and eats into the active area

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric.name: Hot phosphoric acid
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric.description: Silicon nitride is attacked by hot concentrated phosphoric acid and by nothing else practical, so a boiling phosphoric acid bath is the standard way to remove it - which is why LOCOS needs an acid tank that no other step in the line does. The acid was made by burning phosphorus, itself from phosphate rock, in excess air and absorbing the oxide in water.
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.phosphoric.note: The chemistry is high confidence; the specific tank temperature (~150-180 C) is a standard process figure but is not verified against a 1983 datasheet.

facts.label: Selectivity
facts.value: attacks Si3N4, leaves SiO2

mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.name: The silicon nitride masking film
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.description: A layer of amorphous silicon nitride, deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition from silane and ammonia at about 800 C. It is used in three places in a CMOS line: as the mask that protects active areas during field oxidation, as the encapsulant under the nitride passivation at the end, and as a spacer. Nitride is chosen because it is immune to hot steam - which is precisely why it is a good mask for something that is about to be steamed. Its two feed gases are named in `inputs`: monosilane (chem.silane.monosilane) for the silicon, and electronic-grade ammonia (chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide, delivered as anhydrous NH3 sparged into ultrapure water) for the nitrogen. In 1983 essentially all industrial ammonia was made by Haber-Bosch - nitrogen from the air plus hydrogen from steam-reformed natural gas over an iron catalyst at 400-500 C and 200-300 atm - so the film that defines a CMOS transistor's isolation runs, indirectly, on natural gas.
mb.logic.cmos.process.locos.nitride.note: The ammonia sub-branch that used to sit here - ammonia, the nitrogen from the air, the hydrogen from the reformer - duplicated chem.fab-chemicals.ammonium-hydroxide, facility.nitrogen.atmospheric-air and chem.natural-gas.uses.hydrogen, and has been removed. Monosilane and ammonium hydroxide are ingredients, so they hang off `inputs`.

facts.label: Deposition
facts.value: LPCVD, ~800 C

facts.label: Feed gases
facts.value: SiH4 + NH3

facts.label: Ammonia route
facts.value: Haber-Bosch from air nitrogen and steam-reformed hydrogen, ~450 C, 200-300 atm

mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.name: n-well and p-well implants
mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.description: Two masked implants. Phosphorus (or arsenic) goes into the n-well; boron into the p-well. At 3-5 um these were thermal diffusions or, increasingly, implantations - by the early 1980s medium-current implanters were displacing diffusion in CMOS, the opposite trend to bipolar, where diffusion survived much longer. An implantation is done cold and fast: the dopant is accelerated into the surface at tens of keV and stops almost where it is put.

facts.label: n-well
facts.value: phosphorus or arsenic

facts.label: p-well
facts.value: boron

facts.label: Method
facts.value: ion implantation (thermal diffusion still in use)

mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.implanter.name: The medium-current ion implanter
mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.implanter.description: A big steel vacuum chamber with a source, an analysing magnet, an accelerating column and a beamline down to a scan platter that holds the wafer. The dopant is ionised, selected by mass, accelerated to tens of keV, and swept across the wafer. Implanters were expensive, and CMOS was the process that made them a standard line tool rather than a special one.
mb.logic.cmos.process.wells.implanter.note: Implanters were standard in CMOS lines by the early 1980s; diffusion was still the workhorse in bipolar logic, which is one of the more interesting differences between the two processes. The dopant gases are the same three the bipolar line uses - phosphine for the n-well, diborane for the p-well, sometimes arsine - and they are ingredients named in `inputs`, published once at chem.fab-chemicals.dopants. Electricity is a cross-cutting service and is a `from` edge, not a component.

mb.logic.cmos.process.substrate.name: p-type substrate (and the tub)
mb.logic.cmos.process.substrate.description: The wafer is p-type, lightly doped. On top of it two wells are implanted: a deep n-well and a somewhat shallower p-well. The n-well holds every p-channel transistor; the p-well (or the substrate itself, on simpler parts) holds every n-channel transistor. Two tubs, two polarities, one chip - that is the 'twin tub'. The wells must be deep enough that they do not punch through into each other and short the two transistor types together.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: p-type, ~5-20 ohm-cm

si.wafer.name: Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
si.wafer.description: The starting substrate every die in the machine is cut from: a 4-inch (100 mm) Czochralski-grown, boron-doped p-type silicon wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, mirror-polished on one face, 300-350 um thick, with a primary flat and a small secondary orientation flat. 125 mm was not standard until about 1986, and by 1982 every logic die in the C64 was patterned on one of these.
si.wafer.note: Two parts of the machine wanted something slightly different. DRAM wafers were commonly grown to a heavier oxygen content, because a high bulk oxygen-precipitate density lengthens the trapped-charge lifetime and so helps refresh margin on the 4164. Discrete lines of the era were happy with 10-40 ohm-cm and many of them ran 75 mm wafers, because they did not need fine geometry at all.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: 100 mm (4 inch); 125 mm not standard until ~1986

facts.label: Resistivity
facts.value: 10-20 ohm-cm p-type, boron doped

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: (100) with a (111) secondary flat

si.clean.name: Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic
si.clean.description: A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles rather than yield models set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic at 1.6 MHz in deionised water, a hot Piranha of 3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, then RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O 1:1:5 at 75-80 C) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. Between every mask level the same sequence ran again.
si.clean.note: Difference from today: 1980s practice leaned on wet chemistry and megasonic tanks rather than on cassette single-wafer cleaning, and hydrogen peroxide was routinely kept hot enough to be a genuine hazard.

facts.label: Piranha
facts.value: 3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C

facts.label: Megasonic
facts.value: 1.6 MHz, 0.5-2 kW per tank

facts.label: RCA SC-1
facts.value: NH4OH:H2O2:H2O 1:1:5 at 75-80 C

facts.label: Water
facts.value: 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm per die across the whole flow

facts.label: Resist stripper
facts.value: hot H2SO4 or 1,1,1-trichloroethane

si.wafer.finish.name: Lapping, chemical polish and edge rounding
si.wafer.finish.description: Saw-cut wafers are lapped double-sided on a rotating cast-iron plate against a conditioning plate, in a slurry of colloidal silica or alumina in water, taking them to about 300 um with several micrometres of total thickness variation left across the wafer. They are then polished chemically in hot alkaline peroxide or in HNO3/HF/acetic acid, which removes the last 10 um or so of saw damage and leaves an atomically flat surface, and finally the razor edge is rounded by a brief hot KOH or NH4OH etch so that photoresist cannot build up on it and so the wafer will not chip in handling.
si.wafer.finish.note: Difference from today: a modern wafer goes through CMP in a rotary single-wafer polisher with a soft pad and slurry. Chemical-mechanical polishing did not reach volume production until the late 1980s, so this step was purely chemical in 1982.

facts.label: After lapping
facts.value: ~300 um, several um of total thickness variation

facts.label: Polish
facts.value: hot NaOH/H2O2 or HNO3/HF/acetic, removing ~10 um of damage layer

facts.label: Edge
facts.value: rounded in hot KOH or NH4OH

si.wafer.slicing.name: Sawing the ingot and laser-scribing the flats
si.wafer.slicing.description: The boule is ground round, a sapphire-orientation-reference crystal is used to find the (100) direction, and the wafer flats are laser-scribed with a ruby or Nd:YAG laser before cutting. Slicing was by OD saw, with blades up to 2.2 m in diameter turning at 2000 rpm for a 0.30 mm kerf, or on more advanced 1982 machines by ID saw, with the blade inside the crystal for a 0.25 mm kerf. The result is a 0.7 mm wafer, far too warped and marked to print on.

facts.label: Kerf
facts.value: 0.25-0.33 mm, diamond-impregnated blade

facts.label: OD saw
facts.value: up to 2.2 m diameter at 2000 rpm

si.wafer.saw.name: Diamond-impregnated saw blade
si.wafer.saw.description: A thin steel or resin-bonded wheel whose rim carries a diamond grit. Slicing 100 mm silicon at two to three wafers a minute relies on that grit: 20-40 um for a roughing cut and 3-5 um for the finish cut. Resin-bonded blades were introduced in the mid 1970s and gave a thinner kerf and less bow than the metal bond.
si.wafer.saw.note: Not established: the blade diameter, rotational speed, kerf and grit-size figures, or the date on which resin-bonded blades displaced metal-bonded ones. Diamond-wire sawing is the documented modern method; the OD- and ID-saw numbers given here are not in any source available. Kerf and the 0.7 mm as-sawn thickness remain uncertain.

facts.label: Diamond grit
facts.value: 3-40 um, natural or synthetic

facts.label: Blade
facts.value: resin-bonded, OD up to 2.2 m; ID blades inside the boule

si.wafer.diamond.name: Industrial diamond from graphite
si.wafer.diamond.description: Saw-grade industrial diamond in 1982 was mostly synthetic: graphite pressed and sintered with a diamond-metal catalyst (Fe, Co or Ni) at 5-6 GPa and 1300-1600 C in a belt press. Natural diamond - the harder, scarcer gem and industrial grade - came from kimberlite pipes in South Africa, Botswana and Russia.

facts.label: Synthesis
facts.value: 5-6 GPa, 1300-1600 C, Fe/Co/Ni catalyst

facts.label: Natural source
facts.value: kimberlite pipe; Gaborone and Kimberley, South Africa

mb.logic.bipolar.name: How a 74LS chip is actually made (bipolar TTL)
mb.logic.bipolar.description: The 74LS family was not built on the same kind of line as the Commodore custom chips. This is a junction-isolated, collector-diffused bipolar process: an n+ buried-and-collector structure grown epitaxially on p-type silicon, four thermal diffusion cycles, a sputtered NiCr resistor level, one level of aluminium metallisation, about eight mask levels and sixty to a hundred process steps. Minimum drawn features were 3-5 um - twenty times coarser than a 1983 dynamic RAM - which is exactly why a logic chip cost a fraction of what a 6510 or a 4164 cost.
mb.logic.bipolar.note: This is a generalised description of the standard junction-isolated bipolar logic process as it was run in 1982-84 by TI, Fairchild, National and Motorola. Precise vendors differed: Fairchild also offered a dielectric-isolation variant, and TI ran some processes with ion implantation instead of thermal base diffusion. Confidence is medium rather than high, because the 74LS flows are proprietary and no period process description for a specific vendor's 74LS line has been seen. The transistor structure, the four-diffusion sequence, the NiCr resistor level and the eight mask levels are all well documented industry practice for the era. The resulting geometry is a 0.5-1 um base and a 1-2 um emitter inside an isolation island a few tens of micrometres across, wired with 3-5 um aluminium on one level. For comparison, the 4164 DRAM on the same board was patterned at around 1-2 um with two or three aluminium levels, and the VIC-II and SID at around 2-3 um with two levels, which is why a DRAM cost more than the glue.

facts.label: Process family
facts.value: junction-isolated double-diffused bipolar (collector-diffused epitaxial)

facts.label: Minimum drawn feature
facts.value: 3-5 um (emitter window), base width ~0.5-1 um

facts.label: Mask levels
facts.value: ~8 (7 product levels + passivation window)

facts.label: Diffusion cycles
facts.value: 4 thermal: isolation, base, emitter, plus the epitaxial growth itself

facts.label: Interconnect
facts.value: single aluminium level + sputtered NiCr resistor

facts.label: Process steps
facts.value: ~60-100 front-end steps

facts.label: 4164 DRAM, same era
facts.value: ~1-2 um, two or three metal levels

facts.label: Custom VIC-II / SID NMOS, same era
facts.value: ~2-3 um, two metal levels

mb.logic.bipolar.now.name: What happened to bipolar logic afterwards
mb.logic.bipolar.now.description: The 74LS line described here is essentially extinct as a manufacturing process. CMOS won because it drew almost no static power, scaled, and could hold a whole microprocessor on one die, which bipolar could never do economically. Bipolar survives only in niches - power regulators, high-voltage controllers, low-dropout rectifiers, precision amplifiers, the front end of high-speed analog, microwave amplifiers, Hall sensors - where the transistor's current handling and gain are still hard to beat, and those parts are still grown epitaxially and still use guard rings and deep-trench isolation at the leading edge: the process family survived, the market for plain logic gates in it did not. The two families briefly merged in BiCMOS, which built CMOS logic and bipolar output drivers on the same die for gate arrays and for the output stages of older CPUs; it was abandoned once CMOS could drive high current on its own, and is largely gone from production. And the geometry is unrecognisable: the 3-5 um feature of this line put of the order of 10^1 to 10^2 transistors on a die, where a modern GPU puts about 10^10, on 300 mm wafers. Nothing about the aluminium DIP package, the epoxy, the lead frame or the 0.1 in pitch changed at all through that entire scaling - only the silicon inside.
mb.logic.bipolar.now.note: Three things are worth knowing after following the 1983 flow: which niches bipolar logic survives in, what BiCMOS was, and how far the geometry has moved since.

facts.label: 1983 74LS
facts.value: 3-5 um feature, ~10^1-10^2 transistors per die

facts.label: 2020s logic
facts.value: nanometre nodes, ~10^10 transistors per die on a 300 mm wafer

facts.label: Unchanged by all of it
facts.value: DIP package, epoxy moulding, lead frame, 0.1 in lead pitch

mb.logic.bipolar.fab.name: The merchant logic fab that ran the process
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.description: A 1983 merchant logic line was a long building with a linear flow: wafers came in at the front and moved one way through cleaning, oxidation and diffusion, photolithography, etch and metallisation, then out to probe, then to assembly and test at the back. Because a logic process was so repeatable, one fab ran dozens of different part numbers on the same flow, changing only the mask set - which is exactly why the 74LS catalogue was so cheap.
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.note: That the process ran in a clean room inside a dedicated fab is documented, and that a single process serves many part numbers. Not established: the linear bay layout and its bay order, the water, power and nitrogen as services, the vendor plant list, or that one mask set per part number is why the catalogue was cheap.

mb.logic.bipolar.fab.utilities.name: Fab utilities: water, power, scrubbers
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.utilities.description: A logic fab in 1983 drew tens of megawatts and consumed tens of millions of gallons of ultrapure water a year, and every acid vapour had to be scrubbed. The ultrapure water plant - reverse osmosis then ion exchange, then a final 0.2 um filter - was as large and as capital-intensive as any single machine in the fab.
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.utilities.note: The scale figures are order-of-magnitude for a large logic fab, not verified for a specific plant. Water intensity for semiconductors is high relative to most manufacturing; this is well documented generally. Water and power are named in `inputs`, so they render as `from` edges: following this node's materials should not drag a water treatment plant into a logic supply line.

mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baymetal.name: Metallisation bay
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baymetal.description: The vacuum tool room: the sputterers that lay down the NiCr resistors and the aluminium metal, the evaporation stations, the sinter furnace, and the ion-implantation machines. Vacuum and cleanroom in one room; argon flows constantly.
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baymetal.note: Not established: that sputterers, evaporators, a sinter furnace and ion implanters shared one vacuum tool room with argon flowing, or any of the equipment inventory. Sputtering and evaporation are documented as techniques; the bay is a layout assumption.

mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baydiffusion.name: Oxidation and diffusion bay
mb.logic.bipolar.fab.baydiffusion.description: The hot end of the fab: tube furnaces for oxidation, source drive-in and anneal, plus the epitaxial reactors. This bay determined the cycle time of the whole line, because a diffusion push is hours and a furnace boat takes 20-40 wafers. An operator loaded boats in and out at a slow, deliberate rhythm all shift.

mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.name: Cleanroom air, filtration and the wet bench
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.description: The whole front end runs in filtered air with positive pressure, and the wet benches - the sinks where wafers are etched and cleaned - were the dirtiest place in the fab and the reason it needed a Class 100 (ISO 5) hood over every one. HEPA-filtered air was blown down continuously; nitrogen and dry air purged the tool chambers; and huge volumes of deionised water and process chemicals flowed through the sinks.
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.note: Two nodes were folded into this one in QA. First, the photomask bay, which had been a separate facility child of the photolithography process: coating, exposing and developing happened in a yellow room under filtered mercury light and then in a Class 10 (ISO 4) mini-environment with the aligners under hoods, and it was the largest bay in the building by machine count and by electricity draw after the cleanroom air itself. It belonged here rather than under a process step. Second, the bulk process gases - nitrogen for purging tool chambers and for the sinter anneal, hydrogen for the metal anneal, oxygen for oxidation and for ashing photoresist, dry nitrogen also as the blow-off gas for every wafer before it entered a hot tool - which were a separate child duplicating chem.fab-chemicals.process-gases and are now named in `inputs`. Note on the older US class numbering: Class 100 = ISO 5, Class 1000 = ISO 6, Class 10 = ISO 4; it is a different convention from the ISO class numbers used today. Bulk gases, water and power are cross-cutting services and are `from` edges, not components of the building.

facts.label: Air
facts.value: HEPA filtered, 0.3 um, positive pressure

facts.label: Classes used
facts.value: Class 10 (ISO 4) mask bay, Class 100 (ISO 5) sub-fab and diffusion bay, Class 1000 (ISO 6) wet bays

facts.label: Wet benches
facts.value: polypropylene sinks under Class 100 laminar hoods

mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench.name: The wet bench
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench.description: A row of acid-resistant sinks - quartz or polypropylene - where wafers are rinsed and wet-etched. Because wet chemistry releases acid mist and organic solvent vapour, every wet bench sat under a Class 100 laminar-flow hood and exhausted to a scrubbed stack. The wet bench is the reason a 1980s logic line was not as cheap to run as the 'it is just photolithography' story suggests.
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.wetbench.note: Capital equipment, consumed slowly rather than used up in a single run. The nitrogen blow-off and the water flowing through the sinks are utilities supplied to the tool, not components of it.

mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.ffu.name: The HEPA fan filter unit
mb.logic.bipolar.cleanroom.ffu.description: A box of pleated glass-fibre or PTFE media in a sheet-metal housing, blowing filtered air down over the tool at 20-40 air changes an hour. It is the single most numerous object in a 1980s fab - one every few square metres of ceiling - and it is why the whole building was pressurised and why the electricity bill was dominated by fan motors.

facts.label: Air changes
facts.value: 20-60 per hour

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.name: Eight masks, eight photolithography cycles
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.description: A full bipolar logic cycle is repeated for each of its eight mask levels, and each cycle is the same eight or nine operations: clean, dehydrate, spin-coat resist, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse and dry, hard-bake, then inspect - before the wafer goes back to the furnace, the etcher or the implanter. Eight masks times about nine operations is roughly seventy lithography operations, plus oxidation, etching and deposition steps that need no resist, giving the sixty-to-a-hundred total front-end steps.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.note: The mask set and its order in this tree: (1) isolation, (2) base, (3) NiCr resistor, (4) emitter, (5) contact window, (6) aluminium metal, (7) passivation window, plus the scribe/alignment level - about eight, ordering within the tree illustrative. Every mask is exposed once per wafer batch, and the whole flow through the diffusion and photolithography areas takes a batch of wafers roughly a week to ten days. Written out once, one mask level's cycle is ten operations - dehydrate, coat, soft-bake, align and expose, develop, rinse, hard-bake, wet-etch, strip, clean - then the furnace or the sputterer; eight levels of ten is about eighty lithography-area operations, plus oxidation and diffusion pushes, plus metallisation, plus test. That count was a separate child node ('The full cycle, counted') and has been folded in here.

facts.label: Ops per litho cycle
facts.value: ~10 including etch, strip and clean

facts.label: Flow time per batch
facts.value: ~1-2 weeks

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.name: Stripping the resist
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.description: With the etch done, the resist has served its purpose and is removed. In this era, because resist was often negative and organic, a chlorinated solvent strip in a hot bath was standard - historically xylene, then trichloroethylene, boiling at 87 C. Solvent stripping leaves ionic residue, which had to be followed by a piranha clean, a rinse, and a dehydration bake before the next coat. Trichloroethylene was ubiquitous as a resist strip and a vapour degreaser in this period and was being phased out for toxicity and ozone reasons through the 1980s, replaced by perchloroethylene and then by piranha wet strips.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.strip.note: That the resist is removed after etch by dry stripping or plasma ashing or by a wet resist stripper is documented. Not established: chlorinated solvents as the standard route, the xylene-then-trichloroethylene sequence, the 87 C boiling point, the piranha wet strip, and the phasing out of trichloroethylene through the 1980s.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.name: Etching the oxide window
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.description: The patterned resist is the stencil; the wafer goes into an etchant. Buffered oxide etch - hydrofluoric acid buffered with ammonium fluoride - attacks the silicon dioxide where the resist is gone, opening the window, and stops at the silicon or at the oxide-nitride beneath. The wafer comes out with resist still on it, which is stripped next. In this era the oxide etch was still wet chemistry; dry plasma etching had not yet replaced it for the bulk oxide.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.etch.note: Plasma (reactive ion) etching of silicon dioxide was introduced in the early-to-mid 1980s and became standard later in the decade; a 1983 bipolar logic line used wet HF and BOE for its diffusion and contact windows. Hydrofluoric acid, the buffered-etch process and the fluorspar it is made from are named in `inputs` (chem.fab-chemicals.hydrofluoric-acid and its buffered-hf and fluorspar children); the fluorspar-to-HF chain, including the Derbyshire, Ilkley, Mexican, South African and Chinese fluorspar fields and the limestone by-product, used to be inlined beneath this node and is published at metal.fluorspar.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: HF (HF:H2O 1:1 to 10:1) or BOE (HF + NH4F)

facts.label: Selectivity
facts.value: etches SiO2, stops at Si and Si3N4

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: ~1 um/min

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.name: Developing the image
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.description: The exposed wafer is sprayed with an alkaline developer - for a positive resist, a solution of tetramethylammonium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide; for a negative resist, an organic solvent. The unexposed (positive) or exposed (negative) resist dissolves, leaving the pattern in hardened resist. Then a rinse in deionised water, a dry, and a hard-bake to cross-link the remaining resist so it survives the etch that follows. TMAH was preferred because it left no metal ion residues that would poison the device.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.develop.note: The developer chemistry is named in `inputs` rather than inlined: chem.fab-chemicals.tmah publishes TMAH and its synthesis, and chem.photoresist.development publishes the 0.2-0.3 N spray-development process. A potassium-hydroxide developer, made by chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine alongside chlorine, was the older alkali and was still in use; the sub-branch that used to sit here (potash -> brine -> rock salt) duplicated metal.salt-brine and metal.chlor-alkali and has been removed.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.name: Aligning the mask to the wafer
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.description: The wafer is dried, loaded onto a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and the mask is laid directly on top of it - contact printing - or held just above it with a controlled air gap - proximity printing - or imaged one-to-one through a lens. The machine's job is to align each feature on the mask to the feature already printed on the wafer, usually by optically reading alignment marks etched into the previous level. At 3-5 um, alignment tolerance was generous; at DRAM geometries it was brutal.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.note: Contact printing was cheapest and fastest but printed mask defects onto every die and wore the mask; proximity printing added an air gap for a small resolution penalty. 1:1 projection steppers (like TI's Micralign, and Perkin-Elmer's) were arriving in the early 1980s and gave a clean image without contact wear. Bipolar logic at 3-5 um was comfortable with any of the three.

facts.label: Methods
facts.value: contact, proximity, 1:1 projection

facts.label: Alignment
facts.value: optical, on marks from previous levels

facts.label: Alignment tolerance at 3-5 um
facts.value: about +/- 1 um - comfortable

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: mercury g-line 436 nm or h-line 405 nm

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.lamp.name: The mercury lamp
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.lamp.description: A 1000 W high-pressure mercury arc with a quartz envelope. Its spectrum peaks at 365, 405 and 436 nm; optical filters select one line, almost always 436 nm (g-line) for the finest resolution the era could reach. Newer deep-UV lamps added 248 nm. The lamp is run at constant power because the resist's exposure depends on its intensity, and lamp ageing was a constant yield headache.

facts.label: Deep-UV option
facts.value: 248 nm (ArF excimer in later tools)

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.stepper.name: The 1:1 projection stepper
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.stepper.description: A mask aligner that images the mask through a fixed 1:1 lens onto the wafer with a small gap, so there is no contact and no wear, and no mask-defect printing. TI's Micralign and Perkin-Elmer's units of the late 1970s and early 1980s brought this to the logic lines. It was the technology that eventually killed contact printing entirely.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.printer.name: The contact/proximity mask aligner
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.align.printer.description: A granite or cast base, a Chuck/Hamble wafer stage with micrometer knobs for theta and X-Y, a vacuum frame to pull the mask down onto the wafer, a mercury lamp below, and a pair of binocular microscopes to watch the alignment marks. One operator could run one or two of these, spending most of the cycle walking up and down the level stack.

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: ~20-40 s per wafer including load/align/expose

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: ~60-100 wafers/hour

facts.label: Operator
facts.value: 1 per 1-2 machines

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.name: Dehydration bake before the resist
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.description: Resist will not stick to a wet wafer, so before every coat the wafer goes on a hot plate or in a dehydration oven at 150-250 C to drive off the adsorbed water from the previous wet step. Skipping it causes the single most common resist defect - the film lifting off in patches during development. Every one of the eight cycles repeats this.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.hotpl.name: The dehydration hot plate
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.hotpl.description: A temperature-controlled aluminium or ceramic plate the cassette sits on for a minute or two at 150-200 C. Cheap, essential, and present at every wet bench in the bay.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.dehydration.hotpl.note: Not established: the plate material, the 150-200 C setpoint, the one or two minute dwell, or that such a plate stood at every wet bench in the bay. A hot plate is a necessary piece of photolithography equipment but no source describes it.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.name: Spinning on the resist
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.description: The wafer is put on a vacuum chuck in a bowl, a few millilitres of resist is dispensed, and the bowl spins at several thousand rpm, flinging the resist into a film of a chosen thickness - thicker where a thick layer is needed to etch deep, thinner where fine resolution is needed. The film is then soft-baked to drive off solvent and stabilise the image.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.note: On a bipolar line in 1983 the resist was still often negative: exposure cross-links the resist so it becomes insoluble in the developer, and the pattern left on the wafer after develop is the complement of the mask. That suits diffusion, where you want to open the mask where the oxide is. Positive resists, which behave the intuitive way, had taken over NMOS and CMOS from the late 1970s but lingered on bipolar. Medium confidence on the specific mix in a given vendor's logic bay: by 1983 positive resists were already dominant for MOS processes (Shipley AZ-1350 and its successors) and the trend across all processes was well advanced, but negative resist on bipolar logic persisted into the 1980s. The chemistry itself - novolac plus photoactive group, alkaline development, image reversal - is published at chem.photoresist and chem.photoresist.negative, which is where the inlined copy of it used to be; both are named in `inputs`.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.spinner.name: The coater/developer track
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.coat.spinner.description: A machine with hot plates and spray-heads that automates spin-coat, soft-bake, develop, rinse and bake for a whole cassette of wafers in one pass. The track was the workhorse of the photomask bay: an operator loaded a cassette and pushed a button, and the bay's lithography throughput was set by how many tracks it had.

facts.label: Resist thickness
facts.value: 0.5-2 um typical for logic

facts.label: Track throughput
facts.value: ~25 wafers per cycle, ~1 min per cycle

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.name: The mask set
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.description: A set of eight photomasks, one per level, each a square of glass about 15 cm on a side with the pattern for that level in opaque chrome. They are made once from the circuit layout, then used to print thousands of wafers. Making the mask set - patterning, mask inspection, and a few days of lead time - was itself a multi-thousand-dollar, multi-week undertaking, and the masks were the physical embodiment of the design.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer.name: The mask writer
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer.description: A computer-controlled plotter that draws the pattern onto the chrome layer - a direct-write electron-beam or laser writer, or a mask stepper using photographic reduction for the simpler logic geometries. The mask set for one part number was the output of days of the mask shop's finest-resolution tool, and it was checked by eye under a microscope before use.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.writer.note: For 3-5 um logic geometries, a photographic mask stepper was adequate and much faster than electron-beam writing; beam writing was reserved for the DRAM and custom-chip masks.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.reticle.name: The reticle (1:1 mask)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.reticle.description: A bipolar logic wafer of 1983 was almost always patterned 1:1 by contact or proximity printing, so the mask carried the pattern at full size - a 100 mm wafer printed from a 100 mm mask. Reticles in the sense of 4x or 5x reduction masks were for steppers and mostly for the finer NMOS and DRAM processes, not for the coarse logic line.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.reticle.note: The distinction: contact/proximity printing needs a full-size mask; a 1:1 projection stepper also prints 1:1 but optically; only a reduction stepper (2x-10x) needs a smaller reticle. Bipolar logic in 1983 was 1:1 by either contact or 1:1 projection. Bipolar logic generally did not use reduction steppers at this node.

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: 1:1 for contact and 1:1 projection printing

facts.label: Mask size
facts.value: ~125-150 mm, matching the wafer

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome.name: The opaque chrome layer
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome.description: A layer of chromium, evaporated or sputtered onto the glass and then patterned by a mask writer. Chrome is used because it is opaque to the deep-UV and because it survives repeated contact printing without wearing. The clear areas are just bare glass, which is why a mask is easy to inspect: you look through it.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.chrome.note: Chromium is an ingredient of the mask, so metal.chromium hangs off `inputs` rather than as a child.

mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank.name: The mask blank (soda-lime glass)
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank.description: A plate of low-expansion borosilicate or soda-lime glass, polished flat to a few micrometres over 150 mm. Low-expansion glass (LE glass) was preferred for masks because it did not change size with temperature. Both the blank and the pattern ultimately derive from fused silica.
mb.logic.bipolar.litho.masks.blank.note: Silica is an ingredient of the blank, so metal.silica and metal.quartzite hang off `inputs` rather than as a child.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.name: The junction-isolated bipolar flow
mb.logic.bipolar.process.description: The sequence that turns a plain slice of silicon into a chip of interconnected bipolar transistors. Four diffusion cycles do all the work: an n+ isolation diffusion to separate each transistor into its own island; a p base diffusion under the island to form the transistor base; an n+ emitter diffusion into the base to form the emitter; and the Schottky-barrier levels that give the 'LS' in 74LS its name. Between and inside those cycles sit an epitaxial growth, a thin-film resistor deposition, a metallisation and a passivation.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: p-type, ~5-15 ohm-cm

facts.label: Epilayer
facts.value: n-type, 0.1-0.5 ohm-cm, ~5-12 um deep

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: n+ phosphorus, driven to the substrate

facts.label: Base
facts.value: p boron, Rs ~150-400 ohm/sq

facts.label: Emitter
facts.value: n+ phosphorus or arsenic, Rs ~10-30 ohm/sq

mb.logic.bipolar.process.passivation.name: Passivation over the metal
mb.logic.bipolar.process.passivation.description: A final film - silicon dioxide, usually with a nitride cap - deposited over the finished aluminium, opened again only at the bonding pads and along the scribe lanes. It seals the chip against moisture and mobile ions, which is what lets a 1983 logic part hold a 15-year life in a consumer television.

facts.label: Films
facts.value: phosphorus-doped SiO2 + plasma Si3N4

facts.label: Openings
facts.value: bonding pads, scribe lanes

mb.logic.bipolar.process.sinter.name: Sintering the metal into the contacts
mb.logic.bipolar.process.sinter.description: After aluminium is deposited, the wafer is pushed briefly to 400-450 C in hydrogen or forming gas. This melts the aluminium into the contact windows, welding it to the silicon and lowering the contact resistance, and it anneals out the sputter damage in the silicon. It is a short, cheap step and it is the reason the metallisation recipe ends with a hydrogen firing.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.sinter.note: Aluminium sintering / hydrogen alloying at 400-450 C was standard in the era. Confidence medium on the exact temperature window; the purpose and the technique are not in doubt. The forming gas is an ingredient: nitrogen and hydrogen are named in `inputs`, not hung off as children, because a gas supply line is not part of a wafer.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: forming gas (N2/H2)

mb.logic.bipolar.process.contact.name: The contact window
mb.logic.bipolar.process.contact.description: One more mask, which cuts small windows in the field oxide wherever a metal film needs to reach the silicon underneath - the collector, the base, the emitter. Each window is a hole a few micrometres across. The oxide elsewhere is untouched, and it is the oxide that keeps the aluminium from shorting to the substrate everywhere except where you wanted it to.

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: HF through the oxide to the silicon

facts.label: Window size
facts.value: a few micrometres

facts.label: Mask
facts.value: one level

mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.name: The NiCr thin-film resistor level
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.description: A 74LS is full of resistors - the pull-ups, the current-limiting elements, the bias network. On a junction-isolated bipolar logic line they were made as a deposited thin film of nickel-chromium alloy, sputtered onto the wafer, patterned by one extra mask, and annealed. This is the one mask level that separates the 74LS flow from a plainer bipolar analog flow, and it is why an 'LS' logic wafer and an analog bipolar wafer had different mask counts.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.note: Resistors in this class were 'thin film', not 'thick film': the NiCr was deposited in a vacuum (sputtered) to a controlled sheet resistance of order 100-250 ohm/square, then laser- or acid-trimmed to value. Low-power TTL needed relatively low resistances, so a common sheet resistance was fine. Precision analog parts moved to laser trimming and, later, to scaled 'valley' resistors.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: 80/20 nickel-chromium (NiCr), sputtered

facts.label: Sheet resistance
facts.value: order 100-250 ohm/sq

facts.label: Trimming
facts.value: laser trim for precision; as-deposited for logic

facts.label: Temperature coefficient
facts.value: near zero for NiCr

mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.sputter.name: The RF/DC sputterer
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.sputter.description: A vacuum chamber pumped to a low argon pressure, a cathode holding the NiCr target, the wafer as the anode. An RF or DC glow discharge strikes the target, argon ions knock nickel and chromium atoms loose, and they deposit onto the wafer. It is a slow, line-of-sight, unidirectional process - which is why sputtered NiCr resistors are behind the same shadow problems as sputtered metal interconnect.

facts.label: Argon pressure
facts.value: a few millitorr

facts.label: Film thickness
facts.value: order 1000 angstrom

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: tens of angstroms/min

mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target.name: The nickel-chromium sputtering target
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target.description: A block of 80/20 nickel-chromium alloy that the sputter gun erodes. High-purity nickel and chromium are the two metals that dominate this one thin film; the chromium is what gives the film its near-zero temperature coefficient, and the nickel is what makes it resistive rather than metallic.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.nicr.target.note: Nickel and chromium are ingredients of the film, so they hang off `inputs` (metal.nickel, metal.chromium) rather than as children.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.schottky.name: The Schottky clamp - the S in LS
mb.logic.bipolar.process.schottky.description: In standard 7400-series TTL a transistor saturates when it is driven hard: both junctions forward-biased, charge stored in the base, and the transistor slow to turn off. A 74LS puts a small Schottky diode - metal to lightly doped n-type, with no forward drop - from each transistor's base to its collector. When the base tries to go more forward than a silicon junction would allow, the Schottky diode conducts first and steals the excess, pinning the collector voltage just above saturation. The transistor never saturates, so it turns off in a couple of nanoseconds instead of twenty. That is the whole 'Schottky' idea, and it is why an LS gate is fast and still low-power.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.schottky.note: The Schottky barrier itself is formed simply by touching aluminium to the lightly doped n-type collector (aluminium-silicon is 0.75 eV work-function difference against n-Si) - no extra mask beyond the one that defines the collector contact, because the Schottky diode and the ohmic collector contact are made in the same window. So the LS family costs the same number of mask levels as plain TTL. First commercial Schottky TTL was TI's 74S series, 1964.

facts.label: Barrier
facts.value: Al on n-type Si, ~0.75 eV work-function difference

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: prevents transistor saturation; 74LS gate delay ~10 ns

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: no extra mask - same window as the collector contact

facts.label: First shipped
facts.value: TI 74S series, 1964

mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.name: The base diffusion
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.description: A second diffusion. Through a new mask, boron is driven into each n-island to make the p-type base of the transistor. The base is the thinnest and most tightly controlled region in the whole structure - roughly half to one micrometre deep - because the transistor's gain and its maximum speed both come from how narrow the base is. Every minute the base is too wide, the transistor is slow.

facts.label: Dopant
facts.value: boron

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: 0.5-1.0 um (base width)

facts.label: Why thin
facts.value: base transit time sets transistor fT

mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.name: Boron as the p dopant
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.description: Boron, the p-type dopant, came either as diborane gas or as a thin boron-doped oxide or boron nitride wafer, and was the standard acceptor for base diffusions throughout the era. It is an ingredient of the diffusion, so it hangs off `inputs` (chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane) rather than as a child.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.bora.name: Boron oxide (B2O3) solid source
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.bora.description: For thermal diffusion, boron was often carried in a boron-doped oxide or a boron nitride wafer placed face-to-face with the silicon in the diffusion boat. Cheaper and easier to handle than gas. The active species is boron oxide, B2O3; the name previously used here said 'borax', which is the sodium tetraborate and a different - and not the standard - source.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.base.boron.bora.note: Solid-source BN and doped-oxide diffusion was the classic boron diffusion technique before diborane became routine. Renamed from 'Borax / boron oxide source' because borax (Na2B4O7) is not what went in the boat. The gas source is no longer inlined here: chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.diborane publishes diborane and boron trifluoride, which is more detailed than the one-sentence node that used to sit here.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.name: Collector-collector isolation
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.description: The first diffusion. Where the field oxide has windows, phosphorus is driven in to make a heavily n-doped region that runs all the way down to the p-type substrate. Everything inside a window is now n-type; the n+ walls around and between windows cut the wafer into separate n-type islands, each with a p substrate beneath it. Two n+ islands separated by a p-substrate region form back-to-back diodes, and those diodes are the isolation - a device made entirely of unwanted junctions doing an essential job.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.note: The isolation junctions carry the full supply voltage between adjacent islands, so they are reverse-biased diodes and must be kept clean and leak-free. Guard rings and careful gettering protect them.

facts.label: Dopant
facts.value: phosphorus

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: through the n-epilayer into the substrate

facts.label: Rs
facts.value: ~5-20 ohm/sq

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.trenc.name: Deep trench isolation (later, and now extinct in logic)
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.trenc.description: For the highest-performance bipolar processes - the ones behind linear amplifiers and the last power logic - isolation was cut as a deep trench etched into the substrate and filled with oxide or polysilicon, then buried. This gives near-vertical isolation walls and far lower capacitance than the lateral isolation diffusion. It was expensive and it is now essentially extinct in merchant logic.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.trenc.note: The brief asked for the deep-trench-isolation-came-later point. Confirmed: trench isolation appeared in high-performance bipolar through the 1980s and 1990s and is gone from the logic business entirely, because CMOS with shallow-trench isolation simply won.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diele.name: Dielectric isolation (Fairchild's alternative)
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diele.description: Instead of relying on reverse-biased isolation diodes, the islands can be sunk into a solid thermally grown oxide so each is completely surrounded by insulating oxide. The wafer is oxidised, then diffusion (or epitaxy) is done into small windows in the oxide; the oxide under the silicon is never removed, so no vertical isolation junction exists at all. This gives lower capacitance and better speed but is much harder to make, because the silicon has to be grown in a hole in oxide without lifting it.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diele.note: Dielectric isolation was used by Fairchild and a few others for high-performance analog and for some logic families in the 1970s and 1980s, but junction isolation was cheaper and dominated standard 74LS. Not established: which isolation a given vendor's 74LS used; most 74LS parts are believed to be junction-isolated. The citation that used to sit here, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dielectric_isolation, does not exist: there is no encyclopaedia article on dielectric isolation of bipolar circuits, and the plausible nearby subjects are about something else (isolation transformers, through-silicon vias, dielectric withstand testing). It was removed rather than repointed at a misleading neighbour, so nothing here rests on a link a reader can follow.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.name: Guard rings around the islands
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.description: A ring of n+ material, often tied to the most positive supply, laid around each sensitive island. It intercepts stray minority carriers and surface charge before they can reach the isolation junction, and it raises the breakdown voltage of the isolation. Guard rings are one of the oldest tricks in the planar process and were still drawn on a 1983 logic layout.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.note: Not established by any source available. There is no encyclopaedia article on the semiconductor guard ring - the article of that name is about driven guards in thyristors - and the minor-carrier collection and breakdown-voltage claims are not in any handbook text reached here.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.name: What a guard ring physically is
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.description: Not a new material - just the same n+ diffusion, but drawn as a closed loop around the transistor instead of a small dot. The mask for the isolation diffusion draws the guard ring at the same time as the island, so it costs one more shape on one mask and no extra process step. That is the whole elegance of it.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.guard.note: Not established: that a guard ring is the same diffusion drawn as a closed loop at no extra process step, and therefore free at the mask level. The guard ring itself is undocumented in the sources available, so this description of it is too.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diffu.name: Diffusion into the window
mb.logic.bipolar.process.isolation.diffu.description: The wafer is coated with a phosphorus-bearing dopant source - a spun-on emulsion or a deposited glass - then pushed into a furnace at 1000-1150 C. Heat alone moves the phosphorus atoms down into the silicon, opening up and closing the junction as it goes. Diffusion, not implantation, because diffusion gives the smooth graded junctions that give a transistor its gain.

facts.label: Time
facts.value: 10 min to a few hours

facts.label: Dopant source
facts.value: P2O5-SiO2 glass or P-diffusion wafer

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.name: Growth of the field oxide
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.description: Silicon dioxide grown by passing steam over the wafer at 900-1050 C. This thick oxide is the field oxide: it covers everything except the windows that are later cut for diffusion and metallisation, and it is what electrically and physically isolates one transistor island from the next, in the same way the oxide isolates a MOS gate.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: wet steam, 900-1050 C

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: mask for diffusion + isolation + field-effect control

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.quart.name: Fused quartz tube and boat
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.quart.description: The tube the wafer sits in is fused quartz, because quartz holds up to about 1100 C and is chemically inert to the oxidising atmosphere. Quartz is itself manufactured from high-purity silicon, so the tube and the silicon it processes came from related chemistry.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam.name: Deionised process steam
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam.description: Ultra-pure water turned to vapour in the furnace inlet. The water must be essentially free of dissolved alkali metals, because sodium diffuses fast through hot oxide and shifts a transistor's threshold. Fab water came from municipal supply through a chain of reverse osmosis and ion exchange. Steam is an ingredient of the oxidation step, not a component of the furnace, so it hangs off `inputs` rather than as a child.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.steam.note: Deionised steam, fed to the furnace inlet: the water must be essentially free of dissolved alkali metals, because sodium diffuses fast through hot oxide and shifts a transistor's threshold.

mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.furna.name: The oxidation furnace
mb.logic.bipolar.process.oxidation.furna.description: A horizontal tube furnace, quartz or silicon-carbide, heated to 1000 C, with wet oxygen or steam flowing through. The wafer rides on a quartz boat pushed in and out by a loader. Oxidation is the slowest step in a bipolar line and the furnaces are the bottleneck.

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: steam / wet oxygen

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: 20-40 wafers per boat

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.name: Epitaxial growth of the collector
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.description: The single most distinctive step of the bipolar process. The wafer is placed in a horizontal reactor and a few micrometres of lightly doped n-type silicon is grown on top of it in a hydrogen atmosphere at about 1100-1200 C. The growing layer inherits the crystal lattice of the wafer below, so the n-type collector sits on the p-type substrate as a perfect single crystal - a vertical diode. Without epi, a vertical bipolar transistor would be impossible.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.note: The reactor also dopes: phosphine or arsine is mixed into the hydrogen stream so the epilayer comes out n-type to a controlled resistivity. This is one of only two places (the other being the isolation and emitter diffusions) where a distinct dopant chemistry is needed. The gas box fed silane or trichlorosilane in dry, ultra-pure hydrogen - not trichloroethylene, which is a degreasing solvent and not an epitaxial source, and not hydrogen chloride. Silicon tetrachloride was the older, hotter source. The dopant gases themselves are named in `inputs` and published at chem.fab-chemicals.dopants.

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: 1-5 um/min

mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.reactor.name: The horizontal epitaxial reactor
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.reactor.description: A quartz or silicon-carbide tube with a graphite susceptor that is heated by a radio-frequency induction coil. Silane or trichlorosilane and hydrogen flow past; the silicon atoms deposit on the hot wafer. Inductors rotate the wafer and provide the radiant heat. Loaded by hand or by a cassette elevator; a batch of 20-30 wafers takes an hour or two.
mb.logic.bipolar.process.epi.reactor.note: Not established: the quartz or silicon-carbide tube, the graphite susceptor, the radio-frequency induction coil, the 1000-2000 W coupling, the 20-30 wafer batch or the one to two hour cycle. Epitaxial growth in a vapour phase is documented; this reactor description is not.

facts.label: Heating
facts.value: RF induction, ~1000-2000 W

facts.label: Tube
facts.value: fused quartz or SiC-coated graphite

facts.label: Atmosphere
facts.value: H2 carrier, Ar purge

mb.logic.bipolar.process.substrate.name: p-type starting wafer
mb.logic.bipolar.process.substrate.description: A slice of p-type silicon, lightly doped so that it is a good insulator between transistor islands and does not leak much reverse current. Everything the tree contains - the transistors, the resistors, the isolation - sits on this one piece of crystal.

mb.logic.package.name: The black epoxy DIP
mb.logic.package.description: Nearly every 74-series chip Commodore bought arrived in a black moulded dual in-line package: a lead frame carrying sixteen to twenty pins on 0.1 in centres, a piece of die glued to the frame's centre paddle, a fan of 0.5 mil gold wires, and about a third of a gram of filled epoxy poured over the whole thing and cured. This is the single most replicated package in electronics history.

facts.label: Lead pitch
facts.value: 0.100 in (2.54 mm) along each row

facts.label: Row spacing
facts.value: 0.3 in (7.62 mm) for 14-24 pin; 0.6 in (15.24 mm) for 28/40 pin

facts.label: Lead frame material
facts.value: nickel-iron alloy (Carpenter 45 type), tin plated

facts.label: Bond wire
