facts.value: 0.7-1.0 mil gold, ~20 bonds for a 20-pin DIP

mb.logic.package.marking.name: Marking the top of the package
mb.logic.package.marking.description: Ink printing was still the norm in 1983: a pad or a dot-matrix printer lays the part number, the manufacturer's mark, a date code (year and week, e.g. 8341) and a lot or assembly code on the moulded surface. Laser marking was beginning to appear, mostly for military parts, and would take over within a decade because a laser-marked part cannot be relabelled.
mb.logic.package.marking.note: Commodore bought these chips from several vendors and did not re-mark them, which is why an original C64 board may carry parts branded TI, Fairchild, National, Motorola, Hitachi, Toshiba or a Commodore house number, all mixed together. Laser marking - a Q-switched Nd:YAG or CO2 laser ablating characters into the epoxy surface, or a carbon laser removing the top layer to expose an underlying white layer - was indelible and fast but in 1983 was still a premium option used mostly for military marking, adopted more widely through the mid-to-late 1980s.

facts.label: Typical legend
facts.value: e.g. 'SN74LS257N  TI  8341' or 'MM74LS257N  MOTOROLA'

facts.label: Date code format
facts.value: year + work week, e.g. 8341

facts.label: Packaging of record
facts.value: tubed, then later dry-packed and taped

facts.label: Laser marking in 1983
facts.value: minority of parts; military mostly

mb.logic.package.marking.ink.name: Marking ink
mb.logic.package.marking.ink.description: A phenolic or epoxy ink with a pigment, laid on and baked, or cured by UV. Cheap and utterly routine - but it is why an original C64 chip is still readable today and a modern BGA is not. (Ink marking was also curable by laser ablation of the mould compound, which is the mechanism the laser marking route exploits.)
mb.logic.package.marking.ink.note: That the legend is printed in ink or by laser and carries a four-digit year-and-week date code is documented. Not established: a phenolic or epoxy ink with a pigment, baking or UV curing, or that ink marking is why a 1982 part is still readable and a modern ball-grid array is not.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.name: The ceramic DIP (mostly not used here)
mb.logic.package.ceramic.description: For military and extended-temperature parts the epoxy was replaced by a package made of alumina ceramic, sealed hermetically with a glass frit or a metal lid. It could be baked out, leak-tested, and taken from -55 to +125 C without the epoxy softening. It was also more expensive and much larger, so merchant logic in a home computer was always plastic: the C64's own 74-series parts are all black epoxy, with the ceramic version only appearing in industrial or aerospace equipment.
mb.logic.package.ceramic.note: The 74LS series exists in both CDIP (ceramic) and PDIP (plastic) forms, distinguished by the letter after the temperature grade: N is plastic (0 to +70 C), E or M is ceramic (-55 to +125 C). Commodore specified N-grade parts.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal.name: Glass frit sealing
mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal.description: A paste of powdered borosilicate glass with a small amount of binder is applied around the rim, the lid is set on it, and the assembly goes through a sealing furnace. The glass melts, wets the metallised ceramic and the metal lid, and on cooling forms a hermetic, dimensionally matched bond. The temperature profile - ramp, soak around 700-750 C, controlled cool - is the whole art of it.
mb.logic.package.ceramic.seal.note: Sealing in a continuous belt or pusher furnace at a few hundred degrees per hour rather than 700-750 C soak is the classic profile; the exact numbers vary by package. Medium confidence on the peak temperature.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.lid.name: Kovar lid and nickel seal ring
mb.logic.package.ceramic.lid.description: For parts sealed with metal rather than glass, a lid of Kovar (iron-nickel-cobalt, chosen for its matching expansion) is brazed or welded to a nickel ring around the ceramic. Kovar is the same idea as the lead frame alloy: pick the expansion coefficient of the metal so it matches the ceramic and the seal does not crack.

mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.name: Alumina ceramic body
mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.description: A package shell made of 95-99 percent alumina, formed by pressing or by tape-casting a green body in a serpentine conductor pattern and firing it at 1500-1600 C. Alumina was chosen because it matches silicon and the glass seal closely in expansion, is cheap, and is a good thermal conductor compared with any polymer.
mb.logic.package.ceramic.body.note: The bauxite-to-alumina route is not inlined here: metal.bauxite and metal.alumina publish it, with the caustic digestion and the ion-exchange steps on their side. Note that alumina reaches this package by two unrelated routes a few centimetres apart - as the ceramic body of a CDIP, and as the metal sputtered onto the die of the same part in its PDIP form.

mb.logic.package.probe.name: Probe test before packaging
mb.logic.package.probe.description: Die that fail are thrown away before they are worth a lead frame. The wafer is loaded onto a probe stage, a probe card with one needle per bonding pad is lowered onto it, and a tester runs every pattern and every DC parameter. Only known-good die are cut. This is why probe test and not final test is what sets the economics of a logic wafer: a yield loss after packaging has already cost you the moulding and the wire bonds too.

mb.logic.package.probe.tester.name: The logic tester
mb.logic.package.probe.tester.description: An automated test system running a stored functional pattern and a set of DC limit tests per device type: propagation delay, fan-out current, input current, output high and low voltage, and the truth table at the functional corners. A 74LS04 has a few hundred such tests. The tester was the expensive part of probe test and was amortised across every device type on the line.
mb.logic.package.probe.tester.note: Automatic test equipment: capital equipment shared across every device type on the line, so a tool rather than a part or a consumable.

facts.label: Tests per 74LS quad gate
facts.value: ~200-400 patterns and parameters

facts.label: Instrumentation
facts.value: TTL pattern generator, timing analyser, DC meter

mb.logic.package.probe.card.name: The probe card
mb.logic.package.probe.card.description: A ceramic or printed-circuit substrate carrying one cantilever needle per bonding pad, cantilevered down from an epoxy or quartz shell so the needles survive hundreds of thousands of touches on hard silicon. Building a card for a new part number took days and cost hundreds to thousands of dollars, which is why a device that sold for thirty cents could not afford a new probe card per variant.
mb.logic.package.probe.card.note: Not established: the ceramic or printed-circuit card substrate, the cantilever needle construction, the needle lifetime in touches, or the days and hundreds-to-thousands of dollars to build a card for a new part number. Wafer test before dicing is documented; the card is not.

mb.logic.package.probe.prober.name: The wafer probe station
mb.logic.package.probe.prober.description: A heavy cast stage that steps the wafer die by die under a fixed probe card: a vacuum or hot chuck on an x-y-z stage, a microscope to line the card up, and a needle interface to the tester. An operator loads a cassette of up to 25 wafers and unloads it at the end; everything in between was automatic.
mb.logic.package.probe.prober.note: Not established: the cast stage, the vacuum or hot chuck on an x-y-z stage, the 25-wafer cassette, the 1-4 die per second probing speed or the 20-80 g per needle contact force. No prober specification is in any source available.

facts.label: Wafers per run
facts.value: up to 25 (25-wafer cassette)

facts.label: Probing speed
facts.value: 1-4 die per second

facts.label: Probe force
facts.value: ~20-80 g per needle

mb.logic.package.assembly.name: Die attach, wire bond, moulding
mb.logic.package.assembly.description: Three operations turn a loose die and a loose lead frame into a component. The die is brazed to the frame's central ledge. Twenty-ish gold wires are ball- or wedge-bonded from pads on the die to the inner ends of the pins. Then about 0.3-0.5 g of filled black epoxy is transfer-moulded over everything and cured.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.name: Transfer moulding the black epoxy body
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.description: A slab of thermosetting epoxy loaded with 75-85 percent spherical silica is melted at 175 C and forced through a small orifice into a multi-cavity steel mould - the transfer mould - that holds the wired frame in one cavity per die. The compound flows around the wire loops, fills voids, and cures in three to five minutes. Because it is filled with silica it is not really a plastic in the loose sense: it is a ceramic-filled thermoset whose job is to hold the die in place, carry heat away, and keep moisture out. Moulding compounds are incompletely polymerised at the mould temperature, so the parts are then baked for hours at 175 C to complete the cure and drive off the last of the residual stress - a batch operation, thousands of parts in a tray, on a schedule that ran overnight.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.note: The post-mould stability bake: thousands of parts in a tray, overnight, completing a cure that the mould itself cannot finish.

facts.label: Transfer pressure
facts.value: 8-15 MPa

facts.label: Cure in mould
facts.value: 3-5 min

facts.label: Post-mould bake
facts.value: 175 C for 4-24 h - completes cure and moisture equilibration

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.tool.name: The mould cavity and ejector pins
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.tool.description: A hardened, polished steel block with one to hundreds of identical cavities. For a DIP the cavity is a rectangle with fourteen to twenty pin-shaped slots; the mould also carries the moulded cavity number, the vendor's part-number embossing, and ejector pins that push the finished part out without scuffing it. Moulds lasted a few hundred thousand to a few million shots.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.tool.note: A consumable tool, not a machine: it is bought, used up over its shot life and thrown away, so `part` rather than `tool`. Its earlier `inputs: [metal.silica]` was wrong - nothing in a hardened steel mould is silica - and has been removed.

facts.label: Cavity marks
facts.value: the number 1 or a letter, moulded into the underside

facts.label: Tool life
facts.value: ~0.2-2 million shots

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Epoxy moulding compound
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: A blend of roughly 15-20 percent resin system and 80-85 percent filler by weight. The resin is an epoxy-novolac cured by a phenolic novolac; the filler is spherical fused or precipitated silica graded from a few microns up to about 100 microns so the compound can be both thin enough to flow around a 25 um wire and stiff enough to survive handling; and there is a trace of carbon black pigment to make the part black, plus a trace of mould release. Green compounds arrived in the mid-1980s.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.note: The silica filler is an ingredient, not a component, so it hangs off `inputs` (metal.silica, metal.quartzite) rather than as a child. Green compounds arrived in the mid-1980s. The resin and the pigment really are constituents of the compound, so those two stay as children; everything the resin is itself made from is an ingredient of the resin, one level down.

facts.label: Filler loading
facts.value: 70-85 wt% spherical silica

facts.label: Resin system
facts.value: epoxy cresol novolac + phenolic novolac hardener

facts.label: Pigment
facts.value: ~0.5-1 wt% carbon black (or none, for 'clear')

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Carbon black pigment
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: About half a percent by weight of furnace black, dispersed into the compound, to make the package opaque black. Black rather than natural-coloured because a black package hides internal voids, and because it was what the whole industry had standardised on since the first plastic DIP.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.note: The pigment is a trivial mass fraction of the whole computer but it is the same furnace black that goes into carbon-film resistors and into the photoconductor of a laser printer drum. Its feedstock is heavy petroleum residuum or natural gas fed to an air-cooled sooting furnace, the soot scraped off water-cooled rotors and pelletised.

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.name: Epoxy cresol novolac resin
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.description: The workhorse of chip packaging in every decade since 1970. Cresol-formaldehyde epoxy novolac is made from epichlorohydrin and a cresol-formaldehyde novolac; cured with a phenolic novolac and catalysed with a small amount of hexamethylenetetramine, it cures without volatiles and without ionising anything, so it does not damage the die. The epoxy end comes from epichlorohydrin, which industry has always made by chlorohydrination of propylene - propene plus hypochlorous acid to 1,2-dichloropropane, then base dehydrochlorination to close the epoxide ring - so the propylene came off a steam cracker, the chlorine out of a chlor-alkali cell, and the caustic soda out of the same cell: the plastic body of every 74LS chip traces back to salt and to crude oil.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.compound.note: Bisphenol A epoxy (the older, less package-friendly EPON-type system) was still used on some parts; cresol novolac had largely displaced it in logic packaging. The epichlorohydrin -> propylene -> cracker -> chlorine -> brine chain used to be inlined beneath this node as seven nodes of its own; it is not inlined here. chem.epoxy.dgeba.epichlorohydrin publishes the molecule, chem.propylene.sources.cracker-c3 the C3 stream, metal.chlorine and metal.chlor-alkali the chlorine, metal.salt-brine the brine and metal.caustic-soda the caustic. The chain is named by id in `inputs` so there is one copy of it in the tree.

facts.label: System
facts.value: epoxy cresol novolac

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: phenolic novolac + hexamine, 175 C, no by-products

facts.label: Route to epichlorohydrin
facts.value: propylene chlorohydrination, then caustic dehydrochlorination

mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.press.name: The transfer press
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.press.description: A heated platen press with a pot and plunger that transfers melted compound into the mould. Modern machines are multi-cavity and run at thousands of shots an hour; a 1980s line used 20- to 100-shot multi-cavity tools and got through a few hundred thousand DIPs a month.
mb.logic.package.assembly.mould.press.note: Capital equipment, so a tool rather than a part.

facts.label: Cavities per tool
facts.value: 20-100 for logic DIPs

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: ~10-20 s for the moulding operation

mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.name: Gold wire bonding
mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.description: A machine called a wedge bonder presses a hair-thin gold wire onto an aluminium bonding pad with a tungsten or ceramic tool while a hydrogen torch or arc welds them together, then repeats at the inner end of the pin. Each joint is a small aluminium-gold intermetallic wedge, and the wire is parted by tearing it rather than by cutting it. It is the cheapest way ever devised to connect a chip to the outside world, and it is why every 1983 logic chip has that characteristic fan of gold legs.
mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.note: Ball bonding, with a 2.5 mil wire and ~25-50 bonds per second, was displacing wedge bonding for high pin counts in this period. Wedge bonding at ~10 bonds per second dominated merchant logic.

facts.label: Wire diameter
facts.value: 0.7 mil (18 um) to 1.0 mil (25 um)

facts.label: Speed
facts.value: 8-15 bonds/second wedge

mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.bonde.name: The wedge bonder
mb.logic.package.assembly.wirebond.bonde.description: A two-station machine that draws wire from a spool, forms a loop, drives a wedge onto the die pad under a hydrogen flame, swings 90 degrees, and drives the second wedge onto the pin, then snaps the wire. Twenty or forty of these sat in a row along a packaging line, each attended by one operator feeding frames in and taking packaged parts out.

facts.label: Cycle rate
facts.value: ~10 bonds/s, ~2 s per part

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 1.0 mil gold, spool-fed

facts.label: Weld
facts.value: hydrogen torch, ~1000 C

mb.logic.package.assembly.attach.name: Die attach to the frame paddle
mb.logic.package.assembly.attach.description: The die is placed face-down onto a small ledge in the middle of the lead frame and brazed there with a preform of gold-silicon eutectic at 350-400 C. The eutectic melts before the silicon itself does, so the joint is made without heating the chip to a temperature that would damage it. Cheap parts instead used a silver-filled organic paste cured on a hot plate, or conductive epoxy, and some logic used glass-frit die attach for thermal cycling.
mb.logic.package.assembly.attach.note: Organic die attach became common in the late 1980s-90s for cost reasons. In 1983 Au-Si eutectic brazing was still the standard on logic and memory.

facts.label: Au-Si eutectic
facts.value: ~3-5 wt% Si, melts ~360 C

facts.label: Typical die weight
facts.value: ~3 mg for a 14-pin logic die

mb.logic.package.die.name: The separated, tested die
mb.logic.package.die.description: Between the diffusion bay and the packaging line, the wafer is scribed into rectangles, diced, and every rectangle is probed while still in wafer form. The die that arrives at the assembly line is a bare rectangle of silicon, perhaps 1.5 by 2.5 mm, with a scratched pattern of aluminium bonding pads on one face and a bare oxide film over the circuitry on the other.

facts.label: 74LS04 die size
facts.value: ~1.5 x 2.4 mm (measured, high confidence)

facts.label: Bond pads
facts.value: ~70 x 70 um, pitch ~150 um

mb.logic.package.die.hardtest.name: Why 4164 DRAMs die but 74LS parts mostly do not
mb.logic.package.die.hardtest.description: A 74LS gate is a handful of transistors with enormous margin; it either works or the diffusion is cracked. A 64Kx1 DRAM stores charge in a capacitor about 100 femtofarads across a transistor with a leakage path, and it has to be refreshed every few milliseconds. That is why the eight 4164s on the C64 are the board's failure-prone chips and the 74-series glue is almost always fine.
mb.logic.package.die.hardtest.note: The mechanism (charge storage and refresh) is high confidence; the comparative failure rate is a well-attested field observation rather than a measured statistic.

mb.logic.package.die.passivation.name: The glass over the aluminium
mb.logic.package.die.passivation.description: After metallisation the whole wafer is coated in a thick film of silicon dioxide, usually with a plasma-deposited nitride cap. This passivation layer is what protects a 1983 logic die from the humidity and mobile ions that would otherwise creep under the aluminium and shift the threshold of a transistor. Openings in it are the bonding pads and the scribe lanes.
mb.logic.package.die.passivation.note: Early 1980s nitride deposition was increasingly low-pressure or plasma-enhanced CVD from silane and ammonia; furnaces using TEOS plus ammonia still ran in parallel.

facts.label: Oxide thickness
facts.value: 1-2 um (heavily doped, phosphorus glass)

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: moisture barrier and sodium gettering

mb.logic.package.die.scribe.name: Scribing and dicing the wafer
mb.logic.package.die.scribe.description: A diamond stylus is dragged along the scribe lanes between dies, not to cut through but to fracture the crystal along the damage tracks buried in the oxide. For the narrow lanes the wafer is turned edge-on and run through a rotating diamond blade, or more recently a tensioned wire loaded with abrasive, which leaves far less chipping than a blade.
mb.logic.package.die.scribe.note: The diamond itself - natural or, by 1983, mostly synthetic from graphite in a belt press - is not inlined here; si.wafer.diamond in the silicon fragment publishes it, and `inputs` resolves to it.

facts.label: Blade kerf
facts.value: ~0.15 mm for a resinoid dicing saw

mb.logic.package.leadframe.name: Nickel-iron lead frame
mb.logic.package.leadframe.description: A continuous strip of metal, punched and formed into a repeating chain of DIP skeletons joined by tie-bars. It arrives at the assembler as a reel of maybe 3000 frames; the frames are cut out one at a time, plated, and then become the skeleton of the package - the seventeen or more separate pins, the two rows, and the little central ledge the die sits on.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.note: Carpenter 45 (42% Ni / 58% Fe, balance carbon and manganese) and similar low-expansion nickel-iron alloys were the standard logic lead frame material because the thermal expansion coefficient was tuned to match the alumina-and-epoxy package, so the die, the frame and the mould compound do not fight each other over temperature cycling. It was a commodity ferronickel-like alloy made in ordinary steel melts - the same order of chemistry as the ferronickel made from laterite in the metals branch, but at 42% Ni rather than 60-75%, and made to a coefficient spec rather than to a nickel content spec.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: Fe-Ni, ~42% Ni (Carpenter 45 / Alloy 42 family)

facts.label: Iron fraction
facts.value: ~58 wt% - the majority of the frame by mass, and commodity steel

facts.label: Forms per metre of strip
facts.value: ~40-60, joined by tie bars

mb.logic.package.leadframe.c4.name: Copper-clad C4 lead frame (later, not 1983)
mb.logic.package.leadframe.c4.description: A lead frame fabricated not from a bulk alloy strip but from an aluminium or copper leadframe clad on both faces with a controlled thickness of copper, so the surface the solder sees is copper rather than a flash plate. Known by the trademark C4. It solved the tin-whisker and solderability problems at once and became standard for fine-pitch packages from the late 1980s onward.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.c4.note: Included to mark the boundary: a C64 from 1983 contains no C4 frames. The technology existed in the late 1980s but was not standard on through-hole merchant logic. Copper is an ingredient, so it hangs off `inputs` rather than as a child.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.name: Lead plating: tin, gold flash, nickel
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.description: Bare nickel-iron leads solder badly and gall when the DIP is pushed into and out of a socket, so every logic lead frame came out of the stamping press already plated. The common 1983 finish was an electroless or electrolytic nickel pre-plate followed by a matte tin or tin-lead overlay; gold flash over nickel was used where a part had to survive many insertions. A small fraction of frames used silver.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.note: Matte tin plating on lead frames later became a reliability problem - tin whiskers - and the industry spent two decades fixing it. Copper-clad (C4) frames that carry a thicker, more solderable surface metal appeared in the late 1980s and 1990s, which is why the C64's successors used them and the C64 did not.

mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.name: Tin plating bath
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.description: A chemical or electrolytic tin deposit, typically 1-3 micrometres thick, over a nickel underlayer. Tin is soft, wets solder readily and costs almost nothing, and it is why a logic chip could be soldered onto a two-layer board with a plain iron in an automated wave-solder machine with no special flux. The refined tin came from cassiterite smelted in Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand or Bolivia.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.plating.tin.note: The name is kept as-is because two nodes in the silicon fragment resolve their 'tin plating bath' ingredient to this id by name; renaming it would silently break those edges and the repoint is proposed rather than applied. The deeper tin chemistry - cassiterite, the Southeast Asian belt and the 1985-86 International Tin Council price collapse - is not inlined here: metal.cassiterite and metal.tin publish it. The general plating process for steel and copper alloys is metal.tin.plating.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 1-3 um over Ni

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: matte tin, sulphate or fluoroborate

mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.name: Progressive-die stamping of the frame
mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.description: The strip is fed through a sequence of steel dies on a mechanical press. Each station cuts, pierces, forms and bends a little more; by the last station the strip has a repeating row of completed DIP skeletons still joined by their tie bars. Ten to twenty tonnes of press capacity for a strip that is a tenth of a millimetre thick and has to be dimensioned to a few microns.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.note: Photo-etched lead frames from copper and copper alloys were an alternative for high-lead-count parts, but the stamping route dominated through-hole logic DIPs in this period.

facts.label: Strip feed rate
facts.value: ~1000-3000 strokes/min

facts.label: Tooling life
facts.value: ~100k-1M strokes before regrind/retool

facts.label: Tie bars
facts.value: left until after the die is attached, to hold the frame rigid

mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.tool.name: The progressive die set
mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.tool.description: A stack of hardened tool-steel plates, each with apertures and forming punches cut by wire EDM or grinding, bolted into a set between the press bolster and the ram. Making the tooling for one frame number was a days-to-weeks job and was why a lead frame number was never changed casually: the tooling, the mould, the socket and the board artwork all had to change together.
mb.logic.package.leadframe.stamp.tool.note: A press toolset, consumed over hundreds of millions of strokes - capital equipment rather than a part.

mb.logic.package.geometry.name: Why 0.1 inch and 0.3 inch
mb.logic.package.geometry.description: The two dimensions that made the DIP work at all, and the reason for both. The 0.100 in (2.54 mm) lead pitch was chosen so a cheap single-row socket, and a hole in a piece of perforated board on the same grid, would accept the part. The 0.3 in (7.62 mm) row spacing was a compromise: close enough that a 14-pin body clears a 0.05 in hole-pad on 0.1 in centres, far enough apart that the leads are stiff enough to survive insertion into a socket and that the part can sit on the older, wider 0.6 in grid alongside the 40-pin devices. Bodies too wide for 0.3 in moved to 0.6 in rows.
mb.logic.package.geometry.note: The choice of 0.3 in over a wider spacing was a manufacturability and socket-compatibility compromise rather than a single published decision, so this is the conventional account rather than a quotation.

mb.logic.package.geometry.rowspacing.name: 0.3 inch row spacing and its wider variants
mb.logic.package.geometry.rowspacing.description: The distance between the two rows of pins. Standard JEDEC practice in 1983 was 300 mil for packages up to 24 pins and 600 mil for 28-pin and 40-pin parts, so a 40-pin device and a 16-pin device could share a footprint grid. A 900 mil (22.9 mm) body was used by some hermetic and high-current ceramic parts but was never common in merchant logic.
mb.logic.package.geometry.rowspacing.note: The 0.3 in / 0.6 in rule is high confidence; the existence of a 0.9 in (22.9 mm) row spacing in the same era is medium confidence - such spacings appear on hermetic and high-power ceramic packages, but none has been confirmed on a merchant logic part.

mb.logic.package.geometry.pitch.name: 0.1 inch (2.54 mm) lead pitch
mb.logic.package.geometry.pitch.description: The distance between adjacent pins on one row of the DIP. It is the same pitch as the holes on a piece of perforated board, and it is the reason a 74LS04 could be dropped into a socket or a perfboard without any special tooling. The pin itself is a 0.25 x 0.5 mm rectangular wire, the narrow dimension facing the chip.

facts.label: Lead length (DIP-14)
facts.value: ~7.6 mm from body shoulder to tip

mb.logic.not-on-this-board.name: 74-series parts that are NOT on a C64
mb.logic.not-on-this-board.description: A warning about the part list, kept so a reader can trust the sibling nodes. Frequently published lists of '74-series chips in the Commodore 64' include 74LS157, 74LS165, 74LS161, 74LS138, 74LS32, 74LS02, 74LS20, 74LS10, 74LS11, 74LS125 and 74LS181. None of those are on the ASSY 250407. They belong to other machines - the 74LS181 look-ahead carry and the 74LS165 shift registers are Apple II parts, the 74LS157 multiplexers are VIC-20 and BBC Micro parts - and they are almost always the result of copying a generic 'TTL in home computers' list rather than reading a parts list. This is commentary about the supply chain, not an entity, so it is a note.
mb.logic.not-on-this-board.note: Which machine each wrongly-attributed part actually belongs to is a verified finding, held at medium confidence. Twelve of the parts really are fitted to the ASSY 250407.

mb.logic.cmos-4000.name: CMOS logic on the board: 4066 switches and MC4044
mb.logic.cmos-4000.description: Four of the C64's glue chips are CMOS rather than bipolar TTL: two 4066 quad bilateral switches (U16, U28) and one MC4044 phase/frequency comparator (U32), plus the 74LS629 above. The 4066 is four independent CMOS transmission gates used as analogue multiplexers to route luma, chroma and audio and to hand the shared pins between the VIC-II and the outside world. The MC4044 compares the VCO's phase against the colour-subcarrier reference and generates the control voltage that locks the dot clock. Both were Motorola/RCA 4000-series parts, normally sold as CD4066B and CD4044B.
mb.logic.cmos-4000.note: These are 4000-series CMOS, not 7400-series, so strictly they sit outside a '74-series' scope. They are included because they are the clearest demonstration that a single 1983 Commodore board carried two completely different semiconductor processes, and because the brief asked for the CMOS branch to be covered from a real machine.

facts.label: 4066 count
facts.value: 2 (U16, U28), PDIP-14 each

facts.label: Named suppliers
facts.value: Motorola (MC prefix), RCA/Intersil (CD prefix), TI CD-prefix

mb.logic.cmos-4000.u20-lm556.name: LM556 dual timer (U20) - adjacent, not a logic part
mb.logic.cmos-4000.u20-lm556.description: Two 555-class monostable timers sharing one package, in a 14-pin DIP. It sits in the analogue paddle-input path, producing the timed pulse whose width the SID measures to report joystick and paddle position. Included here for completeness because it is off-the-shelf, because it is bipolar, and because it was made on the same diffusion lines as the TTL glue - just a different circuit on them.
mb.logic.cmos-4000.u20-lm556.note: An analogue bipolar part, not a 7400-series logic IC. Its internal process is a linear bipolar flow - epitaxial collector, deep wide-base, large-area emitters, no Schottky clamps and no thin-film resistor level - rather than the junction-isolated Schottky logic flow the bipolar branch describes.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual timer (dual 555)

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-14

facts.label: Process
facts.value: linear bipolar, not Schottky logic

mb.logic.u31-74ls629.name: 74LS629 dual voltage-controlled oscillator (U31)
mb.logic.u31-74ls629.description: Two voltage-controlled oscillator sections plus an enable and a range control, in a 14-pin DIP. The C64 has no crystal governing its video dot clock: one half of U31 amplifies the colour-subcarrier reference coming out of the video circuitry, the other half generates a free-running dot clock whose frequency is pulled by a control voltage. That is the oscillator half of the phase-locked loop completed by the MC4044 at U32. Despite the 'LS' prefix this part is CMOS internally, not bipolar TTL.
mb.logic.u31-74ls629.note: Part number, position and PLL role are high confidence and corroborated by scope measurements of the 250407 clock circuit published at tech.guitarsite.de/c64_scope.html. That the 74LS624-629 family is fabricated in CMOS rather than bipolar TTL despite the LS prefix is medium confidence: the family descends from Signetics/National designs and behaves like CMOS in pinout and power-up, but no period datasheet sentence stating the process has been found. Some vendors did not offer it at all, which is itself suggestive.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual voltage-controlled oscillator with enable and range control

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-14

facts.label: Family
facts.value: 74LS prefix, CMOS internals (medium confidence)

mb.logic.u30-74ls193.name: 74LS193 synchronous 4-bit up/down counter (U30)
mb.logic.u30-74ls193.description: A four-bit presettable binary counter with separate up and down clocks and a clear, in a 16-pin DIP. It sequences the multiplexed dynamic-RAM cycle - stepping through address states and generating the refresh strobes - and helps step the VIC-II's raster counters. This is the chip that turns 'one address bit is high right now' into 'we are on the nth step of a cycle'.
mb.logic.u30-74ls193.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence (service manual). Its exact role is low confidence: sources call it a 'binary counter', a divider, and part of the clock-generation chain, and the 250407 does share a cluster of counters and flip-flops (U29/U30) around the DRAM and raster timing that is hard to allocate from the parts list alone.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: synchronous presettable 4-bit up/down binary counter with clear

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-16

mb.logic.u29-74ls74.name: 74LS74 dual D-type flip-flop (U29)
mb.logic.u29-74ls74.description: Two positive-edge-triggered D flip-flops with asynchronous preset and clear, in a 14-pin DIP. In the C64 they sit in the DRAM timing chain: shaping and stretching the column strobe and dividing or retiming the phase clock so the 4164s get a valid /CAS pulse on the right edge. A flip-flop is what turns a combinational AND into a one-shot wide enough to meet the memory's timing spec.
mb.logic.u29-74ls74.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence. The functional description is low confidence: hobbyist references variously call U29 a 'divider', a 'dual D-type flip-flop', and part of the VIC-II raster timing, and the 251138 schematic was not traced net by net to settle it.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual D positive-edge-triggered flip-flop with preset and clear

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-14

mb.logic.u27-74ls08.name: 74LS08 quad 2-input AND gate (U27)
mb.logic.u27-74ls08.description: Four independent two-input AND gates in a 14-pin DIP - the most ordinary chip on the board and the one that does the most unglamorous work. ANDing is how the machine makes qualified control signals: a decode line ANDed with a clock phase becomes /RAS, /CAS or /WE for the DRAMs, and ANDed with the read/write phase becomes the chip select for the VIC-II, SID or CIA. Commodore also second-sourced it as house-number part 7712.
mb.logic.u27-74ls08.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence. The specific AND terms are inferred from the topology of a dynamic-RAM controller rather than read off the schematic net by net, hence medium.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: quad 2-input positive AND gate

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-14

facts.label: Family
facts.value: 74LS - Schottky-clamped bipolar TTL

mb.logic.u26-74ls373.name: 74LS373 octal D latch, three-state (U26)
mb.logic.u26-74ls373.description: Eight transparent D-type latches with three-state outputs in a 20-pin DIP. The VIC-II has only eight address pins but must reach two different memories - the 1 KB screen/bitmap RAM and the character-generator ROM - so it puts one byte on its own pins while this latch holds the other byte. The three-state outputs let the CPU read the latched byte back whenever the VIC is not driving. A dead U26 corrupts text and bitmap graphics but leaves everything else alive, which is why it is the classic 'screen is garbage but the machine boots' fault.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: octal transparent latch with three-state outputs

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-20

facts.label: Latch width
facts.value: 8 bits, single enable

mb.logic.u15-74ls139.name: 74LS139 dual 1-of-4 decoder (U15)
mb.logic.u15-74ls139.description: Two independent four-way decoders with common active-low enables and active-low outputs, in a 16-pin DIP. Given four address bits and an enable, each half asserts exactly one of four outputs. Commodore uses it to expand the sparse decode coming out of the PLA into individual chip selects - VIC-II banking, the I/O devices - and to qualify them with the read/write phase. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the house-number part 7708/7711.
mb.logic.u15-74ls139.note: Part number and quantity are high confidence (service manual). The exact set of selects it generates is medium confidence because most of the C64's address decoding lives in the 82S100 PLA at U17, and secondary sources disagree about which outputs the 74LS139 finishes off. MOS house-number versions of this decoder were a notorious C64 failure; they are more fragile than the TI/Fairchild/National parts.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: dual 1-of-4 line decoder / demultiplexer

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-16

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: active low

mb.logic.u14-74ls258.name: 74LS258 quad multiplexer with three-state outputs (U14)
mb.logic.u14-74ls258.description: The same four 2-to-1 selectors as the 74LS257 but with outputs that can be switched into a high-impedance state. This is the bus arbiter for VIC-II memory access: when the VIC-II is allowed to take the bus, the multiplexer's outputs are disabled so the VIC-II's own address pins can drive directly instead of fighting them. A failed U14 shows up as the VIC-II being unable to fetch screen data from RAM.
mb.logic.u14-74ls258.note: Some third-party board listings incorrectly give U14 as a 74LS373. The Commodore service manual parts list for #250407 says 74LS258.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: quad 2-to-1 multiplexer, three-state outputs

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-16

facts.label: Output disable
facts.value: per nibble

mb.logic.u13-u25-74ls257.name: 74LS257 quad 2-to-1 multiplexer (U13 and U25)
mb.logic.u13-u25-74ls257.description: Two identical 16-pin packages, each holding four independent 2-to-1 data selectors with non-inverting outputs. They exist for one reason: the 4164 DRAMs are multiplexed parts with only nine address pins, taking a row address first and a column address a few hundred nanoseconds later on the same wires. The CPU has sixteen address bits to deliver, so eight of them have to be time-division multiplexed onto four wires. One 74LS257 multiplexes four bits; two are needed for eight.
mb.logic.u13-u25-74ls257.note: A 74LS257 differs from a 74LS258 only in having totem-pole (push-pull) outputs instead of three-state outputs. This distinction is why U13/U25 and U14 do different jobs.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: quad 2-line to 1-line data selector/multiplexer

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-16

facts.label: Select inputs
facts.value: 1 per 2-to-1 selector, shared by the two selectors of each 4-bit nibble

mb.logic.u8-7406.name: 7406 hex inverter buffer, open collector (U8)
mb.logic.u8-7406.description: Six inverting buffers whose outputs are open collectors rather than totem poles, in a 14-pin DIP. On the 250407 they invert and buffer the 6510's cassette-port output lines (CASS MOTOR, CASS SENSE, CASS WRITE, CASS DATA) and the shared user-port / serial lines. Open-collector outputs with pull-ups are how those lines could be wired-OR and level-shifted without contention, and a pin that shorts to ground leaves the CPU reading the defined 'off' state rather than floating.
mb.logic.u8-7406.note: The service manual lists U8 as '7406 sub 7416'. Commodore also second-sourced it internally as the MOS house-number part 7707, and those MOS-made 'equivalent' parts are notoriously unreliable - a 7406/7707 failing high is a classic cause of a dead datasette or a stuck serial bus. Confidence is medium on the exact nets driven; high on the part number and function class.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: hex inverter / buffer, open collector

facts.label: Package
facts.value: PDIP-14, 0.3 in row spacing

facts.label: Family
facts.value: plain 7400-series TTL, not Schottky (LS)

facts.label: Open-collector sink
facts.value: ~16 mA per output

mb.discretes.name: Discrete semiconductors on the board
mb.discretes.description: The handful of non-IC semiconductors in the machine: small-signal NPN and PNP planar transistors (2N3904, 2N3906, 2N4124) for the serial/parallel port buffers, the colour-amplifier and video-driver stages and the cassette/joystick input switching; higher-voltage NPN power transistors (2N3055, 2N3792) in the power supply's regulator and short-circuit crowbar; rectifier, switching and zener diodes (1N4001, 1N4148, 1N47xx); one or two indicator LEDs; and a metal-oxide varistor across the AC input. Each of these was made in a bipolar or compound-semiconductor plant completely unrelated to the Norristown logic fab.
mb.discretes.note: Placement notes: the 1N4001 rectifiers and the 2N3055/2N3792 sit in the PSU, not on the logic mainboard - the power subsystem is another agent's tree. The exact transistors and diodes on a given C64 PCB revision vary; treat the list as representative rather than a BOM.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-92 epoxy mould for small signal; TO-3 or TO-220 plastic for power

facts.label: LED colours available in 1982
facts.value: red, amber, green - no blue LED existed

facts.label: Varistor
facts.value: ZnO disc, typically 275 V AC rated

mb.discretes.test.name: Probe, gain binning and final test of the discretes
mb.discretes.test.description: Discretes are probed on the wafer with a 3- or 10-needle card, then tested after packaging on a curve tracer or a dedicated bin tester. Bipolar small-signal parts are binned by hFE and by VCEO - the 2N3904's hFE spread runs roughly 100-300 - so a given lot is graded, and the C64's assembly only ever saw parts within the standard bin. Rectifiers are tested for reverse leakage and forward drop at rated current.
mb.discretes.test.note: That wafer-level binning by automatic test equipment is standard practice is documented. Not established: the 3- or 10-needle card, the hFE and VCEO grade bands, the 100-300 hFE spread at a stated bias, or that gain binning rather than lot screening was what the C64 assembly received.

facts.label: 2N3904 hFE
facts.value: 100-300 at Ic 10 mA, Vce 1 V

facts.label: VCEO
facts.value: 40 V minimum

mb.discretes.varistor.name: Zinc oxide varistor disc
mb.discretes.varistor.description: A MOV disc across the mains input: a disc of ZnO powder mixed with a few percent of glass and pressed and sintered at 1000-1200 C in air. Its resistance is nonlinear - about 1 kohm/mm at low voltage, collapsing to tens of ohms at the 275 V clamping point - because the grain boundaries are thin depleted zinc-oxide grain-boundary phases that break down. Organic or glassy coating and epoxy moulding complete the disc.
mb.discretes.varistor.note: ZnO itself comes from zinc concentrate or from the reduction of zinc oxide; that chain belongs in the metals tree. The MOV is in the PSU, not the logic mainboard.

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: 275 V AC, 14-20 mm disc

facts.label: Clamping
facts.value: ~710 V peak at rated current

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ~95-99% ZnO + glass + small dopants

places: China (the dominant ZnO supplier by the 1990s)

mb.discretes.varistor.zinc.name: Zinc oxide powder from zinc concentrate
mb.discretes.varistor.zinc.description: Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed at 900-1000 C to zinc oxide, then reduced with carbon in a shaft or electrothermic furnace at 900-1100 C to zinc metal, burned back to ZnO, and purified to high-purity ZnO for the varistor mix.

facts.label: Zinc content
facts.value: 50-60% in run-of-mine sphalerite

mb.discretes.led.name: Indicator LED (red/green/amber only)
mb.discretes.led.description: The C64's power indicator is a 3 mm or 5 mm epoxy-domed LED: a liquid-phase epitaxially grown GaP or GaAsP junction die, die-bonded into a reflector cup on the cathode post, wire bonded to the anode, and encapsulated in a semi-transparent epoxy lens that also acts as a light pipe. Red (GaAsP, ~660 nm) and green (GaP, ~555 nm) were common; amber (GaAsP ~590 nm) and the increasingly cheap GaP red were also in use. Blue LEDs did not exist in 1982 at any price - the first practical blue GaN/InGaN device was 1993, and an efficient one 1995.

facts.label: Colours available 1982
facts.value: red 660, amber 590, green 555 nm

facts.label: Blue LED
facts.value: did not exist commercially until 1993-1995

facts.label: Die
facts.value: 0.25-0.5 mm GaP or GaAsP junction

mb.discretes.led.substrate.name: GaP or GaAsP substrate wafer
mb.discretes.led.substrate.description: The LPE junction layers grow on a polished, Czochralski-grown substrate of n-type or semi-insulating GaAs, or on GaP grown by the same kind of pull used for silicon. GaAs itself is made by liquid-phase or VGF growth from a melt of gallium and arsenic, with the arsenic fed from a boiler of high-purity arsenic metal in hydrogen.
mb.discretes.led.substrate.note: GaAs substrate supply was treated as a strategic material in the 1980s; Japan, the USSR and the UK were the main sources.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: Czochralski from a Ga/As melt near 1250 C

facts.label: Arsenic feed
facts.value: 7N+ arsenic metal distilled in hydrogen

mb.discretes.led.gallium.name: Refined gallium
mb.discretes.led.gallium.description: Gallium refined from bauxite residue or from zinc residues by repeated ion-exchange in alkaline solution or by amalgam/hydroxide extraction, to 99.9-99.99% metal, then to GaP by reaction with high-purity phosphorus at 1000-1100 C in a sealed quartz ampoule.
mb.discretes.led.gallium.note: Gallium is almost entirely a byproduct of bauxite refining (and of zinc), not a primary ore - this is the same trace metal that makes gallium nitride LEDs possible today.

mb.discretes.led.epi.name: Liquid-phase epitaxy of the GaP junction
mb.discretes.led.epi.description: A GaP or GaAsP wafer is dipped in a molten, boron-doped Ga/GaP/P solution in a horizontal tilting boat inside a long quartz tube furnace at ~850-900 C. The substrate is swept through many alternating supersaturated melts so that dozens of GaP layers a few microns thick grow in, alternating p-type (Zn-doped) and n-type (S-doped) to form the double-heterostructure junction that makes the bright 1980s LED. The process is epitaxial in the strict sense - it is the same technique used for GaAs microwave chips.
mb.discretes.led.epi.note: Liquid-phase epitaxy is the documented route for the bright GaAsP/GaP junction of this period, and the double heterostructure came from it. Not established: the 850-900 C melt temperature, the boron-doped Ga/GaP/P charge, the alternating-supersaturation sweep, or the zinc and sulphur dopants as such. Gallium phosphide is documented as dissociating above about 900 C and being grown from a 1500 C melt, which does not match the temperature given here.

facts.label: Junction depth
facts.value: 2-5 um

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: quartz tube with tilting boat and zone pulls

mb.discretes.diodes.name: Rectifier, switching and zener diodes
mb.discretes.diodes.description: Three diode families with completely different construction. The 1N4001 is a diffused rectifier: an n- epitaxial layer on an n+ substrate with a heavily p-doped anode, rated 1 A / 50 V. The 1N4148 is a planar switching diode: a small npn with a Schottky-clamped base shorted to the cathode, rated 200 mA / 100 V, fast enough for 300 ns recovery. The 1N47xx is a zener: a heavily doped junction with a knee of 2.4-75 V, usually a diffused planar or, in the low-current versions, a temperature-compensated bandgap reference. All three were made by alloying or diffusing junctions into small silicon dice and moulding them in DO-35 glass or DO-41 plastic.
mb.discretes.diodes.note: The C64 parts list names a rectifier, a switching diode and two zeners on the board, with part numbers. Not established: the internal construction of each (diffused rectifying junction, planar switching junction with a Schottky-clamped base, bandgap-compensated zener) and the current and voltage ratings quoted here. Those are part numbers plus datasheets, and no datasheet is cited.

facts.label: 1N4001
facts.value: 1 A, 50 V; N diffusive rectifier

facts.label: 1N4148
facts.value: 200 mA, 100 V, ~4 ns; N planar switching

facts.label: 1N47xx
facts.value: zener, 2.4-75 V, 1 mA test current

mb.discretes.bjt-package.name: TO-92 epoxy mould package
mb.discretes.bjt-package.description: Discretes were diced, attached to the tab of a stamped lead frame, wire bonded or solder dipped, and transfer moulded in a black epoxy (a filled phenolic or epoxy compound loaded with carbon black for colour) with the leads formed to a 0.25 inch pitch. The 2N3904's die is under 1 square mm; the package volume is almost all mould compound.
mb.discretes.bjt-package.note: Not established: the carbon-black filler loading, the silica content, the mould mass, the cure schedule or the 0.25 in lead pitch as measured. That the discretes are epoxy-moulded through-hole parts on a solder-through board is supported by the C64 parts list, which names 2N4401, 2N3904, TIP29B and five 2N2222.

facts.label: Mould compound
facts.value: carbon-black-filled epoxy, 60-70% silica, ~0.1 g per TO-92, 150-180 C cure

mb.discretes.leadframe.name: Discrete lead frame, 0.25 inch pitch
mb.discretes.leadframe.description: A transistor's leads are a stamped 0.25-0.30 mm strip of nickel or copper alloy, plated with tin or tin-lead so they solder into a phenolic or epoxy-moulded phenolic board. The C64 mainboard is a solder-through board, so lead-frame plating was the difference between a working assembly and a cold joint.

mb.discretes.isolation.name: Isolation diffusion and its moat
mb.discretes.isolation.description: A boron diffusion deep enough to reach the subcollector creates a p-type tub around each transistor, isolating it from its neighbours through reverse-biased pn junctions rather than an oxide. The same oxide that covers the tub is later cut away in the base and emitter windows - this is the 'planar epitaxial' process invented at Fairchild in 1959 and still the standard discrete recipe in 1982.

mb.discretes.epi.name: Radiant-heated epitaxial reactor
mb.discretes.epi.description: After the n+ subcollector diffusion, a 1-3 um n-type epitaxial layer was grown in a radiant-heated vertical reactor: the wafers sat on a graphite susceptor inside a quartz bell jar, inductively heated to 1150-1250 C, with AsH3 or PH3 in H2 flowing over them. Epitaxy gave the collector the uniformity and the carrier concentration that a diffusion simply could not, which is what made the 2N3904's gain and its saturation voltage repeatable.
mb.discretes.epi.note: Not established: the reactor geometry (radiant-heated vertical, graphite susceptor in a quartz bell jar), the inductive coupling, the 1150-1250 C setpoint or the 1-3 um epitaxial thickness. Epitaxial growth of a doped layer on a crystalline seed is documented in general; the reactor description is not.

facts.label: Dopant
facts.value: arsine or phosphine in hydrogen

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 1-3 um

mb.discretes.bjt.name: Planar epitaxial small-signal BJT process
mb.discretes.bjt.description: The 2N3904, 2N3906 and 2N4124 are all the same architecture, differentiated by polarity and voltage rating: a p-type substrate, a heavily arsenic- or phosphorus-doped n+ subcollector, then a 1-3 um epitaxial n collector layer grown in an ATCP radiant-heated reactor at ~1150-1250 C with AsH3 or PH3 in H2. Isolation diffusions of boron create the tub, then the base (boron, ~0.5-1 um deep) and finally the emitter (arsenic or phosphorus, heavily overdoped to a low base resistance) through separate photolithography steps. Aluminium metallization is deposited by evaporation, alloyed at 400 C to make ohmic contacts, then the wafer is probed.
mb.discretes.bjt.note: Motorola registered the 2N3904/2N3906 in the mid-1960s as a pair, which is why almost every 1982 household electronics catalog lists them as Motorola parts even when another firm made them.

facts.label: Epi layer
facts.value: 1-3 um, arsenic or phosphorus doped

facts.label: Base
facts.value: boron diffusion, 0.5-1 um deep

facts.label: Emitter
facts.value: arsenic or phosphorus, ~97% of emitter area (GEOR)

facts.label: 2N3904 rating
facts.value: 40 V VCEO, 200 mA Ic, 625 mW Pd

facts.label: 2N3906 rating
facts.value: complementary PNP, 40 V, 200 mA, ~250 MHz fT

si.litho.name: Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop
si.litho.description: Every layer of every die is defined the same way. The wafer is coated on a spinner at 2000-5000 rpm to 1-3 um of positive photoresist, soft-baked at 90-100 C, aligned to the mask on a 1:1 contact or proximity aligner, exposed through the chrome plate at 30-50 mJ/cm2, spray-developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard-baked, stripped, and cleaned. Shipley AZ-1350 was the workhorse thin-film resist of the whole industry and the higher-solids AZ-1354 was used wherever the film had to stand up to a deep etch.
si.litho.note: The step order, the 1:1 contact and proximity print modes, the alkaline developer and the strip chemistry are documented. Not established: the spin speed and film thickness, the bake temperatures, the exposure dose, the AZ-1350 and AZ-1354 resist choices, the Shipley location and the broken-grid alignment scheme giving plus or minus 0.5 um.

facts.label: Soft bake
facts.value: 90-100 C; hard bake to 120 C

facts.label: Exposure
facts.value: mercury lamp, 30-50 mJ/cm2

facts.label: Developer
facts.value: 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide

facts.label: Resist
facts.value: AZ-1350 thin film, AZ-1354 for thick film

si.litho.aligner.name: Contact and proximity mask aligner
si.litho.aligner.description: A 1:1 mask aligner: mercury or xenon source, a 20x-100x binocular microscope, a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and either hard vacuum contact with the mask pressed straight down onto the resist, or a 100-500 um proximity gap. Typical 1982 units were the Coburn 2400, the Kasper 2400, the Universal Exposure Systems machines, and the Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2, whose 5x optical projection removed the "mask lifts off the wafer" failure mode that plagued pure contact printing. Mask work in the 1980s was often done on the same machines, by flashing an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster.
si.litho.aligner.note: Named machines are illustrative of the period rather than a documented inventory of the Norristown line. Reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire, later ASML) were arriving in 1982-83 and were the next generation, not this one.

facts.label: Overlay tolerance
facts.value: ~+-0.5 um with a broken-contact or grid-broken layer

facts.label: Typical machines
facts.value: Coburn 2400, Kasper 2400, Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2, UES

si.litho.spinner.name: Spin coater and hot-plate track
si.litho.spinner.description: A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer, followed by a convection hot plate or an infrared bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed at a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified nitrogen purge and amber-safe lighting.

mb.pla.name: U17 PLA 906114-01 (mask-programmed NMOS)
mb.pla.description: The C64's Programmable Logic Array at U17: it decodes the 6510's address lines and generates the chip-select and bank-switching strobes for every other chip on the board - RAM, ROMs, VIC-II, SID, CIAs, VIA, colour RAM - which makes it the single point of failure for the whole machine. Commodore part number 906114-01, alternate designation MOS 8700-001, die marked MOS 7700R1 / 8700R2. It is a mask-programmed NMOS clone of the Signetics 82S100 bipolar array, in a 28-pin 600 mil epoxy DIP, and it is by far the most failure-prone and most counterfeited part in the machine.
mb.pla.note: Correction to the brief: the part is a 28-pin DIP, not 14 or 16 pin. The 28-pin package is confirmed both by the 'C64 PLA Dissected' reverse-engineering report and by the MOS Technology products list. Also note that early C64s used a bipolar Signetics 82S100 (or Fairchild 93459 clone); the NMOS 906114-01 came later and became the standard part.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 28-pin, 600 mil wide DIP, usually plastic

facts.label: Function
facts.value: 16 inputs, 8 tri-state push-pull outputs, 1 output enable

facts.label: Programming
facts.value: MASK programmed at wafer stage - not user-programmable

facts.label: VOH
facts.value: ~3.7-3.8 V (vs 4.2 V for the bipolar Signetics 82S100)

facts.label: Die markings seen
facts.value: MOS 7700R1, MOS 8700R2, with date codes 2683, 2488, 4885

mb.pla.test.name: Probe, truth-table test and final test
mb.pla.test.description: A PLA is uniquely testable because its specification is a truth table rather than a waveform. On probe, a stored truth table is stepped through all 16 inputs x /OE combinations on all 8 outputs - a few thousand vectors - which catches a stuck link, a shorted link or a bad decoder in seconds. Assembled parts get the same vector set in a socket on an automatic tester, plus a timing check that the address decode settles inside a 6510 cycle.
mb.pla.test.note: Not established: the probe-card pin count, the vector count, the 3-6 week cycle, or that exhaustive truth-table testing was standard practice for mask-programmed PLDs. The device has 16 inputs and 8 outputs, so an exhaustive test is arithmetically small, but no source describes the test regime.

facts.label: Probe card
facts.value: 28 needles

facts.label: Test vector count
facts.value: ~65536 combinations for 16 inputs and /OE

mb.pla.failures.name: Why it fails more than anything else in the machine
mb.pla.failures.description: Three reasons stack up. First, it is a single point of failure: if any of its eight strobes misbehaves, the symptom is a dead or misbehaving machine rather than one dead chip. Second, its output enable and eight outputs switch hard on every 6510 cycle against the capacitive load of the whole board, so it is the highest-current part on the bus and the one that sees the worst ringing. Third, and decisively for longevity, it is the one chip that cannot be replaced: a dead 6510 can be bought new; a dead 906114-01 cannot, so in practice a dead PLA means a dead machine unless it is re-masked or emulated.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: 8 push-pull tri-state, switched every CPU cycle

facts.label: Replacement parts
facts.value: SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton, PLAtinum - all substitutes, none original

si.trim.name: Trim, form, mark and final electrical test
si.trim.description: After moulding the leads are formed on an 8-16 station trim-and-form press - trimmed, bent to the package pitch, flattened, and dipped in a tin or tin-lead solder pot - the body is marked with a dot-matrix ink printer or a Nd:YAG laser with part number, lot code and date code, and the part is dropped into a socket on an automatic tester and run against a final test program.

facts.label: Marking
facts.value: dot-matrix ink (most common in 1982) or Nd:YAG laser

facts.label: Test
facts.value: Teradyne or Fairchild automatic tester in a socket

facts.label: Forming
facts.value: 8-16 station press

si.mould.name: Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy
si.mould.description: The bonded frame sits in a multi-cavity transfer press and is encapsulated in silica-filled epoxy moulding compound. A typical cycle is 150-180 C at 700-1000 psi for one to three minutes per cavity, and plaques of flash at the parting line are trimmed off in a second press operation. The alternate route for hermetic parts is sintering an alumina ceramic shell at about 850-950 C with a glass frit seal - slower, more expensive, and used for military and aerospace grades.
si.mould.note: Transfer moulding with a pot and plunger forcing compound into a heated cavity is documented. Not established: the 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, 1-3 minute cycle, the post-mould bake, the flash-trimming second operation, or the 850-950 C glass-frit hermetic alternative.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: post-mould bake 175 C for 4-24 h

facts.label: Press
facts.value: 50-100 ton hydraulic, multi-cavity

si.mould.press.name: Hydraulic transfer moulding press
si.mould.press.description: A 50-100 ton multi-cavity transfer press with a heated upper platen, a pot and plunger that pre-form the compound pellet, and the encapsulated lead-frame strip in the cavity. Cycle: close the press, 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, one to three minutes dwell, then open and eject the encapsulated part still on its frame rail.
si.mould.press.note: The pot, plunger and heated cavity of a transfer press are documented. Not established: the 50-100 ton clamping force, the 150-180 C mould temperature, the 700-1000 psi pressure or the 1-3 minute dwell for this era.

si.bond.name: Gold wire wedge bonding
si.bond.description: A wire bonder pulls 25-30 um diameter gold wire from a spool through a ceramic capillary and welds it to the aluminium bond pads: a first wire from each pad out to the frame lead, then interconnect wires pad to pad for internal bussing. Gold is soft, so a wedge-shaped tool presses the wire flat rather than using the ultrasonic ball bond of aluminium bonding. A single 6510 carried about 60 wires, roughly 1.5 m of 25 um gold in total.
si.bond.note: Gold is a documented bond-wire material and wire diameters start below 10 um, which brackets 25 um. Not established: the wire count and length on a 6510, the palladium alloy content, the 0.3-1 m of gold per die, and the gold consumed per year at C64 volumes.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: 25 um Au, 0.5-1% Pd alloy, 99.99%

facts.label: Bonds
facts.value: ~40 pad-to-frame plus ~20 internal on a 6510

facts.label: Method
facts.value: wedge, ultrasonic or thermocompression

si.attach.name: Die attach to the lead frame
si.attach.description: The die is placed circuit-side-up on a pre-plated gold lead frame tab and swept through a die bonder. The hot-tool bond raises die and frame to about 400-450 C: gold and silicon melt together at 361 C and, on cooling, form a hard Au-Si eutectic weld roughly 25-50 um thick. That is both the mechanical bond and the die's low-resistance thermal path out to the frame. The diced dice are inspected under a stereomicroscope at 20-50x, and under dark-field illumination for particles, before they are attached: a chip on a pad costs the whole package.
si.attach.note: That the die is eutectic bonded to the frame is documented for high-power parts. Not established: the 361 C eutectic temperature, the 3.4 percent silicon content, the 400-450 C tool temperature, the silver-filled organic and conductive-epoxy alternatives, and the incoming-inspection magnification.

facts.label: Au-Si eutectic
facts.value: 361 C, 3.4% Si in Au

facts.label: Alternatives
facts.value: silver-filled epoxy, or glass frit in a ceramic package

facts.label: Incoming inspection
facts.value: 20-50x stereo plus dark-field

si.emc.name: Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound
si.emc.description: What actually seals a 1982 plastic IC. A thermosetting epoxy or phenolic compound of novolac resin plus 60-75% crushed quartz filler, a small amount of silicone release agent, catalyst and pigment, compounded on a two-roll mill under heat and then transfer moulded at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi for one to three minutes, with a post-mould bake at 175 C. A 6510 uses on the order of 0.3-0.5 g of it; a 4164 about 0.1-0.2 g.
si.emc.note: The same phenolic resin chemistry, in a different form, is the substrate of the C64's own printed circuit board, and the same ground silica filler is in the keyboard's phenolic boards.

facts.label: Filler
facts.value: 60-75 wt% ground silica, 0.5-3 um

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, 1-3 min; post-mould bake 175 C for 4-24 h

facts.label: Mass per part
facts.value: ~0.1-0.5 g depending on package size

si.emc.silica.name: Crushed quartz filler from quartz sand
si.emc.silica.description: The single largest mass ingredient in any plastic package: 60-75% by weight of angular fused or ground silica of 0.5-3 um mean size, made by firing and grinding high-purity quartz. It is there to control the shrinkage coefficient and the thermal expansion, and it is why a decapsulated die sits in a white ceramic-looking blob.
si.emc.silica.note: Not established: that silica is 60-75 percent by weight of a 1982 moulding compound, the 0.5-3 um mean particle size, or the shrinkage and expansion-control rationale. The filler fraction is a supplier formulation figure and is not in any source available.

facts.label: Filler fraction
facts.value: 60-75 wt% of the compound

facts.label: Mean particle size
facts.value: 0.5-3 um, angular

si.emc.resin.name: Epoxy novolac resin from phenol and epichlorohydrin
si.emc.resin.description: Phenol and formaldehyde condensed under acid to a novolac resin, which is then reacted with epichlorohydrin and caustic soda to give the epoxy novolac that forms the backbone of the moulding compound. Phenol itself came from cumene-process oxidation of benzene - overwhelmingly a coal-tar derivative in 1982 - or from chlorobenzene hydrolysis.

si.leadframe.name: Stamped DIP lead frame
si.leadframe.description: The die and its leads emerge from a stamped, plated strip. Frames were made from FeNi 42/58 (C4-29) alloy 0.15-0.20 mm thick by progressive die stamping on a 400-800 ton press, then plated - a nickel strike and gold for hermetic parts, or a matte tin or tin-lead plate over nickel for plastic parts. The strip is indexed on a 0.3 inch tape through the bonder and the moulder, and a 40-pin DIP cavity set produces dozens of packaged parts per moulding cycle.

facts.label: Strip
facts.value: 0.15-0.20 mm FeNi 42/58 (C4-29) or copper alloy

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 0.6 inch (15.24 mm) dual row on DIPs; 0.25 inch on TO-92

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: Au over Ni for ceramic; Sn or SnPb over Ni for plastic

facts.label: Indexing
facts.value: 0.3 inch carrier tape

si.leadframe.plating.name: Nickel strike and gold or tin plating of the lead frame
si.leadframe.plating.description: A nickel strike first, because gold will not adhere directly to the iron-nickel alloy and the leads have to solder. Hermetic parts get a heavier gold plate over the nickel; plastic parts get tin or tin-lead over the nickel so the leads solder into the machine's sockets. The bonding tab is always gold-plated, because the die is eutectic-bonded to it.
si.leadframe.plating.note: Not established: the nickel strike, the gold plating of the bonding tab, or the tin and tin-lead plate over nickel for plastic packages. The lead-frame article documents the base alloy (copper, copper alloy or iron-nickel such as alloy 42) and stamping or etching, but not the plating sequence or its thicknesses.

si.leadframe.alloy.name: FeNi 42/58 lead frame alloy strip
si.leadframe.alloy.description: The standard low-CTE frame alloy: 42% nickel, 58% iron, with a coefficient of thermal expansion close to that of the die, so the bond survives temperature cycling. Melted in a vacuum induction furnace, cast, hot-rolled, then cold-rolled and annealed to 0.15-0.20 mm. Copper alloy C194 with 2.3% lead, and nickel itself, were the alternatives.
si.leadframe.alloy.note: Melted in a vacuum induction furnace, cast, hot-rolled, then cold-rolled and annealed. In 1982 the nickel in it came overwhelmingly from sulphide concentrates - Sudbury in Ontario, the Norilsk-Talnakh massif and the Philippines - won either by the Mond carbonyl loop or by high-pressure acid leach of laterite, then electrolytically refined. The low-carbon steel half came from hematite ore, coke and limestone.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: FeNi 42/58 (C4-29); alternatives Cu C194 with 2.3% Pb, or nickel

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.15-0.20 mm after cold rolling and annealing

places: specialty alloy strip mills, US and Japan

si.package.28.name: 28-pin 600 mil DIP package
si.package.28.description: A wide-body package, because the PLA needs 16 inputs, 8 outputs, an output enable, the unused FE/NE pin, VCC and VSS. Die attach is a gold-silicon eutectic bond on a gold-plated tab, about 28 pad bonds on a 25 um gold wedge bonder, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy, with the leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch in a 28-socket trim-and-form operation. A ceramic variant exists but is uncommon on a C64.

facts.label: Body width
facts.value: 600 mil, 0.6 inch row to row, 28 leads

facts.label: Wires
facts.value: ~28 pad bonds, 25 um Au

facts.label: Ceramic variant
facts.value: exists but uncommon on a C64

mb.pla.economics.name: The economics of one custom mask set
mb.pla.economics.description: The 906114-01 encodes the entire C64 memory map in a die smaller than the fingertip, and Commodore sold millions of C64s, so once the mask was paid for the part was dirt cheap per unit. But the flip side is that the function exists nowhere else in the world. Any machine needing a different bank-switch map needs a different mask, a different lot and a different lead time - which is why C64Cs needed a different PLA (MOS 8721) to support the cartridge port's new banking. It is also why the cost of a single counterfeit or of a dead original is disproportionate to the value of the silicon inside it.
mb.pla.economics.note: No published figure was found for the specific dollar cost of a mask set in 1982; period sources put a full 8-10 level NMOS mask set in the low tens of thousands of dollars, with mask plates alone a few hundred to a couple of thousand per level.

facts.label: NRE
facts.value: artwork + mask set + verification, once per function

facts.label: Unit cost
facts.value: trivial once masked - the die is tiny and needs no exotic process

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: single-sourced, no drop-in replacement, counterfeiting pressure

mb.pla.provenance.name: Reverse-engineered from a Signetics 82S100
mb.pla.provenance.description: Early C64s shipped with a bipolar Signetics 82S100, or the Fairchild 93459 clone of it; Signetics was acquired by Philips, which renamed the part PLS100. Commodore's engineers then decapped the bipolar part, photographed it with a Polaroid camera and rebuilt the function as a mask-programmed NMOS design - Bil Herd's recollection is 'We reverse engineered the PLA from Signetics using a polaroid camera'. The resulting die is marked MOS 7700R1 or 8700R2, and it runs at a slightly lower VOH than the bipolar original (about 3.7-3.8 V against 4.2 V), which is part of why early and late C64s behave marginally differently.

facts.label: Original
facts.value: Signetics 82S100 / Philips PLS100 (bipolar, 1975)

facts.label: Clone
facts.value: Fairchild 93459 (bipolar)

facts.label: Commodore version
facts.value: 906114-01, NMOS, mask programmed

mb.pla.vs-pal.name: PLA versus PAL: why the name misleads
mb.pla.vs-pal.description: The C64's part is called a PLA, but the parts most readers know by that name - the 16L8, 16R8, 20L8 - are PALs, and the two are not interchangeable in sourcing or programming. A PAL is a generic catalogue device: every 16L8 from every vendor is the same silicon, and the buyer programs it. A mask-programmed PLA is a custom device: the buyer cannot program it, and nobody else ever made this function. That is the whole reason fakes are so common - the SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton and PLAtinum parts sold as replacements are typically GAL/EPROM emulations or freshly mask-programmed parts from a third party, and the C64's PLA is precisely the component where a substitute can fail in ways that are hard to trace.
mb.pla.vs-pal.note: Also worth knowing: the 906114 family covered several Commodore machines - 906114-01 for the C64, 906114-04 for the B256, and MOS 8721 (315012-01, 48-pin) elsewhere - but each is a different custom mask.

facts.label: PAL 16L8
facts.value: 10 inputs x 8 registered outputs, 64 x 32 fuse AND array, fusible, generic

facts.label: GAL 16V8
facts.value: fuse-programmed, EEPROM fuse link, generic catalogue part
mask programmed, one-off function, no equivalent catalogue part

mb.pla.alternatives.name: Fusible-link and antifuse PLAs
mb.pla.alternatives.description: The two field-programmable routes a PLD could have taken instead, and the reason a mask-programmed part is a different commercial animal. A fusible link is a real wire of chromium or nichrome, 1-3 um thick, burned out by a laser programmer through the package's FE/NE pin - this is how the PAL 16L8 and 20L8 worked, and why a PAL is a catalogue part you can buy in thousands of functions. An antifuse starts as a conducting amorphous-silicon or silicon-dioxide film which a 20-40 V pulse converts into high-resistance insulation; it needs no laser but was slower to program and harder to test. Commodore could use neither for a part sold in the millions at commodity logic prices.
mb.pla.alternatives.note: The 82S100 that gave the C64 PLA its name was originally marketed as a field-programmable bipolar array of this kind. Whether early C64 82S100 parts arrived pre-programmed from Signetics or were programmed in-house is not established.

facts.label: Fusible link
facts.value: chromium or nichrome film 1-3 um thick; seconds to program

facts.label: Antifuse
facts.value: amorphous silicon or SiO2 film blown open by a ~20-40 V pulse

facts.label: Mask route
facts.value: 3-6 week cycle from artwork to tested parts; minimum order one wafer run

mb.pla.mask-programming.name: Mask programming of the link pattern
mb.pla.mask-programming.description: This is the practical heart of a mask-programmed PLA. The AND array, the OR array and the decoders are all routine NMOS layers, but the pattern of which links exist is frozen into a single additional mask level - drawn as one extra colour plane in the layout database and cut like any other plate. That one extra mask is what makes each unique logic function expensive: artwork generation, mask fabrication and inspection all have to be repeated, and the wafer run cannot be short because the lot must be big enough to be worth the NRE. The whole array is physically small, so a 4-inch wafer holds many thousands of dies - the constraint on order size is mask and engineering cost, not silicon.
mb.pla.mask-programming.note: This is the mechanical reason the 906114-01 is unreplaceable in practice: there is no second source, no substitute function, and no way to change the logic without new silicon.

facts.label: Extra mask levels
facts.value: 1 (the link/contact pattern)

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 3-6 weeks artwork to tested parts

facts.label: Die per 4-inch wafer
facts.value: several thousand

facts.label: Revisions
facts.value: each logic change costs a whole new mask set

facts.label: Programming step
facts.value: none: every 906114-01 off the line is already a C64 address decoder

facts.label: Where the cost sits
facts.value: non-recurring engineering, paid once per unique logic function

mb.pla.process.name: NMOS process for the 906114-01 (node not claimed)
mb.pla.process.description: The device-level facts are solid: it is NMOS, mask programmed, made at Norristown, and running a lower VOH than the bipolar original. The process details are not published anywhere. On the evidence of die markings, the era and the same fab, it is almost certainly the house silicon-gate NMOS flow used for the 6510, 6522 and 6526 - n+ diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, LPCVD polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, one aluminium layer, PSG or nitride passivation - run at whatever line width that flow was at the time. No specific figure is asserted for that line width, because no source states one for this part.
mb.pla.process.note: Explicitly low confidence and deliberately vague. The 906114-01's internal process has never been documented; inferring it from the rest of the CSG part family is an assumption, not a fact. What is not in doubt is the programming mechanism, which is the point of this branch.

facts.label: Technology
facts.value: N-channel silicon gate, mask programmed

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: aluminium; no barrier metal in this period

facts.label: Line width
facts.value: NOT ESTABLISHED - see note

mb.pla.array.name: What a PLA physically is
mb.pla.array.description: Two arrays of transistors and a set of 'links'. The fixed AND array is a matrix of diode or transistor junctions arranged so that each row implements one product term - every possible AND of a subset of the 16 inputs. The programmable OR array adds up to eight of those product terms per output. Each product-term-to-output connection is a physical link in that array, and 'programming' the part simply means deciding which links exist. Commodore's version is pure combinational logic with no registered terms, which is why it is fast enough to sit directly on the 6510's address bus and settle inside a 6510 cycle.
mb.pla.array.note: The 'FE/NE' pin on this package is used for programming field-programmable variants of the device and is left unconnected internally in the mask-programmed 906114-01 - a detail decapping shows.

facts.label: AND array
facts.value: fixed, generates the product terms

facts.label: OR array
facts.value: 8 outputs, each an OR of product terms

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: 16, of the 6510's address and control lines

facts.label: Output enable
facts.value: /OE tri-states the eight push-pull outputs

mb.ppi.name: 6522 PPI/VIA, 40-pin DIP
mb.ppi.description: The 6522 Versatile Interface Adapter at U15 on the C64 mainboard: two 8-bit parallel ports (the user port at $D420 and the cassette port at $D800), two 1-bit handshake lines, an 8-bit shift register for the cassette serial interface, two 16-bit timers with pulse output, four interrupt inputs and an I/O port with three latched control bits. It is the same 40-pin DIP silicon-gate NMOS part as the CIAs, from the same mask-family era and almost certainly the same process.
mb.ppi.note: MOS listed the 6522 as 'VIA' (Versatile Interface Adapter); 'PPI' is Fairchild's name for the same architectural family (the 6820/6821) and is what Commodore's own documentation often called it.

facts.label: Part
facts.value: 6522 (6520 is the older, incompatible PIA)

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 40-pin DIP, 0.6 inch pitch

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, single aluminium

mb.ppi.test.name: Wafer probe and final test of the 6522
mb.ppi.test.description: Probe with a 40-needle card: both 16-bit timers clocked against a reference, the shift register stepped, both ports and the handshake lines cycled, and the interrupt inputs verified. Assembled parts repeat the program in a socket on the automatic tester, then go into the C64's machined-pin socket.

facts.label: Probe card
facts.value: 40 needles
