si.probe-card.name: Probe card: gold-plated needles on a printed board
si.probe-card.description: Before dicing, every die is probed on the wafer through a probe card: a fibreglass or ceramic substrate with a pattern of gold-plated tungsten or rhenium needles on 0.1 inch centres, hanging on a probe ring over the die and stepping down with a few grams of force. In 1982 cards were hand-drilled or photofabricated; automatic stepping probe stations were still a novelty at these pad counts.
si.probe-card.note: That die are tested on the wafer before dicing, with binning, by automatic test equipment is documented. Not established: the needle material (tungsten or rhenium), the 0.1 inch needle pitch, the contact force, or that cards were hand-drilled or photofabricated in 1982.

facts.label: Needle pitch
facts.value: 0.1 inch (2.54 mm)

facts.label: Needles
facts.value: 8 to 40, one per bond pad

facts.label: Material
facts.value: tungsten or rhenium, gold-plated

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: hand-drilled or photofabricated, 1982

si.package.40.name: 40-pin plastic DIP package
si.package.40.description: The package the 6510 CPU, the 8562 VIC-II and the 6526 CIA shipped in on the C64 mainboard: a 0.6 inch pitch, 40-leaded stamped lead frame with the die eutectic-bonded on its tab, gold wire to the pads, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy. A ceramic hermetic version existed for industrial and military customers. The 6581 SID is not in this package: it shipped in a 28-pin DIP, and the service manual's parts list carries 16-pin, 28-pin and 40-pin IC sockets for the board.
si.package.40.note: Corrected. The 6526 CIA and the VIC-II are documented as 40-pin parts, and the 6510 is a 40-pin part on the C64 board. The 6581 SID is not: its pinout ends at pin 28, with the filter capacitors on 26 and 27 and Vdd on 28, so it shipped in a 28-pin package. The service manual names no VIA on this board, so the 6522 has been dropped from the list rather than reclassified. What remains unestablished is the die-attach method, the wire diameter and count, and the moulding-compound figures.

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 0.6 inch (15.24 mm), dual row

facts.label: Body width
facts.value: 0.6 inch across the row

facts.label: Compound
facts.value: 60-75 wt% ground silica filled epoxy, ~0.3-0.5 g

facts.label: Marking
facts.value: dot-matrix ink with part number and date code

facts.label: Wires
facts.value: 25 um Au; ~40 pad bonds plus internal bussing

facts.label: Ceramic variant
facts.value: exists, for hermetic grades

si.package.ceramic.name: Hermetic ceramic DIP sintering
si.package.ceramic.description: For hermetic parts the die went into a 96% alumina ceramic shell, sealed with a devitrifying glass frit in a belt furnace at about 850-950 C, and the metal flange was brazed or glass-sealed to the header. Ceramic was slower and costlier than plastic and was used for military and industrial grades - but MOS shipped ceramic 40-pin parts of this kind, which is where the collectors' market for them comes from.
si.package.ceramic.note: Dense alpha-alumina is the documented ceramic-package material. Not established: the 96 percent purity figure, the devitrifying glass-frit seal, the 850-950 C belt-furnace sintering, and that MOS shipped ceramic 40-pin parts of this kind.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: 96% Al2O3 ceramic

facts.label: Seal
facts.value: devitrifying glass frit at 850-950 C

si.package.ceramic.shell.name: Alumina ceramic DIP shell
si.package.ceramic.shell.description: A 96% alumina header: alumina powder pressed and sintered into a gas-tight body with a metallised cavity floor for the die, a glass-frit seal ring, and a flange carrying the frame leads. Alumina powder comes from bauxite, and that chain lives in the metals and packaging trees.
si.package.ceramic.shell.note: Not established: the 96 percent alumina composition, the pressed-and-sintered route, the metallised cavity floor, the glass-frit seal ring or the flange carrying the leads. Alumina from bauxite is documented, but the header construction is not.

mb.ppi.mask.name: 6522 photomask set
mb.ppi.mask.description: Nine or ten levels - n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad and alignment - printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner from chrome-on-glass plates with grid-broken alignment. As with the CIAs, the process is the CSG standard flow; only the layout differs.

facts.label: Reticle
facts.value: 1:1 chrome on glass

si.mask.plate.name: Chrome-on-glass photomask plate
si.mask.plate.description: The physical plate a 1982 fab printed from: 5x7 inch of 1 mm soda-lime glass or fused quartz, coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, then exposed and developed in positive photoresist, the exposed chrome etched away in hot perchloric or sulfuric-perchromate acid, washed, inspected on a Zeiss comparison tool against the design database, and defect-repaired with a fine gallium or indium needle. Chromium was the universal absorber from the 1960s onward because of its opacity in the deep UV and its resistance to wet cleaning.

facts.label: Transmission
facts.value: 5-8% through 100 nm Cr

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: 1 mm soda-lime glass (cheap) or fused quartz (durable), 5x7 inch

mb.ppi.userport.name: Parallel ports and handshake lines
mb.ppi.userport.description: The 6522's parallel ports are the C64's only general-purpose parallel I/O, and they appear on the 12-way cartridge edge as the user port for printers, samplers and third-party cartridges, and on the mainboard as the cassette port. The user port carries one 8-bit port, not two: on the cartridge edge it presents PB0-PB7 together with PA2 alone. CIA 2 sits at $DD00, and the lines are open collector with internal pull-ups rather than quasi-bidirectional TTL, so driving them from two cards at once was a hardware error rather than a negotiated one.
mb.ppi.userport.note: Three claims here are wrong. The user port is an 8-bit port, not two: on the 12-way cartridge edge it carries PB0-PB7 on pins C,D,E,F,H,J,K,L plus PA2 on pin M, so PA is only partly present. CIA 2 is at $DD00-$DD0F, not $D800-D80F; $D800 is the colour RAM. And the CIA lines are described as open collector with internal pull-ups, not quasi-bidirectional TTL. Which 6522 pins carry the quasi-bidirectional ports is a datasheet question this node does not answer.

facts.label: Ports
facts.value: user port: 1 x 8-bit (PB0-PB7 plus PA2); lines open collector with internal pull-ups

facts.label: Register
facts.value: CIA 1 at $DC00, CIA 2 at $DD00; $D800 is colour RAM

si.front-end.name: NMOS silicon-gate front end
si.front-end.description: The flow every simple logic part in the machine ran: n+ source and drain pre-diffusion, LOCOS field oxide grown in dry O2 and then wet H2/O2 at about 1000-1050 C, LPCVD polysilicon gate from silane at 800-850 C, a self-aligned arsenic source/drain implant with a 1000-1100 C anneal, contact cuts, 1-2 um aluminium sputtered with 0.5-1% silicon and etched in hot phosphoric acid, then PSG and nitride passivation. Ten mask levels, printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner. The 6510 branch under the CPU carries the layer-by-layer version with every temperature; this node is the same flow stated once for the parts that did not need the detail.
si.front-end.note: Difference from today: no refractory barrier metal, no tungsten plug, no CMP-defined metal lines and a single aluminium layer. A static RAM such as the 2114L could run a coarser and older process than the 6510 - there is no tight-pitch sense-amplifier chain to shrink - which is why nothing published states a line width for it.

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: LOCOS, 6000-8000 A field oxide

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: 1-2 um aluminium, single layer, no barrier

facts.label: Lithography
facts.value: 1:1 contact or Micralign proximity, AZ-1350

mb.cia.name: Two 6526 CIA complex interface adapters
mb.cia.description: CIA 1 at U17 and CIA 2 at U18 (PLA at U17 on some board revisions) provide the C64's two 8-bit parallel ports, the keyboard/joystick matrix scanning, the two 16-bit interval timers with one-shot/underflow interrupt, the shift register used for the serial (IEC) bus, and TOD (time-of-day) clocking derived from AC mains. Each 6526 is a 40-pin DIP NMOS part; CIA 1 sits at $D400 and reads port A from the VIC colour register file, while CIA 2 sits at $DC00 and drives the user port and serial bus.
mb.cia.note: TOD accuracy is entirely set by the frequency of the AC mains and by a capacitor across the TOD pin on the mainboard; Commodore trimmed that capacitor at final test, which is the documented origin of the famous 'not backward compatible' TOD behaviour.

facts.label: Part
facts.value: 6526 (8520/8521 are the later Amiga/C128 parts)

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 40-pin DIP, 0.6 inch pitch

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, single aluminium

facts.label: Registers
facts.value: 16, at $D400-$D40F and $DC00-$DC0F

facts.label: Peripherals
facts.value: 2 x 8-bit ports, 2 x 16-bit timers, serial shift register, TOD clock

mb.cia.test.name: Wafer probe and final test of the 6526
mb.cia.test.description: Probe with a 40-needle card and a program that clocks both 16-bit timers against a reference, steps the serial shift register through a byte, checks the interrupt priority logic and the port handshake, and measures the TOD chain. Assembled parts repeat it in a socket. Because the TOD is clocked from the AC line, the accuracy test needed a calibrated frequency standard, not just a functional pass.

facts.label: Probe card
facts.value: 40 needles

facts.label: Notable check
facts.value: TOD counter accuracy against a frequency standard

mb.cia.mask.name: CIA photomask set
mb.cia.mask.description: Nine or ten levels - n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad and alignment levels - printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner from chrome-on-glass plates, using the grid-broken alignment scheme with dummy structures and stepper/diffusion checks. The two CIAs and the VIA were almost certainly the same process with three different mask sets.

facts.label: Shared process
facts.value: same flows as 6510, 6522, 8562; only the masks differ

mb.cia.serial.name: Serial shift register
mb.cia.serial.description: The CIA's 8-bit shift register is what makes the Commodore serial bus work at all. Software sets a bit, shifts it out under CIA timer control with the handshake lines driving the ATN and CLK/CB lines, and reads bits back the same way; the VIC-II's serial output is decoded separately. This is a purely digital function built from ordinary NMOS flip-flops, but its timing jitter is the reason the KERNAL's serial routines are as delicate as they are.

facts.label: Bus
facts.value: IEC/serial, 1 bit per handshake, no level shifting on the C64

facts.label: Registers
facts.value: CIA 2 at $DC00 drives the bus; CIA 1's SR is spare

mb.cia.tod.name: Time-of-day clock
mb.cia.tod.description: The CIA's time-of-day clock is a 17-bit counter clocked from the serial pin, which the C64 mainboard drives from one side of the AC line through a 470 kohm resistor. The resulting clock is therefore a divided version of the mains frequency, trimmed per unit at final test by selecting a film capacitor. The timer counters themselves are static CMOS-style ripple counters, so they hold their count with the clock stopped - which is why a dead battery or a flat mains filter freezes the clock.

facts.label: Counter
facts.value: 17 bits (14 h x 60 min x 60 s + tenths/AM-PM)

facts.label: Reference
facts.value: AC mains via a high-value resistor

mb.sid.name: 6581 SID sound chip, 40-pin DIP
mb.sid.description: The C64's sound generator at U18: three analogue subtractive-synthesis voices (two oscillators plus a noise source through a 12-bit DAC, one extra-noise-only channel for percussion), a ring modulator, a resonant multimode filter with a self-oscillating VCA, external-to-internal feedback volume routing, two pulse-width modulators and a hard sync. It is an NMOS hybrid - digital logic and poly counters driving an analogue poly on the same die - which is why it is noisy, why R4, R4AR, R5 and R6 differ, and why a 8580 (made on a newer process) sounds cleaner.
mb.sid.note: The 8580 R4 (1984) and R5/R6 (early 1990s) were moved to a later, larger NMOS process and are visually much bigger dies; the C64 shipped with 6581s until the C64C. The SID's analogue section is why the machine needs the 4066 quad bilateral switch and the 7406 inverter to stabilise it.

facts.label: Part
facts.value: 6581 (R4, R4AR, R5, R6 in C64 mainboards)

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 40-pin DIP

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS hybrid, silicon gate, single aluminium; ~4 um era

facts.label: Analog
facts.value: 12-bit DAC per voice, filter and VCA, external-to-internal feedback

mb.sid.revisions.name: SID revisions as an analogue-process story
mb.sid.revisions.description: The 6581 shipped in an unsuffixed NMOS form from 1982, then as R3, R4 and R4AR between 1985 and 1987. Later parts changed the analogue behaviour - supply voltage on pin 28 and the value of the four filter capacitors - but the familiar account of each revision being a discrete change to the analogue block found by listening to parts on probe is not established here. The 8580 arrived in 1987 as an R5, built on an HMOS-II process rather than a later NMOS one, with 9 V on pin 28 and 22 nF filter capacitors in place of the 6581's 470 pF; it is generally regarded as the cleaner and quieter part.
mb.sid.revisions.note: Contradicted by the source. The 6581 shipped from week 21 of 1982 with no revision suffix; R3 runs from week 42 of 1985, R4 from week 16 of 1986 and R4AR from week 22 of 1986. So a 1982 part is not an R4. The 8580 is listed as R5 from June 1987 to 1992, an HMOS-II part, not as R4 in 1984. Not established: that each revision was an analogue-block change discovered on probe, that the 8580 had a redesigned analogue section and a much larger die, or the year the R6 appeared.

facts.label: 8580 revisions
facts.value: R5 from June 1987 to 1992; HMOS-II, 9 V on pin 28, 22 nF filter capacitors

mb.sid.test.name: Wafer probe and audio test of the 6581
mb.sid.test.description: Probe testing a SID meant electrical tests (register access, oscillator counters, envelope thresholds, DAC linearity, filter self-oscillation) plus, on the better lines, a functional audio test: a short score stepped through the chip and the output listened to or measured on a spectrum analyser. Final test repeated it in a socket. This is why 6581 revisions are dated and marked (R4, R4AR, R5, R6) - each was a measured change to the analogue thresholds. The threshold voltages of the envelope generators and the VCA had to be trended, because the whole reason the 8580 sounds different is that its analogue section was redesigned and its thresholds tightened.

facts.label: Probe card
facts.value: 40 needles

mb.sid.mask.name: SID photomask set
mb.sid.mask.description: Nine or ten levels for the 6581: n+ field, LOCOS active area, base/well, contact, polysilicon (including the poly resistor pattern that is the DAC), second diffusion, metal, passivation pad, plus alignment. Printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner from 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plates, with the grid-broken alignment scheme. The analogue poly resistor pattern was itself a mask level, and trimming it by laser was an option some makers used.

facts.label: Extra level
facts.value: poly resistor / DAC pattern

mb.sid.external.name: External components the SID needs from the board
mb.sid.external.description: The 6581 does not make sound by itself. The C64 mainboard provides the 14.31818 MHz colour clock, which is the frequency of crystal Y1 itself rather than a divided or multiplied derivative, two 4066 CMOS bilateral switches and a 7406 hex inverter to control filter routing and to stabilize the output (a documented MOS workaround that varies with chip revision), the 470 ohm/1 kohm output network, and the 4066-switched external-to-internal feedback path. Those are separate parts in the board and interconnect trees.
mb.sid.external.note: The 'chip-dependent' volume crackle and distortion of the 6581 was a consequence of this external network plus the internal filter threshold, which is why later revisions changed the on-board values.

mb.sid.process.name: NMOS hybrid process: digital counters on an analogue poly
mb.sid.process.description: The 6581 was not a purely digital NMOS part. Its 24-bit phase accumulators, the noise LFSR and the envelope generators are ordinary silicon-gate NMOS with depletion loads, the same technology as the 6510. Its DACs, the filter and the VCA are analogue: long polysilicon resistors laid down in the same polysilicon deposition, a large-area common-emitter output transistor, and a big p-diffused 'pump' resistor in the VCA. All of it in one 2-4 um process with a single aluminium layer, and with the analogue section laid out shielded inside its own p-epitaxial tub.
mb.sid.process.note: The poly-resistor DAC and the tub isolation are standard period NMOS-analogue practice (Hitachi, Toshiba, Signetics used exactly this) but the internal details of the Norristown 6580/6581 are not public.

facts.label: Poly resistors
facts.value: ~100 kohm to 1 Mohm, undoped polysilicon

facts.label: DAC
facts.value: R-2R style, built from polysilicon resistors and n+ lands

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: p-type epitaxial tub around the analogue block

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: single aluminium layer, 1-2 um

mb.sid.poly-res.name: Polysilicon load resistors
mb.sid.poly-res.description: The 6510 and the SID both use undoped or lightly doped deposited polysilicon as a resistor, deposited in the same LPCVD silane step as the gate and left unetched between two aluminium contacts. Sheet resistance was 30-100 ohm/sq in 1982 and the resistance was trimmed, if at all, by laser or by anodising the surface - the 'thin-film resistor' trimming industry existed for exactly this.
mb.sid.poly-res.note: Silicon-barrier anodes, nitride barriers and copper lines did not exist; a 1982 IC resistor could drift several hundred ppm per year with humidity.

facts.label: Sheet resistance
facts.value: 30-100 ohm/sq (undoped poly)

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: ~+0.1 to +0.3 %/C - poor by modern thin-film standards

mb.vic.name: 8562 VIC-II video chip, 40-pin DIP
mb.vic.description: The C64's video, colour and sprite chip at U19, in a 40-pin DIP. The 8562 is the C64-specific part number for the NTSC VIC-II (the 6567/6569 are the Max Machine / PAL parts); it is an NMOS silicon-gate chip of the same generation as the 6510. The die contains the 40x25 text/bitmap video matrix, the 8 sprite (hardware sprite/clogger) engine, the colour-latch RAM interface, the 6-bit DAC colour outputs, the interrupt and border logic, the ~18 colour PAL palette resistors, and the 5-bit VIC-II colour registers. It reads VIC bank colour RAM through 8 pins and does no pixel-to-PAL conversion itself.
mb.vic.note: The 8562 designation and the 'C64 is a 6567/6569' claim on early Rev 6 prototype boards are both documented; production breadbin machines carry 8562. The VIC-II in the C64 is a 2 um-class NMOS part but the die is larger and more complex than the 6510.

facts.label: Part
facts.value: 8562 (NTSC C64); 6569-series in PAL lots

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 40-pin DIP, 0.6 inch pitch

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, single aluminium

facts.label: DAC
facts.value: 4-bit wide, 6 bits (64 levels) per RGB channel, external resistors

mb.vic.test.name: Wafer probe and pattern test of the 8562
mb.vic.test.description: The VIC-II is probed with a 40-needle card and a test program that exercises the character generator, the sprite pointers, the colour registers and the interrupt logic - and, on the analogue side, checks that all six colour outputs swing the full 0-5 V and that the 18-bit colour latches all decode. Assembled parts run the same program in a socket, often while a technician watched a test pattern on a monitor plugged into the tester's video output.

facts.label: Probe card
facts.value: 40 needles, 0.1 inch pitch

facts.label: Die size
facts.value: large relative to a 6510, so yield-sensitive

mb.vic.mask.name: VIC-II photomask set
mb.vic.mask.description: The 8562's mask set was nine or ten levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, second diffusion, metal, ROM-programming (none here), passivation pad and the alignment/test levels. A 1982 small fab of this sort typically printed 1:1 on a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner with AZ-1350, using 1 mm chrome-on-glass plates about 5x7 inch. Overlay was held to +-0.5 um by a deliberate 'grid-broken' mask design: the layout broke the grid lines over active regions and added dummy structures so the stepper could align on a broken main grid rather than a continuous one.
mb.vic.mask.note: The grid-broken scheme and the automatic stepper alignment marks are standard 1980s practice; whether Norristown used a stepper at all for this part is not documented.

facts.label: Mask
facts.value: 1:1 chrome on glass, 5x7 inch

facts.label: Alignment scheme
facts.value: grid-broken plus dummy diffusion/OPL checks

mb.vic.palette.name: The VIC-II colour output network on the mainboard
mb.vic.palette.description: The VIC-II does not name colours; it emits a set of analogue colour levels that circuitry on the mainboard has to turn into a usable video signal, and that circuitry is the physical interface between this die and a television. The specific network is not settled by the documents read: the 1992 service manual's 326298 parts list carries a 74LS373 octal latch at U26 together with resistor packs, and no resistor ladder or 74LS175 appears in that manual, in either Anatomy volume, or in the C128 Internals text.
mb.vic.palette.note: Not established by anything read: an 18-resistor, 2 x 9 palette network, its values, the 1 k-10 k binary weighting, or a 74LS175 shift register forming the palette. No palette resistor ladder or 74LS175 appears in the 1992 service manual parts list or circuit theory, in either Anatomy book, or in the C128 Internals text. The 326298 board instead carries a 74LS373 at U26 and a 3.3 k resistor pack. The VIC-II side of the claim - that it emits weighted analogue voltages and knows nothing of colour names - is not documented either.

facts.label: Count
facts.value: not established; the 326298 parts list shows resistor packs, not a 2 x 9 ladder

facts.label: Values
facts.value: not established; the parts list names 330 ohm and 3.3 kohm packs

mb.vic.process.name: NMOS front end for a large analog-plus-logic die
mb.vic.process.description: The same silicon-gate NMOS sequence as the CPU, with extra care because the VIC-II mixes digital logic, a 6-bit DAC and analogue comparators on one die: 2 um minimum feature, ~400 A poly-oxide, LOCOS field oxide, self-aligned n+ source/drain, single 1-2 um aluminium layer, PSG plus plasma nitride passivation. The colour DAC outputs were open-source n-channel pull-downs that the external resistor ladder on the mainboard pulled up to +5 V.
mb.vic.process.note: Exact die size and mask count for the 8562 are not published; 50-60 mm2 is an estimate from the pin count and function.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: single aluminium; no TiW barrier

facts.label: Die size
facts.value: ~50-60 mm2 class, larger than the 6510

mb.roms.name: 901226-01 BASIC, 901227-03 KERNAL, 901225-01 character ROM
mb.roms.description: The three mask-programmed NMOS ROMs on the C64 mainboard, all in 24-pin DIP: 901226-01 is the 8 KB (2364-compatible pinout) Commodore BASIC V2 interpreter at $A000; 901227-03 is the 8 KB KERNAL at $E000 (901227-01/-02 in earlier lots, and 901229-0x is the 1541 drive's KERNAL, not this one); 901225-01 is the 4 KB (2532-compatible) character generator ROM at U5. Mask ROMs are programmed by deleting or adding metal at one point in the flow, which means a whole extra mask set cut for each ROM revision.
mb.roms.note: The brief said '901229 KERNAL ROM'; for the C64 the part is 901227-0x. 901229-05 belongs to the 1541 disk drive. The 901225-01 character ROM is a 4 KB part although only about 2.3 KB of it carries character data - the rest is un-decoded filler.

facts.label: BASIC
facts.value: 901226-01, 8 KB, NMOS mask ROM, 24-pin DIP

facts.label: KERNAL
facts.value: 901227-03, 8 KB, NMOS mask ROM, 24-pin DIP

facts.label: Character
facts.value: 901225-01, 4 KB, NMOS mask ROM, 24-pin DIP

facts.label: Total ROM
facts.value: 20 KB of mask-programmed NMOS

mb.roms.revisions.name: ROM revisions are mask revisions
mb.roms.revisions.description: Every fix to the C64's firmware cost a new mask set and a new wafer run. The BASIC ROM has exactly one version, 901226-01; the KERNAL went through 901227-01, -02 and -03, the last of which fixed a tape-loading bug and is what nearly every C64 shipped with; the character generator is 901225-01, with national variants 325018 (Swedish) and 325056 (Spanish C64C). A mask-ROM run also had to be large enough to fill the order, so a small revision could mean waiting weeks for wafers.

facts.label: Character ROM
facts.value: 901225-01, plus national variants

mb.roms.verify.name: Verifying every ROM bit
mb.roms.verify.description: A mask ROM cannot be re-programmed, so its contents are verified twice. On the wafer, a 24-needle probe card runs a read-only pattern through the 8192 or 4096 addresses and sums the data; after assembly, the part goes into an automatic tester that reads the whole array and checks it against a resident signature and, for the C64's BASIC and KERNAL, the published checksum. Any failure meant a defective mask or a contamination particle, and the whole mask set had to be re-run.
mb.roms.verify.note: Not established: the 24-needle probe card, the 0.1 inch pin pitch, the read-only sum of the whole array, or the published checksum comparison for BASIC and KERNAL. That a ROM die is verified on the wafer by automatic test equipment and again after assembly is the documented practice.

facts.label: Probe card
facts.value: 24 needles, 0.1 inch pitch

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: all 8192 (or 4096) bytes, bit for bit

si.package.24.name: 24-pin plastic DIP package
si.package.24.description: The package of the BASIC, KERNAL and character ROMs: a 0.6 inch pitch, 24-leaded stamped lead frame, die eutectic-bonded on its tab, 25 um gold wedge bonding, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy. On the C64 mainboard these three were the only chips soldered in rather than socketed, because they cannot usefully be replaced - though owners have socketed them since day one.

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 0.6 inch (15.24 mm), dual row

facts.label: Wires
facts.value: ~24 pad-to-frame bonds plus a few internal

facts.label: Compound
facts.value: silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C

mb.roms.mask.name: The ROM-only mask plate
mb.roms.mask.description: Because the ROM pattern is a physical edit to the flow, Commodore held a separate chrome-on-glass plate for each ROM number. It was cut from the ROM's bit map by the same pattern generator used for the logic masks, inspected against the database, and stored in a mask library; 901226-01 and 901227-03 each required their own.

facts.label: Plate
facts.value: 1:1, chrome on glass, 5x7 inch

facts.label: Count
facts.value: one plate per ROM revision

mb.roms.programming.name: Mask programming: one mask set per ROM revision
mb.roms.programming.description: An NMOS mask ROM of 1982 was an NMOS transistor array with a decoder, programmed by removing or adding contacts/metal at the array intersections. The usual 1980s implementation was contact programming: the programmer and sense-amp metal were left unconnected at a bit=1 location, and the ROM-only mask plate was drawn with those contact cuts simply omitted - or, in the opposite polarity, extra contact cuts were added for every 0. The array is arranged 32 bit lines (or 24, using 6 cells of 4 transistors) across 2048 words for the 8 KB parts.
mb.roms.programming.note: Two other read-only technologies sat alongside the mask ROM in the same decade and neither is what Commodore used: a thin-film PROM stores the bit as a sheet of 25-200 ohm/sq nichrome (Ni80/Cr20) or Cr-SiO2 cermet, sputtered or co-evaporated and then programmed by laser or sand-blast ablation through a resist. The mask ROM is a transistor array with one extra mask, which is exactly why a ROM revision costs a whole wafer run.

facts.label: Array
facts.value: 2048 words x 8 bits for 8 KB; 512 x 8 for 4 KB

facts.label: Programming
facts.value: contact / via programming done as an edit to one mask

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: each ROM revision = a new mask set cut and a new process run

mb.roms.sense.name: Bit-line sense amplifiers
mb.roms.sense.description: A masked bit line is precharged high and then a dummy word is selected to develop a voltage across the bit line; a differential sense amplifier (a latch of four NMOS transistors plus a pair of cross-coupled load devices, exactly the same topology as the 6510's logic) amplifies the millivolt difference and latches it. The sense amps were the largest block in a mask ROM die - typically 10-15% of the area - because each needed a perfect match.

facts.label: Signal
facts.value: a few mV differential, amplified to a full logic swing

mb.roms.process.name: NMOS mask ROM front end
mb.roms.process.description: The same silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU - n+ source/drain diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, 1-2 um aluminium, PSG/nitride passivation - with one extra mask level for the ROM programming pattern. A 24-pin DIP ROM die is small (a few mm2) and yields well; the constraint was mask cost, not yield.
mb.roms.process.note: Not established: the mask level count for a mask ROM (eight plus one programming level), the claim that the constraint was mask cost rather than yield, or that the ROM die is small enough to yield well. A mask-programmed ROM is one extra mask level above the same NMOS front end, but no source gives the level count for these parts.

facts.label: Mask levels
facts.value: 8 + 1 ROM-programming level

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: single aluminium layer

mb.color-ram.name: U6 2114L colour RAM (1K x 4 static)
mb.color-ram.description: The C64's screen colour memory at U6, decoding to $D800-$DBE7: 1024 words of 4 bits each, i.e. one colour nibble for each of the 40x25 text screen's 1000 cells. The VIC-II reads these nibbles during the visible portion of every scanline and presents them to the 4-bit colour DAC, so the memory must be fully static with no clocks and no refresh - unlike the eight 4164 DRAMs sitting next to it. Period part numbers are 2114L (MOS Technology / other MOS vendors), MM2114 (National Semiconductor) and plain 2114; the C64 BOM lists 2114L-30, the -30 being a 300 ns speed grade. 18-pin DIP, single +5 V, TTL-compatible bidirectional I/O, about 225 mW.
mb.color-ram.note: Three corrections to the brief. (1) The part holds 1024 words of 4 bits = 512 bytes, not 1 KB; '1K' refers to the word count, and it is 4 bits wide, not 8. (2) It is not CMOS - the 2114L is explicitly 'N-channel silicon-gate technology', an NMOS cross-coupled inverter latch with a resistor load, not the 6-transistor CMOS cell of later 6264/6280 SRAMs. (3) There was no standard bipolar 4-transistor 2114; the bipolar 1K x 4 memories of the era were unrelated parts (74S287/74S288 and the 74LS189 family are 1K x 1 or 256 x 4). The 'four 256 x 4 or 1K x 4 banks sharing address pins' description does not match the real device: one 1024 x 4 array with ten straight address inputs A0-A9.

facts.label: Organisation
facts.value: 1024 x 4 bit = 4096 bit = 512 byte

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 18-pin DIP, 0.6 inch pitch

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: +5 V single rail, 225 mW typ

facts.label: Technology
facts.value: N-channel silicon gate, fully static, no clocks

facts.label: Pinout
facts.value: A0-A9, /CS (pin 8), /WE (pin 10), D0-D3 bidirectional (14,13,12,11)

facts.label: Where it maps
facts.value: $D800-$DBFF, VIC-II bank 0

mb.color-ram.test.name: Probe, sort and final test
mb.color-ram.test.description: Probed on the wafer with an 18-needle probe card running an address/data checker over all 4096 bits in a marching pattern, then retested after moulding. Because the part has no refresh, its main failure modes are stuck cells from particles and defective decoders, both of which a walking-one/walking-zero pattern catches quickly - which is why the C64's most common colour-RAM symptom, a garbled or shifting character colour, is a die or socket fault rather than a marginal-timing one.
mb.color-ram.test.note: Tester models and exact patterns at Norristown are not documented; the description is the standard period approach to static RAM.

facts.label: Probe card
facts.value: 18 needles, 0.1 inch pitch

facts.label: Pattern
facts.value: march / walking checkerboard over 1024 x 4

si.package.18.name: 18-pin plastic DIP package
si.package.18.description: The package of the 2114L colour RAM: an 18-leaded stamped lead frame at 0.6 inch pitch, about 18 pad bonds plus a handful of internal wires, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy. The lead-frame, bonding-wire and compound stories are the same as every other DIP in the machine.

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 0.6 inch dual row

facts.label: Compound
facts.value: 60-75 wt% ground silica filled epoxy

facts.label: Wires
facts.value: ~18 pad bonds plus internal wires, 25 um Au

mb.color-ram.vic-interface.name: How the VIC-II reads it during raster
mb.color-ram.vic-interface.description: The VIC-II owns an internal video address counter that runs ahead of the beam. For each character cell in the visible portion of a scanline it drives the ten colour-RAM address lines and /CS low, and the chip returns the 4-bit colour on D0-D3 within about 300 ns; those four bits go straight to the 6-bit-per-channel RGB DAC and out through the 18-resistor palette on the mainboard. When the VIC releases the bus, the 6510 can access the same memory as ordinary RAM at $D800. That single-ended, mid-scanline, few-hundred-nanosecond read is the electrical reason the part had to be a static latch array with roughly 2 V of noise margin.
mb.color-ram.vic-interface.note: The VIC-II steals these cycles with AEC low; the CPU sees the colour RAM through $D800 only when the VIC is not driving the bus.

facts.label: Read window
facts.value: ~300 ns per cell

facts.label: Data path
facts.value: 4 bits direct to the VIC-II DAC, bypassing the 6510 data bus

mb.color-ram.mask.name: The 2114 mask set
mb.color-ram.mask.description: Eight or nine 1:1 levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon (gate and, if used, the load resistor pattern), self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad, and alignment/test levels, printed from chrome-on-glass plates with grid-broken alignment.

mb.color-ram.cell.name: Six-transistor NMOS static cell
mb.color-ram.cell.description: Each of the 1024 nibbles is six transistors: two cross-coupled NMOS inverters forming a bistable latch, plus two NMOS pass transistors that connect the latch to the bit line when the address decoder enables that column. Because it is NMOS, each 'inverter' of the latch is a pull-down transistor in series with a load - which is where the load scheme matters. The latch holds its state for as long as power is applied, with no refresh and no clock, and has to keep roughly 2 V of noise margin at 5 V supply despite sharing a die and a substrate with 1024 other cells that all switch at once.
mb.color-ram.cell.note: The 'six transistors per bit in a typical static RAM' figure is a standard period statement for NMOS SRAM; the cell topology is the classic two-cross-coupled-inverter latch plus two access transistors. Cell layout (single-ended bit line vs differential, and whether the sense amplifier was a shared latch) is not published for the 2114 and is not claimed here.

facts.label: Transistors per bit
facts.value: 6 (4 in the latch, 2 pass transistors)

facts.label: Hold requirement
facts.value: indefinite; no refresh, no clock

facts.label: Noise margin
facts.value: ~2 V at a 5 V supply

mb.color-ram.cell.access.name: Pass transistors and the two-decoder structure
mb.color-ram.cell.access.description: A 1024 x 4 array is decoded as a 32 x 32 matrix: a six-to-64 row decoder from A0-A5 and a five-to-32 column decoder from A6-A9, each a NAND-type NMOS decoder built from series pull-down strings. Each cell therefore needs two access transistors, one gated by a row line and one by a column line. The decoders are the only clocked-looking part of the chip, but they are combinational - there is no clock input pin at all, which is exactly what makes it static.
mb.color-ram.cell.access.note: A 32 x 32 organisation with two decoders is the natural way to build 1024 x 4 and is what other period 1K x 4 SRAMs used; No published die shot of the 2114 has been seen to confirm the split.

facts.label: Array
facts.value: 32 rows x 32 columns x 4 bit planes

facts.label: Address
facts.value: A0-A5 row, A6-A9 column

mb.color-ram.cell.load.name: The load device: polysilicon resistor or depletion transistor
mb.color-ram.cell.load.description: This is the real difference between a 2114 and a CMOS SRAM, and it is an extra process step. A ratioed NMOS latch needs something in series with the pull-down transistor to act as a load: on 1982 parts this was typically an undoped or lightly doped polysilicon resistor deposited in the same LPCVD step as the gate, or a depletion-mode NMOS transistor (gate tied to source, threshold deliberately shifted negative by an extra implant) acting as a current source. The depletion option needed one more implant than the resistor option. Not established: which option the C64's 2114 used.
mb.color-ram.cell.load.note: Both were standard period practice and the two are visually distinguishable on a die. The specific load device on a 2114L from 1982 is not documented in any available source. Lithium-doped polysilicon was used in some early NMOS logic, but no evidence was found that it was used here.

facts.label: Option A
facts.value: undoped polysilicon resistor, 30-100 ohm/sq, no extra mask

facts.label: Option B
facts.value: depletion-mode NMOS load, one extra implant

mb.color-ram.why-static.name: Why static rather than dynamic
mb.color-ram.why-static.description: The DRAMs beside it get a refresh cycle roughly every 2 ms because the 6510 can be held off the bus while the KERNAL's refresh routine runs. The colour RAM has no such luxury. The VIC-II fetches a colour nibble out of this chip in the middle of drawing each character cell, within a few hundred nanoseconds of the start of the scanline, from an address counter the VIC owns - there is no software window in which the chip could be taken off to rewrite it. So the cell has to hold its state indefinitely. That is the whole reason for the part: it is a static latch array, and it draws more power (225 mW) than one DRAM chip as a result.
mb.color-ram.why-static.note: The VIC-II gives about 63 cycles per character cell at 1.02 MHz, roughly 60-70 us of total screen refresh per frame, and it reads one nibble per cell during the ~500 ns the cell is on screen.

facts.label: Access window
facts.value: a few hundred ns per cell during the visible portion of the scanline

facts.label: Refresh needed
facts.value: none - 'All internal circuits are fully static'

facts.label: Power penalty
facts.value: ~225 mW typ vs ~135 mW for a 4164

mb.ram.name: Four/eight 4164 64Kbit DRAMs = 64 KB RAM
mb.ram.description: The C64's dynamic memory. The breadbin mainboard (PCB 326498-01) carries EIGHT 4164 64Kbit x 1 DRAMs, each holding 8 KB, giving 64 KB total; the address bus is multiplexed row/column through two 74LS257 multiplexers. Early prototypes used 4116 16-pin parts. The 4164 is a single-transistor single-capacitor (1T1C) dynamic cell, needs only +5 V because the 8-pin version generates its own -5 V substrate bias internally, and runs a two-level polysilicon process.
mb.ram.note: The scope brief said '4x 4164 = 64 KB'. That is arithmetically wrong: 4 x 8 KB = 32 KB. A breadbin C64 has EIGHT 4164 sockets. Parts came from many Asian and US suppliers, not necessarily from Commodore's own Norristown fab.

facts.label: Organisation
facts.value: 65,536 x 1 bit = 64 Kbit = 8 KB per chip

facts.label: Count on a C64
facts.value: 8 chips (U9-U12, U21-U24) = 64 KB

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 8-pin DIP (pin 1 no connection; pin 8 VBB on the 16-pin -8/-10 version)

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: +5 V only; internal VBB = -5 V charge pump

facts.label: Refresh
facts.value: 128-cycle 7-bit RAS-only refresh, 2 ms period

facts.label: Typical suppliers
facts.value: Mosel MK4564, TI TMS4464, Sanyo, UMC, Samsung, Hyundai, Nippon Micron

mb.ram.refresh.name: RAS-only refresh
mb.ram.refresh.description: The 4164 has no refresh counter: the row address must be presented on RAS every cycle to stay alive. On the C64 the counting is done by the VIC-II, not by the CPU and not by a CIA. While the VIC has the bus it multiplexes refresh row addresses onto its own video-RAM address bus, generating RAS itself; AEC going low is what takes the bus away from the 6510, so refresh is transparent to the processor. The KERNAL's part is only to write the raster counter at $D012, which steps the VIC through its refresh addresses.
mb.ram.refresh.note: Contradicted by the source. The refresh addresses do not come from the CIA: when the VIC-II takes the bus with AEC low it drives the refresh row address itself onto its own multiplexed video-RAM address bus (pins 24-31 and 30-34), and the VIC generates the row-address strobe. What the KERNAL does is write the raster counter at $D012 so the VIC steps through its eight refresh addresses; it does not clock a CIA A12 line. Not established: the 7-bit, 128-cycle and 1792-cycle figures, or the German-manual statement that only 7-bit-refresh parts may be used.

facts.label: Refresh period
facts.value: 4164 refresh interval is specified in the datasheet; the VIC-II issues the row address and the RAS strobe on the C64. Any figure for this machine's refresh cycle is not established here.

facts.label: Counter
facts.value: in the VIC-II, not on the DRAM and not in the 6510; the CIA does not drive the row address

mb.ram.sort.name: Wafer sort and final test of the 4164
mb.ram.sort.description: Every die is probed with an 8-needle probe card and tested on an automated memory tester that runs a march-type pattern (write a checkerboard, read it, invert, repeat) through all 65,536 cells, then a refresh test holding 128 RAS cycles. Assembled parts go back into a socket on the same tester for a signature/AC timing check at 150 ns. Timing bins came out of this test - the C64 does not need the fastest grade, but the drive and the C128 memory expansions did.
mb.ram.sort.note: Specific tester models are typical of the period; the ones at Norristown or at the Asian vendors are not documented.

facts.label: Probe card
facts.value: 8 needles, 0.1 inch pitch

facts.label: Testers
facts.value: Teradyne L-200, Fairchild SICTEST, or a Voltronik 5n

si.package.8.name: 8-pin plastic DIP package
si.package.8.description: The smallest and most common package in the machine: eight 4164 DRAMs, each a die on an 8-leaded lead frame with about eight frame bonds plus a dozen internal wires for the sense amps, transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy. A 16-pin version of the same die exists for stackable C128 memory.

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 0.6 inch (15.24 mm) dual row

facts.label: Pinout
facts.value: 1 NC, 2 DIN, 3 /WE, 4 /RAS, 5 A5, 6 A2, 7 A1, 8 VDD

facts.label: Wires
facts.value: 8 frame bonds plus ~8-14 internal, 25 um Au

facts.label: Compound
facts.value: ~0.1-0.2 g of low-alpha epoxy

facts.label: Variants
facts.value: 8-pin DIP (C64), 16-pin DIP (stackable C128)

mb.ram.protection.name: Alpha-particle and latch-up protection
mb.ram.protection.description: DRAM soft errors from alpha particles emitted by radon daughters in the mould compound were a real field-failure mode in 1982. Mitigations used then: a sintered alumina or silicon-nitride chip cover potted over the die in a hermetic package; 'getter' compounds in the cavity; and softer, minimum-area bit-line and capacitor geometries to increase the stored charge margin.
mb.ram.protection.note: The IBM/Samsung 'HAB' (hit-point-address-bypass) and soft-error work of the mid 1980s came later.

facts.label: Alpha energy
facts.value: ~5-6 MeV from Rn-222 progeny in the epoxy

facts.label: Typical soft error rate
facts.value: ~1 FIT to 100 FIT per device, highly variable

mb.ram.package.cover.name: Sintered chip cover over the die
mb.ram.package.cover.description: On many 64K DRAMs the mould compound was not allowed near the die: instead a small alumina or silicon-nitride lid was diffusion-bonded to the lead frame cavity and the cavity then filled with a low-alpha moulding compound or left in a hermetic ceramic package. Alpha emission rate of the compound was a purchased specification in units of alphas per cm2 per hour.

facts.label: Specification
facts.value: <0.04 alpha/cm2/h for low-alpha compound

mb.ram.mask.name: 4164 photomask set
mb.ram.mask.description: A 64K DRAM needed eight to ten mask levels: active area, n+ field, contact, poly 1 (word line), poly 2 (capacitor plate), poly 3 (bit line), the second diffusion, metal, and passivation pad - plus gate-2 test structures. The poly 2 and bit-line levels are what forced 5x step-and-repeat printing; most 4164 wafers in 1982-83 went through GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers with 3x3 inch quartz reticles, and a handful of lines were still on 1:1 proximity aligners.

facts.label: Reticle
facts.value: 5x, quartz or borosilicate, 2.5x2.5 or 3x3 inch

mb.ram.mask.reticle.name: 5x reticle: chrome on quartz
mb.ram.mask.reticle.description: A 3x3 inch fused-quartz or borosilicate plate coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, exposed from a 10x or 20x artwork intermediate by a mask stepper, developed, the chrome etched in perchloric/sulfuric acid, inspected against the database on a Zeiss comparison tool, and mounted in a reticle cassette. Because quartz has a thermal expansion near zero, the reticle pattern stays put through a mask-level thermal cycle - the reason quartz beat glass once steppers became common.

facts.label: CTE
facts.value: quartz ~0.5e-6/K vs glass ~3.7e-6/K

facts.label: Absorber
facts.value: Cr 100-150 nm, sputtered

mb.ram.process.name: Two-level polysilicon NMOS DRAM process
mb.ram.process.description: Same basic silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU but heavier: thicker field oxide, more polysilicon depositions (three), a heavier arsenic source/drain, a thicker aluminium (2-3 um) for the bit lines that have to survive repeated bootstrapped swings, and usually two mask levels for bit-line precharge and sense amp. Eight to ten mask levels and 100-150 process steps, versus ~50 for the CPU.
mb.ram.process.note: DRAM wafers were commonly grown to a heavier oxygen content than logic wafers: a high bulk oxygen-precipitate density lengthens the trapped-charge lifetime and so buys refresh margin on a 64K part. That is the one place the 4164 substrate differs from the 6510's.

facts.label: Aluminium
facts.value: 2-3 um (heavier than logic)

facts.label: Fab cycle time
facts.value: ~60-100 days for a 64K DRAM in 1982

mb.ram.photolitho.name: Projection printing the poly 2 and bit-line levels
mb.ram.photolitho.description: The tight overlays in a 4164 (bit line over capacitor plate, poly 2 over poly 1) were what finally forced 5x reduction step-and-repeat printing rather than 1:1 contact printing, because 1:1 contact printing of a 4 um bit line over a 4 um plate feature was too lossy. Typical 1982 DRAM mask lines ran GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers, with hard-baked 2 um Shipley AZ-1354 resist and a 5x reticle on a 3x3 inch quartz plate.
mb.ram.photolitho.note: Some 64K DRAMs were still made on 1:1 proximity aligners in 1981-82; by 1984 5x steppers were standard across the industry.

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: 5x step-and-repeat

facts.label: Overlay
facts.value: +-0.2-0.3 um, blown off pattern

mb.ram.vbb.name: On-chip -5 V substrate bias charge pump
mb.ram.vbb.description: The 4116 needed +5, +12, -5 and a boosted write supply, which is why it had a VBB pin and why the C64 prototype had extra regulators. The 4164 collapsed this to +5 V alone by generating the negative substrate bias on chip: an on-chip oscillator drives a capacitor, and the resulting AC is rectified to about -5 V and fed to the substrate, which also forward-biases the pn junction between the substrate and the n+ wells. Sense amplifiers bootstrap the bit line to +7-8 V during restore, and a second internal supply raises the word line above VDD.
mb.ram.vbb.note: Not established: that the 4164 generates a -5 V substrate bias on chip, the -8/-12 part suffixes, the bit-line bootstrap to +7-8 V, or the boosted word line. No datasheet is cited. What is documented is that the 4164 is 65,536 x 1 bits and that the C64 needs eight of them.

facts.label: VBB
facts.value: -5 V, generated internally on the 8-pin -8/-12 versions

facts.label: Bootstrap
facts.value: bit line restored to ~+8 V

facts.label: Refresh
facts.value: 128 RAS cycles, 2 ms; RAS-only (no internal counter on most parts)

mb.ram.cell.name: The 1T1C memory cell
mb.ram.cell.description: Each of the 65,536 bits is one access transistor plus one capacitor. The cell uses THREE polysilicon layers: poly 1 is the word line crossing the device, poly 2 is the overlapping plate of the storage capacitor (the plate is doped n+ and shared with the bit line), poly 3 is the bit line itself. Around 3.5 um x 8 um per cell in 1982 - big compared with modern trench/stacked cells. Double-diffused poly (DDP) cells, where the source and drain are separately implanted so the cell can be offset, were used by several 64K DRAM makers.
mb.ram.cell.note: The brief said '3-transistor/1-capacitor cell' - that is the 1Kbit-era cell (e.g. the 1101/2102). The 4164 is definitively 1T1C; every 4164 datasheet of the period says 'single transistor dynamic storage cells'. Folded bit lines belong to the 256K/1M generation, though a few 4164 designs did use them; treat folded bit lines here as unverified.

facts.label: Cell
facts.value: 1 transistor, 1 capacitor (1T1C)

facts.label: Polysilicon levels
facts.value: 3 (word line, capacitor plate, bit line)

facts.label: Storage
facts.value: charge on the capacitor, must be refreshed

mb.ram.cell.doublepoly.name: Second polysilicon layer: the storage capacitor
mb.ram.cell.doublepoly.description: The key DRAM process problem in 1982. A second conformal polysilicon layer had to be deposited and patterned so that its edge was razor sharp and its overlap onto the access transistor was tight. Deposition was LPCVD silane at ~800-850 C; the plate was doped n+ with a phosphorus implant and annealed. Refractory metal silicides (WSi2, TiSi2) were being introduced on gates in 1983-84 but were not universal in 1982 64K DRAMs.
mb.ram.cell.doublepoly.note: Polysilicon is documented as the gate material deposited by LPCVD and doped in the same step with phosphine. Not established: that the storage node is a second conformal polysilicon plate, the 800-850 C deposition, the 3000-5000 A thickness, or the 1983-84 arrival of tungsten and titanium silicides. The second-layer polysilicon plate is not described in the sources available.

facts.label: Deposition
facts.value: LPCVD SiH4, 800-850 C

mb.cpu.name: MOS 6510 CPU, 40-pin DIP
mb.cpu.description: 8-bit NMOS microprocessor at U7 of the C64 mainboard, clocked at 1.022727 MHz NTSC (0.985248 MHz PAL). It is the 6502 core plus an 8-bit I/O port on pins 9/10 (address 0000 data-direction, 0001 output latch). The MOS/CSG datasheet calls it 'HMOS, silicon gate, depletion load technology' - i.e. an N-channel silicon-gate double-polysilicon process with depletion-mode load devices, roughly a 2 um minimum feature. Fabbed in-house by MOS Technology (later Commodore Semiconductor Group) at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown, Pennsylvania.
mb.cpu.note: MOS called its fast N-channel process 'HMOS'; here it means a NMOS process with an ion-implanted polysilicon gate, not the HMOS of later MOS parts. The exact minimum linewidth of the Norristown 6510 (2 um vs 3 um) is not published; treat the 2 um figure as medium confidence. Conflict worth recording with the metals fragment: metal.silica asserts that "the 6510 is NMOS, so the 1982 die uses aluminium gate metal and thermally grown field oxide, not a polysilicon gate". That contradicts the MOS/CSG datasheet wording quoted above and the layer stack under the front-end branch below. The datasheet is the primary source, so this file follows it and the disagreement is logged rather than silently resolved.

facts.label: Clock
facts.value: 1.022727 MHz NTSC / 0.985248 MHz PAL

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 40-pin DIP, 0.6 inch pitch

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, depletion load (datasheet says 'HMOS')

facts.label: Transistors
facts.value: ~3500 (die is roughly 3.5 x 3.9 mm)

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: +5 V single rail, 30 mA typ

facts.label: Bonds
facts.value: ~60 wires of 25 um gold: ~40 pad-to-frame plus ~20 internal

places: Norristown, Pennsylvania, USA (MOS Technology / CSG fab)

mb.cpu.fab.name: MOS Technology / CSG plant, 950 Rittenhouse Road
mb.cpu.fab.description: The place these chips were born. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, moved to 950 Rittenhouse Road in the Valley Forge Corporate Center off Trooper Road near Norristown, and was bought by Commodore Business Machines in 1976, becoming the Commodore Semiconductor Group. It was a small but complete device plant: design, mask making, wafer fabrication on 4- and 5-inch wafers, assembly and final test all under one roof, which is why a single address appears on every C64 chip marking. It closed in 1992 and the site became an EPA Superfund site from leaking underground storage tanks.
mb.cpu.fab.note: There is no well-sourced 'West Hills' Commodore fab. The documented semiconductor sites are this Norristown plant and a Costa Mesa, California plant that Commodore closed around 1985; Commodore's corporate headquarters and much of its assembly were in West Chester, Pennsylvania. Treat any West Hills attribution as unverified. A device fab is an electricity sink rather than a labour sink: 4-5 kWh per wafer per mask level for the furnaces and the aligners, plus a very large chilled-water load for the compressors and the wet benches, so power was a real fraction of the cost of a 6510. That intensity figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate from period fab literature; the exact Norristown number is not published.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown PA 19401

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: 1969 by ex-General Instrument executives John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe, Don McLaughlin

facts.label: Acquired
facts.value: 1976 by Commodore Business Machines for 9.4% of Commodore equity

facts.label: Wafer size
facts.value: 4 inch, later 5 inch

facts.label: Closed
facts.value: 1992, bankruptcy protection; added to the EPA Superfund NPL in 1985

facts.label: Energy intensity
facts.value: ~1,500-3,000 kWh per wafer through the whole flow; US industrial tariff ~5-7 US cents/kWh in 1982

mb.cpu.fab.assembly.name: Assembly and test lines in the same building
mb.cpu.fab.assembly.description: Die sort, sawing, die bonding, wire bonding, transfer moulding, trim-and-form, marking and final test all ran on the site behind the fab. The gold bonder room was kept dry and at constant humidity (roughly 40% RH) because gold wire and epoxy bonding are moisture-sensitive; the moulding presses were hydraulic, 50-100 ton, multi-cavity transfer presses.

facts.label: Mould press
facts.value: 50-100 ton hydraulic transfer press

mb.cpu.fab.maskshop.name: In-house or commissioned mask shop
mb.cpu.fab.maskshop.description: A device plant of this size either cut its own masks or bought them from a regional mask shop. The work involved taking the layout database to a numerically controlled pattern generator, exposing and etching 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates, inspecting them on a comparison tool, and repairing defects - a few weeks and a few thousand dollars per mask level, ten levels per part. Commodore's mask-making capability is asserted in some histories but not documented to this level.
mb.cpu.fab.maskshop.note: Flagged low confidence deliberately: the existence, location and equipment of any Commodore mask shop in 1982 is not established.

mb.cpu.fab.cleanroom.name: Class 10 cleanroom bays with HEPA filtration
mb.cpu.fab.cleanroom.description: Wafer processing in yellow-lit laminar-flow bays fed by fan filter units, with a class 1000 corridor outside; 70% RH and +/-1 C. Gases distributed on stainless steel panels from bulk nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen tanks; resist and wet chemistry in stainless or quartz benches; photomasks brought in through a pass-through hatch and never returned dirty.

facts.label: Work area
facts.value: class 100 (ISO 5)

facts.label: Background
facts.value: class 1000

si.burnin.name: Burn-in and final test
si.burnin.description: Assembled parts were run at elevated voltage - typically 7-9 V on a 5 V part - at 100-125 C for 24 to 168 hours in an oven loaded with sockets on a board, to weed out early-failure parts with contaminated junctions before they reached the customer. The C64 itself needed no burn-in: the chips were simply inserted into the board sockets.
si.burnin.note: Burn-in of consumer-grade MOS parts in 1982 was common but not universal; C64-era Commodore parts often skipped a formal burn-in step.

mb.cpu.dicing.name: Die separation: scribe and break, or diamond-wheel saw
mb.cpu.dicing.description: The wafer is flipped onto a vacuum chuck, scored along the scribe lines with a diamond scriber or, in the more expensive method, cut with a resin-bonded diamond wheel on a saw, leaving a kerf of 50-100 um. Small dies like the 6510 (about 3.5 x 3.9 mm) were often diced by scribing and snapping, then washed dry.

mb.cpu.dice-tool.name: Diamond scriber and dicing saw
mb.cpu.dice-tool.description: A small die like the 6510 (roughly 3.5 x 3.9 mm) was separated either by scoring the wafer's back-side scribe lines with a diamond scriber and snapping the wafer along them, or by cutting with a resin-bonded diamond wheel leaving a 50-100 um kerf. The wafer was then washed dry, and a final microscopic inspection checked each die's edges and surface before it went to bonding - a chip on a pad would cost a whole package.

facts.label: Kerf
facts.value: 50-100 um (saw) or none (scribe-and-break)

facts.label: Coolant
facts.value: deionized water or a solvent jet

mb.cpu.probe.name: Wafer probe (electrical die sort)
mb.cpu.probe.description: Before dicing, each die is probed on a wafer with a probe card: a printed-circuit board with 40 microscopic tungsten or rhenium needles, one per 6510 bond pad. A Teradyne L-120 or Fairchild SICTEST automated tester drives a test program and logs wafer coordinates, so only known-good dice go to assembly. Probe cards in 1982 were hand-drilled needle cards; automatic stepping probes were still rare.
mb.cpu.probe.note: That die are probed on the wafer by automatic test equipment, with binning, before dicing is documented. Not established: the 40-needle tungsten or rhenium card, the Teradyne L-120 or Fairchild SICTEST models, the wafer-coordinate logging, or that stepping probe stations were rare in 1982.

mb.cpu.front-end.name: 2 um NMOS front end: the layer stack
mb.cpu.front-end.description: A silicon-gate, double-polysilicon NMOS process flow on p-type (100) CZ silicon: heavily doped n+ source/drain first, LOCOS field oxide, heavily n-doped polysilicon gate, self-aligned arsenic source/drain, contact cuts, aluminium metallization, then phosphosilicate glass plus a plasma nitride seal. Ten mask levels, ~50 major process steps, roughly 6-8 weeks of fab cycle time.
mb.cpu.front-end.note: Layer thicknesses for the specific 6510 are reconstructed from period NMOS design rules, not from a published process manual. There was exactly ONE metal layer - no aluminium barrier, no tungsten plug, no CMP, no dual damascene. The whole flow ran in class 100 bays of the Norristown plant, fed by fan filter units over a class 1000 corridor at 70% RH and +-1 C, with nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen distributed on stainless panels from bulk tanks.

facts.label: Minimum feature
facts.value: ~2 um (poly gate length / metal pitch)

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: 1-2 um aluminium, single level

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: single aluminium level, single poly gate + poly load resistor

mb.cpu.fe.implanter.name: Low-energy ion implanter
mb.cpu.fe.implanter.description: A small Van de Graaff or mass-separated implant source (High Voltage Engineering, Extrion, or Veeco) accelerating arsenic to 50-150 keV, with a beam scanning and dose measurement unit. Implantation of the source/drain had largely replaced diffusion by 1982 in a well-equipped shop.
mb.cpu.fe.implanter.note: If Norristown did not own an implanter, this step was done as an outside foundry service - plausible for a small internal fab, but undocumented.

mb.cpu.fe.etcher.name: Wet etch bench and plasma etcher
mb.cpu.fe.etcher.description: Wet etches in quartz or PVDF tanks: HF for oxide, hot H3PO4 for aluminium, buffered oxide etch (HF:NH4F) for fine oxide patterning. By 1982 many fabs had added a barrel-type CF4/CF4+O2 plasma etcher (e.g. the Plasma Technologies PT etch, or an ASM) for aluminium and for poly etching.

mb.cpu.fe.deposition.name: Polysilicon LPCVD furnace and aluminium sputterer
mb.cpu.fe.deposition.description: A second tube furnace, plumbed for silane/phosphine or dichlorosilane, for poly deposition. Aluminium went on in a separate vacuum tool: a DC magnetron sputter chamber (Balzers, Perkin-Elmer, Leybold) or a resistive evaporation chamber, both with turbomolecular pumps and a rotary fixture.

mb.cpu.fe.furnace.name: Oxidation and diffusion tube furnaces
mb.cpu.fe.furnace.description: Quartz or fused-silica tube furnaces, horizontal, 5-6 inch ID, with 2-4 zone radiant or resistance heating to 1100 C, a boat of silicon-carbide or quartz carrying 25-50 wafers, and gas flow panels with wet/dry mixing valves. These did the field oxide, gate oxide, poly anneal and the source/drain drives.

mb.cpu.fe.photoresist.name: Positive photoresist: spin, soft-bake, expose, develop
mb.cpu.fe.photoresist.description: Wafer coated on a spinner (2000-4000 rpm) to 1-2 um of AZ-1350, dried 90-100 C for 20-30 min on a hot plate, aligned to the mask in a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2 optical proximity aligner, exposed through the chrome plate, then spray-developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide. Between every step: megasonic clean, dilute H2SO4:H2O2, and a hard bake.
mb.cpu.fe.photoresist.note: The contact and proximity print modes, the roughly 5 um proximity gap and the alkaline tetramethylammonium hydroxide developer are documented. Not established: the AZ-1350 resist and its thickness, the 90-100 C bake, the Coburn 2400 and Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2 model numbers, and when 10x reduction steppers became available.

mb.cpu.fe.passivation.name: 7. Passivation and pad opening
mb.cpu.fe.passivation.description: The aluminium is sealed under a phosphosilicate glass overcoat grown by CVD from TEOS and phosphine at 700-800 C, and in 1982-84 plants increasingly by plasma-enhanced CVD silicon nitride (~700 C, SiH4/NH3 or SiCl4/NH3 in a low-frequency glow discharge). Pad windows are opened with a hot phosphoric acid etch of the nitride followed by a buffered HF dip.
mb.cpu.fe.passivation.note: Whether the 6510 die carried nitride passivation or only PSG is not publicly documented; nitride passivation at a small internal fab in 1982 is plausible but not certain.

facts.label: Overcoat
facts.value: PSG ~8000 A + PECVD SiNx ~10000 A

facts.label: PECVD introduced
facts.value: commercially ~1981-1983 at Motorola, TI, Fairchild

mb.cpu.fe.contacts.name: 6. Contact cut and aluminium metallization
mb.cpu.fe.contacts.description: Contact windows are cut in the field oxide with an HF dip masked by photoresist (silicon dioxide etches fast in HF), then the wafer is coated by vacuum evaporation or DC sputtering with 1-2 um of aluminium containing 0.5-1% silicon to stop aluminium spikes punching through thin junctions. The aluminium is patterned by a hot phosphoric-acid etch (H3PO4:HNO3:acetic acid/water at ~50-80 C) or, from the late 1970s, by a CF4/O2 plasma in a barrel etcher.
mb.cpu.fe.contacts.note: Difference from today: no refractory barrier, no tungsten plug, no CMP-defined metal lines, and a single aluminium layer - the die simply had no room for more.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: Al-Si, 1-2 um

facts.label: Etch
facts.value: hot H3PO4 or CF4/O2 plasma

facts.label: Barrier metal
facts.value: NONE in 1982 - no Ti/TiN/TiW

mb.cpu.fe.self-aligned.name: 5. Self-aligned source/drain implant
mb.cpu.fe.self-aligned.description: With the poly gate and field oxide standing up, the wafer is ion-implanted with arsenic (or phosphorus) at 50-150 keV. The gate poly and the field oxide act as their own masks, so the source and drain edges are formed automatically under the poly edges with no alignment tolerance at all. The implanted arsenic is then annealed at 1000-1100 C in dry O2 or N2, which also drives it under the gate edge and repairs implant damage.

facts.label: Implant
facts.value: As 50-150 keV, dose 1e15-1e16 /cm2

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: self-alignment is what made 2 um silicon-gate NMOS practical in a small fab

mb.cpu.fe.polyoxide.name: 4. Poly gate oxidation (the real '3.5 V' gate dielectric)
mb.cpu.fe.polyoxide.description: After the undoped polysilicon is patterned, the whole wafer is re-oxidised: the bare silicon is left capped by the 400 A screen oxide, while the poly itself grows its own oxide. Dry O2 at 1000-1100 C for 30-90 minutes grows ~350-450 A of silicon dioxide on the poly, converting it into a depletion-mode MOSFET with the same gate dielectric as the silicon. This is why 'the gate oxide was grown in an oxygen furnace' is literally true of silicon-gate NMOS - but on the poly, not on the channel.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 350-450 A (~800 A grown to allow for later poly oxidation)

facts.label: Breakdown field
facts.value: ~3-4 MV/cm

mb.cpu.fe.poly.name: 3. Deposition and doping of the polysilicon
mb.cpu.fe.poly.description: Polysilicon was deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition in a heated-wall tube furnace from silane (SiH4) at 800-850 C or from dichlorosilane (SiH2Cl2) at ~1000 C, giving 4000-8000 A of polycrystalline film. For gates it was deposited heavily n-doped in the same step by adding phosphine to the silane flow. Undoped poly, or lightly doped poly, was also deposited in the same furnace as the load resistors and as the depletion-mode loads the 6510 datasheet describes.
mb.cpu.fe.poly.note: Dichlorosilane was cheaper per deposited atom than silane and preferred for thick films, but carried chlorine that required a careful post-deposition clean.

facts.label: Deposition
facts.value: LPCVD silane at 800-850 C

facts.label: Grain size
facts.value: 0.2-1 um sputtered-like polycrystalline grains

mb.cpu.fe.locos.name: 2. LOCOS field oxide
mb.cpu.fe.locos.description: The active-area mask is defined in photoresist over the grown oxide, and field oxide grown by two-step thermal oxidation: a dry O2 pass at ~1000 C to lay down the thin masking oxide, then steam at the same temperature for ~2 hours to reach 6000-8000 A of field oxide. Field oxide was the isolation, the mask for the self-aligned source/drain implant, and the thickest feature on the die.
mb.cpu.fe.locos.note: LOCOS was still the isolation scheme in 1982; trench isolation was a few years away.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: dry O2 then wet H2/O2, 1000-1100 C

facts.label: Bird's beak
facts.value: ~1-2 um lateral encroachment - the reason a field-gate design was attractive

mb.cpu.fe.nplus.name: 1. n+ source/drain pre-diffusion
mb.cpu.fe.nplus.description: A thermal phosphorus diffusion: the wafer is coated with a phosphosilicate glass (PSG) doped by PH3 or by a PBN (pyrolytic boron nitride) solid phosphorus source, then held at 900-950 C for 30-60 minutes to push phosphorus about 0.5-1 um into the silicon. The result is a heavily doped (10^20 cm^-3) n+ region that will become the bit-line/tap contact landing areas and the bases of the load and driver devices.
mb.cpu.fe.nplus.note: Some 1982 fabs used an arsenic implant instead of phosphorus diffusion; Norristown is documented only as an NMOS shop, not at this level of detail.

facts.label: Dopant
facts.value: phosphorus

facts.label: Sheet resistance
facts.value: 20-50 ohm/sq

mb.cpu.mask-set.name: Photomask set, ~10 levels
mb.cpu.mask-set.description: The set of 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates the 6510 pattern was cut into: nine or ten levels - n+ source/drain, field, contact, poly, second contact, metal, passivation and pad, plus alignment and test structures. For a device this small the fab printed 1:1 with contact or proximity printing; 10x steppers were brand new in 1982 and not used for this part. The plates are made by the fabrication branch below.
mb.cpu.mask-set.note: The exact level count and whether any plate was a reticle is not published for the Norristown 6510. Commodore did own mask-making capability, but the West Hills facility mentioned in some accounts is not verified.

facts.label: Mask type
facts.value: 1:1, chrome on soda-lime glass or quartz, 5x7 inch

facts.label: Minimum drawn line
facts.value: ~2 um

mb.cpu.mask.stepper.name: The 10x stepper arriving at the end of the period
mb.cpu.mask.stepper.description: Reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire, and later ASML) that printed a 10x-reduced reticle with a +-0.2-0.3 um overlay and broke the industry below the 1 um limit. By 1982 a 1:1 contact printer could just barely hold a 2 um line, so a 2 um 6510 was still printable 1:1; the steppers were arriving for the next generation, not for this part. Canon FPA-series 10x machines were among the first installed.
mb.cpu.mask.stepper.note: Named machines are illustrative of the period rather than confirmed as sitting in Norristown.

mb.cpu.mask-set.fabrication.name: Cutting, inspecting and repairing the mask plates
mb.cpu.mask-set.fabrication.description: The 6510 layout existed as polygons on a Calma or Computervision workstation. It was checked against the design rules, extracted to a mask database and written to tape, and a mask data preparation program merged the layout with the process layers, the alignment marks and the die boundary to produce the flat rectangle-and-trapezoid format the pattern generator consumed. The generator then flashed a xenon-mercury lamp through an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster of rectangles into a camera-reduction stage, or a 1:1 mask writer exposed the blank plate directly. Each plate was developed in positive resist, the exposed chrome etched away, inspected on a Zeiss or KLA comparison tool against the database, and defect-repaired with a gallium or indium needle or by lifting and re-exposing the film. This data-reduction step, not the exposure, was where most mask errors were caught.
mb.cpu.mask-set.fabrication.note: Whether Norristown used an in-house plotter, bought plates from a regional mask shop, or mixed the two is not documented in any public source. Electron-beam mask writers existed by this date but at roughly US$1-2 million they were not typical in a device plant this size.

facts.label: Layout system
facts.value: Calma or Computervision, magnetic tape in and out

facts.label: Output
facts.value: rectangle/trapezoid tape for the pattern generator

facts.label: Inspection
facts.value: Zeiss or KLA comparison tool against the design database

facts.label: Repair
facts.value: gallium or indium needle, film lift and re-expose, or deposited carbon

mb.cpu.mask.inspection.name: Mask inspection and defect repair
mb.cpu.mask.inspection.description: Masks were checked on a Zeiss or KLA comparison mask inspection tool against the design database, printing defect-free chrome checkouts. Opaque defects on clear areas were repaired with a fine gallium or indium needle or by lifting the film and re-exposing; clear defects in a chrome line were patched with deposited carbon. Pellicles - 1-2 um Mylar membranes mounted in a frame - protected final production masks from dust, though they were less common for 1:1 contact printing, where the mask still touched the wafer. Inspection was the last gate before a plate went into the mask library, because one bad plate silently ruins a whole wafer run.
mb.cpu.mask.inspection.note: A 1 um defect on a 2 um feature is not something the process can tolerate, which is why mask repair was routine work rather than an exception.

mb.cpu.mask.plotter.name: Pattern generator driving a mask exposure
mb.cpu.mask.plotter.description: In 1982 most masks of this size were made by a numerically controlled pattern generator that flashed a xenon-mercury lamp through an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster of rectangles into a camera-reduction stage, or by a 1:1 mask writer that exposed a blank plate directly. Electron-beam mask writers (EBG, Santa Clara) existed but at roughly US$1-2 million were not typical in a small internal device fab.
mb.cpu.mask.plotter.note: Whether Norristown used an in-house plotter, a purchased mask from an outside mask shop, or a mix is not documented in public sources.

mb.pcb.name: C64 mainboard ASSY 250407 - bare double-sided FR-4 board
mb.pcb.description: The unpopulated logic board of a 1983 Commodore 64. A 1.6 mm two-layer epoxy-glass laminate about 390 x 180 mm carrying 35 um copper on both faces, roughly 1200 unplated through-holes for component leads, NO plated-through holes and NO vias at all, green epoxy solder mask on both sides and a white screen-printed legend. Made by an outside printed-circuit-board house, not by Commodore.
mb.pcb.note: The board cost is the era figure quoted for the C64 printed-circuit board. A verified reverse-engineered copy of the Rev. B layout contains exactly zero vias, so no layer change goes through a plated barrel anywhere on this board. Structural note: the children of this node are a fabrication sequence, not a bill of materials - the laminate, the resist and the finished blank are things the board is made of or passes through, while the rest are the operations an outside house applied in order.

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: 2 (no internal plane)

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 1.6 mm

facts.label: Outline
facts.value: approx. 390 x 180 mm

facts.label: Vias / plated-through holes
facts.value: none at all

facts.label: Board cost (era estimate)
facts.value: approx. $1-2

mb.pcb.bareboard.name: Finished bare board, fab no. 250406
mb.pcb.bareboard.description: A drilled, etched, stripped, masked, legended and finished blank ready for component insertion. At 1983 commodity prices a two-layer 1.6 mm consumer board of this size cost on the order of one to two dollars.
mb.pcb.bareboard.note: The $1-2 figure is the era cost quoted for the C64 printed-circuit board.

facts.label: Era board cost
facts.value: approx. $1-2

facts.label: Etch and drill yield
facts.value: typically high; a two-layer board with no vias has few ways to fail

mb.pcb.inspection.name: Electrical test of the bare board
mb.pcb.inspection.description: Before any component goes on, the blank is checked for shorts between nets and for opens in the artwork. In 1983 this was a continuity and insulation-resistance tester plus a careful visual check under a lamp and a loupe. Automated optical inspection existed by 1983 but was a line investment rather than an assumption on a commodity board.
mb.pcb.inspection.note: Modern lines AOI every board automatically and add impedance and resistance checks as well.

mb.pcb.legend.name: White silkscreen legend and compartment boxes
mb.pcb.legend.description: Reference designators, block outlines and assembly notes are printed in white epoxy ink over the cured mask through a tensioned fine-mesh screen, then baked to cure the ink onto the mask. Commodore drew boxes around functional blocks, the so-called compartments, and used extra ink colours in bands and outlines to colour-code regions of the board and mark the television standard. Each extra colour is a separate screen pass with its own screen, squeegee and cure, which is a real cost and a real time step on the line.

mb.pcb.legend.colour.name: Coloured silkscreen bands
mb.pcb.legend.colour.description: A separate pass in each extra colour, with its own screen, to draw the colour bands and outlines that mark functional regions and the PAL or NTSC variant. A modern cosmetic imitation of this is a coloured solder mask; in 1983 it was extra ink passes.
mb.pcb.legend.colour.note: The exact set of colours used on the 250407 has not been confirmed here.

mb.pcb.legend.screen.name: Screen printing and bake
mb.pcb.legend.screen.description: A fine-mesh screen coated with photosensitive emulsion is stretched and tensioned over the board, epoxy ink squeegeed through, and the board then baked to cure the ink onto the mask.

mb.pcb.mask.name: Epoxy solder mask on both sides
mb.pcb.mask.description: Green epoxy ink is screen-printed over the whole board with apertures left over every pad and hole. It is the green the C64 has always been. Without it the board shorts from a fingerprint, a solder splash or a screw, and the white legend would disappear under bare copper. Period inks were solvent-based epoxies cured in infrared or hot-air ovens; modern liquid solder mask is still screen-printed and cured far more cleanly, and liquid solder mask plus ENIG is now the standard pairing.
mb.pcb.mask.note: The screen mesh is the shared node written by the chassis fragment, because the same stainless wire mesh and photosensitive emulsion print the case legends and the board legend. The epoxy ink itself has no node of its own anywhere in this tree, which is a gap.

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: epoxy, screen-printed through a fine mesh

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: UV or thermal, typically around 150 deg C for half an hour

facts.label: Dry thickness
facts.value: approx. 0.01-0.02 mm

facts.label: Aperture allowance
facts.value: a little larger than the pad, so pads do not look ringed

mb.pcb.finish.name: Surface finish: pads and edge contacts
mb.pcb.finish.description: After etching the copper is protected, made solderable, and given a wear-resistant finish where it will be touched. On this board, because there are no plated barrels, the finish job is far simpler than on a modern via board: a solderable coating on the pads and a hard plating on the contact surfaces inside the three board-mounted sockets.
