Exposed copper that is neither coated nor plated gets an anti-tarnish treatment - a benzotriazole-type organic protectant that stops it darkening in storage and handling, which is cheap, invisible, and easy to skip until someone notices the boards going brown in the box.

mb.pcb.finish.pth.name: No plated-barrel line on this board
mb.pcb.finish.pth.description: A deliberate absence, recorded here so it does not read as an omission. The C64 mainboard skips the entire through-hole plating sequence a via board runs: hole desmear, electroless copper seed, electrolytic copper build, nickel, gold. None of that equipment ever saw this board, and any account that puts electroless copper into a C64 mainboard is describing a different machine.
mb.pcb.finish.pth.note: Not established: that the board has no plated barrels. The replica layout has no vias, but a bill of materials cannot evidence the absence of a plating line.

mb.pcb.finish.selective.name: Selective plating of the edge contacts
mb.pcb.finish.selective.description: Only the contact surfaces get a hard, wear-resistant metal. The board is either plated overall and the gold stripped back from everywhere except the contacts, or the contacts alone are exposed to the bath with the rest shielded by a fountain-plater weir or a plating rack. The usual route is a nickel underplate followed by electrolytic gold: gold dissolves in a cyanide complex with a fine gold anode and plates onto the rack-held board, which is still the standard because the bath is stable and fast and still needs the same destruction-and-recovery regime. Sometimes the whole board was immersion gold-plated instead, which is simpler and gives softer gold.
mb.pcb.finish.selective.note: On the C64 mainboard specifically these contacts are inside the female expansion, user and cassette sockets, so the gold belongs to a purchased connector; the mating plug cards carry the fingers. The plating chemistry is the same either way.

facts.label: Underplate
facts.value: nickel, commonly electroless with a thin electrolytic strike

facts.label: Gold thickness
facts.value: hard gold, roughly 1-2.5 um for a card-edge finger

facts.label: Gold bath
facts.value: cyanide-based, gold cyanide or gold sulfite

mb.pcb.finish.hasl.name: HASL solder level on the pads
mb.pcb.finish.hasl.description: Exposed copper is coated in molten solder by carrying the board through a wave or a drag of 63/37 tin-lead and blowing or brushing off the excess, leaving a flat solderable layer that will not corrode. This is the period default for a two-sided consumer board with no vias, and it lines up with the solder the wave machine is already using.
mb.pcb.finish.hasl.note: Modern boards use ENIG, immersion tin or OSP instead; HASL went out of fashion because its coating is soft and its thermal expansion mismatch causes failures in thermal cycling. It was, however, ideal for a board that was going straight into a tin pot.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: 63/37 tin-lead, matching the wave solder

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: a few micrometres of tin-lead over copper

facts.label: Bath temperature
facts.value: hot enough to keep the alloy molten, several degrees above 183 deg C

mb.pcb.vias.name: Layer changes without vias
mb.pcb.vias.description: The most distinctive fact about the C64 mainboard, and the reason its copper is shaped the way it is. There are no vias and no plated-through holes at all. A connection that has to move from the component side to the solder side goes through the hole of a component lead: every resistor, capacitor, diode and DIP pin doubles as a via. Where a layer change was needed with no component available, the board carried a short single-core tinned wire jumper, hand-fitted and hand-soldered after wave soldering. There are exactly two of those on the 250407, referenced E1 and E2 on the artwork.
mb.pcb.vias.note: The saving was real: skipping the barrel plating line removed a whole wet-chemical operation and let the board stay two-sided and cheap. The cost was longer traces and a harder time with high-speed return current, which is why the layout leans on wide pours instead of a plane. A modern board would put a via or a zero-ohm resistor in both places.

facts.label: Wire jumpers
facts.value: 2 (E1 solid, E2 dashed on the artwork)

facts.label: What they connect
facts.value: a top-side signal to a bottom-side return

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: 2 copper layers, no internal plane

mb.pcb.vias.plane.name: Ground pour instead of a ground plane
mb.pcb.vias.plane.description: With no internal plane layer, the two signal layers have to carry return current on their own copper, so the layout used wide ground pours and heavy copper wherever return current had to flow. Modern boards solve the same electromagnetic problem with a dedicated plane, which is the main reason vias became universal. This is an aside on the layout rather than a separate operation.

mb.pcb.drill.name: Drilling every component hole
mb.pcb.drill.description: The board is drilled on a numerical-control drill for every component lead, jumper, jack and mounting hole. Because there are no vias, the drill programme is just a component position list; there is no barrel to plate afterwards and no second drill file to reconcile.
mb.pcb.drill.note: That a through-hole board has one drilled hole per component lead is established: originally, every electronic component had wire leads, and a PCB had holes drilled for each wire of each component, and the component leads were then inserted through the holes and soldered to the copper PCB traces. Not established: the order-of-1200 hole count, the 1.1 mm dominant diameter, the 1.6-4.3 mm larger diameters, or that the drill programme was a bare component position list with no second drill file to reconcile. 0.6 mm leads sat in roughly 0.8-1.0 mm holes. The oversize is deliberate: the wave has to fill the hole, and a tight hole makes an unfilled, dry joint.

facts.label: Holes on this board
facts.value: of the order of 1200

facts.label: Dominant diameter
facts.value: approx. 1.1 mm for DIP and leaded parts

facts.label: Larger diameters
facts.value: approx. 1.6-4.3 mm for trimmer, fuse and mounting holes

facts.label: Fit
facts.value: hole set slightly oversize so the lead drops in freely for wave soldering

mb.pcb.drill.bit.name: Carbide drill bit
mb.pcb.drill.bit.description: Tungsten-carbide or high-speed-steel bits, ground and resharpened. Laminated glass plus copper is abrasive, and the hole is the one feature that cannot be reworked once drilled wrong.

mb.pcb.drill.ncd.name: NC drill and tool change
mb.pcb.drill.ncd.description: A tape-fed drill head steps through the tool table, swapping bits for the several diameters the board needs, over pinned or vacuum-held fixtures. A bit-management and drill-jig system holds sub-millimetre position accuracy; drill wander is what breaks a fine-pitch DIP row.

mb.pcb.mill.name: Routing and outline cutting
mb.pcb.mill.description: In 1983 the board outline, the internal cut-outs and the expansion-port routing slot were milled mechanically on a CNC router with a carbide cutter. The slot is cut so that a thin projecting ear of laminate is left standing with copper on both faces: that ear is the board's edge-connector receptacle, and its copper is then selectively plated, so the slot geometry fixes the finger width and spacing that the case connector has to mate with. Laser routing existed but was not yet the commodity default for a board with no fine geometry.
mb.pcb.mill.note: That last point is worth stating plainly, because it is a common misreading of a photograph of this board: on the C64 the mainboard carries the socket and the expansion adapter carries the gold fingers. Modern high-mix shops use CO2 or ultraviolet lasers for routing and depanelising because they need no tooling and leave no router burr; for this board either would have been far slower than milling.

facts.label: Edge connector
facts.value: a female receptacle milled into the board, plated afterwards; the C64 mainboard has no board-edge fingers of its own

mb.pcb.mill.cutter.name: Carbide router cutter
mb.pcb.mill.cutter.description: A tungsten-carbide end mill, often with a diamond-like coating, cutting laminate that is mostly glass fibre. Glass dust is abrasive, so tool life is short and the cutter is changed on a schedule.

mb.pcb.strip.name: Resist stripping and clean-up
mb.pcb.strip.description: The cross-linked resist film is dissolved away in an aqueous caustic or ammoniated stripper, then the board is rinsed, given a mild acid clean to knock back any last residue, dried, and inspected.
mb.pcb.strip.note: Stripping and cleaning are where the etched board stops being a chemistry problem and starts being a mechanical one.

facts.label: Stripper
facts.value: aqueous caustic soda or an ammoniated solvent

facts.label: Follow-up
facts.value: mild acid clean and deionised rinse

mb.pcb.etch.name: Ferric chloride etching
mb.pcb.etch.description: The masked laminate goes into warm ferric chloride solution, which dissolves the unmasked copper and leaves traces, pads and ground pour standing. Copper removed along the way is recovered, and the etchant is periodically replenished or dumped. Because copper in solution poisons the bath, an etching line of this period was a chemical operation with a disposal problem attached, not just a tank.
mb.pcb.etch.note: The general step is established: chemical etching divides the copper into separate conducting lines called tracks or circuit traces, pads for connections, vias to pass connections between layers of copper, and features such as solid conductive areas for electromagnetic shielding. The 2 FeCl3 + Cu -> 2 FeCl2 + CuCl2 stoichiometry follows from that and is not separately cited. Not established: that this line used ferric chloride rather than sodium persulphate or a cupric chloride bath, the 42 deg Baume figure, the 40-50 deg C, the 20-45 minute etch time for 35 um copper, and the practice of dumping and remaking the bath as copper accumulates. Period text consistently quotes 42 deg Baume ferric chloride around 45 deg C. Sodium persulfate was a real alternative for some shops. Modern practice is still ferric chloride, but with tighter control and a copper-recovery loop. The etchant itself, its Baume range and its regeneration are the shared node chem.pcb-chemicals.etching.ferric-chloride; this node is the board-shop step that uses it.

facts.label: Etchant
facts.value: ferric chloride, commonly quoted at about 42 deg Baume, warmed to approx. 40-50 deg C

facts.label: Time for 35 um copper
facts.value: roughly 20-45 min

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 2 FeCl3 + Cu -> 2 FeCl2 + CuCl2

facts.label: Chemistry limit
facts.value: copper in solution poisons the bath, so it is dumped and made fresh

mb.pcb.exposure.name: UV exposure through the artwork film
mb.pcb.exposure.description: The artwork negative is laid against the resist and the board is flood-exposed in a vacuum-frame unit. In 1983 the lamp was a mercury-vapour or metal-halide source rich in the near ultraviolet where the acrylate resists are sensitive; fibre-optic exposure systems that pipe collimated light into a bed of glass rods were spreading through the later 1980s and gave far more even illumination.
mb.pcb.exposure.note: An air gap between film and resist is the classic cause of a fuzzy, partly-etched trace edge on a two-sided board.

facts.label: Exposure time
facts.value: seconds to tens of seconds, set by an integrating light meter

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: film pressed into the resist under vacuum to avoid any air gap

mb.pcb.exposure.lamp.name: Mercury-vapour exposure lamp
mb.pcb.exposure.lamp.description: A quartz envelope filled with mercury vapour struck by an arc, rich in the near ultraviolet where the acrylate resists are sensitive. Needs a water-cooled jacket and a choke.

mb.pcb.exposure.vacframe.name: Vacuum exposure frame
mb.pcb.exposure.vacframe.description: A hinged platen with a rubber diaphragm. Film and resist are clamped and then evacuated so the film sits hard against the resist with no bubbles and no shadowing.

mb.pcb.photoresist.name: Dry-film photoresist, negative working
mb.pcb.photoresist.description: A dry film about 25-40 um thick, on a polyester carrier, laminated onto the copper. Where the artwork film lets ultraviolet light through, the acrylate resist cross-links and hardens; the hardened areas stand up to the ferric chloride. Everything else dissolves away and the copper under it etches out. For a two-sided consumer board in 1983 dry film was already the default; modern shops more often print liquid resist, so the choice has flipped but the principle has not.
mb.pcb.photoresist.note: Period suppliers included Kodak and Dynachem. The resist chemistry itself is the shared node chem.photoresist; this node is the board-shop form factor of it.

facts.label: Dry film thickness
facts.value: approx. 25-40 um

facts.label: Chemistry
facts.value: negative-working acrylate photopolymer on a polyester carrier

facts.label: Lamination temperature
facts.value: approx. 90-110 deg C

mb.pcb.photoresist.coat.name: Surface clean and tack-free prep
mb.pcb.photoresist.coat.description: Before the resist goes on, the board is degreased and dried so the film lies flat. A tack-free prep was unusual on period boards; wet resist had an easier time of it, which is one reason modern processes moved.
mb.pcb.photoresist.coat.note: Wet resist offered the no-prep advantage; dry film offered the thickness control. Dry film won on thickness.

mb.pcb.photoresist.laminate.name: Film lamination of the resist
mb.pcb.photoresist.laminate.description: The board is baked dry, the film is fed from a spool, heated, and pressed onto the copper by rubber-covered nip rollers. The rubber hardness matters: too hard and it embosses the fragile 35 um foil.

facts.label: Control
facts.value: nip rollers and a chill roll to set the film down

mb.pcb.photoresist.carrier.name: PET carrier film
mb.pcb.photoresist.carrier.description: The polyester backing the resist is laminated from, peeled off after lamination and before exposure, leaving the resist on the copper. It is the same dimensionally stable polyester film as the artwork film stock, and it exists so the 25 um resist can be handled and rolled without touching.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.name: Hot platen press and the lamination cycle
mb.pcb.laminate.press.description: The machine that turns loose foil and cloth into a sheet. A hydraulic press pack carries several heated platens so several laminate books can be pressed in one loading, and a stack of foil, prepreg, core and prepreg goes between them. Pressure squeezes out the excess resin and forces it into the weave; the heat completes the cure. The platens are cast and then surface-ground, because a laminate that is not flat is not 1.6 mm everywhere. This one machine is the reason a period FR-4 board has a flatness tolerance tighter than anything the component designer asked for.
mb.pcb.laminate.press.note: Modern high-Tg FR-4 laminates press hotter (200-220 deg C) and harder. Period FR-4 at 175 deg C and 1.4 MPa is the classic cycle.

facts.label: Press temperature
facts.value: approx. 175 deg C

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: approx. 1.4 MPa (200 psi)

facts.label: Cycle
facts.value: roughly an hour including cool-down

facts.label: Heat
facts.value: steam coils or embedded electric resistance elements in the platens

mb.pcb.laminate.press.heat.name: Press heat source
mb.pcb.laminate.press.heat.description: Steam coils or electric resistance elements in the platens. Gas- or oil-fired central steam was the norm in a laminate plant of this era, which is what makes the press the largest single fuel load on such a site.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.release.name: Release paper between books
mb.pcb.laminate.press.release.description: Bleached or unbleached kraft paper laid between each laminate book so resin does not bond one book to the next and the platen stays clean. The same sheet doubles as the cushion that distributes pressure evenly across the book.
mb.pcb.laminate.press.release.note: Kraft paper is lignin-rich cellulose pulp; the paper chain itself is owned by the packaging fragment.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.hydraulic.name: Hydraulic press pack
mb.pcb.laminate.press.hydraulic.description: The pressure side of the press: cylinders and platens arranged so that several laminate books are pressed in one loading. The circulating hydraulic oil is a petroleum-derived lubricating fluid, refined from crude alongside almost every other lubricant on the line.

mb.pcb.laminate.press.platen.name: Heated platens
mb.pcb.laminate.press.platen.description: Cast iron platens, machined and surface-ground flat, heated by embedded steam coils or electric resistance elements. The cast iron is chosen for dimensional stability and thermal mass rather than for strength, and the grind is what guarantees that a stack of books comes out of the press uniformly 1.6 mm thick. Grey cast iron is iron ore reduced with coke in a blast furnace.

facts.label: Body
facts.value: grey cast iron, machined and surface-ground

mb.pcb.laminate.name: FR-4 copper-clad laminate panel, 1.6 mm
mb.pcb.laminate.description: The structural core of the board: woven E-glass cloth in a brominated epoxy matrix, faced with 35 um copper foil on both sides. A merchant laminate plant presses it as a panel roughly 1.2 x 2.4 m, which the printed-circuit-board house cuts into working blanks. The cloth is pulled through epoxy, squeezed between metering nips to a controlled resin content and dried to a partly cured, slightly tacky B-stage prepreg that can be stacked and stored; a stack of foil, prepreg, core and prepreg is then press-bonded in one cycle, which turns loose foil and cloth into a single homogeneous 1.6 mm sheet with copper bonded to both faces. Commodore pressed none of this itself: it bought copper-clad laminate from a merchant plant and did only the imaging, etch, drill and finish, at an outside house.
mb.pcb.laminate.note: The foil is bonded to the resin by a deliberate surface treatment, not by pressure alone. Electro-deposited foil carries a natural fine-pebble or nodular (peckled) surface that grips epoxy; rolled annealed foil is smooth and would delaminate along the copper interface without further roughening. That interface is what the laminate peel-strength test measures, and for a 1 oz consumer board in 1983 electro-deposited foil was the normal, cheaper choice - rolled foil was reserved for high-speed or high-temperature laminate. The glass, the resin and the foil are not repeated here: they are the shared nodes chem.glass-fiber, chem.epoxy.dgeba, chem.epoxy.brominated-epoxy and metal.copper.foil. The press that bonds them together is not inside the panel, so it hangs off mb.pcb as a separate machine, mb.pcb.laminate.press.

facts.label: Copper
facts.value: 35 um (1 oz) per side

facts.label: Core
facts.value: approx. 1.5 mm woven E-glass in brominated epoxy

facts.label: Dielectric constant
facts.value: approx. 4.2-4.7 at 1 MHz

facts.label: Prepreg resin content
facts.value: approx. 45-60 % by weight of glass

facts.label: Gellation
facts.value: approx. 140-160 deg C

c64.io-panel.name: Connectors and operator controls
c64.io-panel.description: Everything that plugs into the machine, and the three things a person touches to run it. The rear edge of the board carries the 44-pin cartridge expansion socket, the integral RF modulator with its channel adjust and RCA antenna socket, an 8-pin DIN for composite video plus separate luma and chroma and audio in and out, the 6-pin DIN serial bus, the 2 x 6 card-edge datasette port and the 24-pin card-edge user port, and the panel also takes a 7-pin DIN power input and two DE-9 control ports. Power arrives as 5 V DC and 9 V AC on that 7-pin socket rather than as mains, because the transformer, rectifier and regulators are in the external supply - which is why the machine's own earthing arrangement is an interwinding screen and a bond inside the brick. The operator controls are a power rocker in the right-hand case panel and two slide potentiometers on the top deck, one for volume and tone and one for brightness, wired straight into the SID's audio output and the VIC-II's analogue video level.
c64.io-panel.note: Checked against c64.connector-jacks, which carries one subtree per connector - user port, cassette port, expansion port, video/audio DIN, serial DIN, control ports and power inlet - plus the shared contact-stamping and housing-moulding sequences and one connector deliberately left off this list, the keyboard ribbon header, which is an internal board-to-board header rather than something a user plugs into. Two qualifications worth keeping: the earliest boards, PCB 326498, carry a 5-pin DIN video connector with composite and luminance but no chroma, the 8-pin part appearing part-way through production; and this subtree is listed once, here, rather than also hanging off the mainboard.

facts.label: Video / audio
facts.value: 8-pin round DIN, 262-degree horseshoe: composite out, separate Y and C out, audio in and out

facts.label: Serial bus
facts.value: 6-pin round DIN, Commodore's serial variant of the IEEE-488 handshake, 300 baud

facts.label: Datasette
facts.value: 2 x 6 card edge: read, write, sense, motor, +5 V and ground

facts.label: User port
facts.value: 24-pin card edge: 17 TTL signals plus 7 ground and voltage pins, one of them 9 V AC

facts.label: Expansion
facts.value: 44-pin dual-row card edge carrying the CPU address and data buses

facts.label: Control ports
facts.value: 2 x DE-9 subminiature D, Atari-compatible

facts.label: Power input
facts.value: 7-pin round DIN: 5 V DC and 9 V AC from the external supply

facts.label: RF modulator
facts.value: integral on the breadbin; RCA antenna output, channel set on the board by a trimmer

c64.switches.name: Switches and slide potentiometers
c64.switches.description: Three human-operated controls on a C64: the mains-free power slider SW1 on the right-hand case panel, and the two slide potentiometers for volume/tone and brightness on the top surface. The power switch gates the incoming 5 V rail; the two potentiometers are wired directly into the SID audio output and the VIC-II's analogue video level.

facts.label: SW1 position
facts.value: right-hand case panel, between the control ports and the power socket

facts.label: Type
facts.value: single-pole slide switch, SPST, mains-rated style body

facts.label: Potentiometers
facts.value: 2 x miniature slide potentiometer, ~10 kOhm linear

facts.label: Slider location
facts.value: top surface of the case, right-hand end

c64.switches.level-sliders.name: Volume and brightness slide potentiometers
c64.switches.level-sliders.description: Two miniature slide potentiometers on the mainboard whose sliders protrude through the top of the case. One sets the audio level at the SID output; the other sets the analogue video brightness level. Both use a printed resistive track and a spring-loaded wiper.
c64.switches.level-sliders.note: The exact resistance and taper of the two C64 slide pots are not established from a primary source. Contemporary photographs and the schematic suggest a linear-law miniature slide pot in the 1 kOhm-100 kOhm range; treat the value as uncertain.

facts.label: Law
facts.value: linear

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: printed carbon track on a ceramic or phenolic substrate

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.name: Single and ganged (twin) sections
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.description: A potentiometer is made in two or three mechanically independent sections that share a common wiper shaft, so one slider knob moves the end terminal, the wiper and the middle terminal together. A 'ganged' pair means two complete potentiometers on one shaft; the C64's two sliders are physically separate parts rather than a ganged pair, since they control completely unrelated signals in different parts of the machine.
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.note: The C64 does not use a ganged pair: its two sliders are physically separate parts driving unrelated signals. Ganging was standard on stereo audio controls of the period, not on a home computer.

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.name: Self-lubricating bushing
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.description: A moulded nylon or PTFE-impregnated bushing in the chassis that the shaft runs in. Dry, it is what makes a slider pot feel smooth rather than gritty.

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.name: PTFE-impregnated bushing
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.description: A nylon or bronze-impregnated bushing with a PTFE (Teflon) lubricant. PTFE is made by polymerising tetrafluoroethylene, whose monomer is made from fluorspar via hydrofluoric acid and chloroform.
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.bushi.note: PTFE is polymerised from tetrafluoroethylene, whose monomer is made from fluorspar via hydrofluoric acid and chloroform. Fluorspar is metal.fluorspar.

c64.switches.level-sliders.section.shaft.name: Common wiper shaft
c64.switches.level-sliders.section.shaft.description: A drawn steel shaft pressed through the moulded wiper carriers, so all the potentiometer sections move together. Drawing the shaft from steel rather than moulding it in plastic is what keeps the alignment over millions of slider cycles.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.name: Moulded housing and slider knob
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.description: A small injection-moulded thermoplastic body with the moulded detent rails for the slider, and a moulded knob with the finger rib that protrudes through the case cut-out. The same polymer families as the switch body: nylon, ABS or a filled phenoxy.
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.note: ABS is one canonical node, chem.abs, shared with the keycaps and the joystick knob; it is linked here by id.

facts.label: Typical polymers
facts.value: ABS, PA66, PBT, filled phenoxy

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob.name: Moulded slider knob
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.knob.description: A small moulded knob with a moulded-in guide rib that engages the body's rails, protruding through the case cut-out. The knob and the body were often moulded in the same tool family so the fit is guaranteed.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injec.name: Injection moulding of the pot body
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injec.description: The body is injection moulded with the three terminal slots, the detent rails and the wiper guide all in one shot, in a multi-cavity tool shared with the rest of the world's miniature slide pot production.
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injec.note: That a potentiometer comprises a resistive element, a wiper, end terminals, a mechanism and a housing is documented. Not established: one-shot injection moulding of the terminal slots, detent rails and wiper guide, or that the tool was shared with world miniature slide-pot production.

c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injec.name: Moulded housing polymer (ABS or PBT)
c64.switches.level-sliders.housing.injec.description: Either the same ABS as the keycaps or a glass-filled PBT. Both are chosen for stiffness at a thin wall - a pot body has to hold a wiper alignment over millimetres of travel without creeping.

c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.name: Spring-loaded wiper
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.description: A small sprung metal clip or blade, usually a copper-nickel-plated spring steel or nickel strip, presses onto the carbon track and taps the voltage off at whatever point along it the slider has dragged it to. It must carry current through a sliding contact, so its plating and its spring force are the two design limits.
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.note: A worn carbon track is the classic reason a 1980s volume pot develops noise or drops to one end of its travel; contact cleaner and a rebuild pen were the standard fixes.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: Ni-plated spring steel, or phosphor bronze

facts.label: Wear
facts.value: the carbon track is deliberately sacrificial - it wears before the wiper

c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.precont.name: Pre-contact break and noise
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.precont.description: A resistive track and a sliding contact inherently generate noise, and a cheap carbon track generates a lot. C64 volume pots are a well-known source of a faint hiss or crackle in the audio output - a real consequence of the printed-carbon technology, not a fault.

c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-.name: Plated spring-steel strip
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-.description: The wiper is stamped from spring strip and plated in a nickel or precious-metal bath so that it both springs correctly and carries current across a sliding contact without galling the carbon track.
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-.note: A springy wiper contact on a potentiometer element is documented, described as phosphor bronze. Not established: stamping from spring strip and plating in a nickel or precious-metal bath for this wiper, or the anti-galling argument against the carbon track.

c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-.name: Nickel plating bath
c64.switches.level-sliders.wiper.nickel-.description: The same nickel chemistry as the resistor lead plating and the connector underplate: a sulfamate or pyrophosphate bath, or electroless nickel-phosphorus where the deposit had to be hard.

c64.switches.level-sliders.track.name: Printed carbon track on a ceramic substrate
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.description: The resistive element is a track of carbon ink printed onto a flat ceramic or phenolic substrate, with metal end lands at each end. Printing is what makes a slide pot cheap: the geometry of the track, its length and its taper, sets both the total resistance and the law.
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.note: A printed carbon track and a printed cermet track are the same manufacturing route as the thick-film resistor networks on the same board; only the geometry differs. For low-level audio pots in 1982, carbon ink on ceramic was still the norm and cermet was the higher-quality option.

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: carbon/graphite in an organic binder, or a cermet (RuO2 + glass) paste

facts.label: Print
facts.value: screen-printed through a mesh, cured in a tunnel oven

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: flat alumina ceramic or glass-filled phenolic

c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvatu.name: Fired substrate and end lands
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvatu.description: The carbon track is printed between two metallic end lands, usually fired silver, one at each end of the travel. The wiper bridges them; the centre terminal taps the wiper. All three terminals are solder pins on the pot's tail.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: flat ceramic or glass-filled phenolic

c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvatu.name: Firing of the printed substrate
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvatu.description: The carbon or cermet track is fired into the ceramic substrate in a tunnel oven at several hundred degrees, fusing the binder and the glass frit so the track cannot be scratched off by the wiper.
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.curvatu.note: Not established: firing the printed carbon track into the ceramic substrate in a tunnel oven at several hundred degrees to fuse the binder and glass frit. No document consulted describes how a printed potentiometer track is cured.

c64.switches.level-sliders.track.carbon-.name: Printed carbon ink
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.carbon-.description: Carbon black ground into a binder to a printable ink, screen-printed along the substrate and cured in a tunnel oven. The track length sets the nominal resistance and its taper sets the law; the two C64 sliders are linear, so the printed geometry is constant width.
c64.switches.level-sliders.track.carbon-.note: The carbon-black furnace is mb.passives.resistors.discrete-axial.carbon-film.powder.carbon-black, linked here by id.

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: carbon black in an organic binder, screen-printed and cured

c64.switches.power-slider.name: SW1 power slider switch
c64.switches.power-slider.description: A single-pole, double-throw or single-throw slide switch on the mainboard, actuated by a moulded slider that protrudes through a rectangular cut-out in the right-hand side of the case. Its only job in the C64 is to interrupt the incoming +5 V rail - everything else on the board runs off the switch's output side.
c64.switches.power-slider.note: The function is confirmed on the 250407 board: the external supply's regulated 5 VDC is applied to pins 5 and 1 of CN7, is filtered by L5, C97 and C100, and is then controlled by on/off switch S1, so the switch's only job is to interrupt the +5 V rail. Not established: the 6 A at 250 VAC resistive rating, the assertion that it is single-pole, and the positive detent at both ends.

facts.label: Poles
facts.value: 1 pole

facts.label: Rating
facts.value: ~6 A at 250 VAC resistive, far beyond the C64's ~1 A load

facts.label: Actuation
facts.value: positive detent at both ends

c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.name: Leaf contacts and contact plating
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.description: A pair of formed leaf springs - phosphor bronze or stainless - carry the current; one is fixed and one moves with the slider, wiping against its mate over a small spring pressure so the electrical contact area is always fresh. The wipe is the whole reason slide switches do not corrode: an oxide film is continuously displaced.
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.note: Wiping contacts are documented for potentiometers and rheostats. Not established: phosphor bronze or stainless leaves on this switch, silver or gold plating on a 5 V power contact, and the 50-200 g per-contact pressure.

facts.label: Leaf alloy
facts.value: phosphor bronze (Cu-Sn-P) or stainless

facts.label: Contact plating
facts.value: silver, silver-nickel, or a gold flash for low-level signals

facts.label: Contact pressure
facts.value: tens to hundreds of grams per contact

c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.name: Phosphor bronze leaf stock
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.description: A copper-tin alloy with a few tenths of a per cent of phosphorus, valued for springiness, fatigue resistance and a low and stable contact resistance. Drawn strip, blanked, pierced and formed in a progressive die; the standard contact alloy of the whole electronics industry.
c64.switches.power-slider.contacts.phosp.note: The copper and the tin of this alloy are metal.copper and metal.tin.ingot. It is the same alloy as the cartridge-socket contacts, documented on that connector.

facts.label: Strip thickness
facts.value: ~0.1-0.3 mm for switch leaves

c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.name: Slide mechanism, actuator and detent
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.description: The actuator is a moulded slider with ribs that engage moulded detent ramps in the body, so it clicks into a definite position at each end rather than resting ambiguously. A moulded spring or a bent leaf spring inside supplies the return force and the over-centre snap that gives the switch its tactile 'click'.
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.note: The detent geometry (moulded ramp plus leaf spring) is standard 1980s miniature-switch practice; No teardown-level measurement of the specific C64 switch is available.

facts.label: Force
facts.value: ~1-3 N at the detent

facts.label: Mechanical life
facts.value: 10,000 cycles typical rating

c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.dete.name: Moulded detent ramp
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.dete.description: A stepped ramp moulded into the nylon body or actuator over which the slider rides, giving a definite position at each end. Moulding the detent rather than machining it is what keeps the part cheap at the volumes a consumer switch sold in.

c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf.name: Return leaf spring
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf.description: A bent spring steel leaf that provides the over-centre force and the return to OFF. It is the part that fatigues: after enough actuations it loses tension and the switch no longer snaps crisply.

c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf.name: Spring steel strip
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf.description: A high-carbon strip steel, hardened and tempered, cut and blanked. Blade and coil spring steel of this quality came from the same integrated steel plants as the razor blades and the automotive leaf springs.
c64.switches.power-slider.mechanism.leaf.note: Not established: high-carbon hardened-and-tempered strip steel for this switch, and the shared origin with razor blades and automotive leaf springs.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.name: Moulded switch body (melamine / phenolic / nylon)
c64.switches.power-slider.body.description: The insulator the whole mechanism lives in. Small slide switches of this generation used a filled thermoset (melamine-formaldehyde or glass-filled phenolic) or a glass-filled nylon; both mould well in simple two-plate tools and stand a soldering iron's heat. Melamine was the industry default because its arc resistance in a mains-adjacent switch is better than polystyrene's. The switch body was riveted or snapped into the mainboard and located by a moulded boss in the case; the boss and its snap feature are part of the case tooling, not the switch tooling.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.note: The C64 switch handles only 5 V DC from the external brick, not mains, so its insulation requirement was modest - but the part was bought from a mains-switch catalogue and over-specified.

facts.label: Materials used
facts.value: melamine-formaldehyde, glass-filled phenolic, PA66, PBT

facts.label: Tool
facts.value: two-plate injection mould, ~10,000 shots/tool life

c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal.name: Solder terminals and anchor
c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal.description: The pins of the switch are brass, either solid or a brass tube over a steel mandrel with a solder tail. Brass is used because it wets tin-lead solder reliably and does not need nickel underplate for a low-voltage contact.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal.note: Not established: brass pins solid or brass tube over a steel mandrel, and the claim that brass needs no nickel underplate at low voltage. No document consulted describes the switch's terminal construction.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal..name: Brass terminal stock
c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal..description: Solid brass wire or a brass tube over a steel mandrel, cut and headed. Brass is chosen because it is springy enough to survive the assembly line and soft enough to take a solder joint.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.terminal..note: Not established: this terminal's brass wire or brass-over-mandrel stock, the springy-and-solderable property argument, and the heading operation.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.name: Nylon 6,6 (PA66)
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.description: The base polymer of PA66, a condensation polymer of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid - not of caprolactam, which makes nylon 6, a different nylon with a lower melting point. The 6,6 grade was preferred for mechanical parts because of its moisture stability and its higher melting point, and both of its monomers are petrochemical.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.nyl.note: This node previously claimed that nylon 6,6 was made by hydrolytic ring-opening polymerisation of caprolactam. That is the route to nylon 6; the 6,6 chain is hexamethylenediamine plus adipic acid. Corrected here, and the caprolactam branch was deleted with it.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.name: Glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF)
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.description: A tough, self-lubricating engineering thermoplastic used where a moving slider needs low friction and good wear resistance against the moulded track. Injection-moulded into the actuator and often into the switch's own guide body.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.note: Which of these the C64's switch actually used is not documented in any available source; the materials above are the standard options for a 1982 miniature slide switch.

facts.label: Glass content
facts.value: 30 % for the actuator grade

facts.label: Why
facts.value: self-lubricating against the moulded case

c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.fil.name: Glass filler in the nylon
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.fil.description: 30 % chopped glass fibre in the PA66, for stiffness at a thin wall and for dimensional stability against the moulded detent. The same filler as in the connector housings.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.nylon.fil.note: Glass-filled thermoplastic composites are documented at 25-30 % glass fibre, with glass filling increasing structural strength and rigidity. Not established: 30 % chopped glass in PA66 for this switch body, that this body is nylon rather than a thermoset or PBT, and that the filler matches the one in the connector housings.

c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine.name: Melamine-formaldehyde thermoset
c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine.description: A thermoset built from melamine and formaldehyde, filled with cellulose or glass fibre, and compression-moulded hot. It is rigid, arc-resistant, dimensionally stable and cheap - the standard insulator for mains switches and domestic electrical accessories of the period.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine.note: Not established: that this switch body is melamine-formaldehyde, the cellulose or glass fibre fillers, compression moulding at 150-180 C and 10-30 MPa, and the arc-resistant property claim. Melamine-formaldehyde as an insulator for mains switches is plausible and the tree cites it elsewhere, but no source was consulted for this body.

facts.label: Fillers
facts.value: cellulose, glass fibre, mineral

facts.label: Moulding
facts.value: compression moulded at ~150-180 C, ~10-30 MPa

c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine..name: Melamine resin from urea and formaldehyde
c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine..description: Melamine is made by condensing urea with formaldehyde. Urea comes from ammonia and carbon dioxide, both cheap industrial gases; formaldehyde comes from oxidising methanol, which comes from the catalytic conversion of synthesis gas. Both halves were pure petrochemical by 1982.
c64.switches.power-slider.body.melamine..note: Not established: the urea-plus-formaldehyde route, the 150-200 C pressure condensation, and the methanol-from-synthesis-gas then silver-catalysed oxidation route to formaldehyde. No source consulted establishes melamine or formaldehyde.

facts.label: Melamine route
facts.value: urea + formaldehyde, ~150-200 C, pressure

facts.label: Formaldehyde route
facts.value: methanol from CO/H2, silver-catalysed oxidation to formaldehyde

c64.connector-jacks.name: Front and rear I/O connectors
c64.connector-jacks.description: Every plug-in interface on a C64: the 24-pin user port, the 2x6 cassette port, the 44-pin cartridge socket, the 8-pin DIN video/audio and 6-pin DIN serial connectors, the two DE-9 control ports, the 7-pin PSU inlet and the keyboard ribbon header. They share one manufacturing sequence: stamped-and-formed brass contacts, nickel underplate, gold flash, and an injection-moulded thermoplastic or glass-filled phenolic insulator.
c64.connector-jacks.note: The breadbin C64 has no RCA jacks. Composite video, luma, chroma, audio and the RF modulator output all leave through a single round 8-pin DIN connector on the rear panel, and an earlier 1982 revision used a 5-pin one; RCA sockets appear on the C64C and on Commodore's own 1701 and 1702 monitors. The datasette port is not a DIN socket either - it is a 2x6 card-edge socket on the motherboard, and the round DIN plug lives on the datasette cable. The PSU inlet is 7-pin.

facts.label: User port
facts.value: 24-pin card edge, 3.96 mm pitch, gold over nickel

facts.label: Cassette port
facts.value: 2 x 6 card edge, 3.96 mm pitch

facts.label: Expansion port
facts.value: 44-pin dual female card edge, 2.54 mm

facts.label: Video/audio
facts.value: 8-pin round DIN, 180 degree, nickel-plated shell

facts.label: Serial bus
facts.value: 6-pin round DIN, 180 degree

facts.label: Control ports
facts.value: 2 x DE-9 subminiature D, plastic shell, gold-flashed

facts.label: Power inlet
facts.value: 7-pin round DIN (DIN 45329 / IEC 10 style)

facts.label: Keyboard
facts.value: soldered board header at the front-left edge carrying a flat ribbon

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.name: Keyboard ribbon header
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.description: A soldered pin header at the front-left edge of the mainboard carrying the keyboard's flat ribbon cable. The keyboard's matrix lines and the shift-lock return run out of the machine this way; it is the one connector on the board that is not an industry-standard part but a plain 2.54 mm row of pins.
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.note: The exact position count of the C64 keyboard header is not established from a primary source. C64 repair references consistently describe a 2.54 mm-pitch male header along the front-left board edge, and replacement parts are sold as 2.54 mm rows of varying length. The matrix needs at most 8 column lines plus 8 row lines plus shift-lock and the 6510 I/O port lines, so a 2 x 12 (24-way) header is plausible but unverified.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: soldered straight male header on the PCB

c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.name: Wave-soldered pin header
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.description: The header's pins were pushed into the board and wave-soldered in one pass with the rest of the components, in 63/37 lead-tin solder. That is why the pin material is brass with a tin plate rather than nickel: it wets tin-lead, and it does not need the corrosion resistance a gold-plated control-port contact does.
c64.connector-jacks.keyboard-header.sold.note: The solder alloy is metal.solder, the wave machine is mb.solder.wave and the flux chemistry is chem.solder-chemicals.rosin-flux; each is a single node shared with the rest of the board rather than a copy living here. Rosin itself is the sticky resin of conifers, metal.pine-resin. Commodore did not use lead-free solder on the breadbin mainboard - the lead-free transition in consumer electronics began in the 1990s. Rosin flux dissolved in alcohol is what let 63/37 solder wet a slightly oxidised lead and a slightly oxidised pad. The ionic residue it leaves behind is why the board is washed after the wave, because that residue is what makes a board drift or corrode. Rosin is the sticky resin of conifers, and metal.pine-resin is where the tree is grown.

facts.label: Solder
facts.value: 63/37 lead-tin, melting point ~183 C

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.name: Power inlet, 7-pin round DIN
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.description: The rear-panel socket the external PSU brick plugs into. A 7-pin round connector in a large 'type C' shell, following the DIN 45329 / IEC 10 form: pins 1 and 5 carry the regulated +5 V DC and pins 6 and 7 the 9 V AC from the transformer, with the switched side feeding the board through L5, C97, C100 and SW1.
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.note: Sources agree on 7 pins; some 1982 supplies shipped a lead with only four populated contacts, which is a different and well-documented issue - the pin 5 damage fault.

facts.label: Standard
facts.value: DIN 45329 / IEC 10 style, large type C shell

facts.label: Pin 1 and 5
facts.value: +5 V DC from the regulator, filtered by L5, C97 and C100

facts.label: Pin 6 and 7
facts.value: 9 V AC unregulated

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.name: Friction-lock and pull-proof contacts
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.description: A mains-adjacent DC supply connector needs its contacts to survive being tugged by the cable. The mating pins are a friction type with a deliberately stiff crimp barrel so a pull is taken by the metal, not the solder fillet; some Commodore supplies additionally used a friction-lock retention ring on the plug body.
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.note: Friction lock on this connector means the pull-proof crimp on the mating pins; no C64-specific retention-ring part number is established.

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.pin-5-fa.name: The pin 5 damage fault
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.pin-5-fa.description: One of the best-known Commodore power faults: a partially populated or incorrectly wired supply lead damages the 5 V pin in the machine's socket, so the machine will not power up even with a known-good supply. It is a wear-and-misalignment problem on a friction contact carrying a DC load that the connector was not designed to be unplugged under.
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.pin-5-fa.note: Widely reported in Commodore service literature; no primary factory bulletin on it has been located.

c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.name: Crimp barrel construction
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.description: The pin is a hollow brass tube with an interference crimp onto the conductor rather than a solder joint. That is the actual meaning of a friction-lock contact: the metal grips the metal, so a tug on the cable is carried by a mechanical interference fit and not by the solder fillet.
c64.connector-jacks.power-inlet.friction.note: Not established: that this contact is a hollow brass tube with an interference crimp rather than a solder joint. No document consulted describes the C64 power-inlet contact construction; the parts list gives only '7 PIN MALE DIN'.

c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.name: Control ports, 2 x DE-9 subminiature D
c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.description: The two nine-pin D-sub sockets on the rear panel for joystick or paddle controllers, a light pen or a mouse. Each is a DE-9 female in a plastic D-shaped shell with gold-flashed brass contacts dimpled for reliable mating - the connector everyone remembers from Atari, Commodore and Amiga alike.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: DE-9, female, right angle, plastic shell

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: stamped brass, gold-flashed over nickel, dimpled

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: glass-filled nylon or PBT with a nickel-plated metal shroud on some types

c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.shroud.name: Metal shell shroud and strain relief
c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.shroud.description: On the machine side the socket is a plastic-shell type with no metal shroud; the shroud is on the cable plug, where it is what provides the plug's shell ground and its mechanical strength. Both were stamped and plated the same way.

c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.insula.name: DE-9 insulator
c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.insula.description: A black glass-filled thermoplastic insulator carrying the nine contacts, keyed to the metal shell. It has to hold position to a few hundredths of a millimetre because the contacts must all engage simultaneously in a stiff nine-pin plug.

c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.insula.name: Glass-filled nylon insulator
c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.insula.description: Glass-filled PA66 holds nine contact positions to a few hundredths of a millimetre over a plastic D-shell, and takes the insertion force of a stiff nine-pin plug without cracking. The base polymer is nylon 6,6 from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid; caprolactam is the route to nylon 6, a different grade.
c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.insula.note: The polymer distinction is documented: nylon-6,6 from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid, caprolactam for nylon 6, and glass-filled variants for stiffness and impact strength. Not established: that this particular insulator is glass-filled PA66, that it holds nine contact positions to a few hundredths of a millimetre, and that PA66 rather than a filled polyester or PBT was used. Note that polyamide is hygroscopic and moisture changes its electrical resistance.

c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.d-sub-.name: D-subminiature (MIL-DTL-24308) standard
c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.d-sub-.description: The D-sub was standardised for military/aerospace use in the 1950s and became universal electronics furniture. Its 2.77 mm pitch, D-shaped polarised shell and 2.5 mm panel-mount screw pattern are defined by the standard; the C64's control ports are ordinary commercial DE-9 sockets.
c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.d-sub-.note: The service manual's parts list confirms the control ports as 'Plug Assy, 9 Pin MINID' / 'Plug Assy, 9 Pin Rt. Angle', i.e. ordinary 9-pin D-sub hardware. Not established: MIL-DTL-24308 as the governing standard, the 1950s military/aerospace origin, the 2.77 mm pitch and 2.5 mm panel screw pattern figures as stated, and that DE-9 sockets are 'commercial' rather than the MIL-qualified variant.

c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.dimple.name: Dimpled socket contact
c64.connector-jacks.control-ports.dimple.description: Each female contact carries a dimple on its mating face. Dimpling pushes the two contact surfaces into a defined line contact rather than a random point contact, which lowers the contact resistance and stops the surfaces rolling on each other. The plug's outer shell also contacts the socket shroud, so the plug's ground comes from its metal shell rather than from its pins.

facts.label: Contact plating
facts.value: 30 microinch gold over nickel, standard for the era

c64.connector-jacks.serial-din.name: Serial bus connector, 6-pin round DIN
c64.connector-jacks.serial-din.description: The IEC serial bus that daisy-chained the 1541 disk drive, printers and the rest of Commodore's peripheral family. Same body and same stamping technology as the video connector, smaller pin count, and the same sprung centre pin.

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: 180 degree, nickel-plated steel

facts.label: Carries
facts.value: serial data in/out, clock in/out, atn in/out, ground, +5 V

c64.connector-jacks.serial-din.protocol.name: IEEE-488-style handshake on 6 wires
c64.connector-jacks.serial-din.protocol.description: Commodore's bus ran clock and data in both directions with attention lines and handshaking on every transfer - an IEEE-488 descendant. That is why a C64 could sit between two 1541 drives and still address the right one: the addressing is on the bus, not in the drive.
c64.connector-jacks.serial-din.protocol.note: Commodore's serial bus is an IEEE-488-influenced protocol but not literally IEEE-488; the source reference is indicative. The bus pin count and function split are well documented.

c64.connector-jacks.av-din.name: Video/audio connector, 8-pin round DIN
c64.connector-jacks.av-din.description: One round DIN on the rear panel carrying composite video, separate luma and chroma (for a Commodore 1701 monitor's RGB-with-separate-luma input), mono audio, and the RF modulator's composite and audio out. Very early 1982 boards used a 5-pin version instead, with luma and chroma combined.

facts.label: Pins
facts.value: 8 (5 on the earliest 250407 revision, part 326106)

facts.label: Shell
facts.value: 180 degree style, nickel-plated steel

facts.label: Centre pin
facts.value: sprung, split-tulip contact

facts.label: Mounting
facts.value: screwed to the case and soldered to the board

c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.name: Nickel-plated steel shell and shield can
c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.description: The outer barrel is a drawn steel shell, nickel-plated for corrosion resistance and solderability, and crimped around the insulator. On a metal-panel or rear-case mounting it doubles as the shell ground. Nickel plate on steel is the standard 1982 finish for a mains-adjacent chassis connector. The knurled ring on a DIN plug is what a user grips to unscrew it, and on a socket the threaded barrel screws into the panel; the knurl is rolled into the shell in the same draw, because knurling a plated can afterwards would cut through the nickel.
c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.note: The service manual's parts list confirms an '8 Pin Din' video/audio connector. Not established: a drawn nickel-plated steel shell, the knurl being rolled in the same draw, the reasoning about plating after knurling, and that nickel plate on steel was the 1982 standard finish for this chassis connector.

c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.steel-s.name: Drawn steel shell stock
c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.steel-s.description: The barrel is deep-drawn from nickel-plated steel strip - a two-and-a-half type can be drawn in a few progressive strokes. The nickel plate carries the shell ground and resists the corrosion a rear-panel connector sees.
c64.connector-jacks.av-din.shell.steel-s.note: Not established: deep drawing from nickel-plated steel strip in a few progressive strokes, and the shell-ground function. No document consulted describes the DIN shell's manufacture.

c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.name: Sprung split-tulip centre pin
c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.description: The centre contact is a thin slotted pin that is sprung into a slight taper, so it plugs into a matching conical socket and self-aligns. The slot lets it flex elastically and also means a slightly undersized mating hole still makes contact at two lines rather than at a point - which is why DIN connectors are famously forgiving.

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: gold or nickel, slotted, ~1.0-1.2 mm

facts.label: Engagement force
facts.value: low, thanks to the tapered split

c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.con.name: Contact plating of the DIN pin
c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.con.description: The centre pin is nickel-plated with a gold or silver flash; the signal level here (composite video and line-level audio) is high enough that nickel alone would work, but gold was used for consistency with the other connectors. It is the same nickel-then-gold sequence as every other contact on the machine, on a tin or nickel base.

c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.mat.name: Conical mating socket
c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.mat.description: The socket the tulip pin plugs into has a matching taper, usually machined or stamped with a broach, so the two surfaces self-align on insertion. The taper is the reason a DIN plug feels forgiving and a plain pin-and-socket does not.

c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.mat.name: Broached taper
c64.connector-jacks.av-din.tulip-pin.mat.description: The mating socket's cone is broached rather than turned, so the surface finish is controlled by a single multi-form tool. The broach was hardened steel, so this was another tool-steel consumer.

c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.name: Cartridge / expansion port, 44-pin dual card edge
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.description: The slot along the bottom of the case into which cartridges plug. A 44-position dual female card-edge socket in a black glass-filled polyester body, with phosphor-bronze contacts gold-flashed over nickel. It is the single most-scrutinised connector on the machine: its contacts carry the entire address and data bus and have to survive thousands of cartridge insertions.

facts.label: Positions
facts.value: 44, dual row, 2.54 mm pitch

facts.label: Body
facts.value: black glass-filled polyester (phenolic), UL94 V-0

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: phosphor bronze, gold-flashed over nickel

facts.label: Gender
facts.value: female socket; the cartridge has the male edge

c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.name: Card-edge contact alloy (phosphor bronze)
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.description: Phosphor bronze was the standard card-edge contact alloy for this connector, gold-flashed over nickel. It is springy, fatigue-resistant and takes a good plating - the combination a card-edge socket needs, because it is wiped hard on every insertion.
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.note: The 44-pin card-edge form factor is documented twice - 'CARTRIDGE / EXPANSION (44-PIN FEMALE) CN6' in the circuit theory and '44 Pin Card Edge' in the parts list. Not established: phosphor bronze as the contact alloy, the gold flash over nickel, or the fatigue and wiping argument.

c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.name: Selective gold plating of the contact area
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.description: The contact is selectively plated by tabbing: the terminal is masked or wired as a cathode so only the mating area is gold-flashed.

c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.spec.name: Commodore expansion port specification
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.spec.description: The 44-pin socket's pin assignment, pitch and card thickness were Commodore's own definition rather than a JEDEC standard, which is why cartridges for the C64, C128 and VIC-20 are interchangeable and C64C cartridges are not.

c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.name: Contact wear and the 'dead cartridge' problem
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.description: A card-edge socket is a wear item: each insertion plucks the leaf contacts and sweeps the mating gold edge. Dust, oxide from the cartridge's board and accumulated plasticiser eventually make one or two contacts intermittent, which is the classic 'dead cartridge' symptom. Contact cleaning and, on a well-used machine, contact replacement were the routine repair.
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.note: Not established: the dead-cartridge symptom sequence and the routine-repair claim. Wear of card-edge sockets is general connector practice; no source consulted quantifies it for this connector.

c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.name: Contact cleaning regime
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.conta.description: The routine service answer to a marginal cartridge socket: an alcohol swab on the contacts, a foam rod through the slots, and a bend of the leaf if it has lost tension. It is one of the few repairs on a 1982 machine that needs no parts.

c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.card-.name: Moulded card guide and polarising key
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.card-.description: The socket body doubles as the mechanical guide: a moulded channel sets the card's insertion depth, and an asymmetric keyway stops a cartridge being inserted the wrong way round. Because the body is a thermoset, the guide is machined or moulded in one piece and cannot flex.
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.card-.note: The C64 cartridge connector's guide and keyway are visible in photographs of the underside of the board; the keyway dimensions have not been measured.

c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.card-.name: Machined guide features
c64.connector-jacks.expansion-port.card-.description: Because the socket body is a thermoset, the card channel, the stop face and the polarising key cannot be melted into place - they have to be present in the compression tool or machined afterwards. Both were normal for this part in 1982.

c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.name: Cassette (datasette) port, 2 x 6 card edge
c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.description: The port that reads and writes Commodore DATAsette tapes. It is a 12-position card-edge socket - six contacts on each face, 3.96 mm pitch - that mates with a 6-pin connector on the datasette lead. Carrying analogue audio, motor control and a sense line, it is a reminder that in 1982 'I/O' still meant tape.

facts.label: Positions
facts.value: 12 (2 x 6), 3.96 mm pitch

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: ground, 5 V, motor control, serial read, serial write, sense

facts.label: Mating
facts.value: 6-pin connector on the DATAsette cable

c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-u.name: Cassette read pull-up resistor
c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-u.description: One leg of the datasette sense line is held high by a single 3k3 1/4 W resistor on the mainboard - the same value and the same carbon-film part as the rest of the discrete resistors. It is a tiny detail that shows the whole board's design logic: discrete resistors where few are needed, a printed array where many identical ones are.
c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-u.note: The pull-up is documented as a discrete 3.3 kOhm resistor rather than as part of RP3/RP4; its reference designator on a 250407 board is not confirmed.

c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-u.name: Why the port exists at all
c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-u.description: The port carries analogue audio plus three DC control lines. The C64 read FSK-encoded data by timing transitions on the read line and generating the tones on the write line - the whole tape interface is three transistors, a resistor and two electrolytics, which is why it is so sensitive to capacitor leakage.
c64.connector-jacks.cassette-port.pull-u.note: The circuit is documented: U7's P3 pin 26 outputs write data to CN3, P4 senses the play switch, P5 drives the cassette motor through Q1 and Q3, and read data enters CN3 to the CIA's FLAG input. The parts list gives CN3 as a 6-pin connector. Not established: that the whole tape interface is three transistors, a resistor and two electrolytics, and that this is why it is sensitive to capacitor leakage.

c64.connector-jacks.user-port.name: User port, 24-pin card edge
c64.connector-jacks.user-port.description: The C64's expansion bus. A 24-position double-row card-edge socket, 3.96 mm pitch, carrying the address, data and control lines plus regulated and unregulated power out to user-port peripherals. Spare parts for this connector are specified as gold-over-nickel contacts in a PBT UL94 V-0 insulator, which is a fair description of the period part.

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: gold over nickel, in PBT UL94 V-0

facts.label: Carries
facts.value: 12 data/address lines, /RESET, /CASS lines, +5 V, 9 V AC, GND

c64.connector-jacks.user-port.pinout.name: User-port pin functions
c64.connector-jacks.user-port.pinout.description: Pins 1-12 carry +5 V out, ground, /RESET, /PPASS (the CPU-select line), the cassette sense/write/read lines and the cassette motor line, plus 9 V AC; pins 13-24 carry the user port's serial bus lines (/EOT, /SERCLK, /ATN IN, /ATN OUT) and the speaker and cassette-slot lines. The C64 6510's on-chip I/O port is wired straight into this connector, which is why a printer interface or a modem could hang directly off it.
c64.connector-jacks.user-port.pinout.note: The broad grouping of signals is well documented, but individual pin numbers are not consistent between the breadbin and the C64C documentation, so they should be treated as unverified.

c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.name: Gold-over-nickel card-edge contacts
c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.description: Each contact is a formed spring leaf whose nose protrudes from the insulator and sweeps the mating card's copper edge as it slides in. The wiping action means the gold never has to be thick to stay clean, and the nickel beneath carries the solder joint to the board.
c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.note: The user port is documented as parallel port B of the second CIA made available on the user port, with SP1/SP2 serial ports and CNT1/CNT2 clocks. Not established: gold flash over nickel on formed spring leaves, the 50-200 g contact force, and the wiping argument.

facts.label: Contact force
facts.value: ~50-200 g per contact

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: gold flash over nickel underplate

c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.s.name: Solder tail and wave-solder attachment
c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.s.description: The tail is formed flat and pierced so it takes a fillet in the wave-solder bath, giving a mechanically strong joint that also resists the repeated flexing of a plugged-in peripheral cable.
c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.s.note: Not established: the flat pierced solder tail and the wave-solder fillet, and that it resists cable flexing. No document consulted describes the user port contact termination.

c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.l.name: Spring leaf alloy
c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.l.description: The leaf has to both wipe the mating edge and hold a contact force, so it is a hard-worked copper alloy - phosphor bronze or a brass-tempered strip. It is the same material family as the switch contacts and the cartridge socket.
c64.connector-jacks.user-port.contacts.l.note: A springy phosphor bronze wiper/contact alloy is documented for potentiometer contacts. Not established: phosphor bronze or brass-tempered strip for this card-edge socket leaf, and the claim that it is the same material family as the switch and cartridge contacts.

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.name: Connector housing: injection-moulded thermoplastic or phenolic
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.description: The insulator every connector sits in. Card-edge and card-guide style connectors used black glass-filled polyester or phenolic because it machines cleanly, has almost no moulding flow and stands soldering temperatures; D-sub and DIN shells used glass-filled nylon or PBT. All were injection-moulded in multi-cavity tools.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.note: The 24-pin user-port replacement connectors on sale today are specified as PBT UL94 V-0 insulator with gold-over-nickel contacts, which is a reasonable period-accurate call as a substitute for whatever Commodore's original supplier used.

facts.label: Phenolic
facts.value: black glass-filled polyester (e.g. glass-fibre reinforced phenolic), UL94 V-0

facts.label: Thermoplastics
facts.value: PBT UL94 V-0, PA66 + 30-50 % glass, or LCP

facts.label: Tooling
facts.value: multi-cavity steel tools, 10^4-10^6 shots

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-p.name: Injection moulding press and tool
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-p.description: A multi-cavity tool clamped between the platens of a screw injection moulder. The housing is a commodity: the same part is made in hundreds of thousands for the entire electronics industry, which is why connector housings cost less than the contacts inside them.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-p.note: Engineering-grade thermoplastics are documented as processed by extrusion, casting and injection moulding. Not established: the multi-cavity tool, P20 or H13 steel at 48-52 HRC, a tool life of 10^5-10^6 shots, and the commodity-cost argument.

facts.label: Tool steel
facts.value: P20 or H13, hardened to ~48-52 HRC

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-p.name: Mould tool steel
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-p.description: P20 stainless tool steel was the industry standard cavity steel in 1982, hardened to ~48-52 HRC and polished to a fine finish. A connector housing's surface is entirely a function of the cavity polish.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-p.note: Not established: P20 stainless as the standard cavity steel in 1982, the 48-52 HRC figure, or that the housing's surface finish is entirely a function of cavity polish.

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-p.name: Injection screw and barrel
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-p.description: A nitrided steel screw and barrel, heated to 230-280 C, plastifying the polymer and injecting it into the tool. The screw is itself a wear part made from tool steel, so the moulding industry is a steady consumer of alloy steel.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.injection-p.note: Not established: a nitrided steel screw and barrel at 230-280 C for this moulding. Processing temperatures of that order are general injection-moulding practice, but no source consulted ties them to this tool.

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.name: PBT thermoplastic housing
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.description: Polybutylene terephthalate is moulded at normal injection temperatures, so a connector body can carry snap-fit features, pivot pins and cable strain-relief arms that a thermoset cannot. Glass-filled PBT was the standard D-sub and DIN shell material of the era, chosen for stiffness and low creep.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.note: PBT was the dominant D-sub shell material through the 1980s; LCP (liquid crystal polymer) took over on premium parts later in the decade.

facts.label: Filler
facts.value: 20-30 % chopped glass

facts.label: Mould temperature
facts.value: ~80-120 C tool, 240-260 C melt

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.uv-stab.name: UV stabiliser and glass filler
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.uv-stab.description: PBT needs an ultraviolet absorber because it yellows and embrittles in light, plus a glass filler for stiffness. The absorber is a benzotriazole, and both additives are minor mass but were cost-relevant in a moulded part sold in tens of millions.

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.dmt.name: Dimethyl terephthalate and butanediol
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.dmt.description: PBT is a condensation polymer of DMT and 1,4-butanediol. DMT comes from paraxylene; butanediol came in the 1980s largely from maleic anhydride hydrogenation (a coal/route) or from butanediol dehydrogenation. Both are petrochemical or coal-chemical intermediates.

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.dmt.px.name: Paraxylene and DMT
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.dmt.px.description: Paraxylene is oxidised to terephthalic acid, esterified with methanol to DMT, then condensed with butanediol. Methanol was itself a cheap synthesis-gas product of that period, so DMT carries coal and gas chemistry as well as oil.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.pbt.dmt.px.note: Not established: the paraxylene-to-terephthalic-acid-to-DMT route with butanediol, and the synthesis-gas origin of the methanol. No source consulted establishes polyester or DMT.

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.name: Glass-filled phenolic (thermoset)
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.description: Phenol-formaldehyde resin reinforced with chopped glass fibre and moulded under heat and pressure. Extremely dimensionally stable, heat resistant and flame retardant, which is why black glass-filled phenolic is the classic black body of terminal blocks, card-edge sockets and relay bases. The disadvantage is that it cannot be melted and reformed, so every detail - including the card guide slot - has to be in the tool.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.note: Not established: that this housing is glass-filled phenol-formaldehyde rather than PBT or nylon, the 20-30 % by weight chopped E-glass figure, the UL94 V-0 rating, and the dimensional-stability and flame-retardancy claims. Black glass-filled phenolic is a plausible period material for a card-edge socket, but no source consulted identifies this housing's material.

facts.label: Filler
facts.value: chopped E-glass fibre, ~20-30 % by weight

facts.label: UL rating
facts.value: UL94 V-0

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.re.name: Phenol and formaldehyde
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.re.description: Phenol comes from cumene or chlorobenzene, both benzene derivatives; formaldehyde from methanol oxidation. So a black phenolic connector body is, like everything else on this board, two or three steps downstream of a steam cracker.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.re.note: Not established: phenol from cumene or chlorobenzene and formaldehyde from methanol oxidation as the feed for this part. The cumene route to phenol is real; no source consulted ties it to this housing.

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.re.name: Phenol from cumene
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.re.description: Phenol was made almost entirely by the cumene process: cumene oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide, then acid-split to phenol and acetone. Both products of that split fed the phenolic and the epoxy chains.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.re.note: Not established: that phenol was made almost entirely by the cumene process in this period, and the cumene hydroperoxide acid-split sequence as described. No source consulted establishes cumene or phenol process.

c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.co.name: Phenolic compression press
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.co.description: A heated platen press with matched metal dies, pressing the thermoset compound to shape and curing it in the same operation. Compression rather than injection is what makes phenolic bodies cheap: the flow is short and the die is simple.
c64.connector-jacks.moulding.phenolic.co.note: Not established: that phenolic bodies were compression rather than injection moulded for this connector, and the short-flow cheap-die argument. No source consulted establishes thermoset processing.

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.name: Shared contact manufacturing: stamping, forming, plating
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.description: Almost every connector here is made the same way at the front end: a brass or phosphor-bronze strip is blanked, pierced, bent and formed in a multi-slide tool, then plated in a nickel bath and given a thin gold flash on the contact areas.

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.name: Refined gold for contact plating
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.description: Gold is deposited from a cyanide or sulphite bath, by immersion displacement onto the nickel or by electroplating with a gold strike. It is the one precious metal on an entire C64's connector set, applied as a sub-micron skin over several square centimetres - a deliberate economics of just enough gold to make the contact.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.note: Not established: the cyanide or sulphite bath chemistry, the gold strike, the 0.03-0.5 um flash thickness, and the account of gold as the only precious metal on the connector set. No source consulted establishes gold plating; the cyanide-effluent claim belongs to the plating file.

facts.label: Thickness used
facts.value: 0.03-0.5 um (a fraction of a microinch-to-half-microinch flash)

facts.label: Baths
facts.value: gold cyanide, gold sulphite, or immersion displacement

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.do.name: Doré bullion as the metal feed
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.do.description: Most industrial gold plating in 1982 was fed from dore bullion - a semi-pure gold-silver alloy - refined to the fine gold the plating shops bought. The dore itself was mostly refinery production from anode slimes and mined doré bullion, so the plating gold is not a separate supply chain from jewellery gold.

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.im.name: Immersion gold flash
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.im.description: A displacement process: the nickel surface is briefly attacked by a cyanide solution and gold plates itself out by substitution, in a few tenths of a micron, with no current. It is fast, cheap and exactly the right thickness for a connector flash.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.im.note: Not established: the cyanide displacement process with no external current, and the 0.1-0.5 um thickness. Immersion gold flash is standard connector practice, but no document consulted describes it for these contacts.

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.cy.name: Gold cyanide plating bath
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.cy.description: Gold is plated from an alkaline cyanide bath with a gold anode that dissolves to replenish the bath. The bath is deliberately kept extremely low in free cyanide and gold so that the gold itself is plated preferentially rather than the underlying base metal.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: gold cyanide, a few g/L

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.cy.name: Sodium cyanide
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.gold.cy.description: The plating chemistry itself: gold is plated from an alkaline cyanide bath held deliberately low in free cyanide, so that the gold deposits preferentially rather than the base metal underneath.
