The cyanide is made from brine by chlor-alkali electrolysis and then from ammonia and carbon, and it is why the cyanide gold shops of the period carried a persistent effluent-control and safety burden through the late 1970s and 1980s.

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.name: Nickel underplate then gold flash
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.description: Two plating baths in sequence. First a nickel underplate (electroless nickel-phosphorus on some parts, barrel or rack electrolytic nickel on others) is laid down; this is the barrier layer that stops the base copper or brass diffusing into the gold, and nickel is also what the solder actually wets. Then a thin gold flash - typically 0.05-0.5 um over nickel - goes on the mating contact areas only, masked by selective plating or by tabbing the contact.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.note: Commodore specified gold-flashed contacts on the user port and cartridge socket, and the DE-9 control ports and the DIN connectors were gold-flashed too, though the DIN shells were nickel-plated steel rather than gold. The flash itself was applied by immersion displacement from a cyanide bath - a few tenths of a micron, no external current - while electroless nickel was one of the two underplate processes and the other was electrolytic nickel. Both existed in 1982.

facts.label: Nickel
facts.value: ~2-5 um; electroless Ni-P ~2-5 um with ~0.3-5 % phosphorus

facts.label: Why gold
facts.value: gold does not oxidise, so the contact resistance stays low forever

facts.label: Why nickel under it
facts.value: nickel is a diffusion barrier; gold on bare copper/alloy would diffuse and flake

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.name: Electroless nickel-phosphorus deposition
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.description: A hypophosphite bath plates nickel onto the parts without an external current, by catalytic reduction on the brass surface. Because the deposit is amorphous nickel containing a few per cent of phosphorus, it is harder and more corrosion-resistant than pure electrolytic nickel and it does not need to be masked. It became the standard underplate for the whole connector industry by the mid-1980s.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.note: Not established: the nickel sulphate plus sodium hypophosphite bath, the 0.3-5 % phosphorus, the hardness and corrosion-resistance claims, and the dating of electroless nickel as standard underplate by the mid-1980s. No source consulted establishes electroless plating.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: nickel sulphate + sodium hypophosphite

facts.label: Era note
facts.value: electrolytic nickel was still the volume process in 1982; electroless took over later in the decade

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.name: Phosphorus from phosphate rock
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.description: The hypophosphite reducing agent is made from white phosphorus, which was still produced in the 1980s by the electric-furnace reduction of phosphate rock - a route that consumed very large tonnages of low-grade apatite for a few tens of kilograms of elemental phosphorus.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.plating.note: Electrothermal phosphorus production was still standard in 1982; the modern blast-furnace acid-route came in later.

facts.label: Route
facts.value: phosphate rock -> electric furnace -> P4 -> hypophosphite

facts.label: Rock
facts.value: apatite, Ca5(PO4)3F, from sedimentary deposits

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.name: Brass strip (Cu-Zn)
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.description: Cartridge brass, usually 70/30 copper-zinc, drawn into strip. Brass is used because it is easy to form, springs usefully, and takes nickel plating well; a strip's mechanical properties are set by the zinc content and by work hardening from the drawing die.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.note: Not established: 70/30 cartridge brass for this strip, the zinc-content and work-hardening argument, and full-hard strip for spring terminals. The general point that brass is formable, springs usefully and plates well is standard; the specific alloy and its temper for these contacts are not documented in any source consulted.

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: 70 % Cu / 30 % Zn (cartridge brass)

facts.label: Hard-rolled
facts.value: full hard strip for spring terminals

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.name: Copper electrorefining
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.description: Blister copper from the smelter is refined electrolytically to 99.99 % cathode, which is then cast to wire rod and rolled into foil. Electrorefining is what makes the uniform, sulphur-free copper that both brass contact strip and solderable connector plating require.

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: anode slime, the main source of silver, selenium and tellurium

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.name: Zinc of the brass
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.description: Zinc is recovered from sphalerite ore, roasted to the oxide and either smelted to crude zinc or leached and electrowon; it is the element that makes copper springy and hard-working.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.note: The zinc chain belongs to the metals file; referenced here only.

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.name: Roasting and calcination
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.brass-s.description: The concentrate is fluid-bed roasted, oxidising ZnS to ZnO with SO2 recovered as sulphuric acid. The oxide is then either smelted with coke to crude zinc or leached and electrowon.

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-sl.name: Four-slide die forming (blank, pierce, form, cut)
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-sl.description: Contacts are made on a multi-slide machine: a brass or copper-alloy strip is fed as a continuous coil, and each station in the slide performs one operation - piercing the terminal slot, forming the spring barrel, bending the solder tail, then cutting off the finished contact. Hundreds of thousands of identical contacts per hour, which is why connectors are cheap.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-sl.note: High-speed stamping of this sort is how a DE-9's dimpled gold-flashed contact costs fractions of a cent.

facts.label: Strip
facts.value: ~0.3-0.5 mm thick brass or phosphor bronze

facts.label: Stations
facts.value: typically 4-6 slides per contact

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: 10^5 - 10^6 contacts/hour

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-sl.name: Coiled contact strip
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-sl.description: The blank comes off the coil as a continuous ribbon of brass strip, the cheapest way to feed a high-speed press. The whole 44-position cartridge socket's 88 contacts are stamped from one coil.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-sl.note: Stamped progressive-die production from coil is documented as the reason connector contacts are a commodity. Not established: that the 44-position cartridge socket's contacts are 88 pieces from one coil, and the brass-strip specification.

c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-sl.name: Tool steel of the stamping die
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-sl.description: The progressive die is made from hardened tool steel - P20 for the body, D2 or H13 for the cutting edges - with the contact geometry machined and ground. A stamping die outlasts tens of millions of strokes, which is why the contact is a commodity.
c64.connector-jacks.metalworking.four-sl.note: Not established: P20 for the body with D2 or H13 cutting edges, the 55-62 HRC figure, and tens of millions of strokes as the reason the contact is a commodity. No source consulted establishes tool-steel.

facts.label: Hardness
facts.value: ~55-62 HRC on cutting edges

c64.keyboard.name: Keyboard module: 66 keycaps on hybrid switches
c64.keyboard.description: The C64's keyboard is a separate wired module that drops into the bezel: a steel backplate, a single-sided printed circuit board carrying the matrix, sixty-six individually moulded ABS keycaps, and beneath each cap a rubber-dome switch - a moulded plunger riding on a return spring and pressing a carbon-loaded rubber dome that bridges two plated pads on the board. The board is rigid: there is no printed flexible membrane and no silver-ink conductor anywhere in the C64 keyboard, and the only conductive element in the switch is the carbon-filled rubber itself. The legends are printed onto the cap tops with a two-colour pad printer.
c64.keyboard.note: The service manual states KEYS 66 Keys total. The 8x8 matrix covers 64 positions; RESTORE bypasses the matrix entirely, because it drives the non-maskable interrupt, and SHIFT LOCK is a latching key wired to the same lines as the left SHIFT, so to the machine it is indistinguishable from pressing left SHIFT. Counted at 63 rather than 66 in several secondary teardowns, which is a count of matrix domes plus the cursor keys and not of the keys a user presses.

facts.label: Keys
facts.value: 66 total: 2 cursor-control keys, 4 function keys, 2 SHIFT, plus the alphanumerics and named keys

facts.label: Scanned matrix
facts.value: 8 x 8 = 64 positions, read by CIA 1

facts.label: Off-matrix keys
facts.value: RESTORE on a dedicated NMI line, and SHIFT LOCK sharing the left-shift lines

facts.label: Switch construction
facts.value: carbon-loaded rubber dome on a rigid single-sided PCB; not a printed flex membrane

facts.label: Legend route
facts.value: two-colour pad printing, not double-shot moulding

facts.label: Keyboard connector
facts.value: 20-pin header at CN1 on the mainboard, front-left edge

c64.keyboard.cable.name: Keyboard ribbon cable and connector
c64.keyboard.cable.description: A short flat ribbon or discrete-lead cable from the keyboard to the 20-pin header (CN1) on the front-left edge of the mainboard, terminating in a moulded connector housing. It carries the eight matrix rows, the eight columns, the RESTORE line and a ground return - eighteen wires in all.
c64.keyboard.cable.note: In conflict with the primary source. The 1992 service manual parts list for PCB assembly 250407-04 gives CN1 as Header Assy, 20 Pin, part 903331-20, and the same 20-pin header appears in the 250425-01, 250466-01 and 250469-01 lists; the C64C list gives it as Header w/LKG Sil 2.54 CTR 20 Pin, 903364-02, substituting Header 20 Pin 903331-20. A walk of the 1982 schematic finds the keyboard connector labelled pins 1 through 20, of which one is an orientation spacer and one, the +5V line, is not connected, leaving eighteen wires: eight COL, eight ROW, RESTORE and GND. The twenty-four conductor count and the 24-pin header in the description and the facts are therefore wrong, and the arithmetic does not work either, since eight rows, eight columns, RESTORE and two power rails is nineteen. Whether the lead is ribbon or discrete is a per-run detail not established either.

facts.label: Conductors
facts.value: 18 wires (8 row, 8 column, RESTORE, ground)

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: 20-pin header on the mainboard (CN1), part 903331-20; one position an orientation spacer and the +5V position unused

c64.keyboard.cable.conductor.name: Ribbon conductors
c64.keyboard.cable.conductor.description: Either a flat laminated ribbon of stranded copper conductors or a bundle of discrete stranded leads; the ribbon is thinner, discrete leads are more flexible at the fold. Whatever the construction, the keyboard cable is the link to the mainboard and has nothing to do with the switch matrix: the matrix lives on a rigid board inside the module.
c64.keyboard.cable.conductor.note: Whether a given C64 keyboard cable is a flat ribbon or a discrete loom is a per-run detail; both are consistent with the era and with the 20-pin connector. The material is PVC or polyester insulation over stranded copper, not a printed flexible circuit.

c64.keyboard.body.name: Keyboard body and its fasteners
c64.keyboard.body.description: A moulded ABS body that holds the plungers, the PCB and the backplate, and carries the cable. It is retained by about twenty small gold-coloured screws, and on the shift-lock position it has a black-backed keyswitch with one wire running diagonally to the PCB.
c64.keyboard.body.note: That the keyboard is a separable assembly is established: it is listed as its own Commodore part, Keyboard 326165-02, under TOP CASE ASSY alongside Top Case 326113-01, Bottom Case 326114-01, LED Plate 326160-01 and Nameplate 326161-01. Not established: that the body is ABS, that about twenty small gold-coloured screws hold it together, and that the shift-lock position has one wire running diagonally to the PCB. The early keyboard's shift-lock key is described as having a black round bottom and being connected with two long yellow wires to the keyboard PCB, with most subsequent Commodore 64 keyboards having short wires, which does not match the single diagonal wire claimed here. The service manual's own two scans disagree on the keyboard part number, 326165-02 in the 1992 edition and 326166-02 in the earlier printing.

facts.label: Retaining screws
facts.value: ~20 small gold-coloured screws

facts.label: Shift lock
facts.value: black-backed keyswitch, one wire runs diagonally to the PCB

c64.keyboard.body.screws.name: Keyboard retaining screws (gold-coloured)
c64.keyboard.body.screws.description: Roughly twenty small self-tapping screws with a gold or brass finish hold the keyboard backplate and body together. The gold colour is a zinc-nickel or brass-look plating, chosen because it reads as 'quality' on a part the customer never sees.
c64.keyboard.body.screws.note: Not established: the count, the thread and the plating on the keyboard retaining screws. The screws are visible in teardowns but no document records their specification or finish.

facts.label: Finish
facts.value: gold-ish zinc-nickel or brass plating

c64.keyboard.body.keyswitch.name: Shift-lock keyswitch
c64.keyboard.body.keyswitch.description: The shift-lock position carries a tiny mechanically latching slide switch: a black plastic body with a metal leaf contact that holds itself in the shifted position until pressed again. It is not a matrix key at all - it is a separate latch that simply closes the shift lines, which is why the firmware cannot tell it from a held SHIFT. On teardown it reads as a black-backed keyswitch with one wire soldered diagonally across the board.
c64.keyboard.body.keyswitch.note: Retroleum describes the shift-lock device as a black-backed keyswitch with one wire running diagonally to the PCB, a small manufacturing quirk that tells you the module was hand-assembled. Some accounts instead describe a latching rubber dome in the same position; both readings appear in the period literature and the two are not readily distinguished from outside the case.

c64.keyboard.backplate.name: Steel backplate
c64.keyboard.backplate.description: A sheet-steel plate under the printed circuit board with openings punched for each plunger and rolled stiffening beads pressed into it. It carries the return springs, holds the plungers' travel against the board, and is screwed to the keyboard body with about twenty small gold-coloured screws. The openings are pierced on a punch press in a single stroke across the whole sheet and the beads roll-formed afterwards: a high-volume sheet-metal job, where a tonne of steel punched this way costs a fraction of a machined equivalent.
c64.keyboard.backplate.note: Not established: that the C64 keyboard has a steel backplate, its sheet thickness, and that the openings were pierced in one stroke with roll-formed stiffening beads. The plate appears in enthusiast teardowns; the press route and dimensions are not recorded.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: mild steel sheet, about 1-1.5 mm

facts.label: Openings
facts.value: punched (pierced) in one stroke for each plunger

facts.label: Piercing rate
facts.value: hundreds of strokes per minute

facts.label: Stiffening beads
facts.value: roll-formed after piercing

c64.keyboard.pcb.name: Keyboard PCB (matrix and contacts)
c64.keyboard.pcb.description: A single-sided printed circuit board carrying the eight row and eight column traces of the matrix, drilled and plated through in the usual way, with one pair of plated pads terminating each key position. It plugs into a 20-pin header on the mainboard at CN1 and carries no logic of its own: it is a switch matrix and nothing more. It is a rigid glass-epoxy laminate board, not a printed flexible membrane.
c64.keyboard.pcb.note: That the board carries no logic and is a bare switch matrix is established: looking at the keyboard's PCB it is pretty clear that it has no electronics intelligence of any kind. It is merely a collection of switches, and the rest of the keys are arranged into an 8 by 8 matrix. The service manual agrees that both parallel ports of the CIA are used to decode the keyswitches, with PA0-PA7 as outputs and PB0-PB7 as inputs. Not established: that the board is single-sided, that the pads are gold-plated or carbon-plated rather than bare copper, and that the scan is performed by CIA 1 specifically. On the pad finish, the early keyboard's activation pads are described as not protected from oxidation as the later keyboards are.

facts.label: Sides
facts.value: single-sided, rigid glass-epoxy, not a flexible membrane

facts.label: Matrix
facts.value: 8 rows x 8 columns

facts.label: Contacts
facts.value: gold-plated or carbon-plated pads; the dome bridges them

facts.label: Logic on board
facts.value: none; the matrix is scanned by CIA 1

c64.keyboard.pcb.contacts.name: Contact pads (gold or carbon)
c64.keyboard.pcb.contacts.description: Each key position terminates in two pads on the rigid board. The carbon-loaded rubber dome that bridges them is the moving conductor: pressed, it closes the circuit between the pads; released, the pads are open. On gold-plated keyboards the pads are gold over nickel; on cheaper sets they are a carbon or graphite coating on the copper, which is the version that needs cleaning.
c64.keyboard.pcb.contacts.note: The carbon-loaded rubber dome as the moving conductor is established by the repair literature, which lists sanding down the keypad conductive rubber and painting graphite powder onto it among the standard remedies, and measures the resistance of the rubber pads as a diagnostic. The early keyboard's activation pads are described as not protected from oxidation as the later keyboards are. Not established: that later pads are gold over nickel, that cheaper sets use a graphite coating on the copper, and that there is no silver-ink conductor anywhere in this keyboard.

c64.keyboard.pcb.matrix.name: How the 8 x 8 matrix and the two odd keys work
c64.keyboard.pcb.matrix.description: The CIA drives one of eight rows low and reads the eight columns; a pressed key connects one row to one column, and sixty-four positions are scanned. RESTORE is wired straight to the NMI line, bypassing the matrix entirely, which is why RESTORE works even while the CPU is jammed. SHIFT LOCK is a mechanically latching switch wired to the same two lines as the left SHIFT, so the firmware sees a shift and never sees a separate key.
c64.keyboard.pcb.matrix.note: SHIFT LOCK being on the same lines as left SHIFT is why holding shift lock in software is impossible and why BASIC reports a shift rather than a distinct key. An explanation of the wiring rather than a part, so it is a note.

facts.label: RESTORE
facts.value: dedicated line to NMI, not scanned

facts.label: SHIFT LOCK
facts.value: latching; shares the left-shift matrix lines

facts.label: Reader
facts.value: CIA 6526 #1, ports $DC00 / $DC01

c64.keyboard.switches.name: Hybrid switches (Mitsumi-style plunger, rubber dome, spring)
c64.keyboard.switches.description: The C64 does not use a rubber-dome-only membrane like a calculator, nor a mechanical switch like a typewriter. It uses a dome-and-plunger hybrid: a moulded plastic plunger carrying or driving a carbon-loaded rubber pad which bridges two plated pads on the rigid keyboard board when the cap is pressed, with a coil return spring under most keys. That gives a real click, a light touch and a definite bottom-out, which is why a C64 keyboard still feels mechanical in the 1980s sense. The rigid board is the point: there is no flexible membrane and no silver-ink trace layer in this keyboard.
c64.keyboard.switches.note: That the key switches are dome-and-plunger hybrids on a rigid board rather than a membrane is established: the domes function for activating the keys, the activation pads sit on the keyboard's PCB, and the PCB is merely a collection of switches with no electronics of its own. That springs are present on the later keyboards and absent on the earliest is established: the biggest difference is the lack of springs underneath the keycaps on the early keyboard, whose domed rubber feet make it feel sluggish. Not established: the 55-70 gf snap peak, the 3-4 mm travel and 0.5 mm pre-travel, the 10-30 million operation life, and the Type 1 versus Type 2 four-pronged plunger taxonomy. The board material and the copper and gold plating processes belong to the PCB subsystem.

facts.label: Force
facts.value: roughly 55-70 gf at the snap peak for a typical dome-and-plunger switch

facts.label: Travel
facts.value: about 3-4 mm total, of which about 0.5 mm is pre-travel

facts.label: Life
facts.value: 10-30 million operations

facts.label: Conductor
facts.value: carbon-loaded rubber; there is no silver-ink layer

c64.keyboard.switches.force-curve.name: The snap: force-displacement curve of the switch
c64.keyboard.switches.force-curve.description: The feel of a C64 key is a curve, not a number. The plunger rides down the spring, then the rubber dome on the board has to collapse, producing a peak in force; past the peak the force drops as the dome flattens, then rises again into the bottom-out. The peak-to-valley difference is what the finger reads as clicky, and it is the collapse of the dome rather than any metal leaf that produces it.
c64.keyboard.switches.force-curve.note: Typical figures for dome-and-plunger switches of this period, not measured C64 data. C64 keys are famous for a light, crisp action, and the rubber dome collapsing is what gives that characteristic. The figures are recorded as facts because they are the only quantitative handle available on the feel.

facts.label: Peak force
facts.value: about 55-70 gf

facts.label: Valley force
facts.value: about 25-45 gf

facts.label: Total travel
facts.value: about 3-4 mm

facts.label: Bottom-out force
facts.value: about 80-120 gf

c64.keyboard.switches.spring.name: Return spring (music wire)
c64.keyboard.switches.spring.description: A small coil spring under each key that returns the plunger. It is drawn from music wire (a high-carbon, low-carbon-content steel with a tight tensile range) and wound on a automatic spring coiler. Type 1 keyboards spring every key; Type 2 springs only the space bar and relies on the rubber dome elsewhere.
c64.keyboard.switches.spring.note: That a coil return spring sits under each key on the later keyboards, and that the earliest keyboard has none, is established: the biggest difference is the lack of springs underneath the keycaps. Re-tensioning the keyboard key springs is a standard remedy in the repair literature. Not established: that the wire is music wire, the 0.3-0.4 mm diameter, the rate, or that Type 2 springs only the space bar.

facts.label: Wire
facts.value: music wire, ~0.3-0.4 mm diameter

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: set so the snap peak lands at 55-70 gf

c64.keyboard.switches.plunger.name: Switch plunger (moulded, with conductive rubber)
c64.keyboard.switches.plunger.description: A small moulded body with a cross-post on top that the keycap clips onto, one or more arms that carry a conductive rubber pad, and a stem that slides in the keyboard body. Type 2 plungers have four prongs and carry a loose grey 'bubble' contact.
c64.keyboard.switches.plunger.note: That the plungers differ between generations and that the caps will not move between them is established: the plastic pegs are white and not black as in the later C64 keyboard versions, and the shape of the early keyboard's plastic pegs also differs from later ones. Not established: the four-pronged Type 2 geometry, the loose grey bubble contact, and the POM or filled nylon material.

facts.label: Type 1
facts.value: black plungers, springs under every key, metal contact

facts.label: Type 2
facts.value: white four-pronged plungers, grey rubber bubble contacts, spring under the space bar only

c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer.name: Plunger polymer: acetal or filled nylon
c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer.description: The plunger has to be dimensionally stable over millions of strokes and low-friction against the spring and the body. Acetal (POM) is the classic choice for its low friction and stiffness; glass-filled nylon or polycarbonate are also used. All three are moulded on small multi-cavity tools, and the formaldehyde and nylon chains are documented under the other-polymers branch of the case.
c64.keyboard.switches.plunger-polymer.note: Which polymer each production run used is not something the sources pin down; POM and filled nylon were both routine. Acetal has a very low coefficient of friction and never develops the grease-seeking behaviour that nylon can.

facts.label: Friction
facts.value: POM has a very low coefficient of friction and no 'grease needed' behaviour

c64.keyboard.keycaps.name: Keycaps (66 individual moulded ABS caps)
c64.keyboard.keycaps.description: Not a single dished sheet: 66 separate rectangular caps, each moulded in dark brown-grey ABS with a slightly concave top, each dropping through its own square opening in the bezel onto its own plunger. Some breadbin sets had tan-coloured function keys, others grey.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.note: The count of 66 is established twice over: The C64 Keyboard has 66 keys on it, and the service manual specification lists 66 Keys total, 2 Cursor control keys and 4 Function keys. That the caps are individual moulded pieces and are not interchangeable between early and late sets is established: the 2u Return key and the 1.5u Function, Restore and Shift keys only have one female socket, which makes the keycaps non-interchangeable with newer versions of the C64 keycaps. The keyboard is a single Commodore part, 326165-02. Not established: that the caps are dark brown-grey ABS, the slightly concave top, the square openings and pitch in the bezel, that the legends are pad printed in two colours, that some later sets also print shifted characters on the front face, and the 5 mm versus 3 mm cross-point dimensions.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, textured, moulded one shot

facts.label: Fitting
facts.value: cross-point: ~5 mm on early breadbin caps, ~3 mm on later ones

facts.label: Legend
facts.value: printed on the top face; later sets also on the front face

facts.label: Colour variation
facts.value: function keys tan on some sets, grey on others

c64.keyboard.keycaps.cross-point.name: Cross-point fitting and cap underside
c64.keyboard.keycaps.cross-point.description: The underside of the cap carries a moulded cross that clips onto the matching cross-post on the plunger - about 5 mm on early breadbin caps, about 3 mm on later ones. The two are not interchangeable. The underside also has guide ribs that keep the cap square as it travels.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.cross-point.note: In part in conflict: that early and late caps are not interchangeable is established, and the difference is described as 0.25 mm in the material thickness of the cross part of the peg tops. The 5 mm and 3 mm cross lengths are not established by any source read for this node. The underside guide ribs are described by teardowns but not dimensioned.

facts.label: Cross length
facts.value: ~5 mm (early breadbin) vs ~3 mm (later)

facts.label: Material
facts.value: moulded with the cap, same ABS

c64.keyboard.keycaps.colours.name: Keycap colour: no coding on the breadbin keyboard
c64.keyboard.keycaps.colours.description: Breadbin C64 caps are almost uniformly a dark brown-grey, with the function keys sometimes a lighter grey or tan. There is no per-number colour coding on the breadbin keyboard - that belongs to some other machines, and the VIC-20 had differently coloured function keys. What a C64 keycap has is a moulded-in colour, not a printed one, so the keycap colour is pigment in the ABS rather than a decoration applied afterwards.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.colours.note: No colour-coded number row or overlay could be confirmed for the 1982 breadbin. Where a legend colour differs between sets it tracks the cap colour, not the key function. Treat any claim of printed colour-coded number overlays as unverified for this machine.

facts.label: Number-key coding
facts.value: none on the breadbin; legends are all one colour on the cap

c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend.name: Printed front (PETSCII) legends
c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend.description: The graphics characters on the small FRONT wall of the cap - the PETSCII and shifted-symbol set - are printed, not moulded. This is the other half of the keycap story from the double-shot top legends (c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot), and the difference is visible: these characters wear and rub off, so a cap whose front legend is faint while its top legend is crisp is normal rather than damaged. Printing a near-vertical face is harder than printing a top - the pad has to be tilted against the front wall with the cap held in a nest, which wants a second station and a second fixture - so front coverage improves gradually across a production run rather than switching on at a date. On sets with only a single top legend, the front face was left plain.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.legend.note: The front legends are printed and the cap tops are not: this node covers the front wall only. The 1982 breadbin keycap is double-shot moulded on top (see c64.keyboard-switches.keycap.double-shot) and printed on the front. Evidence: Keyboard Wiki (themk.org) - "The front-printed "PETSCII" legends are likely pad-printed"; Deskthority 8102 - "The front legends are printed. If you look closely you should see the difference between double shot on the top and printed on the front of the caps." Confidence is held at medium for a specific reason: that the front legends are PRINTED is well attested by two independent collector sources, but the sources do not agree on the method - the Keyboard Wiki hedges with "likely" while Deskthority only says "printed". The ink and pad-printing detail retained here follows the pad-printing reading and should be treated as the weaker half of this node.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: the front wall only - PETSCII and shifted graphics characters

facts.label: Process
facts.value: printed; the sources say pad printing but hedge it ("likely pad-printed")

facts.label: Wear
facts.value: yes - these are the legends that rub off, unlike the moulded tops

facts.label: Why a vertical face is harder
facts.value: the pad must be tilted against the front wall with the cap held in a nest

facts.label: Front-face coverage
facts.value: improves gradually across the production run rather than switching on at a date

c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool.name: Keycap tool (small multi-cavity, hardened steel)
c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool.description: Keycaps are made in small high-cavity tools - 4, 8 or 16 cavities in one block - because a cap is cheap and the tool has to be small enough to fit a small press. The tool is hardened tool steel and the caps come off a common gate, so the visible faces are identical across the set. A cap is the shortest flow in moulding: a shallow thin-walled box filled through a single gate, which is why the tool is small, multi-cavity and warm-moulded, and why the cycle is 15-30 s against 30-60 s for a case.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.tool.note: Not established: the cavity count, the tool size, the cycle time and the tool life on a Commodore keycap tool.

facts.label: Tool size
facts.value: about 150 x 150 mm

facts.label: Tool life
facts.value: 300,000-1,000,000 shots, replated and repolished on rebuild

facts.label: Fill time
facts.value: under 1 s through a single gate on the inside wall

c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs.name: ABS grade for keycaps
c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs.description: A housing-grade ABS, low rubber content so the moulded texture stays crisp and the cap does not feel gummy. Keycap ABS is usually a slightly higher-gloss, higher-flow grade than the case resin because the caps are thin and have to fill a short, tight flow path.
c64.keyboard.keycaps.abs.note: Not established: the ABS grade, the gloss and the wall thickness on Commodore keycaps. The full ABS chain is documented once under c64.case.abs-resin; the keycap grade is not.

facts.label: Gloss units (60 deg)
facts.value: ~85-100 GU for a glossy cap

facts.label: Wall thickness
facts.value: ~1.5-2 mm, thinnest in the legend area

c64.case.name: Breadbin case: two-piece ABS shell
c64.case.description: The C64 'breadbin' housing is a rear shell and a front bezel, both injection-moulded general-purpose ABS in a warm beige-brown. The rear shell carries the ventilation ribs, moulded screw bosses, connector cut-outs and the rubber feet; the bezel carries the keyboard window with its square key openings, the two knurled thumbscrews, the rainbow badge and the fine 'leather' grain. A foil-on-board RFI shield sits inside over the motherboard.
c64.case.note: The case is universally reported as ABS - it is the polymer that browns under UV and can be reversed with peroxide retrobright bleaching. Commodore's own 2025 C64 Ultimate copy notes the surviving tooling carries a period-correct 2-point flow pattern. The wall is 2.5-3.5 mm throughout: figures of 6-8 mm quoted for thick structural mouldings do not apply to this tool and the thin wall is why the case is prone to flow marks.

facts.label: Nominal wall thickness
facts.value: 2.5-3.5 mm, uniform, texturing excluded

facts.label: Case screws
facts.value: 3 x 12 self-tapping zinc-plated, into moulded bosses

facts.label: Shells
facts.value: rear shell and front bezel, both general-purpose ABS

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: pigmented in the resin at compounding, never sprayed

c64.case.other-polymers.name: Other polymers in the C64
c64.case.other-polymers.description: The ABS case is not the only plastic in the machine. This branch gathers the second- and third-generation polymers that appear in the C64's plastic parts so that their feedstocks are traceable alongside the case resin. Several of them - PVC in the cable jackets, POM in the keyboard plungers, nylon in the connector latches, epoxy in the die attach and the potting - are not case materials at all; they belong to other subsystems and are documented there in more detail.
c64.case.other-polymers.note: A routing point rather than a substance: the honest kind for a branch head that only groups other materials. Each child is a real polymer with its own feedstock chain.

c64.case.other-polymers.methanol.name: Methanol (from synthesis gas)
c64.case.other-polymers.methanol.description: Made by reacting carbon monoxide and hydrogen from natural-gas reforming, a few hundred C and 50-100 bar over a copper/zinc oxide catalyst. Formaldehyde comes from methanol oxidation over silver or iron-molybdenum catalyst.
c64.case.other-polymers.methanol.note: The synthesis-gas route and the copper/zinc oxide catalyst are established; the 200-300 C and 50-100 bar figures are not stated by the source. The formaldehyde branch over silver or iron-molybdenum is likewise uncited.

facts.label: Synthesis gas
facts.value: from natural-gas steam reforming

facts.label: Methanol synthesis
facts.value: 200-300 C, 50-100 bar, Cu/ZnO catalyst

c64.case.other-polymers.polyester-film.name: Polyester / PET film (insulation, overlay)
c64.case.other-polymers.polyester-film.description: Polyester film is used as thin insulation, as overlay film on some keycap legends, and as the amber capacitor sleeve material in the power supply. It comes from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, both of which come out of the aromatics and olefin chains already used elsewhere in the machine.
c64.case.other-polymers.polyester-film.note: PET film and the keycap-overlay question overlap with the packaging and board subsystems; the legend decoration is documented under the decoration branch and the PCB materials under the board subsystem. What matters here is only that the film is a polyester and shares the para-xylene route with the case pigment.

c64.case.moulding.name: Injection moulding of the case
c64.case.moulding.description: The bezel and rear shell are moulded on a large toggle or hydraulic press in a multi-cavity family tool. Dried ABS is melted in a three- or four-zone barrel at 200-260 C, injected through a gate on the parting line at 1000-1500 bar, packed at 50-100 bar until the gate freezes, cooled against water channels at 40-60 C until the part has shrunk onto the tool, and pushed off the core on ejector pins that leave small round marks and a gate vestige on the seam. Because ABS shrinks 0.4-0.7% linearly the tool is cut oversize, and because the wall is only 2.5-3.5 mm the melt has to snake a long, thin, textured flow in under a second or it cools and frosts. That combination is why C64 cases carry visible flow marks: the two-point pattern is the frozen boundary where two melt fronts met and did not fully knit.
c64.case.moulding.note: Not established: the clamp force, the melt and mould temperatures, the injection and pack pressures, the cooling time, the cycle time and the wall thickness on a Commodore breadbin tool. The general sequence of injection moulding is documented; none of these figures is.

facts.label: Press clamp force
facts.value: 300-600 t (the C64 case is a wide but shallow tool)

facts.label: Melt temperature
facts.value: 230-260 C; barrel zones about 200 / 230 / 245 / 250 C

facts.label: Mould temperature
facts.value: 40-60 C, water-jacketed

facts.label: Pack pressure
facts.value: 50-100 bar, held while the gate freezes

facts.label: Cooling time
facts.value: 20-40 s, the dominant term in the cycle

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 30-60 s for a case this size

facts.label: ABS shrinkage
facts.value: 0.4-0.7% linear, so the cavity is cut oversize

facts.label: Ejector pin mark
facts.value: about 3-6 mm diameter, faint circular imprint

facts.label: Screw residence time
facts.value: keep under about 10 min to avoid thermal degradation

c64.case.moulding.press.name: Injection press (300-600 t)
c64.case.moulding.press.description: A toggle or direct-hydraulic injection moulding machine with a screw plasticiser, a heated barrel with three or four zones, an oil or water temperature controller, and a mould base. Toggle machines clamp faster and are what most housing tools ran on. Oil hydraulics drive the toggle or the platen, provide injection and holding pressure, and drive the ejector; hydraulic pressure is the reason injection pressure reached 1000-1500 bar, against the about 500 bar of the older toggle-and-screw machines.
c64.case.moulding.press.note: Not established: the clamp force, the screw diameter and ratio, the barrel zoning and the hydraulic oil grade on the press that moulded the case.

facts.label: Screw
facts.value: nitrided 33CrMoV or bimetallic-lined, 25-40 mm diameter at L/D 20-28

facts.label: Hydraulic oil
facts.value: ISO VG 46-68

c64.case.moulding.hydraulics.name: Hydraulic clamp unit
c64.case.moulding.hydraulics.description: Oil hydraulics drive the toggle or the platen, provide injection and holding pressure, and drive the ejector. A hydraulic press is the reason injection pressure reached 1000+ bar - compared with the ~500 bar of the older toggle-and-screw machines.
c64.case.moulding.hydraulics.note: Not established: the injection pressures, the oil grade and the clamp force on a C64 case press.

facts.label: Oil
facts.value: hydraulic oil, ISO VG 46-68

c64.case.moulding.injection-screw.name: Plasticising screw and barrel
c64.case.moulding.injection-screw.description: A flighted screw turns in a heated barrel, conveying and melting pellets on the way back and injecting on the way forward. The screw is nitrided 33CrMoV or 40Cr steel, bimetallic-lined at the tip in later designs.
c64.case.moulding.injection-screw.note: Not established: the screw diameter, the L/D ratio and the nitrided grade on the C64 case press. The general function of a plasticising screw is documented.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: typically 25-40 mm L/D 20-28 for this shot size

facts.label: Screw material
facts.value: nitrided 33CrMoV, or bimetallic barrel

c64.case.tooling.name: Case tooling: H13 family mould with EDM texture
c64.case.tooling.description: The two breadbin case moulds are large two-plate tools in pre-hardened or hardened hot-work steel, with the leather-grain texture cut by electrical discharge machining and the cavity polished and hard-chromed. A single mould produces thousands of C64 cases; its cost is amortised over millions of parts, so Commodore could afford a 5-cavity family tool.
c64.case.tooling.note: Not established: the tool size, the cavity count, the plating thickness and the tool life on the two Commodore breadbin case tools.

facts.label: Tool size
facts.value: ~450 x 350 mm, two-plate, guided by leader pins

facts.label: Cavities
facts.value: typically 1 large cavity for a case this size; 2-4 on smaller tools

facts.label: Tool life for ABS housing
facts.value: 300,000-1,000,000 shots before re-polish or repair

facts.label: Nickel content of plating
facts.value: hard chrome, or electroless nickel of ~5-10 um

facts.label: Tool life by run size
facts.value: large ABS housing tool 300,000-1,000,000+ shots with periodic rebuild; small high-cavity keycap tool similar; short-run and prototype tools may only see 30,000-200,000

c64.case.tooling.p20.name: P20 pre-hardened tool steel
c64.case.tooling.p20.description: A 0.38% C, 0.9% Cr, 0.4% Mo, 0.2% V steel supplied at HRC 30-35. Because it arrives hard, the whole cavity can be machined and polished with no risk of distortion from a later heat treatment, which is why it dominated housing tooling in 1982.
c64.case.tooling.p20.note: Not established: that the case tools were made in P20 or 1.2311, the stated composition, the 0.9% chromium and 0.2% vanadium, and the 28-36 HRC delivery condition. No document identifies the steel in a C64 case tool.

facts.label: Trade names
facts.value: P20, 1.2311, NAK80 is the corrosion-resistant modern cousin

c64.case.tooling.mould-assembly.name: Mould assembly: guide pins, ejectors, cooling
c64.case.tooling.mould-assembly.description: The finished plates are set into a mould base with guide pillars or bushes, an ejector-plate assembly with pins under every feature that would imprint on the visible face, and water lines carrying coolant through the cores and plates to remove the heat of plasticisation.
c64.case.tooling.mould-assembly.note: Not established: the guide pillar count, the ejector pin diameter, the coolant temperature and the cold-runner choice on a Commodore case tool.

facts.label: Guide elements
facts.value: 4 large guide pillars with bushings

facts.label: Ejector pins
facts.value: hardened, nitrided, about 3-6 mm diameter

facts.label: Cooling
facts.value: water at 30-60 C through baffles and core channels

facts.label: Hot runner
facts.value: unusual on a large ABS housing tool in 1982; cold runner with a pressure-controlled gate was normal

c64.case.tooling.plating.name: Hard chrome plating of the cavity
c64.case.tooling.plating.description: The polished cavity is electroplated in a hexavalent chromium bath to a few microns. Chrome is much harder than the tool steel, so the tool wears far better; it is also what gives the moulded ABS its character - the gloss of a C64 case is the gloss of chrome, not of steel.
c64.case.tooling.plating.note: Hard chromium plating out of a hexavalent chromic acid bath is established. Not established: the 50-60 C bath temperature, the 6-10 V, the 3-8 um cavity thickness, and the practice of baking moulds straight after plating against hydrogen embrittlement. Modern practice has largely moved away from hexavalent chromium for environmental reasons, toward electroless nickel or PVD. In 1982 hard chrome was the standard and there was no practical alternative.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: chromic acid with sulfate catalyst, 50-60 C, 6-10 V

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 3-8 um for a mould cavity

facts.label: Hydrogen embrittlement
facts.value: a real risk; many moulds are baked immediately after plating

facts.label: Why
facts.value: chrome is harder than the tool steel, and its gloss is the gloss of the moulded part

c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid.name: Chromic acid
c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid.description: Made by roasting chromite with soda ash and limestone, leaching the sodium chromate, and acidifying. So the chromium in the plating bath comes from the same chromite that came into the tool steel.
c64.case.tooling.chromium-acid.note: Not established: the roast temperature and the acidification route for the chromic acid in the plating bath, and that the plating bath chromium came from the same chromite as the tool steel.

facts.label: Roasting
facts.value: about 1000 C with soda ash and lime, oxidative roast to Na2CrO4

facts.label: Acidification
facts.value: sulfuric acid to chromic acid

c64.case.tooling.polishing.name: Lapping and polishing the cavity
c64.case.tooling.polishing.description: The cavity is progressively polished - progressively finer abrasives on cloth and stone - to a mirror. On a textured tool the polish is done to the whole surface and the texture simply stays; on flat surfaces it goes to Ra 0.05-0.1 um, which is what makes the plated ABS read as glossy.
c64.case.tooling.polishing.note: Not established: the finished roughness figures, the media sequence and the hand-versus-machine split on a Commodore case cavity.

facts.label: Final flat-surface finish
facts.value: Ra 0.05-0.1 um before plating

facts.label: Polishing media
facts.value: aluminium oxide, then chromium oxide for the final mirror

facts.label: Hand vs machine
facts.value: hand polishing on cast iron blocks for the final mirror; machine polish for bulk stock removal

c64.case.tooling.lapping-compound.name: Abrasive polishing compounds
c64.case.tooling.lapping-compound.description: Aluminium oxide for the bulk stock removal and green chromium oxide for the final mirror, both graded by grain size and applied on cloth and stone. This is the most labour-intensive step in the whole case tool: a large textured housing cavity takes days of hand polishing on cast-iron blocks, which is why such tools cost tens of thousands of dollars and why the economics demanded millions of parts.
c64.case.tooling.lapping-compound.note: Not established: the media grades, the finished roughness and the hand-polishing route used on the C64 case tools.

facts.label: Media
facts.value: aluminium oxide for bulk, chromium oxide for the final mirror

facts.label: Final flat-surface finish
facts.value: Ra 0.05-0.1 um before plating

facts.label: Hand vs machine
facts.value: hand polishing on cast iron for the final mirror; machine polish for stock removal

c64.case.tooling.synthetic-alumina.name: Synthetic alumina abrasive
c64.case.tooling.synthetic-alumina.description: Bauxite is refined to alumina and sintered or fused into corundum, then crushed and graded into abrasive powders. Hardness ~9 on the Mohs scale, second only to diamond, and the workhorse of metal finishing.
c64.case.tooling.synthetic-alumina.note: Not established: the fusion temperature and the abrasive grading applied on Commodore tooling.

facts.label: Fused alumina
facts.value: ~2100 C in an arc furnace

c64.case.tooling.machining.name: Machining of the cavity and core
c64.case.tooling.machining.description: A 1982 tool shop would rough the cavity with large carbide or HSS milling cutters, leaving 0.3-0.5 mm, then finish-mill, then grind the critical faces flat and parallel to 0.01-0.02 mm across the plate. The parting plane is lapped to the same figure and put exactly at the joint line of the two halves, so the flash line around the case seam disappears into the seam. Only after that does the texture go in, because the texture electrode has to follow a cavity that is already dimensionally correct.
c64.case.tooling.machining.note: Not established: the stock allowance, the grinding figures, the parting-plane position and the finishing roughness on a 1982 Commodore case tool.

facts.label: Plate flatness after grinding
facts.value: 0.01-0.02 mm across the plate

facts.label: Parting line
facts.value: lapped, and placed on the case joint line

facts.label: Finish target before plating
facts.value: Ra 0.2-0.4 um on polished faces

c64.case.tooling.edm.name: EDM cutting of the leather grain
c64.case.tooling.edm.description: The texture is the one feature of the case that cannot be milled: a random stochastic pattern of overlapping spherical dimples, 0.3-0.8 mm pitch and 0.05-0.15 mm deep. It is cut by sinking a shaped graphite or brass electrode into the hardened, ground cavity, or by wire-EDM scanning. Sinking EDM gives a whole panel at once and was well established by 1982, having been commercial since the 1960s; wire EDM gives resolution but is slower. What has not changed is that the texture is a negative in the steel and not a coating: on parts made in a second colour it can be partly buried, which is why grey aftermarket cases look so much cleaner than originals.
c64.case.tooling.edm.note: The general mechanism is documented: material is removed from the work piece by a series of rapidly recurring current discharges between two electrodes, separated by a dielectric liquid and subject to an electric voltage. Not established: the 0.3-0.8 mm grain pitch, the 0.05-0.15 mm depth, the 0.2-0.5 mm/s rough-cut rate, the kerosene dielectric, and the switch from graphite to brass for fine features. Where the texture has fine features the electrode is switched from graphite to brass, which machines more accurately but wears faster. Neither is a coating: the grain is cut into the tool steel and is reproduced on every shot the tool makes, for the life of the tool.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sinker EDM standard for area texturing; wire EDM for detail

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: graphite, or brass where the texture has fine features

facts.label: Rough cut
facts.value: about 0.2-0.5 mm/s removal; the finish cut is much slower

facts.label: Dielectric
facts.value: hydrocarbon oil (kerosene) or a synthetic dielectric

c64.case.tooling.brass-electrode.name: Brass electrode for fine detail
c64.case.tooling.brass-electrode.description: Copper-zinc alloy electrodes are used where the texture has fine features, because brass machines more accurately than graphite and can be reworked. Brass comes from copper and zinc ores smelted together.
c64.case.tooling.brass-electrode.note: Not established: that brass electrodes were used on the C64 case texture, and for which features. Electrodes and their relative behaviour are documented generally; the choice on this tool is not.

c64.case.tooling.graphite-electrode.name: Graphite electrode for EDM texturing
c64.case.tooling.graphite-electrode.description: Isostatic-pressed fine-grain graphite, turned or milled to the negative of the texture panel, or a CNC-shaped graphite block. Graphite is used because it is easy to machine, wears predictably as the electrode erodes, and does not damage the workpiece the way a metal electrode would.
c64.case.tooling.graphite-electrode.note: Not established: the isostatic pressing, the grade, and the claim that graphite does not damage the workpiece in a way a metal electrode would. That a shaped electrode is used at all is documented.

c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore.name: Natural graphite flake
c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore.description: Flake graphite is mined in Sri Lanka, Madagascar, China and Brazil, purified by acid (or in the 1980s by chlorination) and pressed with pitch binder into tooling graphite.
c64.case.tooling.graphite-ore.note: Not established: the mining origins, the purification route and that China supplied Commodore tooling graphite.

c64.case.fasteners.name: Case fasteners
c64.case.fasteners.description: The screws that hold the C64 together: a handful of case-assembly screws plus the motherboard and keyboard mounting screws. They are cheap zinc-plated self-tapping screws driven into plain plastic bosses. The wire arrives as EBSD or BQ grade, is drawn, cut to length and cold-headed on a multiple-spindle header that makes tens of thousands an hour, then plated: 5-15 um of zinc from an acid or alkaline bath, usually with a yellow or clear chromate conversion coat for corrosion resistance. Zinc is chosen because it is sacrificial and cheap.
c64.case.fasteners.note: Rolled threads are stronger than cut ones, but on a 3 mm screw of this class the distinction barely matters next to the boss. Repro cases now mould brass inserts into the boss to fix exactly this failure.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: cold-drawn carbon steel, EBSD/BQ wire drawn to about 2 mm

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: 5-15 um zinc, chromate-passivated

facts.label: Thread-forming
facts.value: self-tapping plastics thread, 3 x 12 typical

facts.label: Header output
facts.value: tens of thousands of screws an hour, essentially no machining

facts.label: Common failure
facts.value: a stripped ABS boss, not a rusted screw

c64.case.fasteners.brass-insert.name: Moulded-in brass insert (later practice)
c64.case.fasteners.brass-insert.description: Modern repro cases and late Commodore tools mould a brass or stainless insert into the boss and use a real machine screw. The insert is placed by hand or by gravity feed and captured by the ABS on the next shot, giving a reusable metal thread.
c64.case.fasteners.brass-insert.note: Original 1982 breadbins used self-tapping screws into plain plastic bosses. Inserts are the later improvement, and are the reason a repro case does not break at the boss the way the original does.

facts.label: Insert material
facts.value: brass (Cu-Zn) or stainless

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: serviceable thread, no boss breakage

c64.case.shield.name: RFI shield: aluminium foil on a board spacer
c64.case.shield.description: The C64 needed a conductive screen over the motherboard because a 1 MHz machine with a video oscillator radiates through a plastic case. Commodore used a die-cut sandwich of aluminium foil laminated to a cardboard or plastic-fibre spacer, bent into a box and stapled or taped to plastic standoffs, rather than a full metal can.
c64.case.shield.note: Retroleum catalogues three distinct breadbin foil-shield types (Types 1, 2 and 5) which tells you the shape was not standardised across the production run. Later boards (250425) got a stamped metal shield/heatsink that doubled as a cooler for the linear regulators.

facts.label: Foil thickness
facts.value: 0.03-0.06 mm household-grade aluminium foil

facts.label: Spacer
facts.value: thin cardboard / greyboard, sometimes a plastic-fibre core

facts.label: Attachment
facts.value: stapled or taped to moulded plastic standoffs on the case floor

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: reduce RF radiation and ingress without a metal chassis

c64.case.shield.spacer.name: Shield spacer (board core)
c64.case.shield.spacer.description: A rigidising core so the foil does not crumple and short against the board. Cheap versions use thin greyboard; better ones use a plastic-fibre or corrugated spacer. This is the part that makes the shield stand off the motherboard so it cannot touch solder joints.
c64.case.shield.spacer.note: Board core is a plausible choice because the shield only needs to hold a shape and take handling, and greyboard is the cheapest stiff sheet in existence. Stamped sheet-metal shields were the alternative on later boards.

c64.case.shield.foil.name: Aluminium foil
c64.case.shield.foil.description: Aluminium foil carried on a cardboard backing (catalogued as cardboard foil shields), slit and die-cut. Household foil is 0.016 mm and heavy-duty household foil 0.024 mm; this is not a semi-rugged grade but ordinary foil given stiffness by its backing. Its job is not to be a Faraday cage in the strict sense but simply to be a continuous, grounded-ish conductor over the board so the radiated field collapses.
c64.case.shield.foil.note: Corrected: the 0.03-0.06 mm gauge first stated here is heavier than either standard household foil (0.016 mm) or heavy-duty household foil (0.024 mm). The C64 shields are catalogued as cardboard foil shields, which reads as foil carried on a cardboard backing rather than bare foil, and later breadbin boards used a stamped metal shield and heatsink instead. Foil tears easily, so the practical difficulty of using it is handling, not the material.

c64.case.feet.name: Case feet
c64.case.feet.description: Four small anti-vibration feet on the underside of the bottom case that stop the machine skating on a desk and stop the ABS case from ringing against it. Commodore's own parts documentation lists them as self-adhesive stick-on feet, separate from the case, rather than as elastomer moulded into the shell.
c64.case.feet.note: The mounting method was wrong until the service manual was consulted. Its parts lists for the C64 bottom case assembly and the C64C bottom case both describe the foot as "Foot, Self-Adhesive", i.e. a stick-on pad applied to the case, which contradicts the insert-moulded or pressed-in reading this node previously carried and vindicates the common restorer's replacement with stick-on silicone bumpers: the originals were already adhesive pads. What the manual does not give is the compound, so the styrene-butadiene and soft PVC guesses here are unsupported, and the foot's behaviour in service is not described anywhere. Confidence stays medium because the compound and the age of the adhesive are unestablished.

facts.label: Fixing
facts.value: self-adhesive, stuck to the bottom case; not moulded into the shell

facts.label: Compound
facts.value: a soft dark elastomer; the service manual names no material

c64.case.feet.elastomer.name: Foot elastomer compound
c64.case.feet.elastomer.description: A soft, low-durometer elastomer drop-in-moulded over a small ABS boss, or a moulded-in flexible nub. The chemistry is trivial but the tooling is not: it is a two-shot or insert-mould operation with an elastomer barrel and a much longer cure than the ABS.
c64.case.feet.elastomer.note: The chemistry is trivial but the tooling is not: this is a two-shot or insert-mould operation with an elastomer barrel and a much longer cure than the ABS. It reuses the same butadiene and styrene monomers as the ABS and the SBR, which is a reminder that all four plastics in this machine trace back to the same steam cracker.

c64.case.bezel.name: Front bezel (top half)
c64.case.bezel.description: The dished front panel with the keyboard window. It is the visible part of the machine, so it carries the fine leather-grain texture, the rainbow badge recess, the two knurled thumbscrews and the moulded-in 'COMMODORE' lettering on the lower lip.
c64.case.bezel.note: Not established: the 66 openings and their pitch, the grain depth and pitch, and the screw count on the C64 front bezel. The bezel is the Top Case, Commodore part 326113-01, and the case screws are listed as self-tapping.

facts.label: Keyboard window
facts.value: 66 square openings on about 14 mm pitch

facts.label: Texture
facts.value: fine stochastic leather/pebble grain, 0.05-0.15 mm deep, cut by EDM

facts.label: Screws to rear shell
facts.value: 6 self-tapping, plus 2 at the rear lip

c64.case.logo.name: Rainbow Commodore badge
c64.case.logo.description: The rainbow Commodore badge on the bezel: a shallow raised island, moulded as part of the bezel tool so that it is smooth while the surrounding case carries the leather grain, and printed with coloured and metallised pad-print ink. The ink is the badge; the ABS of the bezel is only the substrate it sits on, which is why the badge has no resin ingredient of its own. Later machines carry the same mark as a flat printed decal applied at the factory rather than as part of the shell.
c64.case.logo.note: An input reading "ABS bezel surface" used to resolve to the case resin, which asserted the badge was made of ABS. It is not: it is a film of ink 10-30 um thick on a raised pad of the same ABS. Corrected here to point at the inks. Replicas, second-hand cases and modern reproductions disagree about whether the badge is raised mould or a bonded medallion; surviving originals show a raised pad-printed area with the ink sitting in the texture, which is the most likely reading.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: raised untextured island in the bezel mould, same ABS

facts.label: Decoration
facts.value: pad-printed colour plus metallised aluminium flake in the bright bars

facts.label: Ink film
facts.value: of the order of 10-30 um

facts.label: Later machines
facts.value: flat printed decal rather than part of the shell

c64.case.bezel.thumbscrews.name: Knurled thumbscrews for contrast/brightness
c64.case.bezel.thumbscrews.description: Two moulded plastic thumbscrews on the bezel that carry small metal shafts to the contrast and brightness potentiometers on the board. The caps are ABS, the shafts are plated steel, and the knurl is moulded rather than cut.
c64.case.bezel.thumbscrews.note: On some breadbin boards the potentiometers were adjusted by reaching into the case with a screwdriver and the two bezel thumbscrews only appear on later board revisions; check the specific assembly.

c64.case.bezel.key-well.name: Keyboard window and key openings
c64.case.bezel.key-well.description: A single rectangular opening spanned by thin webs between the key holes; the caps push through and their plungers sit on the keyboard PCB below. The webs are the highest-risk area of the tool for short shots and flash, because the melt has to snake between 66 holes that are only about 10 mm across.
c64.case.bezel.key-well.note: Whether the bezel was a single moulding with the key openings, or a bezel with a separate keyboard frame, varies between breadbin tooling generations. Photographs of ASSY 250407 show one piece. The webs between the openings are the highest-risk area of the tool for short shots and flash, because the melt has to snake between sixty-six holes of only about 10 mm across.

facts.label: Web width
facts.value: 2-3 mm between adjacent holes

facts.label: Flash tolerance
facts.value: <0.2 mm, visually rejected at final inspection

c64.case.rear-shell.name: Rear shell (bottom half)
c64.case.rear-shell.description: The larger of the two mouldings. It forms the base pan, the raised side walls, the wrap-over top with its row of ventilation slots, the rear and side connector cut-outs, the internal ribs that stiffen the pan, the moulded screw bosses and standoffs, and the feet pads.
c64.case.rear-shell.note: Not established: the 2.5-3.5 mm nominal wall, the material grade and the parting-line position on the breadbin rear shell. The top and bottom case parts are documented as parts 326113-01 and 326114-01; their construction is not.

facts.label: Nominal wall thickness
facts.value: 2.5-3.5 mm (uniform, texturing excluded)

facts.label: Material
facts.value: ABS, general purpose, textured

facts.label: Parting line
facts.value: along the top flange, visible as a faint seam

c64.case.rear-shell.connector-cutouts.name: Rear and side connector openings
c64.case.rear-shell.connector-cutouts.description: Rectangular and keyed cut-outs for the cartridge port, user port, cassette port, serial port, video DIN, power DIN and the two DE-9 control ports. Cut with knife-edged steel on the tool; the moulded lip around each port also acts as a draft and a finger stop, and the mouldings carry the connector bodies as separate inserts.
c64.case.rear-shell.connector-cutouts.note: The list of apertures is established from the ASSY 250407 parts list: CN1 Header Assy, 20 Pin, 903331-20; CN4 6 Pin Din, 903361-01 (cassette); CN5 8 Pin Din, 325573-01 (video, on the later 250407-04; 5 Pin Din, 903362-01 on the earliest); CN6 44 Pin Card Edge, 906100-02 (cartridge/expansion); CN8,9 Plug Assy, 9 Pin MINI-D, 251057-01 (control ports). The cartridge port also has its own moulded guide part, Cartridge Guide 326116-01, and the power rocker and joystick apertures are listed as Connector Panel (ON, OFF, Joystick) 326299-01. Not established: the draft and finger-stop detail on the moulded lip. Note the circuit-theory text calls the later video output an eight pin connector while the 250425 parts list also carries a 7 Pin Din, CN7 251116-01, so the manual is not internally consistent on that connector.

c64.case.rear-shell.bosses.name: Moulded bosses and standoffs
c64.case.rear-shell.bosses.description: Integral cylindrical bosses on the pan floor that carry the four case screws, the motherboard mounting screws, the keyboard PCB screws and the RF shield tabs. Each is a thick section relative to the 3 mm pan, so the tool must be cored to keep them from sinking, and each has a blind hole with a drafted self-tapping thread. Commodore did not mould metal inserts into them; the 1982 bosses are plain ABS and it is the screw that cuts its own thread on first insertion, which is why a snapped boss rather than a rusted screw is the characteristic forty-year failure.
c64.case.rear-shell.bosses.note: Not established: the 3 x 12 screw size, the 2.5 mm bore, the 5-8 mm thread engagement and the 1200 rpm first insertion. The claim that the 1982 bosses carried no metal insert, and that a snapped boss rather than a stripped insert is the characteristic failure, is also unverified.

facts.label: Screw size
facts.value: 3 x 12 self-tapping into 6 mm OD bosses

facts.label: Boss bore
facts.value: about 2.5 mm, with a shallow helix rib

facts.label: Thread engagement
facts.value: 5-8 mm for a 3 mm screw

facts.label: Cycle to first screw-in
facts.value: about 1 s at 1200 rpm on a hand screwdriver

facts.label: Serviceability
facts.value: poor; repeated removal strips the plastic thread

c64.case.rear-shell.vents.name: Ventilation slots in the top wrap
c64.case.rear-shell.vents.description: A row of moulded louvre slots in the curved top panel behind the cartridge port, letting convective air out of the case over the SID and VIC-II. They are negative features cut into the tool, not separate ribs, and because they run across a thick section they leave visible flow lines and are a classic sink-mark site. Behind them the pan is stiffened with cross-ribs tying the top panel down to the base, moulded at roughly 60% of the adjacent wall gauge so the whole panel cools and shrinks as one piece.
c64.case.rear-shell.vents.note: Effectiveness was mediocre and reviewers of the period noted heat trapping inside; the slots are modest. Mould-flow validation in 1982 was done by filling a clear polycarbonate or unfilled-PS prototype tool and watching the flow fronts by eye or on a strobe, long before short-shot first-article reports became normal.

facts.label: Style
facts.value: through-slots, parallel to the long axis

facts.label: Function
facts.value: exhaust for the linear regulator and VIC/SID heat

facts.label: Rib gauge
facts.value: 1.5-2.1 mm against a 2.5-3.5 mm wall, about 60%

facts.label: Tooling rule of thumb
facts.value: ribs capped at about 60% of the adjacent wall thickness
